title: Penobscot Remediation Trust updates Bucksport residents on mercury cleanup
text:
BUCKSPORT, Maine (WABI) — The Penobscot Remediation Trust hosted a community meeting Wednesday night to update residents on progress addressing mercury contamination in the Penobscot River Estuary.
Officials shared results from a recently completed six-acre capping pilot in Orrington, where clean sand was placed to reduce mercury exposure. Ongoing studies into removing contaminated sediment are expected to continue into 2027.
The trust is also responsible for monitoring worms, fish, birds, sediment and surface water every three years to track recovery.
The work stems from a 2022 federal settlement requiring Mallinckrodt to pay at least $187 million for remediation and long-term monitoring over the next 30 to 45 years.

title: Breezy, Sunny, & Cooler Friday. GORGEOUS Weekend!
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Clouds from Post-Tropical Cyclone Josephine have cleared the region as the storm pulls farther east. A cold front moving from northwest to southeast will usher in cooler air and gusty winds for Friday.
Clearing skies are expected for the rest of Thursday night with lows ranging from the upper 20s to the upper 30s. Winds will remain out of the north/northwest and will continue to gust upwards of 30 mph. Secure any loose outdoor items.
Friday: Sunny, Chilly and Breezy
Expect a chill in the air Friday morning, with temperatures climbing above freezing by mid-morning under full sunshine. High pressure building into the region will supply lots of sunshine with highs ranging from the upper 40s in the north to the low 50s for the rest of the region. Winds from sunrise to sunset will be out of the north/northwest gusting 20 to 30 mph on average before finally beginning to weaken during the first part of Friday night. It will get chilly with sub-freezing lows for all early Saturday morning.
Saturday: Cold Start, Gorgeous Afternoon
Despite the cold start, sunshine will help pop temperatures above freezing rather quickly Saturday morning. Expect a sunny day with afternoon highs in the 50s and northwest winds around 5 to 10 mph. Another sub-freezing night is expected Saturday into early Sunday thanks to clear skies and light winds.
Sunday: Pick of the Weekend
Both weekend days are gorgeous. Sunday though will be the warmest. Highs will range from the upper 50s along the coast to the 60s inland with even a few spots trying for close to 70 degrees.
Next Week: Mild Start, Then Cooler and Dry
Mild temperatures in the 50s and 60s return for Monday before a cold front Monday evening knocks highs down into the 40s and low 50s for Tuesday and Wednesday. The rest of October may remain moisture free.
First Alert 7-Day Forecast
TONIGHT: Clear skies with lows ranging from the upper 20s to the upper 30s. NNW winds will gust 20-30 mph.
FRIDAY: Sunny skies with highs in the 40s and low to mid 50s. NNW wind will gust to 30 mph.
SATURDAY: Sunny skies with highs in the low to mid 50s. NW wind 5-10 mph.
SUNDAY: Sunny skies. Highs in the 50s and low to mid 60s.
MONDAY: Mostly sunny with highs in the 50s and 60s.
TUESDAY: Mostly sunny with highs in the 40s and 50s.
WEDNESDAY: Mostly sunny with highs in the 40s and low 50s.
THURSDAY: Mostly sunny with highs in the 50s.

title: Finding purpose by following a Maine stone wall forgotten by time
text:
Stone walls in Midcoast Maine are as ubiquitous to our forests as lobster boats are to our harbors. You don’t have to search far to find one. I cross the street that runs by my house on Youngs Point in Wiscasset, step into the woods, and there it is. Its rocks are covered with green moss, brown pine needles, dead leaves, branches and fallen trees. It is beautiful as it meanders across the landscape, and yet there is a haunting loneliness to it. Abandoned by those who built it, and seemingly by time, it is left to fend for itself. If this stone wall could speak, what would it say?
I decided to follow it. It began inconspicuously, in dense forest, hiding amongst tiny white pine sprouts, sticks, brown needles, bramble, leaves and grass. As the stone wall ascends a steep hill, it wanders through a mix of young and old trees, made up mostly of pine, with some oak and maple. A few of the trees touching the wall are dead but standing. Others lay across it, like fallen sentinels. Neglected, this stone wall still has grandeur. It grows taller the further I follow it. I try to imagine what the landscape looked like more than 100 years ago when it was built. I am left wondering as I step over branches, barbed wire, fallen trees and discarded stones.
This is but one of several stone walls located on a 200-acre nature preserve called Eaton Farm Preserve, managed by the Chewonki Foundation. The land was once used for growing hay and grazing sheep and cows. Given its proximity to the Back River and its mudflats, it was and still is used for clamming and worm digging.
Like many stone walls found winding through the New England forests, it was the result of land being cleared of trees and brush to facilitate farming and grazing. As fertile soil erodes over time due to exposure and overuse, it was common to repurpose the land for growing hay and grazing cows and sheep. A byproduct of soil erosion is stones, pushed up to the surface by frost heaves. Known by many as “Maine potatoes,” moving these stones from the useable, productive part of the field to the edge of the property and creating “tossed walls” rather than piles of stones was regular practice. It was a place to dump unwanted stones, to delineate property lines, and to keep agricultural products and livestock separated when used with wood, other natural debris and later, barbed wire. At the time when many of these stone walls were built, it was common for them to be part of a complete fence that included wood. When the property was later abandoned as a working farm, the wood would eventually rot away leaving just the stone walls.
One can also find stone walls built around ancient Midcoast Maine cemeteries, originally to keep livestock out, preventing them from trampling and soiling the graves. The walls also mark hallowed ground, providing a clear separation from other parcels of land surrounding it. Many of these walls remain intact today because they serve their original purpose. Unlike cemetery stone walls, the stone wall I am following no longer seems to serve a purpose.
I continue my walk and marvel at the construction. The tallest sections are typically thigh high, a practical height when you consider the physical stress that lifting heavy stones must entail. Most of the stones are in contact with multiple stones in the wall. Two stones on one is a common pattern. This interconnection of rock continues down the length of the wall, like individual bones of a skeleton, connecting the neighboring stones together and making the entire structure stronger and more resistant to falling trees, animals, frost heaves and small New England earthquakes.
Even the sturdiest stone wall requires regular maintenance. The purpose for which these walls were built has long since passed and time has moved on, leaving them orphaned in the forest and in the past. The Mainers that built this wall would likely not recognize it in its current condition. And yet it still stands, this wall, devoid of purpose, of attention, of caring. All but forgotten except by the forest and its inhabitants. That is, until this moment.
I follow the wall, purposefully, mindfully, carefully. I stop and observe where I am, and where this stone wall is taking me. A journey back in time, through the woods, to simpler times. I listen and I hear the wind, leaves rustling and birdsong. If this stone wall could speak, what would it say to me?
Live in the moment?
Be grateful for what you have?
Love deeply, live simply?
Loneliness needn’t be?
Perhaps my self-awareness and my appreciation of natural beauty all around me is the wall speaking to me. Perhaps this stone wall does still have purpose. To evoke wonderment, introspection, and inner peace.
Or perhaps, just perhaps, this wall is helping me find my purpose, by just being there.
If you would like to explore old stone walls, local conservation nonprofit land trusts such as the Kennebec Estuary Land Trust in Bath, the Brunswick-Topsham Land Trust in Brunswick, and the Chewonki Foundation in Wiscasset protect and maintain properties where stone walls can be viewed from trails such as BTLT’s Tarbox Preserve in Topsham, KELT’s Thorne Head Preserve trails in Bath, and the Chewonki Foundation’s Back River Trail in Wiscasset. Another notable trail to see Midcoast Maine stone walls is the Pownalborough Courthouse Trails in Dresden.
Patrick Sandefur lives in Wiscasset. He is a proud father, lucky husband, devoted runner, and the founder of Elevate Running, a division of Bass Harbor Group. His 40+ years of running changed his life in so many ways and at so many levels. It unchained him. It helped him to see the possibilities that a life well lived has to offer.

title: Harpswell Community School gets solar array
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
New solar panels on the roof of Harpswell Community School could start generating electricity this year.
Shawn Johansen, director of facilities for Maine School Administrative District 75, said that after contractors receive a few remaining pieces and paperwork is finalized by Central Maine Power, the array will generate about 110,000 kilowatt-hours of energy each year.
The electricity will be sold back to CMP rather than going to the building, but the generation will slightly exceed the school’s current usage. A 2026 report by the architecture and engineering firm Harriman said the building used approximately 87,000 kilowatt-hours in the 2024-25 school year.
ReVision Energy is installing the array. The company also installed solar panels on Mt. Ararat High School when it was rebuilt in 2021. ReVision proposed the array on Harpswell Community School. It is also working with the district to install an array on Bowdoin Central School.
The array is being paid for by a third-party investor, Massachusetts-based Blue Haven Solar. The school district has a 25-year lease for the array and will receive energy credits from CMP, effectively lowering the school’s electricity bill.
The investor, who will get tax credits for their investment, also will pay for the array’s maintenance.
Johansen said the arrangement means there are no additional costs to taxpayers. The agreement does include an option for the district to buy the array after seven years.
Johansen said the district will save a small sum of money, likely about $1,800 in the first year, with the credits from the array. He said adding solar energy is primarily a way to reduce the district’s carbon footprint.
Sam Lemonick is a staff reporter at the Harpswell Anchor. He can be reached at [email protected].

title: Maine's worsening drought leaves more wells dry
text:
Maine's worsening drought leaves more wells dry
Per the latest data, dug wells are suffering most.
Maine's worsening drought leaves more wells dry
Per the latest data, dug wells are suffering most.
Maine’s ongoing drought is shaping up to be one of the worst the state has experienced in more than two decades, with groundwater levels struggling to recover and rainfall deficits reaching up to two feet in parts of the state.
A new study examining 26 years of U.S. Drought Monitor data found that the 2000 to 2001 drought ranks as the worst in recent memory, based on the severity shown on historical drought maps. It was also the last time Maine declared a drought-related state of emergency.
Under the same comparison, the ongoing 2025 to 2026 drought ranks second, followed by the droughts of 2020, 2016 to 2017, and 2021 to 2022.
Although current drought conditions may not appear as severe on the map as they did last November, groundwater levels continue to struggle to recover. Rainfall deficits are also growing, raising concerns for Mainers who depend on private wells for their water supply.
According to data collected by the Maine Emergency Management Agency, 62 percent of self-reported dry wells between September 2025 and October 21, 2026, were dug wells.
Among those who reported their well depths, dug wells had a median depth of just 16 feet, compared with 265 feet for drilled wells.
However, depth alone does not determine whether a well will run dry. Even some wells deeper than 400 feet have experienced recovery issues during the ongoing drought.
Factors such as soil conditions, groundwater levels, and a well’s location on a hill can all affect its water supply.
For homeowners concerned about their wells, officials recommend spreading water use throughout the day and monitoring household consumption. Homeowners should also never pour outside water directly into a well.
Those experiencing problems with their water supply should contact a licensed well driller to discuss potential solutions.
Dozens of homeowners are already facing a growing waiting list for well digging and drilling services, as demand increases amid the prolonged drought. Some may have to wait until spring, with limited staffing and resources adding to the challenge of completing the work before the ground freezes for winter.
The outlook remains concerning, with drought conditions forecast to worsen into spring 2027 unless the state receives significant, beneficial precipitation.
Mainers experiencing dry wells can report their situation through the state’s Dry Well Survey. The information helps state officials track the drought’s impacts and better understand how communities across Maine are being affected.

title: Virginia state Sen. L. Louise Lucas is charged with drug trafficking and money laundering, DOJ says
text:
Virginia state Sen. L. Louise Lucas is charged with drug trafficking and money laundering, DOJ says
Virginia state Sen. L. Louise Lucas, one of the state’s most powerful Democrats, was charged on Thursday in connection with what federal authorities alleged was a role leading a criminal enterprise that acquired and distributed large quantities of marijuana and laundered the proceeds.
An indictment unsealed on Thursday charged Lucas and six other defendants, including several of her relatives, the Department of Justice said in a statement ahead of a news conference scheduled for 10 a.m.
Lucas self surrendered, according to a Justice Department spokesperson
The charges came after the FBI searched Lucas' hometown office and a cannabis shop in which she has a stake in May.
At the time of the search, Lucas — who has been a vocal critic of Republican President Donald Trump's administration — characterized it as an attempt to intimidate her. The Associated Press was making efforts to contact Lucas’ attorneys for comment on the charges.
The brash 82-year-old lawmaker has spent decades ascending the ranks of Virginia politics and has served since 1992 in the state Senate, where she is the president pro tempore, overseeing the chamber in the lieutenant governor’s absence. More significantly, she leads the powerful Senate finance committee, through which all legislation with any budget impact must flow. She’s used the position to stop and ultimately kill legislation she opposes.
The FBI alleges a ‘criminal marijuana enterprise’
FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement that the charges allege “Lucas and a close-knit group of family members and associates orchestrated a multi-year scheme to enrich their own criminal marijuana enterprise, ‘the Lucas Enterprise’ — using Lucas’ position as Chairwoman of the Senate Finance and Appropriations Committee to insulate the enterprise from criminal scrutiny and influencing legislation to financially benefit themselves.”
“No one is above the law," the statement said, "and this FBI will continue to follow the facts with our Justice Department and ensure those responsible for criminal conduct are held accountable.”
Lucas has been a leading voice in Democrats’ ultimately failed attempt to redistrict the state’s congressional map this year, a bid to hedge against Republican efforts in other states to redraw maps for their advantage in midterm elections.
A forceful advocate of legalizing marijuana, Lucas partnered in opening the shop, The Cannabis Outlet, in 2021, selling hemp and CBD products. While marijuana is legal to possess in Virginia, recreational retail sales of the drug are not yet underway, though shops across the state do sell other cannabis-derived products.
Lucas also runs a network of companies that provide residential, transportation and other services to adults with intellectual disabilities.
Court records related to the case for months have been sealed, though earlier this year the Department of Justice sent at least two rounds of letters notifying journalists, politicians and others in Lucas’ orbit that their communications with Lucas had been intercepted as part of a court-approved wiretap that ran for two one-month time spans.
At the time of the search, many Democrats spoke up to defend Lucas, expressing skepticism about the basis for the search, given the Department of Justice’s efforts to establish criminal conduct by perceived Trump opponents.
Lucas has publicly spoken about her ownership stake in the cannabis shop as recently as June, though her most recent financial disclosure forms do not list the business by name.
Lucas, who represents a state Senate district that includes her hometown of coastal Portsmouth, operates with a sometimes-profane, unapologetic style that’s drawn comparisons with Trump.
She amassed a six-figure following on X and national attention, using the social media platform to advocate forcefully for her priorities and to bash her critics, including former GOP Gov. Glenn Youngkin. She’s also occasionally blasted members of her own party, including Gov. Abigail Spanberger, with whom she’s had disagreements.
Earlier this year, Lucas helped lead Democrats’ ultimately unsuccessful plan to gerrymander the blue-leaning state’s congressional districts into a map intended to elect 10 Democrats and only one Republican. Along the way, she posted quips about four GOP members the intended map sought to oust, joking that they soon would be working at McDonald’s. She and other Democrats defended the maps as a reasonable response to Trump-backed efforts to boost the GOP’s midterm advantage in other states.
Lucas has been in politics for decades
Lucas has notched several historic firsts in her career. According to a biography from the state library, in 1971 she became the Norfolk Naval Shipyard’s first female shipfitter, a physically demanding job that involves working on metal assemblies for vessels.
She launched her political career in 1984, when, the biography said, she became the first Black woman elected to the Portsmouth city council.
In her decades in the state Senate, Lucas has been a staunch advocate for abortion rights and increased public school funding and a leading voice on issues of racial justice and civil rights.
In 2019, after Democrats flipped control of the chamber, her peers elected her to serve as president pro tempore. And in 2024, she was tapped to lead the chamber’s budget committee, gaining enormous sway over any legislation tied to the state budget. In that post, she played a leading role in killing Youngkin’s proposal to bring Washington’s NBA and NHL teams to a proposed $2 billion development in Virginia.

Maine Historical Society’s Declaration of Independence Tour concludes at Bowdoin College Museum of Art
text:
After 15 stops, and tens of thousands of visitors, the Maine Historical Society’s rare copy of the Declaration of Independence will finish its tour of Maine’s 16 counties at the Bowdoin College Museum of Art. The Dunlap Broadside will be on view Oct. 30–31.
The Dunlap Broadside is one of just 26 surviving copies of the Declaration printed in Philadelphia on July 4, 1776, and sent out to announce American independence. Since July, approximately 17,000 people have come to see it at libraries, museums, schools, and community spaces across the state.
Ending at Bowdoin brings the tour back to where the Maine Historical Society started. The Society was founded in 1822, and its earliest history is tied to the college. The final stop gives Bowdoin students and Brunswick-area residents a chance to see the document up close, in a setting devoted to learning and culture.
The tour has included public and student viewings, readings, and community programming in each county. It is part of the Maine Historical Society’s effort to help communities across the state take part in America’s 250th anniversary in ways which are locally meaningful, thought-provoking, and engaging.
At Bowdoin Museum of Art, visitors can also view @ 250 on exhibit at the museum, which explores the nation’s history through a series of exceptional artworks created since 1776.
Location: Bowdoin College Museum of Art, 245 Maine Street, Brunswick Dates and hours: Oct. 30, 10 a.m.-5 p.m. and Oct. 31, 10 a.m.-4 p.m. Admission: Free. Timed tickets are available, and walk-ins are welcome. Reserve your spot at mainehistory.org.
Founded in 1822, the Maine Historical Society collects, preserves, and shares the history of Maine and its people through its museum, research library, and Maine Memory Network. Learn more at mainehistory.org.

title: Ukulele group brings island vibes to popular South Carolina vacation area
text:
MYRTLE BEACH, S.C. (Aging Untold)— A ukulele group in South Carolina’s Grand Strand is strumming its way into the hearts of listeners with tropical vibes on the East Coast.
Donning Hawaiian shirts, panama hats and flowers in their hair, the musicians who make up Ukes by the Sea transport audiences to paradise with their breezy sound.
“We say that it’s difficult to play a ukulele and frown at the same time,” Tom Woodle, director of Ukes by the Sea, said. “And it’s got such a happy sound.”
Back to the beginning
Woodle began playing the small-stringed instrument at 4 years old, and his talent quickly blossomed. He started playing on live radio when he was 6, joined bands at 11 and began making money from music at 16.
He even made it onto the top 100 chart with his group, The Reedy Creek Band, playing country and bluegrass in Nashville.
The musician traded spotlights for stained glass and returned to the Grand Strand, where he taught at Coastal Carolina and served as senior rector at The Well by the Sea.
He created the uplifting, toe-tapping ukulele band almost three years ago for all to enjoy.
Diverse repertoire and growing membership
“A lot of rock and roll from the ‘60s and ‘70s, and we do some folk songs, and we do some more contemporary things like Africa,” Woodle said. “It could be anything that hits our fancy.”
The band has 25 members, including seasoned musicians and others strumming for the first time.
Woodle scouted out talent like Kristen Toben, who plays the ukulele and now the steel drum.
“I purchased it, and at least with my musical background, it somehow came easy to me, and Tom has always wanted a steel drum in his band,” Toben said. “It really brought my spirits up, and I remembered how much I love music, and it was just a way for me to just continue on my love of music.”
Woodle taught his wife how to play bass so she could be part of the group.
“And to think that most of these people have never touched an instrument two years ago, I think they should be very proud of themselves,” Toben said.
Community performances
When members of Ukes by the Sea are not practicing, they perform with a purpose throughout the community.
“To spread the love of Jesus with happy music,” Woodle said. “And they love it. They have a good time, and people seem to love watching us, so that’s just a good thing.”

title: Girls Soccer Playoffs: Here's Who County Teams Could Face
Penobscot Valley’s Brooklynn Raymond breaks school girls soccer shutout record
text:
HOWLAND, Maine (WABI) - Penobscot Valley goalkeeper Brooklynn Raymond broke the school’s shutout record in the Howlers’ 7-0 win over Schenck-Stearns on Mon. Oct. 5.
It was Raymond’s 41st clean sheet, moving her past Sami Ireland’s previous mark of 40.
Raymond tied Ireland on Oct. 1 in PV’s 4-0 victory over Houlton-GHCA.
“It just proves that I’ve had talent around me, and it’s not just an accomplishment for me, but everybody that I’ve played with in the past four years. It’s kind of crazy, really, because I didn’t want to be goalie, and I never even thought about breaking a record being goalie. I didn’t even know I was close until we finished the season last year,” said Raymond, senior.
Raymond reached 42 career shutouts in Monday’s 1-0 win over Mattanawcook Academy.
She added that she still plays in the field at practice.
No. 1 Penobscot Valley is set to play No. 8 Schenck-Stearns on Wednesday at 5 p.m. in the Class D North quarterfinals.

title: ‘Praying for everyone affected’: 2 dead following massive fire at senior assisted living center
text:
CLINTON, Miss. (WLBT/Gray News) - Two people died after a fire at an assisted living center in Mississippi.
According to Hinds County Coroner Jeramiah Howard, one of the victims was an 82-year-old man, and the other was an 81-year-old woman.
Hinds County fire officials said the fire broke out at Brookdale Senior Living on East Northside Drive around 5 p.m. on Wednesday.
Firefighters from multiple departments, including the Jackson Fire Department and the Hinds County Volunteer Fire Department, along with several retired Clinton Fire Department personnel, helped put out the fire.
“We are heartbroken by the loss of two residents as a result of the fire at our Clinton community. Our deepest sympathies are with their families and loved ones during this incredibly difficult time,” representatives with the Brookdale Clinton facility said.
Mississippi Gov. Tate Reeves added that the Mississippi State Department of Health and the Mississippi Emergency Management Agency were also assisting in the response.
“Please continue praying for everyone affected. Thank you to all of the first responders who have quickly sprung into action to help those in need,” Reeves said.
According to Clinton Fire Chief Levius Buckley, 85 residents had to be evacuated, with four needing to be hospitalized with what appeared to be non-life-threatening injuries.
Buckley said the fire impacted several wings of the building, “about 45%” of the facility, and that the building would not be livable for a while.
The fire chief also called a rumor that the facility’s sprinklers were not working “not factual.”
Fire officials said the cause of the fire remains under investigation.

title: Top-3 intact in Varsity Maine boys soccer poll
text:
Our Communities. Our Teams. Our Future.
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
Lewiston or Brunswick has occupied the top spot in the Varsity Maine poll for the past six weeks. They’ve been ranked first and second for five straight weeks. For the second week in a row, the Blue Devils are No. 1 and the Dragons No. 2.
Though they’ve established themselves as the clear favorites, the Class A North tournament will be a dogfight. Eight-ranked Edward Little is the region’s third seed, and the Red Eddies’ four losses in the regular season were to Lewiston and Brunswick. Class A South has no clear favorite. title: Maine heating oil price hits record high at $6.04 per gallon
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
MAINE (WABI) - The average price for heating oil in Maine has hit another record high.
According to the Maine Department of Energy Resources, the average statewide price of a gallon of heating oil as of last Monday is $6.04 per gallon.
That is a $0.07 increase from last week and an 83% increase from this time last year.
The previous record high for heating oil in Maine was set last month at $6.02 per gallon.
Based on a standard 275-gallon oil tank, Mainers are now estimated to pay approximately $750 more to fill their tank than they would have one year ago.
The U.S. Department of Energy said Wednesday it would make 315,000 barrels of heating oil available from the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve in hopes of bringing down prices.

title: Microgrants for musicians: Portland group aims to amplify artist voices
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Jo Bacharach is the founder and CEO of the JB Music Org, a Portland-based organization that supports emerging artists through microgrants of up to $500.
The organization focuses on musicians in the hip-hop and rhythm and blues genres or related subgenres. Frustrated by how many artists go unheard, Bacharach launched the organization to help amplify their voices.
Mainebiz: What’s your background?
Jo Bacharach: I have a background in engineering and technical training. I’ve always had a side hobby related to music, especially supporting independent artists. In 2024, I obtained my MBA from UMO [University of Maine in Orono] and decided to take a gap year to establish an organization dedicated to emerging independent artists. That is when the JB Music Org was born.
MB: When did you establish JB Music Org?
JB: We obtained our certificate of formation as an L3C [low-profit LLC] from the state in March 2025.
MB: Where do you operate?
JB: My home office in Gorham — just a normal office space. We would love to eventually expand and build a recording studio on the property.
MB: What was involved in getting this going?
JB: Lots of networking and grassroots support. I originally engaged a consultant out of Toronto who helped me establish the foundation of the grant program and then slowly built our presence in the industry. That required building trust and delivering on the promises of our grant program as well as proactive marketing through our website and socials.
MB: What is your funding model?
JB: To date, the grant program is 100% self-funded. However, we will be launching our first crowdfunding campaign in November through Indiegogo. The long-term funding plan is to attract other investors, sponsors and partnerships as we grow our impact.
MB: How many musicians have you worked with?
JB: We’ve awarded grants to over 50 recording artists, musicians and producers to date. The funds are paid directly to vendors (think recording studios, mastering engineers, etc.) to facilitate the release and promotion of music. Additionally, we leverage our brand and partner network for organic artist promotion. This includes posting on our socials, playlist placement and community events. For example, we worked with a local studio and venue in Portland called [the square] to host a [rhythm and blues] and hip-hop showcase this summer with local Maine artists.
MB: How are you able to self-fund the program?
JB: I work a part-time remote job, typically 10 to 15 hours per week, which helps cover our household’s day-to-day expenses. The grant program itself has primarily been funded through gains from my personal investment portfolio, which has performed well over the years. We also generate modest supplemental revenue through our $25 grant application fee, which helps cover the costs of operating and maintaining our application platform. In addition, we’re beginning to build community-supported funding streams. One example is our Wall of Independent Music campaign, where supporters can pledge contributions.
MB: You mentioned a crowdfunding campaign launching in November through Indiegogo — what’s your target?
JB: Our initial goal is $20,000, with a stretch goal of $30,000. The campaign will help us expand grant funding, strengthen operational capacity and invest in new opportunities that directly benefit the artists we support.
MB: How much have you disbursed in grants so far?
JB: Since launching the grant program in spring 2025, we’ve awarded just shy of $30,000.
MB: How does the program result in a financial return for your organization?
JB: As a low-profit LLC (L3C), our primary objective is maximizing impact rather than profit. As we enter our second year, however, our goal is to secure enough funding to sustainably cover grant awards and operational expenses, while generating modest revenue that can be reinvested into growth. We’ve received interest from sponsors, brand partners and industry collaborators.

title: Are fake spiderweb decorations dangerous to birds and other animals?
text:
Yes.
Fake spiderweb decorations can entangle birds and other wildlife, sometimes causing serious injuries or death.
The Canadian Wildlife Federation says animals caught in the synthetic fibers may be unable to free themselves, leaving them vulnerable to predators, exhaustion and starvation.
WildCare, a California wildlife hospital, has treated various entangled birds. Injuries can include restricted blood flow and tissue damage, according to the National Audubon Society.
The American Bird Conservancy warns that outdoor webbing can trap unsuspecting birds, particularly during fall migration. Other entanglement hazards include fishing line, sports nets, kite strings, wind chimes and balloon ribbons.
Experts recommend only using artificial webs indoors. Outdoor displays should avoid flight paths, trees and shrubs.
The danger is documented by wildlife rehabilitators, although the overall frequency of entanglements and deaths remains unknown. Anyone finding an entangled animal should contact a licensed rehabilitator rather than try to release it.
This fact brief is responsive to conversations such as this one.
The Maine Trust for Local News partners with Gigafact to produce fact briefs — bite-sized fact checks of trending claims. Read our methodology to learn how we check claims.

title: A Fine Representative
text:
To the editor:
The most fateful moment of my life was when I met Richard Goldman, D-Dresden, over the salad bar at Bates College in 1972.
After following our respective educational paths and then doing work in medicine and legal services in the Arctic in Nome, Alaska, we returned to Maine and found our forever home in the Eastern River Valley in Dresden.
While raising our three kids, I worked for 36 years at the Richmond Area Health Center while Rich spent his legal career at his Augusta office helping people navigate through life crises — divorce, personal bankruptcy, disability, and more. He was effective because he understood the law and maybe more importantly he listened with his heart.

title: Perturbed by investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar
text:
I recently read that Homeland Security is looking into Congresswoman Ilhan Omar’s immigration background, possibly trying to take away her citizenship and deport her. This really bothers me.
Ilhan Omar became an American citizen in 2000. She has been a citizen for more than 25 years and was elected to Congress. What about, say, Melania Trump?
In 2016, the Associated Press reported that Melania was paid for modeling work before she had authorization to work in this country. Her attorney disputed that report. She did not become an American citizen until July 2006, several months after Barron was born, although she was legally living here at the time.
Why is our government digging into Ilhan Omar’s past while questions about Melania Trump’s earlier employment history seem forgotten?
I’m not suggesting anyone be deported without proof of wrongdoing. But shouldn’t the same rules apply to everyone? If Homeland Security can investigate one person’s immigration history, why not another’s, especially where questions have been raised?
I find this disappointing. Being married to the president should not result in special treatment, just as disagreeing with him should not result in being treated differently.
I was brought up believing nobody is above the law. I still believe that. Our immigration laws should be enforced fairly, regardless of who we are or whom we’re married to.
Ralph Duquette
Old Orchard Beach

title: Storm Josephine brings high winds and possible coastal flooding to Eastern Seaboard
text:
MIAMI (AP) — Subtropical Storm Josephine pushed north from the U.S. Northeast coast early Thursday, bringing some coastal flooding and possible gale-force winds to the Eastern Seaboard.
The storm had maximum sustained winds of 65 mph (100 kph) and was centered about 265 miles (425 kilometers) south of Nantucket, Massachusetts, and about 585 miles (940 kilometers) southwest of Halifax, Nova Scotia.
The National Hurricane Center in Miami said Josephine was forecast to continue moving away from the United States and remain south of Nova Scotia and Newfoundland.
The National Weather Service posted a gale warning for parts of the Northeast and mid-Atlantic, meaning winds above 39 mph (63 kph) were possible through midmorning Friday. Small watercraft were also advised of hazardous conditions south to North Carolina’s Outer Banks.
Minor to moderate coastal flooding was also expected to continue through the week on the mid-Atlantic coast.
In the Pacific, Tropical Storm Vance was well off Mexico’s southwestern coast and may intensify to a major hurricane.
It had maximum sustained winds of 45 mph (75 kph) late Wednesday and was forecast to become a hurricane Thursday and a major hurricane Saturday, the U.S. center said.
Vance was located about 505 miles (815 kilometers) south of Acapulco, Mexico.

title: A Kittery business park has sat vacant for years. Could new zoning change that?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A 90-acre parcel of land in Kittery has been undeveloped and overgrown for years, waiting for a proposal that could be a catalyst for commerce and housing.
The would-be business park, which sits on the southbound side of Interstate 95 and Dennett Road, was designated as a TIF district — a development zone that leverages new property taxes for town projects — in 2010 to promote business and industrial growth. More than 15 years later, not a single acre has been touched.
Existing zoning rules have town officials at odds over what needs to change to promote growth in the area; some say the land use guidelines for a business park zone don’t support the town’s future development goals. Residents, meanwhile, can’t decide on what’s best for the land.
Now, the planning board is considering two proposals — one from the housing committee and one from the conservation commission — that offer competing visions for a new residential zone.
As written, the business park ordinance prioritizes mixed-use development, with language directing projects to occupy “larger tracts of land.” Proposals should also blend business, residential and entertainment developments to “foster general business growth and a sense of community.”
In other words, a developer who wants to build a retail store in the zone should also try to incorporate some housing or other businesses in a proposal, though multifamily home builds are limited based on the availability of public infrastructure.
“The intent of mixed-use development is to provide a more efficient use of land than might be obtained through segregated development procedures,” the ordinance reads.
COMPETING PROPOSALS
Allowed uses listed in the existing business park land use ordinance include art studios, a mass transit station, motels or hotels, restaurants and several other options. Planning board Chair Russell White, who also sits on the housing committee, said the town should prioritize other uses.
“I’d say two or three years ago, approximately, the Town Council, seeing that affordable housing was a real need, sort of designated it as a high priority,” White said.
The housing committee’s proposal advocates for a full transition away from business developments and aims to maximize public infrastructure investments. The vacant business park — which is already served by public water and sewer infrastructure — offers acres of possibility.
The new residential neighborhood ordinance proposed by the committee would allow several residential uses, including multi- and single-family homes, accessory dwelling units, agricultural developments and recreation spaces. It would also allow some developments outlined in the existing residential suburban land use ordinance, including public utility facilities, religious spaces, a school and a handful of child or elder care facilities.
But members of the conservation commission have called that proposal inadequate.
Most developments in town are required to include open space — areas that are free from development — though the exact area varies based on zoning requirements.
The housing committee proposed that 25% of the land should be open space, but Conservation Commission Chair MaryAlice LaPoint, who is advocating for a green residential land use ordinance, said there’s an issue with the committee’s plan.
“(The housing committee is) claiming that the wetlands that can’t be built on anyway, the wetlands and the setback, counts as open space,” LaPoint said, adding that some land on the business park in the northeast corner is protected wetland.
The conservation commission’s proposal keeps the same priorities in terms of housing density — which LaPoint said the commission supports as long as it keeps natural resources in mind — but sets stricter guidelines on open space requirements. It would formally protect 25% of the land, aside from areas designated by the state to have special significance.
It would also require a tree canopy, implement turfgrass restrictions and demand that at least 80% of planted vegetation should be native.
If those standards aren’t met, LaPoint said, the conservation commission will fight back.
“Unless we get that, we’ll be one of the voices to say, ‘If you can’t do it right, then you can’t do it at all,’” she said.
PAST PROPOSALS FUEL CONCERNS
The area has gone through a series of changes in the past eight years. It was a business park until the Town Council changed it to a mixed-use residential zone in 2018, then reverted back to a business park after residents opposed a massive development proposal in 2022.
The town was a few small steps away from accepting a plan for a $300 million development that would have allowed the construction of an apartment complex called Dennett Landing. The 82-acre, multiuse proposal would have included more than 300 units, plus medical offices, a restaurant, a childcare facility and an assisted-living facility.
But residents were worried about property tax increases and the impacts the development could have on the environment and on public infrastructure. The proposal was shot down by residents via petition, which prompted officials to reject zoning changes that would have been necessary to make it happen.
The Town Council also passed a moratorium on development in the business park until it could come up with a better set of guidelines. It expired in 2023.
White, the housing committee and planning board member, thinks past vitriol in response to the Dennett Landing proposal has led some developers to become reluctant to propose new projects.
“I think there is at least one developer who is interested in the parcel,” White said. “There was so much pushback at the Dennett Landing that he doesn’t want to run afoul of that.”
LaPoint also thinks the design of a nearby apartment complex, Seacoast Residences, has made some residents apprehensive about supporting new proposals. She said there’s a coarse nickname residents have for the building, though she wouldn’t share it.
“I’ll just say that people are very unhappy with the look of that first building,” LaPoint said.
The conservation commission aims to offset any pushback on future designs by setting aesthetic requirements on developments to “honor Kittery’s maritime heritage,” according to the proposed ordinance.
WHAT’S NEXT?
Both LaPoint and White say the best path forward would be to create a proposal that combines the goals of the housing committee and the conservation commission.
LaPoint, who is also a member of the Kittery Land Issues Commission, said officials have been working with the town’s director of planning to help draft an ordinance that reflects a compromise. The Town Council will give the ordinance final approval once it’s ready.
“I think that the housing committee and even the planning board realizes that the conservation commission proposal has a lot of things that aren’t essential and some things that are good ideas,” White said. “But how to put them together is something that may be beyond the capacity of the planning board.”
Officials are set to continue discussion at future meetings and will hold a public hearing in November or December before passing the issue to the Town Council, White said.
The timeline to adopt a new ordinance has shifted a lot in the last few years, White said, and with two competing proposals, it remains unclear when a change will be made final.

title: Trump administration drops appeal to overhaul Public Service Loan Forgiveness program
text:
Trump administration drops appeal to overhaul Public Service Loan Forgiveness program
The Trump administration has dropped its effort to overhaul the Public Service Loan Forgiveness program. Here's what that means for the millions who rely on the program.
Trump administration drops appeal to overhaul Public Service Loan Forgiveness program
The Trump administration has dropped its effort to overhaul the Public Service Loan Forgiveness program. Here's what that means for the millions who rely on the program.
The Trump administration dropped its appeal to overhaul the Public Service Loan Forgiveness program, leaving the program unchanged for now.
The decision comes as a surprising reversal for many borrowers who view the program as a financial lifeline. Currently, more than 2.5 million borrowers are enrolled in the PSLF program, with a total loan balance of over $228 billion, according to Student Loan Planner.
Under PSLF, borrowers must work for government agencies, public schools, hospitals, or eligible nonprofits and make 10 years of payments on their student loans to qualify for debt cancellation.
Last fall, the Trump administration introduced a rule granting Education Secretary Linda McMahon the authority to remove employers from the program if their work was deemed to serve "a substantial illegal purpose."
Critics argued the vague phrasing was intended to target employers who supported undocumented immigrants or transgender youth.
A federal judge later ruled that the administration’s plan overstepped agency power and threatened free speech.
With the appeal now dropped, the PSLF program remains unchanged, allowing eligible borrowers to continue working toward debt forgiveness.

title: Maine heating oil costs just hit a record high — again
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Heating oil costs in Maine just hit a record high for the second time this fall.
The Maine Department of Energy Resources said Thursday that the average gallon of heating oil cost $6.04, breaking the record set last month by two cents. Costs are up by 83% over last October, when that same gallon cost an average of $3.30.
At this price, Mainers will spend about $750 more filling a standard 275-gallon oil tank than last fall.
“Maine has broken yet another record for heating oil prices, putting even more pressure on families as winter approaches,” Acting department Commissioner Celina Cunningham said in a news release.
President Donald Trump and his administration’s officials have long told the public that the U.S. and Israel’s war in Iran, which has constricted the crucial oil passageway of the Strait of Hormuz and driven oil prices up, would be quickly resolved. But Trump said this month that the U.S. would not resume strikes on Iran until after the midterm elections next month, a move that could drag out the conflict.
Since the war with Iran began in late February, Maine heating oil prices have spiked 57%.
With costs at their new record high, Maine’s federally supported heating assistance fund, the Home Energy Assistance Program, won’t go as far as in past winters — even with an early release of those funds and $4 million in a carryover from last year.
Maine, as the state most reliant on heating oil, is most vulnerable to price spikes and stood to gain most from the early release of those federal heating assistance funds. About 45,000 households received the supplemental assistance last year, MaineHousing said — and the primary population served by heating assistance programs are seniors on fixed incomes.
To help ease price concerns, the U.S. Department of Energy announced Wednesday that it would release 315,000 barrels of heating oil through a rarely used emergency stockpile, the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve.
Those 315,000 barrels, which carry about 42 gallons each, would fill about 48,100 standard-size heating oil tanks.
But with the release split between the New England states and New York, which by itself has 1.7 million households dependent on heating oil, it’s unclear how the extra supply will impact prices in Maine.
The Department of Energy is using an “exchange” to release the new heating oil — a process where oil companies bid on and receive at least 25,000 barrels of the strategic reserves, and then must return the entire portion they took, plus at least 5% extra, at a later date. The oil will hit the market next month.
Companies must return heating oil to the federal government by April 2027 or face an additional premium that increases by 2.5% monthly, according to the Department of Energy’s request for bids.
But if the Iran war continues into the spring, long-term supply issues may remain.
Heating oil has become a campaign issue, less than two weeks out from Election Day. Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, and her Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson, have blamed each other for high costs. Gubernatorial candidates have also called for more heating assistance funding.
Applications for heating assistance are open now. Maine residents hoping to apply for HEAP funding or looking for other assistance can contact their local community action program or call 211. The state also releases an annual Winter Heating Guide with cost-saving resources for households of all incomes.

FULL INTERVIEW: Sen. Angus King on Maine heating costs, Iran and Ukraine
In an interview for "Total Maine," Sen. Angus King discussed rising home heating oil costs, the war in Iran, and U.S. support for Ukraine.
FULL INTERVIEW: Sen. Angus King on Maine heating costs, Iran and Ukraine
In an interview for "Total Maine," Sen. Angus King discussed rising home heating oil costs, the war in Iran, and U.S. support for Ukraine.
In an interview on "Total Maine," Sen. Angus King spoke about rising heating costs in Maine, the wars in Ukraine and Iran, and U.S. foreign policy.
King said releasing 315,000 barrels from the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve could increase supply and provide relief to Maine households.
He argued that tapping the reserve was justified due to the scale of the price increase.
“Nothing like this has ever happened. I never can recall heating oil prices going anywhere near $6,” Sen. King said. “So this is really an extraordinary circumstance. And it relates to an extraordinary circumstance, which is the war in Iran.”
The conversation shifted to Ukraine, where King criticized the Trump administration’s treatment of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and called for increased pressure on Russian President Vladimir Putin.
“This isn’t a real estate deal. This is a country that’s fighting for its independence. That’s fighting for its very life against a murderous dictator who invaded his country without any justification,” King said. “And to be pressuring Zelensky to make some kind of deal, to give up part of his country in order to mollify Putin is unconscionable.”
King also discussed his recent op-ed in the New York Times, warning that weakening relationships with longtime allies could harm U.S. national security and take years to repair.

title: What to know as 6 women testify in Russell Brand rape, sexual assault trial
text:
What to know as 6 women testify in Russell Brand rape, sexual assault trial
Six women who accuse Russell Brand of sexually assaulting and raping them in separate instances have described during a London trial their encounters with the British actor and comedian.
Related video: Bipartisan campus safety bill promises help for survivors
The women, who don't know each other, allege they were assaulted by Brand between 1999 and 2009 in locations including workplaces, a hotel room and a bathroom at a bar.
Brand, 51, has pleaded not guilty to three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of indecent assault. He denies all the charges.
Prosecutors allege Brand was a “ruthless” and manipulative sexual predator who at the time had an “indiscriminate and voracious” desire for sexual contact.
Alleged assaults took place over a decade of Brand's career
The first woman alleged that Brand raped her in a hotel room in 1999 after she met him during a performance on the fringe of the Labour Party annual conference.
A friend of Brand's testified that some weeks after the alleged rape, the actor told him he "may have gone a bit too far” with a woman.
Another woman alleged that Brand orally raped her in 2004 in the restroom of a London bar. The woman said that she had just met Brand and was chatting to him at the bar when he suddenly grabbed her breasts then dragged her into the bathroom.
A third woman, a then 21-year-old fan, said that Brand anally raped her at his home after she met him at one of his shows in 2009.
Three other women also testified about alleged assaults in their workplaces.
One of them alleged that Brand grabbed her arm and tried to drag her into the men’s bathroom at her office in 2001. Another woman alleged that he kissed and groped her at the London radio station where she worked in 2004 or 2005. A third woman said that he pressed his face into her groin and demanded a massage while recording for a television project in 2009.
The women said they didn't report the alleged assaults at the time out of shame, and because of concern that they wouldn't be believed because of Brand's celebrity status. They individually went to police to report what happened to them after a 2023 television program broadcast anonymous accusations against Brand.
Brand hasn't testified so far
Brand, who is on bail, has appeared in the courtroom with his wife, Laura Gallacher, throughout the trial. He listened intently from the dock, and sat expressionless much of the time as his accusers told of their encounters with him.
In police interviews, he denied ever engaging in nonconsensual sexual activity.
The actor's lawyer, Ian Winter, questioned the women's accounts during the trial. He's expected to argue that sexual encounters from Brand's past have been “reimagined” when he outlines his case next week.
It's not clear if Brand himself will testify. The trial is expected to last up to 10 weeks.
Brand is known for social media content on conspiracy theories
Known for risque stand-up comedy routines and battles with drugs and alcohol, Brand rose to prominence in the early 2000s, hosting television programs and his own BBC radio show. He appeared in Hollywood films including “Forgetting Sarah Marshall” and “Get Him to the Greek" and was briefly married to pop star Katy Perry.
But in the past decade, he has largely moved away from mainstream media after he relocated to Florida and amassed millions of followers on social media with videos mixing wellness, conspiracy theories and discussions of his religious devotion.
Brand has come under increased scrutiny in recent years after multiple allegations of sexual assault surfaced. Last year, the BBC said that concerns about his behavior — including complaints that he had sex on the broadcaster's premises and exposed himself in the studio — weren't handled appropriately because of his status.
The Associated Press doesn’t name victims of alleged sexual violence, and British law protects their identities from the media for life.

title: Trump promises cash payments ahead of midterms
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - President Donald Trump is promising a series of cash payments to voters as Republicans seek to maintain control of the House and Senate in the midterm elections.
At the RNC midterm convention in September, Trump pledged to send $5,000 to every American adult if the GOP retains control of Congress.
“Because of our tremendous strength and success economically, I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000,” Trump said Sept. 9.
Since the Dallas convention, Trump has continued to make additional promises.
He said he would send $8 billion in direct payments to U.S. farmers, who he said have been hit by tariffs and record diesel prices.
Trump also announced a new program that would provide as much as $30,000 to any American who reports a tip about government fraud.
In Greenville, N.C., Trump made a promise to Marine Corps veterans who have claims against the U.S. over contaminated water at Camp Lejeune.
“If we win the House and the Senate, I am directing the Department of Justice to settle all remaining legitimate claims as soon as possible,” Trump said.
Democrats have accused the president of trying to buy votes with the many promises made in the final weeks of the campaign.
It remains to be seen whether Trump can deliver on the promises, or whether the proposals will affect the outcome of the midterm election.

text:

New England Patriots (4-2) vs. Chicago Bears (4-2), 8:15 p.m.

Prediction: Ravens 28, Bengals 27
Tampa Bay Buccaneers (1-5) vs. Carolina Panthers (3-2), 1 p.m.
Tampa Bay definitely let one slip away last week against Pittsburgh, but that's just the kind of team it is this season. Carolina has a high-flying offense, leading the league with nearly 300 passing yards per game. Bryce Young is a solid quarterback who should have a breakout game here. For the Buccaneers, quarterback Baker Mayfield may return this week, but it won't be enough to pull out this division win. Carolina should run away with the win — and the division — against weaker competition.
Prediction: Panthers 37, Buccaneers 20
New York Giants (3-2-1) vs. Houston Texans (2-4), 1 p.m.
The Giants could come into this one with only a single loss, but that's not the way the season has turned out. Last week against the Saints, New York surrendered 34 unanswered points and it was too little too late when they scored 17 points in the fourth quarter. Quarterback J.J. McCarthy should get the start and carry the Giants to a road win to get the season back on track.
Prediction: Giants 38, Texans 23
Indianapolis Colts (2-4) vs. Minnesota Vikings (5-0), 1 p.m.
Dallas Turner and Byron Murphy Jr. lead a strong Minnesota defensive unit and really give the Colts no chance. The Vikings are second in the league, giving up just 259.8 yards per game. Murphy has three interceptions to set a tie for the NFL lead, while Turners' 5.5 sacks rank third in the league. Colts quarterback Daniel Jones will have a tough time finding holes on the road in this one.
Prediction: Vikings 33, Colts 17
Miami Dolphins (0-5) vs. New York Jets (2-4), 1 p.m.
Two of the AFC's weakest teams will clash in a matchup of mercy. The Dolphins come in after a bye week and should be rested for the road trip up north, while the Jets are reeling after dropping a winnable game against New England. Miami's best chance for its first win comes here at MetLife Stadium.
Prediction: Dolphins 18, Jets 14
Cleveland Browns (4-2) vs. Tennessee Titans (1-5), 1 p.m.
The Browns sit atop the AFC North standings and can keep things rolling in Nashville. The Titans came out victorious in their previous matchup last December, but Cleveland is a completely different team now. The Browns have a great passing attack with sure-handed wide receivers. The offense will keep humming, and the Titans' defense, even though it's their best unit, won't be able to contain Denzel Boston and KC Concepcion.
Prediction: Browns 24, Titans 23
Denver Broncos (4-2) vs. Arizona Cardinals (2-4), 4:05 p.m.
Both teams are coming off nail-biting victories. Broncos quarterback Bo Nix is coming off an interesting performance where he completed over 60 percent of his 27 passes, but did not throw a touchdown or interception. The Cardinals' defense has struggled and Nix should be able to improve this week — maybe replicating his Week 5 performance where he threw for 214 yards and a touchdown. He hasn't thrown an interception since Sept. 27 against the Rams.
Prediction: Broncos 42, Cardinals 24
Green Bay Packers (4-2) vs. Detroit Lions (3-2), 4:25 p.m.
The Packers looked destined to fail through the first few games of the season, but a three-game winning streak has the cheeseheads much more optimistic. Jordan Love is putting together a great season and in his first game back off the Commissioner's Exempt List, Josh Jacobs is looking to ignite the offense and make up for his past sins off the field. The Lions have one of the best offenses in the game, though. Jahmyr Gibbs is one of the league's best receivers right now.
Prediction: Lions 38, Packers 32
Los Angeles Rams (2-4) vs. Las Vegas Raiders (3-3), 4:25 p.m.
The Rams have been the biggest disappointment so far this season. And even though the Raiders have fallen to .500, they still might be the biggest surprise in the league. Matthew Stafford leads the NFL in passing with 1,794 yards, and the Rams have averaged more than 400 yards of total offense in each game this season. However, Las Vegas' Kirk Cousins is as reliable as ever, averaging over 35 passing attempts a game this season. This should be a get-right game for the Rams, though.
Prediction: Rams 31, Raiders 24
Kansas City Chiefs (5-0) vs. Seattle Seahawks (3-3), 8:20 p.m.
Kenneth Walker III spent four seasons with the Seahawks, winning a Super Bowl MVP. But in his first season with the Chiefs, he is reshaping an offense that was not itself a year ago. This season, Walker has tallied 665 yards, putting up more than 100 in all but one game. Kansas City was No. 20 in total offense at the end of 2025, and the team is now No. 1 in the league with 414 total yards per game.
Prediction: Chiefs 28, Seahawks 24
Monday, Oct. 26
Dallas Cowboys (2-4) vs. Philadelphia Eagles (2-4), 8:15 p.m.
This is an important game for both teams as the NFC East title is still up for grabs. A win for either side helps make the pathway to the top a little easier. But it won't be easy for either side to get momentum back. After averaging more than 30 points per game through its first four contests, the Cowboys have scored just 29 points across their last two games. Dallas looked rough in a loss at Green Bay last week. The biggest NFL storyline of the week came when the Eagles placed quarterback Jalen Hurts on the injured reserve. He is now out for the season and Tanner McKee must step up quickly to lead the offense. It may take some time for that to happen, so the Cowboys should steal a much-needed road win.
Prediction: Cowboys 37, Eagles 17

title: Movies to Watch After ‘You Can See Everything’
text:
8 Films to Watch If You Love ‘You Can See Everything’
Everyone is talking about You Can See Everything, Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s provocative, three-hour documentary about disgraced entrepreneur and inventor Elizabeth Holmes. A few weeks ago, almost no one even knew the film existed. Now it’s selling out theaters around the country and earning rave reviews that frequently call it the best film of 2026. It looks like it stands a very real chance to become the first documentary ever nominated for the Academy Award for Best Picture.
You Can See Everything boldly breaks with longstanding documentary traditions; it includes reenactments, elliptical editing, and features on-camera appearances from both filmmakers as they try to determine whether Holmes is a charlatan or a victim. It’s a clever, exciting film — but it’s hardly the first documentary to question its own form, or to blend fiction and non-fiction in a single work.
If You Can See Everything left you hungry for more documentaries like it, here’s what to watch next.
Gimme Shelter (1970)
Directed by Albert Maysles, David Maysles, and Charlotte Zwerin
Currently Streaming on HBO Max
This landmark concert documentary follows the Rolling Stones on their 1969 U.S. tour, which culminated with their performance at the Altamont Speedway, where a young man was killed in the middle of their set. But the film is also about the Stones watching their performances, both on and off camera, and commenting on their shows and the violence carried out by their fans. The way they reckon with their celebrity and their public personas offer some interesting echoes of “the real” Elizabeth Holmes in You Can See Me, and the way Nathan Fielder grapples with his subject on camera.
F For Fake (1973)
Directed by Orson Welles
Currently Streaming on HBO Max and the Criterion Channel
50 years before Oppenheim and Fielder deconstructed the documentary form in the middle of a documentary, Orson Welles performed a similar magic trick with his delightful late-career masterpiece F For Fake. Welles leads viewers through a history of notable frauds and fakers — including himself! — and largely depicts them very sympathetically (another thing it has in common with You Can See Everything).
Sherman’s March (1986)
Directed by Ross McElwee
Currently Available for Rent
Nathan Fielder puts himself in the center of the frame in just about everything he makes, and no matter what else You Can See Everything is about, it’s also about its co-director and his feelings of loneliness and isolation. For a masterclass on that sort of extremely personal filmmaking, check out Ross McElwee’s Sherman’s March, which is self-described on its title screen as “a meditation on the possibility of romantic love in the South during an era of nuclear weapons proliferation.” McElwee originally set out to make a film about the lingering impact of the Civil War in the American South. Instead, Sherman’s March became more and more about him, and his own history and his trouble with relationships.
Close-Up (1990)
Directed by Abbas Kiarostami
Currently Available for Rent
The blurry line between fiction and non-fiction was a pervasive theme throughout the career of the great Iranian filmmaker Abbas Kiarostami; most of his films would make solid candidates for a double feature with You Can See Everything. The obvious place to start if you’re not familiar with Kiarostami’s work is Close-Up, a blend of documentary and fiction about a true-crime case involving an Iranian man who tricked a family into believing he was famous Iranian director Mohsen Makhmalbaf. Kiarostami filmed the man’s trial, and afterwards, convinced both the phony and his victims to reenact their prior interactions for his cameras. Kiarostami blended the reenactments with footage from the trial into a moving story of a fraud with an utterly authentic love of cinema.
Stories We Tell (2012)
Directed by Sarah Polley
Currently Streaming on Hoopla, Kanopy, Tubi, and YouTube TV
You Can See Everything is the perfect title for Fielder and Oppenheim’s film, but if they had needed a backup Stories We Tell would have worked pretty well too — if it hadn’t already been used for Sarah Polley’s terrific autobiographical film investigating the mystery of her own parentage and the way we create and perpetuate stories (or outright lies) about our lives. Like YCSE, the film uses reenactments to depict events from the past where cameras weren’t present.
The Act of Killing (2012)
Directed by Joshua Oppenheimer
Currently streaming on Kanopy
It’s one thing for a documentary to hire actors to reenact certain historical events. It’s another to convince the real-life participants in those events to reenact them in front of the cameras — and still another when those real-life participants are recreating murders that they claim to have perpetrated. That’s what transpires in The Act of Killing, which director Joshua Oppenheimer later said created “perhaps a new form of documentary, a kind of documentary of the imagination,” one that raises a lot of the same questions as You Can See Everything.
Actress (2014)
Directed by Robert Greene
Currently Streaming on Fandor
Acting and performance lies at the center of Robert Greene’s Actress, which he once described as a “nonfiction/melodrama hybrid” about Brandy Burre, an out-of-work actress and mother who tries to resurrect her career after time off spent raising her children. Greene observes Burre’s day-to-day life, but also leaves room for us to ponder the character Burre is portraying, not only for his cameras but for everyone in the world around her.
Ren Faire (2024)
Directed by Lance Oppenheim
Currently streaming on HBO Max
Before he co-directed You Can See Everything, Lance Oppenheim directed and co-created this extremely entertaining documentary miniseries that plays like a real-life Game of Thrones. Visually, it looks very similar to You Can See Everything, a choice that lends an epic feel to the behind-the-scenes power struggle for control of the long-running Texas Renaissance Festival — which, in turn, makes the whole show that much funnier because it’s people fighting for control of a Renaissance festival.
The 10 Most Hilarious Bad-on-Purpose Movies

title: The Home Front
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Don Plourde of Coldwell Banker Plourde Real Estate in Waterville and Kim Gleason of McAllister Real Estate in Hallowell are both agency owners and brokers.
With 43 and 35 years in the industry, respectively, they have seen sales cycles come and go and interest rates rise and fall. Here’s what they had to say about today’s residential real estate market.
Kim Gleason
“Houses seem to be on the market several days longer than in the recent past,” Gleason said, adding that buyers now have more than two or three homes to choose from.
The average purchase price around the state has been about $425,000. Gleason said the average sale price of the transactions she’s involved in are closer to $375,000. “You can’t find a reasonable home under $300,000 anymore,” she said.
Asked about a sweet spot for list prices, Gleason said, “Under $400,000 will get the most interest from buyers, but let’s face it, today’s $400,000 is the pre-pandemic equivalent of $200,000.” She attributes this new standard to the influx of people moving to Maine from out of state and more people working from home.
Gleason thinks the market is entering a new cycle, returning to a balance she last saw 20 to 25 years ago.
“It is no longer a seller’s market, but prices aren’t coming down like you think,” she said. “People are afraid to sell a home they purchased with a 3% interest rate and move somewhere else with a 7% interest rate tacked onto their mortgage.”
However, Gleason noted that “it’s always about supply and demand.” She believes growing housing inventory could bring greater market stability in the coming years.
Don Plourde
“The residential market is still strong,” Plourde said. He agreed with Gleason that high interest rates are keeping some buyers out of the market, although existing homes are retaining their value.
“At the same time, aggressive home pricing is becoming more realistic,” he said. “We recently had one house where the seller was asking $525,000. That dropped to $495,000 and then to $449,000. That last asking price was perceived as a good value, and we got offers.”
Asked about competition among buyers, Plourde said, “We also don’t see bidding wars like we used to. Maybe on occasion, but not like when six or seven offers came in after the first day of showings.” He recalled one extreme situation when he had 30 offers on a house in Vassalboro.
“Those days are gone.”
Asked about the near future, Plourde said, “Because of the continued lack of property available, the market will stay strong for sellers. And we won’t see foreclosures like we did in 2008. People have equity these days.”

title: Mom of boy, 8, injured in golf cart hit-and-run on a mission to find driver who hit him
text:
SUMMERVILLE, S.C. (WCSC/Gray News) - An 8-year-old South Carolina boy was riding his bike home from school when he was suddenly hit by a golf cart and left there, injured and alone. Now, his mother says she’s on a mission to find the driver who hit him.
Leo VanOsdol, 8, was riding his bike home from Cane Bay Elementary School last Wednesday on the Cane Bay Trail when he was hit by a golf cart. His mother, Meaghan VanOsdol, was out of town for work at the time of the incident, but she says the woman who hit Leo just kept driving.
The 8-year-old suffered some scrapes and bruises, and his bike was severely damaged with the entire front tire bent. His mother says multiple people drove around him until finally, another woman stopped, helped him and called 911.
“I remember my hands instantly trembling. I couldn’t even grab the phone quickly enough,” VanOsdol said. “Then, as soon as I got off the phone with Leo and knew that he was OK, it was the rush of emotions like anger, disappointment. I felt very lonely in that moment because we’re in this big community, he was surrounded by a ton of adults and he was just left.”
Leo’s mother says he had gotten the bike for his birthday, which was just days before the incident. Since posting on Facebook, she has seen the community rally in support of buying him a new one.
VanOsdol says she is also on a mission to find the woman who hit her son.
“If it was your kid, you wouldn’t want them sitting there,” she said. “Just put yourself in our shoes and know that what you did wasn’t OK. The accident itself, it happens; it’s an accident, but leaving him is just not acceptable.”
Family can’t file charges
Following the incident, VanOsdol is concerned about the lack of protection for kids going to and from school on the trail.
Under state law, golf carts operated on public roads are legally treated like motor vehicles, meaning they can trigger criminal charges and civil liability. However, VanOsdol was told the family couldn’t file charges in this case since Cane Bay Trail is a private trail and a golf cart isn’t considered an automobile.
“It can’t just be something to where this trail goes into the woods unseen and no one monitors it, especially if it’s private,” VanOsdol said. “There’s nothing that can be done if something does happen.”
Now, she’s pushing for more signage and wants the community to be aware of the dangers in the area.
“I think the same way that a school zone is treated on a road, it should be treated on a trail right next to a school,” VanOsdol said. “So, whether it’s speed bumps put in, signs, the trail being monitored in this area, something along those lines.”
Other parents speak out
Melissa Hunt was following behind her kindergartener while she was riding her bike and when she looped around, she stopped by to help. She says this was one of her fears living in the area and has been concerned about golf cart safety for years now.
Hunt says it’s the “wild, wild west” of golf carts.
“They will take the right-of-way when kids are trying to cross the crosswalk, so the kids are going outside of the crosswalk to get across because the golf carts are taking up the space,” she said. “That needs to be something that’s regulated.”
Hunt says another option could possibly be widening the path to give walkers and runners a side and golf carts another, especially with the growth coming to the Cane Bay area.
“Golf carts are great for the environment,” she said. “It cuts down on the traffic around here as well, but with so many golf carts and it being a viable mode of transportation in the area, there needs to be some regulations and laws. I know there’s a few, but I don’t think a lot of people know them.”
Current golf cart regulations
The South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles currently has several registration and equipment requirements, but parents are concerned not everyone is following them.
In Berkeley County, golf carts must be registered and permitted through the SCDMV for a $5 fee, covered by liability insurance and driven by someone at least 16 with a valid license.
Carts are limited to roads with a speed limit of 35 mph or less, within a 4-mile radius of the registered address and during daylight hours unless they are properly equipped with headlights and taillights.
