title: Girls Soccer Playoffs: Here's Who County Teams Could Face
text:
Aroostook County Girls Soccer Teams Prepare for 2026 Playoffs With Strong Seeds and Local Matchups
The regular season is coming to a close, and Aroostook County girls' soccer fans have plenty to look forward to as the postseason gets underway.
Presque Isle has earned the third seed in Class B North, Fort Kent sits atop Class C North, and six County teams are lined up for three head-to-head quarterfinal games in Class D North.
Add in Wisdom's impressive season in eight-player soccer and Katahdin's preliminary matchup, and there should be no shortage of local teams to follow during the next couple of weeks.
The eight-player preliminary round is scheduled for Friday, October 23, with the remaining preliminaries Saturday, October 24. Regional quarterfinals follow October 26, 27 and 28.
Here's a look at what awaits our County teams.
Class B North: Presque Isle Earns Third Seed and Preliminary Bye
The Presque Isle Wildcats have put together a strong regular season, finishing 9-3-2 and earning the number three seed in Class B North.
That gives Presque Isle a bye through the preliminary round and a home quarterfinal against the winner of sixth-seeded Skowhegan and eleventh-seeded Lawrence.
It's a different path from the one the Wildcats appeared to be heading toward earlier in the standings, but they'll still have an opportunity to begin their playoff run on their home field.
Presque Isle picked up some impressive victories throughout the season, including two wins over Orono, a victory over Fort Kent, and a win against Ellsworth.
The Wildcats also played Hermon to a tie after losing their first meeting with the Hawks.
Two of Presque Isle's three losses came against top-seeded John Bapst, which finished 13-0-1.
With the number three seed, the Wildcats have put themselves in a position to make a run through the Northern Maine tournament. They'll just have to wait for the preliminary round to find out who they'll face first.
Class C North: Fort Kent Leads the Way, Houlton Earns Home Quarterfinal
Fort Kent has been one of the strongest girls' soccer teams in Northern Maine throughout the fall.
The Warriors finished 11-1-2 and earned the top seed in Class C North, giving them home-field advantage as they begin the playoffs.
Fort Kent's first opponent is eighth-seeded Maine Central Institute, which finished 4-10.
The Warriors' only loss came against Presque Isle, and they also played the Wildcats to a tie in their other meeting.
Fort Kent swept its regular-season meetings with second-seeded Orono and fourth-seeded Houlton, and also defeated Madawaska twice.
Those results helped the Warriors earn the top spot in the region and an opportunity to begin their tournament at home.
Houlton and Central Meet for a Third Time
The Houlton Lady Shires finished 7-7, earning the fourth seed and a home quarterfinal against fifth-seeded Central, which finished 6-6-2.
This one has the makings of a pretty entertaining matchup.
Houlton and Central met twice during the regular season, with each team picking up a victory.
Now they'll meet for a third time, with the winner advancing to the regional semifinals.
The Lady Shires also recorded victories over Penobscot Valley and Van Buren during the regular season, showing they're capable of competing against some quality opponents.
With the season series split, this third meeting should be an interesting one.
Class D North: Three All-County Quarterfinals Highlight the Bracket
If you're looking for some great local soccer, Class D North might be the place to find it.
Six Aroostook County teams occupy seeds two through seven, creating three quarterfinal matchups between County schools.
And with top-seeded Penobscot Valley also in the field, there's plenty of competition throughout the bracket.
No. 2 Fort Fairfield vs. No. 7 Washburn
Fort Fairfield finished 12-2, earning the second seed after one of the strongest regular seasons in the classification.
The Tigers will host seventh-seeded Washburn, which finished its season at 7-7.
Fort Fairfield defeated the Beavers twice during the regular season, but the playoffs give Washburn another opportunity to turn things around.
The Tigers also defeated Central Aroostook and Madawaska during the fall, proving they can compete with teams near the top of the standings.
Both schools know each other well, and with a regional semifinal appearance at stake, they'll meet for a third time this season.
No. 3 Central Aroostook vs. No. 6 Van Buren
Central Aroostook put together an 11-3 season, earning the third seed and a home quarterfinal against sixth-seeded Van Buren.
The Crusaders finished 9-5.
Unlike several of the other County matchups, these teams did not meet during the regular season.
Central Aroostook recorded victories over Fort Fairfield, Ashland and Madawaska, while Van Buren earned a win over Ashland and swept its meetings against Washburn.
That should make for an interesting opening matchup between two teams that haven't had a chance to size each other up on the field this fall.
No. 4 Ashland vs. No. 5 Madawaska
This could be one of the most entertaining quarterfinal games in the entire Class D North bracket.
Ashland finished 9-4-1, earning the fourth seed, while Madawaska completed a 10-4 season and enters as the fifth seed.
Both teams have had success against strong competition.
Ashland defeated Central Aroostook during the regular season and also earned a tie against top-seeded Penobscot Valley.
Madawaska recorded victories over Fort Fairfield and Central Aroostook, and the Lady Owls are heading into the tournament following one of the more dramatic finishes we've seen this fall.
In their final regular-season game, eighth-grader Dani Pelletier scored just 57 seconds into the second overtime to give Madawaska a 1-0 win over Washburn.
It was a memorable finish to the regular season, and now the Lady Owls will be looking to carry that momentum into the playoffs.
Ashland and Madawaska did not face each other during the regular season, giving us another first-time matchup in the quarterfinals.
Eight-Player North: Wisdom Earns Second Seed, Katahdin Heads to Penquis Valley
The Wisdom Pioneers have enjoyed another outstanding season, finishing 12-2 and earning the second seed in eight-player North.
Wisdom's only two losses came against undefeated Bangor Christian, which competes in the South region.
The Pioneers also picked up two victories apiece over Lee Academy, Penobscot Christian, Penquis Valley and Katahdin.
Wisdom receives a preliminary-round bye and will host the winner between seventh-seeded Penobscot Christian and tenth-seeded George Stevens Academy in the quarterfinals.
Should Penobscot Christian advance, Wisdom would meet a team it has already defeated twice this season.
Katahdin Opens on the Road
The Katahdin Cougars finished 8-6 and earned the ninth seed, setting up a preliminary-round trip to eighth-seeded Penquis Valley, which finished 4-9-1.
These two teams split their regular-season meetings, which should make their third meeting particularly interesting.
Katahdin also picked up a victory over sixth-seeded Lee Academy during the regular season and has shown it can compete against tournament opponents.
If the Cougars can get past Penquis Valley, they'll advance to face top-seeded Dexter, which finished 11-2-1.
Championship Soccer Is Coming to Aroostook County
The tournament begins October 23 with the eight-player preliminaries, followed by the remaining preliminary games October 24.
The regional quarterfinals are scheduled for October 27 and 28, with semifinals October 30 and 31.
Regional championships follow November 3 and 4, with the state championships scheduled for November 7.
Two of those championship games are coming to Presque Isle Middle School.
The Class D North regional championship is scheduled for Wednesday, November 4, while the eight-player state championship will take place Saturday, November 7.
With so many County teams in the tournament, there's plenty of opportunity for some of our local schools to make a run.
I'll have the finalized brackets, game results, updates and more photos as the tournament moves along.
Good luck to all our County teams as they begin their playoff runs!
The 2026 MPA Soccer Championships on 101.9 The Rock are proudly presented by Pineland Farms in Mars Hill.

title: Watch: Mt. Ararat field hockey is the Varsity Maine Girls team of the week
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
Varsity Maine Girls Team of the Week: Mt. Ararat field hockey
When Krista Chase was first hired to pilot the Mt. Ararat field hockey team in 2014, the program had been in a state of limbo for years.
“ Thirteen years ago, we weren’t winning many games,” Chase said.
Now, the Eagles (14-0) enter the postseason as the top seed in Class A North, thanks to their first victory over Skowhegan in more than a decade, a win that coincidentally was Chase’s 200th as head coach.
Chase said the program’s transformation started the day that she took the helm.
“ The very first thing I did was create the Baby Eagles youth program,” she said. “My juniors and seniors are the original Baby Eagles, and that’s the foundation of Mt. Ararat field hockey.”
Chase’s daughter, Kamryn, now a junior captain for the Eagles, was one of the “OG” members of the Baby Eagles.
“ We were the first preschoolers and kindergartners to come through,” Kamryn Chase said. “It just feels very rewarding to do all that hard work … and when we get to high school to be so successful.”
“ They’re my girls, they’re my family,” Krista Chase said. “They’re who have really made me a better coach and really transformed this program.”
The Eagles have outscored their opponents 70-6, with no opponent scoring more than once since the preseason. Kamryn Chase said that she sees this more as a cause for motivation than celebration.
“In playoffs, we’re gonna need to be ready to see anything, ’cause teams are really gonna wanna beat us,” Kamryn said. “ We’re just gonna need to bring the fire and the hard work and just put it all together.”
Regardless of how the postseason goes, the Chases know that they’re modeling for the next generation of Baby Eagles.
“ (The current Baby Eagles are) getting ready to be just like these girls and to take over once (the originals) leave,” Krista said. “They’re the gift that keeps on giving.”

title: Man executes dentist over bad work before dying in shootout with police
text:
TUCSON, Ariz. (KOLD/Gray News) - A man wanted in the killing of his dentist in Mexico died in a shootout with police two days later, authorities said.
The attorney general’s office in Nogales, Sonora, said Ernest N., 30, an American citizen, was wanted in the death of dentist Amed de Jesus N., 42, on Oct. 15 in Nogales.
Two days later, Ernest N. died when he confronted officers attempting to arrest him in Agua Prieta, Mexico.
According to authorities, Ernest N. had received dental treatment from the victim and went to the office demanding immediate attention on Oct. 15. Unable to receive treatment at that time, he allegedly waited outside, then stalked the dentist and shot him multiple times.
Police believe the motive stemmed from a complaint about a previous dental procedure.
Authorities said the suspect was quickly identified and an arrest warrant was obtained. He was located at a home in Agua Prieta, where officers conducted a tactical operation.
During the operation, Ernest N. opened fire on officers. Authorities returned fire, killing him. Two members of the Mexican police were injured in the operation.
According to the attorney general’s office, Ernest N. had a U.S. criminal record for drug-related crimes. Mexican police are coordinating with the U.S. consulate on the case.

title: John Merry named interim fire chief
text:
Wiscasset selectmen Oct. 20 made Deputy Fire Chief John Merry interim fire chief and emergency management agency director. Robert Bickford resigned from both offices this fall with plans to stay on the department he has been part of for 38 years.
Town Manager Dennis Simmons’ written report, released ahead of the meeting, said fire department members have decided to wait until June to elect the next chief, and Merry has agreed to both interim posts.
Also Oct. 20, selectmen made Code Enforcement Officer George Chase the 911 addressing officer, another duty Bickford had served. Simmons said Bickford took it on years ago when a CEO at the time asked to not do it. “At that time, the Code Enforcement Officer position was part-time, and the Fire Chief did not maintain regular office hours. This sometimes made it difficult for residents to obtain a 911 address. With the Code Enforcement Officer now maintaining regular office hours four days a week, returning these duties to that office should provide more consistent and timely service,” Simmons wrote.
In other action, selectmen accepted T Buck Construction’s $4,520,812 bid for the pump station improvements project, contingent on some documents’ submission. In a five-minute special town meeting before the board meeting, voters, without debate, agreed to spend up to $345,200 in capital reserve toward a match to an Environmental Protection Agency grant for the work.
In public comment, Superintendent of Schools Dr. Kim Andersson reminded residents they decide the 2026-27 school budget offer Nov. 3. Two other tries lost in June and September. Polls are open from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. Nov. 3 at Wiscasset Community Center.
A hearing on the Nov. 3 ballot drew no questions or comment.
The board named Mary Finn and Dennis Wehrly to the ad hoc wastewater treatment plant outreach advisory committee.

title: Trump administration too lax on guns, gun safety
text:
During my lifetime, driving has become safer and safer.
Seat belts, then lap belts and airbags. Newer cars now have drowsiness detection, blind-spot monitors, lane centering assistance and adaptive cruise control. Roads have rumble strips and streets have raised crossings. The list of safety measures goes on.
It used to be that motor vehicle accidents were the leading cause of traumatic deaths in this country. Today, guns are more lethal than cars. So why is the current administration doing its best to thwart gun safety measures?
Funding for the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives has decreased. Handguns can now be purchased by 18-21-year-olds. Silencers are now easier to acquire; same with large- capacity magazines. Funding for community violence prevention measures and school-based mental health resources have been cut or eliminated. This list goes on and on.  
Keep this in mind on Election Day.
Edward Walworth, MD
Lewiston

title: ‘Not the end of life’: She’s battling early-onset dementia with new tools
text:
ATLANTA, Ga. (InvestigateTV) - Controlling your movements, shaping your personality, storing your memory. The brain is powerful, but as we age those calls don’t communicate the way they used to.
When those changes happen before the age of 65 and a person can’t live or work independently, it can lead doctors to diagnose early-onset dementia.
Andrea Lucas keeps a pill box in her home, surrounded by pictures and memorabilia celebrating her father, Bill Lucas, who was the first Black general manager for the Atlanta Braves.
The 61-year-old never needed medicine before and said she hates pills. But now, Lucas manages multiple medications after being diagnosed with mild cognitive impairment, or early-onset dementia.
In Georgia, Lucas is one of at least 385,000 people reported to have a form of cognitive impairment, according to Georgia Memory Net.
The first signs came three years ago. She would miss little things, or someone would tell her she kept repeating herself. Minor issues grew into major problems.
“I did engineering; I did all these different things,” Lucas said. “I created all these different projects and all of a sudden to feel as if I couldn’t do it as I did it beforehand, that I wasn’t quite as sharp as I was. It was a little devastating.”
The diagnosis feels ironic for Lucas. Her elderly mother still has perfect memory. Her late father had a photographic one.
The diagnosis brought loss. Lucas said she grieved who she was. She took early retirement after noticing she wasn’t quite herself in conversations.
She even lost access to her bank account after employees learned she was impaired. She was required to appoint a power of attorney to handle her funds.
“I was in a place of darkness and depression for a while; to have someone take, in the blink of an eye, everything you’ve worked for throughout your career,” Lucas said.
But life looks different for Lucas now. The turning point came through a six-month program at Emory’s Brain Health Center and its Cognitive Empowerment Program (CEP), which is a research and therapeutic solution focused on five areas for early-onset dementia patients:
- physical activity like yoga and cardio;
- cognitive training to keep the mind busy;
- functional independence like home and personal safety;
- coping; and
- the MIND diet of healthy foods.
Early outcomes show promise, according to Program Director Amy Rodriguez.
“Our outcomes so far are showing when in the time people are with us, within that year or up to a year, their cognition is stable and their functioning is stable or improving,” Rodriguez said.
A state report projected dementia in Georgia would increase 26.7% from 2020 to 2025. With figures like that, Rodriguez and her team argue the program does not have to be unique. They are advocating for more facilities like it across the state.
“That’s exactly what’s needed, access to programs like these is very limited and people need these resources,” Rodriguez said.
For those with access, the impact is clear. “They feel empowered with a sense of hope they didn’t have before, and that it’s a lifeline,” Rodriguez said.
The CEP takes patients if they are referred by their doctor. Emory offers online webinars that replicate what is being done in the program.
“People need a real view and need to understand it’s not the end of life, and there’s a lot of life to be had,” Lucas said.

title: Cooper Flagg scores 32 points, Mavs lose opener to Rockets
text:
HOUSTON — Kevin Durant and Jabari Smith Jr. scored 30 points apiece and the Houston Rockets used a big second quarter to build a huge lead and coast to a 128-110 win over the Dallas Mavericks on Wednesday night in the season opener for both teams.
The Rockets led by six after the first quarter before outscoring Dallas 38-12 in the second to take a 32-point lead into halftime.
Durant and Smith each scored 16 points each in the first half. The Rockets were up by 15 midway through the second before using a 19-2 run to make it 70-38 at halftime.
Kyrie Irving had 15 points for Dallas in his first regular-season game since tearing his left ACL in March 2025. But it was a tough debut for Dallas coach Dusty May, who led Michigan to the NCAA championship before being hired to replace the fired Jason Kidd.
Cooper Flagg of Newport, the 2025 No. 1 pick and last season’s NBA Rookie of the Year, led the Mavericks with 32 points. P.J. Washington had 10 points and four rebounds.
The Mavericks used a 9-0 run, with six points from Marcus Sasser, to cut the lead to 103-86 with about nine minutes remaining. But Houston used an 8-2 spurt with 3s from Durant and Fred VanVleet to push it to 111-88 about a minute later.
Alperen Sengun added 23 points with 10 rebounds for the Rockets. VanVleet chipped in six points with 11 assists in his return after missing last season recovering from a torn ACL.
Houston’s Tari Eason was ejected with about three minutes left in the first quarter after receiving a flagrant foul 2 for shoving Washington to the court.
Up next
Mavericks: Visit Indiana on Friday night.
Rockets: Play San Antonio in Austin, Texas on Friday.

title: Taco Bell makes decision on soft drink provider as sister chain KFC switches to Coca-Cola
text:
(CNN) - KFC may be ditching Pepsi for Coca-Cola, but Taco Bell said it’s sticking with Pepsi.
The fast-food chain announced Thursday it’s extending its partnership with PepsiCo through 2036.
The deal is a big win for PepsiCo.
Not only did the company lose its longstanding contract with KFC to rival Coca-Cola, but it recently reported slumping North American beverage sales.
Taco Bell and PepsiCo plan to develop new drinks and Doritos Locos Tacos flavors.
Those include more options for Mountain Dew Baja Blast, which has become a billion-dollar brand.
Taco Bell said it’s also aiming to generate $5 billion in beverage revenue by 2030.

title: Rep. Ilhan Omar says she will move out of her Washington, DC, home after federal search
text:
(AP) - U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar will move out of her Washington, D.C., home that federal agents searched last week, she said Wednesday, noting that attention brought on by the raid has made her feel unsafe there.
Federal authorities are investigating potential fraud in her family’s immigration paperwork and have issued grand jury subpoenas to some of her relatives, a person briefed on the investigation told The Associated Press on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss an ongoing investigation.
Omar, who was born in Somalia and is a naturalized U.S. citizen, said Wednesday in her first interview since the search that she is “confident in the fact that I didn’t do anything wrong.”
The progressive Minnesota Democrat has been a frequent critic and target of President Donald Trump, who has on multiple occasions pushed for the prosecution of his perceived political enemies.
In the interview with MS NOW, Omar said she was rattled by the search weeks out from the Nov. 3 midterms, which will decide control of the House and Senate. She is running for reelection in a deep blue district centered in Minneapolis and is expected to retain her seat.
Omar recalled waking around 6 a.m. to Homeland Security investigators banging on her door with a warrant. They searched for four or five hours and seized 17 items, including phones, notebooks, a Somali language children’s book and a vintage camera that her husband had received as a gift, she said.
The Justice Department has shared few details about the case other than saying it was a criminal investigation.
Omar came with her family to the U.S. at age 12, after they obtained asylum. She became a U.S. citizen five years later, in 2000.
“It would be a huge undertaking to, I suppose, indict a 12-year-old for so cleverly conspiring to defraud immigration services to come to the United States. I’m sure there are a lot of smart 12-year-olds, but that seems like a leap,” she said in the interview.
The search drew sharp condemnation from congressional Democrats, who also questioned the timing. The Justice Department has historically avoided overt investigative actions involving candidates in the immediate run-up to an election.
Omar said the agents were “intrusive but polite,” logging the items they took and putting back everything else in its place.
___
Associated Press reporter Alanna Durkin Richer contributed from Washington.

title: Residents living and sleeping in fear after cockroach infestation
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Cockroach infestation discovered at Portland Housing Authority apartment building
A cockroach infestation is under investigation at an apartment building run by the Portland Housing Authority.
Residents of Solterra Apartments in Portland's Bayside neighborhood said there has been evidence of cockroaches in the trash room and hallways, as well as inside their apartments.
Allison Decato said she and her neighbors are living and sleeping in fear. She has been waking up to cockroaches running around her apartment since she moved in during the spring.
"I'm sick of it," Decato said.
Last Friday, Decato said she and a city code enforcement officer toured the six-story building on Boyd Street. Decato said she just recently found a cockroach on her bed.
"Enough is enough," she said.
According to a violation order that was delivered to the Portland Housing Authority, code enforcement found a roach infestation throughout the entire building.
"A licensed pest control company needs to be hired for proper mitigation," the violation order states.
The Portland Housing Authority did not respond to our request for comment about what it plans to do about this notice of violation.
"I'm on protective mode now. Like, at night, when I wake up, I put on my flashlight on my cellphone and I'm dodging them when I walk," Decato said. "I have a pair of flip-flops now because I know when they walk on a surface, their little tentacle legs carry that whole list of germs and diseases and parasites and everything you can think of that's bad."
Decato said the Portland Housing Authority needs to be held accountable for not diligently looking into the cleanliness of tenants. She has kept a bag of dead cockroaches as evidence and vows to keep the pressure on until the Portland Housing Authority resolves this issue.

title: Maine heating oil price hits record high at $6.04 per gallon
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
MAINE (WABI) - The average price for heating oil in Maine has hit another record high.
According to the Maine Department of Energy Resources, the average statewide price of a gallon of heating oil as of last Monday is $6.04 per gallon.
That is a $0.07 increase from last week and an 83% increase from this time last year.
The previous record high for heating oil in Maine was set last month at $6.02 per gallon.
Based on a standard 275-gallon oil tank, Mainers are now estimated to pay approximately $750 more to fill their tank than they would have one year ago.
The U.S. Department of Energy said Wednesday it would make 315,000 barrels of heating oil available from the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve in hopes of bringing down prices.

title: Edgecomb Fire Annual Fish Fry Nov. 7
text:
The Edgecomb Fire Department Auxiliary’s annual fish fry will take place at the fire station, at 473 Boothbay Road in Edgecomb, from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. on Saturday, Nov. 7.
The community event features fried fish or fried chicken tenders with all the trimmings and is a meaningful way to honor veterans on Veterans Day.
The fish fry is the biggest fundraiser of the year. All proceeds are used to supplement the department’s budget, which helps reduce the town’s taxes.

title: Quest Diagnostics reports cyber breach affecting ‘certain patient records’
text:
CHICAGO (AP) — Medical laboratory operator Quest Diagnostics said it learned of a cyber breach of one of its systems this week, likely compromising some records for patients.
In a Thursday regulatory filing, Quest Diagnostics reported “unauthorized access” to its Quanum Lab Services Manager, a platform where certain clients can place test orders and receive or look up their results. The company said it discovered the hack on Wednesday and notified federal law enforcement.
How many patients and which particular records have been affected is still unknown. Quest Diagnostics said it believes “certain patient records” were accessed in the breach, but that the full scope remains under investigation.
The New Jersey-based company said it’s also working with external cybersecurity experts to assist in its response.
Cyberattacks are on the rise across industries. Beyond healthcare, other breaches have recently disrupted anything from supermarket chains to core education applications.
Governments and companies worldwide are working more broadly on online security updates. Urgency erupted this week, after an AI-assisted discovery of vulnerabilities in a programming language called PHP, which is vital to 70% of websites globally.
Outages and limited service have continued for many as firms rush to patch those risks. But based on the company’s investigation, Quest Diagnostics confirmed to The Associated Press Thursday that its cyber breach was not related to the PHP issue.

title: Health insurance gaps leave families struggling with costs, survey finds
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — A new survey from GoodRx finds that even people who have health insurance are increasingly underinsured.
More than a quarter of people in the survey said they have at least one gap in their insurance coverage. Nearly half reported drug coverage gaps, and more than a third said dental care isn’t fully covered either.
Divya Iyer, a senior vice president at GoodRx, said health insurance is covering less each year.
“It could also be where you’re on a plan which just has large co-pays or co-insurance amounts. Or the plan may not cover your drug or may have certain drugs that are excluded, or you have additional steps and authorized prior authorizations and additional steps that you need to go through in order to be able to get approved to access the drug,” Iyer said.
Iyer said because of coverage gaps, people will delay care or skip their medications. She said it’s worth comparing prices online, and consumers could also consider whether a subscription service will help offset gaps or high out-of-pocket costs.
“This is an interesting solution that sits alongside your insurance. It’s not meant to replace insurance, it complements your existing insurance coverage, and it makes a ton of sense if they’re filling multiple prescriptions,” Iyer said.
Iyer said GoodRx Companion is one option, and there are several more available through a quick search. These services typically charge a flat monthly or annual fee for direct access to discounted prescriptions and some basic services.
That may make sense for people with multiple generic prescriptions. Consumers have to weigh how much they’ll spend in a year against how much the service might save them.

title: Roger Chase Downs Sr.
text:
Roger Chase Downs Sr., 82, of Whitefield, passed away unexpectedly at his home on Oct. 13, 2026 following ongoing cardiac and lung complications.
He was born on July 1, 1944 in Rochester, N.H., the second son of Pearl E. and Warren E. Downs. Roger grew up in Whitefield and attended the Alamo School, a two-room schoolhouse, from kindergarten through eighth grade. He then graduated from Gardiner High School in 1962, where he enjoyed playing football more than any academic class. It was there he met his wife, Rochelle.
After marrying in 1961, they welcomed their children, Vicki, Roger Jr., and Daniel, over the next three years. After graduating, Roger began working for Dessler’s Meat Market in Gardiner, honing his skills as a meat cutter. From there, he moved on to First National Stores, quickly becoming the regional meat manager. The family moved many times over the years as he climbed the ranks.
In 1970, Roger and Rochelle moved their family to Freeport to open Downs Food Store. Together, they worked tirelessly over many years, making many friends and business acquaintances along the way. Thanks to Roger’s expertise, the store became known for its meat and fish department, also selling goods from local farmers and bakers. If you ever eat a country-style spare rib, you can thank Roger for contributing to its cut and design.
Many years later, customers still remarked that they would only use Downs Foods clams for their clam chowder. In 1982, Roger and Rochelle retired from the grocery business, becoming proprietors of several Freeport properties. This allowed them to move back to Roger’s childhood hometown of Whitefield, where he would pursue his longtime dream of becoming a farmer. They built their dream home on their 126-acre property, a former apple orchard, beginning many years of haying, gardening, and raising livestock.
Over the years, he became a self-taught master of the fields, selling hay to local farmers and Agway for over four decades. He was a skilled gardener, harvesting countless crops of beautiful fruits and vegetables from White Heart Farm over the years, using them in the home-cooked meals, treats, and preserves he and Rochelle enjoyed preparing for family and friends.
Countless memories were made on the farm: harvesting pumpkins for Halloween, picking apples, sleigh rides with the tractor, and many Thanksgiving, Christmas and Easter holidays spent together as a family enjoying each other’s company – and always, delicious food.
Following Rochelle’s passing in 2015, Roger was fortunate to meet his current partner of nearly five years, Mary Ellen Anderson, of Nobleboro, at a cribbage event. She and Roger enjoyed many memories together, including gardening, baking and cooking, and playing many games of cribbage together at home and at the Wiscasset Community Center. Their last cribbage game was played the morning of Roger’s passing.
As Roger’s health began to decline, Mary Ellen was instrumental in his care, allowing him to remain at home and continue to do many of the things he enjoyed. She became his eyes, his ears, his travel companion and confidante, and she became a beloved member of his family.
Roger was a jack of all trades, with many hobbies, passions, and interests, many of which he mastered. He was a skilled outdoorsman who enjoyed deer hunting, and participated in the Maine Moose Hunt three times. He traveled many places to fly fish, including Alaska, Labrador, and Nova Scotia, and wetted a fly in many ponds and lakes throughout Maine.
Another hobby that he learned from his grandfather, Harry Chase, was the art of tapping maple trees. He was known for his famous black maple syrup, which he made by collecting sap and boiling it in the same evaporator used by Gramp Chase. He passed on this tradition to his granddaughters, Carly, Blair, and Grace, by collecting sap with them over many chilly afternoons and educating them on how to boil the perfect batch.
He was a lifelong football fan and remained loyal to the New England Patriots and Boston Red Sox through thick and thin. He was also a licensed pilot for many years, flying his beloved Cessnas throughout northern Maine and Canada.
He was a true tinkerer, maker, and jury-rigger, always repairing broken farm equipment with whatever happened to be lying around. He loved sharing his passions with his family, whether it was explaining the mechanical structure of an engine or the timing of the first rain on a hay crop. He was a lifelong learner, attending mycology classes and business classes through Cornell University. He was a passionate personal financier and follower of the stock market, and read many favorite books over the years (Benjamin Franklin was one of his favorite authors).
He always enjoyed the daily paper every morning over a cup of black coffee with just a bit of milk. He was a voracious cribbage player throughout his entire life, with countless games and laughs over the years. He especially loved playing against his son-in-law, Claude, who became one of his best friends over the past several years.
He was an active community member who cared deeply about giving back to the place he called home. He was a lifetime member of the Freeport Lions Club, served on the Whitefield Planning Board, and was a trustee of the Shin Pond Road Association. He contributed generously over the years to the Whitefield Historical Society, the Whitefield Cemetery Corporation, and the Sheepscot Valley Community Church.
Due to his generosity, many historic sites and areas of Whitefield were maintained and refurbished. He will be remembered for his mischievous sense of humor, his generosity to the community, and his constant hospitality to friends and family.
He is predeceased by his wife, Rochelle Parlin Downs; their sons, Roger Chase Jr. and Daniel Howard Downs; his brothers, James Warren and Harry Leonard Downs; his sister, Sallie Ann Curtis; and their parents, Warren Edward and Pearl Emma Downs.
He is survived by his daughter, Vicki L. Legere and her husband, Joseph, of Falmouth; granddaughter, Blair E. Legere and her partner, Warren M. Blood, of Manhattan, N.Y.; granddaughter, Grace V. Hawkes and her husband, Carter, of Norfolk, Va.; granddaughter, Carly M. Downs and her daughter, Elise Danielle, of Waltham, Mass.; son-in-law, Claude A. Castonguay, of Biddeford; brother, John Haley Downs, of Jefferson; and daughter-in-law, Peggy Flanagan, of Whitefield. He is also survived by countless beloved cousins, nieces, nephews, and friends.
A service will take place at Sheepscot Valley Community Church in Whitefield on Saturday, Nov. 7 at noon. Arrangements and guidance are under the direction of Staples Funeral Home & Cremation Care, at 53 Brunswick Ave. in Gardiner. Condolences, photos, and memories may be shared with the family by visiting the Staples Funeral Home website staplesfuneralhome.com.
In lieu of flowers, donations can be made to the Whitefield Cemetery Corporation, the Whitefield Historical Society or the Whitefield Union Hall in Kings Mills.

title: Attorney Ben Crump, Kohen Wiley’s family addressed media after viewing shooting footage
text:
(Gray News) - Attorney Ben Crump joined the family of Kohen Wiley at a news conference Thursday to address members of the media after viewing footage from the shooting that led to the 1-year-old’s death.
In June, a Senatobia police officer shot into a moving car and killed Kohen.
Action News 5 received the footage from Darkhorse Press two days after Mississippi Attorney General Lynn Fitch’s office determined the officers’ actions that day were justified.
The footage includes five videos: three body-camera videos from Senatobia officers and two surveillance videos from Walmart.
Authorities said two women were accused of shoplifting from a Walmart. They ran away from the store with the toddler and got into a car.
Police and Tate County deputies can be heard yelling “stop” before the car drove toward Officer Hunter Foster. Foster was standing in front of the vehicle and opened fire on the passenger side.
Foster later told another officer he could not see that a baby was inside the car.
It is unclear whether the toddler’s family plans to take any legal action.

title: Sleepover safety: Rite of passage or too big a risk
text:
(Aging Untold) — Parents face a difficult decision when their children are invited to sleepovers, weighing the childhood tradition against safety concerns.
At the McElrath home, Fridays are reserved for family time. After a hectic week of work and school, the family of four enjoys quality time together.
“We started protecting our Fridays. Nothing ever gets scheduled on Fridays,” Chris McElrath, a father of two, said.
The no-sleepover camp
As the McElrath children get older and receive invitations to sleepovers with friends, the parents have made a decision.
“With the exception of a time or two that I can count on one hand, we’re in the no-sleepover camp,” Emily McElrath, a mother of two, said.
The couple said they are not comfortable with their 9-year-old son, who suffers from epilepsy, and their 11-year-old daughter spending the night outside their home.
“Not everybody has the same rules that we have in our household, and that’s OK. I don’t know what their social media policy is. I don’t know if their children have phones or devices,” Emily McElrath said.
She is concerned about what online content might be seen by curious young eyes.
“And just some of the stuff that I’m already seeing kids talk about in her grade. If my child sees it, I don’t necessarily get a do-over. I don’t get to have her un-see it or un-experience it,” Emily McElrath said.
Expert warnings
Kristi McVee, a child safety expert, said sleepovers “can actually be a massive risk for children.”
McVee, a former child abuse detective who has interviewed young victims in Australia, said sleepovers open the door for sexual abuse, and not just at the hands of strangers.
“Sleepovers at cousins’, at grandparents’, at other people’s homes that could be family because for the most part, child sexual abuse is perpetrated by someone known to the child,” McVee said.
According to the CDC, more than 90 percent of child sexual abuse is perpetrated by someone the family knows and trusts.
Balancing safety and experience
“I feel like it’s a hot topic more than it’s ever been a hot topic,” Jessica Saggio, a parenting columnist, said.
Saggio said she does not want to give up on what she believes is right about the sleepover experience.
“You have to be balanced. You can’t just trust anybody. You have to be careful about where your kids go and who they’re with, but also, I’m not a hardline ‘no’ because I want them to experience that side of childhood,” Saggio said.
Her two older daughters, ages 10 and 8, are just starting to attend birthday slumber parties.
“The family was in our neighborhood. We know them quite well, again the mom had everything planned out. There was no wiggle room for shenanigans, if you will,” Saggio said.
Saggio said it was an overall good experience for her daughters.
But experts warn that sometimes sleepovers are an opportunity for children to engage in high-risk behaviors while the adults are not looking.
“It’s actually quite common for sleepover parties today for kids to jump online and go and engage in sexual communications with people. Bullying very much so, whether they get together as a group at the sleepover and bully someone else,” McVee said.
What to consider
Licensed clinical psychologist Dr. Carolyn Ievers-Landis at University Hospitals in Cleveland said there are many things to consider.
“How closely are kids being monitored? How safe is that household?” Ievers-Landis said.
Ievers-Landis recommends focusing on the child’s need for emotional security and comfort.
“Some kids might wet the bed sometimes and they’re embarrassed to go to sleepovers. Some kids might have fears at night or fears of the dark, so they’re afraid to be away from their parent. Some kids might just like to do things the way things are always done and so they’re afraid,” Ievers-Landis said.
Some children may need more time to mature before agreeing to a sleepover.
The late-over alternative
The McElraths opted for what is called a “late-over,” where a child attends the party but leaves sometime before midnight.
“Even if it’s 10:30/11 o’clock, she can stay over and come to the party and hang out with the girls, but we have somewhere to be early the next morning, so I need to come pick her up,” Emily McElrath said.
“Ease into it. Try one of those late overs. Try letting them go until 10, pick them up, then start over the next time and go a little bit later the next time,” Saggio said.
If it is not the right time or a good fit for a child, experts say parents should not force it.
“They don’t have to do a sleepover. You don’t have to do it if you don’t want to do it,” Saggio said.
“Once our kids are in high school, I would be fine with sleepovers I think,” Emily McElrath said.
For now, the McElraths’ no-sleepover policy will stand.
“First and foremost, our job is not to be your friend, it’s to be your parent and keep you safe. That’s kind of how we landed on that decision,” Emily McElrath said.
Safety suggestions
The Child Rescue Coalition offers suggestions for parents who decide their child is ready for a sleepover:
- Make sure you know and trust the adults and that they will be present to supervise.
- Know who else will be there at the same time as your child. Studies show that 40 percent of children are abused by older children.
- Have a pre-sleepover talk with your kids.
- Check in on your child and allow them to call you. Designate a code word your child can say if they feel unsafe, so you will know to pick them up immediately.

title: Maine heating oil prices reach new record high
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The price of heating oil in Maine hit a new record high of $6.04 per gallon this week.
That’s according to a survey by the Maine Department of Energy Resources, which found that the price peaked on Oct. 19, at an 83% increase from a year earlier.
Last week, the average price for a gallon of heating oil stood at $5.97 in Maine, down slightly from last month’s record high of $6.02.
“Based on a standard 275-gallon oil tank, residents are now estimated to pay approximately $750 more to fill their tank to capacity than they would have one year ago, prior to the start of the Iran conflict,” the state agency said on Thursday.
The cost may come down after the Trump administration this week tapped into the Northeast heating oil reserves for only the second time in history.
The U.S. Department of Energy believes the release of roughly 315,000 barrels, or 13.2 million gallons, will “put downward pressure on home heating oil costs and make a real difference for Maine homeowners as they prepare for winter,” said U.S. Sen. Susan Collins, who lobbied with Sen. Angus King for the release of the reserves.
High heating oil prices are especially bad for Maine, which uses more residential heating oil per capita than any other U.S. state. Roughly half of all Maine households use oil as their primary heat source, according to the Department of Energy Resources.
The agency noted that the percentage has dropped since 2010 when 70% relied on oil.
BDN writer Christopher Burns contributed reporting.

title: 'It's a great find': Lost silent film found in Japan comes back home to New Hampshire
text:
'It's a great find': Lost silent film found in Japan comes back home to New Hampshire
A lost silent film, made more than a century ago and rooted in New Hampshire, has turned up in Japan.
One film archivist is bringing the piece of history back to the community and hoping more lost films are still out there.
"Van-ar-chy" was shot in the Sunapee area and made by Billy B. Van, a New Hampshire resident and pioneer in the silent film industry.
"He was helping to define what movies were in the production of these early features that he made," said John Tariot, a film archivist.
"Van-ar-chy" is on the list of lost Van films that Tariot had been trying to track down until a Japanese film student found it while researching a project.
"Somebody, we believe, brought it with them to Japan. And there it sat, unknown, unloved, unfound," Tariot said. "It's a great find. It means the world to me to be able to return this to the residents of the area — give something back to the community."
Van was well known around town, and he could often be seen in the Newport Opera House speaking out during town meetings.
"Folks would actually come to the town meetings just to see Billy B. Van orate," said Dean Stetson, of the Newport Historical Society.
Van was also a farmer and entrepreneur who created products like soap and shampoo, but it's his films that are now giving people a new look at the town's past.
"This particular film, 'Van-ar-chy,' does have a number of scenes that were shot and are still quite familiar in our community," Stetson said.
As Tariot prepares to share "Van-ar-chy" during a special screening next month, the discovery is also encouraging him to keep searching for more lost films.
"So the hunt will continue after this. This is not the end by any means," Teriot said.

title: Susan Collins won’t have the same clout in the next Congress
text:
Perhaps the best argument for returning Sen. Susan Collins to Washington is that it is clearly in Maine’s interest to have its senator chair the panel that decides how to divvy up billions of federal dollars each year.
As her campaign website says, “Susan’s position gives Maine an outsized voice at the table when critical decisions are made which allows her to deliver serious results for Maine,” and refers to the “the powerful Senate Appropriations Committee.”
Whether she wins or loses on Election Day, it’s likely Sen. Collins won’t be at the committee’s helm next year.
Nationally, Democrats are closing in on something few thought possible this election cycle: retaking control of the Senate. They’re virtually certain to control the U.S. House as well.
One of the consequences of having the Democrats in charge of the chamber is that every Senate committee will have a Democrat as its chair. Republicans, including Sen. Collins, will no longer enjoy the power that comes with being in the majority.
According to the Center for Politics at the University of Virginia, Democrats are poised to hold 49 seats with Republicans trailing with 46. Five seats are up in the air. Those seats are said to be in Maine, yes, as well as Iowa, Kansas, Ohio and Texas. Democrats need to win two of those five to take over the Senate while Republicans must win at least four.
Should Sen. Collins lose her seat, the math gets even tougher for the GOP. But let’s suppose she wins.
In that case, for Sen. Collins to remain in charge of appropriations her party would need to win three of the remaining four toss-up races. Possible, yes, but to me it seems unlikely.
For the group of voters trying to decide between Democrat Troy Jackson and Sen. Collins, why should this make any difference?
It matters because the strongest argument for Maine’s five-term incumbent is that she holds that position of rare clout on Capitol Hill. Without it, she surely can’t do as much for Maine.
That reality makes it easier for an undecided voter to choose Jackson. If Jackson wins, it would be a serious blow to President Donald Trump, who needs to recognize that he can’t simply ignore Congress and the laws of our nation.
The way I see it, Sen. Collins has demonstrated repeatedly that she is not up to the unique challenge of holding Trump in check. She knows what he is. She just hasn’t shown the gumption to stand up to him.
Whatever his faults, Jackson is tough and ornery enough to defy Trump and join every effort to block the president’s corrupt foolishness.
The leader of Senate Democrats, New York’s Chuck Schumer, told reporters recently that his party, back in power, would have two goals: to lower costs for Americans and “to clamp down on this horrible corruption and to end the chaos.”
I’m not sure why Sen. Collins and her GOP colleagues have failed to focus on the cost of living or reining in Trump and his erratic decisions. I have no doubt that most of them know it needs to be done. They just don’t have the guts to act.
As a result, they’re likely going to lose the Senate. And without a good reason to be sent back to Washington, Sen. Collins is likely going to lose the election.

title: Closing arguments set in trial of man accused of killing UNC student in 2012
text:
Closing arguments are scheduled for Thursday in the trial of a man accused of killing a North Carolina college student 14 years ago.
Faith Hedgepeth was a 19-year-old sophomore at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill when she was beaten to death in her off-campus apartment in September 2012. Miguel Salguero Olivares was arrested nine years later after being pulled over for driving while intoxicated and providing a DNA sample that prosecutors say matched evidence from the crime scene.
He has pleaded not guilty to first-degree murder, rape and burglary charges.
Testimony began Oct. 7 following eight days of jury selection. Salguero Olivares did not testify and his attorneys rested their case Wednesday without calling any witnesses. Nearly two dozen witnesses testified for the prosecution, including Hedgepeth’s roommate and other friends, crime scene technicians, state and local law enforcement and a DNA expert.
Early testimony focused on Hedgepeth’s life and her last night alive, when she and her roommate returned home from a club around 2 a.m. Karena Rosario testified that she was drunk and sick when Hedgepeth drove them home but later called a friend to pick her up and she went out again, leaving Hedgepeth in the apartment alone. She returned hours later that Sept. 7 to find Hedgepeth’s body.
An autopsy showed Hedgepeth suffered extensive skull fractures and cuts to her face and head, and she was also badly beaten on her arms and legs.
Prosecutors allege that Salguero Olivares, now 33, was a stranger who killed Hedgepeth in a fit of rage. They said his DNA was found on a rum bottle covered in blood that investigators identified as the weapon in the killing, in Hedgepeth’s body and on a note written on a fast-food bag found at the scene.
Erin Ermish, a forensic scientist with the state crime lab, testified that she could never say with 100% certainty that a DNA sample came from a particular person. But she said DNA swabbed from Hedgepeth’s body was 170 septillion times more likely to be a mixture of DNA from Hedgepeth and Salguero Olivares than from Hedgepeth and an unknown individual. One septillion is a 1 followed by 24 zeros.
Ermish also said the mixture of DNA from the top of the rum bottle was 48.6 tredecillion times more likely to be from Hedgepeth and Salguero Olivares than two unknown, unrelated individuals. One tredecillion is a 1 followed by 42 zeros.
In cross-examining witnesses, defense attorneys questioned Rosario’s account of that night, the processing of the crime scene and the reliability of some DNA evidence. They pointed out that police failed to search some areas of the apartment and later lost some possible blood evidence.
Several jurors cried after viewing autopsy photos of Hedgepeth, according to local media accounts. Salguero Olivares, meanwhile, cried when prosecutors played video of a jailhouse call between him and a friend who has since died.
___
The story has been updated to correct the spelling of Faith Hedgepeth’s last name on one reference.
___
Ramer reported from Concord, New Hampshire.

title: 25 years of championing Waterville
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
When Mid-Maine Chamber of Commerce President Kim Lindlof was summoned by Thomas College this past March, she expected to be asked for assistance with a capital campaign.
Thomas is her alma mater, where she graduated in 1991 with a degree in marketing management. When President Jeannine Diddle Uzzi and Vice President of Advancement Erin Merrill invited her to lunch at Front & Main, Lindlof couldn’t anticipate what came next: She would be receiving an honorary Doctor of Humane Letters degree in recognition of her 25 years of service as chamber president and advocacy for Waterville and surrounding towns.
“It was nice to skip the master’s and just go straight to the doctorate,” Lindlof joked. “I figured they were going to hit me up for money, so when they told me that, I was stunned. Just shocked.”
Chamber work
Lindlof marked her 25th anniversary on May 30. When she started, the chamber employed her full time and two others part time. Today, it has five full-time employees and 22 board members.
Lindlof expressed gratitude that the chamber invested in her own career when she first started in her role, allowing her to attend the four-year Institute for Organization Management through the U.S. Chamber of Commerce. The chamber has transformed under her leadership. Once operating without computers, voicemail or employee benefits in rented office space, the organization now owns its headquarters at 50 Elm St. outright.
“We have no debt,” Lindlof said. “Every step we’ve taken here, we’ve saved and paid cash.” That includes a renovation, addition and solar panels. Assets and funds have grown from approximately $54,000 to $1.2 million.
“We try to do everything sustainably and thoughtfully, so that we’re putting our members’ investment to the best and highest use,” she said.
Membership offerings have expanded beyond marketing packages and advertising. Every member now receives a dedicated business web page, particularly valuable to small businesses without their own websites, which Lindlof said is invaluable to smaller businesses that may otherwise lack the resources to have an online presence.
A day in the life
Lindlof starts her day with locally roasted Mbingo Mountain Coffee, decaf because she avoids caffeine. On days involving events or city tours, she may be seen driving a six-passenger golf cart nicknamed “Elm City Ellie” through downtown, occasionally stopping at Bolley’s for a loaded small fry.
Her colleagues know her as a science fiction fan. At her wedding last year, which doubled as a fundraiser for the Mill Island Park Restoration Fund, she walked down the aisle to the “Star Wars” main theme. She admits “Star Trek” is her true favorite, but its theme wasn’t suited to a wedding march.
Her personable, supportive nature and professional accessibility have inspired a bit of a fandom in the business community.
Chamber board member Matt Hunt, co-founder and owner of Great Reach Communications, is in his second year of service. He said he joined the board simply because Lindlof asked. “I have known Kim for 25 years, and I’ve been in business for 30. She has always been extremely helpful, personable, professional. She has guided this organization extremely well.”
“There’s nothing negative I could say about this woman,” Hunt said. “She is incredible.”
Hunt credits Lindlof with helping guide both the chamber and Waterville’s economic development. He will move on to the chamber’s executive board next year, continuing his involvement in the organization she has helped build.
Lindlof credits her longevity to the support and respect of her board and staff. She never really considered a multi-decade career, just that there was always something more that needed to be done.
Beyond regional marketing, she prioritizes education and advocacy, keeping members informed about everything from road closures to business legislation. Events and newsletters help ensure that business owners have access to information affecting their operations.
Since 2014, Lindlof has also served as executive director of the Central Maine Growth Council. She credits its staff and President and CEO Garvan Donegan for successes including partnerships with Colby College and the city that helped bring two-way traffic downtown.
“We are doing an epic number of ribbon cuttings,” she said. “I’ve never seen anything like it.”
In 2025, 34 new businesses opened in Waterville. Lindlof expects that number to grow in 2026.
Despite her involvement in major projects, she considers herself a conduit rather than a ringmaster. Her role, as she sees it, is to connect people and support initiatives that can benefit the community, whether those efforts address an immediate concern or require years of planning.
“I think I have the ability to relate to people where they’re at,” she said. “I can talk to a CEO, and I can talk to a contractor or union person. I have a problem: I like everybody. I know all my chamber members. They’re all my friends.”
Memorable milestones
One of Lindlof’s proudest achievements was helping bring Exit 124 at Trafton Road in Waterville to fruition in July 2017. The $5.3 million project took more than six years to develop and nearly a year to build.
Lindlof championed the Interstate 95 interchange through letters of support and community meetings. The project improved access to Waterville businesses and reduced travel times during peak tourism season through a collaboration involving the Maine Department of Transportation, Trafton Properties, the Economic Development Administration and others.
“I was a supporter of it, and a cheerleader for it,” she said. “That was a huge undertaking, a private-public partnership, the first one in Maine, so it was substantial and significant to our region.”
During the pandemic, water main upgrades and the Ticonic Bridge replacement brought years of roadwork and traffic disruptions. For nearly four years, Lindlof focused on helping small businesses remain viable despite construction that affected access to their storefronts.
Her commitment is rooted in personal history. Born in Waterville, she now lives in Fairfield with her husband, Ted, in the house where her mother grew up, formerly owned by her maternal grandparents.
Lindlof is proud of Waterville’s transformation, including its thriving arts scene and 23 independently owned restaurants within a four-block downtown radius. Now, she wants to bring similar attention to surrounding communities, recognizing that the region’s economic health extends beyond Waterville’s downtown.
“There are empty storefronts in Oakland and in Fairfield, and I would like to see new life breathed into those as well,” she said.
She also hopes to preserve the region’s papermaking industry, including Sappi and Huhtamaki, and advocates for retaining local dams. For Lindlof, supporting new businesses and protecting heritage industries are both essential to the area’s future.
“When we talk about advocacy, we are very keen on retaining the dams. It’s a huge focus, and what I see my next five years working on.”
Lindlof plans to retire in five years, at her 30th anniversary with the chamber. Her service has included numerous community boards, more than 250 Business Breakfasts and more than 250 Business After Hours events.
But her enthusiasm remains undiminished.
“I love our members, and I want to see every single one of them succeed,” she said. “That’s why we get up in the morning, and that’s why we do so many things in different ways.”

title: Sunday may be Mike Rowe’s final race. Is he the best auto racer in Maine history?
text:
It’s a question Mike Rowe has been pondering for nearly a decade. And now, on the heels of his eighth Super Late Model championship at Oxford Plains Speedway, the 76-year-old driver from Turner might be ready to answer it.
When will the Maine racing legend retire?
The PASS 400 at Oxford Plains Speedway on Sunday could be the final race of his career. After winning the track title last month, Rowe seemed to be leaning closer to retirement than in years past.
“My crew keeps saying, ‘One more year,’ but I’m definitely slowing down,” Rowe said. “I love racing the (Pro All Star Series) races, but the longer races, I don’t think I should do. I don’t really know right now. I should retire, this would be a good time to do it. When you get long in age (it’s something to think about).”
Rowe confirmed Tuesday he is still on the fence about retirement. His focus is on the PASS 400, then he’ll take time to make a decision about his career, he said.
“My son and grandson are racing now, my great-grandson is racing now,” Rowe said. “It’s time for me to sit back and watch them. I don’t really have anything to accomplish, I guess, anymore. I’ve done everything I can do. Especially this year. We didn’t have expectations about running all the (PASS) races this year, but we went out on a good note and kept going.”
Rowe’s career is filled with accolades. He won the Oxford 250 time times (1984, 1997 and 2005), has eight Oxford Plains titles (1976, 1978-81, 1989, 1990, 2026), three Beech Ridge Motor Speedway Pro Series championships (2009, 2010, 2013), a Pro Stock title at Wiscasset Speedway (1991) as well as championships for PASS (South champion in 2006, North champion in 2016), the American-Canadian Tour (1994) and the Northeast Pro Stock Association (1999).
Where does Rowe’s career stack against Maine’s best drivers? He stands alone, according to his peers.
“He’s had a hell of a run and he’s been very good,” said Unity’s Ralph Nason. “Ever since I first raced him … He’s right at the top (of the list).”
Nason, 86, would know. Like Rowe, Nason is a three-time Oxford 250 champion, and the only driver to win Maine’s biggest race in three consecutive years (1998-2000). He and Rowe shared an intense rivalry for years.
“You don’t train to get in the car to be second,” Nason said. “He had the same talent and the same amount of drive (as me), that’s why we were as competitive as we were.”
There are Maine stock car drivers with careers that compete with Rowe.
Ralph Cusack has the most series titles at one Maine track. He won 12 championships at Beech Ridge — the Scarborough track that closed in 2021 after 72 years — including seven Class A championships (1953, 1958-59, 1962-65).
Dick Wolstenhulme was another Beech Ridge legend, winning 10 track championships, including three consecutive crowns from 1960-63.
Both Cusack and Wolstenhulme had excellent success at one track, but not across multiple tracks or multiple series like Rowe.
Rowe is the all-time wins leader at Oxford Plains Speedway, with 157 victories, ahead of Jon Lizotte (113) and David Smith (112).
“It’s pretty cool to have that amount of longevity and success,” said Farmingdale driver Johnny Clark, 46, a seven-time PASS North champion and the 2020 Oxford 250 champion, who has been racing against Rowe for nearly 30 years. “What a way to go out (if this is the end). He’s one of the best, that’s for sure. … I don’t think there is anybody that could get as much out of a car.”
Chelsea native Dave Darveau was a dominant racer at Unity Raceway and Wiscasset Speedway, winning 692 races in a 44-year career (1952-1996). He won the Sportsman series championship at Wiscasset three times (1976, 1978, 1984).
Rodney Maynard was an Aroostook County racing legend, collecting over 100 career wins and five track championships at Spud Speedway in Caribou. Maynard’s most famous victory came in an exhibition race in 1983, when he defeated NASCAR champion Bobby Allison.
The most notable name from Maine at the national level remains Newburgh’s Ricky Craven, now owner of the former Speedway 95 in Hermon. Craven, 60, ran 278 races in the NASCAR Cup Series from 1991-2004, with two victories, and a third-place finish at the 1997 Daytona 500, behind Jeff Gordon and Terry Labonte.
Locally, Craven won track championships at Unity and Wiscasset, and captured the Busch North Series title in 1991, a year that included an Oxford 250 win.
A strong run in the Maine racing scene, but not as strong or as long as Rowe.
If Sunday is Rowe’s final race, there’s no argument that a major piece of Maine racing history goes with him.
“He’s got to go down as one of the best, he’s raced the longest,” Clark said. “I’ve raced with so many great racers in Maine over the years, but you don’t know what they could have or would have done, because you only raced them for 15 years and they just didn’t put in the time that Mike did.”

title: Gas tax holidays will be paid for by road users
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
At this point in time, roughly one-third of the states (at the president’s urging) have passed emergency legislation reducing or suspending the taxes they impose on gasoline. This reduces the short-run cost of gasoline borne by the public.
Simultaneously, the president, by executive order, has reduced the federal tax on some diesel fuels for a similar purpose, i.e., reducing the short-run cost of these fuels. When and whether these steps (said to be temporary) will be rescinded is unknown. Tellingly, no supplementary revenue source to maintain the nation’s highway infrastructure has been offered by the president.
What President Trump and now one-third of the states have failed to acknowledge is that gasoline and diesel tax dollars are committed to the building and repair of essential roads and bridges in all 50 states. In most states, these budgets are already underfunded. Shrinking these budgets puts all users of our highway infrastructure at greater risk.
Bear in mind, too, that shrinking highway maintenance budgets does not stop the deterioration of our highway infrastructure that present levels of use give rise to. In short, the president’s tactic is both disingenuous and dangerous. Lives will be lost. He has sent a third of the states on a fool’s errand. One can only hope Maine will not be joining them.
Orlando Delogu
Portland

title: Man sentenced to 80 years for murdering sex offender who assaulted his relative
text:
GOSHEN, Ind. (WNDU) - An Indiana man convicted of shooting and killing a sex offender who assaulted one of his relatives has been sentenced to 80 years in prison.
According to the Elkhart County Prosecutor’s Office, Nicholas Stanley received 65 years for murder and 15 years for a firearm enhancement he admitted to during his trial.
Stanley, 36, was found guilty last month of killing Allen Cogswell, 35, at the Daylite Inn on Cassopolis Street on June 24, 2025.
Cogswell was released from prison in May 2025 and was living at the motel. Court records showed Stanley was a close family member of one of Cogswell’s past victims.
The Goshen News reported that Stanley testified during his trial that he planned to confront Cogswell and beat him up. He said seeing Cogswell through the motel window caused his brain to “explode like a tsunami” and led him to decide to kill him.
Stanley was said to have gone to his car, grabbed a shotgun, knocked on Cogswell’s motel room door before shooting him twice that early morning.
“I decided that I had to do what I had to do to protect my [family]; I had to kill him,” Stanley was quoted as saying under oath.

title: Rep. Ilhan Omar says she will move out of her Washington, DC, home after federal search
text:
Rep. Ilhan Omar says she will move out of her Washington, DC, home after federal search
U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar will move out of her Washington, D.C., home that federal agents searched last week, she said Wednesday, noting that attention brought on by the raid has made her feel unsafe there.
Previous video: Federal agents search Rep. Ilhan Omar's house
Federal authorities are investigating potential fraud in her family's immigration paperwork and have issued grand jury subpoenas to some of her relatives, a person briefed on the investigation told The Associated Press on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss an ongoing investigation.
Omar, who was born in Somalia and is a naturalized U.S. citizen, said Wednesday in her first interview since the search that she is “confident in the fact that I didn’t do anything wrong.”
The progressive Minnesota Democrat has been a frequent critic and target of President Donald Trump, who has on multiple occasions pushed for the prosecution of his perceived political enemies.
In the interview with MS NOW, Omar said she was rattled by the search weeks out from the Nov. 3 midterms, which will decide control of the House and Senate. She is running for reelection in a deep blue district centered in Minneapolis and is expected to retain her seat.
Omar recalled waking around 6 a.m. to Homeland Security investigators banging on her door with a warrant. They searched for four or five hours and seized 17 items, including phones, notebooks, a Somali language children’s book and a vintage camera that her husband had received as a gift, she said.
The Justice Department has shared few details about the case, other than saying it was a criminal investigation.
Omar came with her family to the U.S. at age 12, after they obtained asylum. She became a U.S. citizen five years later, in 2000.
“It would be a huge undertaking to, I suppose, indict a 12-year-old for so cleverly conspiring to defraud immigration services to come to the United States. I'm sure there are a lot of smart 12-year-olds, but that seams like a leap,” she said in the interview.
The search drew sharp condemnation from congressional Democrats, who also questioned the timing. The Justice Department has historically avoided overt investigative actions involving candidates in the immediate run-up to an election.
Omar said the agents were “intrusive but polite,” logging the items they took and putting back everything else in its place.
___
Associated Press reporter Alanna Durkin Richer contributed from Washington.

title: Morning Update: What you need to know in Maine today
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A version of this story first appeared in the Morning Update newsletter. Sign up here to receive the Morning Update and other BDN newsletters directly in your inbox.
Happy Thursday!
The Trump administration has made numerous moves in recent days to address rising energy costs stemming from the president’s war with Iran.
On Tuesday, the U.S. Department of Agriculture began promoting a new $8 billion fund to give one-time payments to fishermen and farmers who have been hard hit by spiking prices for diesel, which in Maine went Wednesday for $6.43 a gallon, up 66% from a year ago.
Then, on Wednesday, the Trump administration tapped the Northeast heating oil reserves for only the second time in their 26-year history. The stockpile was last tapped in 2012 after Hurricane Sandy devastated the Northeast.
That will inject approximately 315,000 barrels, or 13.2 million gallons, into the market.
While public officials like Gov. Janet Mills and U.S. Sens. Susan Collins and Angus King welcomed the move, Mills and King stressed the need for long-term solutions, especially before winter sets in.
Heating oil is going for an average of $5.97 a gallon in Maine, up 80% from a year ago. That means Mainers will spend an additional $731.50 to fill a standard 275-gallon tank.
It’s unclear how this latest move from the administration will affect prices. More than 300,000 households rely on heating oil to stay warm and will consume between 2 and 7 gallons a day. Assuming those households consume 5 gallons a day (1.5 million gallons), the heating oil from the Northeast stockpile would last about nine days.
Of course, Maine isn’t the only state that needs those reserves.
Beyond the conflict with Iran, intensified fighting between Ukraine and Russia and Yemen’s Houthis and Saudi Arabia threaten to further strain global energy supply chains.
Mild temperatures are continuing to stick around, with highs ranging from the low 50s up north to the low 60s down south. Gusty winds move in later today and will stick around into the weekend, along with our dry weather, delaying any relief from the lingering drought.
Simones’ Hot Dog Stand in Lewiston is known for its red snappers and, through some turn of tradition, as a campaign stop for politicians. Accordingly, it’s a good place to take the political temperature ahead of Election Day.
U.S. Sen. Susan Collins dropped by Wednesday, joined by former U.S. Sen. Joe Manchin of West Virginia, who aimed to give her a boost in a heated race with Democrat Troy Jackson.
Protesters with signs depicting Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh’s face picketed and chanted outside the hot dog stand while red-shirted Collins supporters chanted back to drown them out.
As BDN politics writer Benjamin Kail reports, the event brought into focus the anger, enthusiasm and apathy that the tight race may hinge on.

From the Opinion Page

title: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez appeals to Maine women at rally with Troy Jackson
text:
PORTLAND, Maine — U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez urged Maine women to back Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Troy Jackson at a Portland town hall Thursday, arguing health care and families would be best served by ousting Republican Sen. Susan Collins.
The New York Democrat targeted Collins’ vote on the motion to advance the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, though she voted against the final bill. She also cited the senator’s vote to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh before he helped overturn federal abortion rights. Collins voted against final passage of Trump’s spending bill, as she stressed during debates with Jackson.
Ocasio-Cortez said Collins, as one of the few Republican women in the Senate, had been in a unique position “to protect every woman in America,” but failed.
“If we want to be able to deliver our children safely and for our men to protect our families in moments of crises like these, the most important thing we can do for women in Maine is vote for Troy Jackson,” she said to resounding applause.
Jackson is in a toss-up election with Collins that could decide control of the Senate. The visit from one of the country’s top progressives came 12 days before Election Day and two weeks after rallies with Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vermont, that looked aimed at revving up an angry Democratic base.
Hosted by progressive nonprofit More Perfect University, the packed event at the State Theatre was billed as “Students vs. Billionaires.” It hit on Jackson’s core argument that Collins and a Republican-led Congress are beholden to wealthy donors and have failed to check the Trump administration, something the senator has disputed during her campaign.
Jackson pledged to fight for Medicare for All and for research investments to curb Alzheimer’s and cancer, which has been a major priority for Collins. He dismissed arguments that universal health care is too costly, saying his initial priority would be ending “blank checks” for the war in Iran, which has driven up fuel and gas prices nationwide.
“We can make people’s lives even better,” Jackson said. “It’s going to start with research.”
Supporters came from across the state and country, and many described the narrow, increasingly heated Maine race in national terms.
“It’s like we don’t have a Congress,” said Paul Joyce, a New Hampshire resident whose daughter has joined the Jackson campaign. “There’s a real danger of losing our democracy.”
Collins campaigned in Lewiston on Wednesday with former Sen. Joe Manchin, I-West Virginia. Outside Simones’ Hot Dog Stand, Manchin touted their bipartisan work on infrastructure and health care, called Collins “the soul of the Senate” and chastised Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-New York, for targeting the chamber’s leading centrist.
“Troy is spending his time with far-left progressive office holders who either don’t know or don’t care about the difficulties that he has had working with women,” Blake Kernen, a Collins campaign spokesperson, said in a statement nodding to the rural health care fund and reports on his temper in the State House.
Ocasio-Cortez credited Jackson for ignoring Washington consultants who may have urged him not to share a stage with her. She said the ruling class that has long run Congress is trying to protect Collins by painting Jackson as a communist.
“They’ve been afraid of a waitress in the House and a logger in the United States Senate,” she said, referencing her job when she was elected to a New York City seat. “They critique how he looks, how he talks, [but] when you have someone like Troy, it disrupts and makes it harder for everyone to get away with gladhanding.”

To the editor:
What happened at Silver Rail Elementary School is a tragedy. It is thankful that the threat was eliminated before more lives were lost.
However, the individual mentioned by name in the press and thanked by the governor was not the only hero. According to the police report, a teacher, who is unnamed at this writing, threw her cellphone at the assailant and then tackled him. She did not have a gun. She had a cellphone. She certainly, not “almost certainly,” saved lives.
