title: Mom of boy, 8, injured in golf cart hit-and-run on a mission to find driver who hit him
text:
SUMMERVILLE, S.C. (WCSC/Gray News) - An 8-year-old South Carolina boy was riding his bike home from school when he was suddenly hit by a golf cart and left there, injured and alone. Now, his mother says she’s on a mission to find the driver who hit him.
Leo VanOsdol, 8, was riding his bike home from Cane Bay Elementary School last Wednesday on the Cane Bay Trail when he was hit by a golf cart. His mother, Meaghan VanOsdol, was out of town for work at the time of the incident, but she says the woman who hit Leo just kept driving.
The 8-year-old suffered some scrapes and bruises, and his bike was severely damaged with the entire front tire bent. His mother says multiple people drove around him until finally, another woman stopped, helped him and called 911.
“I remember my hands instantly trembling. I couldn’t even grab the phone quickly enough,” VanOsdol said. “Then, as soon as I got off the phone with Leo and knew that he was OK, it was the rush of emotions like anger, disappointment. I felt very lonely in that moment because we’re in this big community, he was surrounded by a ton of adults and he was just left.”
Leo’s mother says he had gotten the bike for his birthday, which was just days before the incident. Since posting on Facebook, she has seen the community rally in support of buying him a new one.
VanOsdol says she is also on a mission to find the woman who hit her son.
“If it was your kid, you wouldn’t want them sitting there,” she said. “Just put yourself in our shoes and know that what you did wasn’t OK. The accident itself, it happens; it’s an accident, but leaving him is just not acceptable.”
Family can’t file charges
Following the incident, VanOsdol is concerned about the lack of protection for kids going to and from school on the trail.
Under state law, golf carts operated on public roads are legally treated like motor vehicles, meaning they can trigger criminal charges and civil liability. However, VanOsdol was told the family couldn’t file charges in this case since Cane Bay Trail is a private trail and a golf cart isn’t considered an automobile.
“It can’t just be something to where this trail goes into the woods unseen and no one monitors it, especially if it’s private,” VanOsdol said. “There’s nothing that can be done if something does happen.”
Now, she’s pushing for more signage and wants the community to be aware of the dangers in the area.
“I think the same way that a school zone is treated on a road, it should be treated on a trail right next to a school,” VanOsdol said. “So, whether it’s speed bumps put in, signs, the trail being monitored in this area, something along those lines.”
Other parents speak out
Melissa Hunt was following behind her kindergartener while she was riding her bike and when she looped around, she stopped by to help. She says this was one of her fears living in the area and has been concerned about golf cart safety for years now.
Hunt says it’s the “wild, wild west” of golf carts.
“They will take the right-of-way when kids are trying to cross the crosswalk, so the kids are going outside of the crosswalk to get across because the golf carts are taking up the space,” she said. “That needs to be something that’s regulated.”
Hunt says another option could possibly be widening the path to give walkers and runners a side and golf carts another, especially with the growth coming to the Cane Bay area.
“Golf carts are great for the environment,” she said. “It cuts down on the traffic around here as well, but with so many golf carts and it being a viable mode of transportation in the area, there needs to be some regulations and laws. I know there’s a few, but I don’t think a lot of people know them.”
Current golf cart regulations
The South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles currently has several registration and equipment requirements, but parents are concerned not everyone is following them.
In Berkeley County, golf carts must be registered and permitted through the SCDMV for a $5 fee, covered by liability insurance and driven by someone at least 16 with a valid license.
Carts are limited to roads with a speed limit of 35 mph or less, within a 4-mile radius of the registered address and during daylight hours unless they are properly equipped with headlights and taillights.

title: Setting the record straight on Troy Jackson
text:
Negative ads on TV and mailings are wasting money and spreading rumors.
Regarding Troy Jackson and allegations of intimidation of women: In an incident between Troy Jackson, at age 19, and Lana, his partner of about 40 years, Lana has strongly said Troy was not violent toward her.
Regarding Jackson’s desire to raise taxes on Social Security, he does, but not for ordinary people. Jackson wants the wealthy to pay their fair share into Social Security. This year, according to U.S. News and World Report, only income up to $184,500 is subject to Social Security payroll taxes. If this cap goes away, like Jackson wants it to, we could save the program for those with less.
About “Oh, shut up.” Jackson said this during the fourth debate in an “Oh, come on,” tone. It did not sound harsh — like Susan Collins’ inappropriate comment about the heckler.
Victoria Adams
Kennebunk

title: Farmington career and tech school selected for more apprenticeship funding
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
FARMINGTON — Foster Career and Technical Education Center is preparing to expand apprenticeship and pre-apprenticeship opportunities across Franklin County after being selected for additional state funding, building on a program that has served 104 young people and established partnerships with eight employers.
The center is awaiting final approval for funding through the Expanding Maine Apprenticeship Program, administered by the Maine Department of Labor. Although an earlier Regional School Unit 9 announcement identified the award as $304,650, Director Galen Dalrymple said the final amount could be closer to $250,000.
“We are not sure of the amount just yet, I believe it will be closer to $250,000 but again I do not have a hard number,” Dalrymple said in an Oct. 16 email.
Jordan McMullen, Foster Tech’s Jobs for Maine’s Graduates apprenticeship navigator, said the center has not received confirmation of the funding amount or payment schedule.
“Unfortunately I cannot provide information about the incoming grant, as we still do not have information from the state about the amount or when we will receive the funds,” McMullen said.
Despite that uncertainty, the center has already begun preparing for the next phase of its apprenticeship program.
Under its original Maine Apprenticeship Program grant, Foster Tech enrolled 27 apprentices and 82 new pre-apprentices. Four apprentices have completed their programs, with another expected to finish within weeks.
The program served 104 young people overall and established eight apprenticeship occupations with eight participating employers.
Those employers include Franklin Savings Bank in Farmington, Sugarloaf Mountain in Carrabassett Valley, Kenway Composites Manufacturing in Augusta, IEC in Strong and Farmington, A1 Plumbing in Farmington, White Wolf Inn in Stratton and The Square Downtown in Wilton. RLH Enterprise in Strong was a previous partner.
The apprenticeships cover occupations ranging from electricians, plumbers and heavy equipment mechanics to bank tellers, line cooks, composite laminators, vehicle maintenance mechanics and golf course maintenance technicians.
Foster Tech has registered three career and technical education programs as pre-apprenticeships: composite manufacturing, bank teller training and culinary arts.
McMullen said the center is already incorporating additional career preparation into its composite manufacturing and culinary programs.
“The JMG Apprenticeship Navigator is working with the Composite Manufacturing and Culinary pre-apprenticeships to provide the GenUS Competency to Credential Framework, where students will be given the opportunity to earn the Job and Career Ready Credential,” McMullen said.
The initiative emphasizes workplace skills that can transfer across industries, rather than preparing students exclusively for one occupation.
“They will be focusing on building their durable skills that can be used in any form of job or career they would like to pursue,” McMullen said.
The center hopes to use the next round of funding to broaden apprenticeship and pre-apprenticeship opportunities in additional industries.
“We are hoping to expand apprenticeship and pre-apprenticeship opportunities within healthcare, education, manufacturing, heavy trades, digital media, and more,” McMullen said.
Dalrymple said the additional award represents another opportunity to build on the center’s existing work. “It is our second award for development of our Apprenticeship Program,” he said. “Our goal is to continue to expand our Apprentice and Pre-Apprentice programs across Franklin County.”
The additional funding is intended to support continued development and expansion over the next two years, although the center is awaiting confirmation of the final award and when the money will become available.

title: Plane crash-lands on highway, shutting traffic down for hours
text:
STOREY COUNTY, Nev. (Gray News) - A plane’s crash-landing onto a Nevada highway blocked traffic for hours as crews worked to clear the scene.
The Nevada Department of Transportation reported the crash around 8 a.m. on Interstate 80 westbound near USA Parkway in Storey County, east of Reno. All westbound lanes were closed for about two and a half hours.
Officials said that no major injuries were reported.
The cause of the crash was not known at the time of publication.

title: How credit card companies profit from your debt — especially if you have bad credit
text:
How credit card companies profit from your debt — especially if you have bad credit
You can be responsible with your credit cards. You can pay your card bills in full each month and never owe a dollar in interest. And for all that effort, your credit card company will still consider you a “deadbeat” — the industry’s term for its least profitable customers.
Credit card companies make most of their money when you stay in debt. People who pay off their balance each month — “transactors,” in industry shorthand — don’t generate much revenue for card issuers. Instead, they count on “revolvers” (cardholders who carry a balance) to keep feeding their bottom line.
Americans owed a collective $1.26 trillion on their credit cards in the second quarter of 2026, which is near the record high of $1.28 trillion set in the fourth quarter of last year, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. These numbers don’t inspire optimism. Credit card debt, after all, is expensive and can be toxic to your financial health. It’s persistent, too: 47% of cardholders report having a credit card balance as of December 2025, and 22% of debtors don’t think they’ll ever pay it off, according to Bankrate’s 2026 Credit Card Debt Report.
For the people carrying those balances, that’s a problem. For the companies that issued the cards, it’s business as usual.
“Credit card companies make a lot of money on people who carry over credit card debt month to month,” says Lauren Saunders, senior attorney at the National Consumer Law Center. “The people’s payments heavily go to interest rather than reducing their principal.”
And the lower a cardholder’s credit score, the easier for the credit card issuer to make money on the debt they carry. Issuers profit from keeping Americans in debt, and consumers like you pay billions in interest and fees. Protect yourself by knowing the facts and avoiding the trap of revolving debt.
Credit card issuers depend on you staying in debt
Credit card companies make money in three ways:
- Interest, or what you’re charged for carrying a balance
- Other card fees, such as late fees, annual fees, cash advance fees, balance transfer fees and others
- Interchange fees, or fees the merchant pays every time a customer uses a credit card for payment
The biggest share of these profits comes from interest. In 2024, consumers paid $160 billion in interest charges, up from $105 billion in 2022, according to CFPB’s Consumer Credit Card Market report. In fact, interest accounts for about 80% of credit card profitability, according to 2022 Federal Reserve research. With other consumer fees making up most of the remaining 20%, it’s safe to say that cardholders who carry a balance drive most credit card revenue — so issuers rely on them and seek them out.
Interest is also a lucrative revenue stream because the issuers keep the rates steep. Currently, the average credit card interest rate is close to 20%, according to Bankrate’s data. For people with bad credit (or a FICO Score below 580), the rate can be even higher, often exceeding 30%. Issuers price their card products with lending risk in mind, ensuring they remain profitable even if more likely-to-default consumers eventually default.
A card interest rate consists of a Prime Rate (currently 7.00%) and a margin set by the issuer, often about 13%. And yet, “you see cards charging 35.99% in any interest rate environment,” says Adam Rust, a financial director at the Consumer Federation of America.
“It’s interesting to see how the margin between the consumer credit rate and the federal funds rate has gone up over time,” he says. “There’s been a consistent widening of that gap… Large issuers generally charge higher interest rates on a risk-adjusted basis, and yet they still get more market share.”
That means that if you expect to carry a balance, you can’t assume that a major bank will give you a competitive rate. You need to shop around and see what smaller issuers offer. For example, federal credit unions currently cap their interest rates at 18%.
Cardholders with lower scores carry a burden
Issuers rely on customers being in debt, and they do little to steer people with low scores away from it. The industry has a significant incentive to extend credit to borrowers who are already stretched too financially thin, rather than steer them away. And issuers purposefully seek out such customers when marketing certain cards.
“The data brokers are providing thousands of granular points of information on consumers,” Rust says. “An issuer doing its homework doesn’t have any trouble identifying which customers are liquidity-constrained and likely to carry a balance. That’s not hard.”
About half of all general-purpose card accounts carried a balance in 2024, according to the CFPB’s 2025 report. That overall rate hides a huge spread by credit tier: In 2024, 83% of cardholders with subprime scores and 88% with deep subprime scores carried a balance.
“It’s natural that people who are struggling more paycheck to paycheck, who have lower credit scores and have had trouble meeting their expenses, turn more to credit cards and have trouble paying them off every month,” Saunders says.
And the reason they turn to cards is usually not what people assume. Among cardholders carrying a balance, 41% said that an emergency or unexpected expense was the primary cause, while another 33% pointed to day-to-day expenses as the biggest cause of their debt, according to Bankrate’s 2026 Credit Card Debt Report. Only 7% carry a balance because of vacations or entertainment.
Carrying that balance costs low-score borrowers more per dollar, too. Cardholders with subprime and deep subprime scores who revolve a balance pay two to four times more in interest and fees than the superprime borrowers, the CFPB found.
To credit card companies, the riskiest borrowers are also the most profitable ones. In fact, prime borrowers are only about half as profitable, according to research published by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York in 2025. Return on assets for subprime borrowers with FICO Scores in the 600s sits at around 11%, then drops sharply and levels off near 5% for prime borrowers above 750.
What it means for you
For every $1,000 in balances, issuers keep about $110 a year from cardholders with scores in the low-to-mid 600s. To compare, they only make about $50 per $1,000 from cardholders with scores above 750. If you carry a balance at a high APR, you’re a lucrative customer for your card issuer — even if you don’t qualify for its lucrative card products.
“Despite a significantly higher charge-off risk, subprime and deep subprime revolvers are some of the best customers for a card issuer,” Rust says. “The returns on revolvers are so much higher even after factoring in all the expenses for operations and rewards, that it’s hard to ignore.”
Issuer profits aside, offering a revolving line of credit to consumers with bad credit is both necessary and exploitative. On the one hand, it allows people who struggle financially access credit without turning to truly predatory options, such as payday or title loans. On the other hand, with how high fees and interest rates are on cards for bad credit, a credit card can easily make a bad situation worse.
“Anybody who has ‘bad credit’ is probably already deep in debt and really shouldn’t be taking on more,” Saunders says.
But while the cardholder is left to pick the lesser evil, the issuer always wins. A credit card company doesn’t need to choose between serving a subprime borrower and profiting from them. It gets to do both.
How credit cards turn into debt traps
While the healthiest credit card habit is paying off the balance in full every month, credit card issuers don’t make it easy.
Saunders explains that the way credit cards are structured doesn’t encourage swift repayment. Minimum payments are very low — often 1% of the balance amount plus any accrued interest. Paying only the minimum can keep you revolving a balance for years and paying interest on interest, until your total interest exceeds what you borrowed in the first place.
“I don’t think people have any idea of how long it would take to repay their credit card debt just making the minimum payments,” Saunders says. “There is a minimum payment warning that is required on statements from the Credit Card Act of 2009, but… unless you’re really looking at that on your paper statement or on the PDF online, which most people probably never [do], you’re not going to see it.”
Then there are the cards designed to be expensive from the start.
“There are some credit cards aimed at subprime consumers that have very high fees,” Saunders says. “Those fees can be monthly fees. Those are fees that really reduce the amount of credit they’re even getting. We call those fee harvester cards that are really just designed to take fees out of people rather than to give them useful forms of credit.”
These offers usually arrive in the mail. To accept, you’re sent to a website that leads with the promise of a credit card, even with bad credit, but buries the terms under easy-to-miss links. If you check the links, you’ll likely find a range of junk fees, including an application fee, monthly fees and fees for “premium design” (which will still be a regular plastic card). These are signs to look elsewhere for a card.
Saunders also warns against potentially predatory credit card types that can get you in a revolving cycle when you don’t expect it. Be wary of deferred interest cards, which advertise 0% or low APR for several months. You’ll often see these at department stores, big-box stores and sometimes in medical and dental offices. No interest sounds like a good deal, but if you don’t repay the balance in full before the promotional period ends, you’ll owe the interest on the entire original balance, retroactive to the day you bought. Those charges can easily total hundreds of dollars.
“It’s a real trap,” Saunders says.
How much it costs to be a revolver
Let’s say you have a $1,000 balance on a card charging 21%. Your budget is stretched thin, so you only make minimum payments (interest + 1% of the balance). It will take you 119 months — almost 10 years! — to get rid of your debt. You’ll also pay $1,125 in total interest charges, more than your original balance.
It seems like a lot. But for many American revolvers, the numbers are even more significant.
In the Fed’s 2022 research, the average light revolver (or someone who revolved a balance for 11 months out of a year or less) spent $637 on their card per month and had a monthly balance of about $1,700, of which almost $1,000 was revolving balance. Light revolvers held about 22% of total revolving balances and comprised a quarter (25%) of all card accounts. They paid around $15 in interest monthly, which makes up about 20% of all interest.
In contrast, the average heavy revolver (or a person who rolled a balance every month of a year) only spent just $206 a month on their credit card. However, their balance was almost $4,500, and they rolled $4,100 month over month. Overall, heavy revolvers held more than half (53%) of total balances and about two-thirds of total revolving balances. They paid more than $60 per month in interest charges on average — and more than 70% of all interest.
Only 1 in 5 credit card accounts (21%) were transactors. However, they accounted for 39% of all credit card purchase volume, with average monthly spending of $826. They also paid almost no interest.
This underscores the dynamic between revolvers and transactors. The people who consistently carry a balance spend the least on purchases and pay the most in interest. The so-called deadbeats spend the most on purchases on average, yet they avoid interest altogether.
And that’s the tension at the center of the credit card business: What’s best for the issuer’s profits is a financial burden for the cardholder. Fewer than half of cardholders in debt (48%) have a plan to pay it off, according to Bankrate’s 2026 Credit Card Debt report. Worse still, almost 1 in 5 debtors (19%) think they might miss a minimum payment at some point in the next six months.
If credit card debt is straining your finances and dragging down your credit score, you’re not alone. But your credit card habits don’t lessen your value as a customer. Quite the contrary: You’re making your issuer more money than someone with a much higher score and a premium card you can’t qualify for.
How to stop being your issuer’s best customer
Your relationship with your credit card issuer is a two-way street. You follow the terms and conditions, pay your bills and spend within your credit limit. In exchange, your issuer offers access to a line of credit and sometimes certain benefits. What you don’t owe them is a monthly contribution to their margin.
Twenty-two percent of cardholders in debt don’t believe they’ll ever get out of it. It’s not easy, but paying off your credit card debt is possible. Pay more than the minimum whenever you can. Attack your highest-rate card first. And move the balance somewhere cheaper if you can qualify — a balance transfer card with a 0% promotional period will generally want a score of at least 670. Whatever approach you pick, the one that works is the one you stick with.
If you feel completely overwhelmed by debt, get help from a nonprofit credit counseling agency, which can set up a debt management plan to pay down your card balances. Be skeptical of any organization that charges upfront fees or promises to settle your debt for pennies on the dollar.
When you clear your balances, you can become a transactor: someone who uses a card for the perks without paying the issuer a dime in interest. If you’re already there, keep using your cards wisely. Your credit card company might call you a “deadbeat,” but that’s exactly what you want to be.
© 2026 Bankrate.com

title: Recreation helps Lewiston find a way forward three years after mass shooting
text:
Recreation helps Lewiston find a way forward three years after mass shooting
Arthur Barnard studies the pool table before taking his turn. He walks around it, considering the angles while thinking ahead before taking his shot.
"My favorite part about pool is the competition," he said.
The game also connects him to his son, Arthur "Artie" Strout. When Strout was growing up, Barnard used the pool table in his kitchen to teach his son the game and bond with him.
"I used to make my son do these drills before I'd play a game of pool with him," Barnard said.
On Oct. 25, 2023, they both decided to play a couple rounds of pool at Schemengees Bar and Grille in Lewiston, Maine.
“We were just having a time like any other,” Barnard said.
After a couple of games, Barnard decided to go home, while his son stayed.
“I wish I had walked around that pool table and hugged him,” he said.
Minutes after he left, Barnard received a call that a shooter was at the bar.
"In my heart, I knew he was gone," he said.
Ten people were killed at the bar, including Strout.
But Schemengees was not the first place the gunman opened fire that night. Minutes earlier, the attack had begun at another Lewiston gathering place.
Earlier in the evening
Just before 7 p.m., the same shooter opened fire at Just-In-Time Recreation, a bowling alley where eight people were killed. That night, youth league matches were happening. Justin Juray, the bowling alley's owner, was also bowling when the attack began.
"Traumatic, life-changing," Juray said. "I had just walked off the approach when the first shot rang out. I looked across and saw him with a gun. Then I saw the muzzle flash."
Juray rushed into action, helping people escape through an emergency exit door.
In total, 18 people died and many more were injured across the two locations.
Following the shootings, a manhunt began and ended days later when the gunman was found dead.
Moving forward through resilience
The Maine Resiliency Center opened 19 days after the shooting. Its director, Danielle Parent, said the center's approach grew from listening to what people in Lewiston needed.
"What I learned really quickly was that people in this community want a community," Parent said.
But Parent said accepting help was difficult at first for some.
"Initially we had a lot of folks who did not seek services and supports because they felt like either they weren't a victim enough or impacted enough, or somebody else might need those services more than they do," Parent said.
The center offered support groups and access to services, but it also organized game nights, potlucks, art activities and recreation.
Those gatherings often became a way for people to get the help they needed, Parent said.
“We do game nights and we have potlucks and we do arts and we recreate,” she said. “And then what it really turns into is it turns into kind of an impromptu support group. It turns into folks supporting each other, getting access to the clinicians and the advocates and the support folks from the center who intermingle in those environments and are able to provide support in those contexts.”
It became apparent that shared activities gave people a way to be together, find support and practice returning to places they may have stopped visiting.
Back to the places that brought them together
After the shooting, Juray wasn't sure the bowling alley could reopen.
“I didn't know what to expect,” Juray said. “It was scary to consider reopening and knowing that I was afraid to come back in.”
But six months later, the bowling alley welcomed the community back.
Some people returned quickly; others needed more time. Juray said he's seen people come back even a year or two later, as soon as they felt ready.
The return of young bowlers mattered to him, too. Juray said young people who had been there that night came back and invited their friends. He said that's part of the community’s resilience.
“This community made this happen,” Juray said. “We had youth here that night, and our youth program is the largest in the state. That's resiliency.”
Going back to recreation has brought other groups together, too.
At Schemengees, members of a cornhole team for deaf people were hosting an evening of games. Juray said the bowling alley now gives the local cornhole community a more stable place to play, after years without a regular home.
"Bringing those two worlds together,” he said, “to me, that's the definition of resiliency.”
Parent echoed that sentiment, saying these spaces are what people have needed, letting them show up knowing that whatever state they're in, the community will support them.
"We see more need for emotional well-being and support. We see need for feeling heard and feeling known, for being seen."
The way forward
Barnard still plays pool, the game that connected him to his son. He has also become an advocate for gun safety laws in Strout’s memory.
“The only thing I'm asking is that we find a way to make people responsible for the guns that they own,” he said.
When Barnard remembers his last night with his son, he returns to the time they shared at the pool hall.
“I got to spend two and a half hours with him just before he died. And he was happy,” Barnard said.
An ongoing recovery process
Parent said it's easy to forget about a community after a mass violence event, but among those affected after a tragedy, the dynamic can be difficult to navigate.
"It's something that the people learn to build a life around, and learn to fill their lives with positive things and to reengage in their communities. It's always going to be a part of the lives of those who are impacted," Parent said. "I think that having community around them and the people in their lives that acknowledge that, and who don't try to dismiss that experience, has been a challenge."
Parent went on to say that the divide has grown bigger between the people who can live day-to-day and not think about what happened on Oct. 25, and those that can't not think about it. Those who lost someone, those who were injured and those who were at either of the locations don't have a choice in thinking about it.
Parent said people also forget that the impact of events like this one can have a ripple effect. She expressed that everyone can experience trauma, from first responders, interpreters (like those who responded to be present for every press conference and funeral) and funeral home directors to cleaning crews and others. Sometimes, the need for support can go unnoticed for those not directly impacted in a tragedy.
The main lesson we've learned from Lewiston is that the approach to recovery is different for everyone. People can approach their trauma from different angles, but as long as they keep moving forward together, the community grows stronger.
"It takes time for folks to feel safe again ... for people to be able to reengage in the life that they lived prior," Parent said.

title: Bobby Charles is set to talk with critics next week. You can be one of them.
text:
Republican gubernatorial candidate Bobby Charles said Thursday that he is inviting voters, especially “people who do not support” him, to sit down with him at an event in Auburn next week and ask him anything.
The 66-year-old Leeds lawyer said the format of the Oct. 29 event at the Androscoggin County Republican Committee’s headquarters in the Auburn Mall is “simple”: Charles will sit at a table, a voter will sit across from him and the two will talk, with the voter welcomed to ask “tough questions” or “challenge his positions.”
“I’m inviting people who disagree with me to sit across from me and ask anything,” Charles said in a statement. “You can tell me I’m wrong. To my face.”
It is a move by the Republican to project openness in the closing stretch of a gubernatorial contest to succeed Gov. Janet Mills that former Maine House Speaker Hannah Pingree, a Democrat, is expected to win.
Pingree, a 50-year-old North Haven resident who helmed Mills’ policy office and is the daughter of U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree, has consistently held a double-digit lead in the polls over Charles, who previously worked in drug enforcement and domestic policy roles under former Presidents George W. Bush, George H.W. Bush and Ronald Reagan. Independent Rick Bennett, a 63-year-old former Maine Republican Party chair and state senator, has been well behind those two in polls.
A news release from the Charles campaign said he “especially welcomes people who do not support him” to the Auburn Mall event that will go from 5-7 p.m. and is free, with no registration required. Charles is holding “as many one-on-one conversations as time allows,” the release said.
He specifically invited “Hannah Pingree supporters, Kamala Harris voters, Gen Z liberals, frustrated Democrats, undecided independents and Somali immigrants.”
Charles rose quickly to the top of a crowded Republican primary field in June in part by pitching himself as an outsider who supports many of President Donald Trump’s policies. But in the general election, he has noticeably attempted to back away from Trump and some of his positions while portraying himself as a more independent-minded figure.
His rhetoric has at times drawn both Democratic and Republican rebukes during the primary and general portions of the race. Last year, for example, Charles referred to state Rep. Deqa Dhalac, a South Portland Democrat who immigrated to the U.S. from Somalia more than three decades ago, as a “radical Somalia-first” lawmaker, drawing criticism.
Charles invited voters to visit an optional registration page for next Thursday’s event at secure.winred.com/bobby-charles-for-maine/disagree-event.
“If you think I’m wrong about something, tell me. If you’re skeptical of my plans, challenge me,” Charles said. “If there’s an issue you think I’m overlooking, let’s talk about it.”

title: Health insurance gaps leave families struggling with costs, survey finds
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — A new survey from GoodRx finds that even people who have health insurance are increasingly underinsured.
More than a quarter of people in the survey said they have at least one gap in their insurance coverage. Nearly half reported drug coverage gaps, and more than a third said dental care isn’t fully covered either.
Divya Iyer, a senior vice president at GoodRx, said health insurance is covering less each year.
“It could also be where you’re on a plan which just has large co-pays or co-insurance amounts. Or the plan may not cover your drug or may have certain drugs that are excluded, or you have additional steps and authorized prior authorizations and additional steps that you need to go through in order to be able to get approved to access the drug,” Iyer said.
Iyer said because of coverage gaps, people will delay care or skip their medications. She said it’s worth comparing prices online, and consumers could also consider whether a subscription service will help offset gaps or high out-of-pocket costs.
“This is an interesting solution that sits alongside your insurance. It’s not meant to replace insurance, it complements your existing insurance coverage, and it makes a ton of sense if they’re filling multiple prescriptions,” Iyer said.
Iyer said GoodRx Companion is one option, and there are several more available through a quick search. These services typically charge a flat monthly or annual fee for direct access to discounted prescriptions and some basic services.
That may make sense for people with multiple generic prescriptions. Consumers have to weigh how much they’ll spend in a year against how much the service might save them.

title: Aging Untold: What caregivers can do when dementia makes meals difficult
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we explore how dementia can make eating challenging for your loved one and offer practical strategies to help at mealtime.
We discuss mental health support in later life and examine how moving past the stigma of therapy can promote healing at any age.
Finally, we visit a lively coastal ukulele band in South Carolina, spreading joy, friendship and tropical tunes throughout their community.
Eating can become more difficult for someone with dementia as the disease progresses.
It can disrupt the part of the brain that controls hunger, thirst and appetite signaling, Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said.
And the process of getting food to the mouth is complex, requiring motor skills and sensory response.
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said families can make meals easier by serving finger foods and being flexible.
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke added that caregivers should stay open to sudden changes in taste as well.
The idea of therapy can carry a stigma for some older adults.
Cradduck said many older adults were raised in a time when mental health was not discussed. It was often “hidden underneath the rug.”
O’Rourke said she does not use the word “therapy,” choosing to use other words instead.
She will say education or recommend taking a class or buying a book to introduce the older adult to the idea that talking might be helpful.
A parent’s decision about whether children should attend sleepovers can come down to weighing the childhood tradition against safety concerns.
Ukes by the Sea is bringing tropical vibes to the East Coast.
The ukulele group performs in South Carolina’s Grand Strand, where it is strumming its way into the hearts of listeners.

title: Boys Soccer Playoffs: County Matchups and a Big Bracket Twist
text:
Aroostook County Boys Soccer Teams Head Into 2026 Playoffs With Plenty of Local Storylines [VIDEO]
The boys' high school soccer playoffs are almost here, and there's plenty to talk about as our local teams get ready for their tournament runs.
Madawaska has earned the top seed in Class D North, Presque Isle has secured a preliminary-round bye in Class B, and Fort Kent is preparing to host a Class C quarterfinal.
Meanwhile, the eight-player tournament has a particularly interesting possibility, with Wisdom and Katahdin potentially meeting in the quarterfinals if the Cougars can get through their preliminary game.
Add in Caribou, Central Aroostook, Fort Fairfield, Hodgdon, Easton, Washburn, Van Buren and Houlton, and there's no shortage of County soccer to follow.
The eight-player preliminary round begins Friday, October 23, with the Class B preliminary games following Saturday, October 24.
Regional quarterfinals are scheduled for October 27 and 28.
Here's a look at the boys' tournament picture.
The 2026 MPA Soccer Championships on 101.9 The Rock are proudly presented by Pineland Farms in Mars Hill.
Class B North: Presque Isle Earns Home Quarterfinal, Caribou Opens in Preliminaries
The Presque Isle Wildcats finished 8-5-1 and earned the fourth seed in Class B North.
That gives Presque Isle a bye through the preliminary round and a home quarterfinal against the winner of fifth-seeded Erskine Academy and twelfth-seeded Skowhegan.
The Wildcats had some memorable moments during the regular season, including an impressive comeback victory over Foxcroft Academy.
Trailing by two goals, Presque Isle battled back to pick up a 3-2 victory in one of the more exciting finishes of the fall.
The Wildcats also swept their regular-season meetings against Caribou and Fort Kent.
Presque Isle's five losses came against John Bapst, Orono and Foxcroft Academy, all teams that have shown they can compete at a high level.
With the fourth seed, the Wildcats have an opportunity to begin their tournament at home and build on what they've accomplished this season.
Caribou Faces Medomak Valley in Preliminary Round
The Caribou Vikings finished 4-8-2, earning the eighth seed and a preliminary matchup with ninth-seeded Medomak Valley, which finished 6-8.
The teams did not meet during the regular season.
Caribou's victories included two wins over Fort Kent and two against Hermon. The Vikings also earned ties against Foxcroft Academy and Brewer.
If Caribou can advance through the preliminary round, the Vikings would face top-seeded John Bapst, which finished 13-0-1.
John Bapst defeated Caribou twice during the regular season, so the Vikings know the level of competition waiting in the quarterfinals.
First, though, they'll need to get past Medomak Valley.
Class C North: Fort Kent Earns Fourth Seed
Fort Kent finished 7-6-1, earning the third seed in Class C North and a home quarterfinal against sixth-seed Washington Academy.
The Raiders finished with a 6-6-2 record.
The Warriors have faced some challenging competition throughout the fall, including games against Presque Isle, Caribou, Orono and Madawaska.
Fort Kent recorded two victories over Madawaska, which finished as the top seed in Class D North, and also earned a tie against top-seeded Class C Orono.
The Warriors split their two meetings with George Stevens Academy/Deer Isle-Stonington and swept Washington Academy.
The Warriors have shown they can be competitive against strong opponents, and they'll be looking to carry that experience into the postseason.
Class D North: Madawaska Leads a Field Filled With County Teams
If you're looking for a bracket with plenty of local interest, Class D North has it.
Seven of the eight teams in the current tournament field are from Aroostook County, with several familiar opponents meeting again in the postseason.
And at the top of the standings are the Madawaska Owls.
No. 1 Madawaska vs. No. 8 MSSM
Madawaska finished 12-2, earning the top seed in Class D North.
The Owls' only two losses came against Class C Fort Kent, and they swept the rest of their regular-season opponents.
Madawaska finished its regular season with a 6-1 victory over Washburn on Senior Night.
Josh Querze scored twice, while Aiden Gagnon, Oliver Pelkey, Bradley Kennedy and Ashton Guerrette each added a goal.
The Owls will begin the tournament against eighth-seeded Maine School of Science and Mathematics from Limestone, which was 1-7-2 in the supplied standings.
Madawaska defeated MSSM during the regular season.
With the top seed and an impressive regular-season record, the Owls have given themselves a great opportunity to make a run through the Northern Maine tournament.
No. 2 Central Aroostook vs. No. 7 Penobscot Valley
Central Aroostook has also enjoyed an outstanding fall, finishing 11-3 and earning the second seed.
The Panthers are lined up against seventh-seeded Penobscot Valley, which enters with a 5-8 record in the supplied standings.
Central Aroostook's only three losses came against Madawaska twice and Fort Fairfield once.
The Panthers also defeated Fort Fairfield in their other meeting, giving them a split against the Tigers.
Central Aroostook picked up victories over Easton and Washburn during the regular season and has been one of the more consistent teams in the classification.
The Panthers did not face Penobscot Valley this fall, so they'll be preparing for a new opponent when the quarterfinals begin.
No. 3 Fort Fairfield vs. No. 6 Washburn
Fort Fairfield finished 6-6-2, earning the third seed in Class D North.
The Tigers are matched up against sixth-seeded Washburn, which was 3-8-2 in the supplied standings.
These teams split their regular-season meetings, with each picking up a victory.
Fort Fairfield also recorded an important win over second-seeded Central Aroostook, along with a victory over Hodgdon.
Washburn, meanwhile, picked up victories over both Hodgdon and Fort Fairfield, showing that the Beavers can compete with teams seeded above them.
With the season series tied at one game apiece, a third meeting in the quarterfinals should be worth watching.
No. 4 Hodgdon vs. No. 5 Easton
Hodgdon has also put together a strong season, sitting at 9-3-1 in the supplied standings and earning the fourth seed.
The Shires are lined up against fifth-seeded Easton, which finished 8-6.
Hodgdon defeated Easton in both regular-season meetings, and the Shires also recorded victories over Penobscot Valley.
Easton had some impressive moments as well, including two victories over Fort Fairfield.
While Hodgdon had the advantage in the first two meetings against Easton, the Bears will have another chance to change that story when the playoffs begin.
It should be an interesting matchup between two County schools that know each other well.
Eight-Player North: Wisdom Moves to Third, Potential Katahdin Rematch Ahead
The eight-player boys' tournament has one of the more intriguing possibilities for County soccer fans.
Wisdom is entering the postseason as the number three seed, while Katahdin is sixth after finishing with twelve victories.
If both teams advance to the quarterfinals, they'll meet for a third time this season.
But there's plenty of soccer to be played before that can happen.
No. 3 Wisdom Awaits Katahdin or Lee Academy
The Wisdom Pioneers finished 11-3 and earned the third seed in eight-player North.
Wisdom receives a preliminary-round bye and will host the winner of sixth-seeded Katahdin and eleventh-seeded Lee Academy.
The Pioneers have had plenty of success against other tournament teams this season, including two wins over Van Buren and two over Penquis Valley.
Wisdom also split its regular-season meetings with Katahdin.
That creates an interesting possibility for the quarterfinals.
If Katahdin advances past Lee Academy, the Pioneers and Cougars will meet for a third time, with a regional semifinal berth at stake.
No. 6 Katahdin vs. No. 11 Lee Academy
Katahdin finished 12-2, one of the best records among the local boys' soccer teams.
Despite that record, the Cougars enter the eight-player tournament as the sixth seed, based on the Heal point standings.
They'll open against eleventh-seeded Lee Academy, which finished 5-7-2.
Katahdin's only two losses came against Wisdom and Van Buren.
The Cougars also earned victories over both teams in their other meetings, giving them a split against each.
Katahdin did not face Lee Academy during the regular season.
Should the Cougars advance, they'll travel to face third-seeded Wisdom in what could be one of the more interesting County matchups of the tournament.
No. 7 Van Buren vs. No. 10 Schenck-Stearns
The Van Buren Crusaders finished 7-6-1, earning the seventh seed.
Their preliminary-round opponent is tenth-seeded Schenck-Stearns, which finished 7-7.
Van Buren defeated Schenck twice during the regular season and will be looking for a third win against the Wolverines.
The Crusaders also recorded a victory over Katahdin and played Mattanawcook Academy to a tie.
The winner will move on to face the second seed in the quarterfinals.
No. 9 Houlton/GHCA vs. No. 8 Penquis Valley
The Houlton/Greater Houlton Christian Academy Shiretowners finished 4-8-2, earning the ninth seed.
Houlton will travel to eighth-seeded Penquis Valley, which finished 7-7.
These teams did not meet during the regular season.
The Shiretowners picked up two victories over Schenck-Stearns during the fall, along with wins against Ashland and Van Buren.
The winner of the preliminary game will advance to face top-seeded Mattanawcook Academy.
Houlton has already faced Mattanawcook twice this season, with the Lynx winning both meetings.
Tournament Championships Coming to Presque Isle
The postseason begins with eight-player preliminary games Friday, October 23, followed by the Class B preliminaries Saturday, October 24.
Quarterfinals are scheduled for October 27 and 28, with regional semifinals October 30 and 31.
The regional championships follow November 3 and 4, and the state championships are scheduled for Saturday, November 7.
Two major championship games will take place right here in Aroostook County.
Presque Isle Middle School will host the Class D North regional championship on November 4 and the eight-player state championship on November 7.
With so many County teams involved, there's plenty of opportunity for some local schools to advance into the later rounds.
I'll have the finalized brackets, results, updates and more photos as the tournament gets underway.
Good luck to all our local boys' teams as they begin their playoff runs!

title: 'Ghostbusters' creator reveals great-grandfather was a real-life paranormal investigator
text:
'Ghostbusters' star reveals great-grandfather was a real-life ghostbuster
Bustin' may feel good for Ray Parker Jr., but for Dan Aykroyd, it runs in the family.
Aykroyd, one of the creators and stars of "Ghostbusters," has shared on his social media pages that his great-grandfather, Dr. Samuel Augustus Aykroyd, was also something of a paranormal investigator.
Related video above: Haunting retro find explores if ghosts are real
"These are my great-grandfather Dr. Sam Aykroyd's transcripts from the Seances he hosted in the Old Farmhouse," Aykroyd posted on Instagram, along with a series of images showing bound books of handwritten notes.
The books, titled "The Journals of a Kingston Spiritualist, Volume II" and "Sitting for Materialization," chronicle Sam Aykroyd's experiences hosting séances in the Aykroyd family's ancestral home outside of Kingston, Ontario. The journals date back to 1921 and feature pages supposedly containing quotes from the spirits.
Dan Aykroyd has referred to the home in the past as the "old haunted farmhouse."
In the book "A History of Ghosts: The True Story of Séances, Mediums, Ghosts, and Ghostbusters," by Sam Aykroyd's grandson, Peter Aykroyd, the younger Aykroyd says Dr. Aykroyd invited a medium named Walter Ashurst to be his houseguest in 1921. According to the book, Ashurst stayed in the Old Farmhouse for 12 years.
This is not the first time in recent months that Aykroyd has discussed his ancestor's activities. In an appearance on "The Tom Green Farmcast" in June, Aykroyd credited the family history with playing a big role in the creation of "Ghostbusters."
"My grandfather, Sam, was a dentist in Kingston," Aykroyd said. "And he was a spiritualist paranormal researcher. And so he wrote journals and articles related to everything that was going on — apparitions, levitations. And so that's why I wrote the movie; I was steeped in that as a kid."
Aykroyd has referred to his family's paranormal interests as a key source of inspiration for writing "Ghostbusters," which went on to become one of the most influential horror comedies of all time.
"It was the spirit of his work passed down through the generations that inspired my interests," Aykroyd said. "He's the original Ghostbuster."

title: Cumberland’s Victoria Bossong gains fame in Philippines for running success
text:
More than 8,000 miles from where she was born and raised, Victoria Bossong has celebrity status.
The Cumberland native can hardly walk down the street in the Philippines without being recognized. People will look closely, making sure it’s really her. Some will want photos, or maybe even autographs. When she visited the country two weeks ago, she needed a private escort.
“They gave me a little security team at the airport to make sure I made it everywhere safe,” Bossong said. “It’s fun to have that kind of lifestyle. When I go over there, I’m always recognized. I feel the love from people in the Philippines so much, and that keeps me very motivated.”
There’s a reason Bossong, 23, gets superstar treatment on the other side of the world. Representing the Philippines, the 2021 Cheverus High graduate took bronze in the 800 meters at the recent Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, becoming the first Filipina to medal in track and field at the competition in 32 years.
At Cheverus, Bossong was a Maine high school track all-time great. She holds Class A outdoor championship meet records in the 100 (11.73 seconds), 400 (55.08) and 800 (2:10.66), as well as the Class A indoor record in the 400 (56.95). She was Gatorade Girls Track and Field Athlete of the Year in 2019-20 and 2020-21.
Even after she graduated from Cheverus and began competing for the women’s team at Harvard, Bossong didn’t envision a professional career. But during her senior year, when she placed second in the NCAA women’s 800, the neuroscience major changed her mind.
“I was all ready to go straight to med school, but I was able to be so consistent in my progression as an athlete, and it opened a new door,” Bossong said. “I think that’s part of how I’ve been able to be successful, saying ‘yes’ to new things, whether it’s new training techniques or going professional and delaying my academic progression.”
Bossong, who is half-Filipino by way of her mother, became an official citizen of the Philippines in April. On July 1, she changed her sporting nationality from the United States. Having beaten the Asian Games qualifying standard of 2:05.21 multiple times, she was assured a spot in Japan.
Bossong had her sights on gold. The women’s 800 record at the Asian Games, set by Kazakhstan’s Margarita Mukasheva in 2014, stood at 1:59.02, a time Bossong had beaten over the summer. She posted the top time of 2:02.34 in the Sept. 28 qualifiers, but in the finals the following day, her time of 2:05.34 lost out to Wu Hongjiao of China (2:04.49) and Nelly Korir of Bahrain (2:05.16).
“One thing I’ve learned is that you can prepare all you want, but what happens on the day, you can’t fully prepare for it,” Bossong said. “It was just a tactical race, and I haven’t run a race like that in my entire life. Now, just having more experience, if a race went out that slow again in the future, I would make different moves.”
Still, Bossong she knew what the medal meant to the Philippines. Not since Elma Muros took bronze in the 1994 long jump had a Filipina woman won a track and field medal at the Asian Games. It wasn’t her only notable performance in Nagoya, as she also competed on a mixed 1,600 relay team that set a national team record in 3:19.68.
Returning to the Philippines, Bossong received hero status — “EVERY ASIAN MOM’S DREAM DAUGHTER,” read one headline that referenced her medal and Harvard degree. Every media outlet in the country wanted to speak with the bronze medalist, including GMA and ABS-CBN, the nation’s two largest TV news networks. Allure and Cosmo’s Philippine editions also presented her with brand opportunities.
“I would probably have three to four hours of sleep every night, and then it was interviews, interviews and all these collaborations,” Bossong said. “It was a very sleep-deprived week, but I knew I had to make the most out of my time there. … I knew the Philippines was a very supportive country, but being able to witness that firsthand has just been so special, and it’s why I do it.”
Bossong said competing for the Philippines and spending time in the country has allowed her to get more in touch with her Filipino roots. Her platform, she said, has helped her to serve as an inspiration to other Asian athletes, something she lamented not having in the sport as a young girl.
Bossong lives in Cambridge, Massachusetts, where she continues to train at Harvard’s facilities. She still has plenty of ties to Maine, with her family still residing in her childhood home in Cumberland Foreside. It’s a challenge, she said, to get from New England to the Philippines, which can take 24 hours (not counting a 12-hour time difference).
Next on Bossong’s agenda? Los Angeles 2028. Competing for the Philippines at the Olympic Games in her native country would be a dream come true, not to mention that greater Los Angeles is home to more than 500,000 Filipinos — one of the largest Filipino diasporas.
“It would be really special because it’s ‘home turf’ on both ends (in that sense),” Bossong said. “I just hope I’m able, first of all, to make it there, but also to represent the country very proudly and show the world what the Philippines can achieve on the international scale.”

title: LePage casts ballot, calls election ‘most important for decades to come’
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) - Former Gov. Paul LePage went to the polls Thursday and urged Mainers to do the same.
The Second Congressional District Republican candidate and former governor spoke with the press after casting an absentee ballot at Augusta City Hall.

title: Maine’s older residents are ‘aging into crisis’
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
This is the second story in the series Stretched Thin: The cost of getting by in Maine, which looks at the financial hardships Mainers face. Social services reporter Gillian Graham reported this story as a USC Annenberg Center for Health Journalism 2026 National Fellow and a participant in the Center’s engagement initiative.
BOOTHBAY PENINSULA — By the end of each month, Linda Walls has only pennies left.
Nearly half of her $1,100 monthly income pays for the room she rents from a friend. Food, medical costs and bills quickly eat up the rest.
It was one unexpected health crisis that caused her financial stability to unravel. She said she was homeless for a short time and, living only on Supplemental Security Income, has spent years rebuilding her life.
Walls, 71, said she was comfortable — then had nothing.
She’s not alone.
Older Mainers are struggling to keep up with rising costs, access transportation to get to appointments and maintain aging homes on fixed incomes. New data shows that about half of households in the state headed by people 65 and older struggle to afford basic expenses. Those challenges are especially acute in rural areas, according to experts.
“When there’s high inflation and costs go up, they’re kind of stuck,” said Lindsay MacDonald of Spectrum Generations, central Maine’s area agency on aging. “If they can’t work, what else can they do?”
According to data from 2024 released in June by the United Ways of Maine, 52% of older households live below the federal poverty level or are part of a population called ALICE — Asset Limited, Income Constrained, Employed. At that income level, people don’t always qualify for assistance but often struggle to pay for basic needs and are not able to set aside money for emergencies.
Nearly a quarter of the state’s residents are 65 or older, according to U.S. Census data. Projections by the Office of the State Economist show that group is expected to grow in Maine over 11% between next year and 2032.
As people live longer, even those with savings are finding they don’t have enough, said Jess Maurer, executive director of the Maine Council on Aging. About a third of older Mainers have no savings and rely solely on Social Security, she said.
Maurer said the stories she hears are haunting: Older Mainers cutting up and burning furniture for heat. Retirees skipping meals and visits to the doctor because, without transportation, there’s no way to leave home. People isolated and alone, using chamber pots and going without showers because they aren’t mobile enough to get to their bathrooms.
“People are aging into crisis,” she said.
HEATING HOMES AS OIL COSTS RISE
Tourists and seasonal residents flock to the Boothbay peninsula in the summer.
The scenic point of land juts out into the Gulf of Maine between the Sheepscot and Damariscotta rivers. Small boats tender cruise ship passengers to shore, where they flood shops and restaurants. Visitors show up by the thousands to wander through the Coastal Maine Botanical Gardens.
And on a dirt lot behind the Boothbay Public Works garage, the Woodchucks have been busy thinking about winter.
Twice a week year-round, the volunteers behind the region’s wood bank split, chop and stack firewood to bring to people on the peninsula who need help heating their homes. Most of the Woodchucks are retired and have spent years growing the operation into one of the larger wood banks in Maine.
“We’re old men with chainsaws,” volunteer Tom Churchill quipped during a break from chopping in July. “What can go wrong?”
The wood bank, which operates on a lot rented from the town for $1 a year, has become a lifeline for residents who struggle to keep up with heating costs in a region where many people live in older homes.
It will be even more critical this winter, said Holly Stover, director of the nonprofit Community Resource Council, which oversees the Woodchucks program. In late September, as oil prices shot up and state officials urged people to apply for heating assistance as soon as possible, Stover said she had heard from people terrified of what winter will bring.
“I think this year the panic is going to set in,” Stover said.
The Woodchucks delivered 100 cords of wood last year and said they anticipate requests for help will be even higher this season. The CRC also stocks its 24-hour food pantry with emergency bundles of wood — they usually disappear within hours — and runs a local fuel fund that pays for heating oil.
About half of all homes in Maine rely on oil as a primary heat source, making it the most heating oil-dependent state in the country, according to the Natural Resources Council of Maine. In late September, heating oil in the state reached a record $6.02 per gallon. The governor’s office estimates it will cost $740 more to fill a standard 275-gallon tank this winter than it did last year.
In early October, Gov. Janet Mills sent a letter to Maine’s Congressional delegation saying current federal funding for the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program is insufficient to meet the increased need. She wrote some residents will be forced to choose between staying warm and putting food on the table this winter.
David Cornforth, who runs Spectrum Generation’s Ramping Up Repairs program, sees firsthand the challenge facing older residents of Lincoln County and surrounding counties, as they try to heat and maintain their homes with limited money.
The program, which started two years ago, funds critical home repairs for qualifying low-income residents. It is not the only program of its kind in Maine — a similar one operates on a small scale on the Boothbay peninsula — but experts say there is not enough help considering the age of the state’s housing stock.
The first Ramping Up Repairs project was to replace multiple broken windows in an old farmhouse owned by a couple in their 60s with health problems. Cornforth said the windows were fixed just before winter set in.
“They called in the spring and said it was a godsend,” he said. “They said they didn’t know what the winter would have looked like for them.”
POVERTY UNSEEN
When people think of coastal Maine, they’re unlikely to associate it with poverty. In the Midcoast, it’s not uncommon to see high-priced homes near the water selling to out-of-state buyers looking for a summer getaway. But even in the wealthiest communities, there are people facing financial hardship.
“The pockets of poverty are unseen,” Stover, from the Community Resource Council, said. “You don’t see the people living in the woods or in rundown trailers.”
According to 2024 data released this summer, 47% of households in Boothbay and 46% of those in Boothbay Harbor are below the ALICE threshold. Lincoln County, with a median age of 51.4, is among the oldest counties in Maine, which has the highest median age in the country at 44.9, according to Census data.
While money pumps into the region during summer, there are still families barely getting by throughout the year.
“Those who have two or three homes come in to enjoy Vacationland,” said Nicole Evans, executive director of the United Way of Mid Coast Maine. “Their dollars disappear in the dead of winter.”
People who need assistance on the peninsula often turn to the Community Resource Council. In addition to firewood and heating oil assistance, the CRC arranges rides to medical appointments, helps people sign up for assistance programs, and provides food.
Last November, when there were fears that Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program payments would be delayed because of a government shutdown, CRC bought $250 grocery store gift cards for 283 families.
A few years ago, the CRC opened a community fridge behind Boothbay’s town office that is accessible all the time. Stover said a survey of local residents showed people who work different shifts had a hard time making it to food pantries during the day. Others, she said, prefer to stop in for food without the pressure of being seen or talking to people.
The community fridge is a small building with a freezer, refrigerator and shelves for bread and dry goods. Produce comes from local stores, farms and gardeners, and restaurants sometimes stock it with prepared meals.
“You can fall behind once and not go hungry,” said the Rev. Todd Weir, president of the CRC board. “Or you could fall behind every month and not go hungry.”
‘IT’S REALLY TOUGH’
On a crisp Tuesday in early October, Walls stood behind the counter of the small thrift store at the Edgecomb Community Church, chatting happily with the other volunteers and customers browsing the shop.
After several years of hardship, she’s found a supportive community in this historic white church perched on a grassy hill.
Walls spent most of her adult life in southern York County, where she said she raised six children and worked in local stores and pharmacies. She never had enough to set aside money for retirement, but lived comfortably.
Then she got sick.
Four years ago, Walls was living in Limerick when she woke up with stomach pain so bad she ended up in the hospital, where doctors told her she had a perforated colon. Her recovery was a difficult one with multiple setbacks.
Unable to work or pay rent after she was released from the hospital, she said she had no choice but to leave her home. She gave her cat to her granddaughter and put all of her belongings in the trash or on the curb for free because she couldn’t afford to store them. She said she left with three shirts, two pairs of pants and a pair of shoes.
Walls said she was scared to go to a shelter and spent four nights sleeping on the ground in a cemetery in Scarborough before her son found out and brought her home to his apartment.
A caseworker helped her navigate resources and sign up for Medicaid. Walls said she got a job and eventually a new apartment, but is now unable to work because of her health issues.
A couple years ago, Walls said, she moved into a friend’s trailer in Wiscasset. She pays $500 in rent and helps around the house, but he covers most of the utilities.
She said she can’t afford to live on her own.
“If you’re alone and in your 70s, it’s really tough,” she said.
According to the U.S. Census Bureau, 9.5% of Mainers 65 and older are living in poverty.
Women over 75, who typically earned less during their careers and had to take time off for caregiving, live in poverty at twice the rate of men, according to the Maine Council on Aging.
Maurer, from the Council on Aging, said Social Security “masks poverty” because people receive just enough to not qualify for assistance programs. That is the case for Walls, who said she makes too much for SNAP to help pay for food.
In October, the Social Security Administration projected the annual cost-of-living adjustment for older adults and people with disabilities will go up by 3.6% beginning in 2027. That translates to $75 extra per month for recipients, but some don’t think it will be enough to offset soaring prices, according to an AARP survey.
Without government assistance, many people turn to a patchwork of local agencies. But Maurer said others may fall through the cracks because they won’t ask for help or don’t know where to find it.
“People in their 80s and 90s, they’re not going to say, ‘I don’t have enough money for food.’ They’re just not going to eat,” she said. “They’re going to keep their house at 50 degrees. They’re going to take their meds once a day instead of twice a day.”
ONE PROBLEM AWAY FROM CRISIS
On Tuesday mornings, two rooms at the Community Center in Boothbay Harbor are crowded with tables of older women playing mahjong. The clickity-clack of their tiles is nearly drowned out by the conversations about book clubs, grocery prices and grandchildren.
The center, in a nondescript strip mall, started after the local hospital closed and people were concerned about the impact on seniors in the community.
The center combats social isolation and improves people’s quality of life, but has also become a place residents can turn to for help with transportation and medical supplies, said office manager Jane Carpenter.
Down the hall from the rooms where people gather to knit and play games is the medical equipment closet. The brightly lit room is lined with walkers, wheelchairs, shower chairs and canes. Shelves are crammed with incontinence supplies, braces and blood pressure cuffs.
All of it is free to take for anyone who needs it. Carpenter said the program used to serve just the immediate area, but now caseworkers from elsewhere in the county know they can call if they need to find supplies for someone.
Sometimes people seem hesitant to take what they need, but Carpenter said the no-questions-asked policy aims to reduce the stigma.
“People are very proud in this area,” she said. “They don’t want to admit they need help.”
Transportation is one of the biggest issues in Lincoln County, which has multiple peninsulas, said Katie MacDonald, director of Healthy Lincoln County, an organization that aims to improve health outcomes through food security and substance use prevention programs.
“There are some places in Maine where you really can’t get there from here,” she said. “You can see it across the bay, but it’s 45 minutes up and around to get there.”
Healthy Lincoln County is trying to meet the needs of low-income residents, including those who can’t get to stores or food pantries, through its Community Routes program. Each month, the program delivers groceries, clothing, hygiene products and other items to people in 10 towns across the county.
Community Routes coordinator Samantha Mehlhorn said delivering these items directly to people has been “huge” for them.
“We have some great resources in our area — there are a number of food pantries — but that doesn’t mean there’s going to be one they can get to,” she said.
On the Boothbay peninsula, both the Community Center and CRC recruit volunteers to bring older residents without cars to medical appointments and to run errands, but it’s not always easy. Most of the appointments, according to organizers, are in Portland, Brunswick or Damariscotta, a distance that’s harder to get volunteers to cover as gas prices go up.
At the CRC, many of the volunteers who used to drive have aged and now need drivers themselves, Stover said.
“Transportation is a real concern for us. We don’t seem to have a good town or county generated alternative,” said Carpenter, from the Community Center. “We scramble every day to see who can drive.”
In recent years, Maine’s Area Agencies on Aging and others who work with older residents have lobbied the Legislature to support the Older Mainers Act to put more money toward various services, including transportation, meal programs, caregiver support and wellness initiatives.
Legislation introduced in the last session would have allocated $9.75 million toward those programs. At the time the bill was presented, more than 700 people were on waitlists to receive Meals on Wheels.
In 2025, the Legislature approved $3 million in one-time funding from the general fund to support the programs and services provided by the Area Agencies on Aging. But the leaders of those agencies say more support is needed as the number of older residents increases.
Gerard Queally, president and CEO of Spectrum Generations, said the services provided by Area Agencies on Aging prevent social isolation, help people navigate benefits, and are cost-effective alternatives to frequent emergency department visits, long hospitalizations and early placement in nursing homes.
Despite committee support, the Older Mainers Act died on adjournment in April without being funded. Advocates say they will continue to push for more funding to support Maine’s aging population.
Sharon Foerster, who was vice president of the Maine Council on Aging Board of Directors, said in written testimony last year in support of the bill that people wait to ask for help until they really need it.
“Far too many older Mainers,” she testified, “are ‘one away’ — one health problem away, one unexpected expense away, one home system failure away, or one loss away from crisis.”

title: Oregon school attack survivor says she had no chance to protect children at Silver Rail Elementary
text:
‘The shooter was already there’: Oregon teacher recalls Bend school attack
A teacher wounded in last week's attack on a special education classroom at an Oregon elementary school says she never had a chance to try to shelter any of the children inside.
In a statement issued by a family friend, Becky Drury said Wednesday that she ran to see what was going on when she realized something was happening — but immediately saw the shooter and rushed back to the classroom.
Related video above: Safety experts weigh in on additional measures schools could take to prevent or delay a shooter from gaining entry
“I turned to shut the door behind me, but the shooter was already there,” Drury said. “Before I could do anything more, he shot me at close range and I fell to the ground.”
Her left hand was nearly severed by a gunshot, and her right arm was struck as well. Unable to get up or defend herself or others, she said, “I did the only thing I could do, which was to pretend to be dead in the hope he would not shoot me again.”
Three children — ages 5, 8 and 11 — and a teacher were killed at Silver Rail Elementary in Bend, Oregon, last Thursday when a former student there, 16-year-old Griffin J. John II, blasted his way through locked doors with a shotgun and attacked the classroom. Another student was critically injured.
Authorities said another teacher threw her phone at the gunman and then tackled him and wrestled with him for control of the weapon, likely saving lives before the gunman was shot by a father who followed him into the building.
Some news reports had suggested that Drury threw herself on top of one student to protect her. Drury, who remains hospitalized, said she wanted to correct the record.
“Accurate, respectful reporting is a truly important service that will help heal the wounds inflicted by that awful day,” she said.
School reopened in the district Wednesday for the first time since the shooting. Dozens of officers were on hand at each school to welcome children back, the Bend Police Department said.
In a social media post, the department said it continues investigating the attack, including serving search warrants at the attacker's home, as well as on his electronic devices and his social media accounts on a variety of platforms.
The statement said police have confirmed that the pump-action shotgun used in the attack had been legally purchased. The Associated Press previously reported it had been purchased by the suspect's mother, according to a law enforcement source who was not authorized to discuss the investigation. But investigators said they were still looking into how the boy obtained it.

title: Man executes dentist over bad work before dying in shootout with police
text:
TUCSON, Ariz. (KOLD/Gray News) - A man wanted in the killing of his dentist in Mexico died in a shootout with police two days later, authorities said.
The attorney general’s office in Nogales, Sonora, said Ernest N., 30, an American citizen, was wanted in the death of dentist Amed de Jesus N., 42, on Oct. 15 in Nogales.
Two days later, Ernest N. died when he confronted officers attempting to arrest him in Agua Prieta, Mexico.
According to authorities, Ernest N. had received dental treatment from the victim and went to the office demanding immediate attention on Oct. 15. Unable to receive treatment at that time, he allegedly waited outside, then stalked the dentist and shot him multiple times.
Police believe the motive stemmed from a complaint about a previous dental procedure.
Authorities said the suspect was quickly identified and an arrest warrant was obtained. He was located at a home in Agua Prieta, where officers conducted a tactical operation.
During the operation, Ernest N. opened fire on officers. Authorities returned fire, killing him. Two members of the Mexican police were injured in the operation.
According to the attorney general’s office, Ernest N. had a U.S. criminal record for drug-related crimes. Mexican police are coordinating with the U.S. consulate on the case.

title: Wrong turn leads stranger to rescue family of 14 from house fire
text:
LYERLY, Ga. (WRCB) - A wrong turn may have saved 14 lives in northwest Georgia after a man driving home to Alabama spotted a house on fire and rushed inside to warn the family.
James Burke fell asleep in his recliner Saturday night while his wife, 11 children and one grandchild slept in their beds. He woke up to a man standing in his living room.
“The next thing I know, some guy was telling me in my living room, ‘Hey, you’ve got to get out of here. Your house is on fire,’” James Burke said.
The man, identified as Mr. Casey, was driving home to Alabama with his son. A wrong turn sent them down Highway 114 south of Lyerly.
“He was on the wrong road. His GPS put him on the wrong path. He’s never been down that road before. And he said that he knew that something kept bringing him down our road. When he saw the fire from the top of the hill, he knew he had to take action,” James Burke said.
Rescue from the home
James Burke said Casey helped pull all 12 children from the burning home and helped get firefighters to the scene.
“If it had been another five minutes, it would’ve been a different situation. We wouldn’t have made it,” Larita Burke said.
Community response
After the shock wore off Sunday morning, the Burkes said they were met with kindness from strangers, this time in their own community.
“It’s overwhelming how much, immediately, people called to ask, ‘Hey, what do you need? What can we do?’” James and Larita Burke said. “It has been a wonderful feeling. There are so many wonderful people in this community that have reached out. I didn’t realize this county was as wonderful as it was until something like this happened.”
Family looks ahead
The Burkes said the loss of their belongings is fresh in their memories and hard for the younger children to understand.
“They keep asking. My little three-year-old keeps asking, ‘Daddy, when do we go home?’ I said, ‘Soon,’” James Burke said.
“They see the burnt house, but we remind them that it’s still our house. It just needs to be fixed,” Larita Burke said.
The Burkes said they are focusing on the future.
“We are traumatized, of course, but you know what? We’re gonna turn this page, and we’re gonna get on with our lives because we have so much to live for. All of our babies made it out,” James Burke said.
The Burkes said they have fostered more than 500 children over the past 15 years. They said they hope to continue fostering once their home is rebuilt.
The cause of the fire remains under investigation.
