title: Rep. Ilhan Omar says she will move out of her Washington, DC, home after federal search
text:
(AP) - U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar will move out of her Washington, D.C., home that federal agents searched last week, she said Wednesday, noting that attention brought on by the raid has made her feel unsafe there.
Federal authorities are investigating potential fraud in her family’s immigration paperwork and have issued grand jury subpoenas to some of her relatives, a person briefed on the investigation told The Associated Press on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss an ongoing investigation.
Omar, who was born in Somalia and is a naturalized U.S. citizen, said Wednesday in her first interview since the search that she is “confident in the fact that I didn’t do anything wrong.”
The progressive Minnesota Democrat has been a frequent critic and target of President Donald Trump, who has on multiple occasions pushed for the prosecution of his perceived political enemies.
In the interview with MS NOW, Omar said she was rattled by the search weeks out from the Nov. 3 midterms, which will decide control of the House and Senate. She is running for reelection in a deep blue district centered in Minneapolis and is expected to retain her seat.
Omar recalled waking around 6 a.m. to Homeland Security investigators banging on her door with a warrant. They searched for four or five hours and seized 17 items, including phones, notebooks, a Somali language children’s book and a vintage camera that her husband had received as a gift, she said.
The Justice Department has shared few details about the case other than saying it was a criminal investigation.
Omar came with her family to the U.S. at age 12, after they obtained asylum. She became a U.S. citizen five years later, in 2000.
“It would be a huge undertaking to, I suppose, indict a 12-year-old for so cleverly conspiring to defraud immigration services to come to the United States. I’m sure there are a lot of smart 12-year-olds, but that seems like a leap,” she said in the interview.
The search drew sharp condemnation from congressional Democrats, who also questioned the timing. The Justice Department has historically avoided overt investigative actions involving candidates in the immediate run-up to an election.
Omar said the agents were “intrusive but polite,” logging the items they took and putting back everything else in its place.
___
Associated Press reporter Alanna Durkin Richer contributed from Washington.

title: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
text:
(Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep.
Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.”
The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening.
Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.”
The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before next weekend’s time change.

title: UMaine faculty senate wants more say in upcoming budget amid shortfall
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Amid a $19 million shortfall, the University of Maine faculty senate is requesting more involvement in the university’s upcoming budget decisions.
In a resolution recently adopted in a 46-2-2 vote, faculty senate members asked for UMaine administrators to have more consultation with the senate about next year’s budget, any future budgets and academic impacts of proposed layoffs and reduced costs.
UMaine’s budget shortfall has ignited responses from the university’s faculty senate and union members across the University of Maine System. While the university announced plans to close the budget shortfall to $3 million Wednesday, faculty members are asking for more transparency and involvement in a budget process that will require layoffs and cutting costs.
The requests in the resolution, which echoes concerns the faculty senate expressed in April, are not new, but the budget crisis has put a time crunch on when faculty members and administrators can come together before the budget is presented to the University of Maine System Board of Trustees, Faculty Senate President Brian McGill said.
“We can have shared governance or we cannot have shared governance around this budget crisis and we’re past the point of talking about what does it mean and how do we do it and we’re into the point of let’s just do it,” McGill said.
UMaine administrators responded to the resolution Wednesday, McGill said. According to McGill, the response didn’t guarantee more conversations would occur and documents administrators pointed to in it don’t answer faculty’s questions.
“It was pretty disappointing. It was pretty confrontational and petty,” McGill said.
Information on how retrenchments fit into strategic reenvisioning was shared, McGill said. Other questions weren’t answered, but the response did say administrators want to have conversations to better understand what faculty want to know, McGill said.
Faculty’s questions have already been laid out and are specific, he said. The response shows the university is “slow walking” discussions that are on a short timeline, McGill said.
“[This response] is not stepping up to show leadership in a budget crisis. We have a massive crisis happening and serious leadership is needed,” McGill said.
In recent years, there’s been little to no information about the budget shared with faculty before the board of trustees reviews it in January, McGill said. When the board of trustees approves the budget, it’s shown as a total of roughly 25 line items with little to no supporting information, McGill said.
With layoffs and retrenchment being proposed, faculty want more budget information before January to understand what cuts are coming and how they will affect academics, McGill said. Although job cuts will affect faculty members most directly, the resolution also asks for information about future enrollment projects, priorities in future years and how the university got into a budget shortfall.
“These questions are really fundamental questions about the future of the university that everybody should be asking and paying attention to,” McGill said.
In a September letter announcing the $19 million shortfall, President Joan Ferrini-Mundy and Provost Gabriel Paquette said the university would seek input from faculty members and stakeholders as outlined in UMaine’s shared governance policy, which was adopted in 2009 and states that faculty members have an advisory role in the budget process. At a town hall meeting earlier this month, Ferrini-Mundy said more budget information would be shared when it’s available.
Administrators are still seeking input and “believe that transparency, trust and meaningful consultation, communication and collaboration between the administration and our employees are essential to most effectively serving our students and the state, and to the long-term strength and success of Maine’s flagship public university,” University of Maine System Spokesperson Samantha Warren said.
“The university’s budget challenges are real and require difficult decisions, as well as constructive engagement focused on solutions,” Warren said.
Following the resolution vote, the faculty senate sent 36 questions on the upcoming budget to UMaine administrators. The questions are based on conversations faculty members have had, McGill said.
Although the questions were sent to administrators with a 15-business day deadline that has come and gone, they have not been answered, McGill said. A response is usually expected within 30 days but an expedited answer was requested due to the crisis, McGill said.
With just over two months before UMaine’s budget is sent to the board of trustees, where it could be amended — but in recent years has not been — faculty want the opportunity to hear responses and give feedback while it could be impactful, McGill said.
“I know changes can still happen, but I don’t think the faculty feel like they’re going to be part of that conversation to any significant degree, after it goes [to the Board of Trustees] in January,” McGill said.

title: The Grand's 'Into the Woods' enchants
text:
ELLSWORTH — Once again, The Grand has assembled a superb cast of singers and actors to perform its annual fall musical with a production crew and pit orchestra to match.
This year, it’s one of my favorites, Stephen Sondheim’s “Into the Woods,” which I must have seen a dozen times in many forms — high school, show choir and even on Broadway — but this story about dreams coming true and what happens after “happily ever after” never fails to amuse and move me.
And this production is especially enchanting from the moment the Narrator (the always excellent Benjamin Carter) steps on stage and starts relating the fairytale stories of Cinderella, Jack and the Beanstalk, Little Red Riding Hood, and The Baker and his Wife; the conductor Sky Kust strikes up his small but mighty orchestra; the lights come up on Joe Lewis’ gorgeous set and, ABRACADABRA, like magic, we are all plunged deep into the woods on an adventure that will make us laugh, cry and at times, question our own life choices.
It begins with Cinderella, as ever scrubbing the floors, wishing she could go to the ball, (well, in this instance, festival) while her horrid stepsisters and stepmother taunt her.
We last saw Jess Immel as the spunky aspiring Jo March, just a few months ago in The Grand’s spring show “Little Women.” Well, she is just as wonderful here as the sweet girl who does make it to the festival but finds herself overwhelmed by it all. Immel’s lovely soprano couldn’t be better suited to the role and Sondheim’s challenging music. As her stepmother, Jessica Smith is delightfully dreadful and Amelia Ashmore and Tori Smith as Cinderella’s stepsiblings, Florinda and Lucinda, are hilariously horrible.
It should be noted here for parents who plan to bring their youngsters to see this, Sondheim has borrowed largely from the Grimm versions of these tales, which can at times — especially in the second act — be pretty, uh, grim, with some blindings, bludgeonings, smushings and munchings.
A couple of toddlers, who were perhaps too young for this fare, could be heard wailing during last Sunday’s matinee. Like it says in the play, “children will listen.”
We can blame their distress on young Jack (an excellent Matt LeVasseur) who trades his beloved Milky White cow (beautifully puppeteered by Amanda Cole) for five magic beans, which, of course, turn into a huge beanstalk that Jack uses to reach and pillage the home of Mr. and Mrs. Giant.
The sturm und drang that ensues when the giants come seeking revenge is pretty darn scary. The other “delinquent” youngster in this show is Red Riding Hood, played to bratty perfection by the well-named Moxie Breairty.
As Red heads off into the woods to bring Granny a basket of treats, she not only eats most of them on the way, she strays from the path and encounters a wolf (an appropriately sleazy Chris Madigan) who charms her into telling where Granny lives. We all know how that turns out.
Small note here: what happens at Granny’s house, unfortunately stays largely in Granny’s house as the shadow puppetry scrim walls are a little too opaque to see anything but blurs.
Now we come to the heart of this show, The Baker and his wife, a couple cursed with childlessness by a grudge-bearing witch. Mike Smith as The Baker, who for some reason reminds me more and more of John Malkovich (if that fine actor had a fabulous singing voice), plays this role with so many layers of emotion one can’t help but fall a little in love with him.
But Ruby M. MacGregor as his fierce wife is the true ringer in this show. This woman sings, acts, moves and commands the stage like a pro, and, it turns out, she is one. She has performed on stage in her native North Carolina in musicals, operas, cabarets, nightclubs, you name it. And her experience, timing and extraordinary talent is apparent in everything she does here. I just hope we can keep this southerner around after she experiences her first Maine winter.
Another astounding performance is delivered by Leslie Michaud as the grudge-bearing witch who sets all these magical wheels spinning over the theft of some garden greens by The Baker’s father. It is wonderful to see Michaud, who more often is tasked with directing these musicals, back in the spotlight. Her witch is both hateful and heart-wrenching when we learn the only joy in her life is derived from her garden (I get that!) and keeping her daughter Rapunzel (a wonderfully fey gone-to-mad Seneca Maddocks-Wilbur) close, as in locked-in-a-tower close.
Enter the princes charming. As Cinderella’s Prince, Andy Phinney, who has recently played a crustacean and Huck Finn’s drunken, abusive dad, once again demonstrates his chameleon superpowers by looking like the cover of a romance novel here with his flowing blond locks. Zachary Field as Rapunzel’s secret lover gets to show what a truly fine voice he has when not disguising it for a comic character such as Lord Farquad in “Shrek.” These two swanning about with their capes and swords singing their duet “Agony” are to die for.
Actually, every one of these lead characters have their diva moments in this show and take full advantage of them. When they team up in duets, trios, quartets and full choruses, well, it is simply stunning.
Oh dear, I am running out of time and space here, but have to give a shout-out to Di Klausmeyer for her small but spot-on performance as Jack’s beleaguered mom; Dan Mills as the riddling Mysterious Man; the great bird puppeteers who transform from Cinderella’s sweet, little seed-sorting friends to bloodthirsty predators; and Sky Kust’s fabulous orchestra, which I don’t believe hit a wrong note the entire show; Melissa Egolf’s wonderfully fanciful costumes, which also hit all the right notes and Stephanie Bradshaw’s lively and complex direction.
But about that set. Joe Lewis was not only tasked with creating an enchanted forest and a credible bakery for the first act, he also had to engineer its destruction which he manages very effectively. The only things that don’t quite work are the aforementioned Granny’s shadow house and the beanstalk illusion that can’t be seen from the theater’s left section and a couple of flats representing Cinderella’s and Jack’s houses that look unfinished. I would suggest scrapping those, as in this form they only detract from the magic he has created elsewhere. (Oh, that mother tree! Rapunzel’s tower — wow!)
With a few first weekend miscues, Jeff Ferrell’s lighting design and Neil Graham’s sound engineering helped create the magic, fun and the horror for this truly outstanding show.

title: Medicare Advantage plans will be discontinued next year for more than 49K Mainers
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
More than 49,000 Mainers have Medicare Advantage plans that will be discontinued next year, according to the state Bureau of Insurance. And while new ones will be offered, consumers are scrambling to sort it all out.
Open enrollment just started last week, but Medicare counseling appointments at Area Agencies on Aging are already full, said Betsy Sawyer-Manter, president and CEO at SeniorPlus in Lewiston.
“The phones are ringing off the hook,” Sawyer-Manter said. “And, unfortunately, the demand is incredibly outpacing the resources we have to answer people’s questions.”
Sawyer-Manter said some Medicare Advantage plans for next year have reduced benefits, such as eye and dental care. Understanding different options is complex, and Sawyer-Manter hopes that the market stabilizes next year so people don’t have to switch from plans they like.
More than 30% of Medicare Advantage enrollees in Maine have plans with Martin’s Point. A spokesperson said some of its plan changes were required by the Center for Medicare and Medicaid Services. They said Martin’s Point is replacing many terminated plans with new ones and is still offering options in every county.
This story appears through a media partnership with Maine Public.

title: Iran says 7 oil tankers were attacked in the Strait of Hormuz as fears grow of a return to war
text:
TEL AVIV, Israel (AP) — Seven oil tankers caught fire or were damaged in the Strait of Hormuz overnight after being hit by Iran or striking naval mines, Tehran said Thursday, a markedly high number as tensions rise over concerns about a return to all-out war.
With days before a close election in Israel in which Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu could lose power, and before next month’s U.S. midterm election in which war-linked high prices have sparked voter anger, there are concerns that U.S.-Israeli attacks on Iran could resume.
“Netanyahu wants to attack Iran, that’s not even a question,” Danny Citrinowicz, a researcher at Israel’s Institute for National Security Studies and a former Iran specialist in Israel’s military and intelligence services, told The Associated Press.
He accused Israel of rushing into another round with Iran without revamping its strategy. A clear Netanyahu victory in the Oct. 27 election means an attack is almost guaranteed, he said.
Main opposition candidates are likely to focus on domestic issues first, but Citrinowicz said he believed the region is on the way toward “another kinetic escalation.”
Iran repeats threat to attack U.S. bases in the region
Iranian state television reported the claims about the latest attacks on ships, which the AP couldn’t independently confirm. The report cited the Revolutionary Guard Corps navy, which again threatened to strike U.S. military bases in the region if the U.S. keeps helping to guide commercial ships through the strait.
The report didn’t mention casualties. Iran still asserts control over the waterway, a central point of leverage in any talks with the U.S. over the war.
October has had the most reported attacks on commercial shipping since March in the war’s opening weeks, according to a British military monitor, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations. UKMTO didn’t report the latest attacks, but it has noted new reluctance by some shippers to report incidents.
Oil producers have found ways to keep crude flowing, experts say, but at a mounting cost.
Tankers continue moving through Strait of Hormuz despite attacks
Oil tankers are still moving oil through the strait under U.S. military protection despite the recent upsurge in attacks, according to shipping data and analysis company Lloyd’s List Intelligence.
Tanker operators willing to risk the voyage have been shuttling oil from Gulf producers through the strait at night with their location systems and mobile phones turned off using a U.S.-protected lane near the coast of Oman. Those tankers transfer oil to other tankers waiting in the Gulf of Oman for shipment to customers in Asia.
Those “active Gulf operators show little sign of retreating” despite 28 attacks on ships in October, the highest since the start of the war, Lloyd’s said in an online webinar Thursday.
The so-called “dark shuttle” overseen by U.S. Central Command has helped return oil shipments from the Gulf at roughly prewar levels, but at high costs in time, money and sailors’ lives. Spot charter rates for tankers have soared into the hundreds of thousands of dollars a day, while the ship-to-ship transfers can take several days.
UN urges US and Iran to return to diplomacy to end conflict, reopen strait
U.N. spokesman Stephane Dujarric said no commercial ships should be attacked and called for diplomacy between the U.S. and Iran to reopen the strait.
“For the sake of the people of the region and for the broader world, we need to see that waterway reopen, and we need to see tensions go down,” he told reporters Thursday.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on Wednesday said Tehran remains open to diplomacy, but is ready to defend itself.
Iran has warned that it learned important military lessons from the war that began with U.S. and Israeli attacks on Feb. 28, indicating in recent days that it could expand targets to include infrastructure such as undersea cables and data centers.
The United States, for its part, is sending more military assets to the region, including a third aircraft carrier and thousands of troops, to join the largest force of American warships and aircraft in the Middle East in decades.
Mediators, meanwhile, have been trying to bring Washington and Tehran back to formal talks.
Iran still promotes its latest proposal to end the war and fully open the strait within a week if the U.S. meets several conditions, including ending the U.S. blockade of Iranian ports. It echoes conditions in the deal that fell apart within days of both sides signing it in June.
U.S. President Donald Trump rejected the latest proposal last month, but both sides acknowledged that indirect discussions have continued.
The stakes are even higher if all-out war resumes
A return to full fighting would again endanger civilians throughout the region and complicate global deliveries of oil, natural gas and related products like fertilizer from the region and likely bring another spike in prices.
The head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, this week acknowledged that the Islamic Republic will suffer under a prolonged U.S. blockade. But economic pain and strategic collapse are not the same thing, he added, according to Iran’s state-run IRNA news agency.
Now the conflict has widened with the recent surge in fighting between Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia. The Saudi kingdom backs a coalition of forces with Yemen’s internationally recognized government that is fighting the rebels.
The Houthis’ repeated deadly attacks on airports and other facilities inside Saudi Arabia have pressured the close U.S. ally, which has sought military aid.
The escalation also has threatened a crucial shipping corridor, the Bab el-Mandeb at the southern end of the Red Sea.
Meanwhile, the president of Saudi oil company Aramco, whose sites have been targeted by the Houthis, said the amount of oil moving through a pipeline that bypasses the Strait of Hormuz has increased threefold in light of the global energy crisis.
The East-West pipeline’s capacity has surged from two million to seven million barrels each day, Amin Nasser said in an interview with Saudi-owned television Al Arabiya Business. He said the company has been using drones to assess any damage to the pipeline and help with firefighting.

title: Voting-related measures on November ballots include a voter ID push targeting mail-in ballots
text:
Advocates for greater voter identification requirements are pursuing a new approach in some states: a mandate to place driver’s license or partial Social Security numbers on mail-in ballots.
Variations of the voter ID proposals are being decided in the midterm elections in California, Colorado and Nevada — three states where conservative activists collected petition signatures to bypass Democratic-led legislatures and place the issue directly before voters.
The voter ID measures are among about 30 questions on November ballots affecting state policies on voting and elections. They account for roughly 1 in 5 of all state ballot measures nationwide. Some mirror policies that President Donald Trump has pushed unsuccessfully at the national level and build off a Republican narrative that noncitizen voting is a problem, though data indicates it is rare.
Several measures address changes to congressional voting districts, as part of a national redistricting battle spurred by Trump. Others could change the way primaries are conducted, make it more difficult for voters to amend their state constitutions or — in Missouri — make it harder for lawmakers to change measures that voters approve.
Taken together, the measures highlight a long-running debate about who can participate in elections and how to ensure voting is both accessible and secure.
“Ballot measures have become a battle zone for the future of American democracy, including direct democracy itself,” said Chris Melody Fields Figueredo, executive director of the Ballot Initiative Strategy Center, a group that backs progressive ballot issues.
California proposition is one of several voter ID measures
When voting by mail, most states already require a voter’s signature for a ballot to count. Only Georgia, Minnesota, New Mexico and Ohio require some sort of government-issued identification number to be included with mail-in ballots.
California’s Proposition 39 would require a government-issued ID to vote in person or the last four digits of that identification number to vote by mail.
In the August primary, nearly 90% of California’s ballots were cast by mail, and more than 52,000 ballots — less than 1% of the total — were rejected for nonmatching or missing signatures, according to the secretary of state’s office.
The proposed constitutional amendment doesn’t directly repeal California’s current signature requirement. But the intent is for the four-digit verification to replace it, said Carl DeMaio, a Republican state Assembly member whose organization Reform California backed the voter ID initiative.
“If California gets this done through citizens, maybe it will shame the politicians into getting this going in a moderate and reasonable and bipartisan way nationwide,” DeMaio said.
Though Trump hasn’t endorsed the California proposition, opponents contend it is similar to a bill he backed in Congress to require a photo ID to vote, or a photocopy for ballots returned by mail.
“Prop 39 is just another Trump power grab that is intended to make voting harder, less secure and more expensive for Californians,” said Brittany Stonesifer, a voting rights attorney at Common Cause California.
About 7 in 10 registered voters nationally favor requiring all voters to provide valid photo identification at their voting place in order to vote, according to an October poll by The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research. Though support is stronger among Republicans, a majority of Democratic voters also favor a voter ID requirement.
In addition to citizen initiatives in Colorado and Nevada, voter ID amendments also were referred to the November ballot by Republican-led legislatures in Arizona, North Carolina and Ohio.
Citizen voting measures spread to six states
Ballot measures in Alaska, Arizona, Arkansas, Kansas, South Dakota and West Virginia would reinforce current election practices limiting voting to U.S. citizens. Since 2018, at least 15 states have adopted similar measures, including all eight states where they appeared on the ballot in 2024 and in Texas last year.
Many critics argue the measures are largely symbolic and unnecessary, because voting by noncitizens is rare and already forbidden in most states.
No state constitutions explicitly allow noncitizens to vote. But some municipalities in California, Maryland and Vermont, as well as the District of Columbia, do allow voting by noncitizens in some local elections such as for school board and city council.
States need to act because the nation’s founders “gave the states the rights to determine who can vote,” said Becky Arps, research director for Americans for Citizen Voting.
Changes to primaries are proposed in Massachusetts and Alaska
A pair of Massachusetts ballot measures could reshape state elections. One amendment would scrap separate party primaries in favor of an open primary in which the top two vote recipients — no matter the party — advance to the general election.
Another would allow people to register to vote on the same day as the election, instead of the current 10-day-in-advance deadline.
In Alaska, voters are again being asked whether to repeal a system of open primaries and ranked choice voting. A similar measure narrowly failed two years ago.
Redistricting efforts face voter referendums
Republican lawmakers in Missouri passed new congressional districts for the midterm elections, after Trump urged GOP-led states to redistrict to try to win additional House seats. But the Missouri Supreme Court and U.S. Supreme Court both blocked the new map from being used in the November election because of a referendum petition.
Voters now will decide whether to uphold or reject the new districts. If approved, the map could be used in the 2028 election.
Maryland voters, meanwhile, will decide whether to approve a redistricting amendment backed by Democratic state lawmakers that could pave the way for a new U.S. House map ahead of the 2028 election. Proponents’ campaign signs urge a “yes” vote as a means to “stop Trump.”
In Colorado, where some Democrats also want to redistrict, a ballot initiative backed by a conservative group would instead prohibit any mid-decade redistricting from favoring one political party and require approval from both an existing independent commission and the state Supreme Court.
Ballot initiatives could get new hurdles or protections
Proposed amendments in North Dakota and South Dakota would make it harder to amend their state constitutions by requiring 60% approval from voters instead of a simple majority. A similar 60% threshold is proposed in Utah for future citizen initiatives that raise taxes. All were referred to the ballot by Republican-led legislatures.
Several states already have supermajority requirements for certain ballot measures, including 60% thresholds to pass constitutional amendments in Florida and tax initiatives in Arizona. Two years ago, amendments to legalize recreational marijuana and create abortion rights both received majority support but still failed because of Florida’s supermajority threshold.
Measures in several other states seek to strengthen citizen ballot initiatives. A Missouri amendment proposed by a citizens group would make it harder for lawmakers to change voter-approved citizen initiatives by requiring revisions to get an 80% vote in the state House and Senate. That comes after the Republican-led Legislature last year repealed a paid sick leave law approved by voters and referred a new constitutional amendment to the November ballot to reverse voter-approved abortion rights.
A Montana ballot measure would make the citizen initiative process a fundamental right, and a Colorado measure would require ballot questions to be written “in plain language at no more than an eighth-grade reading level.”
___
Associated Press writer John Hanna contributed to this report.

title: 'Looksmaxxing' streamer known as Clavicular pleads not guilty to rape charge
text:
'Looksmaxxing' streamer known as Clavicular pleads not guilty to rape charge
The "looksmaxxing" livestreamer Braden Peters, better known by his stage name Clavicular, pleaded not guilty Thursday to charges that he raped a 17-year-old girl at his family’s Massachusetts home.
The 20-year-old influencer is accused of bringing a 17-year-old girl to a family home in Chatham in May of last year, where he allegedly assaulted the victim.
Peters arrived for his Orleans District Court appearance with a dog on a leash that barked at reporters as he entered the building.
He was held on $10,000 bail and ordered to stay away from the alleged victim and to not post about her on social media. He is scheduled to return to court next month.
Peters faces charges of rape, drugging a victim for sexual intercourse and providing liquor to a person under age 21, according to court documents.
Police said a woman walked into the Chatham Police Department's headquarters to report the sexual assault allegation on June 4. According to the report, the victim alleged that the incident happened on May 23, 2025.
Video below: Peters arrives with dog at court
She told officers that she had met Peters through Instagram and that she was later paid to make some videos for social media, the document states. On the day of the alleged rape, she said Peters ordered her a ride to his family's residence in Chatham, where they did a live stream.
"Before entering his bedroom, he instructed her to lie on the live stream to say that she is 18 years old. He also instructed her to say that the alcohol is water, so that neither his Twitch account nor live stream gets banned," the officer wrote in the report.
The woman told police she drank vodka and became "really drunk." According to the narrative, she told officers that she fell asleep in his bed and woke up to Peters having sex with her without consent.
"I asked... if she said anything to him as he was on top, to which she stated, 'No. I was, like, in shock,'" the officer wrote.
According to the narrative, police reviewed video of the relevant Twitch stream and saw that it included the woman and Peters kissing.
Peters has more than 1 million social media followers resulting from this promotion.
Peters has denied any wrongdoing.

title: Woman accused of poisoning friend’s tea after being confronted about suspicious bank activity
text:
(Gray News) - A woman in New Jersey is accused of poisoning a friend after being confronted about suspicious bank activity.
Rohweniven Bacani, 52, was charged with third-degree aggravated assault after allegedly poisoning the woman’s tea with a benzodiazepine, according to New Jersey authorities.
The two women had arranged to meet at a restaurant in Fort Lee on Sept. 8 to discuss unauthorized activity the alleged victim had discovered in financial accounts to which Bacani had shared access, prosecutors said.
When the woman arrived, Bacani was already there with a cup of tea waiting for her.
The woman allegedly drank some of the tea but stopped after noticing an unusual taste. She collapsed while leaving the restaurant and later regained consciousness in a hospital, with no recollection of how she had gotten there, prosecutors said.
She remained hospitalized for several days.
Following a weeks-long investigation, detectives concluded that Bacani had allegedly added a benzodiazepine to the woman’s tea.
Bacani was charged and arrested outside her home.
She was taken to the Bergen County Jail pending her first court appearance.

title: Access nature with these 5 new accessible Maine trails
text:
Many Mainers like to spend time outdoors on the state’s thousands of trails. Increasingly, more of these trails are being built so that people using wheelchairs, pushing strollers, and with other mobility devices or disabilities can use them, too.
While what makes a trail accessible is complex based on both environmental conditions and user needs, the U.S. Forest Service offers trail accessibility guidelines. The service outlines that accessible trails should be 3 feet wide, have a firm and stable surface, limited obstacles and a low grade and cross slope — essentially, accessible trails should be relatively smooth and flat.
Other accessible trail infrastructure includes resting spots throughout the route and near steeper sections, clear signage about the terrain, and connected accessible facilities and parking areas.
While constructing accessible trails is often more expensive due to these considerations, land trusts and other outdoor organizations in Maine are steadily building them.
“This decision to be as inclusive as possible is exactly what we should be doing,” said Maine Audubon President Judy Camuso about the organization building a new accessible trail in Falmouth. “After all, the outdoors are for everyone.”
From Kennebunk to Damariscotta, here are five accessible trails that opened within the past year for you to explore.
GILSLAND FARM AUDUBON CENTER, FALMOUTH
The All Persons Trail at Maine Audubon’s wildlife sanctuary in Falmouth opened this month. Its wheelchair-accessible hard-packed stone dust surface and a wooden boardwalk go through shaded woods and grassy meadow in a half-mile loop. An additional spur trail has views of the Presumpscot River. Three accessible benches along the trail offer scenic rest stops.
ALEWIVE WOODS PRESERVE, KENNEBUNK
Kennebunk Land Trust opened the Alewive Access Trail in July. The trail is 1 mile long, offering an out-and-back journey through the woods of West Kennebunk. About halfway through the trail is an accessible curved bridge, built by a land trust volunteer.
WINDHAM COMMUNITY FOREST, WINDHAM
The Universal Access Trail in Windham is 1 mile of hard-packed stone dust that gradually leads to an overlook of the White Mountains. The trail, which opened this month, is in the newly formed Windham Community Forest, also created in October following the combination of Lowell Preserve and the East Windham Conservation Area.
WOODWARD POINT PRESERVE, BRUNSWICK
Andy’s Trail in Brunswick is a half-mile, hard-packed stone dust trail that circles a hay field that juts into Casco Bay. The path offers views of Little Bull Pen cove and the preserve’s main field, a favored habitat of bobolinks. Resting areas are available at vistas and by steeper portions of the trail. The Brunswick-Topsham Land Trust and Maine Coast Heritage Trust collaborated to open this ADA-complaint project in fall 2025.
CASTNER BROOK COMMUNITY FOREST, DAMARISCOTTA
The all-persons trail at the Coastal Rivers Conservation Trust’s Castner Brook Community Forest is a 0.35-mile out-and-back path. It goes through a hemlock forest to reach Castner Brook for a view of the bubbling stream. The trail opened in fall 2025.

title: Severe turbulence injures several flight attendants on flight heading to Los Angeles
text:
HONOLULU (KHNL/Gray News) - Several flight attendants needed medical attention after a reported rough flight from Honolulu to Los Angeles.
United Airlines flight 1157 landed safely just before 9:30 p.m. on Wednesday.
The pilot of the Boeing 777 told air traffic controllers that they were hit by about five seconds of turbulence during the descent and requested medical assistance at the gate.
No reports of passenger injuries but four flight attendants needed medical attention and one needed to be taken to the hospital.

title: FEMA wants states to shoulder more disaster costs. Can they afford it?
text:
FEMA wants states to shoulder more disaster costs. Can they afford it?
The Trump administration wants states to take on more responsibility for disaster response and recovery. But some states are questioning whether they can afford a reduced federal role.
FEMA wants states to shoulder more disaster costs. Can they afford it?
The Trump administration wants states to take on more responsibility for disaster response and recovery. But some states are questioning whether they can afford a reduced federal role.
More than 4 feet of floodwater swept through Liz Ayala's family home in Kerr County, Texas, in July. Months later, her parents still cannot move back in.
"We were raised in that home, that neighborhood. So it has a lot, a lot of value and memories in that home," Ayala told Hearst Television.
Without flood insurance, her parents hoped federal assistance would help them rebuild. But FEMA denied Texas's request for Individual Assistance following the flooding.
"With that being denied, we're back to square one," Ayala said.
The denial comes as the Trump administration pushes to shift more disaster response and recovery responsibilities to states. Those proposed changes have not been linked to the Texas decision.
FEMA argues state and local officials know their communities best and should take the lead when disaster strikes.
But can states afford it?
Hearst Television sought answers from FEMA, state emergency management officials, an independent expert and a family still struggling to recover.
What FEMA wants to change
In an Oct. 15 memo, FEMA Administrator Cameron Hamilton outlined four agency priorities, with reducing federal government dependency at the top.
In a statement to Hearst Television, FEMA emphasized that it is "not the first responder" and that federal assistance is intended to support state and local efforts, not replace them.
The administration argues that giving states more responsibility will make disaster recovery more effective.
A Trump-appointed FEMA Review Council has also proposed reducing the federal government's share of certain disaster recovery costs.
Currently, FEMA generally covers at least 75% of eligible costs under its Public Assistance program, which helps governments repair infrastructure and recover from disasters.
The council proposed starting the federal share at 50%, potentially increasing it to 75% based on performance and even higher in certain circumstances.
For a disaster with $100 million in eligible recovery costs, that could mean state and local governments paying $50 million instead of $25 million.
The proposal has not been finalized and could require congressional action. It also applies to Public Assistance, not the separate Individual Assistance program that Ayala's family hoped to receive.
FEMA also announced a separate $400 million flood prevention funding opportunity Thursday, allowing eligible communities to seek money for projects including home elevations, property buyouts and drainage improvements.
The funding targets future flood risks, particularly involving properties insured through the National Flood Insurance Program. It is not intended to reimburse uninsured families for damage they have already suffered.
Which states receive the most federal disaster assistance?
An analysis of FEMA data by MoneyGeek found the federal government approved or obligated approximately $42.9 billion in disaster assistance between January 2020 and May 2026, excluding COVID-19 emergencies. Five states: Florida, Louisiana, North Carolina, Texas and California accounted for more than half that amount. Louisiana received the most assistance per resident, at $1,916, followed by Vermont at $660.
North Carolina faces billions in unmet recovery needs
Hurricane Helene caused nearly $60 billion in damage and recovery needs in North Carolina, according to state officials. More than $41 billion remains unfunded.
North Carolina has committed roughly $3.1 billion toward recovery, but officials told Hearst Television that affected communities cannot absorb the remaining costs alone.
"Those are the events that could truly bankrupt states," said Andrew Rumbach, a disaster policy expert at the Urban Institute.
Rumbach warned that shifting more recovery costs to states could force significant increases in property or sales taxes.
His own research raises questions about whether states have the money to take on that burden.
In a 2025 Urban Institute analysis, Rumbach examined how earlier proposals to reduce FEMA funding would have affected state budgets. Using 2019 figures, they found only five of 31 states receiving federal disaster assistance had enough money in dedicated disaster reserves to cover the projected shortfall.
"And I think it's probably fair to say that many of them are not prepared to take on that cost immediately," Rumbach said.
The research examined an earlier proposal, but Rumbach says the financial challenge remains especially serious for states repeatedly hit by catastrophic disasters. States that rarely face major disasters may be better positioned to take on additional responsibilities.
Pennsylvania prepares while Texas relies heavily on federal funding
Pennsylvania officials say the state is already preparing for a reduced federal role.
Gov. Josh Shapiro's administration has doubled funding available to state agencies for disaster response, from $20 million to $40 million. The state has also established a disaster recovery assistance program and ordered agencies to strengthen emergency preparedness.
But Pennsylvania officials warned Hearst Television that significant federal funding reductions could weaken the state's ability to respond effectively to emergencies.
Texas, meanwhile, relies heavily on Washington.
The state budgeted approximately $1.9 billion for emergency response spending in 2027, with just $37 million coming from state funds, according to The Texas Tribune.
Following the July floods, FEMA approved certain government recovery assistance but denied Texas's request for aid to individual survivors. Gov. Greg Abbott's office told The Texas Tribune it was reviewing the decision and considering an appeal.
FEMA also announced a separate $400 million flood prevention funding opportunity Thursday, allowing eligible communities to seek money for projects including home elevations, property buyouts and drainage improvements.
The funding targets future flood risks, particularly involving properties insured through the National Flood Insurance Program. It is not intended to reimburse uninsured families for damage they have already suffered.
Back in Kerr County, Ayala's parents still cannot return home.
"The flood's gone, but the damages are still there," Ayala said. "Families are still dealing with damaged homes, of financial hardship, and the loss of things that they can't get back."

title: UMaine defenseman brings extensive pro experience to Black Bears
text:
ORONO, Maine — Even though University of Maine senior defenseman Dru Krebs is only 23 years old, Black Bear head coach Ben Barr said he is like a “grandfather on the team.”
“He is extremely mature and he’s a great human being,” said Barr.
Krebs’ resume is different from most college hockey players’.
He came to UMaine after playing 142 professional games: 140 in the ECHL and two in the American Hockey League. He has also played in a National Hockey League exhibition game.
“I thought it was an opportunity to get some school done and also elevate my game play,” said the 23-year-old Krebs, who has been a steady stay-at-home presence on the blue line paired with offensive-minded Lukas Peterson. “There is a lot more practicing (at the college level) and the games are (more) high-intensity. This puts me in position to re-enter pro after a year and make a step forward.”
Krebs, who is 6-foot-1 and 185 pounds, said he needed to gain weight, and the additional workouts at the college level help him do so and put him in a better position to be a pro hockey player.
“I’ve heard from other guys that playing in the NCAA is an unbelievable experience,” he said. “I knew some guys who played at Maine and they absolutely loved it here so I said there is nothing to lose coming to play for Maine.”
Even though he has yet to register a point, he is plus-one in plus-minus and is averaging 18 minutes and 9 seconds of playing time per game. He has three blocked shots.
Players receive a plus-one when they are on the ice when their team scores an even-strength or shorthanded goal and a minus-one if the other team scores one.
While the ECHL plays 72 regular season games, there are only 34 in college hockey.
“For college games, everybody is so pent up to play these two games a week. And every game is so much more important. There are a lot more games in pro hockey so the players play a little bit more passively and tend to play within the system a little bit more,” Krebs said. “College is kind of run-and-gun. It resembles how playoff games are in pro hockey in terms of the intensity for every single game.”
He played his first two games at Alfond Arena two weekends ago when the Black Bears split with nationally ranked Quinnipiac, and he said he will never forget the experience.
“It was unbelievable. For the first warmup, I had some shivers and goose bumps,” said the Okotoks, Alberta, native. “To see everybody around and hear the band was really cool to experience for the first time. It was pretty sweet.
“I really enjoy playing with these guys. And playing with my partner (Peterson) has been good.”
Peterson said he feels the same way.
“It has been awesome. It has been a pretty smooth transition for him. He is honestly very easy to play with,” Peterson said. “He plays a very simple game. He knows his role out there. After playing with (Brandon Holt) last year, he’s kind of a similar player. It has been an easy transition.”
UMaine graduate student left wing and captain Owen Fowler said when Peterson and Krebs are on the ice “it’s always a good thing.”
Barr called Krebs’ game “very efficient.”
“He does really well getting the puck out of our zone. He has a good stick,” Barr said. “He has been a great addition not just as a hockey player but as a person for our locker room.”
“He’s a good leader out there, a veteran guy,” said senior center and alternate captain Max Scott. “He makes good plays and a good guy to have in the locker room. He is a very well-spoken guy. He holds down the back end with (Peterson). We love having him.”
Krebs played in 67 regular season games and 15 playoff games for the ECHL’s Fort Wayne Komets a year ago. He had 4 goals and 15 assists during the regular season and was plus-31 and had a goal and two assists in the playoffs and was a plus-four.
He had played in 58 regular season games for the Greenville Swamp Rabbits in the ECHL in 2024-25 and had 2 goals and 10 assists. He also played in two games for the AHL’s Ontario Reign and didn’t register a point.
Krebs has two older brothers, Dakota and Peyton, who both played hockey. Peyton is a forward with the NHL’s Buffalo Sabres with 400 career NHL games to his credit between Vegas and Buffalo.
He said both have been major influences in his career.
Krebs was a sixth round draft choice of the Washington Capitals in 2021, and Peyton was a first round choice of Vegas in 2019. They wound up playing against each other in an NHL exhibition game.
“I had to defend him. It was all good. I didn’t get scored on. He doesn’t have anything on me. It was pretty fun,” Krebs said. “I always watch him play and he watches me and gives me some pointers. He has been such a big influence on me. I look up to him and model myself after him. He is such a great human being.”
The 2-2 Black Bears entertain 0-4 Colgate for a two-game series this weekend.
Krebs said his goal for the rest of the season is to “play a simple game, support my teammates and play the way I can to earn my coaches’ trust and work off of that.”
Fowler said Krebs is “unreal.”
“He has a lot of experience at a different level, and he is wise in his play and his off-ice habits,” Fowler said. “He knows what it takes. He has been a great add.”

title: UMaine outlines non-academic cuts to address budget shortfall
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
MAINE (WABI) - The University of Maine and University of Maine at Machias have announced planned non-academic cuts to help close a projected $19 million budget shortfall for Fiscal Year 2028.
In a previous letter, University President Joan Ferrini-Mundy announced $10 million would be cut from academic affairs, which makes up roughly half of the budget.
In a letter posted to the university’s website Wednesday, leaders outlined the non-academic changes, though they say they are limited in adjustments due to existing collective bargaining agreements.
University leaders say they hope the changes will account for about $6 million of the $9 million non-academic shortfall, adding that plans to close the remaining $3 million gap will be their main focus in the coming weeks.
Strategies include changing the length of annually appointed contract staff, cutting back on overtime, eliminating vacant positions, consolidating units, seeking outside funding through sponsorships and licensing opportunities, added facility fees for those outside of the university, fee increases, and the sale of property and other assets.
The adjustments will impact multiple departments including athletics, student life, research, strategic partnerships, resources, innovation and engagement, Finance and Administration & Facilities Management, and the President’s Office, which includes Cultural Affairs and Marketing and Communications.
The university says it also hopes to increase revenue by hosting more events and conferences on campus while planning around numerous variables, including projected enrollment as well as state and federal funding.

title: Susan Collins reminds us of the rationale for ‘country before party’
text:
Apparently Sen. Susan Collins doesn’t adhere to a guiding principle many Americans learned
in their youth. “Remember, country always comes before party,” my Republican father admonished me — long before I was of age to vote.
Sen. Collins, in an August 2016 Washington Post op-ed, described her attachment to
the Republican Party: “Being a Republican is what defines me as a person.” In the same op-ed, Collins declared Donald Trump not qualified to be president, and did this in no uncertain terms. 
Yet, she now asks us to reelect her to the Senate, where she would vote for Trump’s Republican Party. This would add greatly to Trump’s power as president, a position she did not believe he was qualified to hold in the first place.
Sen. Collins provides a clear case of placing party before country — and a clear reason why Americans have long believed in placing country before party.
Parker Albee, Jr.
Falmouth

title: Pediatrician felt 'drugged,' planned bloodwork for morning she was found dead: Docs
text:
Pennsylvania wife felt 'drugged,' planned bloodwork for morning she was found dead: Docs
Interviews with Julia Pederson's relatives, friend and co-worker revealed that she had reported feeling "drugged" and experienced dizziness and lethargy after consuming drinks delivered by her husband and daughter in the weeks before her death, according to a search-warrant application filed in Pennsylvania by the Harrisburg Bureau of Police.
Police said Pederson's husband, Jonathan Gatto, strangled her and then set fire to her body.
Crews respond to Green Street fire
Police and firefighters responded to the couple’s home in the 2900 block of Green Street at about 7:05 a.m. Oct. 10 for a reported house fire.
Firefighters entered the home and found Pederson. Emergency responders performed CPR before taking her to Holy Spirit Hospital in Camp Hill, Pennsylvania, where she was pronounced dead, according to the warrant application.
Investigators determined the fire had been intentionally set. A blood test measuring the level of carboxyhemoglobin in Pederson’s body indicated she had died before the fire began, the application states.
An autopsy conducted Oct. 13 determined Pederson died from multiple traumatic injuries, and her death was ruled a homicide, according to the warrant.
Pederson told mother she felt 'drugged,' docs say
Pederson's sister provided investigators with text messages Pederson had sent to their mother, police said.
In a Sept. 10 message, Pederson said she felt as though she was "being drugged" because she could barely walk, according to the warrant. She also reported feeling groggy and said she had canceled appointments with five patients before lying down to sleep.
Gatto would bring Pederson drinks daily, docs say
A friend told investigators that Gatto and the couple's daughter frequently brought drinks to Pederson at work, according to the warrant.
The friend stated that Pederson did not want the drinks but that Gatto would have their daughter carry them inside while he waited in the car, according to police.
A co-worker provided a similar account, telling investigators that Gatto and the child delivered drinks to Pederson almost daily.
Pederson’s symptoms appeared to worsen after she finished a drink, the co-worker told police. She reportedly became dizzy and lethargic, experienced more severe migraine symptoms and developed a very dry mouth.
Pederson planned to get bloodwork the morning she was found dead
On Oct. 9, the day before the fire, Pederson was "so lethargic" that she was lying on her office floor and appeared "very out of it," the co-worker told investigators.
Pederson said she planned to have bloodwork performed the following morning, according to the warrant. She was found dead that morning.
Police sought DNA, security cameras
Investigators requested authorization to search the Green Street residence, the surrounding property and a Toyota Prius associated with the home.
Police sought hair or other DNA samples from Gatto, Pederson and the couple's daughter, along with water bottles and other beverage and food containers Pederson might have used.
The warrant application also listed documents concerning the couple's relationship, records related to Pederson's medical symptoms and containers that might have held flammable liquids or chemicals.
Investigators also sought security cameras, alarm systems and surveillance recordings, including footage from a Ring doorbell system.

title: UMaine men’s hockey hosting Colgate on Homecoming weekend
text:
Following a rare early season weekend off, the University of Maine’s hockey team returns to Alfond Arena for a two-game series against Colgate University on Friday and Saturday nights as the two teams renew their non-conference rivalry.
It is Homecoming weekend in Orono, and both games begin at 7 p.m.
This will be the third time in four years the 2-2 Black Bears and 0-4 Raiders will be meeting for a two-game set in Orono, with the Black Bears holding a 2-1-1 edge in the close, hard-fought games. The teams split 3-2 decisions a year ago, with Colgate winning the first game and UMaine taking the second one in overtime.
During the 2023-24 season, UMaine notched a 3-1 victory and then rallied from a 3-0 deficit to earn a 4-4 tie.
UMaine traveled to Hamilton, New York, for a two-game series in 2022-23, and the Raiders posted a 5-2 triumph before the teams skated to a 1-1 tie.
So far this season, the Black Bears have split a road series with Holy Cross (4-1 win, 3-2 overtime loss) and a home set with Quinnipiac (2-1 loss, 5-3 win) while the Raiders dropped a pair at Stonehill (2-1 in overtime, 4-2) and were swept at home by New Hampshire (5-2, 2-0).
UMaine head coach Ben Barr said Colgate’s record is irrelevant.
“They’re just like everybody else. They’ve been in a bunch of close games, just like us,” Barr said. “They’re going to be extremely motivated. They always play us great up here.”
Barr said his team needs breakthroughs from players in every game, but he’s not worried whether they’re going to work hard.
“But then we have to go out and execute as well,” he said. “There have been games that we’ve done that and games that we haven’t and that’s been the story of our team.”
“We don’t really look at any team’s record,” UMaine sophomore defenseman Lukas Peterson said. “Every team in college hockey is good. And they are always going to come out [ready to play] especially when they have an opportunity to come up to Maine and play in our arena.”
UMaine graduate student left wing and captain Owen Fowler said Colgate will be a “hungry group.”
“They wanted to come up here and play again, and we have to be ready for them,” Fowler said. “They definitely want to upset us. We have to play our game, stick to what we’re doing well and play with a lot of energy and physicality.”
Colgate is coming off a 13-20-4 season, 9-10-3 in the ECAC, and was picked to finish ninth in the 12-team league in the preseason coaches poll.
UMaine was chosen to finish seventh in Hockey East.
Coach Mike Harder’s Raiders have returned six of their top 10 scorers and starting goalie Reid Dyck, but among their losses were co-leading scorer Simon Labelle, who graduated, and fifth-leading point-producer Michael Neumeier, a defenseman who was the 2024-25 ECAC Rookie of the Year and transferred to Western Michigan.
Colgate has scored only five goals in four games, with senior right wing Jake Schneider being the lone Raider with two goals.
Defenseman Isaiah Norlin headlines the list of returnees after collecting 28 points on 8 goals and 20 assists a year ago to tie Labelle (13 goals, 15 assists) for the team scoring lead. Max Nagel had 11 goals and 15 assists, Ryan Sullivan had 7 goals and 19 assists and Jack Brandt had 8 goals and 10 assists, with three of his eight goals coming against UMaine.
Dyck started 27 games and was 10-15-3 with a 3.17 goals-against average and a .900 save percentage. He made 25 saves in the win over UMaine.
The 6-foot-4 sophomore has started all four games this season and has a 2.78 GAA and a .911 save percentage.
UMaine has four players sharing the scoring lead led by right wing Lee Parks, who has 3 goals and an assist and will bring a three-game goal-scoring streak into the series. Defensemen Isa Parekh and Peterson and senior center Max Scott are the other four-point producers.
Eight Black Bears have scored at least a goal and nine have at least two points.
Left wingers Tanner Klimpke, Fowler and Will Gerrior and center Sully Scholle each have three points.
Goalie Albin Boija is 2-1 with a 2.03 GAA and a .906 save percentage.

title: Obituary: Gregory “Greg” Im
text:
WOOLWICH – With great sadness, the Im and Locke families share the passing of Gregory “Greg” Im of Woolwich, on Oct. 11, 2026.
Born on Sept. 23, 1965, Greg grew up in Timonium, Md., and attended Dulaney High School before graduating from Cornell University in 1987 and the University of Maine School of Law in 2009. After college, Greg traveled extensively throughout the U.S., visiting 47 of its 50 states. Eventually leaving the road, he settled in Maine with his wife, Courtney Locke, where they built a life farming, restoring a 200-year-old farmhouse, and enjoying a quiet life with their children, Will and Tallulah.
A lifelong master of reinvention, Greg moved seamlessly through roles and careers during his life – from child-college student and pianist to master carpenter, rock and roll roadie, flower farmer, and exceptional home chef. All that, and he still managed a day job! At the time of his death, Greg was a partner at Drummond Woodsum law firm, where he served as the head of the Public Finance Group, working in municipal and school law.
New skills came easily to Greg. He could install bathroom plumbing and prepare a Michelin star-worthy meal with little more than a Sunset how-to plumbing book, a 10-inch chef’s knife, and the conviction that “If a guy named Earl can do it, then so can I.” He approached every challenge with thoughtfulness and quiet determination, whether he was single-handedly replacing a load-bearing wall with a half-ton steel beam for his demanding wife, or building a backyard waterpark with PVC pipe and hoses for his son. He could sew a plush flying squirrel costume for his daughter, then turn around and style a 15-person, winter-themed dinner party for his in-laws – with an hour’s notice and nothing on hand but evergreen fronds, candles, and confectioners’ sugar. Greg could do it all and do it well.
Greg was singularly smart, funny, creative, and curious, and he valued his family, close friends, a great meal, privacy, and a good laugh above all else. He loved an inside joke and would ride it for years. He loved great guitar solos, math, cooking for family and friends, precise language, Maine, and building beautiful things. He hated arrogance, inefficiency, and dishonest fries.
Despite his exceptional skills and many accomplishments, Greg remained humble and kind throughout his life. He adored his family, friends, and colleagues, always acting to improve their lives. He was a born giver, and he gave freely and without expectation, wanting only to delight and uplift. In doing so, he made everyone else’s life a little easier, happier, and calmer.
Greg is survived by his wife, Courtney Locke of Woolwich; son, Will Im of Gorham; daughter, Tallulah Im of Portland; parents, Michael and Minja Im of North Ridgefield, Ohio; sister, Kathy Im, and Mark Laschinsky of Halethorpe, Md.; in-laws, William J. Locke of Brunswick, Laura Locke and Paul Mourning of Brooklyn, N.Y., Tracy Locke and Patricio Adams of Bayonne, N.J., Kimberly Locke and Richard Heim of Austin, Texas, and Merrill Lee Jones of Harpswell; five nieces, one nephew, one grand-nephew and two grand-nieces; the Village; and countless family members and friends who mourn his loss and whose lives are better for having known him.
A remembrance service honoring Greg will be held at The Brunswick Hotel, 4 Noble Street, Brunswick, ME 04011 on Saturday, Nov. 7, 2026, from 2-5 p.m.
The family thanks Team Benton at New England Cancer Specialists and CHANS Hospice staff for their exceptional care during Greg’s final months.
Memories and condolences can be shared at http://www.brackettfh.com.
Please consider making a donation to Defenders of Wildlife or planting a tree in Greg’s honor.

title: The search is on for the perfect spruce for the holidays
text:
LEWISTON, ME – Somewhere in Lewiston, the perfect spruce waits for its chance to become the centerpiece of one of the City’s most anticipated holiday traditions.
Lewiston Public Works (LPW) invites residents to see if they have the perfect Spruce for this year’s Holiday Tree. The Tree will be decorated and lights turned on during Holiday at the Plaza festival on Sat., Dec. 5 at 4:27 PM.
But first, the City needs to find the perfect tree. That’s where you come in!
Lewiston’s City Arborist, Steve Murch says the ideal tree is a Spruce, approximately 30 to 35 feet tall that is free from overhead power lines making it accessible from the road so LPW crews can safely remove and transport it to Dufresne Plaza. LPW hopes to identify a suitable tree in the coming weeks and complete its removal by Thanksgiving. There is no cost for the tree removal.
In previous years, one resident collected cereal box tops to get his Spruce. He waited since the 1970s to finally have LPW display it at Holiday At The Plaza. Another gentleman was hunting in the County when he spotted what he thought was the perfect Spruce. He took it home to Lewiston and waited decades before contacting Murch who presented it for Holiday At The Plaza too.
Think you may have it? Maybe you saw it on your way into work? Ask Steve by contacting him at 207-513-3000, ext. 3443, or SMurch@LewistonMaine.gov.

title: Stephen King Wrote a Vampire Classic in a Small Maine Garage
text:
Stephen King Wrote a Vampire Classic in a Small Maine Garage
One of the King of Horror’s most recognizable works was written in a small room in a garage here in the Pine Tree State.
👇 KEEP READING: 13 Best Stephen King Movies According to Rotten Tomatoes 👇
According to his official website’s biography, Stephen King gained the financial means to leave teaching and write full time after learning of a major paperback sale for “Carrie” in May 1973.
At the end of that summer, his family moved to southern Maine because of his mother’s declining health and rented a summer home on Sebago Lake in North Windham for the winter.
There, King wrote 'Salem’s Lot in a small room in the garage, initially calling the novel “Second Coming” and later "Jerusalem’s Lot” before settling on its final title.
His mother died of cancer at age 59 during this period.
King’s 'Salem’s Lot follows writer Ben Mears as he returns to the small Maine town of Jerusalem’s Lot, where he spent part of his childhood, hoping to write a novel.
When residents begin disappearing or becoming vampires, Mears joins a small group of townspeople trying to stop the spreading threat.
And there you have it! One of King’s most recognizable horror novels took shape during a pivotal period of his life in North Windham.

title: Hall of Fame basketball coach Bob Huggins has a 'progressive cognitive condition,' family says
text:
Hall of Fame basketball coach Bob Huggins has a 'progressive cognitive condition,' family says
Retired Hall of Fame basketball coach Bob Huggins has a "progressive cognitive condition" that has started to impact his memory "and aspects of his daily life,” his family said.
Video above: Bob Huggins returns to Cincinnati, praises new UC basketball coach Calhoun
Huggins' family released a statement on his health in coordination with the University of Cincinnati Athletics Department ahead of the 73-year-old's induction into the school's Athletics Hall of Fame.
The family kept the matter private over the past several months but believes now is "an appropriate time to share the news with the many people who have supported Bob throughout his remarkable career," the statement said.
Cincinnati’s Hall of Fame induction is Friday night. Other inductees include Jason Kelce and former Philadelphia Eagles teammate Connor Barwin. The statement said Huggins was "looking forward to returning to Cincinnati this weekend, celebrating with former players and friends, and sharing in a moment that recognizes not only his accomplishments, but also the enduring bonds formed along the way."
"Although Bob and his family recognize the challenges that lie ahead, they remain focused on the relationships, experiences, and moments that bring him joy," the statement said.
Huggins compiled a 935-414 head coaching record at five colleges that included 16-year stints each at Cincinnati and West Virginia, where he took both schools to the Final Four.
Former Huggins pupil Jerrod Calhoun was named Cincinnati’s coach in March. Calhoun graduated from Cincinnati in 2004 and was a student assistant under Huggins during the 2003-04 season. He also spent five seasons on Huggins’ staff at West Virginia from 2007-12.
Huggins' teams were NCAA Tournament staples, and included All-Americans Danny Fortson and Steve Logan and 2000 AP national Player of the Year Kenyon Martin for the Bearcats. Cincinnati reached the Final Four under Huggins in 1992 before losing to Michigan in the national semifinals.
At West Virginia, Huggins landed few high-profile recruits. The 2010 West Virginia team won the Big East tournament and defeated top-seeded Kentucky along its ride to the national semifinals before losing to Duke.
Huggins was inducted into the Naismith Basketball Hall of Fame in September 2022.
Eight months later during an appearance on a Cincinnati radio station, Huggins used a homophobic slur to refer to Xavier fans while also denigrating Catholics. Under an agreement with West Virginia after the remarks, Huggins was suspended for three games at the start of the 2023-24 season, took a $1 million salary reduction and was required to undergo sensitivity training.
Then, in June 2023, Huggins was arrested on suspicion of drunken driving in Pittsburgh. He resigned the next day and issued his second public apology in a month.
It was his second drunken driving arrest. The other occurred in 2004 while he was at Cincinnati and led to his firing in 2005 in a power struggle with the school’s president. After spending one season at Kansas State, Huggins took his dream job at West Virginia in 2007. He was born in Morgantown, West Virginia, grew up in Ohio where his father molded three state high school champion teams, and was a three-year letter winner in basketball at West Virginia.

title: Taco Bell makes decision on soft drink provider as sister chain KFC switches to Coca-Cola
text:
(CNN) - KFC may be ditching Pepsi for Coca-Cola, but Taco Bell said it’s sticking with Pepsi.
The fast-food chain announced Thursday it’s extending its partnership with PepsiCo through 2036.
The deal is a big win for PepsiCo.
Not only did the company lose its longstanding contract with KFC to rival Coca-Cola, but it recently reported slumping North American beverage sales.
Taco Bell and PepsiCo plan to develop new drinks and Doritos Locos Tacos flavors.
Those include more options for Mountain Dew Baja Blast, which has become a billion-dollar brand.
Taco Bell said it’s also aiming to generate $5 billion in beverage revenue by 2030.
