Athletes, coaches and athletic directors can nominate teams by emailing sports editor Bill Stewart at [email protected] or Varsity Maine editor Lee Horton at [email protected].
Varsity Maine Boys Team of the Week: Biddeford football
Biddeford was a clear underdog heading into its game against then-undefeated Marshwood. The Tigers, though, were unfazed.
“ I tell the kids to pursue excellence,” coach Steve Allosso said. “They grasped excellence the second half of that game, because Marshwood is an outstanding team.”
With a 5-2 record, Biddeford is ranked third in the Class B South Heal point standings heading into its regular-season finale Friday against Cheverus. Last year, the Tigers finished 1-7.
Senior quarterback Ernie Dore says that experience has played a large role in this season’s turnaround.
“ A lot of guys this year (were) starting last year on both sides,” Dore said. “I think that’s really played a factor.”
Despite injuries that forced Biddeford to use second- or third-string players at points this fall, including against Marshwood, junior receiver/running back Estevao Lembissa says that the win over an undefeated team is just a glimpse of the Tigers’ potential.
“ It’s the best we played all season, in my opinion,” Lembissa said. “ We gotta bring that to next week, because we have nothing to lose.”
A win over Cheverus would likely give Biddeford the No. 2 seed in the playoffs and a first-round bye. It would also mean a chance for the Tigers to play in front of a home crowd in the semifinals.
“ Last year, they supported us a lot, even when we were 1-7,” Dore said. “ Now, there’s a lot more people supporting us.”

title: Powerful Democratic Virginia lawmaker accused of leading a marijuana criminal conspiracy, money laundering
text:
NORFOLK, Va. (AP) — Virginia state Sen. L. Louise Lucas, one of the state’s most powerful Democrats, was charged Thursday with leading what authorities alleged was a wide-ranging criminal enterprise that acquired and distributed large quantities of marijuana and laundered the proceeds.
Lucas, who has been in elected office for decades, used her political power to insulate the operation from scrutiny, according to an indictment charging her and six other defendants, including several of her relatives. She “put her own financial interests before the people she was elected to serve,” said U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche, who spoke at a news conference with FBI Director Kash Patel.
Lucas surrendered, the Justice Department said. She made a brief appearance in federal court in Norfolk on Thursday afternoon, where she was released on her own recognizance, according to court records. She left the court without addressing journalists who shouted questions her way and went straight into a waiting vehicle.
The charges, including drug trafficking and money laundering, came after the FBI searched Lucas’ hometown office and a cannabis shop in which she has a stake in May. At the time of the search, Lucas — who has been a vocal critic of Republican President Donald Trump’s administration — characterized it as an attempt to intimidate her.
Lucas says she won’t be bullied by the federal government
A statement attributed to Lucas posted on her social media account did not directly address the substance of the charges but said Thursday’s actions amounted to the federal government wielding its “full weight” against a great-grandmother.
“I will not be intimidated. I will not be bullied. And I will not back down,” Lucas said in the statement. Her attorney at the hearing declined comment outside.
The brash 82-year-old lawmaker has spent decades ascending the ranks of Virginia politics and has served since 1992 in the state Senate, where she’s the president pro tempore, overseeing the chamber in the lieutenant governor’s absence. More significantly, she leads the powerful Senate finance committee, through which all legislation with any budget impact must flow. She’s used the position to kill legislation she opposes.
Justice Department denies politics played a role
The indictment comes as Trump’s Justice Department has faced intense scrutiny over investigations and prosecutions against foes of the president that critics have called politically motivated.
Blanche rejected any suggestion politics played a role in Lucas’ case, noting the investigation began well before the second Trump administration started in January 2025.
“We don’t do political paybacks,” Blanche told reporters.
A person familiar with the May search told The Associated Press at the time that the probe was opened during Democratic President Joe Biden’s administration. The person spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss a continuing criminal investigation.
FBI alleges a ‘criminal marijuana enterprise’
Patel said in a statement that “Lucas and a close-knit group of family members and associates orchestrated a multi-year scheme to enrich their own criminal marijuana enterprise, ‘the Lucas Enterprise’ — using Lucas’ position as Chairwoman of the Senate Finance and Appropriations Committee to insulate the enterprise from criminal scrutiny and influencing legislation to financially benefit themselves.”
The indictment describes Lucas as the “leader of the enterprise” who “approved and directed criminal activities,” including arranging for the acquisition and distribution of marijuana and supervising the laundering of the proceeds.
The indictment alleges Lucas worked this year with another of the defendants to use her political position to obtain a recreational marijuana license for him, with the understanding that the proceeds from sales under the license would be shared with her to support the “enterprise.”
Since 2021, marijuana has been legal to possess in Virginia, and many shops across the state have sold cannabis-derived products. But full recreational sales are not yet underway; legislation enacted earlier this year will allow them beginning in July 2027.
Law enforcement made multiple controlled purchases of marijuana from Lucas’ shop, which purported to sell hemp products, in 2024 and 2025, the indictment said.
In addition to drug and money laundering charges, Lucas faces charges of racketeering conspiracy, conspiracy to commit honest services fraud and maintaining a drug-involved premises. An arraignment is scheduled for next month.
Among the other defendants who face a mix of those and other charges are two daughters, Lisa Lucas Burke and Theresa Lucas-Lamb, and a grandson, Ryan Eichelberger. All three also made brief court appearances and were released on their recognizance, according to court records.
Attorneys for Lucas-Lamb and Eichelberger declined comment; Andrew Sacks, who was listed in court records as an attorney for Burke, didn’t respond to requests for comment. Attorneys for two other defendants who are not family members declined comment; a third who was also released Thursday had no attorney listed in court records.
Virginia officials react
A forceful advocate of legalizing marijuana, Lucas partnered in opening the shop, The Cannabis Outlet, in 2021. She has publicly spoken about her ownership stake as recently as June, though her most recent financial disclosure forms do not list the business by name.
At the time of the search — when marijuana was recovered at The Cannabis Outlet, according to the indictment — many Democrats spoke up to defend Lucas.
On Thursday, Scott Surovell, the Democratic leader of the state Senate, said in a statement that the indictment contained “serious allegations” but emphasized that “Senator Lucas has the right to defend herself, and she has my full support as she does so.” Attorney General Jay Jones, a Democrat who is close with Lucas, said the allegations against her must be tested in a “full and fair” legal process.
House Speaker Don Scott, Lt. Gov. Ghazala Hashmi, and Gov. Abigail Spanberger, all Democrats, echoed those sentiments, with Spanberger adding that the timing of the indictment so close to the midterm election would “further erode” Americans’ trust in the Justice Department. Lucas herself is not on the ballot this year.
Ryan McDougle, the Senate Republican leader, said he would not comment while the court proceedings play out.
The senator draws comparisons to Trump
Lucas, who represents a district that includes her hometown of coastal Portsmouth, operates with a sometimes-profane, unapologetic style that’s drawn comparisons to Trump.
She amassed a six-figure following on X and national attention, using the social media platform to advocate forcefully for her priorities and to bash her critics, including former GOP Gov. Glenn Youngkin. She’s also occasionally blasted members of her own party, including Spanberger, with whom she’s had disagreements.
Earlier this year, Lucas helped lead Democrats’ ultimately unsuccessful plan to gerrymander the blue-leaning state’s congressional districts into a map intended to elect 10 Democrats and only one Republican. Along the way, she posted quips about four GOP members the intended map sought to oust, joking that they soon would be working at McDonald’s. She and other Democrats defended the maps as a reasonable response to Trump-backed efforts to boost the GOP’s midterm advantage in other states.
Lucas has been in politics for decades
Lucas has notched several historic firsts in her career. According to a biography from the state library, in 1971 she became the Norfolk Naval Shipyard’s first female shipfitter, a physically demanding job that involves working on metal assemblies for vessels.
She launched her political career in 1984, when, the biography said, she became the first Black woman elected to the Portsmouth city council.
After Democrats flipped control of the Senate in 2019, her peers elected her to serve as president pro tempore. And in 2024, she was tapped to lead the chamber’s budget committee.
___
Rankin reported from Richmond. Associated Press journalists Eric Tucker in Washington and Steve Helber in Norfolk contributed to this report.

title: Looking for the cheapest holiday flights? Here's when to book, according to Google Flights data
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The best times to book holiday travel, according to Google Flights
The cheapest fares may appear sooner than expected, especially for Christmas, according to five years of Google Flights data.
The best times to book holiday travel, according to Google Flights
The cheapest fares may appear sooner than expected, especially for Christmas, according to five years of Google Flights data.
Holiday travel gets expensive fast, but a new report by Google Flights based on five years of data reveals key ways to save on flights this season.
Travelers paid an average of nearly $900 for a round-trip domestic flight last holiday season, according to AAA.
When to book Thanksgiving and Christmas flights
If you're looking for cheap fares this Thanksgiving, don't wait any longer to book. Google Flights says the historical window for the lowest prices has already passed.
The lowest prices historically hit about 34 days before departure, with lower prices typically appearing three to eight weeks before, making October a key time to book.
For Christmas, the best deals generally appear from late October through mid-November. The fares typically hit their lowest average point around 56 days out, which is five days earlier than last year's report. 
For domestic trips, the best time to book is 39 days ahead, while international flights are lowest around 89 days out, or three months. Waiting for a better price usually doesn't pay off.
For Europe, the lowest prices hit about 90 days out, with the lowest price range starting 49 days before departure.
For Mexico and the Caribbean, the lowest prices hit 43 days before departure, with the low-price range spanning 24 to 69 days.
The best days and dates to save on airfare
Looking for more ways to save? The day you buy matters less than you might think.
Google's analysis found Wednesday to be the cheapest day, but the savings compared with Sunday were minimal, at just 1.4 percent.
What may matter more is your travel schedule. But prioritize what matters most to you.
Departing Monday and returning Tuesday or Wednesday saved about 14 percent compared to weekend itineraries.
Connecting flights can also cut costs, with nonstop tickets averaging 20 percent more.
When to book for spring break and summer
For spring break, the lowest prices hit 56 days before departure, which was five days earlier than last year. The best deals fall between late-October and mid-November.
For summer vacation trips in July and August, the lowest prices hit 21 days before departure.

title: 3 Maine football storylines to follow against Campbell
text:
Make it six consecutive losses for the University of Maine football team. The Black Bears had their chances last week against visiting Bryant, but three fumbles were costly in a 17-14 defeat to the Bulldogs that assured Maine of a losing season.
Homecoming week for Maine pits the Black Bears (1-6, 1-3 Coastal Athletic Association) against 16th-ranked Campbell (6-1, 3-0 CAA) at 1 p.m. Saturday (FloSports). Here are three storylines ahead of Maine’s third consecutive home game:
Is Drezek the guy?
Until last week, Maine’s starting quarterback job still belonged to Eddie Buehler. The sophomore had started every game and was atop the depth chart the team released two days before the Bryant game.
But junior Caden Drezek played from start to finish against Bryant, completing 18 of 34 passes for 234 yards — most by a Maine QB this year — with a touchdown and no interceptions. Drezek had already been eating into Buehler’s playing time, so is the job now his?
“We have not decided on that yet,” coach Jordan Stevens said in the CAA press conference on Monday. “We’re going to meet with those guys and really decide how that’s going to play out this weekend.”
Maine defense has its hands full
It’s hard to pin too much of Maine’s losing streak on the defense. That unit hasn’t been perfect, but it has put the Black Bears in position to win many of those six games. Now comes a much bigger challenge.
Campbell is first in the CAA and 11th of 124 Football Championship Subdivision teams in yards per game (455). Senior quarterback Kamden Sixkiller is 10th in the FCS in passing yards with 1,899.
“Sixkiller is just doing an excellent job distributing the football,” Stevens said. “Their intensity is seen through the film, and that shows (in) how they block — how they block up front, how they block on the perimeter and how hard their backs run.”
Homecoming heroics?
If you’re looking for a good omen for the Black Bears against Campbell, consider what week it is. Homecoming has yielded great success recently for Maine, which has won nine consecutive homecoming games since losing to Yale in 2015.
Even some years of struggles have yielded homecoming wins for Maine, which won against Monmouth in 2022 and LIU in 2023 — both two-win seasons. Perhaps Saturday could produce similar magic for the Black Bears.

title: Cheverus, the Varsity Maine field hockey poll’s unanimous No. 1, turns attention to playoffs
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
As has been the case all season, Cheverus is the unanimous No. 1 team in the Varsity Maine field hockey poll. The Stags are undefeated (14-0) and take the top seed into the Class A South tournament. And they have won the past three state championships.
A fourth straight title won’t be easy. To win their region, the Stags will have to get past the likes of third-ranked Biddeford and Sanford/Kennebunk, who have each played Cheverus twice this season, and the Stags won all four matchups by only one goal. No. 8 Thornton Academy should also be in the mix.
Then there’s A North, which is topped by another unbeaten, second-ranked Mt. Ararat, and the Stags’ usual state title game foe, No. 4 Skowhegan. The Eagles and the River Hawks also have to survive ninth-ranked Camden Hills, which took Mt. Ararat to overtime on Tuesday.
The B North and B South tournaments could be even more chaotic. Nokomis, which moved up from eighth last week to No. 7, is B North’s top seed, but the Warriors might have to face two-time reigning state champion Belfast in the semifinals. Fifth-ranked Leavitt beat the top contenders in the region but finished a distant second to Nokomis. That means the Hornets will have a tough second-round matchup with third-seeded Cony or sixth-seeded Gardiner, which has shown itself to be more than capable of winning the region.
Sixth-ranked Yarmouth is B South’s No. 1, but Freeport, which rejoins the poll at No. 10, dealt the Clippers their first loss of the season on Monday. Those two squads also need to be wary of third-seeded Greely.

title: Kohen Wiley’s family pushes for federal investigation after baby’s shooting deemed justified
text:
SENATOBIA, Miss. (WMC/Gray News) - The family of 1-year-old Kohen Wiley is pushing to have the Department of Justice open an investigation into his death.
Kohen was shot and killed by a Senatobia police officer back on June 14 at the Senatobia Walmart parking lot.
Earlier this week, Mississippi Attorney General Lynn Fitch’s office announced the officer was justified in his actions.
The Wiley family is represented by civil rights attorneys Ben Crump and Van Turner. The two held a press conference alongside the Wiley family and community activists Thursday morning.
“I’m having a difficult time understanding the word justified. I just don’t understand,” said LaSandra Williams, Kohen’s paternal grandmother.
Williams and Kohen’s maternal grandmother, Veronica Roberson, say they remain heartbroken.
According to Crump’s team, the Wiley family was able to review all of the surveillance and body camera footage from the shooting provided by the Mississippi Bureau of Investigation Thursday morning.
“Disgusted me. First, I want to say, the word justified has haunted me since Monday,” said Roberson.
Roberson and Williams said they will not stop pushing for justice.
“We’re going to petition the Department of Justice to open an investigation to make sure that we get justice for this baby. It just won’t end here,” said Turner.
Turner and Crump said the videos from MBI match the results of their independent autopsy.
Kohen was shot through the side, right to left. According to Crump, MBI said a total of three bullets were fired.
“The third bullet from the side, the bullet that killed one-year-old baby Kohen Wiley, was not justified,” said Crump.
After being cleared by the Mississippi Attorney General, Senatobia Police Officer Hunter Foster reportedly resigned, according to Turner.
Kohen’s family, Crump’s team, and the community said they want Foster decertified.
“It’s not a white or Black issue. It’s a right or wrong issue,” said Brackin Camp. “This was way too much force; it’s unbelievable what happened in the Walmart parking lot that day.”
A special meeting was called by the Senatobia Board of Aldermen and the Mayor on Wednesday. WMC news crews were there; however, a motion was passed to turn the meeting into a closed executive session regarding police personnel.

title: Avid birders flock to Cape Elizabeth after rare grey heron sighted
text:
CAPE ELIZABETH — For a moment, no one spoke.
Eyes were glued to scopes, and binoculars were trained beyond the piles of mulch and gravel and fields of sprouting rows.
“Look at how white the thighs are,” Jose Ramirez, of Scarborough, said as he squinted into his scope. “This is the one.”
A grey heron. A bird seen for the first time in Maine on Sunday, Oct. 18.
To the uninitiated, it looks like a great blue heron, its distant relative. But grey herons, which are native to Europe, Africa and Asia, have white on the bend of their wings and thighs. Their more common counterparts have rusty red accents. Grey herons are daintier and more compact, with shorter legs and smaller bills.
And they are incredibly rare, especially on this continent.
There have been just a handful of grey heron sightings in North America ever (a couple in Alaska, a few in Canada). One was spotted on an island off the coast of Nantucket in 2020, the first time the bird made its way to the lower 48 states. Presumably that same bird was seen in Virginia a little while later.
But this time is different. This bird is hanging out in an accessible spot, in the fields and marsh that surround Jordan’s Farm in Cape Elizabeth, on the corner of Spurwink Avenue and Wells Road.
On a sunny Thursday afternoon, the heron was unknowingly hiding from a gaggle of birders, some of whom had traveled a long way in search of the bird.
The birders were patient. They traded field stories and chatted about other species they’ve chased. Tim and Erin Metcalf, who drove up from Richmond, Rhode Island, plan their vacations around spotting different species (They’re 29 states into seeing 100 birds in every state, and they’ve already crossed off big birding states like Texas and Arizona).
The heron strutted back into view, a diva returning to the spotlight. The crowd of onlookers excitedly followed it with their binoculars.
‘WE’VE ALL BEEN DYING TO SEE IT’
This part of Cape Elizabeth has become a zoo this past week, driven by a Beatlemania-like craze by birders from both Maine and away.
“It’s one of those birds we’ve all been dying to see for a long time,” said Doug Hitchcox, a naturalist with Maine Audubon.
Portland-based birder Peter Griffin first spotted the grey heron on Sunday. By Monday, people had already arrived from Massachusetts, New York and Connecticut to see it, according to Hitchcox.
Hitchcox set up a scope by the marsh on Monday from 6 a.m. to noon, and around 200 people came to take a peek. At times, the area has become a bit of a traffic nightmare, with some birders stopping their cars in the middle of the road, anxious to see the bird.
Liz Bullis, who works for Jordan’s Farm, said people from North Carolina, Connecticut and Pennsylvania have popped into the store to pick up donuts, apples and other snacks. Some of the farmers have named the bird Sheldon.
“If we served hot beverages, we’d be really popular,” she said. Each morning when she drives to work, the crowd — with different members each time — is back.
On Wednesday, Hitchcox spoke with an enthusiastic birder who flew in from Michigan, got a look at the bird and flew home the same day.
“That’s having a lot of faith that it would be there,” he said.
With each successive day that the heron remains here, birders from farther away grow more confident traveling to see it, Hitchcox said.
‘WORTH A SECOND LOOK’
It’s a difficult field identification.
Some juvenile great blue herons have pale patches, fooling even experienced birders.
It took hours of close observation and encouragement from a few birding friends before Griffin believed what he suspected: He had indeed spotted a grey heron.
“I had to explain this to my mom,” he said.
He drove by the bird, which was located 20 or 30 yards from the road, on his way to scope out other birds in a nearby pumpkin patch. Like many hobbyists, he got into birding during the COVID-19 pandemic, and his interest grew from there.
“A thought popped into my head that this one was worth a second look,” he said. “It seemed a little different.”
He snapped some photos when it flew away, which highlighted some of its trademark characteristics, like those vibrant white patches. He texted a friend: “There’s no way this is a grey heron, right?”
Other birders confirmed the sighting within a couple of hours.
And there’s photo evidence that this rare bird has been camping out in the marshy field since the beginning of October, under the noses of the many experienced birders who frequent this part of southern Maine, according to Hitchcox.
“It’s funny to think that people have seen it and probably thought ‘Oh, a great blue heron,’” Hitchcox said.
On a sunny Thursday afternoon, a group of birders gathered on the wrong side of a road near the Jordan’s Farm stand, about a hundred yards from another clump of birders. Their scopes were trained on the wrong bird. A friendly birder invited them to join the rest of the watchers.
No one knows how long the bird will stay, fueling a feverish desire to get to Cape Elizabeth as soon as possible. Some great blue herons in the area are already starting to migrate south.
“Birds have wings,” Hitchcox said. “They can disappear at any moment.”
Southern Maine has been no stranger to visits from rare birds.
In 2018, a great black hawk was sighted in Portland, a first in the North American record, and a statue was built in its honor after the hawk, which took up residence in Deering Oaks park, died.
A couple of years ago, a Steller’s sea eagle (nicknamed Stella), appeared in towns like Georgetown along the midcoast. Birders traveled from other countries to take a look at the giant eagle from Siberia with an eight-foot wingspan.
Maine Audubon has a Maine Rare Bird Alert group chat, which now has more than 4,000 members, that people can sign up for on their website. It’s the go-to source for minute-by-minute updates about the grey heron’s whereabouts.
Not all of those trying to catch a glimpse of the grey heron are fanatical birdwatchers.
Peter and Sara Merrill live in Cape Elizabeth, just a couple of miles from Jordan’s Farm. They perched their scope right next to their car.
They consider themselves “backyard birdwatchers.”
“Well, when this is your backyard,” Peter Merrill said, gesturing to the field as the heron stood gracefully in the distance, “you have to come take a look.”

title: AOC tells voters Troy Jackson will get billionaire influence out of politics
text:
PORTLAND — Onstage at the State Theater, before a lively crowd, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez repeatedly said the best antidote to the influence of the ruling class in Washington would be to elect Troy Jackson to the U.S. Senate.
“They’ve been afraid of a waitress in the House, and a logger in the United States Senate,” Ocasio-Cortez said. “So they want to critique how he talks, how he looks, the way he says things. Because if you’re not one of them, they at least want you to act like you are.”
The New York congresswoman, one of the most prominent members of the Democratic Party’s progressive wing, came to Portland on Thursday — less than two weeks before voters will decide between Jackson and Sen. Susan Collins — for an event billed as a students vs. billionaires town hall.
“When you have someone like Troy go to the United States Senate and call everything for what it is, it disrupts and makes it harder for everyone to get away with all the glad-handing that goes on over there,” she said.
The latest polls show Jackson leading slightly in a tight race against Collins, a five-term incumbent.
For a bit more than an hour, Ocasio-Cortez and Jackson took questions from local high school and college students, tackling topics from AI regulation to student debt to rural labor and delivery centers. While Ocasio-Cortez did most of the talking, bringing the crowd to its feet several times, Jackson cemented his stances on healthcare, Immigration and Customs Enforcement and U.S. aid for Israel.
Jackson said his first actions — were Democrats to take back the Senate — would be repealing President Donald Trump’s signature One Big Beautiful Bill Act to restore billions in Medicaid funding, then to push for Medicare for All.
He called for no more “blank checks to (Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin) Netanyahu,” for the abolition of ICE, and for an end to stock trading by members of Congress.
In response to a question from a Portland High School student about pitching progressive policies like Medicare for All to more rural or conservative communities in Maine, Jackson said people would get on board if presented with the facts.
“I just think we have to get the greed out of our healthcare system,” Jackson said. “It’s just taking the time to explain to people that you’re not going to get bad insurance, you’re going to get awesome insurance, and that we can do it, just don’t let these billionaires tell us differently.”
Both Ocasio-Cortez and Jackson delivered hits on Collins, especially on her voting record and her personal finances. Ocasio-Cortez told audience member Leah Hurwitz, an advocate against the closure of rural labor and delivery units, that Collins paved the way for hundreds of billions in healthcare cuts around the country by supporting the procedural motion to advance the Big Beautiful Bill to the floor. (Collins later voted against the bill, and she’s argued her procedural vote did nothing to affect its eventual passage.)
Hurwitz had asked about what could be done to stop the loss of maternal healthcare centers in the state. She said after the event that Ocasio-Cortez’s answer was a good open-ended response, but she was looking for more concrete solutions to bring back delivery services to rural communities that have lost them. She had a baby about 11 months ago at Lincoln Hospital, who was born breech. That hospital’s birthing center is now set to close by the end of the year.
“I know better than most,” she said. “Minutes mattered in my situation”
In response to a Bowdoin student’s question about how Jackson would stay in touch with Mainers from Washington, he criticized Collins’ reluctance to hold town hall events in the state, calling it “a major failing” of her tenure.
“It’s no secret that I’ve changed my opinion on a number of major issues,” Jackson said, alluding to his history of, among other things, opposing abortion. “I was presented with people who had better information, really made me think critically about where I was, and that I wouldn’t have gotten if I wasn’t willing to take the hard questions, go out and hear from people.”
In a race that could be decided by a small number of moderate swing voters, Republicans have attacked Jackson for courting national progressive heroes like Ocasio-Cortez; Bernie Sanders, who attended a Lewiston rally earlier this month; and Elizabeth Warren, who was in Portland over the weekend at a No Kings protest.
The town hall came one day after Collins emphasized her bipartisan credentials by hosting former Democratic Sen. Joe Manchin of West Virginia for lunch at a Lewiston hot dog stand.
Manchin, an old friend of Collins’ who left the Democratic Party in 2024, emphasized to reporters after their meal that Collins is “the most independent-minded person” he has ever met and described her as not a “Trump senator.”
On Wednesday, Maine GOP Chairman Jim Deyermond held a news conference criticizing Ocasio-Cortez’s visit to the state and Jackson’s alliance with her.
“AOC is far outside the mainstream of Maine politics. She is very, very far left, ” Deyermond said. “And that’s who Jackson is campaigning with here in Maine.”
It didn’t take long for Ocasio-Cortez to point out that sentiment herself at Thursday’s event. There are a lot of consultants in Washington that would tell Jackson not to sit on a stage next her, she said.
“It takes a lot to say, ‘You know what, I know my people, I know who I am, and I’m going to do things my way,”‘ Ocasio-Cortez said. “So thank you, Troy.”
“Why wouldn’t I want to sit alongside of someone who just talked like that,” Jackson said a few minutes later, after Ocasio-Cortez gave an impassioned response about military spending and domestic affordability.

title: Aging Untold: What caregivers can do when dementia makes meals difficult
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we explore how dementia can make eating challenging for your loved one and offer practical strategies to help at mealtime.
We discuss mental health support in later life and examine how moving past the stigma of therapy can promote healing at any age.
Finally, we visit a lively coastal ukulele band in South Carolina, spreading joy, friendship and tropical tunes throughout their community.
Eating can become more difficult for someone with dementia as the disease progresses.
It can disrupt the part of the brain that controls hunger, thirst and appetite signaling, Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said.
And the process of getting food to the mouth is complex, requiring motor skills and sensory response.
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said families can make meals easier by serving finger foods and being flexible.
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke added that caregivers should stay open to sudden changes in taste as well.
The idea of therapy can carry a stigma for some older adults.
Cradduck said many older adults were raised in a time when mental health was not discussed. It was often “hidden underneath the rug.”
O’Rourke said she does not use the word “therapy,” choosing to use other words instead.
She will say education or recommend taking a class or buying a book to introduce the older adult to the idea that talking might be helpful.
A parent’s decision about whether children should attend sleepovers can come down to weighing the childhood tradition against safety concerns.
Ukes by the Sea is bringing tropical vibes to the East Coast.
The ukulele group performs in South Carolina’s Grand Strand, where it is strumming its way into the hearts of listeners.
“We say that it’s difficult to play a ukulele and frown at the same time,” Tom Woodle, director of Ukes by the Sea, said. “And it’s got such a happy sound.”

title: Group urges Penobscot County voters to reject jail referendum
text:
Members of the No Penobscot County Jail Expansion group are asking local voters to reject a ballot measure that would allow a new county jail to be built in Hampden, outside the county seat.
Group member Larry Dansinger said the county should be spending its money on diversion programs instead of building a new facility to house more inmates.
“Vote no. Send a message to the county commissioners: We don’t want a new jail. We want fewer people in the jail, and we want money to be used instead for diversion, and not another high bill for county taxpayers,” he said.
County officials have argued that the population of the current jail is well over capacity and the number of inmates boarded out to other jails has skyrocketed in recent years.
Penobscot County Sheriff Troy Morton said the existing jail in Bangor only has 157 beds but the population averages about 230 inmates a day.
Speaking at a recent news conference, opponent Doug Dunbar said the county should expand diversion programs to reduce the number of people held at the jail.
“What helps people is treatment for mental health issues, for substance use disorder, help to get connected with housing resources, and that doesn’t happen in a building like this,” he said.
Dunbar was incarcerated at Penobscot County jail in 2017 for charges related to drunk driving. While there he participated in a diversion program that has helped him stay sober.
He wants to see that opportunity extended to more inmates.
The November referendum addresses the location of the jail but does not include additional funding.
This story appears through a media partnership with Maine Public.

title: Letter: Does Paul LePage live in the 2nd Congressional District?
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
It’s been widely reported that Paul LePage claims a legal address in an apartment above a car rental agency in Augusta. But is that where he and his wife retire at the end of the day and greet the morning sun?
Furthermore, he states he’s a “snowbird” (BDN Oct. 17-18 edition), an admission I believe that he doesn’t value full-time Maine state residence. Second Congressional District voters deserve a candidate who actually lives with them in the district he hopes to represent. A suggestion that he might purchase a home in Aroostook County if he is elected also hints that he might hightail it back to Florida, as he has done before, if he is not elected.
So does he live with us or not? His commitment to us seems pretty thin.
It’s long past the time for him to speak the truth and answer the question directly: as a candidate, does he live in the Second Congressional District with the voters he hopes to represent? It’s a question that needs a definitive answer.
David Wildes
Hancock

title: New study traces van Gogh's famed 'Starry Night' to an actual night sky from 1889
text:
New study traces van Gogh's famed 'Starry Night' to an actual night sky from 1889
Researchers say the scene may have been what van Gogh saw as he gazed up from a French asylum
New study traces van Gogh's famed 'Starry Night' to an actual night sky from 1889
Researchers say the scene may have been what van Gogh saw as he gazed up from a French asylum
Scientists doubling as art detectives have traced Vincent van Gogh's "The Starry Night" to a celestial scene that suggests a new date for one of the world's most famous paintings.
Related video above: Insect found in decades-old van Gogh painting
Their findings indicate that rather than being a product of van Gogh's imagination, "The Starry Night" may have been inspired by what he saw as he gazed heavenward from his French asylum 137 years ago.
A South Korean team reported Thursday that after years of forensic astronomy and research into the Dutch artist, they have matched his masterpiece to a predawn sky over France's Saint-Rémy de Provence right around July 22, 1889.
That's a month later than the long-accepted timeframe for the postimpressionist painting depicting a crescent moon and Venus surrounded by a sky of swirling stars with a village nestled below and cypress trees looming on one side.
Art historians have long dated the painting to June 1889, soon after Van Gogh checked into the asylum. He'd cut off his left ear several months earlier during an argument with painter Paul Gauguin.
A team led by Elijah Jeong-hyun Kim, the CEO of a Seoul telescope maker, is now disputing that date in a study appearing in the journal Scientific Reports.
The sky that is most similar to the painting occurred around July 22, 1889, said Kim, who is also a doctoral candidate at Kyung Hee University. He noted that the few days before and after could have inspired van Gogh as well.
"No two skies are the same. Something always changes. I believe Vincent noticed those changes and put them into the painting," Kim said in an email.
He added: "I am confident that July 22 is the better date. I will bet on this date."
The latest study addresses "a real puzzle" around the fact that in mid-June 1889, the moon was not the thin crescent painted by van Gogh, said Jose Luis Aragon at the National Autonomous University of Mexico. He has studied "The Starry Night" as a physicist, but did not take part in the new research.
"Still, I would see the July date as an intriguing hypothesis rather than a settled answer," Aragon said in an email.
Long fascinated by van Gogh's art, Kim traveled to France in 2019, the first time in mid-June and the second around July 22. He found brilliant stars rising in July's predawn sky, unlike June.
Kim and his team discovered through further celestial sleuthing that around July 22, 1889, the shape of the moon before dawn appeared like the one in the painting, with the Hyades star cluster in the constellation Taurus rising in the east alongside Venus. The sky should have been clear enough for van Gogh to see all this, based on their weather analyses.
Van Gogh is thought to have suffered a seizure around that time in July. But Kim and his team contend that the seizure occurred later in July, based on their analyses of letters between the painter and one of his brothers. Some of those letters refer to cicadas, another clue that points toward the hotter July, according to Kim.
The researchers tested and verified their methods on night skies in other paintings, making for what Aragon considers "a careful and genuinely interdisciplinary study."
Since van Gogh painted in a studio at the asylum from sketches and memory, "the sky is likely a composite of many nights as the authors themselves acknowledge," Aragon said.
"What I find most convincing is the broader message: The painting is not pure fantasy. Van Gogh watched the real sky very closely," Aragon said.
Despite all his research, Kim has never seen "The Starry Night" at the Museum of Modern Art in New York.
"Now that the paper is out, I really have to go and see 'The Starry Night' in person, don't I?" he said.

title: Meta ordered to pay New Mexico $25 billion for deceiving users about privacy on Facebook
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(AP) - A judge on Wednesday ordered Meta to pay New Mexico $25 billion after a jury found the company liable for deceiving users about privacy on Facebook, marking the biggest fine ever against the tech giant.
Facebook’s deception was intentional and executives consistently misled users about how the platform worked, state District Court Judge Francis J. Mathew wrote in his ruling.
“Facebook promised users that they (the users) controlled their data. This was false,” he said.
Jurors in September found Meta liable for over 43 million violations of New Mexico consumer protection laws for making misleading public statements about how it handled users’ personal data. The case was brought after political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica harvested Facebook data to generate targeted political ads during the 2016 election season.
The award will serve as a warning to tech companies that New Mexico will hold them accountable, state Attorney General Raúl Torrez said at a news conference.
“This judgment should be a signal, an unambiguous message, to Silicon Valley,” he said.
Meta said the ruling and Torrez’s office’s approach to enforcement “makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico.”
“At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online. We are confident we will prevail on appeal,” C.J. Mahoney, the company’s chief legal officer, said in a statement.
The Menlo Park, California, company has a market value of $1.8 trillion and brought in more than $200 billion in revenue last year. Company shares traded 2% higher after Wednesday’s announcement, and it was scheduled to report its quarterly earnings later in the day.
New Mexico goes it alone
In August, Meta reached a settlement with nearly all states and territories — except New Mexico and Florida — to pay $18 billion and add stronger child-safety measures to its Facebook and Instagram platforms.
The settlement ended a trial over teen social media addiction and resolved a pivotal case years in the making that sought to hold the tech giant accountable for the role its platforms played in undermining children’s mental health. The effort targeted features designed to grab young people’s attention.
New Mexico didn’t join the multistate settlement, choosing to go after the company on its own.
The director of a nonprofit that supports stronger policies toward corporations said $25 billion is “a drop in the bucket for Meta,” but demonstrates people want accountability.
“Right now, they are rolling out Muse, an AI assistant encouraging people to trust it with everything from their bank accounts to their medical information,” added Nidhi Hegde, executive director of the American Economic Liberties Project. “Which is why we need more enforcers with courage and laws with actual teeth to rein them in.”
At the trial, attorneys for the state cited a 2010 Washington Post op-ed in which Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg wrote that the company didn’t sell user data.
“You have control over how your information is shared,” Zuckerberg said. “We do not and never will sell any of your information to anyone.”
New Mexico officials sought fines of $35 billion to $40 billion, arguing the company would only change if its stock price were impacted.
Meta’s lawyers, meanwhile, asserted that the state failed to prove the company made misleading statements and that content moderation actually harmed people in New Mexico. They wanted the company to pay $3.4 billion at most and said an award many times larger would be unconstitutional.
Although interest would accrue on the penalty during the appeal process, Meta could succeed in reducing the number of violations for which it is found liable.
The $25 billion award far exceeds a $5 billion fine the Federal Trade Commission levied against Facebook in 2019.
Peter Ormerod, an associate law professor at Villanova University, was surprised by the size of the New Mexico judgment because previous legal settlements over Cambridge Analytica were much lower.
“It comes out to about $12,000 per person in New Mexico,” he said. “It’s quite unlike anything else we’ve seen.”
Under the New Mexico Constitution, fines for violating consumer protection laws go toward education spending. It could take years for the state to get the money while the company appeals.
Company argues that the state failed to prove harm
The trial focused on accusations Facebook deceived users about a breach stemming from a third-party personality quiz that harvested data from roughly 87 million profiles and sold it to Cambridge Analytica. The now-defunct firm’s clients included Donald Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign.
Attorneys for New Mexico argued that the state’s entire population was deceived, and that Facebook allowed misinformation or violent content to proliferate.
Meta’s lawyers argued the state failed to prove people were harmed by deceptive statements. Zuckerberg in a video deposition denied that Facebook profited off harmful content and said the company had to balance free speech with content moderation.
In a partial win for the company, jurors rejected assertions that Facebook made false claims about removing harmful content, including misinformation about the COVID-19 pandemic.
Meta lawyers said it has changed policies since the lawsuit was filed in 2021 and catches and removes an estimated 99% of content violating its standards.
___

title: 100.3 WKIT forecaster returns to Bangor to sign calendars for charity
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Fans lined up before dawn to meet a Bangor radio personality and support a cause he started decades ago.
Longtime weather forecaster Jim Witt, who lives in New York, returned to Chase’s Restaurant to sign his long range calendars. Witt is heard on the Rock and Roll Morning Show on 100.3 WKIT FM in Bangor.
Proceeds from the calendars benefit Witt’s HOPE for Youth Foundation, which he founded to help children in the Hudson Valley. The foundation has raised more than $7 million.
“Many years ago, a fella on a different radio station liked the long range forecasts and said is there some way that we can make money on it? I said well, I can do a calendar. He said that’s great. I said the only stipulation is the money we make does not come to you or me, or anybody else but the kids. He said that’s fine with me and that was 42 years ago. So since then I’ve done 42 calendars,” Witt said.
“It’s very impressive. I love having him come and if they want to eat breakfast they can and I hope we can do it again,” said Terri Chase, owner of Chase’s Restaurant.
Witt’s calendar sale is the largest annual fundraiser for the HOPE for Youth Foundation.

title: Bangor Beautiful plants native trees, removes invasive species at farmers market
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - The Bangor Farmer’s Market is a favorite spot for many during the fall. One organization is helping to plant trees to make the spot a little more beautiful.
Sixteen tree saplings were planted Thursday morning by the Bangor Beautiful nonprofit. Native plants like pitched pine and serviceberry trees were provided by Maine Audubon.
The organization also helped to remove invasive plant species in the area, including burning bush and buck thorn. The new, native plant species will not only help create ecosystems, but help to reduce runoff, making sidewalks more pedestrian friendly.
“We can’t let our native species decline because the invasive species are coming in. We want to create habitat. This ecosystem needs native plants so that we can feed the caterpillars that feed the birds that make us all happy in the end,” said Bangor Beautiful President Annette Dodd.
The organization had also repainted a shipping container in the area earlier this year. Bangor Beautiful will be planting more trees in the area this coming spring.
You can learn more by reaching out to Bangor Beautiful on their website and Facebook page.

title: Former NHL star Ron Duguay, known later for relationship with Sarah Palin, dies of cancer at 69
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Ron Duguay, who played nearly 1,000 games in the NHL from the late 1970s through the ’80s, has died of cancer. He was 69.
A spokesperson for the New York Rangers said Thursday that Duguay’s family informed the team of his death.
Duguay played his first six seasons with the Rangers after they selected him with the 13th pick in the draft in 1977. The Sudbury, Ontario, native was an All-Star as a point-a-game producer in 1981-82.
A series of trades led him to spend time with the Detroit Red Wings, Pittsburgh Penguins and Los Angeles Kings with another Rangers stint, as well. Duguay finished his career in the league with 673 points in the regular season and playoffs, then played in Germany and the minors.
“The New York Rangers organization mourns the loss of Ron Duguay, one of the most popular players in franchise history,” the club said in a statement. “Ron’s signature skating style — with his hair flowing as he moved down the ice — captivated the (Madison Square) Garden faithful, and his skill, tenacity and charisma earned him the admiration of all New Yorkers. We join the hockey community in sending our condolences to Ron’s friends, family and loved ones during this difficult time.”
Duguay was known late in life away from hockey for dating former Alaska governor and 2008 Republican U.S. vice presidential nominee Sarah Palin. His family started a GoFundMe earlier this year to offset the costs of travel and treatments.
“It’s with a shattered heart but also deep peace knowing Ron is with Jesus now,” Palin posted on social media. “He fought so hard. Love never ends.”

title: Sen. Susan Collins and Troy Jackson condemn use of attack ads in Maine’s Senate race
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WMTW) - Both candidates running for the U.S. Senate in Maine condemned attack ads against each other on Wednesday.
Republican incumbent Sen. Susan Collins spent Wednesday morning campaigning with former Sen. Joe Manchin, a longtime Democrat from West Virginia who became an independent just months before departing the Senate in January 2025.
“This is a United States senator who basically is a Maine senator,” Manchin said. “She’s not a Trump senator. She’s not a Republican senator or a Democrat senator. She’s an American senator.”
Collins was asked about a recent radio advertisement that was paid for by the Senate Leadership Fund PAC.
The ad was to the tune of a song and included lyrics such as: “If he screws his own family, he’ll screw yours too.”
“Well, first of all, I had nothing to do with that ad, and I said that it should be taken down,” Collins said.
Collins said that she cannot legally contact the PAC. She added that she had nothing to do with the advertisement.
Collins was first elected to the Senate in 1996. She said this race has not been like one she’s ever been involved with before.
“This campaign has been unique in Maine’s history, in the number of personal attacks,” Collins said. “I’ve been accused of all sorts of things.”
In Augusta, several women, many of whom worked with Jackson in the Maine Legislature, gathered to host a “Women for Troy” event.
The speakers pointed toward the radio ad along with a separate anti-Jackson television ad. They said that ad portrayed the former lawmakers as “victims and villains.”
According to the group, this wasn’t their experience with Jackson in Augusta.
“He lifted up the voices of women,” said former Democratic state lawmaker Rebecca Millett. “He appointed them into leadership positions. He trusted us with the important work of leading powerful committees and our colleagues.”
Many members of the group also spoke on the unique style of attack ads in the Senate race. Some also said the level of the advertisements was at a level they’ve never seen before.
“They can’t defend Susan Collins’ record, so they are resorting to personal attacks,” Millett said. “This TV ad and the disgusting radio ad that goes along with it reek of desperation. And it says a lot more about Sen. Collins and her backers than it says about Troy.”
Jackson wasn’t in attendance for Wednesday’s event. His campaign spokesperson Dan Gottlieb provided a statement in response to the radio advertisement.
In part, Gottlieb said in his statement: “If Collins believes these attacks are wrong, she owes Troy’s family an apology for spreading them herself and must take responsibility for her allies pushing the same personal attack on his family on TV right now.”
Maine Women’s Lobby also spoke at the event, publicly endorsing Jackson. Members of the lobby mentioned Jackson’s voting record and their approval of his work in childcare and the state’s paid family and medical leave program.

title: Gas tax holidays will be paid for by road users
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
At this point in time, roughly one-third of the states (at the president’s urging) have passed emergency legislation reducing or suspending the taxes they impose on gasoline. This reduces the short-run cost of gasoline borne by the public.
Simultaneously, the president, by executive order, has reduced the federal tax on some diesel fuels for a similar purpose, i.e., reducing the short-run cost of these fuels. When and whether these steps (said to be temporary) will be rescinded is unknown. Tellingly, no supplementary revenue source to maintain the nation’s highway infrastructure has been offered by the president.
What President Trump and now one-third of the states have failed to acknowledge is that gasoline and diesel tax dollars are committed to the building and repair of essential roads and bridges in all 50 states. In most states, these budgets are already underfunded. Shrinking these budgets puts all users of our highway infrastructure at greater risk.
Bear in mind, too, that shrinking highway maintenance budgets does not stop the deterioration of our highway infrastructure that present levels of use give rise to. In short, the president’s tactic is both disingenuous and dangerous. Lives will be lost. He has sent a third of the states on a fool’s errand. One can only hope Maine will not be joining them.
Orlando Delogu
Portland

title: Federal regulators can't police campaign finance violations during midterms due to vacancies
text:
Federal regulators can't police campaign finance violations during midterms due to vacancies
The Federal Election Commission hasn't been able to launch investigations or issue penalties for well over a year.
Federal regulators can't police campaign finance violations during midterms due to vacancies
The Federal Election Commission hasn't been able to launch investigations or issue penalties for well over a year.
A record amount of money is pouring into the midterm elections, but there's currently no cop on the beat.
The Federal Election Commission is charged with policing campaign finance laws, but it has been unable to conduct investigations or issue penalties for well over a year.
That's because the agency doesn't have enough commissioners to hold a vote. President Donald Trump fired the Democratic chair last year, and three other Republicans on the panel resigned for different reasons. Currently, two commissioners remain in place.
Trump announced two nominees earlier this year, which would be enough to restore enforcement, but their approval has stalled in the Senate for months.
In a statement dated Feb. 18, 2026, Senate Rules Committee Chairman Mitch McConnell (R-KY) praised Trump's picks and promised a "timely hearing and confirmation process."
"A functioning FEC is essential to maintaining the integrity and transparency of our federal elections, and restoring a quorum is an important step toward that goal," McConnell wrote.
McConnell returned to Capitol Hill last month after an extended absence due to health issues. 
Asked if a confirmation hearing would be scheduled before the current Congress ends in January, a spokesperson for McConnell, David Popp, wrote in an email, "I’ll be sure to let you know if I have any scheduling announcements or guidance for you."
Sen. Alex Padilla of California, the top Democrat on the committee, didn't immediately respond to a request for comment on Wednesday.
Meanwhile, the FEC's latest quarterly report shows there are 307 pending cases.
Adav Noti, a former FEC lawyer who currently serves as executive director of the Campaign Legal Center, says enforcement at the agency was lacking before the vacancies.
"The voter perception that there's something wrong with the system isn't just a product of the FEC being sort of non-functional right at this moment. It's a much longer-term issue of the rules going unenforced and voters going unprotected," Noti said.
Noti said there is a five-year window for legal action after an alleged violation occurs, meaning the FEC will still have an opportunity for enforcement after new commissioners have been installed.
"At that point, the spending will have already happened, and voters will have already had a full election without the benefit of the transparency or the protection that the FEC is supposed to provide," Noti said.
Trump accused of campaign finance violation
The Campaign Legal Center recently filed a complaint stemming from Trump's statements that he "controls" money collected by the super PAC MAGA, Inc. It alleges that these comments amount to a "remarkable admission of a serious campaign finance violation," pointing to rules barring federal officeholders from operating groups that aren't subject to contribution limits.
"If somebody is giving millions of dollars, or tens of millions of dollars, or in the case of Elon Musk, hundreds of millions of dollars, there is a very high likelihood that that money could corrupt the officeholders who it's benefiting," Noti said.
The White House didn't immediately respond to a request for comment on Wednesday, nor did MAGA, Inc.
Other vacancies not expected to impact midterms
Trump also removed members of the U.S. Election Assistance Commission earlier this year. The agency currently has no sitting members.
Matt Weil, vice president of the Bipartisan Policy Center's Governance Program, said those vacancies are not expected to have a big impact on the midterm elections.
Weil, a former policy analyst at the EAC, said that agency staff can continue certifying voting systems and distributing federal election funds. However, he said the vacancies could slow down future updates to voting equipment standards.
"Certainly, for this election and even for the next election, the standards are not going to be changed, and you're not going to be voting on different equipment than you would have been if the EAC commissioners were there," Weil said, "But in the long term, this will slow down the next update for voting system guidelines, and it will lengthen the timeline before we'll see new voting system equipment."

title: Just like the temperatures, summer home prices rose across much of central Maine
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
During what is typically the busiest season for residential real estate transactions, the market across central and western Maine showed mixed signals, with higher home prices in most counties but uneven sales volume.
According to the Maine Association of Realtors, median prices increased or held steady across counties in this publication’s coverage area during the three-month period ending Aug. 31, 2026, compared with the same period in 2025.
Kennebec County recorded the largest price increase among the five counties, rising 10.36% to $365,000 since last year. The county also had the greatest number of completed sales, with 420 single-family homes changing hands, four fewer than a year earlier.
Franklin County followed with an 8.06% increase in median sale price, reaching $337,700, although sales declined 3.08%.
Somerset County remained the most affordable of the five markets, with a median sale price of $251,250. But it experienced the strongest growth in sales activity, with 188 homes sold, an increase of 11.24% from the previous year.
In Oxford County, the median sale price climbed 4.62% to $342,500, while the number of homes sold remained nearly unchanged at 207.
Androscoggin County’s median price held steady at $360,000, but sales volume declined 7.14%, from 308 homes to 286.
Statewide, the median price for existing single-family homes reached $429,000 during the June-August period, up 2.75% from a year earlier. Sales increased 1.92%, to 4,831 homes.
The figures illustrate why looking at sale prices alone does not capture the differences among Maine’s regional housing markets. Higher prices do not necessarily translate into more transactions, and the number of homes changing hands can vary considerably even between neighboring counties.
Source: Maine Association of Realtors and Maine Listings. Figures represent existing single-family home sales from June 1 through Aug. 31, 2026, compared with the same period in 2025. Statistics are subject to revisions from late reporting

title: Cop accused of taking control of deceased man's home after welfare check
text:
Police officer accused of creating scheme to take control of deceased man's home after welfare check
A Florida police officer is facing felony charges after officials said a welfare check led to a scheme in which the officer tried to take control of an individual's home following his death.
Related video: QR code scams
The Broward Sheriff’s Office said Brian Louis Sguros, 35, a Lauderhill police officer, responded as backup officer for a welfare check at a home in the area on July 11, 2022.
Officials said 71-year-old Dennis West was found dead inside the home. He died of natural causes.
Following West's death, detective said Sguros became involved in the individual's post-death affairs, saying he represented himself to the Broward County Medical Examiner’s Office as West’s friend.
Sguros stated to the medical examiner's office that West had no living family.
The department said there is no indication they both knew each other, and that West still has living family members.
The investigation revealed that Sguros paid the taxes and utilities at the home in West’s name and used West’s identification to make it appear that he was still alive to get the city of Lauderhill to issue a permit to facilitate repairs.
In addition, the department said the officer forged West's signature on the permit.
According to investigators, Sguros also filed paperwork with Broward County Property Appraiser in Feb. 2025, stating his possession of the property dated back to Aug. 2022, just weeks after West’s death.
Authorities took Sguros into custody on Oct. 20, 2026.
He faces several charges, including official misconduct, criminal use of deceased personal identification, criminal use of personal identification information, offense against a computer user and unlawful use of a two-way communication device.
An investigation into the incident remains ongoing.

title: Discussion focuses on employee performance evaluations
text:
Woolwich selectmen are revising the way they conduct employee performance evaluations and considering implementing a similar review process for first responders. The board met with the town administrator to talk over changes to its policy Wednesday afternoon, Oct. 21.
Selectman Tommy Davis, who has been drafting the changes, said the revisions were long overdue. One of the initial steps he explained is for the selectboard to bring its evaluation process in line with other municipalities. He recommended they begin by having employees complete a “self-evaluation” prior to their yearly performance review. Davis recommended dropping a scoring method the selectboard had been using and introduce a written process on which to base salary adjustments, training and corrective action.
The selectboard currently doesn’t require performance evaluations for fire department and EMS employees, although that could change starting in the new year. Selectman Dale Chadbourne, however, wasn’t convinced evaluations for first responders were needed. “Why? That’s the responsibility of the fire chief and EMS director,” he commented. Fire Chief Shaun Merrill and EMS Director Danny Evarts were unable to attend the meeting.
Selectman Jason Shaw thanked Davis for the research and work he’d done. “My thought is, we as a board enter into this new evaluation process slowly,” he commented.
In his monthly report to the selectboard, Evarts wrote the ambulance department responded to 13 calls so far in October. Thirteen patients were seen, 10 were transported, and MC1 was called eight times. Evarts noted the department will be holding a cardiac training session Nov. 8 at the municipal building.
A wire cage containing free firewood provided by Midcoast Wood Bank has been removed from the parking area across from the town office. “We’re not dropping out of the program. We’ll continue to have information about it at the town office. We’re just no longer interested in having the cage sitting out front,” David King Sr., selectboard chairman, told Wiscasset Newspaper. “We weren’t able to find anyone in the community willing to volunteer their time to refill the cage which was a condition of having it.” An “all-volunteer” non-profit organization, Midcoast Wood Bank based in Topsham offers up to two cords per household of free firewood to residents in need as a source of winter heat. The cage contained split firewood residents were permitted to help themselves to. Residents needing firewood assistance, or information about the program, can call Midcoast Wood Bank at 207-800-1658 or email the organization at info@midcoastwoodbank.org
In other business, the board renewed a recreational cannabis license for Landrace Cannabis Co. on Route One.
Selectmen are hoping for a large turnout when the Station 46 Bridge is renamed the “Veterans Memorial Bridge" at 11 a.m. Saturday, Nov. 14. The ceremony will take place in the parking area of the Taste of Maine Restaurant beneath the osprey nest. The selectboard has invited Smith-Tobey American Legion Post 21 and Veterans of Foreign Wars Post 7738, both based in Bath, to attend the dedication ceremony. Nina Ryan, a Woolwich resident, has been asked to sing the national anthem. Woolwich’s annual Veterans Day program will take place as usual at 11 a.m. Wednesday, Nov. 11 at Nequasset Meetinghouse.

title: Powerful Democratic Virginia lawmaker accused of leading a marijuana criminal conspiracy, money laundering
text:
NORFOLK, Va. (AP) — Virginia state Sen. L. Louise Lucas, one of the state’s most powerful Democrats, was charged Thursday with leading what authorities alleged was a wide-ranging criminal enterprise that acquired and distributed large quantities of marijuana and laundered the proceeds.
Lucas, who has been in elected office for decades, used her political power to insulate the operation from scrutiny, according to an indictment charging her and six other defendants, including several of her relatives. She “put her own financial interests before the people she was elected to serve,” said U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche, who spoke at a news conference with FBI Director Kash Patel.
Lucas surrendered, the Justice Department said. She made a brief appearance in federal court in Norfolk on Thursday afternoon, where she was released on her own recognizance, according to court records. She left the court without addressing journalists who shouted questions her way and went straight into a waiting vehicle.
The charges, including drug trafficking and money laundering, came after the FBI searched Lucas’ hometown office and a cannabis shop in which she has a stake in May. At the time of the search, Lucas — who has been a vocal critic of Republican President Donald Trump’s administration — characterized it as an attempt to intimidate her.
Lucas says she won’t be bullied by the federal government
A statement attributed to Lucas posted on her social media account did not directly address the substance of the charges but said Thursday’s actions amounted to the federal government wielding its “full weight” against a great-grandmother.
“I will not be intimidated. I will not be bullied. And I will not back down,” Lucas said in the statement. Her attorney at the hearing declined comment outside.
The brash 82-year-old lawmaker has spent decades ascending the ranks of Virginia politics and has served since 1992 in the state Senate, where she’s the president pro tempore, overseeing the chamber in the lieutenant governor’s absence. More significantly, she leads the powerful Senate finance committee, through which all legislation with any budget impact must flow. She’s used the position to kill legislation she opposes.
Justice Department denies politics played a role
The indictment comes as Trump’s Justice Department has faced intense scrutiny over investigations and prosecutions against foes of the president that critics have called politically motivated.
Blanche rejected any suggestion politics played a role in Lucas’ case, noting the investigation began well before the second Trump administration started in January 2025.
“We don’t do political paybacks,” Blanche told reporters.
A person familiar with the May search told The Associated Press at the time that the probe was opened during Democratic President Joe Biden’s administration. The person spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss a continuing criminal investigation.
FBI alleges a ‘criminal marijuana enterprise’
Patel said in a statement that “Lucas and a close-knit group of family members and associates orchestrated a multi-year scheme to enrich their own criminal marijuana enterprise, ‘the Lucas Enterprise’ — using Lucas’ position as Chairwoman of the Senate Finance and Appropriations Committee to insulate the enterprise from criminal scrutiny and influencing legislation to financially benefit themselves.”
The indictment describes Lucas as the “leader of the enterprise” who “approved and directed criminal activities,” including arranging for the acquisition and distribution of marijuana and supervising the laundering of the proceeds.
The indictment alleges Lucas worked this year with another of the defendants to use her political position to obtain a recreational marijuana license for him, with the understanding that the proceeds from sales under the license would be shared with her to support the “enterprise.”
Since 2021, marijuana has been legal to possess in Virginia, and many shops across the state have sold cannabis-derived products. But full recreational sales are not yet underway; legislation enacted earlier this year will allow them beginning in July 2027.
Law enforcement made multiple controlled purchases of marijuana from Lucas’ shop, which purported to sell hemp products, in 2024 and 2025, the indictment said.
In addition to drug and money laundering charges, Lucas faces charges of racketeering conspiracy, conspiracy to commit honest services fraud and maintaining a drug-involved premises. An arraignment is scheduled for next month.
Among the other defendants who face a mix of those and other charges are two daughters, Lisa Lucas Burke and Theresa Lucas-Lamb, and a grandson, Ryan Eichelberger. All three also made brief court appearances and were released on their recognizance, according to court records.
Attorneys for Lucas-Lamb and Eichelberger declined comment; Andrew Sacks, who was listed in court records as an attorney for Burke, didn’t respond to requests for comment. Attorneys for two other defendants who are not family members declined comment; a third who was also released Thursday had no attorney listed in court records.
Virginia officials react
A forceful advocate of legalizing marijuana, Lucas partnered in opening the shop, The Cannabis Outlet, in 2021. She has publicly spoken about her ownership stake as recently as June, though her most recent financial disclosure forms do not list the business by name.
At the time of the search — when marijuana was recovered at The Cannabis Outlet, according to the indictment — many Democrats spoke up to defend Lucas.
On Thursday, Scott Surovell, the Democratic leader of the state Senate, said in a statement that the indictment contained “serious allegations” but emphasized that “Senator Lucas has the right to defend herself, and she has my full support as she does so.” Attorney General Jay Jones, a Democrat who is close with Lucas, said the allegations against her must be tested in a “full and fair” legal process.
House Speaker Don Scott, Lt. Gov. Ghazala Hashmi, and Gov. Abigail Spanberger, all Democrats, echoed those sentiments, with Spanberger adding that the timing of the indictment so close to the midterm election would “further erode” Americans’ trust in the Justice Department. Lucas herself is not on the ballot this year.
Ryan McDougle, the Senate Republican leader, said he would not comment while the court proceedings play out.
The senator draws comparisons to Trump
Lucas, who represents a district that includes her hometown of coastal Portsmouth, operates with a sometimes-profane, unapologetic style that’s drawn comparisons to Trump.
She amassed a six-figure following on X and national attention, using the social media platform to advocate forcefully for her priorities and to bash her critics, including former GOP Gov. Glenn Youngkin. She’s also occasionally blasted members of her own party, including Spanberger, with whom she’s had disagreements.
Earlier this year, Lucas helped lead Democrats’ ultimately unsuccessful plan to gerrymander the blue-leaning state’s congressional districts into a map intended to elect 10 Democrats and only one Republican. Along the way, she posted quips about four GOP members the intended map sought to oust, joking that they soon would be working at McDonald’s. She and other Democrats defended the maps as a reasonable response to Trump-backed efforts to boost the GOP’s midterm advantage in other states.
Lucas has been in politics for decades
Lucas has notched several historic firsts in her career. According to a biography from the state library, in 1971 she became the Norfolk Naval Shipyard’s first female shipfitter, a physically demanding job that involves working on metal assemblies for vessels.
She launched her political career in 1984, when, the biography said, she became the first Black woman elected to the Portsmouth city council.
After Democrats flipped control of the Senate in 2019, her peers elected her to serve as president pro tempore. And in 2024, she was tapped to lead the chamber’s budget committee.
___
Rankin reported from Richmond. Associated Press journalists Eric Tucker in Washington and Steve Helber in Norfolk contributed to this report.

title: ‘Gloves are off’ in Maine’s U.S. Senate race
text:
ORONO, Maine (WABI) - The gloves are off in Maine’s U.S. Senate race.
UMaine Political Science Professor Mark Brewer says advertising is getting more aggressive, and the debates between Sen. Susan Collins and Troy Jackson have gotten testy, with both candidates complaining about personal attacks.
“In Maine at least this is still somewhat unusual. Maine politics tend to be more civil on the whole,” Brewer said. “If you look at American politics more broadly, we’ve almost been now in two decades plus period where the gloves are always off. Our politics haven’t been civil for quite some time.”
Brewer says it just takes a little longer for that tenor to reach Maine, but it shouldn’t be a surprise to anyone watching national politics in recent years.
He thought this week’s visit to Maine by Democrat-turned-Independent Joe Manchin with Collins may have curried favor with undecided voters.
He thinks the high-profile appearance by Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez stumping for Jackson in Portland will not have a similar impact.

title: Perturbed by investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar
text:
I recently read that Homeland Security is looking into Congresswoman Ilhan Omar’s immigration background, possibly trying to take away her citizenship and deport her. This really bothers me.
Ilhan Omar became an American citizen in 2000. She has been a citizen for more than 25 years and was elected to Congress. What about, say, Melania Trump?
In 2016, the Associated Press reported that Melania was paid for modeling work before she had authorization to work in this country. Her attorney disputed that report. She did not become an American citizen until July 2006, several months after Barron was born, although she was legally living here at the time.
Why is our government digging into Ilhan Omar’s past while questions about Melania Trump’s earlier employment history seem forgotten?
I’m not suggesting anyone be deported without proof of wrongdoing. But shouldn’t the same rules apply to everyone? If Homeland Security can investigate one person’s immigration history, why not another’s, especially where questions have been raised?
I find this disappointing. Being married to the president should not result in special treatment, just as disagreeing with him should not result in being treated differently.
I was brought up believing nobody is above the law. I still believe that. Our immigration laws should be enforced fairly, regardless of who we are or whom we’re married to.
Ralph Duquette
Old Orchard Beach
