title: An mRNA cancer vaccine helps reduce the chances of melanoma patients' tumors returning
text:
An mRNA cancer vaccine helps reduce the chances of melanoma patients' tumors returning
A first-of-its-kind cancer vaccine is significantly reducing the chances that melanoma patients' tumors come back, according to results of a major study released Thursday by drugmakers Moderna and Merck.
Video above: Hep B vaccine policy changes spark concerns for U.S. infants
The vaccine was custom-brewed for each patient to match their tumor. Adding it to a standard post-surgery treatment reduced by 42% the risk of melanoma returning two years after surgery, according to the most advanced study to date of this new strategy for fighting cancer.
"The field has been looking for a win, and I think this one is a big one," said Dr. Hussein Tawbi of MD Anderson Cancer Center in Houston, one of the researchers in the international study.
The vaccine, called intismeran, is made with the same Nobel Prize-winning mRNA technology that was behind COVID-19 vaccines. Experimental personalized cancer vaccines made with mRNA and some other approaches also are being tested against other types of cancer.
Experts not involved with the new study say its success bolsters the field.
"This is a new frontier," said Karen Knudsen, CEO of the Parker Institute, which helps fund cancer immunotherapy research.
"It's a big step forward for science, for oncology, because this vaccine will apply to many different cancers," said Dr. Michael Atkins, deputy director of Georgetown University's Lombardi Comprehensive Cancer Center.
Moderna and Merck had announced in August that the late-stage trial of intismeran was successful, but the detailed results were set to be released Saturday at a meeting of the European Society of Medical Oncology in Madrid. Some of the data was leaked publicly late Thursday, prompting a full release ahead of the weekend's scientific presentation.
Most people think of vaccines as preventing an infection, like measles or whooping cough. There are already two cancer-preventing vaccines — the HPV and hepatitis B shots that block infection from those tumor-causing viruses. And research is underway to prevent some types of inherited cancer such as Lynch syndrome-caused colorectal cancer.
But a personalized vaccine designed to block surgically-removed cancer from returning is very different. For the intismeran study, scientists hunted gene mutations unique to each patient's tumor, mutations that create proteins which shouldn't be in the body unless those cancer cells start to grow again. The custom vaccine — nine doses given three weeks apart — teaches the patient's immune system to watch out for and attack those so-called neoantigens.
How did it work? The study included more than 1,100 people with high-risk melanoma that was surgically removed. Everyone was given the standard follow-up therapy: Merck's immunotherapy named Keytruda. The participants were randomly assigned to also receive custom-brewed vaccine doses or a placebo.
Two years later, 82% of the people in the vaccine group were still living without a recurrence of their cancer compared to 70% who had gotten standard Keytruda alone. The trial is continuing to track participants' longer-term outcomes.
The vaccine's side effects were mainly the sore arm, fatigue and other reactions typical of mRNA coronavirus vaccination, Tawbi said.
Moderna shares dropped 18% Thursday after the study's full results were made public, but they remained more than 200% higher than they were in late August before investors were first told of the initial results.

title: Voters want the next Congress to focus on costs and Iran, not on Trump, a new AP-NORC poll shows
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Regardless of the outcome in the coming election, a new AP-NORC poll shows voters from both major political parties want the next Congress to focus on making life more affordable and ending the war in Iran, while fewer are looking for an emphasis on President Donald Trump — whether it’s investigating him or supporting his agenda.
The results suggest that voters are ready for Congress to tackle core issues, despite Trump’s centrality in the midterm campaign.
About 8 in 10 registered voters, including a large majority of Republicans and Democrats, say lowering the cost of living should be one of the highest priorities for the session coming up, the survey from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research finds.
Justin Campbell, a 31-year-old Democrat from Brookhaven, Mississippi, said he wants the government to focus on helping people like him rather than wealthy people.
“I’m not a millionaire and probably won’t ever be,” he said. “I prefer policy that helps me instead of someone I’ll never be.”
Most voters also want Congress to prioritize ending the war with Iran, with roughly 7 in 10 saying this should be a top focus. Substantially fewer voters, about 4 in 10, want Congress to make investigating the Trump administration a high priority, and only about 2 in 10 want Congress to prioritize supporting the Republican president’s agenda.
But the poll also indicates that there are deep divisions within the parties on what to focus on, with moderate Democrats and Republicans differing sharply from voters on the left and right wings of their parties.
Most Democratic voters who identify as supporters of democratic socialism are hoping for a Congress that will investigate the Trump administration, and many want to end military aid to Israel, while MAGA Republicans are interested in Congress supporting Trump’s agenda.
Moderates in both parties, meanwhile, are much likelier to want Democrats and Republicans to find common ground.
Most voters want Congress to focus on reducing costs and ending the war
Lowering the cost of living and ending the Iran war overshadow a wide range of other issues as voters consider priorities for the next Congress.
While most registered voters say reducing costs and ending the war should be among the highest priorities for Congress, only about half say reducing the budget deficit and finding common ground between the two parties should be high priorities. About 4 in 10 want investigating the Trump administration and passing new laws regulating artificial intelligence to be high priorities.
Fewer, about 3 in 10, prioritize ending military aid to Israel, and only about 2 in 10 want a focus on supporting Trump’s agenda.
Though most registered Democrats want Congress to investigate the Trump administration, that falls behind the larger priorities of lowering costs and ending the conflict with Iran. About 6 in 10 registered voters who identify as Democrats call investigations into the Trump administration “one of the highest priorities.”
Arthur Brown, a 71-year-old Democrat in Magee, Mississippi, wants to see the next Congress work on making the economy stronger and prices lower. He feels less urgently about holding Trump accountable, mostly because there’ll be only two years left in Trump’s term. He thinks it’s more important to try to turn the economy around.
“They should just focus on, you know, trying to tackle these problems,” he said. “Eventually down the road, justice will come.”
For Republican voters, bolstering Trump’s goals also falls behind lowering the cost of living, ending the war in Iran and reducing the budget deficit.
In a strikingly tepid show of support for the president, only about 4 in 10 Republican voters say the next Congress should make supporting the Trump administration’s agenda one of its highest priorities.
Most democratic socialists want Congress to investigate Trump
House Democrats have begun planning an ambitious 100-day agenda for what they would do if they win control of Congress in November. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York has said the Democratic Party’s top priorities include making life more affordable and conducting vast oversight of the Trump administration.
But there are potential schisms in the party awaiting Democrats if they win a governing majority. The Democratic Party has reckoned in primary campaigns with a growing wing of democratic socialists. Their progressive stances on some issues have divided the party — including on whether to continue military aid to Israel, whether to compromise with Republicans and how strongly to investigate the Trump administration.
About three-quarters of Democratic voters who identify as supporters of democratic socialism say one of the top priorities should be investigating the Trump administration, compared with slightly less than half of Democrats who say they’re not democratic socialists.
Democratic socialists are also more likely to want Congress to end military aid to Israel and less likely to say it’s a top priority to find common ground between the two parties.
Campbell, the Democrat in Mississippi, identifies as a democratic socialist and wants Congress to hold the Trump administration accountable.
“It feels a little cliche to just say roll back the past two years, but honestly, mostly just roll back the stuff he’s done the past two years,” Campbell said.
Most MAGA Republicans want Congress to support Trump
Republicans are broadly aligned on what they want the next Congress to do, regardless of whether they identify with the Make America Great Again movement — except when it comes to Trump.
At least half of MAGA and non-MAGA Republicans want leaders to lower costs, end the Iran war and reduce the federal budget deficit.
Richard Longo, a 74-year-old Republican in Lake Forest, California, wants to see the president’s agenda pursued in the next Congress but is especially worried about balancing the budget.
“You’re not going to balance the budget in one year, but you have to have a plan,” Longo said.
But while about 6 in 10 MAGA Republicans want Congress to prioritize supporting the Trump administration’s agenda, only about 2 in 10 Republicans who are not supporters of MAGA say the same.
Lisa Ostlund, a 46-year-old from Wayland, Massachusetts, who identifies as a MAGA supporter, wants to see the next Congress prioritize Trump’s agenda. She doesn’t support everything Trump does, but she credits his policies with her recent ability to find housing after struggling with homelessness for several years.
“You got to care about your American people,” Ostlund said. “He definitely doesn’t say it right, but you do have to put them first.”
___
The AP-NORC poll of 1,119 adults was conducted Oct. 8-12 using a sample drawn from NORC’s probability-based AmeriSpeak Panel, which is designed to be representative of the U.S. population. The margin of sampling error for adults overall is plus or minus 3.9 percentage points.

title: Obituary: Clement “Nick” Nickerson
text:
BROOKSVILLE, Fla. – Clement “Nick” Nickerson, 92, passed away on Oct. 15, 2026.
Born on June 30, 1934, Nick was the son of Kermit and Doris Nickerson. He graduated from Waterville High School and went on to attend the University of Maine at Farmington, where he earned his master’s degree in administration. It was there that he met Patricia “Pat” Craig. They married in 1958 and settled in Brunswick where they raised their family and built a life together.
Nick enjoyed a long career with Ginn & Company, retiring after 33 years. His work in textbook sales kept him busy throughout his career, and retirement gave him more time to pursue one of his favorite pastimes: golf.
Following Pat’s passing in 1996, Nick began spending winters at Silverthorn, a golf community in Brooksville, Fla., returning to Brunswick for the summers. There he met Lorraine Phoenix, and they enjoyed many happy years together, sharing their love of golf and splitting their time between Florida and Maine. Their companionship continued until Lorraine’s passing in 2014.
In 2016, Nick met Alice Vanoyen, and they shared many years of companionship, enjoying life together until his passing.
Nick is survived by his children, Kimberly Nickerson and Craig Nickerson and Craig’s wife, Kathi, and Sarah (Nickerson) Newbury and her husband, Mike; along with extended family and friends.
Nick will be remembered for his dedication to his career, his love of golf, and the many friendships and relationships that enriched his life. He enjoyed a long and full life, with cherished connections to both Maine and Florida, and will be dearly missed by those who knew and loved him.

title: He’s been rehabilitating birds in his backyard for 42 years and counting
text:
WILLIAMSVILLE, Vt. (InvestigateTV) - A licensed bird rehabilitator in Vermont has spent more than four decades healing injured birds, driven by a childhood memory that shaped his life’s work.
“I think our kids grew up thinking every kitchen has an owl,” Fred Homer said.
There’s Jasper, the crow, who didn’t enjoy this reporter’s company. And then there’s Stella, the blind-in-one-eye Barred owl, who has been a fixture in Fred Homer’s kitchen for years.
His wife, Debbie Fiener, is okay with Stella... for the most part.
“It’s springtime in Vermont, and the rivers running free. There’s no place else on earth that I was born to be,” Homer sings.
That place is Williamsville, a hamlet in the southern Vermont town of Newfane.
“I love interacting with the land,” Homer said. And wasting time could be a cardinal sin.
Reporter Joe Carroll: You don’t believe in the afterlife...
Fred Homer: That’s true.
Reporter Joe Carroll: Does that make life even more special?
Fred Homer: Absolutely... And there’s the emotional part, “Ah s---, this is too good a ride.”
“He’s sort of a Renaissance man,” Fiener said.
And for over four decades, the former teacher has spent much of his time in the barn. The 87-year-old is a licensed bird rehabilitator. He’s been healing birds for as long as they’ve lived here: 42 years.
Reporter Joe Carroll: Why do this?
Fred Homer: Why? Good question.
The answer goes back 80 years, to a hay wagon in New Jersey.
“We were going down the road, and there was an injured bird in the road, and I was climbing out of the wagon to help,” Homer said. He and his family were at a day camp when young Fred made the move. An employee got his feathers ruffled. “‘Don’t you dare get out.’ And I just... The wagon pulled away, and that little bird was just sitting in the road, and I just, my heart went out.”
Homer has attempted to save over 4,000 birds. But sadly, not every one can be saved. “Injured birds seem to invoke and promote the best in people,” he said.
Homer built his own coffin 20 years ago as a daily reminder that life is precious.
“I walk past my coffin every single day and I say, ‘Fred, exploit this day and don’t let it slip by and don’t be grumpy,’” he said.
Reporter Joe Carroll: So, you’d be happy if this collects dust for the next 20 years or so.
Fred Homer: That would be fine with me.
Homer said Jasper the crow was distressed when he first arrived. He believes Jasper will soon be strong enough to be released.
Reporter Joe Carroll: He’s getting used to me, I think.
Fred Homer: I think so, too.
For Homer and his wife, Williamsville is his “heaven on earth.”

title: Hundreds turn out for AOC rally with Troy Jackson in Maine
text:
Hundreds turn out for Rep. Ocasio-Cortez rally with Troy Jackson in Maine
Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez held a rally with Troy Jackson, Maine's Democratic Senate candidate, on Thursday in Portland, where hundreds of attendees cheered her calls to expand healthcare and get the United States out of Iran.
Ocasio-Cortez is stumping for progressive candidates in the run-up to the midterm elections. Jackson is running against five-term Republican Sen. Susan Collins. He and Ocasio-Cortez dedicated a lot of the event to calls for changing America's priorities from foreign conflicts to domestic cost-of-living issues.
Ocasio-Cortez said the nation's spending priorities are leaving working people behind by focusing on war.
"How are we going to afford Iran, how are we going to afford Gaza, when our people back home can't eat, can't afford healthcare, can't afford to build a bridge to get to work?" Ocasio-Cortez said.
Jackson also took a jab at Collins for appearing with retired Sen. Joe Manchin, a former Democrat who became an independent, in Lewiston on Wednesday.
Thursday's event at the State Theatre was billed as a "Students vs. Billionaires" town hall and hosted by More Perfect University, the campus program of the progressive media organization More Perfect Union.
The town hall is the latest event Jackson has attended with a high-profile politician during his Senate campaign. On Saturday, Oct. 17, Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) joined Jackson and Maine gubernatorial candidate Hannah Pingree for a No Kings rally in Portland. The weekend prior, Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) campaigned with Jackson in Bangor, Lewiston and Biddeford.
Ocasio-Cortez is seeking a fifth term representing New York's 14th Congressional District in the U.S. House. She recently visited Michigan to campaign for Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, as well as Ohio to support fellow Congresswoman Emilia Sykes.

title: Execution staff warned IV site might have ‘blown’ during Christa Pike’s execution attempt
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (AP) — Tennessee execution team members failed multiple times to establish working IV lines in Christa Pike’s arms before her attempted execution and warned that some of her veins may have ruptured, or “blown,” before she was injected with the lethal drug, her attorney wrote in a court document filed Thursday.
The IV team went through about 10 needles and tried several IV sites on both arms, attorney Randy Spivey wrote in the document, which provides the most detailed account of the execution attempt so far. They even struggled to push saline through the last IV site they established, Spivey wrote.
Pike, 50, was hospitalized after surviving two doses of pentobarbital as the state tried to execute her on Sept. 30 for the 1995 stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer. She was 18 when she tortured and killed Slemmer with her boyfriend, becoming one of the youngest women to be sentenced to death.
State protocol calls for a second dose of pentobarbital if the first doesn’t result in death, but it doesn’t spell out what to do if a person survives the second injection.
After being taken to a hospital, Pike was on a ventilator for several days. At one point, her attorneys did not expect her to survive. She ultimately regained consciousness and returned to prison after being discharged.
The failed execution has brought renewed scrutiny to how Tennessee carries out death sentences. The court document was part of a separate legal proceeding in which people on the state’s death row are challenging Tennessee’s lethal injection procedures.
“Our predictions about the likelihood of botched executions have come true — and will continue to come true — without substantial change,” Kit Thomas, an attorney representing people on death row in the case, said.
Nearly an hour of IV attempts
The execution team began trying to place the two IVs required by Tennessee’s execution protocols at 6:34 p.m., Spivey wrote, and when they struggled Pike helped, advising them to look in her upper arm for a viable vein.
They managed to set an IV in Pike’s right arm within about 6 minutes, but it took them nearly an hour to complete the same process in her left arm.
Pike was “wincing and grimacing” as the IV team members moved the needles around inside her left arm, Spivey wrote, and the team members repeatedly expressed doubts after inserting the needles.
One team member said a vein “might be blowing” at 6:57 p.m. while examining an IV in Pike’s left arm, but two others said they couldn’t tell, Spivey wrote. “One of them said something like, ‘it’s either blood or blown, I need to know,’” Spivey wrote.
The team tried again with a different spot in her left arm, and the needle appeared to be severely bent when they pulled it out, the attorney said. “I think it’s blown,” the attorney recalled one of the IV team members saying at 7:07 p.m. After more attempts, the team decided at 7:13 p.m. that they had successfully placed an IV in Pike’s left arm, and they taped her hands down and hooked her up to a heart monitor.
Pike complained of burning arm pain
A series of phone calls were made to the execution chamber starting about five minutes later. Spivey said it appeared the execution team members responsible for pushing the pentobarbital into the lines — a process that happens in an adjoining room — were asking the IV team for repeated checks of Pike’s left arm.
It’s not clear exactly when the pentobarbital was pushed into the IV lines, but at 7:34 p.m., Pike said her arm was hurting.
“I feel like my arm is about to bust. It burns,” she said, according to her attorney. She continued to talk to her spiritual adviser for the next 10 minutes before she began making an “agitated snoring sound,” Spivey wrote.
Over the next 30 minutes Pike strained, flinched, moved her head and seemed to struggle to breathe, Spivey said, and when he asked to use a phone he was led on a circuitous, seven-minute route through the facility instead of being allowed to use the phone in the execution witness room.
Spivey called fellow attorneys at 8:22 p.m. and asked them to stop the execution because a third dose of pentobarbital isn’t authorized under the state’s protocol. He then went back to the witness room and told the deputy attorney general that Pike needed immediate medical care.
Spivey was told an ambulance was on the way at 8:50 p.m., and 20 minutes later he was told that medical staff were providing life-saving measures, he wrote. An ambulance was seen arriving at the hospital at 9:14 p.m.

title: John Anderson, Country Music Hall of Fame singer, dies at 71
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WSMV/Gray News) — Country music singer John Anderson has died, according to a statement shared by his family on his official social media pages.
“It is with the heaviest of hearts that we share the passing of our beloved husband, father, grandfather, and best friend,” the family said in the statement.
Anderson was 71.
Family statement
“To the world, he was a gifted country music singer whose voice and songs touched countless lives. To us, he was so much more. He was the heart of our family, the one who made us laugh, loved us fiercely, and made every ordinary moment feel special,” the statement said.
“We are completely heartbroken,” the family said. “His music will live on, but for us, his greatest legacy will always be the love he gave his family and the memories we will carry with us forever. Please keep our family in your thoughts and prayers as we grieve this unimaginable loss.”
Career highlights
Anderson was known for hits including “Straight Tequila Night” and “Seminole Wind.”
Throughout his career, Anderson opened shows for other artists including Merle Haggard, George Jones and Willie Nelson.
Anderson received the CMA Horizon Award and the CMA Single of the Year award for “Swingin’.” He also received the Academy of Country Music Career Achievement Award.
He was inducted into the Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame in 2014.
According to the Country Music Hall of Fame, which inducted Anderson in 2024, he earned 20 top 10 country hits.
Hall of Fame tribute
“John Anderson was a one-of-a-kind song stylist who proved that fresh innovations were best born from time-honored traditions,” said Kyle Young, CEO of the Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum. “Whether he borrowed inspiration from Lefty Frizzell’s vocal bends or the Florida swamp land, he brought dynamic distinction and creative soul to a world that needed to hear his voice. In 1981, John famously gave life to Billy Joe Shaver’s lyric, ‘I’m just an old chunk of coal, but I’ll be a diamond someday.’ He was already a diamond then, and a diamond he always will be.”
Anderson’s family has not released information about what caused his death.

title: Pres. Trump to hold midterm rally in Fort Myers on Friday
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - President Donald Trump is scheduled to host a midterm campaign rally in Fort Myers, Fla. on Friday afternoon.
GOP organizers said the event aims to mobilize Republican voters for the November elections.
“The midterms are a game of turnout, and nobody turns out voters quite like President Trump,” said Emma Hall, RNC Southeast Regional Communications Director.
The event will be held at Florida Gulf Coast University’s Alico Arena, beginning at 2 p.m. eastern.
Southwest Florida is considered one of the most Republican corners of a state that has been known as a GOP stronghold for years.
Hall said the election is critical for the party.
“Protecting our majorities in the House and the Senate is critical to continuing the Republican agenda of tax cuts, safe communities, secure borders, you know, investment booms in states like Florida,” she said.
Republican gubernatorial nominee and Congressman Byron Donalds is also scheduled to appear at the rally.
Donalds and other GOP candidates in the state have been favored in polling for months. But, a new University of North Florida poll found that the party’s leads in the gubnatorial and U.S. Senate races have been lessening.
José Javier Rodríguez, a Democratic candidate running for Florida attorney general, said he sees the president’s visit as a sign of desparation.
“It’s clear that they feel a little desperation to get turnout,” he said. “And to kind of actually give Republicans a reason to vote Republican instead of crossing the aisle. But it’s unclear why they’ve chosen the president as the messenger when, you know, he’s sort of the billboard for broken promises on the economic front.”

title: Northern Light Health lab manager suffers data breach
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Medical laboratory operator Quest Diagnostics said it learned of a cyber breach of one of its systems this week, likely compromising some records for patients.
Quest acquired Northern Light Health’s outreach lab services in 2023. Quest says through the partnership with the health system, their company provides laboratory management services for nine of Northern Light’s hospital laboratories, along with its cancer center laboratory in Brewer.
The hospital system says there is no indication right now that their patients were impacted by the breach.
“We have been in close communication with Quest Laboratories regarding their reported data breach,” Suzanne Spruce, Senior Vice President, Chief Marketing and Communication Officer for Northern Light Health said in a statement. “At this time Quest has not indicated that any Northern Light Health associated data was involved and we have put additional monitoring in place as they work through this issue.”
Spruce added that hospital lab services have not been affected, and are operating as normal.
In a Thursday regulatory filing, Quest Diagnostics reported “unauthorized access” to its Quanum Lab Services Manager, a platform where certain clients can place test orders and receive or look up their results. The company said it discovered the hack on Wednesday and notified federal law enforcement.
How many patients and which particular records have been affected is still unknown. Quest Diagnostics said it believes “certain patient records” were accessed in the breach, but that the full scope remains under investigation.
The New Jersey-based company said it’s also working with external cybersecurity experts to assist in its response.
Quest Diagnostics has seen hacks impacting patient records before. In 2016, for example, the company said data including lab results and contact information of about 34,000 people was exposed in another online breach. And in 2019, other personal information belonging to about 11.9 million Quest patients was affected after a separate hack at American Medical Collection Agency, a billing collections service provider.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: The renovated Maine State Museum opens Saturday. Here’s what’s new.
text:
AUGUSTA — Six years after shutting its doors for renovations, the staff at the Maine State Museum is ready to welcome the public back to the museum and showcase Maine’s history through brand-new exhibits.
The museum closed in 2020, along with the State Archives and Library, as the Cultural Building was set to undergo significant building renovations. Now, after spending the closure planning and designing new exhibits, the museum is set for a grand reopening starting at 10 a.m. Saturday.
The museum will reopen in phases, with the main floor and second floor exhibits opening first. Museum staff hope to reopen exhibits on the lower two levels, including the Made in Maine and 12,000 Years in Maine exhibits, in the next two years after they finish planning and raising money.
In its first major redesign of the main floor exhibits since its opening in 1971, museum staff focused on telling Maine’s stories in new and interactive ways. From whale skeletons to quilts to snowmobiles and everything in between, here’s a guide to what’s new at the Maine State Museum.
VECTOR THE WHALE
As visitors move through the updated museum, they’ll be greeted by a new face: Vector the whale.
Suspended from the ceiling, the 45-foot-long whale skeleton belongs to a female humpback whale who lived in the Gulf of Maine. Up until the whale died at age 35, scientists tracked and studied her movements, naming her Vector because of patterns on her tail.
Next to Vector is the skeleton of a 5- to 6-month-old humpback whale calf, both positioned like a mother whale would protect her calf.
It is the only museum exhibit in the world to showcase two humpback whale skeletons displaying the species’ range and size.
“We really want our visitors to understand that the whales relate to them, that they have some responsibility,” Museum Director Bernard Fishman said. “We really do have a responsibility to try to make sure that creatures like this can survive and flourish, if possible, and that the ecology of the Gulf of Maine can remain healthy and something we’re proud of.”
The two skeletons are surrounded by interactive and educational displays that provide information about the lives of humpback whales in the Gulf of Maine. The exhibit also features the jaw and flipper bones of a right whale, an endangered species, that died from entanglement.
Visitors can walk under and around the skeletons, which were installed by Dan DenDanto, the owner of Maine-based whale skeleton restoration company Whale and Nails.
“These are important ecological stories,” Fishman said. “That’s why they’re here.”
BEYOND THE POSTCARD
While planning new exhibits, museum staff wanted to focus on telling Maine’s history through the stories of people in Maine.
They developed the “Beyond the Postcard: Stories of the Maine Experience” exhibit centered around lesser-known stories of historical and contemporary Maine people around the themes of work, recreation, community, service and innovation.
Visitors can learn about Cornelia Thurza “Fly Rod” Crosby, the first registered Maine Guide, and William Wilberforce Ruby, a black U.S. Army private from Maine who served in the Spanish-American War.
The exhibit features objects that tell stories from Maine’s history, like the first registered snowmobile in the state and a Lombard Log Hauler, a vehicle invented and manufactured in Maine for hauling logs.
Visitors can see a 40-foot partial reconstruction of the St. Mary, one of the last full-rigged wooden ships built in Phippsburg in 1890, which crashed off the Falkland Islands. In the first six months after reopening, Teresa Murphy, the museum’s objects conservator, will be completing a conservation treatment on the ship in a gallery where visitors can watch and ask questions.
The highlighted stories in the exhibit will change over time, according to Angela Goebel-Bain, chief curator for the exhibit.
“We’re gonna take a story out and put a new person in, and so we can keep telling these stories and keep broadening the stories we tell,” Goebel-Bain said. “It also gives us an opportunity to engage with the audience, so that we can kind of hear what kind of stories they want to hear, and maybe we can develop stories with them, and maybe develop our collections at the same time.”
LUNDER EDUCATION CENTER
Fishman said he was particularly excited about the new Lunder Education Center, as the museum finally has a space dedicated to education to support the thousands of students that visit the museum each year.
The new space, funded by the Lunder Foundation, features a presentation area, rotating exhibits, interactive displays and spaces for educational demonstrations.
Throughout the renovation, Fishman said museum staff focused heavily on incorporating interactive elements. Many of the prior exhibits were several decades old and didn’t incorporate technology in any way, he said.
“It expands educational horizons,” Fishman said. “And it makes the exhibits more accessible.”
One of the new interactive displays is a table that allows visitors to experience what an archaeological dig might have been like by finding and learning about objects on The Defence, a privateer rig from the 1770s that was scuttled by American forces during the Penobscot Expedition in June 1779, a failed American project to expel British troops from Fort George in upper Penobscot Bay.
Visitors will be able to explore the ship through the interactive table and find and repair objects that were actually found on the original ship.
MAINE QUILTS
On the upper floor of the museum is the new “Maine Quilts: 250 Years of Comfort and Community” exhibit curated by Laurie LaBar.
The exhibit showcases quilts from the early 1800s to today, highlighting the work of the women and communities who quilted throughout Maine’s history.
Many of the quilts are brightly colored, despite being hundreds of years old. Different styles and trends of quilting throughout the decades are on display and the intricate craftsmanship is highlighted.
LaBar wrote a companion book for the exhibit, also titled “Maine Quilts: 250 Years of Comfort and Community,” which explores the history of quilting in Maine and Americar.
The exhibit also highlights textile objects from Wabanaki and Passamaquoddy people throughout Maine’s history.
WHAT TO KNOW BEFORE VISITING
Admission to the museum will be free from the grand reopening through the remainder of the year.
The grand reopening celebration is set to take place from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. on Saturday, with a ribbon-cutting to start. The event will also feature live music, refreshments and educational demonstrations.
The museum’s regular weekly hours will be Tuesday through Sunday, 10 a.m.–4 p.m.

title: Cruise passengers unexpectedly end up in Canada, even though their destination was the Bahamas
text:
(CNN) - Thousands of passengers set to travel on Royal Caribbean’s giant “Oasis of the Seas” had their bathing suits, sunscreen and floppy hats ready to go, heading for the Bahamas.
Just hours before they had to be on the ship, they were told that bad weather forced a change of itinerary.
A big one.
Now, instead of heading south, they would sail north, to Halifax, Canada.
The travelers had to quickly trade bikinis for hoodies, but most of them took it all in stride.
“Of course, it’s not the 80-degree Bahamas, so, you know, make from lemons, you make lemonade,” one passenger said.
Now, the ship will spend three days at sea before returning to New Jersey.
Royal Caribbean gave passengers 50 percent off travel vouchers in exchange for the inconvenience.

title: 3 Maine football storylines to follow against Campbell
text:
Make it six consecutive losses for the University of Maine football team. The Black Bears had their chances last week against visiting Bryant, but three fumbles were costly in a 17-14 defeat to the Bulldogs that assured Maine of a losing season.
Homecoming week for Maine pits the Black Bears (1-6, 1-3 Coastal Athletic Association) against 16th-ranked Campbell (6-1, 3-0 CAA) at 1 p.m. Saturday (FloSports). Here are three storylines ahead of Maine’s third consecutive home game:
Is Drezek the guy?
Until last week, Maine’s starting quarterback job still belonged to Eddie Buehler. The sophomore had started every game and was atop the depth chart the team released two days before the Bryant game.
But junior Caden Drezek played from start to finish against Bryant, completing 18 of 34 passes for 234 yards — most by a Maine QB this year — with a touchdown and no interceptions. Drezek had already been eating into Buehler’s playing time, so is the job now his?
“We have not decided on that yet,” coach Jordan Stevens said in the CAA press conference on Monday. “We’re going to meet with those guys and really decide how that’s going to play out this weekend.”
Maine defense has its hands full
It’s hard to pin too much of Maine’s losing streak on the defense. That unit hasn’t been perfect, but it has put the Black Bears in position to win many of those six games. Now comes a much bigger challenge.
Campbell is first in the CAA and 11th of 124 Football Championship Subdivision teams in yards per game (455). Senior quarterback Kamden Sixkiller is 10th in the FCS in passing yards with 1,899.
“Sixkiller is just doing an excellent job distributing the football,” Stevens said. “Their intensity is seen through the film, and that shows (in) how they block — how they block up front, how they block on the perimeter and how hard their backs run.”
Homecoming heroics?
If you’re looking for a good omen for the Black Bears against Campbell, consider what week it is. Homecoming has yielded great success recently for Maine, which has won nine consecutive homecoming games since losing to Yale in 2015.
Even some years of struggles have yielded homecoming wins for Maine, which won against Monmouth in 2022 and LIU in 2023 — both two-win seasons. Perhaps Saturday could produce similar magic for the Black Bears.

title: Actor Tom Skerritt, known for roles in 'Alien,' 'Top Gun,' and 'M*A*S*H,' dies at 93
text:
Actor Tom Skerritt, known for roles in 'Alien,' 'Top Gun,' and 'M*A*S*H,' dies at 93
Tom Skerritt, the Emmy-winning actor who embodied a solid, wry authority figure, whether as a flight instructor in "Top Gun," a tough-but-fair sheriff on TV's "Picket Fences" or the doomed captain of "Alien," has died. He was 93.
Skerritt died Wednesday of natural causes, his family said in a statement. "While the world knew Tom through his remarkable acting career, we knew him for his humor, curiosity, wisdom, generosity and the love he brought into our lives. He cared deeply about imagination, creativity, storytelling, service, veterans, the natural world and helping others find and share their own voices," the statement said.
Skerritt was twice nominated for an Emmy — both for "Picket Fences," winning outstanding lead actor in a drama series in 1993. Other career highlights include playing the patient husband of Shirley MacLaine in "Turning Point," Sally Field's husband in "Steel Magnolias" and a scheming opportunist who stands in the way of Jodie Foster's attempt to communicate with extraterrestrial life in "Contact."
"A writer once described me as a character actor locked in a leading man's body, and I've always loved that. It's a nice compliment. I've been able to walk the line between television and features," he told the Seattle Post-Intelligencer in 1997.
Onstage, he was the narrator in "Our Town" at Seattle's Intiman Theatre in 2004 and made his Broadway debut in 2013 in an adaptation of John Grisham's "A Time to Kill," in which The Associated Press wrote he "nicely pulls off a charming disgraced and drunken lawyer."

title: Dresden Readies to Reexamine Comprehensive Plan
text:
During a period of growth for the town, Dresden is organizing a committee to examine its comprehensive plan.
A town’s comprehensive plan is an overview of the town and the direction it wants to take with planning. It includes information on a town’s resources, population, and demographics as well as a vision statement about its desired future.
Lincoln County Regional Planning Commission Executive Director Emily Rabbe said while the state no longer has a “hard and fast” requirement for a town to update its plan every decade, it is still best practice to do so.

title: Execution staff warned IV site veins might have 'blown' during Christa Pike's execution attempt
text:
Execution staff warned veins may have 'blown' during Christa Pike lethal injection attempt, court filing says
Tennessee execution team members failed multiple times to establish working IV lines in Christa Pike’s arms before her attempted execution and warned that some of her veins may have ruptured, or “blown,” before she was injected with the lethal drug, her attorney wrote in a court document filed Thursday.
The IV team went through about 10 needles and tried several IV sites on both arms, attorney Randy Spivey wrote in the document, which provides the most detailed account of the execution attempt so far. They even struggled to push saline through the last IV site they established, Spivey wrote.
Related video above: How could a lethal injection go wrong?
Pike, 50, was hospitalized after surviving two doses of pentobarbital as the state tried to execute her on Sept. 30 for the 1995 stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer. She was 18 when she tortured and killed Slemmer with her boyfriend, becoming one of the youngest women to be sentenced to death.
State protocol calls for a second dose of pentobarbital if the first doesn’t result in death, but it doesn’t spell out what to do if a person survives the second injection.
After being taken to a hospital, Pike was on a ventilator for several days. At one point, her attorneys did not expect her to survive. She ultimately regained consciousness and returned to prison after being discharged.
The failed execution has brought renewed scrutiny to how Tennessee carries out death sentences. The court document was part of a separate legal proceeding in which people on the state's death row are challenging Tennessee's lethal injection procedures.
"Our predictions about the likelihood of botched executions have come true — and will continue to come true — without substantial change,” Kit Thomas, an attorney representing people on death row in the case, said.
Nearly an hour of IV attempts
The execution team began trying to place the two IVs required by Tennessee’s execution protocols at 6:34 p.m., Spivey wrote, and when they struggled Pike helped, advising them to look in her upper arm for a viable vein.
They managed to set an IV in Pike’s right arm within about 6 minutes, but it took them nearly an hour to complete the same process in her left arm.
Pike was “wincing and grimacing” as the IV team members moved the needles around inside her left arm, Spivey wrote, and the team members repeatedly expressed doubts after inserting the needles.
One team member said a vein “might be blowing” at 6:57 p.m. while examining an IV in Pike's left arm, but two others said they couldn’t tell, Spivey wrote. “One of them said something like, ‘it’s either blood or blown, I need to know,'” Spivey wrote.
The team tried again with a different spot in her left arm, and the needle appeared to be severely bent when they pulled it out, the attorney said. “I think it's blown,” the attorney recalled one of the IV team members saying at 7:07 p.m. After more attempts, the team decided at 7:13 p.m. that they had successfully placed an IV in Pike's left arm, and they taped her hands down and hooked her up to a heart monitor.
Pike complained of burning arm pain
A series of phone calls were made to the execution chamber starting about five minutes later. Spivey said it appeared the execution team members responsible for pushing the pentobarbital into the lines — a process that happens in an adjoining room — were asking the IV team for repeated checks of Pike's left arm.
It’s not clear exactly when the pentobarbital was pushed into the IV lines, but at 7:34 p.m., Pike said her arm was hurting.
“I feel like my arm is about to bust. It burns,” she said, according to her attorney. She continued to talk to her spiritual adviser for the next 10 minutes before she began making an “agitated snoring sound,” Spivey wrote.
Over the next 30 minutes Pike strained, flinched, moved her head and seemed to struggle to breathe, Spivey said, and when he asked to use a phone he was led on a circuitous, seven-minute route through the facility instead of being allowed to use the phone in the execution witness room.
Spivey called fellow attorneys at 8:22 p.m. and asked them to stop the execution because a third dose of pentobarbital isn’t authorized under the state’s protocol. He then went back to the witness room and told the deputy attorney general that Pike needed immediate medical care.
Spivey was told an ambulance was on the way at 8:50 p.m., and 20 minutes later he was told that medical staff were providing life-saving measures, he wrote. An ambulance was seen arriving at the hospital at 9:14 p.m.

title: The Lincoln County News
text:
To the editor:
Canvassing voters throughout Lincoln County has offered me the opportunity to visit with folks from across the economic spectrum: farmers, fishermen, retired and employed, white-, blue-, green-, and even pink-collar workers.
Here are two snapshots from my interactions:
A young woman answers the door with a generous smile riven with untreated tooth decay, a reminder that dental care isn’t a luxury. It’s healthcare.
After my knock, a disabled fisherman struggles, but finally reaches the door on two canes. We talk at length about Democrats offering a hand up, not a handout.

title: Postseason Is Here: Week Eight Nominations Are Open
text:
The Postseason Is Here: Week Eight Athlete of the Week Nominations Are Open
The regular season has given way to postseason pressure, and now every goal, save, race and big moment means a little more.
Fall Week Eight Athlete of the Week nominations are officially open! For games and performances held between October 19th - October 24th!
With soccer tournament games beginning across Northern Maine and cross country entering championship season, we are looking for the Aroostook County athletes who step up when the stakes are highest.
Maybe it is a game-winning goal that keeps a season alive.
Maybe it is a goalkeeper coming up with the save a team desperately needs.
Maybe a runner delivers a huge championship performance, or an athlete simply turns in the kind of effort that deserves to be recognized.
Whatever the performance, we want to hear about it.
When submitting a nomination, include the athlete's name, school, sport and as much information as possible about what they accomplished during the week.
Stats, scores, opponents, meet results and other details all help us build the strongest boys and girls ballots possible.
Who Deserves a Spot?
Athlete of the Week is about more than simply finding the leading scorer.
Big offensive numbers certainly matter, but so do defensive performances, goalkeeping, championship finishes, leadership and the moments that make a difference when a team's season is on the line.
Public nominations are an important part of the process, so if you saw someone deliver a performance that should not be overlooked, make sure we know about it.
Fall Week Eight nominations are open through Sunday, October 25 at 6 p.m.
After nominations close, the boys and girls finalists will be selected and Athlete of the Week voting will begin.
The Week Eight winners will be announced Friday morning.
The postseason has arrived.
Now tell us who is rising to the moment.

title: Respected attorney was battling cancer when foster son murdered her for her money, officials say
text:
SAN DIEGO (KFMB) - A California attorney and foster mother disappeared while battling cancer in 2024. Now, her foster son is accused of poisoning her with fentanyl and burying her body.
Nadine Jett, a 64-year-old attorney and foster mother, disappeared in January 2024. She was battling cancer at the time and failed to show up for a medical appointment. Last year, her remains were found buried on her 20-acre Valley Center property.
The San Diego District Attorney’s Office announced Wednesday that they’ve made an arrest in the case. Jett’s foster son, 34-year-old Cedric von Ferdinand, is accused of poisoning her with illicit fentanyl in order to get his hands on her money.
“This is a case of deadly greed,” said San Diego County District Attorney Summer Stephan.
When Jett disappeared, von Ferdinand had been living with her, pretending to care for her, Stephan says. He allegedly told friends and family she would die soon and that she wanted to be cremated without a funeral service.
Von Ferdinand allegedly told a caretaker that was due to come to the house that she was no longer needed because Jett had died around Jan. 17, 2024. Stephan alleges it’s around that time that Von Ferdinand killed his foster mother.
Von Ferdinand raised suspicions when he tried to sell all three properties Jett owned, Stephan says. He allegedly forged a real estate document using his thumbprint, pretending it was hers. During a search, investigators also found a fake marriage license for von Ferdinand and his foster mother that he is accused of forging with a co-defendant.
“It was signed and notarized well after her death,” Stephan said.
In July 2025, Jett’s remains were found wrapped in a bedsheet in a 6-foot hole about 30 yards from her home. The medical examiner’s office determined she had massive amounts of illicit fentanyl in her system, and her death was ruled a homicide.
Bianca Lucci and her quadruplet sisters are Jett’s foster daughters, and they deeply miss her.
“Nadine took us in at a young age after about 10 foster homes, and she was the mom we needed. She gave us a fair chance at life,” Lucci said. “It is sad we’ll never get to see her again, but I do believe she’s looking from above, proud of us.”
Von Ferdinand is scheduled to be arraigned Thursday on a murder charge as well as two special circumstance allegations.

title: He’s been rehabilitating birds in his backyard for 42 years and counting
text:
WILLIAMSVILLE, Vt. (InvestigateTV) - A licensed bird rehabilitator in Vermont has spent more than four decades healing injured birds, driven by a childhood memory that shaped his life’s work.
“I think our kids grew up thinking every kitchen has an owl,” Fred Homer said.
There’s Jasper, the crow, who didn’t enjoy this reporter’s company. And then there’s Stella, the blind-in-one-eye Barred owl, who has been a fixture in Fred Homer’s kitchen for years.
His wife, Debbie Fiener, is okay with Stella... for the most part.
“It’s springtime in Vermont, and the rivers running free. There’s no place else on earth that I was born to be,” Homer sings.
That place is Williamsville, a hamlet in the southern Vermont town of Newfane.
“I love interacting with the land,” Homer said. And wasting time could be a cardinal sin.
Reporter Joe Carroll: You don’t believe in the afterlife...
Fred Homer: That’s true.
Reporter Joe Carroll: Does that make life even more special?
Fred Homer: Absolutely... And there’s the emotional part, “Ah s---, this is too good a ride.”
“He’s sort of a Renaissance man,” Fiener said.
And for over four decades, the former teacher has spent much of his time in the barn. The 87-year-old is a licensed bird rehabilitator. He’s been healing birds for as long as they’ve lived here: 42 years.
Reporter Joe Carroll: Why do this?
Fred Homer: Why? Good question.
The answer goes back 80 years, to a hay wagon in New Jersey.
“We were going down the road, and there was an injured bird in the road, and I was climbing out of the wagon to help,” Homer said. He and his family were at a day camp when young Fred made the move. An employee got his feathers ruffled. “‘Don’t you dare get out.’ And I just... The wagon pulled away, and that little bird was just sitting in the road, and I just, my heart went out.”
Homer has attempted to save over 4,000 birds. But sadly, not every one can be saved. “Injured birds seem to invoke and promote the best in people,” he said.
Homer built his own coffin 20 years ago as a daily reminder that life is precious.
“I walk past my coffin every single day and I say, ‘Fred, exploit this day and don’t let it slip by and don’t be grumpy,’” he said.
Reporter Joe Carroll: So, you’d be happy if this collects dust for the next 20 years or so.
Fred Homer: That would be fine with me.
Homer said Jasper the crow was distressed when he first arrived. He believes Jasper will soon be strong enough to be released.
Reporter Joe Carroll: He’s getting used to me, I think.
Fred Homer: I think so, too.
For Homer and his wife, Williamsville is his “heaven on earth.”

title: Quest Diagnostics reports cyber breach affecting ‘certain patient records’
text:
CHICAGO (AP) — Medical laboratory operator Quest Diagnostics said it learned of a cyber breach of one of its systems this week, likely compromising some records for patients.
In a Thursday regulatory filing, Quest Diagnostics reported “unauthorized access” to its Quanum Lab Services Manager, a platform where certain clients can place test orders and receive or look up their results. The company said it discovered the hack on Wednesday and notified federal law enforcement.
How many patients and which particular records have been affected is still unknown. Quest Diagnostics said it believes “certain patient records” were accessed in the breach, but that the full scope remains under investigation.
The New Jersey-based company said it’s also working with external cybersecurity experts to assist in its response.
Quest Diagnostics has seen hacks impacting patient records before. In 2016, for example, the company said data including lab results and contact information of about 34,000 people was exposed in another online breach. And in 2019, other personal information belonging to about 11.9 million Quest patients was affected after a separate hack at American Medical Collection Agency, a billing collections service provider.
Governments and companies worldwide are working more broadly on online security updates. Urgency erupted this week, after an AI-assisted discovery of vulnerabilities in a programming language called PHP, which is vital to 70% of websites globally.
Outages and limited service have continued for many as firms rush to patch those risks. But based on the company’s investigation, Quest Diagnostics confirmed to The Associated Press Thursday that its cyber breach was not related to the PHP issue.

title: Cambria’s own air-monitoring records show silica levels sometimes exceeding federal limits, documents show
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Copies of Cambria’s own air-monitoring records show tests at fabrication shops run by the nation’s largest engineered-stone slab manufacturer repeatedly recorded silica dust above federal limits. That’s despite its chief legal officer’s January testimony to Congress that its shops stay below half the legal limit. The records recently surfaced in litigation and were obtained by InvestigateTV.
Dust from cutting engineered stone countertops — made from crushed quartz bound with resin and containing 90% or more crystalline silica, far higher than granite or marble — has sickened hundreds of workers around the country with silicosis, an incurable lung disease.
In California alone, the state has confirmed 668 silicosis cases and 35 silicosis-related deaths among countertop workers since 2019 as of October 20, according to California Department of Public Health data. Public health experts say cases are undercounted nationally.
Cambria, headquartered in Minnesota, has repeatedly said that smaller fabrication shops around the country need to follow federal regulations and silica dust limits to stay safe, and has held its own facilities out as examples of safely-run shops. But its own testing documents show that on numerous occasions, the company has itself failed to meet federal Occupational Safety and Health Administration safety standards.
Company says safety is a priority
“Safety is a hallmark of the Cambria organization,” Micah Aberson, Cambria’s executive vice president, said in December at the company’s manufacturing facility and fabrication shop in Minnesota. He said eliminating dust while fabricating engineered stone countertops is key to that safety.
“I mean, we would contend that no dust is good dust,” Aberson said.
The dust created by cutting slabs contains respirable crystalline silica. Hundreds of workers who cut and shape countertops around the country have been diagnosed with silicosis. Thirty-five have died in California alone.
At a House subcommittee hearing in January, Cambria’s chief legal officer, Rebecca Shult, said the company keeps workers safe by abiding by federal regulations that set a limit for the amount of silica allowed in the air, known as the permissible exposure limit, or PEL.
“We know that workers can be protected by following OSHA regulations and controlling silica exposure to below the permissible exposure limit. And in fact, at our shops, we control exposures below the action level, which is half of the PEL,” Shult said.
What the thresholds mean
In 2018, OSHA set two thresholds for silica dust in the air. The Action Level, 25 micrograms per cubic meter, triggers closer monitoring of workers. The Permissible Exposure Limit, or PEL, 50 micrograms, is the maximum amount a worker can legally be exposed to in an eight-hour workday.
OSHA also requires medical surveillance when workers are exposed at or above the Action Level for 30 or more days per year.
Shult told Congress Cambria stays under the lower number, half the legal limit, and called for all fabrication shops to do so.
Records show repeated violations
But copies of Cambria’s own air-monitoring records, recently surfaced in litigation and obtained by InvestigateTV, show the company has failed to meet those standards on numerous occasions.
InvestigateTV reviewed Cambria test results from facilities in Minnesota, California, Ohio and Indiana going back to 2018. The tests show Cambria’s own facilities have repeatedly recorded higher levels of breathable crystalline silica in the air than federal rules allow.
Among about 170 tests from 2018 to 2026, 57 — about a third — were at or above the federal Action Level, the threshold Shult told Congress her company stays under. Eight showed more silica than the legal limit itself, the PEL. In Ohio in 2020, one sample came back more than five times the legal limit.
In December, Aberson told InvestigateTV that Cambria does not medically test its own workers for silicosis because, based on its own air monitoring tests, OSHA does not require it.
“We have no evidence of anyone having contracted silicosis at Cambria,” Aberson said. He said Cambria officials “would have heard about it” if any workers had been diagnosed with the disease.
Former OSHA official responds
David Michaels, who served as assistant secretary at OSHA for eight years, testified at the same congressional hearing as Cambria’s chief legal officer, Shult.
“When these stones are cut safely, workers are not overexposed to silica dust,” Shult testified.
After hearing about the test results, Michaels said: “Cambria may insist that it’s possible to do this safely, but certainly from these documents, it does appear that Cambria has not been successful in following essentially that premise.”
Cambria declined to comment for this story.
California moves toward a ban
After hearing from sick workers and their families, California officials have taken the first steps toward banning engineered stone. Public Citizen, a consumer group, joined last month in calling for a ban and a nationwide screening and prevention program for workers.
Australia banned engineered stone in 2024, becoming the first country to do so.

text:

The fun starts with the Trunk-or-Treat located in the heart of Downtown Orono, on Mill Street. From 4-6PM families will be able to make the rounds, from trunk to trunk and to all the area businesses, to gather candy in abundance!
According to organizers, as they have in the past, this year they'll be shutting the street down to make it safe for little ones to run around.
"This family-friendly event transforms Mill Street into a safe, traffic-free trick-or-treating zone, allowing families to enjoy Halloween in a centralized and supervised setting."
They will also have an option for those kids who have allergies to certain ingredient, who still want to have fun and gather treats.
"Orono’s Trunk or Treat proudly participates in the Teal Pumpkin Project, offering non-food and allergy-friendly items so children with food sensitivities can join in the fun."
People looking to participate in the Trunk-or-Treat as guests can park down behind the Town Office building off of Goodridge Drive. Those who wast to decorate a trunk and hand out candy are also encouraged to do so.
Read More: Bangor, Maine Dog Park's Halloween Party Brings Costumed Pups Together
This year, directly following the Trunk-or-treat for the kids, there's something new for the grownups!
They're calling it Halloween After Dark! And it's set to run from 6PM to 9:45PM.
The HOME committee, who put this new event together, says its a local restaurant crawl, with eateries like the Family Dog, Marsh Island Brewing, Orono Brewing Co., Thai Orchid, Woodmans Bar & Grill and Yama's Bar & Grill all taking part.
"We'll have a photo booth, raffle, food/drink specials, and a FREE trolley ride around town—looping from the UMaine Student Union, Orchard Trails, and to Downtown Orono and Orono Brewing Company."
While costumes are encouraged, they are not mandatory.

title: Mother, 4 young children killed in overnight Texas mobile home fire
text:
VAN ZANDT COUNTY, Texas (KLTV/Gray News) - Four young children and their mother died following an overnight house fire, authorities said.
Van Zandt County Fire Marshal Kevin Palmer said firefighters were dispatched shortly after 12:30 a.m. Wednesday to a fire at a mobile home at 482 County Road 4127 with reports of people trapped inside.
Palmer said when crews arrived, three people had escaped on their own, but four children remained inside. Firefighters breached an exterior wall to get in and quickly located the four children.
Officials said three of the children were pronounced dead on scene and a fourth child was flown to a hospital. The children’s mother was also flown to the hospital. Officials later announced the child and mother died at the hospital.
The children were a 3-year-old girl and three boys, ages 5, 8 and 10. The family has not been publicly identified, however Canton Independent School District confirmed some of the children were students.
“It is with profound sadness that we share the heartbreaking news of the loss of students at Canton Elementary and Canton Intermediate Schools. Our thoughts and prayers are with the family, friends, classmates, teachers, and everyone affected by this tragic loss,” the district said.
Two other people were taken by ambulance to the hospital as a precaution, Palmer said.
The Fire Marshal’s Office is in the early stages of investigating the fire.
When the Canton Fire Department got to the fire, the mobile home was half on fire, according to South Van Zandt Volunteer Fire Department Battalion Chief Jason Foster. He and his crew were called in as backup.
“As I got there, I went up to go in and help them search. They handed me the first one out. We pulled him out, started doing CPR immediately, and then they went in searching for the rest,” Foster said.
Foster said the fire was heaviest to the middle and right of the mobile home. The children were found inside a bedroom.
Foster says he’s been a firefighter for 28 years.
“Unfortunately, not my first time in a situation like this. But they never get any easier,” Foster said.
Foster says the fire was controlled in about 20 minutes.

title: Man convicted of killing mother who threatened to evict him, believed she was ‘possessed’
text:
OREGON CITY, Ore. (KPTV/Gray News) — An Oregon man has been found guilty of murdering his mother, whom he believed was possessed by demons.
Ronald Joseph Kirk, 38, was convicted of second-degree murder and being a felon in possession of a firearm in Clackamas County court on Tuesday.
Prosecutors said Kirk was living with his mother, 61-year-old Rosa Leyva, in her small Gladstone home when Leyva didn’t come into work early on Nov. 26, 2024.
People who knew Leyva had concerns about Kirk and testified in court that he was volatile, dangerous and frequently drunk or high on meth.
Gladstone police went to the home to conduct a welfare check that same day after Leyva did not answer calls from coworkers and loved ones. Kirk answered the door and told officers that his mother was inside and had not been conscious for about a day, according to prosecutors.
Officers found Leyva’s body sitting at the dining room table in front of her laptop, covered in pillowcases with a single gunshot wound to the head.
Investigators learned that Leyva expressed concern about her son’s behavior fueled by alcohol and drug use, and that Kirk became obsessed with exorcism and demonic possession while under the influence.
A month before Leyva’s death, Kirk had left her a voicemail in which he claimed she was possessed and had “almost” put a bullet in her head the day before.
Leyva had planned to legally evict Kirk and texted him that she wanted him out of her house on Nov. 8, 2024.
Kirk is scheduled to be sentenced on Nov. 4 and faces a potential life sentence with a minimum of 25 years in prison.

title: Northern Light Health lab manager suffers data breach
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Medical laboratory operator Quest Diagnostics said it learned of a cyber breach of one of its systems this week, likely compromising some records for patients.
Quest acquired Northern Light Health’s outreach lab services in 2023. Quest says through the partnership with the health system, their company provides laboratory management services for nine of Northern Light’s hospital laboratories, along with its cancer center laboratory in Brewer.
The hospital system says there is no indication right now that their patients were impacted by the breach.
“We have been in close communication with Quest Laboratories regarding their reported data breach,” Suzanne Spruce, Senior Vice President, Chief Marketing and Communication Officer for Northern Light Health said in a statement. “At this time Quest has not indicated that any Northern Light Health associated data was involved and we have put additional monitoring in place as they work through this issue.”
Spruce added that hospital lab services have not been affected, and are operating as normal.
In a Thursday regulatory filing, Quest Diagnostics reported “unauthorized access” to its Quanum Lab Services Manager, a platform where certain clients can place test orders and receive or look up their results. The company said it discovered the hack on Wednesday and notified federal law enforcement.
How many patients and which particular records have been affected is still unknown. Quest Diagnostics said it believes “certain patient records” were accessed in the breach, but that the full scope remains under investigation.
The New Jersey-based company said it’s also working with external cybersecurity experts to assist in its response.
Quest Diagnostics has seen hacks impacting patient records before. In 2016, for example, the company said data including lab results and contact information of about 34,000 people was exposed in another online breach. And in 2019, other personal information belonging to about 11.9 million Quest patients was affected after a separate hack at American Medical Collection Agency, a billing collections service provider.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Is it worth paying a processor to butcher your deer?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Outdoors
The BDN outdoors section brings readers into the woods, waters and wild places of Maine. It features stories on hunting, fishing, wildlife, conservation and recreation, told by people who live these experiences. This section emphasizes hands-on knowledge, field reports, issues, trends and the traditions that define life outside in Maine. Read more Outdoors stories here. 
Have you filled a deer tag yet? Here we are, headed toward the end of archery season, and I have yet to let an arrow fly. The closest I’ve come to a deer is when my wife pushed one a few yards behind me the other night as we headed for our usual rendezvous point after a late-afternoon and evening sit.
I heard the sound of running hooves first and, as I turned, all I saw was a dark silhouette against an evening sky, running under a full burst of steam. Up to that point, I was beginning to have some doubt about hunting one of my favorite “hotspots,” blaming everything from the weather to this year’s abundant acorn crop for my abhorrently bad archery season.
But that one ghostlike blur was enough to put things back in proper perspective. It’s just the way some years go and a reminder of how important it is to keep the faith. Deer season has a long way to go yet.
Truth be known, my wife and I eventually figure things out or just get lucky and fill our tags. At that point, it’s off to our local deer processor.
We long ago gave up the notion of processing our own deer. We didn’t have the space, tools or expertise, and still don’t. Although the processing fee took a bite out of the monthly budget then and still does, dropping our deer off at a local processor has proven to be the best way to go after weighing the options.
The bottom line is that no matter which way you go, do-it-yourself or professional processing, both options cost money. But there are upsides and downsides to consider with both.
DIY processing calls for an upfront financial investment. Investing in a grinder for burger, a slicer, skinning and other butchering equipment, a bone saw, a vacuum sealer and bags or freezer wrap, among other necessities, can run up a considerable tab. Plus, you need a place to get the job done.
It’s also a good idea to have some knowledge of skinning, quartering and deboning, as well as making the proper cuts.
True, the initial cost will more than pay for itself over time and will save money if you process multiple deer annually. But there’s also the time involved, and convenience is difficult to put a price tag on for many people.
Perhaps the biggest upside of DIY processing is that you know what you’re getting. Processing can be done immediately, and if you want special cuts or 10% or 20% beef fat added to your burger, the choice is yours at no extra cost.
With professional processing, you’re paying for expertise and convenience, which remain the most important factors for us.
Over the years, we’ve grown appreciative and increasingly spoiled by simply dropping off our deer, telling the processor what cuts we want and providing any other particulars, then picking it up a few days later, ready for the freezer.
The downside of commercial processing is the cost, which comes every year we tag out. The fee still bites into the budget, but we’ve come to accept it as part of the cost of hunting and doing something we love.
It’s also worth it to us because we know where our food comes from. And considering the cost of good beef these days at the supermarket, we may even be saving money.
We’re lucky, too. We have a processor in the next town over that we’ve used for years. It’s run by experienced professional meat cutters, some retired and others still working
They’re reasonably priced, deliver prompt service even during the busy rifle season and do a great job.
But professional processing price structures and fees vary, so it pays to do your research beforehand. Basic cuts, which generally include skinning, wrapping and cuts such as chops, burger, stew meat and roasts packaged in your desired weights, can cost $1.25 to $1.40 per pound of hanging weight.
Any custom cuts or products, such as cutlets, minute or shaved steak, sausage, jerky and snack sticks, or adding beef or beef fat to burger, can jack up the cost considerably.
Hunters can find a list of deer processing facilities on the Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife’s website under Hunting and Trapping, in the Deer Hunting Information section.

(CNN) - Thousands of passengers set to travel on Royal Caribbean’s giant “Oasis of the Seas” had their bathing suits, sunscreen and floppy hats ready to go, heading for the Bahamas.
Just hours before they had to be on the ship, they were told that bad weather forced a change of itinerary.
A big one.
Now, instead of heading south, they would sail north, to Halifax, Canada.
The travelers had to quickly trade bikinis for hoodies, but most of them took it all in stride.
“Of course, it’s not the 80-degree Bahamas, so, you know, make from lemons, you make lemonade,” one passenger said.
Now, the ship will spend three days at sea before returning to New Jersey.
Royal Caribbean gave passengers 50 percent off travel vouchers in exchange for the inconvenience.

title: U.S. Marshals Apprehend Suspect In Westbrook After Waldo Street Incident In Rumford
text:
They Found Him: U.S. Marshals Catch Up With Fugitive Sought In Rumford Manhunt In Town Of Westbrook Tuesday
Less than a week after he disappeared from the scene of a drug raid in Rumford prompting a statewide manhunt for him, 21-year-old Blake Lachance of Lewiston has been apprehended by authorities.
Read More: Rumford Police Seek Armed Suspect After Waldo Street Raid
The Backstory
Authorities issued a warning to residents that Lachance should be considered armed and dangerous following raid on home on Waldo Street in Rumford. Reports of drug activity and shots fired prompted a large police presence in the area. Once the place was secured, it was discovered that Lachance had fled the scene before police arrived.
What Took Place This Week
The U.S. Marshals Service says they caught up with Lachance this week, and that he is now in custody.
"On October 20, in Westbrook, members of the emergency services units apprehended Lachance after he attempted to flee the residence on foot. A perimeter team subsequently took him into custody without further incident. Lachance was then turned over to the custody of the U.S. Marshals Service and transported to a local jail, where he remains pending his initial appearance on the state charges."
Lachance faces felony state charges including criminal mischief, aggravated assault and aggravated reckless conduct.
As is often the case with serious situations in the state, the U.S. Marshals Service says the Lachance's arrest came about as a result of multiple agencies working in cooperation with each other, including the Homeland Security Task Force, the Maine Violent Offender Task Force, Cumberland County Sheriff's Office, Maine State Police, and the South Police, Westbrook, Rumford and Lewiston Police Departments.
Teamwork Makes The Dream Work
U.S. Marshal David St. Pierre says this cooperation across the board is key positive outcomes and arrests.
“This arrest demonstrates the importance of investigative collaboration among federal, state, and local law enforcement partners who work seamlessly across jurisdictions to identify, locate, and apprehend violent offenders who pose a direct threat to our communities. Joint fugitive investigations such as this one help ensure that individuals accused of violent crimes are brought before the courts and that potential threats to public safety are addressed."

If you have details about individuals who are being sought for alleged crimes, or about criminal activity in your area, authorities encourage you to reach out to your local police departments. Do not try to engage these individuals directly. You can also connect with U.S. Marshals at MED.TIPLINE@usdoj.gov.
