title: What to know about McArthur Library’s new internet education program
text:
Biddeford’s McArthur Library is on its way to helping residents navigate the digital world.
The library recently received a $50,000 digital resilience grant from Maine Connectivity Authority, which will be used to conduct programming around internet literacy and safety.
“It’s amazing,” Library Director Nicole Clark said. “It’s really, really wonderful. So much of the world has gone digital, so it’s such a great tool to reach folks across our Maine community.”
Using the grant money, McArthur Library staff will host digital literacy training for targeted audiences across York County, helping to provide access to the internet.
Some of those trainings will take place in schools to help students navigate cyberbullying, internet accessibility and artificial intelligence. Others will be focused on the older population, many of whom find it challenging to stay connected in an increasingly digital world.
This type of programming brings the library’s mission to create access outside of the institution’s walls, Clark said.
“When people get this training, it helps them to feel not only more safe, but more confident,” she added.
Corie LeClair, technical coordinator at McArthur, will be working alongside Teen Services Librarian Claudia Spelman to host digital literacy trainings at libraries in five communities: Biddeford, Kennebunk, Limerick, Sanford and York.
Each of those libraries is connected to several different towns, LeClair said, effectively spreading the programming across the county.
“It’s a very large outreach program,” he said. “We’ll be able to hit every single town in York County.”
The grant funding will also be used to purchase equipment like laptops, Amazon Echo Dots and hotspots. LeClair and Spelman will then be able to help residents learn how to use their devices.
In the first round of outreach programming, participants will receive a free Echo Dot to help with accessibility. The Echo Dot is a helpful tool for vulnerable populations, Clark said. It can help people ask for emergency help, control their lights, check the weather or news, make calls to friends and family, set alarms and reminders, play music, and receive medication alerts.
In a state with the oldest median population age in the country, with 23% of the population being 65 or older, accessibility is important. Knowing how to avoid internet scams is also important, LeClair said.
“Maine has a very large problem with digital scams,” he said.
Starting in 2022, a Falmouth couple was scammed out of $1.3 million. China couple Barbara and Larry Cook, both in their 80s, were also scammed out of $1.3 million last year.
Both scams involved cryptocurrency. Among people 60 and up, scams of that nature more than tripled from 2022 to 2024, from 9,991 incidents worth $1 billion to 33,369 incidents worth $2.8 billion.
It’s those types of scams that LeClair hopes he can teach older Mainers to avoid.
“I see people come in all the time, and they’re scammed out of thousands of dollars,” he said. “We just want to help them out.”
The first learning session will take place on Nov. 17 at the York Public Library, followed by a session at McArthur Library on Nov. 20.
The Sanford session will take place at Goodall Library on Dec. 8, followed by a session at Kennebunk Free Library on Dec. 11 and a session at Limerick Library on Jan. 13. All sessions will take place at 12 p.m.
To register (and request transportation assistance if needed), those interested can email [email protected] or call the library at 207-286-9326.

title: What is cychlorphine, the opioid said to be 10 times more dangerous than fentanyl?
text:
What is cychlorphine, the opioid said to be 10 times more dangerous than fentanyl?
After years of fentanyl causing fatal overdoses, public officials are now warning of an even more powerful opioid.
Video above: Doctor talks decrease in opioid-related fatalities
Cychlorphine (sy-KLOR-feen) is a synthetic, or lab-made, opioid — specifically, a class of drugs known as orphines. Created by researchers who were trying to find powerful painkillers in the 1960s, orphines were ultimately considered too strong and dangerous, and the U.S. Food and Drug Administration never approved cychlorphine for medical use.
This story was originally published on PolitiFact.com.
Cychlorphine is a Schedule I drug that cannot be possessed or sold under federal law, but it has been increasingly linked to overdoses after China banned synthetic opioids called nitazenes.
People who track illicit drugs in the United States first identified cychlorphine in the drug supply in 2024, and Reddit users were talking about it online that same year. The drug is now making headlines in connection with U.S. overdose deaths.
It was linked to a 16-year-old’s death in San Francisco in April. And in Knoxville, Tennessee, officials said cychlorphine had been detected in about 50 suspected overdose deaths from July 2025 to early June.
Officials in Louisiana and Los Angeles County have issued public alerts warning residents of its risks as well.
How prevalent is cychlorphine in the U.S.?
In 2024, there was one report of cychlorphine in the U.S. drug supply, according to the White House Office of National Drug Control Policy. In 2025, there were 16 reports of it in 10 states.
Nationally, orphines don’t currently appear to be widespread, but “prevalence and trends are hard to discern,” said Jason R. Williams, a research scientist at the University of Washington’s Addictions, Drug & Alcohol Institute.
Hospitals and medical examiners’ toxicology tests and even crime labs sometimes fail to detect any given drug until it becomes a substance that officials are interested in tracking or collecting data on, he said.
The National Drug Control Policy office said it is currently most prevalent in Ohio, Texas and Tennessee.
Following a fatal overdose in Los Angeles County, public health officials there warned that cychlorphine is being mixed into the illicit drug supply without people’s knowledge. It has been found in powders, rocks or crystals, liquids and counterfeit pills made to look like prescription medications, they said.
How strong is cychlorphine?
The Drug Enforcement Administration describes fentanyl — a synthetic opioid that is approved for medical use — as about 100 times more potent than morphine.
Laboratory tests show cychlorphine is about 10 times more potent than fentanyl, said Alex Krotulski, director of toxicology and chemistry at the Center for Forensic Science Research and Education.
“That’s the only data that we have right now,” Krotulski said in July. Fentanyl has been studied in humans, but cychlorphine has not been studied in humans or animals, he said. “So we’re really finding out in real time what its effects on humans are.”
The drug’s potential effect on a person, however, depends on the dose, not just cychlorphine’s potency.
What are the signs of a cychlorphine overdose?
The signs that a person has been exposed to a toxic amount of cychlorphine are similar to those from other opioids like fentanyl. Pupils become constricted. Breathing is slowed or shallow. And other brain and spinal cord functions such as heart rate slow as the central nervous system becomes depressed.
Even “a very small amount” of cychlorphine can cause someone to stop breathing, Los Angeles County health officials said.
Can naloxone help during a cychlorphine overdose?
Yes, the opioid-overdose reversing drug naloxone can help.
But, much like fentanyl overdoses, cychlorphine’s potency means that treating an overdose can require multiple naloxone doses.
Naloxone usually comes in two-dose packages, meaning that when people carry it, they typically carry only one or two doses. That’s why it’s important to call 911 for suspected overdoses — first responders can provide additional doses if they’re needed.
It also might be hard to know if someone is overdosing on cychlorphine. The drug isn’t detected in routine hospital opioid urine screens or with drug test strips, so it can easily be missed.
What does data show about cychlorphine overdose rates?
More cychlorphine overdoses are being documented, but not all labs test for it, making it hard to detect trends.
The White House Office of National Drug Control Policy reported 55 deaths linked to cychlorphine in 2025 and through April 2026.
Krotulski said the Center for Forensic Science Research and Education lab started to detect cychlorphine in late 2025, but its prevalence increased in 2026. In about seven months, the lab linked more than 140 deaths to cychlorphine in the United States and Canada, he said.
Most samples that test positive for orphines in the U.S. also test positive for other drugs, and the vast majority of orphine-related deaths had other drugs present as well, Williams said.
That complicates determining what caused someone’s death because a toxicology panel might be limited unless evidence points toward looking for a drug not covered by typical testing, he said.
“It’s really unknown truly how many deaths there have been, but certainly in that short period of time, that is a significant number for a newly emerging drug like this,” Krotulski said.
If someone who died had a history of opioid use and the death circumstances suggest an opioid overdose but fentanyl and traditional opioids aren’t detected, then a medical examiner might test for orphines such as cychlorphine.
But if tests found fentanyl, the death would be explained and the medical examiner might not test further, potentially missing any cychlorphine’s presence, Williams said.
This story was originally published on PolitiFact.com.
It is republished here as part of a reporting and fact-checking partnership between PolitiFact and Hearst Television.

title: Fugitive convicted in murder case captured year after mistaken jail release
text:
MEMPHIS, Tenn. (WMC/Gray News) — A fugitive has been apprehended one year after he was mistakenly released from custody, authorities in Tennessee said.
The Shelby County Sheriff’s Office said deputies and U.S. Marshals agents arrested Anthony Green around 1:25 p.m. Wednesday.
Green had been erroneously released from custody in September 2025.
Background on the case
The Shelby County Sheriff’s Office said Green, then 24, was found guilty in September 2025 in a 2020 murder case after a three-day trial.
The jail had not yet received or processed information from the clerk’s office before Green was released in September 2025 after posting a $2,500 bond in an unrelated misdemeanor theft case, the Shelby County Sheriff’s Office said.
Arrest details
Officers, deputies and U.S. Marshals agents acted on tips and executed a search warrant in the 3300 block of Knights Trail in Memphis.
Green, now 25, was taken into custody and transported to the Shelby County Jail. He faces charges of first-degree murder, attempted first-degree murder and employing a firearm with the intent to commit a felony.

title: F-16 intercepts aircraft minutes before Pres. Trump landed for South Carolina rally
text:
CLEMSON, S.C. (WHNS/Gray Media) - A U.S. fighter jet intercepted an aircraft that violated restricted airspace over Clemson during President Donald Trump’s scheduled rally on Wednesday.
According to the North American Aerospace Defense Command, an F-16 intercepted a general aviation aircraft at about 5:40 p.m.
The aircraft landed safely at a nearby airfield while being monitored.
According to White House pool reports, Air Force One touched down at Greenville-Spartanburg International Airport just after 5:45 p.m., minutes after the intercept.
President Trump got off the plane at 6:08 p.m. and boarded Marine One to head to Clemson.
Marine One landed near the rally venue at Clemson University’s T. Ed Garrison Arena just before 6:35 p.m., according to the pool report. The president began speaking at 7:10 p.m.
NORAD reminded pilots who are intercepted to immediately tune to frequency 121.5 or 243.0 and reverse course until receiving further instructions.
Pilots who violate temporary flight restriction airspace may be met by federal authorities upon landing and face enforcement action.

title: Why older adults avoid therapy — and how to help them open up
text:
(Aging Untold) — For some older adults, the word “therapy” carries a stigma rooted in a generation that was taught to stay quiet and keep going.
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck says that silence has a cost and the Aging Untold experts have practical, low-pressure ways to help older loved ones start talking.
A generation taught to hide it
“Our age community was raised in a time when mental health was not something that we talked about,” Cradduck said. “Mental health was something that was hidden underneath the rug.”
Cradduck said that stigma meant asking for help was often seen as shameful.
“It was looked at with such distaste that for an aged person to say, ‘I need help,’ or ‘I would like to talk to someone’ — and that’s why there’s so much depression, I think, in our aged community,” Cradduck said.
She connected that silence directly to unresolved pain.
“When you haven’t been able to deal with all of the trauma that life has given you and you haven’t processed through, then there’s such a heavy weight on you,” Cradduck said. “Psychotherapy is absolutely an essential part of just being a human being, I think.”
“Survival is not healing”
Older generations were conditioned to push through hardship rather than confront it, Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said.
“I learned how to survive. That’s the older generation — they were always taught they were very stoic and they survive, but survival’s not healing,” Rogers said. “So they never really had a chance to really even heal or even to recognize, do they even know they’re depressed?”
Rogers added that depression in older adults doesn’t always look like sadness.
“It presents so different. It’s not sadness. They may be irritable. They may just feel like they’re fluttered, you know, or just loss of desire or motivation,” Rogers said. “I don’t think they recognize that they’re depressed.”
Reframing therapy as “education”
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said the word “therapy” itself can shut the conversation down before it starts — so she uses different language.
“When I’ve worked with clients that hear therapy and you can just see their eyes are like, no, no, no, I just don’t call it therapy,” O’Rourke said. “I say education. Let’s take a class, let’s buy a book just to get them kind of initiated into the idea that maybe talking would be helpful.”
She described one example of meeting a client where they already were.
“I had one Catholic client and I said, ‘Why don’t you go to confession?’ And he did,” O’Rourke said. “And in that tradition, he got it all out with the priest, and he felt better. And then he was open to going to therapy. It was the thing that just triggered him, so be open to using anything just to get that motion going.”
Friends, clubs and community can help too
Cradduck said licensed therapy isn’t the only path to processing grief and life’s heaviness.
“You don’t have to be a licensed therapist to be a good friend and lend an ear. Most of us have some good advice we can give,” Cradduck said. “But this is the bootstrapped generation — you were told you had to pull your bootstraps up, you had to keep going. And they were left suffering.”
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose pointed to group settings as another outlet.
“Even like Bible studies, book clubs — you know, where you can have discussions,” Ambrose said. “I have people around the country, they’re doing downsizing clubs, and people are really processing all this stuff, all the grief, all the heaviness.”
Ambrose said those groups often lead to deeper conversations than expected.
“They’re talking about the challenges they have communicating with their spouse or adult children, or with the medical episodes that they’ve had. So it’s very cathartic,” she said.
A Medicare benefit many don’t know about
O’Rourke also flagged a federal resource available to older adults seeking mental health support.
“The other resource that I would want people to know about is Medicare. Go to cms.gov. Medicare covers mental health help,” O’Rourke said.
Hospice is another resource, O’Rourke said.
“And if you’ve been involved in losing someone and you’ve had hospice services, you can get help with that grief for 12 months after death,” she said.

title: Maine bill seeks to replace ‘unenrolled’ with ‘independent’ on voter forms
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) - A proposal at the State House could change how Maine identifies voters who are not affiliated with a political party.
Maine state Rep. David Boyer, R-Poland, announced legislation Wednesday to replace “unenrolled” with “independent” on voter registration forms and election records.
Boyer said the term “unenrolled” does not accurately describe voters without a party affiliation. He said confusion surfaced during June’s primary when some voters were unsure whether their “unenrolled” status allowed them to vote in a party primary. Others mistakenly registered with the Green Independent Party.
The bill would change the terminology but not voter rights or Maine’s primary system.
“People identify as independent,” Boyer said. “They don’t go around and, you know, tell somebody that they’re an unenrolled voter and that they don’t have a party. They say they’re independent.”
“This is why it’s a common-sense change,” he said.
Supporters cite voter numbers
Brett Loyd, President and CEO of The Bipartisan Bullfinch Group and Founding Partner of the Independent Center, supports the proposal.
“In Maine, if you look at the voter registration statistics, a third of the vote, there’s more independents in Maine than there are Republicans, and only about a point shy from Democrats,” Loyd said.
“This is something that truly is impacting one in three voters in Maine,” he said.
Clerk raises concern over confusion
Bath City Clerk and President of the Maine Town & City Clerks’ Association Darci Wheeler said the change could create another layer of confusion because Maine already has the Green Independent Party.
“We need to make sure voters can clearly distinguish between someone who is not enrolled in a political party and someone who has chosen to enroll in the Green Independent Party,” Wheeler said.
Wheeler said more voter education outside of the booth may be the better solution. She said clerks can explain that “unenrolled” means “no party choice,” but in order to stay neutral, they cannot explain political parties to voters.
Boyer’s bill is expected to receive a public hearing early next year.

title: Please do not make excuses for Troy Jackson
text:
I write in response to Steve Collins’ column making light of Troy Jackson’s dismissive action of telling Sen. Susan Collins to “shut up” on the debate stage (“Politicians have a rich history of telling each other to zip it,” Oct. 19).
First, Steve Collins suggests that because Sen. Collins did not react to the slight to women — both on the night of the debate and also when Trump may have insulted her — it is somehow on her shoulders to defend herself each and every time she may be insulted. If she does not, it somehow puts her at fault.
I believe Sen. Collins decided not to engage Mr. Jackson, and decided to ignore the slight and not get into a fight about it on stage. She is a lady.
Secondly, Troy Jackson acts like a victim when he says “she [Sen. Collins] is talking down to me.” Mr. Jackson is no victim. Someone once told me that the only person who can make you feel inferior is yourself.
Thirdly, because there have been many other instances of politicians saying “shut up,” does that make it right? I will note that all the examples Steve Collins gave were of men saying “shut up.”
Fourth, although, yes, not the end of the world, is this the kind of behavior we want from a senator? I want to see a gentleman match the professionalism of Sen. Collins.
Joanne Lebel
Auburn

title: Susan Collins reminds us of the rationale for ‘country before party’
text:
Apparently Sen. Susan Collins doesn’t adhere to a guiding principle many Americans learned
in their youth. “Remember, country always comes before party,” my Republican father admonished me — long before I was of age to vote.
Sen. Collins, in an August 2016 Washington Post op-ed, described her attachment to
the Republican Party: “Being a Republican is what defines me as a person.” In the same op-ed, Collins declared Donald Trump not qualified to be president, and did this in no uncertain terms. 
Yet, she now asks us to reelect her to the Senate, where she would vote for Trump’s Republican Party. This would add greatly to Trump’s power as president, a position she did not believe he was qualified to hold in the first place.
Sen. Collins provides a clear case of placing party before country — and a clear reason why Americans have long believed in placing country before party.
Parker Albee, Jr.
Falmouth

title: Buxton voters approve temporary data center ban
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BUXTON — Buxton joined several Maine towns Wednesday in passing a data center moratorium. Voters approved the measure in a special town meeting attended by about 60 residents.
The moratorium bans data centers — facilities designed for processing and storing troves of digital data and artificial intelligence — for 180 days dating from Aug. 12 in Buxton. Opponents of data centers point to evidence that they deplete local natural resources and disrupt infrastructure.
No data centers have been proposed in Buxton. The pause will give town officials time to draft and pass an ordinance to regulate any such facility that might be pitched in the future.
Several towns in southern Maine, including Gorham, Scarborough, Westbrook, Biddeford and Sanford, have enacted similar moratoriums since Gov. Janet Mills vetoed a bill in April that would have temporarily restricted such developments statewide. Some communities are now considering banning data centers outright.

title: Bestselling author Tess Gerritsen releases new novel in Martini Club series
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Internationally bestselling author Tess Gerritsen has released spy thriller “The Shadow Friends,” the latest installment in her Martini Club series.
Series and book summary
The Martini Club series follows five retired spies, now living anonymous lives in a small town in Maine. They use their skills to deal with the crises that arise in their lives and in their community.
The series consists of “The Spy Coast,” followed by “The Summer Guests.” “The Shadow Friends” is the third installment in the series.
Inspiration for the series
Gerritsen says the Martini Club series was inspired by her discover that many CIA and State Department retirees live in Midcoast Maine.
“On the short street where I was living 30 years ago, two of the homes on the street were owned by retired spies. I wondered what retirement was like for them -- whether they got together to gossip, or if they missed their old jobs. It made me look at ALL my older neighbors with new eyes. Suddenly I saw them as more than just Grandmas and Grandpas. I wondered whether their careers had been dangerous, and what secrets they could tell -- if they were allowed to,” said Gerritsen.
Gerritsen says she is working on the fourth book, “The Italian Affair.”
About the author
Gerritsen lives in Camden, Maine. She is a trained medical doctor who built a second career as an internationally bestselling writer. “The Shadow Friends” is one of her 33 novels.
She is also known for her Rizzoli and Isles crime series, which is the basis for the TV series “Rizzoli & Isles.”
Gerritsen’s novels have been translated into 40 languages, and more than 40 million copies have been sold worldwide.
Her novels are available where books are sold. Readers looking for a signed copy can find one at Left Bank Books in Belfast, Maine.
For more information on Gerritsen, visit her website.

title: ‘Top Gun,’ ‘Alien’ star Tom Skerritt dies at 93
text:
(Gray News) - Emmy Award-winning actor Tom Skerritt, known for his roles in “Alien,” “Top Gun,” “M*A*S*H,” and more, died Wednesday. He was 93.
He died of natural causes, according to The Associated Press.
“While the world knew Tom through his remarkable acting career, we knew him for his humor, curiosity, wisdom, generosity, and the love he brought into our lives,” his family wrote in a statement issued to media outlets, including People.
Skerritt was born in 1933 in Detroit.
After enlisting in the U.S. Air Force for four years, he attended Henry Ford College, Wayne State University, and the University of California, Los Angeles. He left school to pursue acting.
Skerritt was twice nominated for an Emmy — both for “Picket Fences,” winning outstanding lead actor in a drama series in 1993. Other career highlights include playing the patient husband of Shirley MacLaine in “Turning Point,” Sally Field’s husband in “Steel Magnolias,” and a scheming opportunist who stands in the way of Jodie Foster’s attempt to communicate with extraterrestrial life in “Contact.”
“A writer once described me as a character actor locked in a leading man’s body, and I’ve always loved that. It’s a nice compliment. I’ve been able to walk the line between television and features,” he told the Seattle Post-Intelligencer in 1997.
Onstage, he was the narrator in “Our Town” at Seattle’s Intiman Theatre in 2004 and made his Broadway debut in 2013 in an adaptation of John Grisham’s “A Time to Kill,” in which The Associated Press wrote he “nicely pulls off a charming disgraced and drunken lawyer.”
Funeral plans were not immediately available.

title: FTC sues ticket broker accused of cheating limits to hoard high-demand event tickets
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray News) - The Federal Trade Commission is suing a ticket broker accused of using unlawful tactics to buy millions of tickets to popular events.
The complaint, filed by the Department of Justice, alleges REPS & Company Inc., along with its CEO Ryan Pancheri, President Brian Archibald and Chief Operating Officer Nicholas Totagrande, violated the Better Online Ticket Sales Act.
The law makes it illegal to “circumvent a security measure, access control system or other technological control or measure on an Internet website or online service that is used by the ticket issuer to enforce posted event ticket limits or to maintain the integrity of posted online ticket purchasing order rules.”
The complaint alleges that since 2022, REPS and its operators used unlawful tactics to bypass ticket issuers’ security measures and exceed posted ticket limits.
REPS purchased more than eight tickets for at least 83,500 events — many in high demand and likely to sell out. REPS spent more than $1.3 billion to amass more than 18.5 million tickets, generating at least $120.8 million in profit by reselling them, the complaint says.
For example, REPS generated $833,000 in profit by using 1,300 accounts to purchase 7,624 tickets to one Beyoncé Renaissance tour concert in Kansas City, Missouri, in 2023, according to the complaint.
“Companies that seek to profit by driving up prices or depriving ordinary fans of access to reasonably priced tickets to their favorite shows or events should be on notice that we are watching and will take action to stop this unlawful conduct,” Christopher Mufarrige, Director of the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection, said.
Ticket issuers such as Ticketmaster and AXS have measures to block resellers from violating purchase limits. The complaint alleges REPS uses employees, most of whom are based in the Philippines, to bypass Ticketmaster and other issuers’ account security measures.
The alleged methods include using thousands of purchasing accounts created with other people’s names, addresses or phone numbers, along with virtual credit card accounts and phone numbers controlled by REPS. Employees also used IP proxy services and multisession browsers that mask a user’s identity and location, the complaint alleges.
When ticket issuers detect attempts to bypass limits, they often block or cancel the purchase. REPS developed strategies to work around those controls, such as making slight changes to an account holder’s address or name, the complaint alleges. Internal company documents show REPS officials discussed tactics to keep accounts from being blocked.
The commission voted 2-0 to refer the complaint to the Justice Department for filing. The department filed the complaint on behalf of the commission in U.S. District Court for the Southern District of California.

title: Quest Diagnostics reports cyber breach affecting 'certain patient records'
text:
Quest Diagnostics reports cyber breach affecting 'certain patient records'
Medical laboratory operator Quest Diagnostics said it learned of a cyber breach of one of its systems this week, likely compromising some records for patients.
Video above: Baylor Genetics data breach
In a Thursday regulatory filing, Quest Diagnostics reported "unauthorized access" to its Quanum Lab Services Manager, a platform where certain clients can place test orders and receive or look up their results. The company said it discovered the hack on Wednesday and notified federal law enforcement.
How many patients and which particular records have been affected are still unknown. Quest Diagnostics said it believes "certain patient records" were accessed in the breach, but that the full scope remains under investigation.
The New Jersey-based company said it's also working with external cybersecurity experts to assist in its response.
Quest Diagnostics has seen hacks impacting patient records before. In 2016, for example, the company said data including lab results and contact information of about 34,000 people was exposed in another online breach. And in 2019, other personal information belonging to about 11.9 million Quest patients was affected after a separate hack at American Medical Collection Agency, a billing collections service provider.
Cyberattacks are on the rise across industries. Beyond healthcare, other breaches have recently disrupted anything from supermarket chains to core education applications.
Governments and companies worldwide are working more broadly on online security updates. Urgency erupted this week, after an AI-assisted discovery of vulnerabilities in a programming language called PHP, which is vital to 70% of websites globally.
Outages and limited service have continued for many users as firms rush to patch those risks. But based on the company's investigation, Quest Diagnostics confirmed to The Associated Press Thursday that its cyber breach was not related to the PHP issue.

title: Meta ordered to pay New Mexico $25 billion for deceiving users about privacy on Facebook
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(AP) - A judge on Wednesday ordered Meta to pay New Mexico $25 billion after a jury found the company liable for deceiving users about privacy on Facebook, marking the biggest fine ever against the tech giant.
Facebook’s deception was intentional and executives consistently misled users about how the platform worked, state District Court Judge Francis J. Mathew wrote in his ruling.
“Facebook promised users that they (the users) controlled their data. This was false,” he said.
Jurors in September found Meta liable for over 43 million violations of New Mexico consumer protection laws for making misleading public statements about how it handled users’ personal data. The case was brought after political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica harvested Facebook data to generate targeted political ads during the 2016 election season.
The award will serve as a warning to tech companies that New Mexico will hold them accountable, state Attorney General Raúl Torrez said at a news conference.
“This judgment should be a signal, an unambiguous message, to Silicon Valley,” he said.
Meta said the ruling and Torrez’s office’s approach to enforcement “makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico.”
“At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online. We are confident we will prevail on appeal,” C.J. Mahoney, the company’s chief legal officer, said in a statement.
The Menlo Park, California, company has a market value of $1.8 trillion and brought in more than $200 billion in revenue last year. Company shares traded 2% higher after Wednesday’s announcement, and it was scheduled to report its quarterly earnings later in the day.
New Mexico goes it alone
In August, Meta reached a settlement with nearly all states and territories — except New Mexico and Florida — to pay $18 billion and add stronger child-safety measures to its Facebook and Instagram platforms.
The settlement ended a trial over teen social media addiction and resolved a pivotal case years in the making that sought to hold the tech giant accountable for the role its platforms played in undermining children’s mental health. The effort targeted features designed to grab young people’s attention.
New Mexico didn’t join the multistate settlement, choosing to go after the company on its own.
The director of a nonprofit that supports stronger policies toward corporations said $25 billion is “a drop in the bucket for Meta,” but demonstrates people want accountability.
“Right now, they are rolling out Muse, an AI assistant encouraging people to trust it with everything from their bank accounts to their medical information,” added Nidhi Hegde, executive director of the American Economic Liberties Project. “Which is why we need more enforcers with courage and laws with actual teeth to rein them in.”
At the trial, attorneys for the state cited a 2010 Washington Post op-ed in which Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg wrote that the company didn’t sell user data.
“You have control over how your information is shared,” Zuckerberg said. “We do not and never will sell any of your information to anyone.”
New Mexico officials sought fines of $35 billion to $40 billion, arguing the company would only change if its stock price were impacted.
Meta’s lawyers, meanwhile, asserted that the state failed to prove the company made misleading statements and that content moderation actually harmed people in New Mexico. They wanted the company to pay $3.4 billion at most and said an award many times larger would be unconstitutional.
Although interest would accrue on the penalty during the appeal process, Meta could succeed in reducing the number of violations for which it is found liable.
The $25 billion award far exceeds a $5 billion fine the Federal Trade Commission levied against Facebook in 2019.
Peter Ormerod, an associate law professor at Villanova University, was surprised by the size of the New Mexico judgment because previous legal settlements over Cambridge Analytica were much lower.
“It comes out to about $12,000 per person in New Mexico,” he said. “It’s quite unlike anything else we’ve seen.”
Under the New Mexico Constitution, fines for violating consumer protection laws go toward education spending. It could take years for the state to get the money while the company appeals.
Company argues that the state failed to prove harm
The trial focused on accusations Facebook deceived users about a breach stemming from a third-party personality quiz that harvested data from roughly 87 million profiles and sold it to Cambridge Analytica. The now-defunct firm’s clients included Donald Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign.
Attorneys for New Mexico argued that the state’s entire population was deceived, and that Facebook allowed misinformation or violent content to proliferate.
Meta’s lawyers argued the state failed to prove people were harmed by deceptive statements. Zuckerberg in a video deposition denied that Facebook profited off harmful content and said the company had to balance free speech with content moderation.
In a partial win for the company, jurors rejected assertions that Facebook made false claims about removing harmful content, including misinformation about the COVID-19 pandemic.
Meta lawyers said it has changed policies since the lawsuit was filed in 2021 and catches and removes an estimated 99% of content violating its standards.
___
This story was updated to correct the spelling of the judge’s last name.

title: Cooper Flagg set new record in Mavericks' season opener
text:
Cooper Flagg set yet another record during Wednesday night’s season opener against the Houston Rockets.
The Dallas Mavericks star completed a fourth quarter jump shot to bring his total points scored to 32, the most any teen has scored during an NBA season opener.
The 19-year-old Newport phenom even outscored Kyrie Irving, who sat out last season because of a knee injury and had 15 points in his return.
Yet Flagg’s performance wasn’t enough to carry the Mavericks to victory. The Mavs lost 128-110.
But Flagg continues to demonstrate why he was a No. 1 draft pick ahead of his rookie season.
During his first season with the Mavericks, Flagg averaged 21 points per game, the most for any rookie; became the youngest player to score 50 points in a single NBA game; and is the second-youngest to score 1,000 points.
Flagg went on to become the second-youngest Rookie of the Year, behind only Lebron James.

title: Gusty winds from the north as storm passes by
text:
Gusty winds from the north as storm passes by
Gusty winds from the north as storm passes by
It is seasonable and mostly sunny Thursday afternoon across Maine, with highs in the 50s and low 60s. Northerly winds pick up as the day goes on, with gusts of 25 to 35 mph possible Thursday evening, overnight, and into Friday.
Subtropical Storm Josephine is located 340 miles south of the Maine coastline Thursday afternoon. The storm will accelerate as it moves east-northeast into tonight, with gusty northerly winds continuing into Friday.
Winds ease up Friday night, and with high pressure overhead, temperatures will fall rapidly after sunset. Lows in the teens and 20s are likely by Saturday morning. Lighter winds and plentiful sunshine make for a beautiful fall weekend.
A slight warming trend is expected through Monday, with highs in the 60s to around 70 degrees at the start of next week. A cold front brings colder air for the remainder of the week.

title: Man convicted of killing mother who threatened to evict him, believed she was ‘possessed’
text:
OREGON CITY, Ore. (KPTV/Gray News) — An Oregon man has been found guilty of murdering his mother, whom he believed was possessed by demons.
Ronald Joseph Kirk, 38, was convicted of second-degree murder and being a felon in possession of a firearm in Clackamas County court on Tuesday.
Prosecutors said Kirk was living with his mother, 61-year-old Rosa Leyva, in her small Gladstone home when Leyva didn’t come into work early on Nov. 26, 2024.
People who knew Leyva had concerns about Kirk and testified in court that he was volatile, dangerous and frequently drunk or high on meth.
Gladstone police went to the home to conduct a welfare check that same day after Leyva did not answer calls from coworkers and loved ones. Kirk answered the door and told officers that his mother was inside and had not been conscious for about a day, according to prosecutors.
Officers found Leyva’s body sitting at the dining room table in front of her laptop, covered in pillowcases with a single gunshot wound to the head.
Investigators learned that Leyva expressed concern about her son’s behavior fueled by alcohol and drug use, and that Kirk became obsessed with exorcism and demonic possession while under the influence.
A month before Leyva’s death, Kirk had left her a voicemail in which he claimed she was possessed and had “almost” put a bullet in her head the day before.
Leyva had planned to legally evict Kirk and texted him that she wanted him out of her house on Nov. 8, 2024.
Kirk is scheduled to be sentenced on Nov. 4 and faces a potential life sentence with a minimum of 25 years in prison.

title: Federal judge orders Trump to sit for deposition in his defamation lawsuit against BBC
text:
Federal judge orders Trump to sit for deposition in his defamation lawsuit against BBC
A federal judge on Thursday ordered President Donald Trump to sit for a deposition in his defamation lawsuit against the BBC by Dec. 11.
The order from U.S. Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett came as BBC’s lawyers complained that Trump had delayed his appearance. Attorney Charles Tobin said that with two months left in the discovery period, “we still haven’t been able to depose the plaintiff.”
He noted there was an agreed-upon date of Oct. 16, but that the Republican president canceled it for a “matter of national importance.” Tobin he said Trump was in fact campaigning in Georgia.
Previous video: BBC leaders resign amid scandal over misleading edit of Trump speech
“He was participating in party politics and prioritized that over sitting for the deposition,” Tobin said.
Lett said Trump must sit for a deposition by Dec. 11, or face sanctions up to dismissal of his lawsuit -– unless the discovery period was extended past Dec. 18.
THIS IS AN APNewsAlert. Check back for updates. AP's earlier story is below.
Lawyers for the BBC and for Donald Trump were tussling in court Thursday over whether former special counsel Jack Smith should be deposed in the president's $10 billion defamation case against the broadcaster — a possibility that Trump strongly opposes.
In a hearing before U.S. Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett in Miami, the parties were also expected to address the thorny issue of when Trump himself will be made available for deposition.
BBC asked the judge last week to compel Trump to appear after they said he canceled an agreed-upon date of Oct. 16, citing "matters of national importance." The British broadcaster says Trump is trying to delay his appearance until January 2027. The judge has threatened sanctions if Trump fails to comply with the court's schedule.
Trump, who has often avoided depositions, filed his lawsuit against the BBC last December, seeking $10 billion in damages. He accused the publicly funded broadcaster of defamation as well as deceptive and unfair trade practices related to a documentary, "Trump: A Second Chance."
The BBC acknowledged that filmmakers spliced together quotes from different sections of the speech Trump delivered to his supporters on Jan. 6, 2021, before the storming of the U.S. Capitol, to make it seem he was directly urging violence. The broadcaster apologized over the editing, and the head of the BBC and its top news executive both resigned. But BBC has denied Trump's claims that it defamed him.
To bolster its defense, the broadcaster subpoenaed Smith earlier this month. Trump's lawyers argued, in a joint filing asking for a hearing on the matter, that there was no good reason for Smith, who is not a party to the case, to appear.
"Smith lacks any personal knowledge regarding the issues in this matter," they argued in the filing. "He was not present when President Trump's January 6, 2021, speech … was made, nor did he participate in its preparation. Smith does not have any personal knowledge regarding President Trump's state of mind at the time the Speech was given."
Trump's side also argued that "Smith's testimony would be duplicative," because he published he lengthy report on the events of January 6 and also testified for many hours. "The entirety of his testimony is publicly available," it argued.
The BBC countered, in the same filing, that there were few more knowledgeable sources about the events of Jan. 6 than Smith, who studied and investigated them for years.
"It is difficult to imagine a more authoritative source on these issues than Mr. Smith, who spent years gathering evidence on those topics with the force of the Justice Department and the power of the grand jury behind him," the BBC's lawyers argued.
"No one forced Plaintiff to file this lawsuit and to dispute that his speech on January 6 incited the violence that followed at the Capitol. But as long as he chooses to maintain the case, he cannot commit the fundamental injustice of preventing the BBC from obtaining the evidence it needs to robustly defend itself on every element of his claim…"
A key question also remains: When will Trump himself appear?
In a filing Oct. 13, BBC lawyers said they first requested dates for a deposition in July, and followed up repeatedly, with both sides eventually agreeing on Oct. 16.
After weeks of silence, they wrote, "Plaintiff's counsel responded on September 28, 2026, indicating that 'the President is no longer available for his deposition on October 16 due to other matters of national importance' and that counsel would 'endeavor to provide you with a replacement date by the end of this week.' He did not."
They said they were then told that Trump "has no availability whatsoever for a deposition" before discovery is set to close on Dec. 18, and that Trump would instead make himself available the second or third week of January.
"Two months of discovery remaining, the BBC still has not been able to depose, and does not even have a schedule to depose, the most central figure in this case: Plaintiff himself," attorney Charles D. Tobin wrote in the filing. "Those delays have flouted the cooperative spirit of discovery and precluded the BBC from obtaining the evidence necessary to robustly litigate its defense."

title: Judge orders Trump must sit for a deposition in his defamation lawsuit against the BBC
text:
MIAMI (AP) — A federal judge on Thursday ordered President Donald Trump to sit for a deposition in his $10 billion defamation lawsuit against the BBC by Dec. 11.
The order from U.S. Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett came as lawyers for the British broadcaster complained that Trump had delayed his appearance in his own lawsuit. Charles Tobin, attorney for the BBC, said that with two months left in the discovery period, “we still haven’t been able to depose the plaintiff.”
Meanwhile, it remained uncertain whether former special counsel Jack Smith would be allowed to sit for a deposition. Federal rules require current and former employees to receive permission from agency heads before testifying in court cases. Smith has requested permission but has not received an answer, and the judge ruled that the department must respond to him by Nov. 2.
In arguments about Trump’s deposition, Tobin noted there had been an agreed-upon date of Oct. 16, but Trump had canceled it for a “matter of national importance.” He said the Republican president was in fact campaigning in Georgia that day. “He was participating in party politics and prioritized that over sitting for the deposition,” Tobin said.
Lett said Trump must sit for a deposition by Dec. 11, or face sanctions up to dismissal of his lawsuit — unless the discovery period is extended by the presiding judge.
Discovery, where lawyers for both sides exchange documents and other evidence, is scheduled to end Dec. 18, and the BBC’s attorneys want to make sure they have Trump’s deposition before that deadline. Lett said only the presiding judge assigned to the case can alter the trial schedule, and the defense said it would be open to scheduling the deposition at a later time if the trial schedule was also changed.
Trump, who has often avoided depositions, filed his lawsuit against the BBC last December. He accused the publicly funded broadcaster of defamation as well as deceptive and unfair trade practices related to a documentary, “Trump: A Second Chance.”
The BBC acknowledged that filmmakers spliced together quotes from different sections of the speech Trump delivered to his supporters on Jan. 6, 2021, before the storming of the U.S. Capitol, to make it seem he was directly urging violence. The broadcaster apologized over the editing, and the head of the BBC and its top news executive both resigned. But the BBC has denied Trump’s claims that it defamed him.
Trump’s attorneys also argued against recording his deposition on video, asking for only a court reporter. The judge ruled that the deposition could be recorded on video but only for attorneys, meaning it wouldn’t be released to the public.
It remained unclear whether Jack Smith would be allowed to sit for deposition
To bolster its defense, the broadcaster subpoenaed former special counsel Jack Smith earlier this month. Trump’s lawyers have argued that there is no good reason for Smith, who is not a party to the case, to appear. The BBC has said Smith has extensive knowledge of what happened that day.
At issue in Thursday’s hearing, though, was whether Smith had received the legally required permission from the Department of Justice. Assistant U.S. Attorney Matthew Feeley told the judge that Smith had sent a letter to the department saying he would not testify without permission, and the agency had not yet responded. Lett ordered the department to respond to Smith by Nov. 2.
It seems unlikely that the department would grant Smith permission, or that he would move forward without it.
Earlier in the hearing, Tobin, the BBC lawyer, argued that Smith has not objected to being deposed for this case, meaning the only objection is coming from Trump. Tobin said the BBC is not trying to relitigate the events of Jan. 6, but Smith is one of the leading experts in what happened that day, and his deposition could lead the BBC to evidence that could help their case.
“We can argue later on whether his testimony is admissible,” Tobin said, “but we are entitled to that deposition.”
Trump’s lawyer, Alejandro Brito, said Smith has no personal knowledge of Trump’s Jan. 6 speech or Trump’s state of mind when he gave it. All of Smith’s knowledge about the case is secondhand, Brito argued, and the special counsel’s report, along with Smith’s testimony before Congress, is all public and available to the BBC’s attorneys.
Judge says the BBC can see membership records for Mar-a-Lago
The judge agreed that the BBC should be allowed to see records for the total number of applications for membership at Trump’s Mar-a-Lago resort in Florida from Jan. 6, 2020, through Jan. 6, 2026, as well as the total cost of membership and initiation fees for new applicants.
Tobin said one aspect of any defamation case is showing actual damages, and the popularity of Mar-a-Lago is a significant indicator of Trump’s reputation. The BBC’s lawyer described the private club as “a place where he exhibits his reputation in front of people who are important to him.”
Brito argued that Trump does not actually run Mar-a-Lago, and that his reputation is not associated with the club.

title: ‘There are no words’: Boyfriend accused of killing girlfriend, her 15-year-old son, and her mother
text:
HAPPY VALLEY, Ore. (KPTV/Gray News) — Three people found shot to death inside an Oregon home on Tuesday have been identified, along with the person who police say is responsible.
According to Happy Valley police, 78-year-old Patricia Lynn Campbell, 47-year-old Katie Lynn Kinder and 15-year-old Evan Scott Kinder were found dead inside their home after officers were called to the residence for a welfare check.
Officers said the welfare check was requested after Kinder did not show up to work.
Neighbors told officers they had not seen anyone at the house for a few days.
The Clackamas County Medical Examiner’s Office said Wednesday autopsies showed all three died from gunshot wounds.
Detectives named 45-year-old Edward Villa as the person believed to be responsible for the family members’ murders.
Police said Villa was Kinder’s boyfriend and lived at the home with her, her son and her mother.
Villa was found dead Wednesday in a motel room at the South Jetty Inn in Hammond of an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound, according to Warrenton police.
Members of the U.S. Marshals Service found him after officers watched his car at the motel.
Officials said Villa had worked for the North Clackamas School District since 2007, most recently as a student and community engagement specialist. The district said he did not show up for work Wednesday.
In a statement, family members said they lost a mother, a sister and a nephew. They described Campbell as someone who helped hold the family together and who was loved as a mother and grandmother.
Loved ones described Kinder as a loving aunt who brought joy and laughter to the family. They said Evan was young and had his whole life ahead of him.
“There are no words strong enough to describe the pain, grief, and devastation we are feeling,” the family shared in part.
The family asked for privacy as they grieved and thanked the community for support.
Villa’s ex-wife, Tiffany Villa, said they share a son and her main concern is his well-being.

title: Strikes and sisterhood: Inside Bangor’s Coffee Cup bowling league
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Thursday mornings at Family Fun Bowling Alley sound like this — pins crashing, cheers, and laughter from the Coffee Cup League.
The league brings together 24 women every week to bowl, socialize and stay active.
Decades on the lanes
For some, bowling is a lifelong love:
- Ruth has been bowling for about 50 years.
- Gloria started about 60 years ago.
- Roxy joined about 17 years ago.
“I joined for exercise and the camaraderie,” Ruth said.
Roxy joined for family: “She talked me into it, she’s my sister.”
A 90th birthday celebration
Thursday was extra special for mother-daughter duo Sherrie Pedersen and Gloria Tapley, as the team celebrated Gloria turning 90 years young.
“There’s three mother-daughter teams,” Sherri said. “Me and my mom, the 97-year-old and her daughter Toby and another couple over here.”
Each week, teams face a different opponent — though scores aren’t the focus.
“We really like it when we get the pins down, we get a strike or a spare,” Sherri said. “Which I’m not doing so hot today,” Gloria laughed.
More than a game
“It’s good for a laugh.” — Roxy
“We all think it keeps everybody young.” — Sherri
“Well, it keeps us on our feet.” — Gloria

title: A mutated virus is driving the US into an early flu season, especially on the West Coast
text:
A mutated virus is driving the US into an early flu season, especially on the West Coast
Flu season is picking up months ahead of schedule with a mutated virus spreading in some parts of the United States, surprising some people who might not even be thinking about their annual flu shots yet.
This year, the season started 2 1/2 months earlier than what’s typical and hit states on the West Coast first, which is unusual, said Dr. Alex Greninger, head of the Division of Infectious Disease Diagnostics at the University of Washington’s Department of Laboratory Medicine.
Related video above: Doctors urge people to get their fall vaccines now before respiratory illness season hits
Usually, the U.S. flu season starts in the South – often in Florida, where it arrives from the Southern Hemisphere. Then, it tends to spread north as fall and winter progress.
“In Seattle, we’re pretty far north. We see a pretty strong peak in January,” Greninger said, noting that the bulk of their cases typically come in late December through February.
That’s not how it’s playing out this year.
‘January levels of flu’
Roughly 1 in 10 people who were tested for the flu last week tested positive in Washington state, according to data from the state Department of Public Health.
“We’re basically seeing January levels of flu in the last week,” Greninger said.
Walgreens says that nationally, this flu season is tracking about four weeks ahead of recent seasons, and it’s dispensing more antiviral prescriptions as well as cough and cold medications than during the same period last year.
Nationally, about 2.1% of doctor visits last week were for influenza-like illness, a rough measure of the misery that flu symptoms like fever and cough are causing across the country. That’s still below the national baseline, however, according to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, meaning the virus hasn’t really taken off everywhere yet.
“All of the Pacific states, I would say, started their season very early,” said Dr. Caitlin Rivers, an epidemiologist who directs the Center for Outbreak Response Innovation at Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health.
In the region that includes Arizona, California, Hawaii and Nevada, the proportion of flu tests that come back positive reached at least 10% last week, indicating significant levels of flu. The South is catching up to those numbers quickly, said Rivers, who closely tracks the flu through her Force of Infection newsletter.
A dominant strain
The wave of flu hitting the Pacific states came from Asia, Greninger said, and is dominated by the H1N1 virus, which sparked a pandemic when it first emerged in 2009.
It represents about 98% of the samples his lab is getting now, he said.
These H1N1 viruses have also picked up a gene mutation that makes them better at evading our immunity.
This version of the virus has already wreaked havoc in Japan, where it forced school and daycare closures after cases surged in kids. It also prompted officials to move up vaccination clinics to help protect people.
The mutation, at a location called G155E, cropped up after strains were already selected for this year’s flu shots, Greninger said. So even though the vaccines target a version of H1N1 and should still offer some protection, the virus can still break through.
Get vaccinated now, experts say
Greninger notes that the Covid-19 pandemic helped experts develop new tools that allow them to track the spread of viral variants almost in real time.
“We’re getting closer and closer to the weather report, right?” he said. “We can get the sequence quickly, so we can say exactly what the mutations are. What this really puts the focus on is, we’ve got to be able to make these vaccines faster.”
The strains used in this year’s flu shots were chosen in the spring, before the new viral variant had become a threat. They’re selected so early because the majority of flu shots are still grown in chicken eggs, a practice that persists, Greninger added, because it is so cheap.
There’s a newly approved flu shot that uses mRNA technology, and he said that has the potential to make better shots available more quickly. Whether it will someday replace egg-based vaccines is a different issue – an economic one.
Doctors often advise getting a flu shot before Halloween, in order to provide the best protection through spring. But Greninger’s best advice now is to get vaccinated as soon as possible. “A lot of people, like even myself, would wait until late October, which we’re sort of in already. But really, the time to get vaccinated was actually two to three weeks ago.”
Other experts agree.
“It is very early, and so I worry about vaccine timing,” Rivers said. “People aren’t thinking about getting their flu vaccine so early in the season.”
Whether that will make the overall season more severe remains to be seen.
Greninger said there could also be a second wave of flu cases after H1N1 peaks.
“I wouldn’t be surprised to see a second flu season, like a normal flu season. You’ll have H1N1 cases that will peak in 2026, and then who knows what comes in January or February or March,” he said. “So maybe interesting to watch.”

title: Maine can do without Susan Collins’ perks
text:
Those conflicted about a vote for Sen. Susan Collins should consider the trade-offs. She could bring perks to Maine far beyond those a freshman senator could ever hope to bring. But she also might well be the senator whose reelection keeps Republicans in the majority.

title: Judi Dench gives health update, says sight loss means she can no longer perform
text:
Judi Dench gives health update, says sight loss means she can no longer perform
Oscar-winning actress Dame Judi Dench gave a heartbreaking health update, saying her eye condition has left her unable to act or read more than a decade after her diagnosis.
Dench, 91, was diagnosed with age-related macular degeneration in 2012, a condition that affects her central vision.
Related video above | Judi Dench says reading scripts has become impossible for her
In an interview with BBC Radio's Emma Barnett, Dench said her condition has progressed to a debilitating point.
"I can't be on stage. I can't do a play anymore. I can't do a film anymore. I can't read anymore," she said. "You’ve got to adjust to all that, and make allowances for it. And just get on and don’t think about it too much.”
Dench told Barnett she couldn't even see Barnett's face during the interview, even though she was sitting directly across from her. Dench also said that she has approached people and hugged them during outings, before realizing they were not who she thought they were.
Dench said aging was "rubbish," but she's choosing to remain positive.
Age-related macular degeneration damages the macula — the part of the retina responsible for sharp, straight-ahead vision — and can blur or distort central vision over time.
Dench's career spans theater, television and film. She made her professional stage debut as Ophelia in “Hamlet” with the Old Vic Company in 1957.
She won the Academy Award for supporting actress for playing Queen Elizabeth I in “Shakespeare in Love” and has received seven other Oscar nominations. Her honors also include a Tony Award and seven Laurence Olivier Awards.
In recent decades, audiences have perhaps best known Dench as M, the head of MI6 in seven James Bond films, beginning with “GoldenEye” in 1995 and ending with “Spectre” in 2015.

title: Woman accused of poisoning friend’s tea after being confronted about suspicious bank activity
text:
(Gray News) - A woman in New Jersey is accused of poisoning a friend after being confronted about suspicious bank activity.
Rohweniven Bacani, 52, was charged with third-degree aggravated assault after allegedly poisoning the woman’s tea with a benzodiazepine, according to New Jersey authorities.
The two women had arranged to meet at a restaurant in Fort Lee on Sept. 8 to discuss unauthorized activity the alleged victim had discovered in financial accounts to which Bacani had shared access, prosecutors said.
When the woman arrived, Bacani was already there with a cup of tea waiting for her.
The woman allegedly drank some of the tea but stopped after noticing an unusual taste. She collapsed while leaving the restaurant and later regained consciousness in a hospital, with no recollection of how she had gotten there, prosecutors said.
She remained hospitalized for several days.
Following a weeks-long investigation, detectives concluded that Bacani had allegedly added a benzodiazepine to the woman’s tea.
Bacani was charged and arrested outside her home.
She was taken to the Bergen County Jail pending her first court appearance.

title: Penobscot Remediation Trust updates Bucksport residents on mercury cleanup
text:
BUCKSPORT, Maine (WABI) — The Penobscot Remediation Trust hosted a community meeting Wednesday night to update residents on progress addressing mercury contamination in the Penobscot River Estuary.
Officials shared results from a recently completed six-acre capping pilot in Orrington, where clean sand was placed to reduce mercury exposure. Ongoing studies into removing contaminated sediment are expected to continue into 2027.
The trust is also responsible for monitoring worms, fish, birds, sediment and surface water every three years to track recovery.
The work stems from a 2022 federal settlement requiring Mallinckrodt to pay at least $187 million for remediation and long-term monitoring over the next 30 to 45 years.

title: Cambria’s own air-monitoring records show silica levels sometimes exceeding federal limits, documents show
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Copies of Cambria’s own air-monitoring records show tests at fabrication shops run by the nation’s largest engineered-stone slab manufacturer repeatedly recorded silica dust above federal limits. That’s despite its chief legal officer’s January testimony to Congress that its shops stay below half the legal limit. The records recently surfaced in litigation and were obtained by InvestigateTV.
Dust from cutting engineered stone countertops — made from crushed quartz bound with resin and containing 90% or more crystalline silica, far higher than granite or marble — has sickened hundreds of workers around the country with silicosis, an incurable lung disease.
In California alone, the state has confirmed 668 silicosis cases and 35 silicosis-related deaths among countertop workers since 2019 as of October 20, according to California Department of Public Health data. Public health experts say cases are undercounted nationally.
Cambria, headquartered in Minnesota, has repeatedly said that smaller fabrication shops around the country need to follow federal regulations and silica dust limits to stay safe, and has held its own facilities out as examples of safely-run shops. But its own testing documents show that on numerous occasions, the company has itself failed to meet federal Occupational Safety and Health Administration safety standards.
Company says safety is a priority
“Safety is a hallmark of the Cambria organization,” Micah Aberson, Cambria’s executive vice president, said in December at the company’s manufacturing facility and fabrication shop in Minnesota. He said eliminating dust while fabricating engineered stone countertops is key to that safety.
“I mean, we would contend that no dust is good dust,” Aberson said.
The dust created by cutting slabs contains respirable crystalline silica. Hundreds of workers who cut and shape countertops around the country have been diagnosed with silicosis. Thirty-five have died in California alone.
At a House subcommittee hearing in January, Cambria’s chief legal officer, Rebecca Shult, said the company keeps workers safe by abiding by federal regulations that set a limit for the amount of silica allowed in the air, known as the permissible exposure limit, or PEL.
“We know that workers can be protected by following OSHA regulations and controlling silica exposure to below the permissible exposure limit. And in fact, at our shops, we control exposures below the action level, which is half of the PEL,” Shult said.
What the thresholds mean
In 2018, OSHA set two thresholds for silica dust in the air. The Action Level, 25 micrograms per cubic meter, triggers closer monitoring of workers. The Permissible Exposure Limit, or PEL, 50 micrograms, is the maximum amount a worker can legally be exposed to in an eight-hour workday.
OSHA also requires medical surveillance when workers are exposed at or above the Action Level for 30 or more days per year.
Shult told Congress Cambria stays under the lower number, half the legal limit, and called for all fabrication shops to do so.
Records show repeated violations
But copies of Cambria’s own air-monitoring records, recently surfaced in litigation and obtained by InvestigateTV, show the company has failed to meet those standards on numerous occasions.
InvestigateTV reviewed Cambria test results from facilities in Minnesota, California, Ohio and Indiana going back to 2018. The tests show Cambria’s own facilities have repeatedly recorded higher levels of breathable crystalline silica in the air than federal rules allow.
Among about 170 tests from 2018 to 2026, 57 — about a third — were at or above the federal Action Level, the threshold Shult told Congress her company stays under. Eight showed more silica than the legal limit itself, the PEL. In Ohio in 2020, one sample came back more than five times the legal limit.
In December, Aberson told InvestigateTV that Cambria does not medically test its own workers for silicosis because, based on its own air monitoring tests, OSHA does not require it.
“We have no evidence of anyone having contracted silicosis at Cambria,” Aberson said. He said Cambria officials “would have heard about it” if any workers had been diagnosed with the disease.
Former OSHA official responds
David Michaels, who served as assistant secretary at OSHA for eight years, testified at the same congressional hearing as Cambria’s chief legal officer, Shult.
“When these stones are cut safely, workers are not overexposed to silica dust,” Shult testified.
After hearing about the test results, Michaels said: “Cambria may insist that it’s possible to do this safely, but certainly from these documents, it does appear that Cambria has not been successful in following essentially that premise.”
Cambria declined to comment for this story.
California moves toward a ban
After hearing from sick workers and their families, California officials have taken the first steps toward banning engineered stone. Public Citizen, a consumer group, joined last month in calling for a ban and a nationwide screening and prevention program for workers.
Australia banned engineered stone in 2024, becoming the first country to do so.

title: A 16-year-old carried out the Bend school shooting. Could his parents face charges?
text:
A 16-year-old carried out the Bend school shooting. Could his parents face charges?
In Oregon, the Bend school shooting investigation has only just begun, but legal experts believe it may follow a similar path of recent school shooting cases.
A 16-year-old carried out the Bend school shooting. Could his parents face charges?
In Oregon, the Bend school shooting investigation has only just begun, but legal experts believe it may follow a similar path of recent school shooting cases.
It’s illegal in Oregon for anyone under 18 to possess a firearm, with a few exceptions. So how exactly did the 16-year-old who carried out a school shooting in Bend, Oregon, last week get access to a gun and ammunition?
That question has yet to be answered and is part of what Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz called an “active criminal investigation.”
Recent cases in Michigan and Georgia suggest either or both parents of the teenage school shooter could be held criminally liable for the killings.
In Michigan, James and Jennifer Crumbley, the parents of 14-year-old school shooter Ethan Crumbley, were convicted of manslaughter and sentenced to 10 to 15 years in prison. In Georgia, Colin Gray, the father of 14-year-old school shooter Colt Gray, was convicted of murder and sentenced to 15 years in prison.
And in a pending case in Wisconsin, the father of a 15-year-old school shooter faces three felony charges for allegedly allowing his daughter access to firearms. Jeffrey Rupnow, 44, has pleaded not guilty, and his trial is set for March, according to court records.
Those cases were part of a broader movement pushing the limits of who is accountable for a mass shooting. For prosecutors, the goal of bringing these cases is to ensure gun-owning parents secure their firearms and thereby prevent future school shootings.
In Oregon, the investigation has only just begun, but legal experts believe it will follow a similar path.
Related video: Bend, Oregon, students return to school after shooting
“It certainly could lead to a situation like we’ve seen recently in the last few years in Georgia and also Michigan, where parents have been charged criminally,” said Andrew McCabe, CNN senior law enforcement analyst.
Like in the Michigan and Georgia cases, investigators are likely to focus on how the Oregon school shooter obtained the firearm and what the parents knew about the potential risks to others.
“I think this investigation will head the same way,” said CNN national security analyst Juliette Kayyem. “How did he get access to guns? What did the parents know?”
Where the Oregon investigation stands
In the Bend school shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School, the armed 16-year-old shooter killed three children and a teacher before he was fatally shot by a student’s parent. Another child and teacher also were injured, officials said.
A pump-action shotgun was found near the gunman, who had about 44 remaining rounds of ammunition, Krantz said.
The gun had been purchased by the teen’s mother, a senior law enforcement official briefed on the investigation told CNN.
The firearm used in the shooting was purchased legally, police said Wednesday, adding: “We are not sharing further information about the firearm at this time.”
Per Oregon law, it’s illegal for a juvenile to possess a firearm but there are exceptions for certain long guns if the firearm was transferred by their parent or is used temporarily for hunting or target practice.
The shooter’s parents were interviewed and were cooperative, a senior law enforcement official told CNN.
A search warrant was executed at the shooter’s house on Thursday and computers and other electronics were taken, the source said.
Detectives served search warrants on the attacker’s electronic devices and his social media accounts “on a variety of platforms,” Bend police said Wednesday. “That work continues, and it takes time.”
The shooter, Griffin J. John II, was a former special needs student at the school, police said. His mother spoke in 2020 with CNN affiliate KTVZ about his special needs and his enrollment in a program described as serving children with “intensive behavioral and social skills challenges.”
“I think it will be great for my son to get the help that he needs from the skilled teachers that he needs to get it from,” she told the station.
The shooter’s mother spoke briefly with CNN off camera from her balcony on Friday. She said there were no warning signs and declined to comment on how her son got access to the gun.
“I’m so sorry, I wish I could have done something. I’m sorry for their loss,” she told CNN.
How the Michigan and Georgia cases unfolded
The criminal cases against the Crumbleys in Michigan and Colin Gray in Georgia featured similar allegations: An unsecured firearm and inattentive parents.
In each situation, a parent purchased a gun for their teenage son as a Christmas gift and left the firearm unsecured. The parents also allegedly knew their son had mental health problems and was a threat to others but did not properly address the issues by putting him into counseling or therapy.
Prosecutors argued the parents’ actions represented “criminal negligence” – and the juries agreed.
For example, in Gray’s trial, police had visited his home a year prior to the school shooting to investigate an online threat to shoot up a school. Colt Gray denied posting the threat and law enforcement was ultimately unable to substantiate the tip.
Colin Gray bought his son an AR-15-style rifle later that year. He testified he sometimes allowed his son to keep the rifle in his bedroom, and left other weapons and ammo lying around the house.
His defense attorney said he tried his best to help his son but simply didn’t have warning about his violent plans. But prosecutors argued he acted negligently by buying a gun and ignoring warnings of the potential risk to others.
“This was a trial about this defendant’s actions, his choices and his responsibility,” Barrow County District Attorney Brad Smith said.
In the Oregon case, there are more questions than answers at this point. How did the 16-year-old get access to the firearm and ammo? What did the parents know of their son’s mental health issues and the potential threat he posed to others? Were there warning signs ahead of time, and what did people around him do about them?
Simply buying a gun for a child is not illegal on its own, legal experts said.
“The purchase, per se, is not necessarily improper,” said Katherine Schweit, a former Chicago prosecutor and FBI special agent.
McCabe said investigators will be looking for more than just a purchase history.
“They’ll need evidence, actual proof that the parent knew that, let’s say, the minor was in a vulnerable state. And the parent, despite knowing that, basically gave the minor access to the firearm, knowing that they might be in a vulnerable position,” he said.
“Those are all hard things to prove after the fact. So we’ll have to see what comes out of the investigation.”

title: Toyota is recalling more than 105,000 vehicles. Which models are affected
text:
Toyota is recalling more than 105,000 vehicles. Which models are affected
Toyota has issued a recall after it said some vehicles may have a faulty fuel tube that could result in a leak and fire risk.
Related video: How to stay ahead of recalls
According to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, the company said 105,794 vehicles are being recalled over the potential issue.
Toyota said the vehicles have a faulty fuel tube connection near the fuel tank that may disconnect and leak fuel. A fuel leak paired with an ignition source can increase the risk of a fire, the car manufacturer said.
The company said on Oct. 14 that "certain 2024-2027 Toyota Land Cruiser Hybrid vehicles" are affected. 
NHTSA said car dealers will inspect the connection and "install a supplemental clamp or, as necessary, replace the resin fuel tube and install a supplemental clamp, free of charge."
Owner notification letters are also expected to be mailed by Nov. 29, 2026.
To see if your vehicle is part of the recall, visit NHTSA's website here.
