title: Maine’s older residents are ‘aging into crisis’
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
This is the second story in the series Stretched Thin: The cost of getting by in Maine, which looks at the financial hardships Mainers face. Social services reporter Gillian Graham reported this story as a USC Annenberg Center for Health Journalism 2026 National Fellow and a participant in the Center’s engagement initiative.
BOOTHBAY PENINSULA — By the end of each month, Linda Walls has only pennies left.
Nearly half of her $1,100 monthly income pays for the room she rents from a friend. Food, medical costs and bills quickly eat up the rest.
It was one unexpected health crisis that caused her financial stability to unravel. She said she was homeless for a short time and, living only on Supplemental Security Income, has spent years rebuilding her life.
Walls, 71, said she was comfortable — then had nothing.
She’s not alone.
Older Mainers are struggling to keep up with rising costs, access transportation to get to appointments and maintain aging homes on fixed incomes. New data shows that about half of households in the state headed by people 65 and older struggle to afford basic expenses. Those challenges are especially acute in rural areas, according to experts.
“When there’s high inflation and costs go up, they’re kind of stuck,” said Lindsay MacDonald of Spectrum Generations, central Maine’s area agency on aging. “If they can’t work, what else can they do?”
According to data from 2024 released in June by the United Ways of Maine, 52% of older households live below the federal poverty level or are part of a population called ALICE — Asset Limited, Income Constrained, Employed. At that income level, people don’t always qualify for assistance but often struggle to pay for basic needs and are not able to set aside money for emergencies.
Nearly a quarter of the state’s residents are 65 or older, according to U.S. Census data. Projections by the Office of the State Economist show that group is expected to grow in Maine over 11% between next year and 2032.
As people live longer, even those with savings are finding they don’t have enough, said Jess Maurer, executive director of the Maine Council on Aging. About a third of older Mainers have no savings and rely solely on Social Security, she said.
Maurer said the stories she hears are haunting: Older Mainers cutting up and burning furniture for heat. Retirees skipping meals and visits to the doctor because, without transportation, there’s no way to leave home. People isolated and alone, using chamber pots and going without showers because they aren’t mobile enough to get to their bathrooms.
“People are aging into crisis,” she said.
HEATING HOMES AS OIL COSTS RISE
Tourists and seasonal residents flock to the Boothbay peninsula in the summer.
The scenic point of land juts out into the Gulf of Maine between the Sheepscot and Damariscotta rivers. Small boats tender cruise ship passengers to shore, where they flood shops and restaurants. Visitors show up by the thousands to wander through the Coastal Maine Botanical Gardens.
And on a dirt lot behind the Boothbay Public Works garage, the Woodchucks have been busy thinking about winter.
Twice a week year-round, the volunteers behind the region’s wood bank split, chop and stack firewood to bring to people on the peninsula who need help heating their homes. Most of the Woodchucks are retired and have spent years growing the operation into one of the larger wood banks in Maine.
“We’re old men with chainsaws,” volunteer Tom Churchill quipped during a break from chopping in July. “What can go wrong?”
The wood bank, which operates on a lot rented from the town for $1 a year, has become a lifeline for residents who struggle to keep up with heating costs in a region where many people live in older homes.
It will be even more critical this winter, said Holly Stover, director of the nonprofit Community Resource Council, which oversees the Woodchucks program. In late September, as oil prices shot up and state officials urged people to apply for heating assistance as soon as possible, Stover said she had heard from people terrified of what winter will bring.
“I think this year the panic is going to set in,” Stover said.
The Woodchucks delivered 100 cords of wood last year and said they anticipate requests for help will be even higher this season. The CRC also stocks its 24-hour food pantry with emergency bundles of wood — they usually disappear within hours — and runs a local fuel fund that pays for heating oil.
About half of all homes in Maine rely on oil as a primary heat source, making it the most heating oil-dependent state in the country, according to the Natural Resources Council of Maine. In late September, heating oil in the state reached a record $6.02 per gallon. The governor’s office estimates it will cost $740 more to fill a standard 275-gallon tank this winter than it did last year.
In early October, Gov. Janet Mills sent a letter to Maine’s Congressional delegation saying current federal funding for the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program is insufficient to meet the increased need. She wrote some residents will be forced to choose between staying warm and putting food on the table this winter.
David Cornforth, who runs Spectrum Generation’s Ramping Up Repairs program, sees firsthand the challenge facing older residents of Lincoln County and surrounding counties, as they try to heat and maintain their homes with limited money.
The program, which started two years ago, funds critical home repairs for qualifying low-income residents. It is not the only program of its kind in Maine — a similar one operates on a small scale on the Boothbay peninsula — but experts say there is not enough help considering the age of the state’s housing stock.
The first Ramping Up Repairs project was to replace multiple broken windows in an old farmhouse owned by a couple in their 60s with health problems. Cornforth said the windows were fixed just before winter set in.
“They called in the spring and said it was a godsend,” he said. “They said they didn’t know what the winter would have looked like for them.”
POVERTY UNSEEN
When people think of coastal Maine, they’re unlikely to associate it with poverty. In the Midcoast, it’s not uncommon to see high-priced homes near the water selling to out-of-state buyers looking for a summer getaway. But even in the wealthiest communities, there are people facing financial hardship.
“The pockets of poverty are unseen,” Stover, from the Community Resource Council, said. “You don’t see the people living in the woods or in rundown trailers.”
According to 2024 data released this summer, 47% of households in Boothbay and 46% of those in Boothbay Harbor are below the ALICE threshold. Lincoln County, with a median age of 51.4, is among the oldest counties in Maine, which has the highest median age in the country at 44.9, according to Census data.
While money pumps into the region during summer, there are still families barely getting by throughout the year.
“Those who have two or three homes come in to enjoy Vacationland,” said Nicole Evans, executive director of the United Way of Mid Coast Maine. “Their dollars disappear in the dead of winter.”
People who need assistance on the peninsula often turn to the Community Resource Council. In addition to firewood and heating oil assistance, the CRC arranges rides to medical appointments, helps people sign up for assistance programs, and provides food.
Last November, when there were fears that Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program payments would be delayed because of a government shutdown, CRC bought $250 grocery store gift cards for 283 families.
A few years ago, the CRC opened a community fridge behind Boothbay’s town office that is accessible all the time. Stover said a survey of local residents showed people who work different shifts had a hard time making it to food pantries during the day. Others, she said, prefer to stop in for food without the pressure of being seen or talking to people.
The community fridge is a small building with a freezer, refrigerator and shelves for bread and dry goods. Produce comes from local stores, farms and gardeners, and restaurants sometimes stock it with prepared meals.
“You can fall behind once and not go hungry,” said the Rev. Todd Weir, president of the CRC board. “Or you could fall behind every month and not go hungry.”
‘IT’S REALLY TOUGH’
On a crisp Tuesday in early October, Walls stood behind the counter of the small thrift store at the Edgecomb Community Church, chatting happily with the other volunteers and customers browsing the shop.
After several years of hardship, she’s found a supportive community in this historic white church perched on a grassy hill.
Walls spent most of her adult life in southern York County, where she said she raised six children and worked in local stores and pharmacies. She never had enough to set aside money for retirement, but lived comfortably.
Then she got sick.
Four years ago, Walls was living in Limerick when she woke up with stomach pain so bad she ended up in the hospital, where doctors told her she had a perforated colon. Her recovery was a difficult one with multiple setbacks.
Unable to work or pay rent after she was released from the hospital, she said she had no choice but to leave her home. She gave her cat to her granddaughter and put all of her belongings in the trash or on the curb for free because she couldn’t afford to store them. She said she left with three shirts, two pairs of pants and a pair of shoes.
Walls said she was scared to go to a shelter and spent four nights sleeping on the ground in a cemetery in Scarborough before her son found out and brought her home to his apartment.
A caseworker helped her navigate resources and sign up for Medicaid. Walls said she got a job and eventually a new apartment, but is now unable to work because of her health issues.
A couple years ago, Walls said, she moved into a friend’s trailer in Wiscasset. She pays $500 in rent and helps around the house, but he covers most of the utilities.
She said she can’t afford to live on her own.
“If you’re alone and in your 70s, it’s really tough,” she said.
According to the U.S. Census Bureau, 9.5% of Mainers 65 and older are living in poverty.
Women over 75, who typically earned less during their careers and had to take time off for caregiving, live in poverty at twice the rate of men, according to the Maine Council on Aging.
Maurer, from the Council on Aging, said Social Security “masks poverty” because people receive just enough to not qualify for assistance programs. That is the case for Walls, who said she makes too much for SNAP to help pay for food.
In October, the Social Security Administration projected the annual cost-of-living adjustment for older adults and people with disabilities will go up by 3.6% beginning in 2027. That translates to $75 extra per month for recipients, but some don’t think it will be enough to offset soaring prices, according to an AARP survey.
Without government assistance, many people turn to a patchwork of local agencies. But Maurer said others may fall through the cracks because they won’t ask for help or don’t know where to find it.
“People in their 80s and 90s, they’re not going to say, ‘I don’t have enough money for food.’ They’re just not going to eat,” she said. “They’re going to keep their house at 50 degrees. They’re going to take their meds once a day instead of twice a day.”
ONE PROBLEM AWAY FROM CRISIS
On Tuesday mornings, two rooms at the Community Center in Boothbay Harbor are crowded with tables of older women playing mahjong. The clickity-clack of their tiles is nearly drowned out by the conversations about book clubs, grocery prices and grandchildren.
The center, in a nondescript strip mall, started after the local hospital closed and people were concerned about the impact on seniors in the community.
The center combats social isolation and improves people’s quality of life, but has also become a place residents can turn to for help with transportation and medical supplies, said office manager Jane Carpenter.
Down the hall from the rooms where people gather to knit and play games is the medical equipment closet. The brightly lit room is lined with walkers, wheelchairs, shower chairs and canes. Shelves are crammed with incontinence supplies, braces and blood pressure cuffs.
All of it is free to take for anyone who needs it. Carpenter said the program used to serve just the immediate area, but now caseworkers from elsewhere in the county know they can call if they need to find supplies for someone.
Sometimes people seem hesitant to take what they need, but Carpenter said the no-questions-asked policy aims to reduce the stigma.
“People are very proud in this area,” she said. “They don’t want to admit they need help.”
Transportation is one of the biggest issues in Lincoln County, which has multiple peninsulas, said Katie MacDonald, director of Healthy Lincoln County, an organization that aims to improve health outcomes through food security and substance use prevention programs.
“There are some places in Maine where you really can’t get there from here,” she said. “You can see it across the bay, but it’s 45 minutes up and around to get there.”
Healthy Lincoln County is trying to meet the needs of low-income residents, including those who can’t get to stores or food pantries, through its Community Routes program. Each month, the program delivers groceries, clothing, hygiene products and other items to people in 10 towns across the county.
Community Routes coordinator Samantha Mehlhorn said delivering these items directly to people has been “huge” for them.
“We have some great resources in our area — there are a number of food pantries — but that doesn’t mean there’s going to be one they can get to,” she said.
On the Boothbay peninsula, both the Community Center and CRC recruit volunteers to bring older residents without cars to medical appointments and to run errands, but it’s not always easy. Most of the appointments, according to organizers, are in Portland, Brunswick or Damariscotta, a distance that’s harder to get volunteers to cover as gas prices go up.
At the CRC, many of the volunteers who used to drive have aged and now need drivers themselves, Stover said.
“Transportation is a real concern for us. We don’t seem to have a good town or county generated alternative,” said Carpenter, from the Community Center. “We scramble every day to see who can drive.”
In recent years, Maine’s Area Agencies on Aging and others who work with older residents have lobbied the Legislature to support the Older Mainers Act to put more money toward various services, including transportation, meal programs, caregiver support and wellness initiatives.
Legislation introduced in the last session would have allocated $9.75 million toward those programs. At the time the bill was presented, more than 700 people were on waitlists to receive Meals on Wheels.
In 2025, the Legislature approved $3 million in one-time funding from the general fund to support the programs and services provided by the Area Agencies on Aging. But the leaders of those agencies say more support is needed as the number of older residents increases.
Gerard Queally, president and CEO of Spectrum Generations, said the services provided by Area Agencies on Aging prevent social isolation, help people navigate benefits, and are cost-effective alternatives to frequent emergency department visits, long hospitalizations and early placement in nursing homes.
Despite committee support, the Older Mainers Act died on adjournment in April without being funded. Advocates say they will continue to push for more funding to support Maine’s aging population.
Sharon Foerster, who was vice president of the Maine Council on Aging Board of Directors, said in written testimony last year in support of the bill that people wait to ask for help until they really need it.
“Far too many older Mainers,” she testified, “are ‘one away’ — one health problem away, one unexpected expense away, one home system failure away, or one loss away from crisis.”

title: Brightening Skies & Breezy This Afternoon... Sunshine, Breezy & Cooler Friday
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Clouds will gradually give way to brightening skies from north to south this afternoon as a cold front exits the area and subtropical storm Josephine pulls away from the region. The pressure gradient between high pressure over the Great Lakes Region and Josephine will lead to a gusty northerly breeze this afternoon with gusts to 25-30 MPH possible. Temperatures will be seasonable with highs in the 50s to near 60°. Skies will clear out this evening... leading to clear skies tonight with low temperatures dropping to the upper 20s to mid-30s. Breezy conditions will continue through the night with the northerly breeze gusting to 25-30 MPH at times.
The northerly breeze will have ushered a colder air mass into the state for Friday. Josephine will continue to pull away from New England during the day while strong high pressure builds in from the west. This will keep the pressure gradient fairly tight over the area Friday... keeping the breezy conditions going through much of the day with northerly winds gusting to 25-30 MPH at times. Otherwise expect a brighter and cooler day with plenty of sunshine and high temperatures in the mid-40s to around 50° north and low 50s elsewhere.
Strong high pressure will bring us a gorgeous weekend with lots of sunshine both Saturday and Sunday. The high will build to our south through the weekend... which will allow warmer air to return as the weekend progresses. Temperatures will top off in the 50s on Saturday then mid-50s to low 60s for highs on Sunday. This fantastic fall weather continues into next week too. A cold front is forecast to move through the state Monday but looks to be lacking moisture and will likely be more of a cloud producer than anything. Look for a mix of sun and clouds Monday with temperatures remaining on the milder side with highs in the mid-50s to low 60s. Cooler weather will move in behind the front for Tuesday. The next best chance for some precipitation will be later in the week with some showers possible in the Thursday/Friday timeframe.
Rest of Today: Brightening skies and breezy. Highs in the 50s. North/northwest wind 10-20 MPH with gusts to 25-30 MPH possible.
Tonight: Clear and breezy. Lows in the upper 20s to mid-30s. North wind 10-20 MPH with gusts to 25-30 MPH possible.
Friday: Sunny... breezy... and cooler. Highs in the mid-40s to low 50s. North wind 10-20 MPH with gusts to 25-30 MPH possible.
Saturday: Mostly sunny. Highs in the 50s.
Sunday: Mostly sunny. Highs in the mid-50s to low 60s.
Monday: Mix of sun and clouds. Highs in the mid-50s to low 60s.

title: Avid birders flock to Cape Elizabeth after rare grey heron sighted
text:
CAPE ELIZABETH — For a moment, no one spoke.
Eyes were glued to scopes, and binoculars were trained beyond the piles of mulch and gravel and fields of sprouting rows.
“Look at how white the thighs are,” Jose Ramirez, of Scarborough, said as he squinted into his scope. “This is the one.”
A grey heron. A bird seen for the first time in Maine on Sunday, Oct. 18.
To the uninitiated, it looks like a great blue heron, its distant relative. But grey herons, which are native to Europe, Africa and Asia, have white on the bend of their wings and thighs. Their more common counterparts have rusty red accents. Grey herons are daintier and more compact, with shorter legs and smaller bills.
And they are incredibly rare, especially on this continent.
There have been just a handful of grey heron sightings in North America ever (a couple in Alaska, a few in Canada). One was spotted on an island off the coast of Nantucket in 2020, the first time the bird made its way to the lower 48 states. Presumably that same bird was seen in Virginia a little while later.
But this time is different. This bird is hanging out in an accessible spot, in the fields and marsh that surround Jordan’s Farm in Cape Elizabeth, on the corner of Spurwink Avenue and Wells Road.
On a sunny Thursday afternoon, the heron was unknowingly hiding from a gaggle of birders, some of whom had traveled a long way in search of the bird.
The birders were patient. They traded field stories and chatted about other species they’ve chased. Tim and Erin Metcalf, who drove up from Richmond, Rhode Island, plan their vacations around spotting different species (They’re 29 states into seeing 100 birds in every state, and they’ve already crossed off big birding states like Texas and Arizona).
The heron strutted back into view, a diva returning to the spotlight. The crowd of onlookers excitedly followed it with their binoculars.
‘WE’VE ALL BEEN DYING TO SEE IT’
This part of Cape Elizabeth has become a zoo this past week, driven by a Beatlemania-like craze by birders from both Maine and away.
“It’s one of those birds we’ve all been dying to see for a long time,” said Doug Hitchcox, a naturalist with Maine Audubon.
Portland-based birder Peter Griffin first spotted the grey heron on Sunday. By Monday, people had already arrived from Massachusetts, New York and Connecticut to see it, according to Hitchcox.
Hitchcox set up a scope by the marsh on Monday from 6 a.m. to noon, and around 200 people came to take a peek. At times, the area has become a bit of a traffic nightmare, with some birders stopping their cars in the middle of the road, anxious to see the bird.
Liz Bullis, who works for Jordan’s Farm, said people from North Carolina, Connecticut and Pennsylvania have popped into the store to pick up donuts, apples and other snacks. Some of the farmers have named the bird Sheldon.
“If we served hot beverages, we’d be really popular,” she said. Each morning when she drives to work, the crowd — with different members each time — is back.
On Wednesday, Hitchcox spoke with an enthusiastic birder who flew in from Michigan, got a look at the bird and flew home the same day.
“That’s having a lot of faith that it would be there,” he said.
With each successive day that the heron remains here, birders from farther away grow more confident traveling to see it, Hitchcox said.
‘WORTH A SECOND LOOK’
It’s a difficult field identification.
Some juvenile great blue herons have pale patches, fooling even experienced birders.
It took hours of close observation and encouragement from a few birding friends before Griffin believed what he suspected: He had indeed spotted a grey heron.
“I had to explain this to my mom,” he said.
He drove by the bird, which was located 20 or 30 yards from the road, on his way to scope out other birds in a nearby pumpkin patch. Like many hobbyists, he got into birding during the COVID-19 pandemic, and his interest grew from there.
“A thought popped into my head that this one was worth a second look,” he said. “It seemed a little different.”
He snapped some photos when it flew away, which highlighted some of its trademark characteristics, like those vibrant white patches. He texted a friend: “There’s no way this is a grey heron, right?”
Other birders confirmed the sighting within a couple of hours.
And there’s photo evidence that this rare bird has been camping out in the marshy field since the beginning of October, under the noses of the many experienced birders who frequent this part of southern Maine, according to Hitchcox.
“It’s funny to think that people have seen it and probably thought ‘Oh, a great blue heron,’” Hitchcox said.
On a sunny Thursday afternoon, a group of birders gathered on the wrong side of a road near the Jordan’s Farm stand, about a hundred yards from another clump of birders. Their scopes were trained on the wrong bird. A friendly birder invited them to join the rest of the watchers.
No one knows how long the bird will stay, fueling a feverish desire to get to Cape Elizabeth as soon as possible. Some great blue herons in the area are already starting to migrate south.
“Birds have wings,” Hitchcox said. “They can disappear at any moment.”
Southern Maine has been no stranger to visits from rare birds.
In 2018, a great black hawk was sighted in Portland, a first in the North American record, and a statue was built in its honor after the hawk, which took up residence in Deering Oaks park, died.
A couple of years ago, a Steller’s sea eagle (nicknamed Stella), appeared in towns like Georgetown along the midcoast. Birders traveled from other countries to take a look at the giant eagle from Siberia with an eight-foot wingspan.
Maine Audubon has a Maine Rare Bird Alert group chat, which now has more than 4,000 members, that people can sign up for on their website. It’s the go-to source for minute-by-minute updates about the grey heron’s whereabouts.
Not all of those trying to catch a glimpse of the grey heron are fanatical birdwatchers.
Peter and Sara Merrill live in Cape Elizabeth, just a couple of miles from Jordan’s Farm. They perched their scope right next to their car.
They consider themselves “backyard birdwatchers.”
“Well, when this is your backyard,” Peter Merrill said, gesturing to the field as the heron stood gracefully in the distance, “you have to come take a look.”

title: How the next 12 days could shape the outcome of the midterm elections
text:
How could the next 12 days shape the outcome of the midterm elections?
President Donald Trump is traveling to Iowa to campaign for GOP candidates in key races as the state faces economic challenges tied to his policies.
How could the next 12 days shape the outcome of the midterm elections?
President Donald Trump is traveling to Iowa to campaign for GOP candidates in key races as the state faces economic challenges tied to his policies.
President Donald Trump is visiting Iowa today to campaign for Republican candidates in a governor's race, a close Senate race, and several races for House seats as the midterm elections approach.
Democrat Josh Turek is facing off against Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson to replace outgoing Iowa Sen. Joni Ernst.
In 2024, Trump won Iowa by 13 percentage points. The state, which is largely dependent on farming, has been impacted by tariffs, rising diesel prices, and fertilizer costs.
According to a CNN poll conducted between late September and early October, 74% of likely voters in Iowa said Trump's policies have increased the cost of living in the state.
Republicans have recently been on the defensive in red states like Kansas, Nebraska, and South Carolina. On Wednesday, Trump held a rally in South Carolina, urging his supporters to back Sen. Darline Graham, who was appointed to fill her late brother Lindsey Graham's seat.
"In this election, I'm asking you to pretend I'm on the ballot because when I'm on the ballot, we get 49% more votes all three times," Trump said. "For the sake of our country, just pretend because you have to get out and vote."
Trump is also expected to return to Ohio next week, marking his third visit to the state in less than a month.
Keep watching for the latest from the Washington News Bureau:

title: Mother accused of drowning newborn whose body was found in motel dumpster days later
text:
FORT WORTH, Texas (Gray News) - A Texas woman is facing charges after investigators say she drowned her newborn daughter in a motel bathtub days before the baby’s body was found in a dumpster.
Avia Lynette Cantrell, 23, is facing a capital murder charge after Fort Worth Police say she drowned her newborn daughter in a motel bathtub. The baby’s body was found in a dumpster outside the motel days later.
Cantrell’s boyfriend, 26-year-old Camron Kyjuan Baker, was also arrested in relation to the case. He is facing a charge of abuse of a corpse.
Police responded about 8:40 p.m. Sunday to a Fort Worth motel after a baby was found in a dumpster outside. The baby was taken to the hospital, where they were pronounced dead, KTVT reports.
Surveillance footage from Sunday afternoon showed a woman putting a box of items, including a car seat, into the dumpster. The motel manager identified the woman as Cantrell, according to an arrest affidavit obtained by The Dallas Morning News.
Investigators questioned Cantrell, who admitted to giving birth last Wednesday morning in her motel bathtub, the affidavit says. She allegedly told detectives she left the baby girl face down in the water for about 30 minutes until she believed the newborn was dead.
Cantrell called Baker at work and told him the baby had died, according to Baker’s arrest warrant. The couple allegedly kept the newborn’s body in a bag near the toilet for four days before police say Baker put the body in the motel dumpster.
“Heartbreaking doesn’t even begin to describe this case,” Fort Worth Police Chief Eddie Garcia told WFAA. “Our thoughts are with everyone affected by the loss of this child.”
Baker told detectives the couple did not seek medical help because they feared facing criminal charges, according to the affidavit. He allegedly disposed of the baby’s body after Cantrell asked him to, saying she couldn’t do it herself.
Cantrell is being held on $2 million bond, and Baker is being held on $250,000 bond, online records show. The investigation is ongoing.
Following the incident, Fort Worth Police are reminding everyone of Texas’ Baby Moses Law. The law allows a parent to safely and legally surrender an unharmed newborn at a designated location without fear of being prosecuted for abandonment.
“Every baby deserves a safe beginning,” police wrote in a Facebook post. “If you or someone you know is facing a situation where caring for a newborn feels impossible, help is available. You are not alone, and there are safe options that can protect both you and your baby.”

title: Portland officials frustrated over Bloomberg housing funding
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Portland city councilors have plenty of ideas about how to use $750,000 from Bloomberg Philanthropies to chip away at the housing crisis, but despite being named as a recipient of the money, those ideas may never come to fruition.
Last week, the philanthropic organization announced Portland as one of 15 cities to test housing reforms that have worked in other parts of the country.
But Portland never applied to be part of the project and Mayor Mark Dion said that he and staff determined the city didn’t have any initiatives that fit the organization’s strict criteria, so he had to decline the offer.
It is unclear how or why Bloomberg included Portland in the announcement. The organization later updated its news release to “reflect that Portland, ME will not be a part of this initiative at this time.”
But city councilors, who hadn’t known Portland was even being considered for money, say Dion was too hasty in turning down the opportunity.
“We left that money on the table,” Councilor Wes Pelletier said in a phone interview. “Maybe there’s a chance for us to go for that money in the future, but we could use it now.”
‘NOT A MATCH’
Using successful models from California, Texas and Georgia, cities in the Bloomberg program will receive between $450,000 and $750,000 as well as expert support to tackle permitting times, accessory dwelling unit approvals and a backlog of stalled affordable housing projects.
Portland already has a digitized permitting system, ADUs have been allowed on all single-family lots statewide for four years and the city has multiple task forces to clear the housing construction pipeline, Dion said.
He asked Bloomberg officials if they could use the money to help digitize the city’s rent control database instead, but the organization wasn’t interested, he said.
“It’s not a match right now,” Dion said last week.
But he also said he was told that if the city develops an initiative in line with Bloomberg’s criteria, it is still considered eligible.
City officials were hopeful that meant if they could come up with a plan quickly, they might not miss out.
But the organization said in a statement Wednesday that “while Portland will not be participating in the initiative at this time, we will be selecting additional cities in the future and would be delighted to consider Portland again.”
MAKING IT WORK
Kate Sykes believes there are obvious ways the city could use the money.
“I just have to ask if there’s a gas leak in here, because we’ve just put forward two social housing … pilot projects that we need staff to help us stand up,” Sykes said at the Housing and Economic Development Committee meeting on Tuesday. “It absolutely addresses the housing pipeline.”
Those proposals are meant to build more “missing middle” housing, including a 40-unit development on Cornell Street near Morrill’s Corner.
“It feels to me like if we can preserve the ability to participate in this and get almost a million dollars toward that, that is a smart idea,” she said.
Pelletier, who is not on the committee, said that while the city’s permitting system is online, it needs serious work.
“Our digital infrastructure is bad, full stop, ” he said at the meeting. “We cannot pretend that it’s a good experience to log onto the city website and to fill out forms”
If there’s a way to improve the “interface” between residents and government, “we should be taking that money,” Pelletier said.
MAYBE NEXT TIME
Portland is still holding out hope for future rounds, and the committee directed Dion to get the materials from Bloomberg for staff to look over.
They will reconsider if there are any programs they could stand up that might be in line with the organization’s requirements.
But it will take time, said Dena Libner, assistant city manager.
“Building programs and conceptualizing them isn’t something that happens overnight,” she said, “but we would focus on that and bring back whatever we come up with as soon as we could.”
It’s not clear whether Portland will be able to find a way to make the program fit with current needs, or even when another round may open up.
Dion and councilors agreed the will-they-won’t-they of Portland receiving the money was confusing and said Bloomberg was unclear about the timeline.
Part of the confusion, Dion said, was that the organization had a short decision-making window because it was used to dealing with executive mayors who can unilaterally make decisions, rather than legislative mayors like Dion, who have to be directed by the council.
Pelletier said he was frustrated that the council wasn’t involved earlier in the process.
“We need to figure out a better process for what happens when someone reaches out with this sort of offer,” he said.

title: Obituary: Ethel L. Collins
text:
SCARBOROUGH – Ethel L. Collins, 85, of Scarborough, passed away peacefully on Oct. 10, 2026, leaving behind a legacy of warmth, unwavering dedication, and a lifetime of cherished memories.
Born on Dec. 26, 1940, Ethel grew up in South Portland, the daughter of the late Robert I. Foshay and Lillian Hogland Foshay. In 1958, she married the love of her life, William A. Collins. The two shared a deeply devoted and happy marriage of 65 years until his passing, building a life centered around family, community, and joy.
In 1963, Ethel and Bill moved to Scarborough, where they built their own home in 1967 and raised their five children. Known to all as the “Collins Ranch,” their home was a welcoming haven filled with laughter, friends, and endless fun. Whether it was the swimming pool, volleyball, horseshoes, pool, ping-pong, or lawn tractor races, Ethel and Bill ensured there was always a safe, happy place for their children and all of the neighborhood kids. A full parking lot at the Ranch was a daily testament to their hospitality and loving spirit.
Ethel was a familiar and beloved face throughout her community. In 1970, she joined the U.S. Postal Service as a rural letter carrier, delivering mail to thousands of hometown friends and neighbors. She took immense pride in her work, famously never missing a delivery regardless of the terrible weather or towering snowbanks she had to climb over. After retiring in 2000 following 30 years of dedicated service, she was still frequently reminded by community members how dearly she was missed, always remembered for her commitment and her bright, happy smile. Not one to slow down in retirement, Ethel happily worked part-time for many years alongside her husband Bill at the Dunstan Dental Center (Joe and Demi) in Scarborough.
Ethel was predeceased by her parents, Robert and Lillian; her beloved husband, William A. Collins Sr.; her son, William A. Collins Jr., her daughter, Maryellen Collins Stevenson; her brother, Ernest Foshay, and her sister, Barbara Dillon.
She is survived by her loving children, Robert M. Collins, Laurie Hanson, and Don T. Collins. She also leaves behind many cherished grandchildren and great-grandchildren, as well as extended family members and countless friends who will miss her dearly.
Visiting hours will be held at Hobbs Funeral Home in Scarborough on Oct. 30, 2026, from 12 to 2 p.m. A service celebrating Ethel’s life will follow immediately afterward.
Ethel’s radiant smile, fierce work ethic, and boundless hospitality touched the lives of everyone she met. Her memory will live on in the hearts of her family and the community she served and loved so well.

title: With MEMIC, safety pays dividends
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Earlier this month, the MEMIC Group announced that its Board of Directors has authorized a $17 million dividend for more than 17,000 Maine policyholders.
For over 30 years now, MEMIC has shown that workplace safety isn’t just good for employees — it’s good for business. The annual dividend is based on MEMIC’s financial performance, claims experience and the collective success of policyholders in maintaining safe workplaces.
Maine Employers’ Mutual Insurance Company (MEMIC) is owned by its policyholders in Maine, who share the success of a safe workplace. When safety improves and claims go down, everybody wins. The $17 million distribution represents a 10.5% return of premiums paid by eligible policyholders and will be distributed in November.
“There’s no question that Maine businesses are navigating a lot of uncertainty right now. We understand that because we work alongside them every day,” said Michael Bourque, president and CEO.
“At a time of rising costs, helping policyholders operate more safely and efficiently matters more than ever. The $17 million dividend is another way we can return value directly to the businesses we serve that drive this economy, employ our neighbors and keep communities moving forward.”
Making a difference for Maine and beyond
Founded in 1993, MEMIC was created with a public purpose: to restore balance to Maine’s workers’ compensation system and ensure every employer had access to coverage. What began as a solution to a statewide crisis has grown into a nationally recognized insurance company serving more than 21,000 employers and 1 million employees across the country. When the company succeeds, its policyholders will succeed. Read more about how this system works for a small business like Paul White Company.
Mutual insurance means mutual success
As a mutual insurance company, MEMIC is owned by its policyholders. Instead of paying profits to shareholders, the company returns them to policyholders as annual dividends, when financial and safety performance allow.
With the 2026 dividend, MEMIC will have returned more than $406 million to Maine policyholders since 1998. These dividends are the direct result of their shared commitment to workplace safety and effective injury management. When the company succeeds, its policyholders will succeed.
Fewer injuries mean lower costs for workers’ compensation insurance, and the potential for dividends. To help prevent injuries, MEMIC employees have traveled millions of miles to redesign work, engineer out risks and train employees to make safety their top priority. And it’s working: since MEMIC began, workplace injuries in Maine have dropped by more than 50%, and insurance costs have fallen by 60%.
And when injuries happen, they’re there to help workers recover and return to work safely, with experienced claims support every step of the way.
For MEMIC, being mutual means “we’re in this together.” When everyone does their part to prevent injuries, safety pays dividends.
MEMIC has grown from its Maine roots to partner with 22,000+ employers and support approximately 1 million employees nationwide, protecting workers and building safer workplaces.
The feeling is mutual. | Find your agent.

title: Russia hits Ukraine with missiles, drones hours after agreeing to peace talks
text:
Russia pounds Kyiv with missiles as Moscow says 808 drones downed in Russian cities
Russia bombarded Kyiv with ballistic missiles in an hourslong nighttime barrage, and the Russian military said Thursday that its air defenses intercepted 808 drones fired by Ukraine at Moscow and other cities, in attacks that dampened new hopes of progress in ending the war.
At least two people were killed in Ukraine and dozens of others wounded, officials said.
Russian President Vladimir Putin on Wednesday agreed “in principle” to resume three-way negotiations involving officials from Russia, Ukraine and the United States, but no date was set for a meeting. Putin's consent came in talks in St. Petersburg with U.S. President Donald Trump’s envoy, Steve Witkoff, who the previous day had met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Norway.
Representatives of those three countries held three rounds of negotiations early this year, meeting twice in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, in January and February, followed by further talks in Geneva in February.
However, little progress was reported beyond exchanges of prisoners of war, and deadly attacks continued. Russia and Ukraine remain far apart in their terms for stopping the fighting.
Zelenskyy, who says only a meeting of leaders can end the deadlock, commented on the prospect of “technical talks” between delegations: “We’ll see what happens this time.”
Zelenskyy sees ‘no change’ in Moscow's attitude
Russia’s aerial attacks hit 12 regions of Ukraine overnight, killing at least two people and wounding 34 others, including five children, Zelenskyy said on social media Thursday.
The Ukrainian capital endured a noisy night as 21 ballistic missiles came in three waves, he said, smashing apartment buildings, energy facilities, a railway station and the Kyiv subway system, shopping malls and businesses. One person was killed in Kyiv.
Multiple attacks on the eastern city of Kharkiv and the surrounding area left one person dead and at least 13 wounded, the State Emergency Service said.
Ukrainians are bracing for the winter, as a recent escalation in Russian attacks targets the power grid to deny civilians heat, light and running water during the bitterly cold months. Ukraine says Russia is stockpiling ballistic missiles for an annual campaign that Ukrainians describe as “ weaponizing winter. ”
The Russian bombardment showed “there has been no real change in (Moscow’s) attitude toward everything that is happening,” Zelenskyy said.
The Ukrainian leader has pleaded with Washington to supply more Patriot air defense ammunition that can stop ballistic missiles and to heap more sanctions on Russia that might make Moscow pursue peace.
But Trump has agreed to a deal with Putin to import diesel from Russia and waived heavy sanctions on Moscow, while U.S. officials say Patriot ammunition is in short supply.
Ukrainians chide Trump envoy for flattering Putin
Witkoff, the Trump envoy who met with Putin in St. Petersburg on Wednesday, was harshly criticized in Ukraine and in the U.S. for praising the Russian leader as a “humanitarian” for ordering the release of a retired American teacher imprisoned on charges of fighting as a mercenary in Ukraine.
The five-year anniversary of Russia’s all-out invasion of its neighbor comes on Feb. 24. The fighting has resulted in hundreds of thousands of troop casualties on the battlefield and thousands of civilians killed in aerial strikes.
Also, assassination attempts against foes of Putin have been common during his more than two decades in power. Those close to the victims and the few survivors have blamed Russian authorities, but the Kremlin has routinely denied involvement.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the “brutal” Russian attacks demonstrated “what Russian ‘humanism’ truly sounds like.”
“Appeasement, servility, and flattery will not stop this war. Only strength will,” Sybiha said on social media.
Russia says it intercepted more than 800 Ukrainian drones
Russia’s Defense Ministry said that air defenses overnight downed 808 Ukrainian drones, with two people reported wounded.
Moscow’s Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said that 630 of the drones were fired toward the Russian capital between late Wednesday and early Thursday. Moscow airports temporarily restricted air traffic overnight.
The Russian military hit the facilities involved in making and storing drones and cruise missiles and transport infrastructure in Kyiv in overnight strikes, the Defense Ministry said. Infrastructure in the southern port of Odesa and vessels used for the Ukrainian armed forces were also hit, it said.

title: Mitchell pushes for larger homestead exemption in bid for Senate District 13
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Edwin W. Mitchell, I-Boothbay, wants to represent both sides of the political aisle in his run for Senate District 13.
Mitchell, who goes by Win, faces Cameron Reny, D-Bristol, to represent Senate District 13, which consists of Lincoln County, excluding Dresden and including Washington and Windsor.
“I don’t have the answers to everything, but I sure have talked to a lot of people that have some great ideas,” Mitchell said. “Their voices need to be shared and heard.”
Originally from Southport, Mitchell volunteered with the Southport Fire Department and later attended Southern Maine Vocational Technical Institute for Marine Science Deck to get his mate’s or captain’s license. Instead of taking the usual route of shipping off on a tanker or tug boat, Mitchell went into the private boat trade, he said.
After a few years of running a boat up and down the East Coast, Mitchell was hired as a boat captain to run boats for the Maine Marine Patrol, first stationed in Southwest Harbor and then Boothbay.
Mitchell retired from the patrol after 12 years and spent his time after lobstering and running different businesses, such as woodcutting and lot cleaning. In 2006, Mitchell and his wife bought the property that his brewery and RV park now sit on. Boothbay Craft Brewery, Tavern, and RV is celebrating 20 years in business this year.
“We did everything ourselves,” Mitchell said.
With the creation of the brewery, Mitchell became a figure in reviving the Maine Brewer’s Guild. He partnered with the owner of Maine Beer Company, Daniel Kleban, and former state representative and senator Heather Sanborn, to reshape the organization. The effort took the guild from 25 breweries to just over 150.
Mitchell has “never been in politics” before because of his employment at the state level. He said he is familiar with numerous laws and how bills are passed.
“But I’m more interested in representing all my fellow Lincoln County people,” Mitchell said.
Mitchell is running as an independent because he believes he can converse with both political parties by being in the middle. During his campaign, he said he has found that more people are willing to talk to him because he is not affiliated with a party.
“I can state unequivocally that I am doing it because I think that’s the only proper way to represent a diverse political area like Lincoln County,” he said.
Mitchell decided to run because his sons are now old enough to start taking over the business. As they do so, he said his plan is to give back to the community.
He said he believes that his experience working in marine patrol and connections across the state from his business make him a good candidate. He referenced his campaign videos that highlight why he loves his community and local industries throughout the district.
“They’re intended to tell why I love living here, why my boys love living here, and we want to be able to stay here and succeed,” Mitchell said.
Another motivator for Mitchell to run was a perceived disconnect between elected officials and the communities they represent. In the 20 years he has run his business, he said that Reny has not stopped by.
Mitchell said once someone is elected to office, it should not be the end of their door knocking.
“It’s not like, ‘Win Mitchell has the answers, he’s going to the state house,” Mitchell said. “It’s, ‘Win Mitchell has the connections and the experience to be able to talk to his constituents and fairly represent them, and then come back and tell them what the result was.”
Mitchell said his strengths are his ability to talk to people, share ideas, and respect other’s opinions.
He also said he has had enough of seeing advertisements putting other candidates down and instead would like to see reasons why he should vote for someone.
“To get elected is for the people to choose, they think that I’m the best one to represent them, but they also have a trust that I’m going to come back to them and get their opinions on things,” Mitchell said.
A major concern for Mitchell is affordability across the board, especially for housing. As a business owner, he spoke about difficulties retaining full-time employees, which forced his operating hours to shift.
“Plenty of business,” he said. “Just can’t get the help.”
For rural healthcare, Mitchell said he understands frustrations around the impending closure of the labor and delivery unit at MaineHealth Lincoln Hospital in Damariscotta, but said people should also look at the reasons for why it closed. He said there needs to be more open and honest conversations between MaineHealth and state representatives to ensure transparency when these decisions are being made.
Mitchell also said that with the attention on the closure announcement, many people did not celebrate the opening of a new oncology and infusion center at Lincoln Hospital. He said the services cater to the age demographics in the area and recalled how his wife would have liked a center like that when she battled and beat cancer 13 years ago.
Noting the trend in labor and delivery units closing across the state, Mitchell said the best way to keep them open is to grow local communities. If elected, he intends to brainstorm ideas on how to attract “the talent” to work in healthcare.
“Young professionals want to give; they want to give service,” Mitchell said. “I don’t blame them. Be like me sitting around here waiting for somebody, you know, to come buy a beer.”
Through running his business, Mitchell said he has also seen the struggle to obtain affordable health insurance. Most employees at his brewery are self-insured, he said. If elected, Mitchell said he does not know how much change a state senator can enact in health insurance, but would like to guide a policy toward making it more accessible.
Additionally, Mitchell wants to address rising property taxes and believes the state is spending more than can be afforded.
“We’ve got to make sure that we don’t depress the people that are already here,” Mitchell said.
Some of the blame for the increase in property taxes can be attributed to the rise in AirBnB and other short-term rentals throughout the state, Mitchell said. If elected, Mitchell said he plans to find ways to increase the homestead exemption, which would lighten the burden of property taxes and incentivize part-time residents to become full-time.
By bringing in more residents, more money will be contributed to the state’s economy, Mitchell said. The attraction of more full-time residents would also create more activities year-round, which would expand business hours, that would then bring in even more employees, he said.
“People will bring industry, but you can’t bring industry and hope that people come,” Mitchell said.
He voiced concerns about the rental properties bought by big corporations, which he said are partially to blame for the increasing costs of living. He said larger houses that are only occupied by visitors during the summer often do not fit in the budget of full-time residents.
“We are literally encouraging people not to live in Maine year-round with our policies,” Mitchell said.
To increase home affordability for families, Mitchell said he will focus on high efficiency regulations.
Also concerned about increasing taxes, Mitchell called the rise in education costs a “Catch-22,” because while the price for schooling is increasing, the number of students enrolled is decreasing because their families cannot afford to live in the area.
“It’s sad because we are losing those people and their votes,” Mitchell said. “Whether they vote Democrat or Republican doesn’t matter. They vote locally in our elections.”
While talking about education, Mitchell said there also need to be more ways to encourage students to pursue a career in trades. He said someone always needs an electrician or a plumber, and that there should be a trade school in every county. With more opportunities like this, he believes more people will move to the area.
“You know, it’s a great place to live,” Mitchell said. “There’s no reason why people shouldn’t be flocking here.”
When it comes to infrastructure, Mitchell said he is considering different paths to improve the safety of local roadways. He referenced the state’s effort in 2010 to build a bypass around Wiscasset meant to improve traffic conditions that was eventually put down by voters.
Mitchell said this was a missed opportunity and that Wiscasset would be “so much more vibrant” if it did not have “every truck and trailer” driving through. He said Damariscotta is an example of a “bypass that worked.”
Throughout the district, Mitchell said there is a need for some infrastructure updates and that by pushing these projects forward; the state can use local contracts.
Considering the working waterfront, Mitchell gave kudos to those working in Department of Marine Resources and said that fisherman should have a voice. If elected, he said he will aim to prevent overregulation in this industry while protecting the natural ecosystems.
A part of protecting the fishing industry is also ensuring fishermen and lobstermen are not driven out of the state by increasing taxes, he said.
“I do think that DMR and scientists have a key role in guiding and working with fisherman to do what’s right for our environment and other uses,” Mitchell said.
Mitchell has local endorsements from friends, families, and neighboring business, including Boothbay Select Board member Russell Pinkham, and Rob Hunt, owner of Hunt Brothers Lumber.
Mitchell said even if he does get elected, his campaign has been a great experience and he encourages others to do the same. As someone who never had any aspirations to be in politics, he said it is important to bring in experiences from all areas to “get people talking again, working together again.”
The election is on Tuesday, Nov. 3.
This article appears through a content-sharing agreement with the Lincoln County News.

title: Missing Wabanaki marker at Cadillac Mountain and the fight over what national parks should tell
text:
At Cadillac Mountain, a missing Wabanaki marker and the fight over what national parks should tell
In the soft light of dawn, an Ohio tourist studied the interpretive sign at the summit of Cadillac Mountain in Acadia National Park, reading about how magma formed the ground under her feet.
There is one sign she and the other 4 million-plus tourists who visit Acadia annually can no longer see at the summit: a marker explaining the mountain’s sacred significance to the Wabanaki people in the region. “Today, visitors from everywhere find meaning on the mountain,” it said.
It was among 30 markers removed from Acadia under a Trump administration campaign to strip national parks of materials deemed disparaging to American history, according to the National Parks Conservation Association.
But when park staff took down the summit sign on the orders of Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, they also unraveled some of the trust that took decades to build between Acadia National Park and the Wabanaki people. The Wabanaki Confederacy, also known as "the people of the dawnland," has inhabited the northern seaboard for over 10,000 years and the Wabanaki were the first known stewards of land that includes much of the national park. It was a gathering place to trade, hunt, fish and pick sweetgrass.
Some of the signs removed from Acadia were developed over years of partnerships with organizations including Friends of Acadia, the Schoodic Institute and the Native Plant Trust — with consultation from citizens of the Wabanaki Nations. They know the mountain in Maine as Wapuwoc — “white mountain of the first light.” From October to March, it’s the first place to see the sunrise in the continental United States.
“Getting to a place where our language is in these parks and it is educational … erasing that or setting that back has big implications for how far we’ve come,” said Maulian Bryant, the Wabanaki Alliance's executive director.
Bryant says the removed signs reflected “the good stuff.”
“These signs don’t say 96% of Wabanaki people died from smallpox, or there were 26 nations and now there’s four,” she said. “If we really want to get into the real history, that’s a whole other slice of cake.”
Other signs removed from Cadillac’s summit addressed issues of climate change, informing visitors that “Acadia’s future will be warmer and wetter” and that “In the last century, average annual precipitation has increased by six inches.”
During their tenure under the Biden administration, former National Park Service director Chuck Sams and former Interior Secretary Deb Haaland — the first Native Americans to hold these positions — aimed to reflect the experiences of all Americans throughout the national parks. Before leaving his post in February 2025, Sams saw parts of his work unraveled by the current administration.
This “attempt to rewrite history into a single narrative … is also counter to our democracy. And counter to the idea that we are a plural nation,” said Sams.
Lawsuit against national park removals advances
Now, a coalition of conservation, history and science organizations is fighting in court to get the Acadia signs and hundreds of other items put back. Under Burgum's 2025 campaign, signs, books, films and exhibits covering topics such as slavery, climate change and the massacre of Native Americans were flagged and removed from national parks and monuments nationwide.
“Some of it’s been put back, and then some of it has been removed again,” said the Center for American Progress' Angelo Villagomez. He was part of the progressive policy group's team that examined a database leaked earlier this year and found that a third of national parks had flagged exhibits featuring history or science. Of those, exhibits featuring Black and Indigenous history were most targeted.
Portions of all flagged material have since been reviewed and cataloged by a committee led by Joy Beasley, a National Park Service associate director. However, in a June affidavit, she writes that the spreadsheet is “unlikely to capture every removal, revision, or replacement.”
The Interior Department did not respond to The Associated Press’ questions about the current status of sign and exhibit removal or the ongoing lawsuit filed by the nonprofit coalition in February against the federal government.
The parks “are America’s storytellers,” said Todd Martin of the National Parks Conservation Association, a plaintiff in the lawsuit. “It’s their duty to preserve and interpret American history, the good, the bad, and the ugly.”
Jenny McBurney, a government publications librarian at the University of Minnesota who co-founded the project Save Our Signs, feels it’s more important than ever for park visitors to document revised signs.
“People are going to go to the parks and think that they will get to learn history there when in fact they will be learning an incomplete history,” said McBurney.
Wabanaki culture — past and present — shared in Acadia
Despite the job cuts, threats of land reduction, talks of privatization and even demolition within some parks, Indigenous groups and park partners have persevered.
In Maine, members of the Wabanaki Confederacy — comprised of the Maliseet, Mi’kmaq, Passamaquoddy, Penobscot and Abenaki principal nations — carry on the cultural traditions and spiritual practices that helped them maintain sovereignty and connection to their ancestral land after settlers arrived. That includes sharing their culture with tourists.
Penobscot Nation citizen Jennifer Neptune had mixed emotions about the attempted erasure of her people from Acadia and their ancestral homeland.
“It’s hard to get good signage in national monuments, in national parks,” said Neptune. “It’s a real gut punch when it (removal) happens, not just for Indigenous people, but for Black people, for the people whose stories don’t get shared.”
Over the past decade, she’s seen real change from the National Park Service, which has played an integral part in bringing Wabanaki voices to the table to create Indigenous-designed spaces.
In partnership with Acadia, the privately owned Abbe Museum, which is largely overseen by Wabanaki people, hosts a program that brings Native voices into the park through music, arts and culture.
Nick Bear and members of a Wabanaki drum circle perform on Cadillac Mountain annually as part of this collaboration. “That’s just like bringing those ceremonies right back to the original sites,” he said.
In July, Passamaquoddy basket maker Lydia Soctomah demonstrated traditional Wabanaki basketry using pounded ash bark and sweetgrass outside the Sieur de Monts Nature Center. Both the ash tree and sweetgrass are part of the Wabanaki creation story, she said.
“Making a basket is worth 1,000 memories for me,” said Soctomah, whose grandmother was a well-known basket maker. “I was always told it holds a part of your spirit.”
Sweetgrass access an example of shared stewardship
Access to sweetgrass has long been difficult for Wabanaki people as they were pushed from coastal lands onto reservations. In Acadia, it’s been nearly nonexistent since the park’s creation in 1916. But over the past decade, park staff and Wabanaki members have collaborated to change that.
In 2017, scientist Suzanne Greenlaw, a citizen of the Houlton Band of Maliseet Indians, partnered with the U.S. Forest Service, Acadia’s Schoodic Institute and 14 traditional gatherers to conduct a Wabanaki-led sweetgrass study in hopes of allowing tribal access.
“It was really impactful because we had never had those kinds of co-stewardship relationships,” said Greenlaw, adding that those relationships, built over time, have not changed.
By the end of the Biden administration, there were over 400 co-stewardship or co-management agreements with tribes, 159 within the National Park Service alone, says Sams. Programs in Acadia were among them.
These programs, he says, allow tribes to fulfill their obligation to protect, preserve and enhance natural resources, and the federal government to fulfill its obligation to allow tribal access for hunting, fishing, and gathering foods and medicines.
Sams cautiously hopes there will be a rebuilding period for the park service under the next administration.
“There are always ebbs and flows with every administration,” he said. “Nobody has seen that more than American Indian tribes.”

title: Massachusetts police officer heads off Bitcoin scam targeting Maine woman
text:
NEWBURYPORT, Mass. — The quick thinking of a local police officer saved a Maine woman from depositing $11,000 in cash into a Bitcoin ATM as part of an attempted scam, according to the chief administrator at the city’s police department, Matthew Simons.
On Tuesday around 5:30 p.m., Officer Nathaniel Kelley was at a Storey Avenue gas station when he was approached by a 75-year-old woman, who feared she may be getting scammed.
The woman said she was nervous because she was on the phone with someone claiming to be a government agent who knew personal information about her, and told her she had to deposit money into a Bitcoin ATM machine to avoid legal repercussions.
Based on his training, Kelley was immediately suspicious and asked to speak to the person on the phone with the 75-year-old, but that individual hung up as soon as a police officer joined the conversation.
Kelley soon learned the 75-year-old had driven from Maine in search of a Bitcoin ATM machine, and that she had withdrawn $11,000 in cash. He then explained the call was likely a scam, and encouraged the woman to keep an eye on her accounts in the immediate future and to report any suspicious activity.
The call was a common type of scam in which suspects pose as law enforcement or government officials and threaten would-be victims with legal consequences if they don’t provide money immediately. Other variations of the scam involve claims that a relative is in jail and needs immediate bail money, according to Simons.
Once cash is deposited into Bitcoin ATM machines, it is often irretrievable unless the entire Bitcoin ATM is seized with a search warrant. Few victims who actually send cash ever get their money back, and arrests are rare, according to local police.
The attempted scam comes weeks after the City Council voted on Oct. 5, to ban cryptocurrency ATMs within city limits. Assuming a procedural second vote goes the same way during Monday’s City Council meeting, all ATMs must be removed in two months. From Jan. 1, 2021, through Aug. 26, 2026, the Police Department has confirmed 10 incidents involving Bitcoin ATMs totaling $134,700.
“Most people don’t even know what Bitcoin ATMs are for, and we mostly only hear about them when they are used to transmit funds to scammers,” Simons said. “These machines provide little service to residents, but represent a real threat to public safety by providing a quick and easy way for residents to be separated from their hard-earned money.”
Story by Dave Rogers, The Daily News of Newburyport. Distributed by Tribune Content Agency, LLC.

title: Maine needs to double down on its Canadian ties
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Douglas Rooks has been a Maine editor and columnist for 41 years. His biography of Gov. Ken Curtis, “Transformational,” is now available. He welcomes comment at [email protected].
I had the chance to travel for a week in Canada recently. It seemed a good time to compare the two countries while traveling north — or in this case, east.
The Maritime provinces (New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia) recall similarities for Mainers. Though our viewpoint usually extends west — uniquely among the “lower 48” states, Maine borders only one, New Hampshire — New Brunswick is an equally interesting pairing.
The two are almost equal in size, though New Brunswick has just shy of 900,000 people against Maine’s 1.4 million. Cities are larger, though, with three — Moncton, St. John and Fredericton, the capital — exceeding Portland’s population.
Throughout the Maritimes, there’s a familiar feel, with the Acadian forest dominating the coast an extension of Washington County. Yes, there’s lots of trees, though Prince Edward Island, whose economy relies on farming (and tourism), resembles Aroostook’s potato-growing regions.
There have been changes since previous wanderings of mine. A bridge to PEI replaced the ferry in 1997. The U.S. Customs station opened in 2009 is four miles upriver from Calais, while Canada’s is still downtown.
Some changes are more recent. Canadians are united behind Prime Minister Mark Carney to a degree unthinkable a few years ago. When Carney and his Liberal Party stood for election in April 2025 after Liberal Party Prime Minister Justin Trudeau stepped down, Carney was widely expected to lose to Pierre Poilievre’s Conservative Party. Pundits called it “unwinnable” for the Liberals.
Instead, Liberals won their first majority since 2019 and Carney may be carving a larger place for himself on the international scene than Trudeau — himself son of legendary Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau, whose 18 years in office made him the most famous Canadian PM to date.
The elder Trudeau, a Liberal Party member from Quebec, held Canada together against a determined separatist movement by the Parti Quebecois aimed at separating the French-majority province from Canada. This week, separatists in Alberta, the conservative, oil-rich western province, held a referendum to explore independence — and 76% voted “No.”
What prompted these events? The actions of President Donald Trump. Upon returning to office, Trump made ludicrous statements about Canada as “the 51st state,” arguing that America’s (and Maine’s) largest trading partner was defrauding us. He aimed to make the world’s “longest undefended border” a battleground.
Carney differs from the international leaders who make soothing sounds to avoid Trump’s ire. Carney plays it straight, defending his nation’s interests. Trump, after his first trade war was struck down by the U.S. Supreme Court, launched another against Canada.
The immediate results: Canadians are increasingly united, Americans disunited. Yet Canadians seem to bear us no ill will for this distressing performance. Rather the opposite: Americans are still welcome, with the attitude “this too will pass.” In our own response to Trumpian vows to annex Canada, Greenland, Iceland, Venezuela, et. al., we might think instead: cooperation.
Let’s ponder a confederation of Atlantic provinces and states, with Maine a charter participant. Our economies have similar strengths and weaknesses. Unlike much of the world, we could use some more people — young people especially.
Where Maine was abandoned by American paper companies, job losses were mitigated in Canada thanks to companies like Irving, with its forest products and petroleum divisions. Along with McCain, the frozen food giant, Irving is now the largest business investor in eastern Maine and Aroostook. Once viewed as a threat, Canadian investment helps sustain Maine’s rural economies — but is now threatened by irrational trade wars.
Long ago, a Maine governor appreciated Canadian ties and built on them. When I researched Ken Curtis’ administration, one surprise was how vigorously and persistently he pursued those ties. He sought to create a public power authority that could buy cheap hydropower from the then-new Churchill Falls project in Newfoundland; CMP and Bangor Hydro opposed him.
Curtis befriended Richard Hatfield, New Brunswick’s longest-serving premier, and signed numerous agreements, some still in force. He established an Office of Canadian Relations and later served a regrettably brief stint as ambassador to Canada. Though Curtis hoped future governors would maintain these efforts, they didn’t.
Gov. Janet Mills traveled this week to Ireland, exploring both the Republic and Northern Ireland as a gateway to the European market, now that Great Britain has “Brexited” the EU. Perhaps the next governor could explore gateways to Canada.
If as well received as I expect a confederation would be, Maine might attract American Atlantic partners, say Massachusetts, New Hampshire and Rhode Island. Then Maine could be the center of something, rather than at the far margins.
Confederation is a useful concept. It’s how Canada moved toward nationhood starting with a conference in Charlottetown, PEI, in 1864, the height of our Civil War. And on that path — unlike our own — no revolution was required.

title: Trump backs Ramaswamy on ad featuring Amy Acton’s estranged mother
text:
COLUMBUS, Ohio (AP) — The backlash over an Ohio campaign advertisement attacking Amy Acton, the Democratic nominee for governor, spread beyond the state’s borders Thursday, causing fresh headaches for Republicans with less than two weeks until the midterm elections.
The latest episode began when Gov. Mike DeWine criticized Vivek Ramaswamy, a fellow Republican that he endorsed as his successor, for running an ad featuring Acton’s estranged mother criticizing her. Acton’s mother lost custody of her children decades ago after her husband was indicted for raping Acton as a child.
But President Donald Trump took the opposite approach hours later, posting on social media that Ramaswamy’s ad was “hitting pay dirt” and questioning DeWine’s loyalty to the party.
Trump’s stance only hardened throughout the day. Speaking to reporters at the White House, Trump said, “Amy Acton’s mother said horrible things about Amy Acton” and “she’s fair game.”
And at a campaign rally in Iowa, Trump regaled the crowd with a story about how Ramaswamy called him to ask for advice.
“You’ve got to ride with it,” Trump recalled telling Ramaswamy, a biotech billionaire and former presidential candidate. Trump expressed jealousy that he didn’t have such a strong ad to run during his own campaigns.
“I told him to leave it up and look upstairs and say: ‘Thank you, God, very much. I appreciate it,’” Trump added. “I only wish I could have had an ad like that against somebody.”
Trump’s aggressive defense of Ramaswamy practically guarantees that more of his party’s candidates will face questions about the issue at a moment when they already risk being dragged down by the president’s low popularity.
Rep. Ashley Hinson, the Republican nominee for U.S. Senate in Iowa, was asked about it before appearing with Trump at the rally.
She told ABC News the ad is “absolutely terrible” and “I think they should take the ad down.”
Ramaswamy’s campaign has said it plans to spend $4 million to show the ad online and on television.
DeWine stops short of pulling his endorsement
The controversy has became the latest test of the bounds of acceptable political discourse.
In western Michigan, former Republican Rep. Fred Upton said the ad had spread throughout his community as people heard about it on the radio and television or were asked about it by others.
“They asked me about it at the bank today,” Upton said, adding that the ad “speaks horribly of the gutter politics that some rely on.”
An influential Ohio Republican, former Rep. Jim Renacci, posted a lengthy essay on social media overnight suggesting that “the floor may have just fallen out from under the Republican campaign for Ohio Governor” and urging everyone in the party to distance themselves from it.
Ohio U.S. Sen. Jon Husted, who is being challenged by former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown, said he would not have run the ad. So did Republican Secretary of State Frank LaRose, who is running for state auditor.
At a gathering with reporters at the Ohio Statehouse on Thursday, DeWine recalled the painful experiences of rape victims he dealt with as a county prosecutor and state attorney general.
“It’s wrong to run this ad,” he said. “And, even at this late time — my wife, Fran, saw the ad just run this morning on TV — I would just urge the Ramaswamy campaign to take this down.”
The governor stopped short of pulling his backing for Ramaswamy. DeWine recalled that a previous line of attack by the Acton campaign had mentioned Ramaswamy’s mother, and the governor said that was also wrong because “family members have always historically been off limits.” However, DeWine noted that the topic was never used in a multimillion-dollar ad campaign.
Acton’s criticism cited an investigative report into Geetha Ramaswamy’s role at a pharmaceutical company run by her son, whom Acton and Democrats described as “hiring his own mother to manipulate clinical trial data.” The Ramaswamy campaign called those claims “slanderous.”
“Governor DeWine is correct that the first and only candidate to attack the mother of her opponent in this race was Amy Acton,” Ramaswamy spokesperson Connie Luck said in a statement, adding, “We refuse to accept the media’s double standards.”
Vance supported Ramaswamy
The Ramaswamy campaign video features Acton’s birth mother, Donna Arthur, calling her “a liar” and insinuating she has mental health issues.
Acton, Ohio’s COVID-19-era health director, has made no secret of facing homelessness and abuse as a child. Arthur lost custody of her children after their stepfather, Arthur’s husband, was indicted on a charge of rape involving Acton.
The abuse allegedly happened from December 1976 to April 1978. Cledith Arthur failed to show for a court appearance and became a fugitive. Donna Arthur remained married to him until his death in 2004.
Acton’s campaign on Tuesday posted a video of her brother, who supported her backstory about living in a tent and being abused.
Republican Vice President JD Vance, an Ohio native son, expressed disgust with Republicans “whining” about the ad while he visited the state on Wednesday.
Amid the turmoil, Ohio Republican Party Chairman Alex Triantafilou posted what sounded like a warning, or a threat.
“The final days of a tough campaign are always the best time to find out who is really with you and who just posts and pretends,” he wrote. “Yes — we are keeping score.” The quote was followed by a winking-eye emoji.
While Republicans are at odds over the ad, Democrats have rallied to support Acton.
“Child abuse and sexual assault should never be weaponized to score partisan points,” Democratic Governors Association spokesperson Izzi Levy said. ”Governor DeWine is right — Vivek Ramaswamy’s ad is beyond troubling, and he should take it down immediately and apologize to survivors everywhere and all those hurt by this reprehensible attack.”
Illinois first lady MK Pritzker said she donated $500,000 to Acton’s campaign because of the ad.
___
Associated Press reporters Joey Cappelletti contributed from Washington and Thomas Beaumont contributed from Sioux City, Iowa.

title: Maine pumpkin farms see high demand as Halloween approaches
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine pumpkin farms see high demand as Halloween approaches
With Halloween just around the corner, pumpkin farms across Maine are seeing a seasonal rush as customers search for the perfect pumpkin.
At Jordan’s Farm in Cape Elizabeth, the team grows its own pumpkins and has been busy keeping up with demand during one of the farm’s final major sales periods before winter.
Elizabeth Bullis, the farm’s project manager, said pumpkin season is an important time for the business as activity typically slows during the colder months.
“Winter is tough. You know, there's not a lot of revenue coming in in the winter as compared to the high season of summer,” Bullis said. “So pumpkins are sort of that last big push for us.”
Pumpkins are a popular part of fall traditions in Maine, whether customers are looking for jack-o’-lanterns, seasonal decorations or a way to celebrate the Halloween season.
Jordan’s Farm plans to continue selling pumpkins through Halloween and beyond, until its supply runs out.
