title: Construction on Trump’s 250-foot triumphal arch in D.C. could begin in just two weeks
text:
Construction on Trump’s 250-foot triumphal arch in D.C. could begin in just two weeks
The Trump administration told a judge Wednesday evening that construction on the president’s controversial 250-foot triumphal arch could begin in just two weeks, days after the midterm elections.
The Justice Department said in Wednesday’s court filing that the National Capital Planning Commission is set to meet on Nov. 5 and could sign off on final plans for the arch that day — and with final authorization from the Department of the Interior — “construction could commence as early as November 5, 2026.”
The administration last week released its final plans for the arch — one of President Donald Trump’s pet construction projects in the nation’s capital. Wednesday night’s court filing comes in one of the lawsuits seeking to stop the arch’s construction.
Related video: Trump Triumphal arch design
Notably, the plans released last week excluded key features of a military complex including drones and snipers that Trump has used as justification for the much-criticized project. In the plans, the contours of the arch do not appear to reflect a national security purpose. Instead, they describe the project as a “ceremonial gateway” to the nation’s capital.
Trump announced in September that the arch would store large numbers of drones and function as a post for military snipers, with a large cache of ammunition. While the plans submitted last week don’t include the military components Trump described, the structure still might feature them.
The massive arch would sit directly across from Arlington National Cemetery, where nearly 430,000 service members, veterans and their family members are buried. Veterans suing to stop its construction argue the towering structure would break the solemnity of funerals at the cemetery, while preservationists argue it would disrupt the sightline of the row of national landmarks that includes the Lincoln Memorial, Arlington House and the Robert E. Lee Memorial.
An Interior Department spokesperson told CNN over the weekend that the structure will “enhance the visitor experience at Arlington National Cemetery for veterans, the families of the fallen, and all Americans alike.”
The proposed arch is among several projects Trump is pursuing in an effort to remake the nation’s capital to his own personal liking, prompting legal battles from preservationists and others. The idea of the arch being needed for national security purposes mirrors an argument Trump has made for building a White House ballroom where the East Wing once stood.
The administration’s assertion that construction could begin next month drew immediate backlash from opponents of the project. Charles A. Birnbaum, CEO and founder of the Cultural Landscape Foundation, a Washington, D.C.-based education and advocacy organization, which has been a vocal critic of Trump’s arch, gave a scathing assessment.
“What better way to celebrate the nation’s 250th anniversary than to shut down the legally required review process, ignore some 100,000 negative public comments, and fast track the construction of a bloated and deeply unpopular monument that the president claims is for him,” he said.

As state senator since 2022, I’ve worked to support legislation aligned with two priorities: the broad issues I campaign on and finding solutions to unique challenges impacting Senate District 13.

title: Maranacook cross country runner is turning heads as a freshman
text:
Our Communities. Our Teams. Our Future.
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone—because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s Go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
READFIELD — Nineteen minutes, 38.50 seconds. It was a time Reagan Mattson had drilled into her head long before she stood at the starting line for her first home cross country meet at Maranacook.
The Black Bears freshman felt she could beat the course record set by Abby Williams four years ago. Was it too big of a thought for someone competing in her first official varsity race? Nope. Mattson did what she set out to do, breaking the record with a time of 19:35.31.
“I knew what the (previous record) was going into the race, and that was my goal for the whole race — I was just focused on that,” Mattson said. “It was close in the end, but I was super excited. I got so many congratulations for it, and it was such a huge confidence-booster for me.”
It was a springboard to what has been a remarkable year for Mattson on trails throughout central Maine and the Mountain Valley Conference. Mattson has won six of the seven races in which she’s competed, and with two course records to her name, she now has her sights set on regional and state titles.
Mattson’s record-setting home meet followed a win in the preseason Laliberte Invitational on Aug. 28 at Cony High School. Then came victories on Sept. 10 at Hall-Dale, on Sept. 17 at Winthrop — her time of 19:56.84 broke the course record by more than a minute — and on Sept. 24 at Gardiner.
A first-place finish at the MVC championships was Mattson’s sixth win and helped guide the Black Bears to the conference title. The only meet she failed to win was the Festival of Champions, but she delivered her proudest performance to date: an 18:55.42 that placed her seventh in a field of 627.
“I was so happy with that time,” said Mattson, who also placed first among 70 runners in the girls 14-and-under age group at the Beach to Beacon 10K (39:46). “Breaking 19 (minutes) was a huge goal I had for myself this season, and doing it there, I was super proud of that.”
Why is Mattson so good? Sure, she’s fast, but Maranacook interim coach Casey Thompson says her success comes down to more than her athletic abilities. It’s that physical prowess and an ability to process a race that exceeds that of most freshmen that makes her the complete package.
“She has such a good sense of race strategy,” said Thompson, who is leading the Black Bears this year while coach Kelsey Barrett is on maternity leave. “She’s very impressive. Even though there are some courses where she hasn’t set the record, she still has her eyes on them.”
The athletic gene runs in Mattson’s family. She developed an affinity for running by listening to her grandmother, Miriam, regale her with stories of her glory days in the sport. Reagan’s sophomore brother, Gage, is also a strong runner for the Black Bears, finishing fifth at MVCs last week.
Mattson insists she and Gage don’t have a sibling rivalry, though the two certainly are very competitive. In addition to being outstanding runners, both are also very good basketball players. Gage was the leading scorer on Maranacook’s Class C South title-winning team last year, and Reagan is a top player in the 2030 class.
“We are so close; we’re best friends — he’s my idol — and I look up to him so much,” Mattson said. “He teaches me a lot about race strategy. … Our 1-on-1 (on the basketball court) get a little heated, but he works with me a lot, and he’s always super helpful to me.”
Mattson knows her biggest goals this season remain in front of her. On the heels of an MVC title, she hopes to complete a sweep of championship season by claiming the Class C South title on Saturday at Twin Brook Recreation Area in Cumberland and the Class C state title next Saturday at Cony.
Mattson could be next in a line of memorable Class C runners. Before her, there was Houlton/Greater Houlton Christian’s Teanne Ewings, the 2024 Varsity Maine Girls Cross Country Runner of the Year. Ewings followed Ruth White, who was Varsity Maine Runner of the Year three straight years from 2021-23.
The Maranacook freshman idolizes those runners. She remembers watching White’s races as a middle schooler and being in awe of how the now-University of New Hampshire standout approached races. Now, she hopes to do as a freshman what White couldn’t because of COVID in 2020: win a state title.
“It would be so amazing to go out and win a state championship as a freshman,” said Mattson, who is Class C’s top-ranked runner. “That’s something not a lot of people get a chance to do. It’s my goal, and I hope I can succeed on that one.”

title: The Lincoln County News

As a 99-year-old voter from Bangor, I’ve learned that one of the most important rights we have is the right to vote. Throughout my lifetime, I’ve seen how elections shape our communities, our state and our future.

title: Trump blasts LeBron James for not standing still during national anthem
text:
Trump blasts 76ers' star LeBron James as 'disgrace' for not standing still during national anthem
President Donald Trump on Thursday accused LeBron James of disrespecting the United States after the NBA star appeared to continue his warmups while the national anthem was performed before Philadelphia's season opener on Tuesday.
"I said right from the beginning that he's no good, a TOTAL DISGRACE," Trump said of James in a social media post sharing the video. "LeBron James should apologize to all of those Great American Warriors and Heroes who died for the American Flag, and all that our Country stands for!"
James appeared to practice a golf swing and jump shot as The Star-Spangled Banner was performed at Tuesday's game in New York. James, starting his first season with Philadelphia, was lined up alongside teammates who mostly stood still during the anthem.
Trump and James have been critical of each another for years, occasionally trading public swipes.
James had not made a public comment or a social media post as of Thursday afternoon about Trump's gripe.
The 41-year-old James, in his record 24th NBA season, was set to make his home debut for the Sixers Thursday night against Cleveland.
Among some of the more notable times James became entangled with the president or politics:
LeBron wears 1 black shoe, 1 white shoe
James was with Cleveland in 2017 when he made a statement during an NBA game with his shoes — one black, one white, with the word "equality" in capital gold letters on the back of each.
Then, after the game, James made a statement about Trump, saying: "This is a beautiful country and we're never going to let one person dictate how beautiful and how powerful we are."
James had called Trump " a bum " on Twitter and also said earlier that season of the president: "He doesn't understand how many kids, no matter the race, look up to the president of the United State for guidance, for leadership, for words of encouragement. He doesn't understand that, and that's what makes me more sick than anything."
Shut up and dribble
James showed determination to speak out on social issues and the nation's political climate after Fox News host Laura Ingraham criticized the four-time NBA champion for his 2018 comments about social issues.
"We will definitely not shut up and dribble," James said. "I will definitely not do that. I mean too much to society. I mean too much to the youth. I mean too much to so many kids that feel like they don't have a way out and they need someone to help lead them out of the situation they're in."
James referenced Muhammad Ali, Jim Brown, Bill Russell and Jackie Robinson as athletes who previously spoke up for equality and change with no concerns about the consequences or any rewards.
"We know it's bigger than us," James said.
Get people to the polls
James was named The Associated Press' Male Athlete of the Year in 2020 in large part for leading the Los Angeles Lakers to a championship and helped convince many — at the peak of Black Lives Matter — who had never voted to finally head to the polls.
"I still know what I do on the floor and obviously, I give everything to the game," James said. "But I can make a greater impact off the floor right now, more than I can on the floor. And I want to continue to inspire people with the way I play the game of basketball. But there's so many more things that I can do off the floor to help cultivate people, inspire people, bring people together, empower them."
James rejects Zlatan's criticism of activist athletes
AC Milan striker and former LA Galaxy star Zlatan Ibrahimovic blasted socially conscious athletes in a 2021 interview. Ibrahimovic called it "a mistake" for James and other athletes to get involved in political causes, saying they should "just do what you do best, because it doesn't look good."
James, naturally, rejected the criticism.
"I would never shut up about things that are wrong," James said.
___
AP White House reporter Collin Binkley in Washington contributed to this story.

title: Man's Tesla video leads to acquittal, police officer's resignation
text:
Man's Tesla video leads to acquittal, police officer's resignation
A Florida man said a judge found him not guilty at trial after video recorded by a camera on his Tesla was shown in court.
More than two years later, the arresting officer resigned from the Winter Springs Police Department.
Kevin Finley said he feels vindicated now that the officer, who falsely accused him of fleeing and then detained him at gunpoint outside his garage in 2024, has left the force.
"I feel it's the first step, yeah, there's some accountability, finally,” Finley told sister station WESH. “It's a little bit of relief. I feel like the community is a lot safer now."
Officer Erik Schwartz can be heard on his body camera video telling Finley to “turn around, get on your knees,” before he placed him in handcuffs for 33 minutes.
"I was very scared,” Finley said. “I had no clue what was going on." 
Finley was driving home after dropping his children off at daycare. He said he wasn’t trying to flee because he didn’t see the lights or hear the sirens when Officer Schwartz initiated a traffic stop near his house for driving through an intersection at a high rate of speed.
Finley was never charged with felony fleeing and eluding.
"So, here's the deal: you're not going to jail today,” Schwartz told Finley in the body camera video. “You are going to be issued multiple citations for your driving. You're also receiving a criminal citation for the reckless driving." 
The next day, Finley said he went to the Winter Springs Police Department and “explained to them like, 'Hey, I have video, like, we can clear this right up?' And they just didn't care." 
When Finley’s case went to trial in July, he proved he never saw the officer coming after him with video recorded by the camera on the back of his Tesla.
"Ah, it made me feel great,” Finley said. “Like, I love the car even more now, you know? It saved me from jail time, which was amazing."
Right before jury deliberations, the judge acquitted Finley of his charges.
While Officer Schwartz wrote in the police report that Finley “lost traction and fish-tailed,” his Tesla video showed that wasn’t the case.
There’s only a brief moment in the Tesla video when the unmarked patrol car’s lights were visible.
"There's no way I could have seen him,” Finley said. “He was going the opposite direction. He had to do a three-point turn, and then you know, like I'm looking forward, like as a driver is supposed to do."
On Tuesday, Winter Springs Police Chief Matthew Tracht announced that Officer Schwartz is no longer employed by the City of Winter Springs.
He resigned amid an ongoing internal investigation after Finley filed a complaint at the conclusion of his criminal case. 
Chief Tracht declined an on-camera interview request from WESH on Wednesday.
"Based on the circumstances surrounding this matter, the conduct did not meet the standards and expectations I have for the officers who serve this department and our community,” Chief Tracht wrote in a Facebook post. "There is no doubt the situation could have been handled differently, and there are lessons to be learned from how it was addressed."
Finley said he was surprised when the chief called to apologize and to tell him the officer resigned.
"I don't think it was a sincere apology,” Finley said. “It was two years too late. The apology should have come the same day that this happened, and these charges should have never been filed."
Finley said he intends to file a civil lawsuit against Winter Springs police.

title: Susan Collins won’t have the same clout in the next Congress
text:
Perhaps the best argument for returning Sen. Susan Collins to Washington is that it is clearly in Maine’s interest to have its senator chair the panel that decides how to divvy up billions of federal dollars each year.
As her campaign website says, “Susan’s position gives Maine an outsized voice at the table when critical decisions are made which allows her to deliver serious results for Maine,” and refers to the “the powerful Senate Appropriations Committee.”
Whether she wins or loses on Election Day, it’s likely Sen. Collins won’t be at the committee’s helm next year.
Nationally, Democrats are closing in on something few thought possible this election cycle: retaking control of the Senate. They’re virtually certain to control the U.S. House as well.
One of the consequences of having the Democrats in charge of the chamber is that every Senate committee will have a Democrat as its chair. Republicans, including Sen. Collins, will no longer enjoy the power that comes with being in the majority.
According to the Center for Politics at the University of Virginia, Democrats are poised to hold 49 seats with Republicans trailing with 46. Five seats are up in the air. Those seats are said to be in Maine, yes, as well as Iowa, Kansas, Ohio and Texas. Democrats need to win two of those five to take over the Senate while Republicans must win at least four.
Should Sen. Collins lose her seat, the math gets even tougher for the GOP. But let’s suppose she wins.
In that case, for Sen. Collins to remain in charge of appropriations her party would need to win three of the remaining four toss-up races. Possible, yes, but to me it seems unlikely.
For the group of voters trying to decide between Democrat Troy Jackson and Sen. Collins, why should this make any difference?
It matters because the strongest argument for Maine’s five-term incumbent is that she holds that position of rare clout on Capitol Hill. Without it, she surely can’t do as much for Maine.
That reality makes it easier for an undecided voter to choose Jackson. If Jackson wins, it would be a serious blow to President Donald Trump, who needs to recognize that he can’t simply ignore Congress and the laws of our nation.
The way I see it, Sen. Collins has demonstrated repeatedly that she is not up to the unique challenge of holding Trump in check. She knows what he is. She just hasn’t shown the gumption to stand up to him.
Whatever his faults, Jackson is tough and ornery enough to defy Trump and join every effort to block the president’s corrupt foolishness.
The leader of Senate Democrats, New York’s Chuck Schumer, told reporters recently that his party, back in power, would have two goals: to lower costs for Americans and “to clamp down on this horrible corruption and to end the chaos.”
I’m not sure why Sen. Collins and her GOP colleagues have failed to focus on the cost of living or reining in Trump and his erratic decisions. I have no doubt that most of them know it needs to be done. They just don’t have the guts to act.
As a result, they’re likely going to lose the Senate. And without a good reason to be sent back to Washington, Sen. Collins is likely going to lose the election.

title: In New Mexico governor’s race, Deb Haaland’s historic bid tests Democrats' political hold
text:
ALBUQUERQUE, N.M. (AP) — If Deb Haaland wins New Mexico’s race for governor this year, she’ll make history as the first Native American woman to lead a state.
But first she has to convince New Mexicans that they should keep Democrats in charge. The state persistently ranks near the bottom nationally on poverty, crime and public education, and disenchanted voters are pleading for change.
A loss would be embarrassing for Democrats, who hold all the top state offices and have controlled the Legislature nearly continuously for almost a century. Haaland blames President Donald Trump for compounding the state’s problems by cutting social programs that New Mexicans disproportionately rely on and increasing the cost of living by waging war against Iran. She proposes expanding existing tax credits and spending more on safety net programs to help families make ends meet.
Haaland, a citizen of Laguna Pueblo in west-central New Mexico, once relied on government assistance as a single mother. She rose through the ranks, serving in Congress for two years before being tapped as President Joe Biden’s interior secretary.
A victory in the governor’s race could elevate Haaland’s standing in the Democratic Party. The party recently named New Mexico as one of the earliest states for its next presidential primary, bolstering its prominence in national politics and ensuring more visits from White House hopefuls.
Gregg Hull, the Republican contender and a former mayor of fast-growing Rio Rancho, said New Mexico can no longer afford more of the same and is “primed for a shift.” If he wins, Hull promises to cut taxes, which he said will fight poverty by allowing people to keep more money in their pockets.
“I think the time has come to have a leader who is going to focus on the true solutions to these problems,” Hull said.
Haaland’s national star power meets Hull’s local pitch
Haaland has leveraged her national profile into a nearly $20 million campaign fund and endorsements from big Democratic names, including former President Barack Obama and former U.S. Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg.
U.S. Sen. Elizabeth Warren joined Haaland at an Albuquerque daycare center this week to read stories to preschoolers and promote New Mexico’s fledgling universal childcare program, which Haaland has pledged to preserve.
“I have known and worked with Deb Haaland for many years, and she is a fighter on behalf of opportunities for all of our children,” Warren said.
Hull, meanwhile, has emphasized his record leading Rio Rancho, a suburb of Albuquerque, through a period of fast economic growth. He says he would apply lessons from that experience to attract large employers to the state and boost workers’ incomes.
That pitch resonates with A.J. Rodriguez, a school security guard who lives in Edgewood and said local success means more to him than federal experience.
“I do like how he was running Rio Rancho,” Rodriguez said. “I liked his stance on crime.”
Soaring oil prices pad state coffers
New Mexico’s next governor will face stubborn challenges but also inherit a financial cushion that could be used to address them.
As the nation’s No. 2 oil-producing state, New Mexico has used record revenues over the years to build substantial budget reserves and multibillion-dollar permanent funds that help pay for schools and childcare. Higher energy prices stemming from the war with Iran have provided an additional boost.
In that windfall, Hull sees an opportunity to reduce New Mexicans’ tax burden. He has a plan to gradually phase out state income tax for all residents while reining in recent growth in state spending.
“If you want to raise people out of poverty, the best way to do that is to improve their personal wealth,” he said.
Haaland favors doubling down on free childcare and free college tuition and shoring up government assistance for healthcare and food after federal cuts under Trump. Once a supporter of the Green New Deal, a sweeping plan for transitioning away from fossil fuels to fight climate change, Haaland acknowledges the oil and gas industry’s role in funding New Mexico’s social safety net.
But she said the surging revenue comes at the cost of higher prices.
“I’m not happy about that because it’s caused people a lot of heartache,” Haaland said.
New Mexico voters focus on affordability
Chris Flores, a volunteer for Hull’s campaign, believes strongly in the candidate’s proposal to eliminate income tax, starting with the lowest income New Mexicans.
“I’ll be able to pay off the biggest debt that I’ve ever had,” said Flores, who lives in Albuquerque. She meant the student loans that have prevented her from fixing up her house and saving for retirement.
Rodriguez is skeptical of the tax break plan and wonders how the state will make up for lost income. Still, he says Democrats have “mismanaged” New Mexico’s persistent problems, and it’s time for a Republican to set the state’s political agenda.
Journeyman plumber Alfred Lujan blamed Republicans for rising prices, and said it costs him $150 to fill up his work truck with diesel. He said Haaland understands what it means to live on a tight budget.
“She’s had setbacks in her life and she’s come back from that,” the 47-year-old Albuquerque resident said. “That’s really what makes me gravitate toward her.”
At a campaign event in Gallup, Haaland’s celebrity status with some Native American voters was on display. She took selfies with students and accepted gifts of handmade jewelry and pottery from supporters.
Generita Francisco and Angela Bahe, both citizens of the Navajo Nation, were attracted to her pledge to help residents enroll in public health benefits. Both said they are priced out of the insurance market and forced to rely on Gallup’s aging and understaffed Indian Health Service hospital.
The two women, who left with autographs, have watched Haaland’s political rise with pride. But if she’s elected, they vowed to hold her to a high standard.
“Everything she’s promising, she needs to fulfill it,” Bahe said.

title: Study offers 'wake-up call' as it finds almost all coral reef ecosystems face risk of collapse
text:
Study provides 'wake-up call' as it finds almost all coral reef ecosystems face risk of collapse
The world’s coral reef ecosystems almost all face a high risk of collapse in the next 50 years, mostly due to warming oceans and heat waves, according to a global assessment released Thursday.
Related video above: Oceans hit record temperatures amid climate change and El Niño
The International Union for Conservation of Nature’s assessment, announced on the sidelines of a U.N. biodiversity conference in Albania, found that 96% of shallow-water reef systems are already critically endangered and could disappear by 2075.
Most of the world’s famous reef systems — including the Great Barrier Reef in Australia, the Coral Triangle in the Western Pacific Ocean and Southeast Asia, the Mesoamerican Barrier Reef System and the Red Sea coral reefs — are critically endangered, the highest level of threat.
“The risk of coral reef collapse is escalating, but this must be a wake-up call rather than a cause for despair," said Mishal Gudka, the scientific lead of the global IUCN Red List of Coral Reef Ecosystems assessment, the first of its kind.
“Coral reefs have shown a remarkable ability to bounce back from devastating bleaching events,” he said. “Pockets of surviving, resilient coral reefs can still remain in the future, so we must do everything within our reach to set them up for success.”
The assessment is the latest dose of bad news for coral reefs, which are critical sources for seafood and tourism and often serve as buffers from coastal erosion and storms. Sometimes dubbed “rainforests of the sea," they have some of the world's richest biodiversity. They support a quarter of marine species as well as coastal communities and businesses.
When a reef collapses, hard corals disappear and are replaced by algae, rubble and sponges. As a result, the reef no longer supports a diverse ecosystem that can include everything from tiny invertebrates to reef fish like grouper.
“Coral reefs are one of the clearest vital signs of the ocean’s health," Grethel Aguilar, the IUCN director general, said in a statement.
The assessment, spanning 127 tropical and subtropical ecoregions and encompassing 72,726 square miles of coral reefs globally, called climate change the “single most consistent threat driving coral reef decline worldwide.”
A week ago, another study in the journal Nature by the IUCN found that nearly 44% of reef-building coral species face an elevated risk of extinction due to climate change. A year ago, a survey found that harmful bleaching of the world’s coral has grown to include 84% of the ocean’s reefs — the most intense of its kind in recorded history.
2024 was Earth’s hottest year on record, and much of that is going into oceans. The average annual sea surface temperature of oceans away from the poles was a record 20.87 degrees Celsius (69.57 degrees Fahrenheit).
Beyond combatting rising global emissions, experts said efforts to reduce pollution, overfishing and coastal development can help reefs survive.
"We know what is needed: ambitious emissions reductions, stronger protection and restoration efforts, and sustained investment in resilient coastal ecosystems and the communities that depend on them,” Aguilar said.

title: Portland home and ‘Hopeful’ sign artist’s studio available for $899K
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Housing
This section of the BDN aims to help readers understand Maine’s housing crisis, the volatile real estate market and the public policy behind them. Read more Housing coverage here.
A mixed-use building and house tucked in a Portland neighborhood that now holds a renowned artist’s workshop is on the market for just shy of $900,000.
Located on Brentwood Street in Portland’s Deering Center neighborhood, the property includes a shop space closest to the street with greenhouses behind and adjacent to it. Then, an updated four-bedroom, four-bathroom house is tucked behind that.
“It looks like this unassuming little building when you drive by, but there’s a ton of space inside,” said Katie Brooke of Vitalius Real Estate Group, the listing agent for the property. “It’s a pitched roof, so there’s just lots of vertical space too.”
The commercial space and greenhouse previously held Dodge the Florist until the business closed in October 2021 after more than 100 years in business. For years the family lived in the house while operating the flower shop, according to Brooke.
Maine-based artist Charlie Hewitt bought the property — both the commercial space and home — in 2021 and converted the shop and greenhouse spaces into an art studio and workshop for himself. The space is now known as the Electric Greenhouse.
Though Hewitt is a multi-media artist, he’s perhaps best known for his work with lights and neon signs. He created the marquee-style “Hopeful” signs in 2019 that can now be found in communities around the state — including Bangor — and in states across the northeast.
“It’s a super unique and funky space and he has loved it,” Brooke said.
Hewitt is selling the property to consolidate his work into one studio in Lewiston, where he was born and raised, he said.
The sellers also gutted and renovated the house in 2022. The two-story space, which is now rented to local students, offers more than 2,500 square feet of living space as well as updated fixtures.
While the property is now a single-family house, it could easily be transformed into a two-unit with the first floor serving as an accessory dwelling or guest space, according to the listing.
The greenhouse and shop spaces were also updated to include new flooring, walls, roofing, heat pumps and solar panels. But, much of the original greenhouse roof remained in place to allow sunlight to stream in, Brooke said.
The building also still has a crank feature that controls vents in the ceiling that can be opened or closed. However, the older greenhouse ceiling does leak in some places, Brooke said.
“When it rains out you will get some puddles inside,” Brooke said. “That’s the sacrifice [Hewitt] wanted to make. He said, ‘The natural light is so good, I’m willing to sacrifice a few puddles.’”
The property sits on a roughly 10,000-square-foot lot with paved parking areas on both sides of the building.
The property, built in 1930, hit the market last week with an asking price of $899,000. The site has drawn the attention of several prospective buyers so far, Brooke said, many of whom have unique ideas for what the greenhouse could hold.
Proposals for the commercial space have ranged from a children’s recreational space to a woodworking shop, Brooke said. A buyer could also live in the home behind it, or continue operating it as a rental to offset the cost of the property.
“Everybody has an idea of what they’d want to do with the space,” she said. “It’s going to take a unique buyer with a unique vision to do what they want with it.”

title: New Pentagon directive bans troops from using nonpublic info to bet in prediction markets
text:
New Pentagon directive bans troops from using nonpublic info to bet in prediction markets
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has issued a new directive telling troops they cannot use "nonpublic information" to make bets on prediction markets.
"Our enemies watch movements in these markets," Hegseth wrote in a memo dated Tuesday and reviewed by The Associated Press. "When an American Service member, intelligence professional, or other Department civilian engages in a financial transaction on a military outcome, they create a signal."
The one-page document, which was reported earlier by CBS News, comes months after a U.S. Special Forces soldier involved in the military operation to capture then-Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro was charged with using classified information about the mission to win more than $400,000 on the prediction market Polymarket.
The memo stresses that troops are forbidden from using both classified and unclassified but nonpublic information to make trades on platforms like Polymarket and Kalshi. It says violators could be subject to administrative punishment and criminal charges under the Uniform Code of Military Justice or federal law.
"Beyond operational security, financial stakes can warp judgment," Hegseth said in the memo. "A logistician with money riding on a strike date has an interest in that date. An analyst with a position on an outcome has an interest in that outcome."
When asked about the new policy, a defense official said the Pentagon had no other information to offer beyond the memo.
In April, 38-year-old Master Sgt. Gannon Ken Van Dyke was charged by federal prosecutors and federal regulators with using his access as a Special Forces member to place a series of bets that totaled more than $32,500 on when Maduro might be removed from power.
According to the federal complaint in his case, he placed those bets between Dec. 30 and Jan. 2, with the vast majority occurring the night of Jan. 2 — just hours before the first missiles would fall on Caracas.
However, the issue of government officials and employees using their access to place bets on prediction markets is not confined to the Pentagon.
A group of new accounts on Polymarket made highly specific, well-timed bets on whether the U.S. and Iran would reach a ceasefire just before President Donald Trump announced it in April, resulting in hundreds of thousands of dollars in profits for the new customers. The White House warned staff against using private information to trade on prediction markets the same day the report came out.
Kalshi also fined and suspended three congressional candidates who the company said wagered on the outcome of their own elections in April.

title: The good, the bad, and the glitched when Mainers take tech abroad
text:
My wife, Connie, and I just returned from a three-week trip to New Zealand and Australia. Technology played a big part in our trip and we learned some things about tech in two countries a long way from the U.S.
A confession: I didn’t do as much preplanning as I should have done. Chris and Jill, my BoomerTECH Adventures colleagues, are experienced travelers and have written a number of articles that I should have reviewed before we left. We carried basic gear: our iPhones, laptops, earbuds and requisite chargers and cables. No extra power bricks, which airlines are very strict about, or portable chargers.
Why laptops for such a long trip? Even though this was a vacation, Connie needed to stay in touch with her job and my device of choice is always my laptop. So, even though our laptops added some extra weight to our carry-ons we appreciated having them and using hotel Wi-Fi to learn more about our travels.
To SIM or not to SIM … that was the question! Before we left home we signed up for an international travel plan for Connie’s phone while I decided that I didn’t need phone access every day. We considered installing SIM cards (which we have used on previous trips) but decided that since we were in two different countries for only a week each, we didn’t want to bother with the different phone numbers that come with SIM cards.
While the international travel plan was more expensive than a SIM card, the convenience of not having to mess with settings, toggle data lines, or fuss with digital installations while on vacation was worth the extra money, especially for our short trip in two countries. It was especially important for Connie, who needed to stay in contact with business contacts as well as our family.
Interestingly, the international travel plan for Connie’s phone, which we had signed up for before we left the U.S., did not work initially. Our first two hours in New Zealand were spent on the phone getting it straightened out. That was not so easy; we talked to an AI bot first and that was not helpful. The bot apologized several times for the poor phone connection we had but couldn’t solve our problems and eventually hung up on us! What was that about? We finally got a human being who stayed with us and we were passed up the ladder to at least three people trying to solve our problem. Eventually it got straightened out and the plan was added. I decided to do the same to my phone so we’d have some backup in case one phone didn’t work.
In retrospect, we should have let Connie use the international travel plan from our carrier and I should have used a SIM Card or an eSIM.
We used our phones everywhere and they worked great. Calls, email, and text and we stayed within the limits of calling time, had unlimited texts, and Google Maps directed us around New Zealand without fail.
How else did tech figure in our trip?
• I watched several YouTube videos (which were very helpful) before we left to get hints about driving on the left side of the road … my first time. Glad to report that except for some minor scraping on a one-lane bridge, I navigated the very narrow, winding New Zealand roads where drivers go very fast. And who thought it was a good idea to put the steering wheel on the right side of the car?
• Both New Zealand and Australia were cashless. We used our credit card exclusively for everything. Australian restaurants had you order and pay directly from a QR code on the table.
• Our phones were useful when we were on the move. To our surprise, we found one of Thomas Dambo’s giant trolls (in western Australia) like those at the Boothbay Botanical Gardens. In New Zealand we learned a great deal about Māori culture because we could read about it as we moved along.
• Wi-Fi worked smoothly throughout our stay everywhere except one hotel in Auckland. No matter what we tried — including borrowing a different charger — our devices refused to connect. When we returned to the hotel on our final night in New Zealand, we faced the exact same blackout, despite our gear working flawlessly everywhere else. Ultimately, unexpected tech glitches are just part of traveling on the go.
• On the flip side, technology delivered an unforgettable highlight during our visit to Fremantle’s Maritime Museum in Australia. The “Life on the Great Barrier Reef” virtual reality experience was nothing short of spectacular.
• Finally, don’t leave your chargers and cord behind as I did in Rotorua, New Zealand. Fortunately, when I checked with Gemini (AI), I found that my iPhone charger worked for my laptop just as well. It would just take longer. Suggestion — don’t put devices or cords in a nightstand drawer!
• One last highlight: We had our first ride in a Waymo in San Francisco. This self-driving car was smooth, safe, and comfortable. As Sebastian Thrun (former head of Google’s self-driving car project) said, “Future generations will find it astonishing that we let humans drive at all.”
Overall, our technology made navigating New Zealand and Australia smoother and more engaging. And when tech did occasionally fail us, we simply had to practice a little patience and roll with the punches.
BoomerTECH Adventures (boomertechadventures.com) helps boomers and older adults navigate the digital world with confidence and competence. Active boomers themselves, they use their backgrounds as Maine teachers to support individuals and groups with online courses through Maine Adult Education (tinyurl.com/BTAclasses) articles, videos and presentations to organizations upon request.

title: AOC tells voters Troy Jackson will get billionaire influence out of politics
text:
PORTLAND — Onstage at the State Theater, before a lively crowd, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez repeatedly said the best antidote to the influence of the ruling class in Washington would be to elect Troy Jackson to the U.S. Senate.
“They’ve been afraid of a waitress in the House, and a logger in the United States Senate,” Ocasio-Cortez said. “So they want to critique how he talks, how he looks, the way he says things. Because if you’re not one of them, they at least want you to act like you are.”
The New York congresswoman, one of the most prominent members of the Democratic Party’s progressive wing, came to Portland on Thursday — less than two weeks before voters will decide between Jackson and Sen. Susan Collins — for an event billed as a students vs. billionaires town hall.
“When you have someone like Troy go to the United States Senate and call everything for what it is, it disrupts and makes it harder for everyone to get away with all the glad-handing that goes on over there,” she said.
The latest polls show Jackson leading slightly in a tight race against Collins, a five-term incumbent.
For a bit more than an hour, Ocasio-Cortez and Jackson took questions from local high school and college students, tackling topics from AI regulation to student debt to rural labor and delivery centers. While Ocasio-Cortez did most of the talking, bringing the crowd to its feet several times, Jackson cemented his stances on healthcare, Immigration and Customs Enforcement and U.S. aid for Israel.
Jackson said his first actions — were Democrats to take back the Senate — would be repealing President Donald Trump’s signature One Big Beautiful Bill Act to restore billions in Medicaid funding, then to push for Medicare for All.
He called for no more “blank checks to (Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin) Netanyahu,” for the abolition of ICE, and for an end to stock trading by members of Congress.
In response to a question from a Portland High School student about pitching progressive policies like Medicare for All to more rural or conservative communities in Maine, Jackson said people would get on board if presented with the facts.
“I just think we have to get the greed out of our healthcare system,” Jackson said. “It’s just taking the time to explain to people that you’re not going to get bad insurance, you’re going to get awesome insurance, and that we can do it, just don’t let these billionaires tell us differently.”
Both Ocasio-Cortez and Jackson delivered hits on Collins, especially on her voting record and her personal finances. Ocasio-Cortez told audience member Leah Hurwitz, an advocate against the closure of rural labor and delivery units, that Collins paved the way for hundreds of billions in healthcare cuts around the country by supporting the procedural motion to advance the Big Beautiful Bill to the floor. (Collins later voted against the bill, and she’s argued her procedural vote did nothing to affect its eventual passage.)
Hurwitz had asked about what could be done to stop the loss of maternal healthcare centers in the state. She said after the event that Ocasio-Cortez’s answer was a good open-ended response, but she was looking for more concrete solutions to bring back delivery services to rural communities that have lost them. She had a baby about 11 months ago at Lincoln Hospital, who was born breech. That hospital’s birthing center is now set to close by the end of the year.
“I know better than most,” she said. “Minutes mattered in my situation”
In response to a Bowdoin student’s question about how Jackson would stay in touch with Mainers from Washington, he criticized Collins’ reluctance to hold town hall events in the state, calling it “a major failing” of her tenure.
“It’s no secret that I’ve changed my opinion on a number of major issues,” Jackson said, alluding to his history of, among other things, opposing abortion. “I was presented with people who had better information, really made me think critically about where I was, and that I wouldn’t have gotten if I wasn’t willing to take the hard questions, go out and hear from people.”
In a race that could be decided by a small number of moderate swing voters, Republicans have attacked Jackson for courting national progressive heroes like Ocasio-Cortez; Bernie Sanders, who attended a Lewiston rally earlier this month; and Elizabeth Warren, who was in Portland over the weekend at a No Kings protest.
The town hall came one day after Collins emphasized her bipartisan credentials by hosting former Democratic Sen. Joe Manchin of West Virginia for lunch at a Lewiston hot dog stand.
Manchin, an old friend of Collins’ who left the Democratic Party in 2024, emphasized to reporters after their meal that Collins is “the most independent-minded person” he has ever met and described her as not a “Trump senator.”
On Wednesday, Maine GOP Chairman Jim Deyermond held a news conference criticizing Ocasio-Cortez’s visit to the state and Jackson’s alliance with her.
“AOC is far outside the mainstream of Maine politics. She is very, very far left, ” Deyermond said. “And that’s who Jackson is campaigning with here in Maine.”
It didn’t take long for Ocasio-Cortez to point out that sentiment herself at Thursday’s event. There are a lot of consultants in Washington that would tell Jackson not to sit on a stage next her, she said.
“It takes a lot to say, ‘You know what, I know my people, I know who I am, and I’m going to do things my way,”‘ Ocasio-Cortez said. “So thank you, Troy.”
“Why wouldn’t I want to sit alongside of someone who just talked like that,” Jackson said a few minutes later, after Ocasio-Cortez gave an impassioned response about military spending and domestic affordability.

title: LePage casts ballot, Dunlap launches more attacks as CD2 candidates make final push
A Susan Collins campaign stop exposes Maine’s split between anger and exhaustion
text:
LEWISTON, Maine — Fernand Asselin didn’t want to talk about politics at first.
But he opened up after polishing off a pair of red snappers during a busy lunch hour at Simones’ Hot Dog Stand. Just hours earlier, U.S. Sen. Susan Collins and former West Virginia Sen. Joe Manchin had stopped at the retail politics mainstay amid a throng of supporters and reporters.
“I’m not for her 100%,” said Asselin, an 81-year-old retired Auburn firefighter, who agreed with Democratic nominee Troy Jackson’s core argument that Collins votes too often with President Donald Trump. “But I know I don’t want to see anyone else but her in the Senate. The left has gone way overboard.”
Asselin said Collins needs strong turnout to blunt a progressive movement that has embraced Jackson and Democrats nationally. He described them as too extreme and bordering on communist.
The visit was part of Collins’ reelection bus tour, 13 days before Election Day. It brought into focus the anger, enthusiasm and apathy that the tight race may hinge on. Several Simones’ patrons expressed disgust with increasingly bitter campaign ads — or politics in general — whether on Capitol Hill or in Augusta.
When a reporter apologized for holding a loud interview over the chatter, sizzling burgers and clattering dishes, one patron paying his check said, “I’m glad I missed it.”
“It’s more volatile,” co-owner Linda Simones, whose family has run the shop since 1908, said of the political environment. “People before, if they knew your points of view, they would be a little more accepting.”
Simones and her husband, Jimmy, are Republicans. Their daughter is a Collins staffer. She said the senator “works really hard for Mainers” and credited her and Manchin, a former Democrat who turned independent in his last year in the Senate for “working with both sides.”
Outside, Democratic protesters who had learned of the visit, which wasn’t announced publicly, held “Retire Collins” signs and cutouts of U.S. Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh’s face. They accused the incumbent of corruption and said she paved the way for health care cuts, the overturning of federal abortion rights and deadly immigration enforcement.
“She is absolutely complicit,” said Michelle Barajas, a 56-year-old retired health care worker. “I’ve never been more angry. We have fewer rights than our grandmothers did? It’s baffling.”
Barajas added that it was “mind-blowing” the race appeared to be neck and neck.
Holly Sysko, a retired state worker from Lewiston who previously voted for Collins, said Jackson is a strong alternative. She alluded to his past opposition to abortion rights, which he has since said was wrong.
“There’s things he’s been challenged on, things he’s changed his mind on over the years … that shows you’re listening to people,” Sysko said.
When Collins and Manchin took questions from a crush of reporters, her red-shirted supporters chanted her name to drown out the protesters until Collins asked her team to quiet them so she could hear. She renewed her calls to ease tariffs on Canada and said a Senate Leadership Fund radio ad mocking Jackson’s family should come off the air.
Simones said patrons still get a kick out of the famous figures who stop by, though some visits have sparked frustration or even boycotts. She takes pride that almost all of the Democrats and Republicans in this year’s gubernatorial primaries came in.
She pointed to two signatures in her guest book as a sign of hope for bipartisanship: Donald Trump Jr. and Maine author Stephen King, a proud Democrat.
“Both ends of the spectrum,” she said. “Politics is part of our life, it’s not all of it.”

title: Scarborough, Old Orchard Beach to vote on $12.4M radio upgrades
text:
Scarborough, Old Orchard Beach residents to vote on $12.4 million radio upgrades
Scarborough and Old Orchard Beach residents are voting on an emergency communications radio referendum in the midterm election. The joint project to replace the current radio system is estimated to cost $12.4 million.
Scarborough voters are being asked to approve up to $6 million in bonds. Old Orchard Beach voters are being asked to approve $3.2 million in spending. Scarborough town officials are working with Sen. Angus King to secure federal grants that will cover the remaining $3.2 million.
The town of Scarborough currently provides emergency dispatch services for both towns, but Emergency Communications Director Joseph Thornton is concerned the existing radio infrastructure for the 150-megahertz analog VHF system is at risk of failing.
"We squeaked out the last five years, basically," Thornton said. "We’re at a point where we’re in danger minute by minute of our system failing completely."
Thornton said it's been challenging to find the parts needed to make repairs to the 1950s-era technology. He also recalled several instances when first responders could not communicate with dispatch and other first responders due to "dead zones" where radio transmissions are blocked.
There has also been trouble communicating with other towns.
"All the areas and all the communities around us have switched to a digital 800-megahertz system, and that puts us on an island," Thornton said. "We can't communicate, and as everyone knows, we rely very heavily, particularly in Southern Maine, on mutual aid."
A study conducted by an external, New Hampshire-based consulting group suggested the switch to a digital system to address those concerns. The new radio system would also connect first responders to other departments in both towns, including public works, community services, recreation, lifeguards, the sanitary district, wastewater and schools.
“I wish we lived in a world where we didn’t have to worry about issues or problems at schools," Thornton said. "Our officers and police officers can’t communicate with staff in the school, and they can’t communicate with each other inside the school.”
Town officials intend for the new, streamlined network to improve interoperability.
Scarborough and Old Orchard Beach residents will vote on the funding for this project separately. If the referendum passes in only one town, the project can still be completed on a smaller scale individually.
Thornton lives in Scarborough and understands concerns about raising taxes, but he is hopeful voters in both towns will support the referendum. “I think we’re at a point where we can’t wait anymore," he said.
On Saturday, Oct. 24, residents are invited to speak with Scarborough town councilors about the project at the public safety building from 10:30 a.m. to noon. Public safety staff will be on-site to answer questions as well.
Scarborough officials are hosting a public information session from 6 to 7 p.m. Monday, Oct. 26, at the public safety building. That session will be livestreamed.
Election Day is Tuesday, Nov. 3. Early voting is underway.

title: From Scotland to Bates: Meet New Women’s Soccer Coach Jonny Macadam
text:
A soccer fan and player from his very first steps, Jonny Macadam is now stepping into the role of Head Coach for women’s soccer. Facing this next chapter of his soccer career, he holds high hopes for the season and for the team.
Soccer History
Growing up in Scotland with a family of soccer fans, it’s no surprise that Macadam ended up on the field. A stone’s throw from the soccer hub of the world, he was exposed to the love of the game from a young age and never outgrew it. According to Macadam, he was “playing pretty much as soon as [he] could walk.”
Macadam’s fervor persisted for years until, fresh out of secondary school, he had to make a choice—staying in Scotland meant either pursuing a degree or becoming a full-time soccer player, not both. He turned his eyes elsewhere, in search of someplace he could expand his academic education while keeping a foot on the field.
With some help from friends among d others who’d sought out the same experience, Macadam found his way to Des Moines, Iowa, and onto the men’s National Association of Intercollegiate Athletics (NAIA) soccer team at Grand View University, where he would go on to earn a spot in the NAIA 2013 Third All-America’s Team roster.
As he made his way through college, Macadam planned to return to Scotland after schooling, but he wasn’t quite ready to let the sport go, a feeling many athletes experience. As retirement arose on the horizon, the chance to train others in the sport sent his plan in another direction, providing a path that kept him connected into professional life.
Luckily for Macadam, he wouldn’t be saying goodbye to his sport just yet. After a few coaching classes, Macadam found another facet of the sport to love, and he realised he would never have to stray far from soccer.
As a coach, Macadam found his way to Bridgeport, where he helped the team to multiple championships, from state-wide to national; Fairfield, as a volunteer for a season; and Fordham, where he helped elevate the team up in the Atlantic 10 Conference and saw some of the highest stats the team had seen in decades, before making his way to Bates.
Why Bates soccer?
Macadam was in love with Bates from his first visit. At first, Bates wasn’t heavy on his radar. Despite his unfamiliarity with the school, he decided to approach the opportunity with an open mind and “left the interview really wanting the job,” he recalls.
One of Macadam’s largest coaching philosophies is individuality. He wants every player to be themself, whether in personality or playing style, a lesson he learned early on in his coaching career, and one which he hopes to instill in all his athletes. Much like Bates as a whole, the soccer team is a conglomeration of people, backgrounds, and interests, and Macadam believes it’s his job to “try and get them all to manage and play together.”
Rather than try the one-play-fits-all approach, Macadam is determined to “focus on the players that we have and then try to maximise.” This mentality persists in his coaching—Macadam doesn’t believe in a single coaching strategy, but rather adjusts his coaching style to match the athletes he has in front of him.
Looking Forward
Macadam hopes to rally the team and take Bates soccer far. To him, every game is a learning opportunity, whether they win or lose, and he aims to take advantage of every one. He’s proud of what the team has done so far, in that “they bring it every day, every session, [and] they want to get better,” and he knows that both they and he will keep working hard to move up in the NESCAC.

title: The Latest: Many states deciding control of the Senate are seeing a big boost in early voting
text:
Voter turnout is soaring compared with the last midterm election in many of the states that are expected to decide control of the U.S. Senate, according to an Associated Press analysis of early voting two weeks before Election Day.
Advocates for greater voter identification requirements are pursuing a new approach in some states: a mandate to place driver’s license or partial Social Security numbers on mail-in ballots. Variations of the voter ID proposals are being decided in the midterm elections in California, Colorado and Nevada — three states where conservative activists collected petition signatures to bypass Democratic-led legislatures and place the issue directly before voters.
The Trump administration moved Wednesday to end its legal fight to overhaul a popular student loan forgiveness program. The Department of Justice appealed after federal judges ruled in June in favor of advocates who said the Public Service Loan Forgiveness program risked becoming a tool for political retribution. But it dropped two appeals Wednesday in single-sentence joint agreements, which stipulated that each side would pay its own fees.
Here’s the latest:
Ashley Hinson shows Republicans’ midterm balancing act as Trump heads to Iowa to boost turnout
Iowa’s Republican nominee for U.S. Senate is navigating a tricky political landscape. Ashley Hinson promises to support Trump when it benefits Iowa but also vows to push back when necessary.
Although many Republicans are walking a political tightrope in this year’s midterm elections, Hinson’s balancing act is more challenging than most. Iowans have been hamstrung by manufacturing job losses, healthcare clinic closures and shrunken farm profits since Trump returned to the White House, but Hinson is also relying on the president’s loyalists to show up for her.
On Thursday, Hinson will join Trump for a rally in Sioux City, which is in Iowa’s conservative northwest corner. The visit to safe territory is geared toward boosting turnout even as it ties her more tightly to an unpopular president.
Trump is expected to visit the state again Nov. 1. He is “anxious for Iowans to hear his message before they vote,” Iowa Republican Party Chair Jeff Kaufmann said in announcing the president’s schedule.
Transgender healthcare case to continue after Supreme Court loss
The Trump administration plans to keep pressing to enforce restrictions on healthcare for transgender people in federal prison after a loss on the Supreme Court’s emergency docket.
A Justice Department spokesperson expressed disappointment with the high court’s Wednesday decision but pointed out that the justices have not made a final ruling.
Lower courts have blocked enforcement of the policy, which would halt surgeries, taper off hormones and end social accommodations like makeup and wigs.
The Trump administration had filed an emergency appeal asking the Supreme Court to intervene, but the justices declined. The government can continue to appeal through lower courts.
Wisconsin Republican Tiffany says Zuckerberg money was the reason he tried to overturn 2020 election
The Republican candidate for Wisconsin governor who supported Trump’s attempts to overturn his 2020 loss in the battleground state said Wednesday he did it because of concerns about election funding from Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg.
“One of the reasons that I did that is ’ Zuckerbucks,’” U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany said in a debate, using a term coined by opponents of the money.
Tiffany also said he opposed certifying Wisconsin’s election results because clerks in Milwaukee and Dane counties advised voters they could claim to be “indefinitely confined” due to the COVID-19 pandemic and receive absentee ballots without showing a photo ID.
More than 200 communities across Wisconsin received about $10 million in grants from the Zuckerberg-funded Center for Tech and Civic Life to help run elections during the pandemic.
The debate exchange was an example of how Trump’s false claims about election fraud and his attempt to prevent Joe Biden from taking office continue to ripple through American politics.
AP-NORC Poll: Most MAGA Republicans want Congress to support Trump
Republicans are broadly aligned on what they want the next Congress to do — except when it comes to Trump, the new AP-NORC poll shows.
At least half of Republicans who identify as supporters of MAGA and non-MAGA Republicans want leaders to lower costs, end the Iran war and reduce the federal budget deficit.
But while about 6 in 10 MAGA Republicans want Congress to prioritize supporting the Trump administration’s agenda, only about 2 in 10 Republicans who are not supporters of MAGA say the same.
Lisa Ostlund, a 46-year-old from Massachusetts who identifies as a MAGA supporter, wants the next Congress to prioritize Trump’s agenda. She doesn’t support everything Trump does, but she credits his policies with her recent ability to find housing after struggling with homelessness.
“You got to care about your American people,” Ostlund said. “He definitely doesn’t say it right, but you do have to put them first.”
AP-NORC Poll: Democratic socialists want Congress to investigate Trump
There may be schisms awaiting the Democratic Party if they win a governing majority in November, the new AP-NORC poll finds.
About three-quarters of registered voters who identify as democratic socialists say investigating the Trump administration should be one of Congress’ top priorities, compared with slightly fewer than half of Democrats who do not align with democratic socialism.
Democratic socialists are also more likely to want to end military aid to Israel and less likely to say it’s a top priority to find common ground between the two parties.
Justin Campbell, a 31-year-old Democrat in Mississippi who identifies as a democratic socialist, wants Congress to hold the Trump administration accountable.
“It feels a little cliché to just say roll back the past two years, but honestly, mostly just roll back the stuff he’s done the past two years,” Campbell said.
AP-NORC Poll: Voters want the next Congress to focus on costs and ending the Iran war
Voters from both parties want the next Congress to focus on making life more affordable and ending the war in Iran, while fewer are looking for an emphasis on Trump — whether it’s investigating him or supporting his agenda.
The results from a new AP-NORC poll suggest that voters are ready for Congress to tackle core issues, despite Trump’s central role in the midterm campaign.
About 8 in 10 registered voters, including most Republicans and Democrats, say lowering the cost of living should be “one of the highest priorities.”
Most voters also want Congress to prioritize ending the war with Iran, with roughly 7 in 10 saying this should be a top focus. Substantially fewer voters — about 4 in 10 — want Congress to make investigating the Trump administration a high priority, and only about 2 in 10 want Congress to prioritize supporting Trump’s agenda.
Vance says Republicans shouldn’t complain about Ramaswamy ad featuring Amy Acton’s estranged mother
Vice President JD Vance defended an ad Wednesday by Vivek Ramaswamy that features the estranged mother of Dr. Amy Acton, his Democratic opponent for Ohio governor, and spotlights the abuse she experienced as a child, even as the Republican in a tight race to retain Vance’s former seat in the Senate distanced himself from the ad.
During a campaign visit to Ohio, Vance told reporters he was “disgusted” by fellow Republicans who were pushing back against the ad, then later drew cheers at a political rally when he defended Ramaswamy, a biotech billionaire and 2024 presidential candidate.
Vance said he has watched Democrats “throw every dirty trick in the political book at Vivek,” who he considers a close personal friend — including calling him a ‘murderer’ — while “the whole time Vivek has stood tall and talked about what he wants to accomplish.”
“I would not have run that ad,” U.S. Sen. Jon Husted said in a statement to The Associated Press. A day earlier, his Democratic opponent, former Sen. Sherrod Brown, called the spot “disgusting” and said everybody — including Husted — should denounce it.
In final Michigan Senate debate, El-Sayed and Rogers question each other’s loyalties
Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers clashed in their final Senate debate Wednesday, with El-Sayed trying to tie his opponent to Trump and Rogers saying his rival’s progressive policies would be too extreme for Michigan.
The debate kicked off a breakneck final stretch in one of the nation’s most closely watched and competitive Senate races. Former President Barack Obama will rally in Detroit on Saturday, followed by Trump on Sunday.
Wednesday’s hourlong debate followed one on Oct. 8 that devolved into personal insults and attacks, with the candidates continuing to argue even during a commercial break. This time, the exchanges were slightly less contentious and focused on policy, though both candidates repeatedly returned to their central attacks.
The most contentious exchange came when Rogers again tried to link El-Sayed to the Muslim Brotherhood, repeating an allegation he and Trump have raised in recent weeks. El-Sayed has denied any affiliation with the group.
Jeffries says Democrats ‘on the verge’ of winning the House. It puts the Speaker’s gavel in reach
Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries listened from the front row at the old Ohio church as the Sunday congregation heard of scripture’s guidance for calming a gathering storm.
“Wind, hush!” the speaker advised, describing the power to bring about change.
Jeffries nodded along, the words resonating beyond the church’s soaring brick walls, days out from the midterm elections that will determine control of Congress for the remainder of Trump’s term in the White House.
“We’re on the verge of taking back control of the House,” Jeffries told The Associated Press in an interview afterward.
Jeffries is on track to become House speaker, if Democrats sweep to power and elect him to the job, one of the most powerful positions in the U.S., second in line to the presidency. He has been campaigning across the country in more than 50 cities for House Democrats as they try to oust Republicans and win back majority control.
Trump administration drops legal fight to overhaul student loan forgiveness program
The Trump administration moved Wednesday to end its legal fight to overhaul a popular student loan forgiveness program.
The Department of Justice appealed after federal judges ruled in June in favor of advocates who said the Public Service Loan Forgiveness program risked becoming a tool for political retribution. But it dropped two appeals Wednesday in single-sentence joint agreements, which stipulated that each side would pay its own fees.
Federal officials provided no explanation, but advocates praised the ruling.
“The Trump administration’s attempt to weaponize public service loan forgiveness against organizations it disagrees with was anti-democratic and unlawful from the start,” Dan Zibel, an attorney for the group Student Defense, said in a written statement. “This is a significant victory for millions of Americans who have dedicated their careers to public service.”
Voting-related measures on November ballots include a voter ID push targeting mail-in ballots
Advocates for greater voter identification requirements are pursuing a new approach in some states: a mandate to place driver’s license or partial Social Security numbers on mail-in ballots.
Variations of the voter ID proposals are being decided in the midterm elections in California, Colorado and Nevada — three states where conservative activists collected petition signatures to bypass Democratic-led legislatures and place the issue directly before voters.
The voter ID measures are among about 30 questions on November ballots affecting state policies on voting and elections. They account for roughly 1 in 5 of all state ballot measures nationwide. Some mirror policies that President Donald Trump has pushed unsuccessfully at the national level and build off a Republican narrative that noncitizen voting is a problem, though data indicates it is rare.
Several measures address changes to congressional voting districts, as part of a national redistricting battle spurred by Trump. Others could change the way primaries are conducted, make it more difficult for voters to amend their state constitutions or — in Missouri — make it harder for lawmakers to change measures that voters approve.
Many states deciding control of the Senate are seeing a big boost in early voting, AP analysis shows
Voter turnout is soaring compared with the last midterm election in many of the states that are expected to decide control of the U.S. Senate, according to an Associated Press analysis of early voting two weeks before Election Day.
In Texas, early voting is up 74% compared with 2022. In Kansas it’s more than doubled. Maine, North Carolina and Ohio also have seen increases of more than 30% in early in-person and mail voting compared with the same point in 2022.
Democrats are trying to flip Republican-held Senate seats in each of those states. In most of them, Republicans are accounting for a smaller share of advance voters than they did four years ago.
The AP’s data, which runs through Tuesday, gives a snapshot of potential voter enthusiasm — and where it might be lacking — after early voting has opened in most states during a midterm cycle that has shifted in often unpredictable ways.

title: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
text:
(Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep.
Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.”
The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening.
Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.”
The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before next weekend’s time change.
