title: She survived a school shooting. Now her children have, too
text:
She survived a school shooting. Now her children have, too
"Mom, there's a shooter," Michelle's fifth grader said through the phone.
Something about her son's serious tone was familiar.
"If you've ever gotten a call that a loved one passed away … that kind of tone," Michelle explained.
The 40-year-old mother would later compare it to the sound of her principal's voice echoing through the loudspeaker 25 years ago: "Lockdown! Lockdown!"
When she was in ninth grade, a former classmate opened fire at her high school in El Cajon, California.
Like then, she immediately knew in her gut the situation was serious.
And Michelle was right. A former student had just shot through the glass doors of her son's school, Silver Rail Elementary in Bend, Oregon, and opened fire on a special needs classroom, killing a beloved teacher and three students.
CNN has agreed to withhold Michelle's last name and the names of her family members for privacy concerns.
Michelle told her son that she loved him, but that he needed to hang up immediately and remain quiet while she called 911.
As a school shooting survivor herself, she knew the importance of her son staying silent and not alerting the shooter to his location, she said.
She immediately fled the Olive Garden where she and her mother had been eating lunch and called 911 as she ran, her mother trailing behind her. Emergency operators in Bend always answered immediately in her experience – but that didn't happen this time.
"It was just ringing, ringing, ringing, and nobody was picking up," she said.
No response bred panic
Police cars and firetrucks crowded the streets as Michelle neared the school. Alarmed parents followed closely as she ran up to Silver Rail Elementary.
"What's going on? Is someone hurt?" she frantically asked parents and police officers when she reached the front of the school. The police informed them that the shooter was dead, though this offered little relief.
Michelle saw a kindergarten class sitting on the ground near the teacher's parking lot. "They were all crying, which was really hard to see because they are tiny," she said.
Even though Michelle had heard from her fifth grader, her mind raced with thoughts of her first grade son who remained inside the school. She texted her first grader's teacher, but didn't get a response, sending her "panic to 100."
She had no other way to reach him.
Memories from her own experience of the shooting at Granite Hills High School in 2001 crept into her thoughts, including brief recollections of the shooter, a boy she had sat next to in physics class. But these flashbacks were overtaken quickly by the thoughts of her own children in their classrooms.
Were they safe? What did they see? On a loop, her brain replayed, "It was your kid who was shot."
Last Thursday "was just honestly the worst day of my life, much worse than when I actually went through it myself as a child," she said.
At one point, she had to sit down on the pavement at her sons' elementary school as she grew faint from the overwhelming emotions.
Lightning strikes twice
Michelle's husband, alerted by her mother on the drive over from the restaurant, had arrived at the school, and the family was redirected to Journey Church, where authorities sent families to be reunited with their children.
As petrified parents filed into the warehouse-like church nestled in a strip mall and took seats on folding chairs, Michelle noticed a woman near the front, sitting alone. The woman's cell phone rang. She answered the call, and soon broke down in tears, collapsing out of her chair. Other parents rushed to comfort her. Inferring what news the woman had likely learned on that call, Michelle stared at the dark screen of her own phone for the next three hours, praying it wouldn't ring.
Later that day, a childhood friend reminded Michelle of her own reunification process decades earlier. After the SWAT team methodically cleared each room, she and her classmates were let out in a single-file line with their hands over their heads to a park where parents waited. All the kids around her were screaming "mom" and "dad," so Michelle screamed her mother's full name to stand out in the crowd and find her mom.
"How can lightning strike twice? How can I go through this and then my children go through this?" she asked.
Knowing her oldest was safe, Michelle and her husband texted their fifth grader to see if he had seen his little brother. Communicating through the tiny screen on his Apple Watch, he said he had. Michelle asked her son again, to which he answered his brother was alive, but Michelle's thoughts still spiraled.
"What if he saw a kid in a blue shirt and thought it was (him)? I was still worried," she said.
Finally, after three grueling hours waiting in the church, Michelle was reunited with her two sons. Her oldest heard the gunshots and the sound of people screaming in the school. As she picked him up and gave him a hug, the first thing he said, through tears, was "Mom, can I be homeschooled? I never want to go in that school again."
Some hours after the shooting in the safety of their home, adrenaline waning, Michelle's mother turned to her and said she better call the Olive Garden to pay the bill they ran out on.
"Mom, I think Olive Garden is gonna be OK," replied Michelle.
Enduring trauma
Later that evening, Michelle spotted her 11-year-old on his iPad reading a news headline that several people had died at his school.
For the first time, she told her son about her own survival story.
"This happened to you?" he asked, his eyes wide, and wondered if anyone had died at her high school.
Three students and two teachers were wounded in the shooting at Granite Hills, but no one was killed.
Michelle reassured her son, but he didn't want to talk about the incident. She told him she would be there to talk when he was ready.
In 2001, Michelle remembers hiding under her desk and hearing helicopters circling over her school. After roughly an hour, when the shooting was believed to be over, but still locked down in their classroom, her teacher put on a movie to pass the time. It was "The Karate Kid." Then, cell phones were rare among students. Michelle recalls her teacher letting students use his computer to email their parents while they waited.
During a work-related meeting this past Monday, Michelle kept thinking of the 18-year-old shooter from her high school. The recurring image of his face clouded her thoughts while she tried to focus.
For Michelle, the trauma of enduring a school shooting has meant never feeling safe in her school or in public spaces again, finding herself always looking for the nearest exit in case of emergency, and later developing panic attacks. Well before last week's shooting, she said she got a pit in her stomach every time she dropped her children off at school, which she previously chalked up to anxiety and her own trauma.
"What if that was just intuition? And I think that's probably pretty ridiculous. But like, I was just in shock," she said.
Now her son seems to be facing similar feelings of dread at the thought of public spaces. The Red Cross and other organizations held a gathering over the weekend for Silver Rail students and families.
"I don't want to go, because what if a terrorist comes and shoots us all?" her fifth grade son told Michelle. They did not attend the event.
Though they're not using many words to talk about what they witnessed that day, comments like these from her oldest, along with her youngest cuddling her "like a baby," illustrate her children's struggles, Michelle said.
Avoiding the school
Michelle doesn't see a path forward at the elementary school at this point and is seriously thinking about homeschooling both of her boys, and says other parents are considering the same.
"I feel like it happened to me twice. Who's to say it's not going to happen a third time?" Michelle said.
In the week since the shooting, she now avoids driving near Silver Rail and opts for different roads instead. She did go to the makeshift memorial on Saturday to put down flowers but tried not to look too closely at the school.
She said seeing the building brought back flashbacks of the excruciating helplessness she felt running up to the school last week but not being allowed inside, which triggered memories of desperately searching for her own parents in a crowd in 2001.
Earlier this week, at a secure FBI location, Michelle retrieved the belongings her children left behind at the school. The process for picking up the items was very well-organized and offered comfort items like therapy dogs, stuffed animals and snacks. Michelle told the FBI agent that they didn't have anything like this after her experience in a school shooting.
"And then (the agent) kind of said to me, 'Unfortunately, we've had 25 years to perfect this process.'"
Baby steps forward
But her family is also taking small steps toward healing, each processing the incident in their own way.
On Sunday, Michelle invited a therapist to their home to chat with her boys.
With the therapist and his mom present, Michelle's 11-year-old finally started to open up about some of the questions on his mind. "Why did this happen?" he asked.
He also wanted to know who the victims were. After they told him, he got his yearbook out and looked at their pictures and explained some of his memories with them. Then he sat in front of the TV, the yearbook still in his hands, for "quite a while," Michelle said.
He left the house on Monday for the first time since the shooting to get his favorite ice cream.
Michelle's husband visited the memorial Monday night, after the kids were asleep, and found himself praying and processing his own grief surrounding the tragedy.
The family has set up a "free toys and books" bin in their yard where neighborhood kids could grab sensory toys and books, with a friend ordering books tailored to help children process this kind of traumatic event.
Her youngest rode bikes with some friends in the neighborhood and asked his mom to schedule playdates.
Michelle is working to cope with the recurring U.S. epidemic of gun violence on school campuses. In the meantime, she's focused on reassuring her boys.
"I went through this. I'm OK. You'll be OK," she told them.

title: Jordan Elliott was released by Titans after pulling out gun in parking lot, coach Robert Saleh says
text:
Jordan Elliott was released by Titans after pulling out gun in parking lot, coach Robert Saleh says
Tennessee Titans coach Robert Saleh confirmed Wednesday that defensive tackle Jordan Elliott was released after pulling a gun in the parking lot of the team facility but said it was a "terrible lapse in judgment that I recognize as a call for help more than a criminal act."
The Titans had announced Tuesday that Elliott was released, saying only that it came after his involvement in an unspecified incident at the team's facility five days earlier.
A person briefed on the incident told The Associated Press on Wednesday that Elliott had a gun in his car and went to the parking lot to retrieve it after a dispute with another player. The person spoke to the AP on condition of anonymity because the incident is being reviewed.
Elliott's agent, Malki Kawa, could not be reached for comment.
The NFL prohibits league personnel from taking a firearm to club facilities, stadiums and team hotels and on team planes or buses.
The Titans promptly notified the league of the incident involving Elliott, which is being reviewed, the NFL said.
Speaking to reporters, Saleh defended Jordan's character.
"Unfortunately, rules are rules with regard to guns on property, and sometimes it's far greater than the knee-jerk reaction of kicking somebody when they're down," the coach said.
"He's a good man. Made a terrible, had a terrible lapse in judgment that I recognize as a call for help more than a criminal act," Saleh added. "He's never committed a crime in his entire life and he pulled a gun, in the parking lot."
Right tackle JC Latham, who was involved in the altercation with Elliott on the practice field, called the episode an unfortunate situation.
"I don't really have too much to say about it," Latham said Wednesday. "There ain't never been no bad blood between us two. We were here on the summer getting treatment. Before that, we hung out whenever we were in the same city together. We actually had never had an argument leading up to it."
Elliott appeared in five games this season with one start and had 11 tackles. He followed Saleh to Nashville after a two-year stint with the San Francisco 49ers, where he played in 31 games with 29 starts.
The 6-foot-4 defensive tackle was selected by the Cleveland Browns in the third round of the 2020 draft. He spent his first four seasons in Cleveland before signing a two-year, $7 million deal with San Francisco.
Tennessee added him as a free agent in the offseason on a two-year, $8 million deal.
___
AP Pro Football Writer Rob Maaddi in Tampa, Florida, contributed to this report.

title: Children remain at risk from gun violence, not transgender people
text:
The BDN Editorial Board operates independently from the newsroom, and does not set policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com.
Republicans, including President Donald Trump, want you to fear that schools are secretly sending children away for gender-reassignment surgery. This is ludicrous. Yet, campaigns across the country are spending millions of dollars to spread this fallacious fear and other trangender hate.
What is happening is that children continue to be gunned down in American schools. Last week, three students and a teacher were killed in Bend, Oregon. The suspected shooter, a 16-year-old former student of the elementary school, who received the gun as a birthday gift from his mother, was killed by a father of children at the school. It was the 52nd school shooting in the U.S. this year.
Gun violence has received little attention this year as control of Congress — and hence the power of Trump — is up for grabs. That is too bad, because gun violence continues to claim far too many lives in America and, as we’ve seen in Maine, there are actions to take that can reduce this violence, while respecting constitutional rights.
Sunday marks the third anniversary of the horrific shooting in Lewiston that claimed 18 lives, injured 13 and reshaped countless lives. In the wake of that tragedy, state leaders, led by Gov. Janet Mills, reconsidered their positions and came together to tackle gun violence, and to improve mental health services. The state’s existing yellow flag law, which was rarely used before the Lewiston tragedy, was strengthened and it has been used much more frequently. Voters later approved a red flag law, allowing family members to petition to remove guns from those they considered a danger to themselves or to others.
Those measures, known officially as extreme risk protection orders, are working. The Maine Attorney General’s Office reports that Maine’s yellow flag law has been used more than 1,600 times since it went into effect in July 2020. Use of the law to disarm people threatening harm to themselves or others has increased markedly since the Lewiston shooting in 2023. Deaths by suicide have been prevented, as recently as this week. Homicides have been stopped.
The newer red flag law, which went into effect this year, has been used five times, The Maine Monitor reported. Three requests under the new law were denied as of late August.
In 2024, Gov. Mills allowed a 72-hour waiting period for gun purchases to become law. The law was quickly challenged in court by gun rights groups. Earlier this week, the U.S. Supreme Court declined to consider the case, leaving in place a lower court ruling upholding the constitutionality of the waiting period. Further court proceedings remain. Research has shown that waiting periods can reduce suicides, homicides and intimate partner violence using guns.
As we remember the victims and survivors of the Lewiston shooting, and their families and friends, we can be proud that Maine acted quickly to avert another such horrible tragedy. The law changes enacted by the Legislature and by the people of Maine have saved lives, while upholding constitutional rights. But, we also know that there is more work to do to keep all Mainers, especially our children, safe from gun violence.
To reach a suicide prevention hotline, call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org.

title: At Cadillac Mountain, a missing Wabanaki marker and the fight over what national parks should tell
text:
BAR HARBOR, Maine (AP) — In the soft light of dawn, an Ohio tourist studied the interpretive sign at the summit of Cadillac Mountain in Acadia National Park, reading about how magma formed the ground under her feet.
There is one sign she and the other 4 million-plus tourists who visit Acadia annually can no longer see at the summit: a marker explaining the mountain’s sacred significance to the Wabanaki people in the region. “Today, visitors from everywhere find meaning on the mountain,” it said.
It was among 30 markers removed from Acadia under a Trump administration campaign to strip national parks of materials deemed disparaging to American history, according to the National Parks Conservation Association.
But when park staff took down the summit sign at the orders of Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, they also unraveled some of the trust that took decades to build between Acadia National Park and the Wabanaki people. The Wabanaki Confederacy, also known as “the people of the dawnland,” has inhabited the northern seaboard for over 10,000 years and was the first known stewards of land that includes much of the national park. It was a gathering place to trade, hunt, fish and pick sweetgrass.
Some of the signs removed from Acadia were developed over years of partnerships with organizations including Friends of Acadia, the Schoodic Institute and the Native Plant Trust — with consultation from citizens of the Wabanaki Nations. They know the mountain in Maine as Wapuwoc — “white mountain of the first light.” From October to March, it’s the first place to see the sunrise in the continental United States.
“Getting to a place where our language is in these parks and it is educational … erasing that or setting that back has big implications for how far we’ve come,” said Maulian Bryant, the Wabanaki Alliance’s executive director.
Bryant says the removed signs reflected “the good stuff.”
“These signs don’t say 96% of Wabanaki people died from smallpox, or there were 26 nations and now there’s four,” she said. “If we really want to get into the real history, that’s a whole other slice of cake.”
Other signs removed from Cadillac’s summit addressed issues of climate change, informing visitors that “Acadia’s future will be warmer and wetter” and that “In the last century, average annual precipitation has increased by six inches.”
During their tenure under the Biden administration, former National Park Service director Chuck Sams and former Interior Secretary Deb Haaland — the first Native Americans to hold these positions — aimed to reflect the experiences of all Americans throughout the national parks. Before leaving his post in February 2025, Sams saw parts of his work unraveled by the current administration.
This “attempt to rewrite history into a single narrative … is also counter to our democracy. And counter to the idea that we are a plural nation,” said Sams.
Lawsuit against national park removals advances
Now, a coalition of conservation, history and science organizations are fighting in court to get the Acadia signs and hundreds of other items put back. Under Burgum’s 2025 campaign, signs, books, films and exhibits covering topics such as slavery, climate change and the massacre of Native Americans were flagged and removed from national parks and monuments nationwide.
“Some of it’s been put back, and then some of it has been removed again,” said the Center for American Progress’ Angelo Villagomez. He was part of the progressive policy group’s team that examined a database leaked earlier this year and found that a third of national parks had flagged exhibits featuring history or science. Of those, Black and Indigenous history were most targeted.
Portions of all flagged material have since been reviewed and cataloged by a committee led by Joy Beasley, a National Park Service associate director. However, in a June affidavit, she writes that the spreadsheet is “unlikely to capture every removal, revision, or replacement.”
The Interior Department did not respond to The Associated Press’ questions about the current status of sign and exhibit removal or the ongoing lawsuit filed by the nonprofit coalition in February against the federal government.
The parks “are America’s storytellers,” said Todd Martin of the National Parks Conservation Association, a plaintiff in the lawsuit. “It’s their duty to preserve and interpret American history, the good, the bad, and the ugly.”
Jenny McBurney, a government publications librarian at the University of Minnesota who co-founded the project Save Our Signs, feels it’s more important than ever for park visitors to document revised signs.
“People are going to go to the parks and think that they will get to learn history there when in fact they will be learning an incomplete history,” said McBurney.
Wabanaki culture — past and present — shared in Acadia
Despite the job cuts, threats of land reduction, talks of privatization and even demolition within some parks, Indigenous groups and park partners have persevered.
In Maine, members of the Wabanaki Confederacy — comprised of the Maliseet, Mi’kmaq, Passamaquoddy, Penobscot and Abenaki principal nations — carry on the cultural traditions and spiritual practices that helped them maintain sovereignty and connection to their ancestral land after settlers arrived. That includes sharing their culture with tourists.
Penobscot Nation citizen Jennifer Neptune had mixed emotions about the attempted erasure of her people from Acadia and their ancestral homeland.
“It’s hard to get good signage in national monuments, in national parks,” said Neptune. “It’s a real gut punch when it (removal) happens, not just for Indigenous people, but for Black people, for the people whose stories don’t get shared.”
Over the past decade, she’s seen real change from the National Park Service, playing an integral part in bringing Wabanaki voices to the table to create Indigenous-designed spaces.
In partnership with Acadia, the privately owned Abbe Museum, which is largely overseen by Wabanaki people, hosts a program that brings Native voices into the park through music, arts and culture.
Nick Bear and members of a Wabanaki drum circle perform on Cadillac Mountain annually as part of this collaboration. “That’s just like bringing those ceremonies right back to the original sites,” he said.
In July, Passamaquoddy basket maker Lydia Soctomah demonstrated traditional Wabanaki basketry using pounded ash bark and sweetgrass outside the Sieur de Monts Nature Center. Both the ash tree and sweetgrass are part of the Wabanaki creation story, she said.
“Making a basket is worth 1,000 memories for me,” said Soctomah, whose grandmother was a well-known basket maker. “I was always told it holds a part of your spirit.”
Sweetgrass access an example of shared stewardship
Access to sweetgrass has long been difficult for Wabanaki people as they were pushed from coastal lands onto reservations. In Acadia, it’s been nearly nonexistent since the park’s creation in 1916. But over the past decade, park staff and Wabanaki members have collaborated to change that.
In 2017, scientist Suzanne Greenlaw, a citizen of the Houlton Band of Maliseet Indians, partnered with the U.S. Forest Service, Acadia’s Schoodic Institute and 14 traditional gatherers to conduct a Wabanaki-led sweetgrass study in hopes of allowing tribal access.
“It was really impactful because we had never had those kinds of co-stewardship relationships,” said Greenlaw, adding that those relationships, built over time, have not changed.
By the end of the Biden administration, there were over 400 co-stewardship or co-management agreements with tribes, 159 within the National Park Service alone, says Sams. Programs in Acadia were among them.
These programs, he says, allow tribes to fulfill their obligation to protect, preserve and enhance natural resources, and the federal government to fulfill its obligation to allow tribal access for hunting, fishing, and gathering foods and medicines.
Sams cautiously hopes there will be a rebuilding period for the park service under the next administration.
“There are always ebbs and flows with every administration,” he said. “Nobody has seen that more than American Indian tribes.”

title: Thos. Moser moving showroom from Freeport to the Old Port
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Thos. Moser, an Auburn company known for crafting furniture that verges on art, is moving its Maine showroom back to Portland after nearly 30 years in Freeport.
Contractors are renovating the storefront at 146 Middle St., where the new showroom will augment the Old Port’s growing contingent of high-end, often Maine-based designers, artists and makers. The company also has showrooms in Boston, San Francisco and Washington, D.C.
Expected to open by January, the Old Port showroom will display new and classic designs and introduce shoppers to the people and processes behind a distinctive furniture line with influences ranging from Shaker to Nakashima.
Founded in New Gloucester in 1972, the company’s workshop is now in Auburn. Its first showroom opened on Cumberland Avenue in Portland in 1984 and moved to Freeport in 1998.
“After many years in Freeport, we are excited to return to Portland,” said spokesperson Kelsey Wing. “We were really drawn to the vibrant community that Portland offers, where design, art, craft and commerce all come together. This new location is an ideal spot to welcome customers, designers, architects and visitors to Maine.”
Thos. Moser isn’t the first Maine-based furniture maker to set up shop in the Old Port. Chilton opened a showroom at 100 Commercial St. in 2020, in addition to its showroom in a former sea captain’s home in Freeport.
In 2013, Ethan Allen, a national high-end furniture retailer, moved from a store near the Maine Mall in South Portland — its home for nearly two decades — to a much smaller space at 145 Commercial St.
The company said at the time that the steady flow of pedestrians on Commercial Street — in the heart of Portland’s tourist district and steps away from the city’s cruise ship terminals — would increase the brand’s exposure to a broader market.
Other high-end Maine retailers in the Old Port include Brunswick leather bag designer Rough & Tumble and Portland handbag designer Alice Yardley; women’s clothing designers Roxi Suger of Biddeford and Jill McGowan of Portland; and local jewelry makers Folia, D. Cole and Designs by CC.
“The growth of high-end retailers in the Old Port reflects Portland’s evolution as a destination for unique, high quality shopping experiences,” said Quincy Hentzel, CEO of the Portland Regional Chamber of Commerce. “As more of these businesses establish a presence, they collectively strengthen the Old Port’s appeal — attracting both residents and visitors who appreciate quality, craftsmanship and a distinctive retail experience.”
The new Thos. Moser showroom will be in the historic Storer Bros. Building, which was built in 1881 and designed by noted architects Francis H. Fassett and John Calvin Stevens. The space was previously occupied by Greenhut Galleries, which moved to the Bayside neighborhood.
“We look forward to bringing our talented Freeport team to Portland, welcoming customers, friends and partners to our new showroom,” said CEO Philip Hussey.

title: Watch: Mt. Ararat field hockey is the Varsity Maine Girls team of the week
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone—because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s Go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
Editor’s note: Each week during the fall sports season, Varsity Maine will highlight a boys and girls team of the week. The teams, picked by staff members, will take into account several factors, including success stories, bounce-back efforts and notable accomplishments, among others. Athletes, coaches and athletic directors can nominate teams by emailing sports editor Bill Stewart at [email protected] or Varsity Maine editor Lee Horton at [email protected].
Varsity Maine Girls Team of the Week: Mt. Ararat field hockey
When Krista Chase was first hired to pilot the Mt. Ararat field hockey team in 2014, the program had been in a state of limbo for years.
“ Thirteen years ago, we weren’t winning many games,” Chase said.
Now, the Eagles (14-0) enter the postseason as the top seed in Class A North, thanks to their first victory over Skowhegan in more than a decade, a win that coincidentally was Chase’s 200th as head coach.
Chase said the program’s transformation started the day that she took the helm.
“ The very first thing I did was create the Baby Eagles youth program,” she said. “My juniors and seniors are the original Baby Eagles, and that’s the foundation of Mt. Ararat field hockey.”
Chase’s daughter, Kamryn, now a junior captain for the Eagles, was one of the “OG” members of the Baby Eagles.
“ We were the first preschoolers and kindergartners to come through,” Kamryn Chase said. “It just feels very rewarding to do all that hard work … and when we get to high school to be so successful.”
“ They’re my girls, they’re my family,” Krista Chase said. “They’re who have really made me a better coach and really transformed this program.”
The Eagles have outscored their opponents 70-6, with no opponent scoring more than once since the preseason. Kamryn Chase said that she sees this more as a cause for motivation than celebration.
“In playoffs, we’re gonna need to be ready to see anything, ’cause teams are really gonna wanna beat us,” Kamryn said. “ We’re just gonna need to bring the fire and the hard work and just put it all together.”
Regardless of how the postseason goes, the Chases know that they’re modeling for the next generation of Baby Eagles.
“ (The current Baby Eagles are) getting ready to be just like these girls and to take over once (the originals) leave,” Krista said. “They’re the gift that keeps on giving.”

title: What the new food sovereignty ordinance means for Buxton residents
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BUXTON — Buxton voters at a special town meeting Wednesday passed a food sovereignty ordinance, making it easier for locals to sell food from their homes.
With the change, any Buxton resident will be able to sell most food products they prepare in their kitchens to neighbors without worrying about state regulations.
Supporters of the ordinance say it strengthens local food systems by simplifying the steps to start and run small farms and businesses, and fosters relationships between residents around food.
The Maine Food Sovereignty Act has allowed municipalities to adopt food sovereignty ordinances since 2017. Over 113 Maine municipalities, roughly 30% of the state’s towns, had food sovereignty ordinances in effect in 2025, according to data from Local Food Rules, an organization that advocates for the law.
Right now, Buxton residents are subject to state law that requires them to secure a home food processor license before selling shelf-stable products prepared at home, such as sourdough and jam. No license is necessary for selling eggs or produce, since they are not altered in the kitchen.
The ordinance will remove the license requirement for residents who want to sell food directly to other individuals, but not for those selling to stores or restaurants. They will also now be able to sell dairy products, which even the state license does not allow because they must be refrigerated.
Though getting the license is fairly simple (it involves a one-time kitchen inspection and a $20 yearly fee), other barriers it creates take more money and time, said Cynthia Gorham, a Buxton resident and home food seller who brought the ordinance to the Buxton Board of Selectmen’s attention.
Some products — anything acidic or fermented, and some types of jam and jelly recipes, for example — must be sent to state regulators for testing with a fee of $100 for a new product and then $80 for a new recipe for that product, a process that can take over a month. The license also requires accurate ingredient labeling for products, creating challenges for sellers when they change recipes.
Those are steps Buxton residents will no longer have to take before stocking farm stands or advertising homemade products via local Facebook groups. Products that can be sold through food sovereign, producer-to-consumer transactions include milk or milk products, fish or fish products, seafood or seafood products, cider or juice, acidified foods, and canned fruits or vegetables.
A food sovereignty ordinance would not apply to farmers markets; transactions must be face-to-face, involving food or food products at the site of production.
Gorham said she hopes the ordinance will provide more opportunities for Buxton residents to buy food from community members at lower prices than they would at the grocery store, result in a healthier local economy and creating more contact between neighbors.

title: Two killed in fire at senior living center in Mississippi
text:
Two killed in fire at senior living center in Mississippi
Two people were killed in a fire at an assisted living facility in Mississippi, Hinds County Coroner Jeramiah Howard confirmed early Thursday.
The fire started just after 5 p.m. Wednesday at Brookdale Senior Living in Clinton, city officials said.
An 82-year-old man and an 81-year-old woman died as a result of the fire, according to the coroner. Their names have not yet been released.
"We are devastated by the fire at our Clinton community," Brookdale Senior Living said in a statement. "Our hearts are with all our residents, their families and our associates during this incredibly difficult time."
Much of the building, which was home to more than 100 people, was destroyed.
Gov. Tate Reeves released a statement on social media following the fire, writing, "Mississippi is praying for the residents, employees and families affected by the terrible fire at the Brookdale assisted living facility in Clinton. Please continue praying for everyone affected. Thank you to all of the first responders who have quickly sprung into action to help those in need."
Clinton is about 10 miles northwest of Jackson.

title: Your Choice, Your Voice: how tariffs and taxes impact Maine businesses
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Your Choice, Your Voice: how taxes and tariffs impact Maine businesses
Michael Knight is the co-owner of Smiling Hill Farm and Hillside Lumber. He said the tariffs are not impacting his product, as much is they're impacting other business costs.
Your Choice, Your Voice: how taxes and tariffs impact Maine businesses
Michael Knight is the co-owner of Smiling Hill Farm and Hillside Lumber. He said the tariffs are not impacting his product, as much is they're impacting other business costs.
At Smiling Hill Farm, co-owner Michael Knight said the dairy industry has been struggling for years.
"We're on life support," he said. "The farmers in Maine, New Hampshire, all across the United States, have seen increase in diesel prices, tariffs and everything. And yet they can't get more money for their milk because of the glut of the milk on the market."
That glut of milk he's referring to is milk from mega farms that Knight said are milking cows three times a day. He added that this has put many generational Maine farms out of business.
"Are the farmers scared of the tariffs? They're more scared of the low milk price right now and staying in business than they are of the tariffs," Knight said.
The tariffs affecting Smiling Hill aren't the dairy tariffs.
"The big thing in the last two months has been the diesel prices. You know, this cost and this company, you know, I estimate anywhere from 8000 to $10,000 more a month, just to keep my trucks on the road because of high diesel prices," he said.
Knight is also the co-founder of Hillside Lumber. The lumber industry is also impacted by tariffs.
He said the market for lumber changes every day, but because of the Canadian tariffs, he has to buy his lumber in the United States instead of in Canada, and that's becoming more expensive.
Taxes are also a priority for people. Just in the last legislature there were new taxes on cigarettes, marijuana, paint, streaming services and millionaires.
At the time the legislature was considering the 2% millionaires tax, small businesses lobbied against it, saying business owners who sell their business would be hit with the tax.
Knight said things are hard now, but his industries have been through it before.
"When Covid hit, lumber prices went way higher than this and they've survived that. So this is just a little blip," Knight said.

title: Cheverus, the Varsity Maine field hockey poll’s unanimous No. 1, turns attention to playoffs
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone—because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s Go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
As has been the case all season, Cheverus is the unanimous No. 1 team in the Varsity Maine field hockey poll. The Stags are undefeated (14-0) and take the top seed into the Class A South tournament. And they have won the past three state championships.
A fourth straight title won’t be easy. To win their region, the Stags will have to get past the likes of third-ranked Biddeford and Sanford/Kennebunk, who have each played Cheverus twice this season, and the Stags won all four matchups by only one goal. No. 8 Thornton Academy should also be in the mix.
Then there’s A North, which is topped by another unbeaten, second-ranked Mt. Ararat, and the Stags’ usual state title game foe, No. 4 Skowhegan. The Eagles and the River Hawks also have to survive ninth-ranked Camden Hills, which took Mt. Ararat to overtime on Tuesday.
The B North and B South tournaments could be even more chaotic. Nokomis, which moved up from eighth last week to No. 7, is B North’s top seed, but the Warriors might have to face two-time reigning state champion Belfast in the semifinals. Fifth-ranked Leavitt beat the top contenders in the region but finished a distant second to Nokomis. That means the Hornets will have a tough second-round matchup with third-seeded Cony or sixth-seeded Gardiner, which has shown itself to be more than capable of winning the region.

title: How this app helps anglers find their fishing crew
text:
HERMITAGE, Mo. (InvestigateTV) - For many anglers, sometimes it’s not the fish but the memories that are keepers.
“Some of my best memories,” John Bledsoe said, “and the best memories I have with regards to fishing, are always about the people I’m with at the time.”
Without a doubt, this lake is a dream spot for many. But for John, this spot launched his dream.
“It was on this lake right here, Pomme de Terre Lake, I was fishing by myself,” John said. “That day I was feeling a little lonely. And I happened to look at my empty seat and got to thinking, man, why didn’t I bring somebody with me? And then the wheels started turning.”
That day, John bought the domain name coangler.com for $13. His idea was an app where people could connect and book fishing trips together.
“Helping people that maybe don’t have the means to get outdoors,” John said about the app, “or maybe people that need help loading and unloading boats, or their wives would feel more comfortable if they had an extra co-angler in the boat with them.”
A chemist by trade, Missouri State’s e-Factory was right next to where John worked. It was there he got advice and attended a 10-month-long coding program.
That led to funding opportunities from various organizations to get Co-Angler launched as smooth as a bass boat off a boat ramp.
“It’s a great way for people to connect and meet each other,” angler Luke Routh said.
Luke’s fished in tournaments all across the nation, but the Co-Angler app is a way for him to have a little more fun.
“A lot of outdoorsmen are good people,” Luke said. “They just want to go outside and have fun, enjoy the lake; a lot of people don’t have access to it.”
“So, if you’re a person that has a boat,” Luke continued, “you ain’t got to show off all your good fishing spots. We’re coming here today, John and I, just fish randomly throughout the lake, and we’ve had a heck of a time.”
“Social media has created this kind of pseudo-social connection, which isn’t really real,” John said. “And so having the ability to use technology in the outdoors to connect people in the real world to go fish together is something I’m really passionate about.”
On the app, you can create your profile, explore trips, rank your activity level, techniques, and target fish you want to catch.
“First and foremost, it’s about human connection,” John said. “It’s about getting people in the outdoors together, sharing each other’s company, having a great time.”
”There’s definitely some natural healing properties to, you know, being around water and the outdoors, and sunshine, getting some of that vitamin D,“ John continued.
Right now, there are over 2,500 users on the app. John says it’s the only app connecting anglers.
Co-Angler is available in the App Store on your cell phone, or you can find it by clicking here to go to coangler.com.
It’s free to join, but you can add on some premium features as well.

title: Husband, wife diagnosed with breast cancer a year apart are now cancer-free
text:
Husband, wife diagnosed with breast cancer a year apart are now cancer-free
For North Carolina couple Joan and Robert Eyster, the traditional wedding vow ‘in sickness and in health’ takes on a different meaning this year.
The couple, who went on their first date in December of 1965, were diagnosed with breast cancer one year apart from each other.
Joan learned that she had breast cancer in 2024, and she remembers how she felt when she found out about the diagnosis.
"When I had my mammogram, I was shocked," Joan said. “I broke out in tears … because I had no idea; it was just a shock.”
Her husband, Robert, found out that he would go down the same path as his wife when he was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2025.
"It was in her right breast and my right breast," Robert said. "And we both had good results, because we both found it early."
The two used the same surgeon and the same oncologist from Novant Health. Robert has the BRCA2 gene, which does raise breast cancer risk.
"He was the first man I had ever heard of who was diagnosed with breast cancer, and it was a huge shock to me," Joan said.
Now, both breast cancer survivors, they want their own story to help others who might be dealing with a similar diagnosis.
"Don't give up just because you get that diagnosis," Joan said. "And we have to be our own advocates as far as medical conditions. If we notice something is not right, we need to get it checked out."
The couple found out early, and at 82 and 83 years old, they say they’re now feeling great.
"Praise the Lord," Robert said. "Because now we sit here cancer-free."
They celebrated their 60th wedding anniversary in August.

title: Maine Hospice Council ceases operations
text:
After careful consideration and extensive evaluation of available resources, the Maine Hospice Council Board members have made the difficult decision to cease operations and close the organization effective Oct. 17, 2026.
Referring to her one-on-one work with people, public speaking, and consulting, MHC Executive Director Kandyce Powell, RN, MSN said, “I will continue to be available to anyone searching for hospice and end-of-life care resources at either (207) 882-4032 or KandycePowell65@gmail.com.”
Over the past 35 years, the MHC has worked to advance the mission of promoting universal access to quality end-of-life and palliative care through innovation, creativity, education, advocacy, and collaboration. The organization has been a leader in advocating for, training, and educating providers and communities about hospice and palliative care.
All of the Council’s work has been grounded in identified needs. Leadership and staff listened to community members-including healthcare providers-to identify needs and gaps in end-of-life and serious illness care, in order to develop meaningful programs.
This approach guided extensive outreach to underserved and disenfranchised populations, including financial support, development, and education for the Maine State Prison’s comprehensive Hospice and Palliative Care Program.
Notable initiatives over 35 years including, but not limited to, policy development; program development such as the Hospice Veteran Partnership and the Maine Pain Initiative; community listening sessions; international human rights presentations and program collaborations; successful grant writing, including support through the Robert Wood Johnson Community/State Partnership; and serving as a host site for numerous academic interns, doctoral students, and other learners.
Throughout its years of operation, the MHC has been honored to collaborate with donors, volunteers, staff, community partners, and supporters who make this important work possible.
“I acknowledge the dedicated work of the Council for all of the years under the leadership of Executive Director Kandyce Powell. The Council has been able to provide services to Maine people because of Kandyce’s commitment and perseverance,” said MHC Board President Alicia Murray, DNP, MSN, RN, CHPN.
“This decision was not made lightly,” Murray added. “We are incredibly proud of the impact our organization has made and deeply grateful to everyone who supported our mission. While closing our doors is difficult, we celebrate the lives touched, the relationships built, and the lasting contributions made to our community.”
The Maine Hospice Council extends its heartfelt appreciation to its employees, volunteers, board members, donors, grant foundations, community partners, and the individuals and families it has served. Their commitment and support enabled the organization to pursue its mission for more than 40 years.
Although the MHC is closing, the values and impact of its work will continue through the individuals, organizations, and communities that carry the mission of quality end-of-life care forward.

title: Maine woman accused of intentionally setting fires at neighboring homes
text:
Maine woman accused of intentionally setting fires at neighboring Ashland homes
A Maine woman is facing arson charges after she was accused of intentionally setting fires at neighboring homes in Ashland.
Brooke Robinson, 26, of Ashland, was arrested Tuesday in connection with an incident that happened on Frenchville Road earlier this month, according to the Maine State Fire Marshal's Office.
On Oct. 10, Ashland police responded to 1158 Frenchville Road after receiving a complaint about ongoing criminal mischief. Officers found Robinson at the property, arrested her and issued a summons for her to appear in court on a criminal mischief charge.
The Ashland Police Department then contacted the State Fire Marshal's Office on Oct. 13 after additional information was developed during the initial investigation.
Investigators identified fire damage to the outside of the home at 1158 Frenchville Road, and after examining that damage, the Fire Marshal's Office determined that the fire was intentionally set by means of holding an open flame against the exterior siding of the home.
The Fire Marshal's Office said investigators also determined that Robinson was responsible for setting fires at 1164 Frenchville Road, a neighboring property, before setting fire to the home at 1158 Frenchville Road.
According to officials, investigators identified two separate areas of fire damage at 1164 Frenchville Road, and determined that the damage was caused by an open flame being held against the home's exterior siding and insulation materials.
The case was submitted to the Aroostook County District Attorney's Office, and an arrest warrant was issued charging Robinson with two counts of arson.
Fire Marshal's Office investigators arrested Robinson with help from the Presque Isle Police Department, and she was taken to the Aroostook County Jail.

title: Patriots’ comeback falls short against Bears
text:
CHICAGO — Caleb Williams threw for 308 yards and two touchdowns, and the Chicago Bears cooled off Drake Maye and the New England Patriots with a 30-24 win on Thursday night.
Williams was 22 of 33 passing in his second game back after being sidelined by a right hamstring injury. He became the first Bears quarterback to throw for more than 300 yards in consecutive games since Mitch Trubisky had a three-game run in 2018.
Williams outdueled Maye in their second meeting since the longtime friends were part of the 2024 NFL draft. Williams went No. 1 to Chicago, and Maye was selected by New England at No. 3.
Luther Burden had four catches for 130 yards for Chicago (5-2), and Colston Loveland had a 12-yard touchdown reception. Cairo Santos kicked a 58-yard field goal with 1:34 left, a career long and matching the franchise record, after he missed a 53-yard attempt earlier in the final quarter.
Maye was 24 of 31 for 321 yards and two touchdowns. He also threw a costly interception in the end zone in the first half.
New England (4-3) had won three consecutive games behind Maye, who threw 10 TD passes and one interception during the streak.
Rhamondre Stevenson had five catches for 93 yards and a touchdown for the Patriots. Eli Raridon had a 30-yard TD catch in the third quarter.
After Santos’ long field goal, Maye drove New England into range for Andy Borregales’ 47-yarder with 37 seconds to go. But Chicago recovered the onside kick.
It was Chicago’s first home game since Mike Ditka died on Oct. 9. The Bears saluted the Hall of Fame tight end and longtime coach with a pregame moment of silence, and they also handed out fake mustaches to the crowd of 60,520 at Soldier Field.
Ditka’s No. 89 jersey dotted the stands, and fans also donned Bears sweaters in a callback to what Ditka wore on the sideline as a coach.
Chicago opened a 20-7 lead on Burden’s 24-yard touchdown with 14 seconds left in the first half. Burden got the ball on a screen on third-and-17, and Loveland, Kalif Raymond and Darnell Wright helped clear the way for his second TD reception of the season.
Set to receive the second-half kickoff, the Bears were in position to pull away. But the Patriots responded with Stevenson’s 48-yard touchdown reception on the final play of the half.
Stevenson slipped out of the backfield and Maye lobbed the ball over the head of Bears safety Cam Lewis. Stevenson ran away from Lewis and got a downfield block from DeMario Douglas before cutting past Bears cornerback Jaylon Johnson on his way to the end zone.
Injuries
Patriots: Cornerback Christian Gonzalez played after being listed as questionable because of an illness. … Safety Kevin Byard departed after he was checked out by trainers with 9:44 left in first half. He later returned. … Defensive tackle Christian Barmore departed late in the game.
Bears: Cornerback Malik Muhammad left in the third quarter because of a toe injury. … Tight end Cole Kmet hurt his right knee on a reception with 5:34 left.
Up next
Patriots: At Miami on Nov. 1
Bears: At Seattle for a Monday night game on Nov. 2

title: Trump administration drops legal fight to overhaul student loan forgiveness program
text:
Trump administration drops legal fight to overhaul student loan forgiveness program
The Trump administration moved Wednesday to end its legal fight to overhaul a popular student loan forgiveness program. 
The Department of Justice appealed after federal judges ruled in June in favor of advocates who said the Public Service Loan Forgiveness program risked becoming a tool for political retribution. But it dropped two appeals Wednesday in single-sentence joint agreements, which stipulated that each side would pay its own fees.
Federal officials provided no explanation, but advocates praised the ruling.
Related video: Trump administration addresses health care price transparency
“The Trump administration’s attempt to weaponize public service loan forgiveness against organizations it disagrees with was anti-democratic and unlawful from the start,” Dan Zibel, an attorney for the group Student Defense, said in a written statement. “This is a significant victory for millions of Americans who have dedicated their careers to public service.”
The PSLF program was designed to make jobs in government, public schools, fire and police departments, public hospitals and nonprofits more attractive by forgiving loans for qualified employees after a decade’s worth of payments.
But last fall, President Donald Trump’s administration wrote a new rule to empower Education Secretary Linda McMahon to kick employers out of the program if she decides their work has a “substantial illegal purpose.”
The vaguely phrased rule was targeted at employers who support undocumented immigrants or transgender youth, potentially affecting borrowers who worked at schools, public hospitals and legal aid groups.
The overhaul amounted to a major reworking of a program that has canceled loans for more than 1 million Americans. 
But just before it was set to take effect in July, U.S. District Judge Myong Joun in Massachusetts vacated the U.S. Education Department’s changes, saying they overstepped the agency’s power and threatened to violate First Amendment protections for free speech. The ruling came in response to a pair of lawsuits filed by more than 20 states along with a coalition of nonprofit groups and cities.
On the same day, District Judge Amir Ali in Washington issued a similar ruling in a case brought by nonprofit organizations.

title: Please do not make excuses for Troy Jackson
text:
I write in response to Steve Collins’ column making light of Troy Jackson’s dismissive action of telling Sen. Susan Collins to “shut up” on the debate stage (“Politicians have a rich history of telling each other to zip it,” Oct. 19).
First, Steve Collins suggests that because Sen. Collins did not react to the slight to women — both on the night of the debate and also when Trump may have insulted her — it is somehow on her shoulders to defend herself each and every time she may be insulted. If she does not, it somehow puts her at fault.
I believe Sen. Collins decided not to engage Mr. Jackson, and decided to ignore the slight and not get into a fight about it on stage. She is a lady.
Secondly, Troy Jackson acts like a victim when he says “she [Sen. Collins] is talking down to me.” Mr. Jackson is no victim. Someone once told me that the only person who can make you feel inferior is yourself.
Thirdly, because there have been many other instances of politicians saying “shut up,” does that make it right? I will note that all the examples Steve Collins gave were of men saying “shut up.”
Fourth, although, yes, not the end of the world, is this the kind of behavior we want from a senator? I want to see a gentleman match the professionalism of Sen. Collins.
Joanne Lebel
Auburn

title: InvestigateTV+: Helping families that travel with breast milk
text:

She said when she asked to speak to a supervisor, she was asked, “Well, where is the baby?” The supervisor then said if her child was with her, “it wouldn’t be an issue,” according to Calandrelli.
She said she was ultimately escorted from the security line and forced to check her ice packs.

Andrea Lucas keeps a pill box in her home, surrounded by pictures and memorabilia celebrating her father, Bill Lucas, who was the first Black general manager for the Atlanta Braves.

title: Trump administration too lax on guns, gun safety
text:
During my lifetime, driving has become safer and safer.
Seat belts, then lap belts and airbags. Newer cars now have drowsiness detection, blind-spot monitors, lane centering assistance and adaptive cruise control. Roads have rumble strips and streets have raised crossings. The list of safety measures goes on.
It used to be that motor vehicle accidents were the leading cause of traumatic deaths in this country. Today, guns are more lethal than cars. So why is the current administration doing its best to thwart gun safety measures?
Funding for the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives has decreased. Handguns can now be purchased by 18-21-year-olds. Silencers are now easier to acquire; same with large- capacity magazines. Funding for community violence prevention measures and school-based mental health resources have been cut or eliminated. This list goes on and on.  
Keep this in mind on Election Day.
Edward Walworth, MD
Lewiston

title: Mobile clinic offers low-cost spay neuter services for cats in Caribou
text:
CARIBOU, Maine (WAGM) - Cat owners throughout the county got the chance to get veterinary care during a low-cost spay and neuter clinic in Caribou this week.
In Caribou, cats received a variety of vet care this week during the mobile spay and neuter clinic. The clinic started Monday morning with a few hiccups, including blowing the power at the Collins Pond facility where they set up. Tuesday, vets said things were going much smoother.
“Kind of everything that could go wrong went wrong and today much smoother sailing. We’ve been here since 6:45 and we’re gonna be done around 4ish. Today we have spayed and neutered 25 cats. Yesterday we did a few more. We did about 30. We’re gonna be here for 2 more days. So, the goal is 120. Some are privately owned and some are through rescue partners,” said Monique McNichol, Protectors of Animal Life Society (P.A.L.S.) veterinary technician.
The clinic provides a wide range of services for cat owners.
“In the rig, we’re doing just spay/neuter but that includes rabies vaccines, FVRCP vaccines. If we see tapeworms, we’re also treating tapeworms. If we see live fleas, you’re getting a Capstar live flea treatment. Everyone’s getting pain medication and then per the owner we’re also doing microchips, snap tests for FIV and FELV, and you can also go home with a cone if you want,” McNichol said.
The mobile clinic drove up from Winthrop, nearly four hours away, and the vets say this is the longest trip they’ve ever made.
“This is the furthest we’ve ever been in the rig. This is our 4th or 5th trip out in our mobile unit. Up here it’s really hard. We would call this a veterinary desert. There’s not a lot of options for spay/neuter. There’s no access to care for low-cost services. It’s just important to have access to care and these low-cost options available for people,” McNichol said.
The clinic says it plans to return in the spring to offer another low-cost spay and neuter clinic. During the next trip to the county, the clinic will drive around to different communities to reach more people in need of vet care.
There are still spots available for this clinic and the spring visit. Cat owners can register by visiting palscatshelterwinthrop.com.

title: The Lincoln County News
text:
To the editor:
It seems like all the news these days is bad. Less a steady stream; more a gushing river. Bad news feels normal.
Every so often the old folks come out with their signs and stand on the sidewalks either side of the Damariscotta-Newcastle bridge. They’re bundled against a chilly wind blowing up the river from the sea. Red and brown and yellow leaves swirl and gather in the gutter. They wave their signs. Some passing cars honk. They stick around for an hour or so and head home for some hot tea. They plod back to their cars, hunched into the wind like they’re pulling the world behind them, signs tucked under their arms to be stowed in the mudroom until next time. The signs all say: “We don’t like any of this stuff.”

title: Bobby Charles is set to talk with critics next week. You can be one of them.
text:
Republican gubernatorial candidate Bobby Charles said Thursday that he is inviting voters, especially “people who do not support” him, to sit down with him at an event in Auburn next week and ask him anything.
The 66-year-old Leeds lawyer said the format of the Oct. 29 event at the Androscoggin County Republican Committee’s headquarters in the Auburn Mall is “simple”: Charles will sit at a table, a voter will sit across from him and the two will talk, with the voter welcomed to ask “tough questions” or “challenge his positions.”
“I’m inviting people who disagree with me to sit across from me and ask anything,” Charles said in a statement. “You can tell me I’m wrong. To my face.”
It is a move by the Republican to project openness in the closing stretch of a gubernatorial contest to succeed Gov. Janet Mills that former Maine House Speaker Hannah Pingree, a Democrat, is expected to win.
Pingree, a 50-year-old North Haven resident who helmed Mills’ policy office and is the daughter of U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree, has consistently held a double-digit lead in the polls over Charles, who previously worked in drug enforcement and domestic policy roles under former Presidents George W. Bush, George H.W. Bush and Ronald Reagan. Independent Rick Bennett, a 63-year-old former Maine Republican Party chair and state senator, has been well behind those two in polls.
A news release from the Charles campaign said he “especially welcomes people who do not support him” to the Auburn Mall event that will go from 5-7 p.m. and is free, with no registration required. Charles is holding “as many one-on-one conversations as time allows,” the release said.
He specifically invited “Hannah Pingree supporters, Kamala Harris voters, Gen Z liberals, frustrated Democrats, undecided independents and Somali immigrants.”
Charles rose quickly to the top of a crowded Republican primary field in June in part by pitching himself as an outsider who supports many of President Donald Trump’s policies. But in the general election, he has noticeably attempted to back away from Trump and some of his positions while portraying himself as a more independent-minded figure.
His rhetoric has at times drawn both Democratic and Republican rebukes during the primary and general portions of the race. Last year, for example, Charles referred to state Rep. Deqa Dhalac, a South Portland Democrat who immigrated to the U.S. from Somalia more than three decades ago, as a “radical Somalia-first” lawmaker, drawing criticism.
Charles invited voters to visit an optional registration page for next Thursday’s event at secure.winred.com/bobby-charles-for-maine/disagree-event.
“If you think I’m wrong about something, tell me. If you’re skeptical of my plans, challenge me,” Charles said. “If there’s an issue you think I’m overlooking, let’s talk about it.”

title: Maine can do without Susan Collins’ perks

title: Facing a ban on horse-drawn carriages, Central Park's drivers fear for their livelihoods
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — The horse-drawn carriages that have cruised through Central Park for more than 150 years are set to be banished soon from New York City, ending an iconic tradition beloved by tourists but long opposed by animal welfare activists.
For the carriage drivers, it’s unclear what comes next.
“No one can come up with an appropriate answer because there is none,” said Alexus Lawson, a 28-year-old carriage driver from Queens who grew up with horses and has worked as a riding instructor. Now, she worries about what would become of 7-year-old Starlight and her other horses. “Without a job, how can I take care of my horses?”
The New York City Council is expected to pass a bill Thursday that would ban horse-drawn carriage rides by June 2028, pulling back the reins after the death of a teenage tourist last spring spurred the latest call to end the rides after decades of opposition from activists.
But the one question that has come up time and again — what to do with drivers whose jobs would be eliminated — remains largely unanswered.
The legislation requires Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s office to develop a plan by next April to help the more than 150 remaining drivers find other work. That would include referrals for job openings in the city’s transit, hospitality and taxi industries, as well as career counseling. It also would anticipate the administration considering some form of compensation for industry workers.
City Hall is working on a detailed plan for the transition of the workforce and has started discussions on potential compensation, a spokesperson for the mayor said. And Mamdani himself has said government has a “civic responsibility to ensure that we are not leaving anybody out to dry.”
Medet Fidan, a former cab driver who traded his steering wheel for a set of reins after ride sharing apps upended the taxi industry, said he felt like he was being targeted.
“I think the city is leaving us a big mess,” said Fidan, 56, who has been driving a carriage for 15 years. “We’re going to lose our businesses, we’re going to lose our jobs, we’re going to lose our livelihoods.”
Council Speaker Julie Menin “will remain engaged in the transition process,” a spokesperson said, adding that the legislation seeks to address the longstanding question of what happens to displaced carriage drivers by setting a firm deadline for City Hall to act.
The union representing the drivers has vowed to file a legal challenge “the minute the ink dries” on the legislation.
Mamdani’s two immediate predecessors as mayor had both called to end the industry, but neither succeeded.
Former Mayor Bill de Blasio campaigned on ending the rides on day one of his administration but the effort wilted amid a backlash from unions and a big media blitz involving actor Liam Neeson. Eric Adams, the mayor just before Mamdani, floated a ban late in his term but the proposal went nowhere.
The latest push began in June after an 18-year-old Indian tourist, Romanch Mahajan, died after jumping from a runaway carriage during a ride. That appeared to be the first fatality involving a horse carriage in Central Park since the rides began.
Mahajan’s family has personally appealed to the city to end the rides, offering tearful testimony that they thought the rides were safe. His father, Deepak Mahajan, told lawmakers that his son jumped from the carriage to help his mother after she was thrown out of her seat after the horse suddenly bolted.
Carriage drivers have expressed sympathy for Mahajan and his family but argue that they are being unfairly targeted because of a single accident.
“It does nothing for alternate employment, for the continuation of our businesses,” said Christina Hansen, a longtime carriage driver and industry spokesperson. “Who’s going to pay my rent while I’m looking for a job?”

title: Former NHL star Ron Duguay, known later for relationship with Sarah Palin, dies of cancer at 69
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Ron Duguay, who played nearly 1,000 games in the NHL from the late 1970s through the ’80s, has died of cancer. He was 69.
A spokesperson for the New York Rangers said Thursday that Duguay’s family informed the team of his death.
Duguay played his first six seasons with the Rangers after they selected him with the 13th pick in the draft in 1977. The Sudbury, Ontario, native was an All-Star as a point-a-game producer in 1981-82.
A series of trades led him to spend time with the Detroit Red Wings, Pittsburgh Penguins and Los Angeles Kings with another Rangers stint, as well. Duguay finished his career in the league with 673 points in the regular season and playoffs, then played in Germany and the minors.
“The New York Rangers organization mourns the loss of Ron Duguay, one of the most popular players in franchise history,” the club said in a statement. “Ron’s signature skating style — with his hair flowing as he moved down the ice — captivated the (Madison Square) Garden faithful, and his skill, tenacity and charisma earned him the admiration of all New Yorkers. We join the hockey community in sending our condolences to Ron’s friends, family and loved ones during this difficult time.”
Duguay was known late in life away from hockey for dating former Alaska governor and 2008 Republican U.S. vice presidential nominee Sarah Palin. His family started a GoFundMe earlier this year to offset the costs of travel and treatments.
“It’s with a shattered heart but also deep peace knowing Ron is with Jesus now,” Palin posted on social media. “He fought so hard. Love never ends.”

Violent Arizona storms bring possible tornado, toppled trees and golf ball-size hail
text:
PHOENIX (AP) — Trees fell onto homes and utility poles were knocked down by a possible tornado in a central Arizona community during a series of violent storms that moved through the state overnight into Thursday.
Storms capable of causing hail and wind damage were traveling through central Arizona early Thursday, with some flood watches and the possibility of tornadoes, the National Weather Service said.
On Wednesday night, northern and central parts of the state saw hail the size of golf balls that pummeled people’s roofs, shattered windows and dented cars, along with damaging wind gusts. The weather service had issued multiple warnings during the severe thunderstorms.
A tornado warning was in effect Wednesday night as a storm moved over Heber-Overgaard in Navajo County, about 140 miles (225 kilometers) northeast of Phoenix. People in the area posted photos and video online of uprooted trees and crumpled structures. Significant damage and minor injuries were reported, the county sheriff’s office said in a statement. There are about 3,000 people in the community.
State Rep. Walt Blackman, whose district covers parts of the county, requested a state of emergency declaration.
“We have families without power, significant property damage, and at least one reported injury,” he said in a statement.
The storm hit as members of the Overgaard Baptist Church were wrapping up a prayer meeting.
“We took some damage, lost a lot of trees, signs, fences and a few windows,” the church posted about the storm Wednesday night. Nerves were rattled, but members were OK.
“We had a great prayer meeting in the women’s restroom,” the post said.
Warm, moist air moving north fuels storms coming off the California coast. Changing winds can make them spin, creating the conditions for tornadoes, said Ryan Bernhart, a weather service meteorologist in Flagstaff.
“This is very unusual for this area at this time of the year,” Bernhart said.
Strong winds toppled trees in Flagstaff and Mesa, with some landing on walls and carports. A few dozen ponderosa pines over 30 feet (9 meters) tall fell down in the Coconino National Forest, northwest of Flagstaff.
“These are not small trees that are down,” Bernhart said. “These are pretty strong trees that had been knocked down.”
___
Hill reported from Las Vegas. Associated Press writer Kathy McCormack in Concord, New Hampshire, contributed to this report.

title: Cooper Flagg scores 32 points in season opener, makes NBA history
text:
Maine's Cooper Flagg scores 32 points in season opener, makes NBA history
19-year-old Newport native sets record for most points scored by a teenager in a season opener
Maine's Cooper Flagg scores 32 points in season opener, makes NBA history
19-year-old Newport native sets record for most points scored by a teenager in a season opener
Maine native Cooper Flagg got his second NBA season off to a great start and set another scoring record in the process.
The 19-year-old from Newport scored a game-high 32 points for the Dallas Mavericks in their 128-110 season-opening loss to the Houston Rockets. Flagg also finished the game with five rebounds, two assists, three steals and one block.
The Mavericks' communications department said Flagg's 32 points are the most scored by a teenager in a season opener in NBA history.
Last season, Flagg became the youngest player to score at least 35 points, 40 points, 45 points and 50 points in an NBA game en route to winning the 2025-26 NBA Rookie of the Year award. He led all rookies with an average of 21.0 points per game and also ranked in the top five among rookies in rebounding (6.7 per game, 4th), assists (4.5 per game, 2nd), steals (1.2 per game, 2nd) and blocks (0.9 per game, 5th).
Kyrie Irving scored 15 points in his first game for the Mavericks since tearing his left ACL in March 2025. It was also the Mavs' first game under head coach Dusty May, who was hired to replace Jason Kidd just two months after leading the University of Michigan to an NCAA title.
Kevin Durant and Jabari Smith Jr. each scored 30 points for the Rockets, who outscored the Mavericks 38-12 in the second quarter and held a 32-point lead at halftime.
Dallas had a 9-0 run to cut the lead to 103-86 with about nine minutes remaining in the game, but Houston went on an 8-2 run to push its lead back out to 23 points about a minute later.
The Mavericks visit the Indiana Pacers on Friday.

title: Drought lowers well levels in northern Maine
text:
AROOSTOOK COUNTY, Maine (WAGM) - About half the country relies on private wells for everyday water use. An ongoing drought is leaving some wells with record low levels, and with winter approaching, local officials say the next few weeks could be critical for the groundwater supplies that keep wells working.
Drought conditions across northern Maine
James Sinko, lead meteorologist and hydrology program manager for the National Weather Service, said much of northern Maine is in a D2 drought, classified as severe.
“Currently across much of northern Maine, we’re in a D2 drought, which is severe drought conditions. This is a water resources type drought. So we’re talking groundwater, stream flows, you know, wells, things like that,” Sinko said.
Sinko said northern Maine is still feeling the effects of rainfall deficits from last year.
“I like to think of it as you’re living paycheck to paycheck and then all of a sudden your automobile breaks down. It’s a massive impact. Well, our automobile was the month of August when we had significant rainfall deficits,” Sinko said.
Sinko said it would take 10 to 15 inches of rain before the ground freezes to end the drought, but that rainfall needs to come gradually.
“Now we don’t want 15 inches all at once. Mother Nature cannot handle that. It would rush all out into the rivers. It would bring the rivers up, sure, but it would not get into the ground where it’s needed,” Sinko said.
Record low levels reported, but no dry wells in county
The Maine Drought Task Force reported that a well in Oxford and a well in Clayton Lakes reached a record low this month. Aroostook County Emergency Management Director Darren Woods said there haven’t been any reported dry wells in the county.
Woods said residents who rely on private wells can take steps now to conserve water and reduce the risk of running low.
“So consider things like reducing use of water whenever it’s not needed. So like instead of putting one shirt and pair of pants in a washing machine, maybe wait till you have a load, you know, so you’re using less water,” Woods said.
Over time, wells can refill through the natural process of precipitation and snowmelt. Woods said he advises against trying to refill a well that runs dry by bringing in a truck of water.
“It can be a waste of money because once you’ve dumped that water, it kind of just seeps into the ground and you might not benefit at all from that. So we’re telling people, just save your money,” Woods said.
Woods said residents should report it if their well runs dry.
Dry wells can be reported through the Maine Emergency Management Agency.

title: Former NHL All-Star Ron Duguay dies at 69 after bout with cancer
text:
Former NHL All-Star Ron Duguay dies at 69 after bout with cancer
Ron Duguay, a former NHL All-Star, has died following a brief battle with colon cancer. He was 69.
A right winger and center, Duguay was best known for his years with the New York Rangers.
The Sudbury, Ontario, native was selected by the Rangers 13th overall in the 1977 draft and reached the Stanley Cup Final with the team in 1979.
Related video above | Remembering those we lost in 2026
He played 864 NHL regular-season games over 12 seasons, scoring 274 goals and 346 assists for 620 points. His best NHL season was 1984–85, when he recorded 89 points for the Detroit Red Wings.
He also represented the Rangers at the 1982 NHL All-Star Game.
The Rangers released a statement Thursday, saying in part, "The New York Rangers organization mourns the loss of Ron Duguay, one of the most popular players in franchise history. Ron's signature skating style - with his hair flowing as he moved down the ice - captivated The Garden Faithful, and his skill, tenacity, and charisma earned him the admiration of all New Yorkers. We join the hockey community in sending our condolences to Ron's friends, family, and loved ones during this difficult time."
After stints with Detroit, Pittsburgh and Los Angeles, he returned to New York and later worked as a Rangers studio analyst.
Duguay revealed in February that he had been diagnosed with stage 4 colon cancer in late 2024. He said the cancer spread beyond his colon and required surgery involving his appendix and gallbladder.
Duguay has been in a relationship with former Alaska Gov. Sarah Palin since 2022. Palin has supported him during his cancer treatment, and his daughter has shared images of her helping care for him in the hospital.
Palin also shared a tribute to Duguay on her social media accounts, saying "It’s with a shattered heart, but also deep peace knowing Ron is with Jesus now. He fought so hard. Love never ends."

title: Hermon football hosts Leavitt in battle of Class C contenders
text:
The Hermon High School football team will look to bounce back from its first loss of the season against the 7-0 Leavitt High School Hornets from Turner in a statewide Class C encounter at Pottle Field in Hermon on Friday night.
Kickoff is at 7 p.m.
Last week, defending state Class C champ Greely of Cumberland dealt the visiting Hawks a 28-14 setback, leaving the Hawks with a 6-1 record.
Greely is also 6-1 with its lone loss being to Leavitt, 30-12, on Sept. 10.
Among the other games this weekend, Bangor, coming off an important 35-14 victory over Edward Little of Auburn, will travel to take on Sanford at 7 p.m. Friday.
Bangor is 3-3 in Class A North while Sanford is 1-6 in Class A South.
