Also at 1 p.m. Saturday, headlining the schedule in southern Maine is the battle of 7-0 Class A South heavyweights between defending state champ Thornton Academy of Saco and visiting Bonny Eagle of Buxton.
At Hermon, Hawks coach Kyle Gallant will be looking for a bounceback performance from his team after the loss at Greely.
Gallant said the first half of the game against Greely was “decent.”
“We played well enough to put points on the board, well enough to stop a really high, prolific offense like they have,” said Gallant. “Then they just kind of ground us out in the second half. We couldn’t get anything going. We had some missed opportunities to tackle the ballcarrier. We couldn’t get out of third-and-longs and fourth downs.”
He knows his team will have its hands full with head coach Mike Hathaway’s Leavitt Hornets, who have outscored their opponents 288-39.
Leavitt reached the state title game a year ago where it lost to Greely 41-6.
“They’re really solid all the way around in all three phases of the game. They’re well-coached. You have to execute and play really, really good football in all three phases to beat a team like that. That’s something we’ve been working on this week,” said Gallant.
The Hawks have never beaten the Hornets, losing 47-14 in the semifinals and 12-7 during the regular season. They also lost to Leavitt in 2019.
He said he will need better play from his offensive and defensive lines after losing the battle of the trenches in the second half against Greely.
“We have to control the football and keep their offense off the field as much as possible,” said Gallant.
Leavitt’s offensive catalyst is standout junior dual-threat quarterback Landon Marquis, who threw for two touchdowns and ran for two more in last weekend’s 36-12 win over Nokomis of Newport.
“He is very good,” said 10th-year head coach Gallant.
Hermon features hybrid slotback/linebacker Sam Hopkins, fullback/running back/linebacker Dylan Yeo, quarterback Ethan Curtis and wide receiver Griffin Dunton.
It will be Homecoming and Senior Night in Hermon.
“That place will be crazy. We’re excited about it. We’re looking to rebound,” said Gallant.
At Sanford, the Rams all but sewed up a berth in the Class A North playoffs with their win over Edward Little last Friday night, and they will be looking to build momentum for the playoffs.
Sanford is better than its record indicates as its six losses have come to teams who have a combined record of 29-13.
Explosive Bangor junior slotback/wide receiver Gavin Hughes scored four touchdowns on three short runs and a game-opening 87-yard kickoff return. He now has seven touchdowns in his last two games.
Steadily improving junior quarterback Alex Tennett, who has thrown for 300-plus yards in two of his last four games, completed 8-of-13 passes for 89 yards against EL and he also ran for a 21-yard TD.
Hayden Summerlin caught five passes for 68 yards.

title: ‘Gloves are off’ in Maine’s U.S. Senate race

ORONO, Maine (WABI) - The gloves are off in Maine’s U.S. Senate race.
UMaine Political Science Professor Mark Brewer says advertising is getting more aggressive, and the debates between Sen. Susan Collins and Troy Jackson have gotten testy, with both candidates complaining about personal attacks.
“In Maine at least this is still somewhat unusual. Maine politics tend to be more civil on the whole,” Brewer said. “If you look at American politics more broadly, we’ve almost been now in two decades plus period where the gloves are always off. Our politics haven’t been civil for quite some time.”
Brewer says it just takes a little longer for that tenor to reach Maine, but it shouldn’t be a surprise to anyone watching national politics in recent years.
He thought this week’s visit to Maine by Democrat-turned-Independent Joe Manchin with Collins may have curried favor with undecided voters.
He thinks the high-profile appearance by Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez stumping for Jackson in Portland will not have a similar impact.

title: Newborn safely surrendered to Safe Haven Baby Box that has been used 3 times since it was installed
text:
KNOXVILLE, Tenn. (WVLT/Gray News) – A newborn baby was safely surrendered at a Safe Haven Baby Box at a Knoxville Fire Department Tuesday.
Station 17 received a baby box alert around 7:45 p.m., according to Timothy Woods with the fire department.
The crew at the station went to the box, where they found a healthy baby inside, Woods said. The child was quickly removed from the box for further evaluation before being taken to the hospital.
Woods said this baby box was installed in February 2023, marking the first one in Tennessee. There are now 33 in the state, with the most recent being installed in Sevierville.
This was the third time the baby box has been used since its installation, according to Woods.
How does a Safe Haven Baby Box work?
When a baby is placed inside the climate-controlled box, a silent alarm immediately alerts firefighters, allowing personnel to respond within minutes while preserving the anonymity of the individual surrendering the child.
Surrendered babies are typically adopted by a family within 30 to 45 days.
Officials with the Department of Child Services conduct interviews to find a home for the newborn.
“The Safe Haven Baby Box provides a compassionate option that protects the health and safety of babies while offering hope during a crisis,” Brad Bailey, chairman of The Woodlands Township, said. “We are thankful this baby is safe and commend the Fire Department for its commitment to providing this lifesaving resource to our community.”
The baby box was installed at the fire station in April 2025 and operates under the Texas Safe Haven law.
Resources for the parents
“To the parent, thank you! Thank you for keeping your baby safe and trusting us and the fire dept to take it from here,” Safe Haven Baby Box founder Monica Kelsey said. “We are praying for you!”
Safe Haven Baby Boxes offer free medical and counseling resources for the mother, should she need them.
Counseling services are available based on the birth mother’s schedule and are done online via Zoom at no cost.
If you need help finding a Safe Haven location or would like to speak to a licensed counselor, call the National Safe Haven crisis hotline at 1-866-99BABY1.
Women in crisis can call the national 24-hour hotline and receive counseling and assistance free of charge.

title: Obituary: Merritt Elton Gooding
text:
ABILENE, Texas – Merritt Elton Gooding was a beloved husband, father, grandfather, brother, uncle, and friend. He passed away peacefully at his home in Abilene, Texas, surrounded by his loving family. He will be remembered for his quiet strength, deep love of family, and perfectly timed wit.
Born on May 2, 1949, in Portland, Merritt was the son of Lawrence Merritt Gooding and Gail Marvis Gooding, who preceded him in death.
Merritt graduated from Greely High School in Cumberland in 1967. Before graduating, he joined the Naval Reserve. In 1968, he enlisted in active duty in the United States Navy, proudly serving as a signalman aboard the USS Elokomin.
On Dec. 14, 1968, Merritt married the love of his life, Roenna Nadeen McInnis, in Cumberland Center. Together, they shared 58 wonderful years of marriage, building a life centered on love, devotion, family, and countless cherished memories.
Merritt was the proud father of two sons. His eldest son, Jonathan Terrence Gooding, preceded him in death and is survived by Patricia and their son, Sean Connor Gooding. Merritt is also survived by his youngest son, Merritt Tracy Gooding, and his wife, Erica, and their son, Merritt Reece Gooding. His children and grandchildren were his greatest joy, and the time they shared will be treasured always.
Merritt is also survived by his sister, Moira Gooding Vincent, and her husband, Glenn. He leaves behind his nephew, Todd Vincent, Todd’s wife, Shanda, and their son, Chandler, as well as his niece, Amy Vincent Cross, Amy’s husband, Bruce, and their daughter, Madison. He cherished his extended family and the special relationships they shared.
Merritt found joy in the things he loved most. He enjoyed riding his Harley-Davidson motorcycle, reminiscing about his beloved 1957 Chevy, walking along the rocks at Two Lights, and spending time with family. These simple pleasures brought him happiness and created many cherished memories throughout his life.
Merritt was a humble man who carried himself with quiet strength. Though he never sought attention, his presence made an impression. When he spoke, people listened, and his thoughtful observations and quick sense of humor often caught others by surprise and brought laughter to those around him.
Merritt will be deeply missed, forever loved, and never forgotten. His memory will live on in the hearts of all who knew him.

text:
Average price of heating oil in Maine reaches new all-time high less than a month after previous record was set
DOER says the average statewide price of heating oil was $6.04 per gallon as of Oct. 19. The previous record high of $6.02 per gallon was set on Sept. 21.
Average price of heating oil in Maine reaches new all-time high less than a month after previous record was set
DOER says the average statewide price of heating oil was $6.04 per gallon as of Oct. 19. The previous record high of $6.02 per gallon was set on Sept. 21.
For the second time in a month's span, the average statewide price of heating oil in Maine has hit a new record high.
The Maine Department of Energy Resources (DOER) announced Thursday that its latest weekly survey of Maine heating fuel prices shows the average statewide price of heating oil was $6.04 per gallon as of Monday, Oct. 19. The previous record high average statewide price of $6.02 per gallon was set on Sept. 21.
According to the DOER's weekly surveys, the average statewide price of heating oil dipped to $5.96 by Sept. 28 and was at $5.97 per gallon the next two weeks before rising to $6.04 per gallon.
The DOER said the average statewide price of $6.04 per gallon marked an 83% increase in price from this time last year. Based on a standard 275-gallon oil tank, Maine residents are estimated to pay approximately $750 more to fill their tank to capacity than they would have one year ago, according to the DOER.
"Maine has broken yet another record for heating oil prices, putting even more pressure on families as winter approaches," Acting DOER Commissioner Celina Cunningham said in a statement. "With rising costs and cold weather on the way, I encourage Maine people to stay informed of current prices, review incentive options through Efficiency Maine, and to contact their Community Action Agency if they need immediate relief."
State officials said Maine consumes more residential heating oil per capita than any other state and consumes significantly more per capita than other New England states. Approximately 50% of all Maine households rely on fuel oil as their primary heat source, but the DOER noted that figure has declined steadily from 70% in 2010.
Last month, projections from the National Energy Assistance Directors Association indicated that Maine households are expected to spend an average of $2,939 to heat their homes with heating oil this winter.
On Wednesday, the U.S. Department of Energy announced that it will make up to 315,000 barrels of heating oil available from the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve in an effort to increase supply and bring down prices.
The latest heating fuel prices are available to view on the DOER website and are updated weekly during the heating season. The DOER is encouraging Maine residents to review the department's Winter Heating Guide for helpful tips and resources related to winter heating, including information about financial assistance for home heating and cost-saving home efficiency incentives.

title: Two-part workshop will explore gentle, mindful approaches to living well with pain
text:
ELLSWORTH — Healthy Acadia invites community members to join a two-part Mindfulness for Pain Management workshop series on Tuesday, Nov. 10 and Thursday, Nov. 12 from 10 a.m. to 12 p.m. at 77 Beechland Road.
Participants will explore practical ways to work with pain by bringing awareness, acceptance, and self-compassion to their experience. This gentle, evidence-based approach can help ease the intensity of pain, reduce stress and support overall well-being.
Led in a supportive, small-group setting, these workshops are designed for anyone living with chronic pain or interested in learning mindful self-care strategies. Sessions will include guided practices, discussion, and simple techniques that can be used in daily life to cultivate resilience and calm.
Participation is free, and all are welcome. Pre-registration is required. To register, visit https://forms.gle/wQVePr11CCeiH8Ux6.
Sonya Connelly has served as Healthy Acadia’s communications and community outreach coordinator since 2020. She holds a master’s degree in counseling and has extensive experience in bereavement support and spiritual formation. With decades of experience in mindfulness, meditation, and contemplative practices, Connelly is passionate about simplicity and the slow living approach.
For additional information about this and future mindfulness events or to learn more about other programs focused on building skills that promote mindful living, please contact Ursula Hanson at ursula@healthyacadia.org or Connelly at sonya.connelly@healthyacadia.org.
Healthy Acadia is a 501(C)(3) community health organization dedicated to building vibrant communities and making it easier for everyone to lead healthy lives. They serve Washington and Hancock counties, providing additional community health support and leadership throughout Maine. title: Celebrating Al Gardner: A life bridging music, martial arts, and community in the Midcoast
text:
In his book “Town Meeting,” Donald Robinson writes about “bridging people” — individuals who bind the fabric of a community together, connecting generations, traditions, and people who might otherwise never cross paths. Al Gardner, also known as Alan Shavarsh Bardezbanian, was one of those people.
On Friday, Nov. 13, at 7:30 p.m., the Chocolate Church will host Celebrating Al, commemorating 20 years since his passing and honoring his extraordinary impact on our community.
Al was many things to many people. For some, he was an extraordinary musician — a virtuoso of the oud, a composer and multi-instrumentalist — who helped bring Armenian, Turkish, Greek, and Arabic music to Maine. For others, he was a grand master of martial arts who taught generations of children and adults at his dojo on Front Street in Bath.
I first learned about Al from Georgetown musician and community organizer Fateh Azzam, who brought us the idea for this celebration.
“Al was the kindest and warmest human being you’d ever want to meet,” Fateh told me. “His impact is still felt today, 20 years after his untimely passing, by the community of Middle Eastern musicians he helped create and nurture.”
That impact is equally felt by his martial arts students.
Leon Doyle began studying with Al at 17. “I wanted something deeper, something more. I found that with him.” When I asked Leon for one word to describe Al, he answered: “Presence. An intensity of presence. That type of thing is rare.”
And Al devoted his life not simply to practicing martial arts, but to bringing people from very different facets of the community together through them. Leon told me, “There was quite a broad spectrum of people as it should be. All these other differences melt away and you’re left with the art form where everyone is united.”
His dear friend Shane McKenna shared, “If you knew Al, you were a better person. He changed and affected a lot of people’s lives.”
What fascinates me is Al’s dual devotion to martial arts and music. Shane McKenna, whose sons studied with Al, told me, “I never knew about his talent as a musician. I never knew he would go home from the dojo and play the oud all night long.”
Having myself studied tae kwon do for over 20 years, while devoting my professional life to the performing arts, I find myself wondering about the connection. Perhaps it’s spirit. Both disciplines cultivate an embodied expression of energy, presence, and something larger than ourselves. Al devoted himself not simply to mastering these practices, but to bringing others along on the journey.
The Nov. 13 celebration will feature Al’s musical compositions and beloved Middle Eastern songs performed by the Al-Mashreq Ensemble, personal remembrances, a martial arts demonstration, and images from his remarkable life.
Another former student, Sensei Heid Fenwicki, recalled, “There was a degree of magic. You could feel it in the dojo.” Twenty years later, that magic is still felt. What a beautiful legacy to celebrate together. And what a great time to remember, it is people like Al, who remind us that it isn’t the people of prominence or political power, but bridging people like Al, who bind us and make us one.
Matthew Glassman is executive and artistic director of the Chocolate Church Arts Center in Bath.

title: CLT’s ‘Cabaret’ continues this weekend
text:
The L/A Community Little Theatre production of the classic musical “Cabaret” continues this weekend, October 22-25.
Since its Broadway debut in 1966, “Cabaret” has captivated audiences with its subversive plot and groundbreaking storytelling. Set in a seedy Berlin nightclub in the final years of the Weimar Republic in Germany, the musical portrays a society on the brink of collapse, using the Kit Kat Club as both a space of liberation and a harbinger of impending authoritarianism. As fascism rises outside its doors, the club’s revelers dance in a haze of sex, cynicism, and cabaret. Costume design has played a crucial role in shaping audience interpretations of the show’s themes, characters, and historical context.
Remaining performances will be held on October 22, 23, and 24 at 7:30 p.m., and October 25 at 2:00 p.m. All shows will be held at CLT on 30 Academy Street in Auburn. Tickets are available online at www.laclt.com and will also be available at the door. Due to the mature themes in this production, parental discretion is advised.

title: FTC sues ticket broker accused of cheating limits to hoard high-demand event tickets
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray News) - The Federal Trade Commission is suing a ticket broker accused of using unlawful tactics to buy millions of tickets to popular events.
The complaint, filed by the Department of Justice, alleges REPS & Company Inc., along with its CEO Ryan Pancheri, President Brian Archibald and Chief Operating Officer Nicholas Totagrande, violated the Better Online Ticket Sales Act.
The law makes it illegal to “circumvent a security measure, access control system or other technological control or measure on an Internet website or online service that is used by the ticket issuer to enforce posted event ticket limits or to maintain the integrity of posted online ticket purchasing order rules.”
The complaint alleges that since 2022, REPS and its operators used unlawful tactics to bypass ticket issuers’ security measures and exceed posted ticket limits.
REPS purchased more than eight tickets for at least 83,500 events — many in high demand and likely to sell out. REPS spent more than $1.3 billion to amass more than 18.5 million tickets, generating at least $120.8 million in profit by reselling them, the complaint says.
For example, REPS generated $833,000 in profit by using 1,300 accounts to purchase 7,624 tickets to one Beyoncé Renaissance tour concert in Kansas City, Missouri, in 2023, according to the complaint.
“Companies that seek to profit by driving up prices or depriving ordinary fans of access to reasonably priced tickets to their favorite shows or events should be on notice that we are watching and will take action to stop this unlawful conduct,” Christopher Mufarrige, Director of the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection, said.
Ticket issuers such as Ticketmaster and AXS have measures to block resellers from violating purchase limits. The complaint alleges REPS uses employees, most of whom are based in the Philippines, to bypass Ticketmaster and other issuers’ account security measures.
The alleged methods include using thousands of purchasing accounts created with other people’s names, addresses or phone numbers, along with virtual credit card accounts and phone numbers controlled by REPS. Employees also used IP proxy services and multisession browsers that mask a user’s identity and location, the complaint alleges.
When ticket issuers detect attempts to bypass limits, they often block or cancel the purchase. REPS developed strategies to work around those controls, such as making slight changes to an account holder’s address or name, the complaint alleges. Internal company documents show REPS officials discussed tactics to keep accounts from being blocked.
The commission voted 2-0 to refer the complaint to the Justice Department for filing. The department filed the complaint on behalf of the commission in U.S. District Court for the Southern District of California.

title: More than 4 million tubes of toothpaste, including popular children’s brand, recalled
text:
(Gray News) - More than 4 million tubes of toothpaste, including a popular children’s brand, have been recalled.
The Food and Drug Administration reported that several varieties of Brush Buddies toothpaste have been recalled. The recalled toothpastes include Barbie-, Hot Wheels-, My Little Pony- and Crayola-branded flavors.

Lots of Evo advanced whitening and sensitive toothpaste, as well as ARU gum health and cavity protection toothpaste were also recalled.
The recalled toothpastes were all distributed by Ashtel Studios Inc. in Ontario, California, and sold nationwide.
A full list of the impacted toothpastes and their corresponding lot numbers can be found on the recall’s enforcement report.
The recall was first initiated on Sept. 10, 2026. Its certification was updated to a Class II recall on Oct. 22.
A Class II recall signifies that using the affected product could result in “temporary or medically reversible adverse health consequences.” However, the likelihood of having a severe “health consequence” is very low.
On the recall’s enforcement report, the reason for the recall is listed as deviations in “current good manufacturing practice.” However, the FDA did not disclose any further details about the cause of the recall.

The teams, picked by staff members, will take into account several factors, including success stories, bounce-back efforts and notable accomplishments, among others. Athletes, coaches and athletic directors can nominate teams by emailing sports editor Bill Stewart at [email protected] or Varsity Maine editor Lee Horton at [email protected].
Varsity Maine Boys Team of the Week: Biddeford football
Biddeford was a clear underdog heading into its game against then-undefeated Marshwood. The Tigers, though, were unfazed.
“ I tell the kids to pursue excellence,” coach Steve Allosso said. “They grasped excellence the second half of that game, because Marshwood is an outstanding team.”
With a 5-2 record, Biddeford is ranked third in the Class B South Heal point standings heading into its regular-season finale Friday against Cheverus. Last year, the Tigers finished 1-7.
Senior quarterback Ernie Dore says that experience has played a large role in this season’s turnaround.
“ A lot of guys this year (were) starting last year on both sides,” Dore said. “I think that’s really played a factor.”
Despite injuries that forced Biddeford to use second- or third-string players at points this fall, including against Marshwood, junior receiver/running back Estevao Lembissa says that the win over an undefeated team is just a glimpse of the Tigers’ potential.
“ It’s the best we played all season, in my opinion,” Lembissa said. “ We gotta bring that to next week, because we have nothing to lose.”
A win over Cheverus would likely give Biddeford the No. 2 seed in the playoffs and a first-round bye. It would also mean a chance for the Tigers to play in front of a home crowd in the semifinals.
“ Last year, they supported us a lot, even when we were 1-7,” Dore said. “ Now, there’s a lot more people supporting us.”

title: Maine man who drove over his wife with a truck dies a year into murder sentence
text:
Maine man who drove over his wife with a truck dies a year into murder sentence
A man from Norway who stabbed his wife and then drove over her body with his pickup truck and left her body in their driveway has died in prison, a year after he was sentenced for murder.
Prosecutors said Andrew St. George, who was 61 at the time of the crime, confessed to his son.
The Maine Department of Corrections says St. George, 64, died at about 9:20 a.m. on Tuesday. He had been incarcerated at the Mountain View Correctional Facility since he started serving a 37-year sentence last year.
His cause of death was not immediately released.
He killed his estranged wife, Barbara St. George, in July of 2023 at their home on Greenwood Road in Norway. Andrew St. George was still at the property when officers arrived. Authorities said he was treated for superficial wounds.
He pleaded not guilty that year.

title: Election night vigil and open sanctuary at Old South First Congregational Church
Maine bill seeks to replace ‘unenrolled’ with ‘independent’ on voter forms
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) - A proposal at the State House could change how Maine identifies voters who are not affiliated with a political party.
Maine state Rep. David Boyer, R-Poland, announced legislation Wednesday to replace “unenrolled” with “independent” on voter registration forms and election records.
Boyer said the term “unenrolled” does not accurately describe voters without a party affiliation. He said confusion surfaced during June’s primary when some voters were unsure whether their “unenrolled” status allowed them to vote in a party primary. Others mistakenly registered with the Green Independent Party.
The bill would change the terminology but not voter rights or Maine’s primary system.
“People identify as independent,” Boyer said. “They don’t go around and, you know, tell somebody that they’re an unenrolled voter and that they don’t have a party. They say they’re independent.”
“This is why it’s a common-sense change,” he said.
Supporters cite voter numbers
Brett Loyd, President and CEO of The Bipartisan Bullfinch Group and Founding Partner of the Independent Center, supports the proposal.
“In Maine, if you look at the voter registration statistics, a third of the vote, there’s more independents in Maine than there are Republicans, and only about a point shy from Democrats,” Loyd said.
“This is something that truly is impacting one in three voters in Maine,” he said.
Clerk raises concern over confusion
Bath City Clerk and President of the Maine Town & City Clerks’ Association Darci Wheeler said the change could create another layer of confusion because Maine already has the Green Independent Party.
“We need to make sure voters can clearly distinguish between someone who is not enrolled in a political party and someone who has chosen to enroll in the Green Independent Party,” Wheeler said.
Wheeler said more voter education outside of the booth may be the better solution. She said clerks can explain that “unenrolled” means “no party choice,” but in order to stay neutral, they cannot explain political parties to voters.
Boyer’s bill is expected to receive a public hearing early next year.

title: Butterstamp Workshop Owners Retire After 47 Years
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A Wiscasset store selling butter stamps and beeswax ornaments is closing its doors on Saturday, Oct. 31.
Opened by Lois and David Kwantz in 1979, Butterstamp Workshop carries reproduction molds of antique butter stamps and beeswax ornaments made by the couple.
A butter stamp is a piece of folk art, an art form Lois Kwantz described as art done by a person with no formal training in the craft. A dairy farmer would stamp butter to decorate it and increase its price, as well as mark the butter as coming from their farm.
Butter stamps are uncommon today because of how butter is shipped, Lois Kwantz said. When butter is stacked, it flattens into the rectangular shapes sold in stores.
Butter stamps and other pieces of folk art appeal to people because they do not look manufactured, according to Lois Kwantz.
“The antique butter molds, the people who did the carving and that type of thing, they just learned it through practice and you know that type of thing, and that’s actually what we did,” Lois Kwantz said.
In 1979, Lois and David Kwantz moved to Wiscasset and began learning how to reproduce antique mold designs from Philip Thomas, a Wiscasset resident and folk artist who used butter stamps to create molds. That same year, they opened a store selling their molds, as well as gravestone carving reproductions they sourced from a friend.
Butterstamps and Gravestones, as the store was originally called, kept its name until the 1990s, when the owners changed the name to the Butterstamp Workshop to better reflect their inventory, David Kwantz said.
The two came to Wiscasset familiar with the area from purchasing antiques. The two had a lifelong love of old houses and items, Lois Kwantz said. They balanced the store with David Kwantz’s work at Bath Iron Works.
While the store specializes in butter stamps, the owners said any shape can be a mold. Lois Kwantz uses polyurethane, a material known for versatility and durability, to recreate the shape of many items.
“I love chocolate and he came in with this package of a claddagh for me, that was a piece of chocolate, a piece of candy,” Lois Kwantz said. “I thought he had brought it for me and I started to open it up and he went, ‘No, no, no!’ he said, ‘You’re going to glue it down into one of the takeout trays and make a polyurethane mold of it.’”
The business later expanded into selling beeswax ornaments. David Kwantz said this was in response to customers asking if they sold anything with lobsters on them. Lois Kwantz found patterns and created molds for him to pour beeswax into.
“It became terribly lucrative,” David Kwantz said. “We worried at first that it would take sales away but in fact, it enhanced sales like crazy.”
The idea to use beeswax was based off folk art, specifically a tradition where German women took their beeswax to the gingerbread bakers’ guild and poured it into their molds, David Kwantz said.
“All of a sudden, farm women could have what city women had, which is some art on their walls, because you could, in fact, hang the piece of beeswax and paint it,” David Kwantz said.
The store was open seasonally, and during the winter, the owners sold their products at fairs or outside stores. Last year, health problems began impeding the owners’ ability to maintain the store’s hours. Keeping the store open also prevented them from spending time with family, Lois Kwantz said.
The owners announced on June 6 on Facebook they would close the store on Oct. 31. Closing the store also meant selling their inventory, including the approximately 325 antique stamps.
On July 11, Instagram user @katyelliott posted about the store to her channel. As of Tuesday, Oct. 20, the video post has 474,000 views, 12,900 likes, and 5,061 shares. After the post gained traction, the store had 200 or more customers each day.
“As ex-teachers, the education of the history and showing people and telling people how they could use a butter mold and all of that was very important to us and with that many people coming in all at once, I couldn’t stop and do that each time,” Lois Kwantz said.
At first, the uptick frustrated her, Lois Kwantz said, as it was hard to keep up with increased demand and David Kwantz had to pause his beeswax pouring. At the same time, the increased sales made a “significant difference” for their retirement fund, she said.
After the closure, Lois and David Kwantz will take time to rest and move to a retirement home in Kennebunk.
“I won’t have to be responsible for anything other than just to go and sing with the church choir,” Lois Kwantz said.
The Butterstamp Workshop is located at 55 Middle St. in Wiscasset. For more information, call 882-7825, find the shop on Facebook, or email [email protected].

title: Affordability and accountability top priorities for Hobson in House 48 race
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
If elected, Erik Hobson, R-Boothbay, said he hopes to bring accountability and transparency to Augusta as the representative for House District 48.
Hobson faces Charlotte Nutt, D-Edgecomb, in the race to represent the district, which consists of Boothbay, Boothbay Harbor, Edgecomb, South Bristol, and Southport. Rep. Holly Stover, D-Boothbay, is serving her fourth and final term.
Originally from Traverse City, Mich., Hobson moved to Maine eight years ago with his family. He now lives on Barters Island in Boothbay. He graduated from Arizona State University in 2002 with degrees in anthropology and psychology.
Hobson began his career in computer sales. He later worked for Child Protective Services while living in Arizona and is now an insurance claims manager.
Although Hobson has not previously held an elected position, he said he believes his experience negotiating and handling stressful situations in the insurance industry has prepared him for legislative work.
“There’s a lot of negotiating … it’s working with others that have a different opinion from what I have,” he said. “So the ability to find that commonality will help (in the Legislature).”
If elected, he said he plans on prioritizing reducing government spending, making housing affordable, and attracting and retaining new Maine residents.
Hobson said he is concerned about barriers faced by young families hoping to move to, or stay in, Maine and find housing. He said affordable housing is one of the most pressing concerns House District 48 voters have voiced to him.
Potential solutions to alleviate the stress of rising housing costs includes a credit or subsidy system for first-time homeowners, as well as improving home internet infrastructure to incentivize remote workers to come to Maine. He referenced Starlink as one of the internet solutions, the company founded by SpaceX.
“We have to build some of that infrastructure as well, but with Starlink, anybody can pop one of those on at their house, so why not have a credit for that?” he said.
Hobson identified the growing usage of homes as short-term rentals, homes owned by private equity firms, and part-time housing as contributing factors to the housing availability and affordability issue.
“We are seeing too many of our homes being purchased by people that do not live here, so they are not invested in our community,” he said.
Another issue brought up by Hobson is property taxes, which he said can pose an “undue burden” on seniors and veterans looking for housing. To counter this, he said he supports expanding the state Homestead Exemption Program, which currently offers permanent residents a property tax exemption of up to $25,000.
In regard to education, Hobson said more accountability and transparency in spending is needed to address both the housing affordability crisis and issues he sees within Maine’s schools.
“If we have continued declining enrollment, why do we continue to throw more tax dollars at our school system?” he said. “I’m not sure that’s the right answer.”
Hobson said he supports evaluating the ratio between administrators and students in a school and investing money from the education budget into small businesses instead. He also voiced concerns about the quality of education in Maine schools, which he said has declined in recent years.
Potential solutions for this decline would come from “focusing on those core subjects: reading, writing, and arithmetic,” he said.
“It seems that every time Maine is mentioned in the papers, especially as far as education goes, we continue to decline,” Hobson said.
Other ideas Hobson has for education includes expanding educational pathways outside of college, such as training programs for different trades, by establishing more vocational learning centers around the state. He said his son attended the Bath Regional Career and Technical Center and that it was a “great experience.”
He said it is important for students to have a stake in their education and that the individual responsibility is a broader value he wants to bring to the legislature if elected.
“We want to make sure that we have opportunities for kids to not only go to a traditional junior college or four-year college but also make sure that we provide assistance for technical (education) as well,” Hobson said. “College isn’t the answer for everybody, so make sure that we have a pathway for trades as well.”
Hobson said the challenges facing House District 48 voters are interconnected and cannot be solved individually. If elected, he plans to address the rising cost of living in the Midcoast region. Hobson said he supports no tax on tips or overtime and wants to reduce state spending as a way to increase affordability.
He said by reducing spending, taxes will also be reduced.
“We can’t simply throw money at healthcare and then expect our, you know, population to increase,” Hobson said. “We can’t throw money at healthcare and expect housing to become affordable, to throw money at housing and expect our education system to get better.”
Hobson is running as a clean elections candidate under the Maine Clean Elections Act. Candidates who participate in the voluntary program must receive a certain number of $5 donations from voters in their district in order to qualify. Once a part of the program, candidates cannot raise or spend any private money and can only use funds granted by the Maine Clean Election Fund, which are disbursed in equal amounts to candidates.
He said Republican Party members advised him run as a clean elections candidate. He opposes lobbyist money in politics and believes the limitations on private donations give all candidates a fair opportunity to run.
If elected, Hobson said he wants to bring compromise into the governing process.
“We then have to find the lowest common denominator, that thing that we all believe in together,” he said. “Do we agree on making Maine better? OK, we can both start from there.”
For more information, go to hobsonforhouse.com or email hobsonforhouse@gmail.com.
The general election is on Tuesday, Nov. 3.

title: Letter: Don’t miss this chance to reelect Susan Collins

title: Retired NYPD detective arrested in road rage killing on George Washington Bridge
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — A long-retired New York City police detective was arrested Wednesday in the road rage killing of a motorist on the George Washington Bridge, police said.
Victor Romero, 62, was charged with murder in the death of Koran Irvine, 46, who was found just after 7 p.m. Tuesday wounded and unconscious in the driver’s seat of a vehicle on the New Jersey-bound side of the bridge’s upper level.
Irvine, of Valley Cottage, New York, was pronounced dead at a hospital. The shooting near the end of the evening rush snarled traffic for hours on the busy Hudson River span that connects Manhattan and Fort Lee, New Jersey.
Romero, of Haverstraw, New York, retired from the New York Police Department in 2001 after he was wounded in the hand and chest in an off-duty shootout with men attempting to rob his family’s Brooklyn laundromat in June 2000. Using his service weapon, Romero shot one of the men in the stomach, arm and leg, and another man in the legs, according to news accounts from the time.
A telephone number listed for Romero in public records rang unanswered. Information on a lawyer who could comment on his behalf was not immediately available. Romero, a drug detective in Brooklyn, had been working for the NYPD for six years when the laundromat shooting occurred, according to a New York Post article from the time.
Irvine worked for Con Edison, the utility said in a statement, calling the shooting a “senseless act of violence.”
“Our deepest condolences go out to his family, friends, colleagues, and everyone who knew and loved him,” the company said.
Closed bridge lanes reopened about five hours after the shooting, the span’s operator, the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey, said.
Opened to traffic in 1931, the iconic, double-decked bridge carries around 100 million vehicles each year, according to the Port Authority, which calls it the world’s busiest. The bridge and its entrances are teeming with cameras.
Its entrances can be difficult to navigate, as drivers often veer across packed lanes, causing heavy traffic even under normal circumstances.

title: Lidl recalls gelato for possible Listeria contamination
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(CNN) — Lidl is recalling some gelato over a possible Listeria contamination, according to the FDA.
The recall involves Gelatelli Coffee & Vanilla Gelato with Coffee Sauce & Cookie Pieces.
The product was sold at Lidl stores in nine states, including Delaware, Georgia, Maryland, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, South Carolina and Virginia. It was also sold in Washington, D.C.
The containers have a best-by date of March 26, 2028.
Lidl said routine testing detected Listeria in a sample.

title: Iran says 7 oil tankers were attacked in the Strait of Hormuz as fears grow of a return to war
text:
TEL AVIV, Israel (AP) — Seven oil tankers caught fire or were damaged in the Strait of Hormuz overnight after being hit by Iran or striking naval mines, Tehran said Thursday, a markedly high number as tensions rise over concerns about a return to all-out war.
With days before a close election in Israel in which Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu could lose power, and before next month’s U.S. midterm election in which war-linked high prices have sparked voter anger, there are concerns that U.S.-Israeli attacks on Iran could resume.
“Netanyahu wants to attack Iran, that’s not even a question,” Danny Citrinowicz, a researcher at Israel’s Institute for National Security Studies and a former Iran specialist in Israel’s military and intelligence services, told The Associated Press.
He accused Israel of rushing into another round with Iran without revamping its strategy. A clear Netanyahu victory in the Oct. 27 election means an attack is almost guaranteed, he said.
Main opposition candidates are likely to focus on domestic issues first, but Citrinowicz said he believed the region is on the way toward “another kinetic escalation.”
Iran repeats threat to attack U.S. bases in the region
Iranian state television reported the claims about the latest attacks on ships, which the AP couldn’t independently confirm. The report cited the Revolutionary Guard Corps navy, which again threatened to strike U.S. military bases in the region if the U.S. keeps helping to guide commercial ships through the strait.
The report didn’t mention casualties. Iran still asserts control over the waterway, a central point of leverage in any talks with the U.S. over the war.
October has had the most reported attacks on commercial shipping since March in the war’s opening weeks, according to a British military monitor, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations. UKMTO didn’t report the latest attacks, but it has noted new reluctance by some shippers to report incidents.
Oil producers have found ways to keep crude flowing, experts say, but at a mounting cost.
Tankers continue moving through Strait of Hormuz despite attacks
Oil tankers are still moving oil through the strait under U.S. military protection despite the recent upsurge in attacks, according to shipping data and analysis company Lloyd’s List Intelligence.
Tanker operators willing to risk the voyage have been shuttling oil from Gulf producers through the strait at night with their location systems and mobile phones turned off using a U.S.-protected lane near the coast of Oman. Those tankers transfer oil to other tankers waiting in the Gulf of Oman for shipment to customers in Asia.
Those “active Gulf operators show little sign of retreating” despite 28 attacks on ships in October, the highest since the start of the war, Lloyd’s said in an online webinar Thursday.
The so-called “dark shuttle” overseen by U.S. Central Command has helped return oil shipments from the Gulf at roughly prewar levels, but at high costs in time, money and sailors’ lives. Spot charter rates for tankers have soared into the hundreds of thousands of dollars a day, while the ship-to-ship transfers can take several days.
UN urges US and Iran to return to diplomacy to end conflict, reopen strait
U.N. spokesman Stephane Dujarric said no commercial ships should be attacked and called for diplomacy between the U.S. and Iran to reopen the strait.
“For the sake of the people of the region and for the broader world, we need to see that waterway reopen, and we need to see tensions go down,” he told reporters Thursday.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on Wednesday said Tehran remains open to diplomacy, but is ready to defend itself.
Iran has warned that it learned important military lessons from the war that began with U.S. and Israeli attacks on Feb. 28, indicating in recent days that it could expand targets to include infrastructure such as undersea cables and data centers.
The United States, for its part, is sending more military assets to the region, including a third aircraft carrier and thousands of troops, to join the largest force of American warships and aircraft in the Middle East in decades.
Mediators, meanwhile, have been trying to bring Washington and Tehran back to formal talks.
Iran still promotes its latest proposal to end the war and fully open the strait within a week if the U.S. meets several conditions, including ending the U.S. blockade of Iranian ports. It echoes conditions in the deal that fell apart within days of both sides signing it in June.
U.S. President Donald Trump rejected the latest proposal last month, but both sides acknowledged that indirect discussions have continued.
The stakes are even higher if all-out war resumes
A return to full fighting would again endanger civilians throughout the region and complicate global deliveries of oil, natural gas and related products like fertilizer from the region and likely bring another spike in prices.
The head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, this week acknowledged that the Islamic Republic will suffer under a prolonged U.S. blockade. But economic pain and strategic collapse are not the same thing, he added, according to Iran’s state-run IRNA news agency.
Now the conflict has widened with the recent surge in fighting between Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia. The Saudi kingdom backs a coalition of forces with Yemen’s internationally recognized government that is fighting the rebels.
The Houthis’ repeated deadly attacks on airports and other facilities inside Saudi Arabia have pressured the close U.S. ally, which has sought military aid.
The escalation also has threatened a crucial shipping corridor, the Bab el-Mandeb at the southern end of the Red Sea.
Meanwhile, the president of Saudi oil company Aramco, whose sites have been targeted by the Houthis, said the amount of oil moving through a pipeline that bypasses the Strait of Hormuz has increased threefold in light of the global energy crisis.
The East-West pipeline’s capacity has surged from two million to seven million barrels each day, Amin Nasser said in an interview with Saudi-owned television Al Arabiya Business. He said the company has been using drones to assess any damage to the pipeline and help with firefighting.

title: ‘Top Gun,’ ‘Alien’ star Tom Skerritt dies at 93
text:
(Gray News) - Emmy Award-winning actor Tom Skerritt, known for his roles in “Alien,” “Top Gun,” “M*A*S*H,” and more, died Wednesday. He was 93.
He died of natural causes, according to The Associated Press.
“While the world knew Tom through his remarkable acting career, we knew him for his humor, curiosity, wisdom, generosity, and the love he brought into our lives,” his family wrote in a statement issued to media outlets, including People.
Skerritt was born in 1933 in Detroit.
After enlisting in the U.S. Air Force for four years, he attended Henry Ford College, Wayne State University, and the University of California, Los Angeles. He left school to pursue acting.
Skerritt was twice nominated for an Emmy — both for “Picket Fences,” winning outstanding lead actor in a drama series in 1993. Other career highlights include playing the patient husband of Shirley MacLaine in “Turning Point,” Sally Field’s husband in “Steel Magnolias,” and a scheming opportunist who stands in the way of Jodie Foster’s attempt to communicate with extraterrestrial life in “Contact.”
“A writer once described me as a character actor locked in a leading man’s body, and I’ve always loved that. It’s a nice compliment. I’ve been able to walk the line between television and features,” he told the Seattle Post-Intelligencer in 1997.
Onstage, he was the narrator in “Our Town” at Seattle’s Intiman Theatre in 2004 and made his Broadway debut in 2013 in an adaptation of John Grisham’s “A Time to Kill,” in which The Associated Press wrote he “nicely pulls off a charming disgraced and drunken lawyer.”
Funeral plans were not immediately available.

title: Retired NYPD detective arrested in road rage killing on George Washington Bridge
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — A long-retired New York City police detective was arrested Wednesday in the road rage killing of a motorist on the George Washington Bridge, police said.
Victor Romero, 62, was charged with murder in the death of Koran Irvine, 46, who was found just after 7 p.m. Tuesday wounded and unconscious in the driver’s seat of a vehicle on the New Jersey-bound side of the bridge’s upper level.
Irvine, of Valley Cottage, New York, was pronounced dead at a hospital. The shooting near the end of the evening rush snarled traffic for hours on the busy Hudson River span that connects Manhattan and Fort Lee, New Jersey.
Romero, of Haverstraw, New York, retired from the New York Police Department in 2001 after he was wounded in the hand and chest in an off-duty shootout with men attempting to rob his family’s Brooklyn laundromat in June 2000. Using his service weapon, Romero shot one of the men in the stomach, arm and leg, and another man in the legs, according to news accounts from the time.
A telephone number listed for Romero in public records rang unanswered. Information on a lawyer who could comment on his behalf was not immediately available. Romero, a drug detective in Brooklyn, had been working for the NYPD for six years when the laundromat shooting occurred, according to a New York Post article from the time.
Irvine worked for Con Edison, the utility said in a statement, calling the shooting a “senseless act of violence.”
“Our deepest condolences go out to his family, friends, colleagues, and everyone who knew and loved him,” the company said.
Closed bridge lanes reopened about five hours after the shooting, the span’s operator, the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey, said.
Opened to traffic in 1931, the iconic, double-decked bridge carries around 100 million vehicles each year, according to the Port Authority, which calls it the world’s busiest. The bridge and its entrances are teeming with cameras.
Its entrances can be difficult to navigate, as drivers often veer across packed lanes, causing heavy traffic even under normal circumstances.

title: Protest over diesel costs tanks Italy's buffalo mozzarella output
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Millions in cheese revenue lost as protest over diesel costs tanks Italy's buffalo mozzarella output
A truckers' protest in southern Italy has halted the production of the famed buffalo mozzarella, causing an estimated loss of 3 million euros in just 24 hours because the milk cannot reach dairies in the Naples region and the finished cheese cannot reach customers, an official said.
Video above: Trump's Russia diesel deal unlikely to curb high costs, experts say
The weeklong strike by truck drivers over the high cost of diesel driven up by the Iran war has also blocked deliveries of other basic goods to supermarkets and left gas pumps empty in much of southern Italy. The government approved new tax breaks for truckers Thursday, but it was too early to tell whether they were enough to end the protest.
The disruption is particularly damaging to buffalo mozzarella because the production of the protected cheese depends on a tightly timed supply chain.
Buffaloes have to be milked regardless of whether dairies are operating, while production rules require that their milk be turned into mozzarella within 60 hours. Buffalo mozzarella is softer, creamier and richer than cow’s-milk mozzarella.
Pier Maria Saccani, director of the Consortium for the Protection of Mozzarella di Bufala Campana DOP, said about 1 million liters of buffalo milk produced on Wednesday couldn't be turned into mozzarella because of the transport blockade. The consortium oversees production standards and protects the designation of origin of the cheese in Italy and abroad.
“Yesterday, no mozzarella was produced,” Saccani said, explaining it was a “3-million-euro block in 24 hours” — a loss of about $3.4 million.
Farmers typically have only enough capacity to hold the fresh milk until dairy trucks collect it and cannot store large quantities for extended periods.
“So this blockade has obviously caused panic among farmers, who say, ‘Where are we going to put it?’” Saccani added.
The dairies making mozzarella cannot afford to accumulate a highly perishable product if trucks are unable to deliver it to customers.
Several dairies have remained closed as a result, Saccani said, describing the situation as a “complete production blockade.”
Unlike false claims this summer that production of Parmigiano Reggiano cheese was in crisis due to extreme heat, buffalo mozzarella output is indeed in jeopardy.
During an extraordinary Cabinet meeting on Thursday, the Italian government led by Premier Giorgia Meloni approved new measures to help truckers and farmers face higher fuel costs, bringing financial aid to those two groups to a combined 540 million euros in tax credits, up from 434 million euros.
Some farmers have resorted to feeding part of the unused milk to their animals because they have nowhere to send it, Saccani said, adding that the transport disruption is also threatening supplies of animal feed and diesel needed to keep farms operating.
“It’s a very, very complex and delicate situation,” he said.
The blockade comes as milk producers and dairies are already confronting higher costs. Saccani said the consortium estimates production costs have risen about 30%, driven by increases in animal feed, diesel, energy, plastic packaging and transportation.
The increases have not been fully passed on to customers, he said, leaving producers to absorb much of the additional expense and cutting into profitability across the supply chain.
Buffalo mozzarella is an important industry in the Campania region, where the city of Naples is located, and in neighboring areas of southern Italy.
Saccani said that in 2025, the production of Mozzarella di Bufala Campana DOP totaled just under 58,000 metric tons, with about 37% of production exported. France is its largest foreign market.

title: Mother accused of drowning newborn whose body was found in motel dumpster days later
text:
FORT WORTH, Texas (Gray News) - A Texas woman is facing charges after investigators say she drowned her newborn daughter in a motel bathtub days before the baby’s body was found in a dumpster.
Avia Lynette Cantrell, 23, is facing a capital murder charge after Fort Worth Police say she drowned her newborn daughter in a motel bathtub. The baby’s body was found in a dumpster outside the motel days later.
Cantrell’s boyfriend, 26-year-old Camron Kyjuan Baker, was also arrested in relation to the case. He is facing a charge of abuse of a corpse.
Police responded about 8:40 p.m. Sunday to a Fort Worth motel after a baby was found in a dumpster outside. The baby was taken to the hospital, where they were pronounced dead, KTVT reports.
Surveillance footage from Sunday afternoon showed a woman putting a box of items, including a car seat, into the dumpster. The motel manager identified the woman as Cantrell, according to an arrest affidavit obtained by The Dallas Morning News.
Investigators questioned Cantrell, who admitted to giving birth last Wednesday morning in her motel bathtub, the affidavit says. She allegedly told detectives she left the baby girl face down in the water for about 30 minutes until she believed the newborn was dead.
Cantrell called Baker at work and told him the baby had died, according to Baker’s arrest warrant. The couple allegedly kept the newborn’s body in a bag near the toilet for four days before police say Baker put the body in the motel dumpster.
“Heartbreaking doesn’t even begin to describe this case,” Fort Worth Police Chief Eddie Garcia told WFAA. “Our thoughts are with everyone affected by the loss of this child.”
Baker told detectives the couple did not seek medical help because they feared facing criminal charges, according to the affidavit. He allegedly disposed of the baby’s body after Cantrell asked him to, saying she couldn’t do it herself.
Cantrell is being held on $2 million bond, and Baker is being held on $250,000 bond, online records show. The investigation is ongoing.
Following the incident, Fort Worth Police are reminding everyone of Texas’ Baby Moses Law. The law allows a parent to safely and legally surrender an unharmed newborn at a designated location without fear of being prosecuted for abandonment.
“Every baby deserves a safe beginning,” police wrote in a Facebook post. “If you or someone you know is facing a situation where caring for a newborn feels impossible, help is available. You are not alone, and there are safe options that can protect both you and your baby.”

title: EMDC Comprehensive Economic Development Strategy approved
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The U.S. Economic Development Administration approved Eastern Maine Development Corporation ‘s Comprehensive Economic Development Strategy, confirming its EDA funding eligibility and reinforcing its designation as an Economic Development District through March 31, 2031.
Through a series of meetings involving 75 participants and several keynote speakers, the CEDS process established a strategic roadmap for regional economic development focused on building local capacity, strengthening economic resilience and advancing long-term prosperity across the region. The EMDC plan was developed in coordination with Maine’s 10-Year Economic Development Strategy to align regional priorities with statewide economic goals and the priorities of the current federal administration.
“Maine has always been nimble in demonstrating resilience and determination in navigating all kinds of economic challenges ranging from mill closures to the COVID-19 pandemic,” EMDC President & CEO Lee Umphrey said. “We are adept at embracing new opportunities made possible by a strong education and workforce development system that prepares communities and businesses for the future. This report reflects Maine’s resilience in attracting new industries and protecting our natural resources while recruiting, training, and retaining the workforce needed for economic growth and prosperity.”
Umphrey added, “Key community stakeholders and several EMDC staff members, especially our colleague Jaida Bolstridge, compliance & development analyst, guided the creation of a report that will serve as a catalyst for new ideas and endeavors.”

title: Country singer John Anderson has died at 71
text:
John Anderson, voice behind 'Seminole Wind,' dies at age 71
Singer John Anderson, a Country Music Hall of Fame member, has died. He was 71.
The Tennessean and Rolling Stone report that representatives for the country music singer confirmed he died Wednesday. The Tennessean reports that Anderson, known for songs like "Seminole Wind" and "Black Sheep," died at his home in Smithville, Tennessee.
Anderson's family also confirmed his death in a post on his official Facebook page, saying that he was a "beloved husband, father, grandfather, and best friend."
Related video above: Remembering those we've lost in 2026
A native of Apopka, Florida, Anderson was inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 2024. He had dozens of hit songs and was best known for his tunes from the 1980s and 1990s, including "Straight Tequila Night," "Money in the Bank," "Swingin'" and "Wild and Blue."
"To the world, he was a gifted country music singer whose voice and songs touched countless lives. To us, he was so much more. He was the heart of our family, the one who made us laugh, loved us fiercely, and made every ordinary moment feel special," his family wrote in the social media post. "We are completely heartbroken. His music will live on, but for us, his greatest legacy will always be the love he gave his family and the memories we will carry with us forever. Please keep our family in your thoughts and prayers as we grieve this unimaginable loss."
Further details about Anderson's cause and manner of death haven't been publicly released.
Anderson's last known public appearance came just a few days before his death, when he attended the induction Medallion Ceremony for the Class of 2026 inductees to the Country Music Hall of Fame in Nashville.
Tim McGraw, Paul Overstreet, and the Stanley Brothers were inducted into the Hall of Fame on Oct. 18, according to the Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum website.
Anderson was in the audience, according to one of the inductees.
In a social media post on Wednesday night, now-fellow Hall of Famer Tim McGraw said he was "completely shook" by the news of Anderson's death.
"I was talking with John Sunday night at the HOF ceremony. He was in such good spirits. We talked, we laughed, we sang his songs that I loved so much together, just goofing off. I am completely heartbroken by his passing. There will never be a stylist in music, any music, that was so defining as his. It’s just devastating. All of our love goes out to his family and the country music community. He was and is one of the defining voices in country music. So great. I am completely shook," McGraw said in posting a black-and-white photo of he and Anderson taken on Sunday.

title: ‘He didn’t deserve this’: Family heartbroken after 4-year-old boy killed in dog attack
text:
LOUISA COUNTY, Va. (WVIR/Gray News) - A 4-year-old Virginia boy with his whole life ahead of him was killed in a dog attack. As the investigation into the incident continues, the boy’s family is speaking out amid their grief.
Days after 4-year-old Garcia Welch was killed in a dog attack, his family is sharing memories of the little boy they lost as they continue to mourn.
“Garcia is just someone that if you met him, you loved him,” said the boy’s aunt, Cynthia Russ. “He lit up the room. His smile was just amazing.”
Garcia loved painting, playing video games with his older brother and music. His mother, Cathleen Russ, recalled the times she and her son would walk to the bus stop to get his brother, 11-year-old Gabriel Welch.
Garcia’s aunt remembered how friendly he was.
“He was a beautiful kid. He was fun and sweet and kind, and he made friends everywhere. And he just — he didn’t deserve this,” Cynthia Russ said.
The attack
Garcia was killed in a dog attack around 4:40 p.m. Sunday along a highway in Louisa County.
Deputies with the Louisa County Sheriff’s Office arrived at the scene to find Garcia seriously injured with an American bully still attacking him. The sheriff’s office said deputies had to put the dog down to stop the attack.
Garcia was taken to a landing zone for air medical transport but was pronounced dead before he could be flown to a hospital.
Cynthia Russ said the family is still trying to understand what happened that afternoon.
“There’s a lot of confusion about how this could happen — why this happened. Still a lot of confusion about that,” she said.
Cathleen Russ said Garcia was at his father’s home for the weekend. Recently separated, she and Barry Welch had a formal custody agreement. On Sunday, she received a call from a non-family member about the incident.
Gabriel was also at his father’s home on Sunday and witnessed the events. Cynthia Russ described a conversation with the 11-year-old later that night where he claimed he “tried to stop it.”
“I talked to my nephew that night, and he was just crying and screaming,” she recalled.
The sheriff’s office says its investigation remains active. Investigators have not publicly confirmed all the circumstances leading up to the attack.
A life cut short
Before his death, Garcia was beginning a new chapter as a preschool student at Thomas Jefferson Elementary School.
Although he had only recently started attending the school, Principal Jesse Cleaver said Garcia had already made an impression on those around him. In a message sent to families Monday, Cleaver acknowledged the little boy’s death and expressed condolences to those grieving his loss.
“This is heartbreaking news for our Patriot family. Though Garcia was just beginning his time at Thomas Jefferson Elementary School, he quickly made a meaningful impression on those around him with his kind, friendly, and respectful personality,” Cleaver wrote.
The school division said counseling and support would be available to students and staff affected by his death.
For Garcia’s family, preschool was one of many experiences they had been looking forward to sharing with him as he grew older.
“He just had so much ahead of him, and we were just excited to see it,” Cynthia Russ said.
Community offers support
Garcia’s family is now working to arrange his funeral. In the days since the little boy’s death, friends, neighbors and people the family had never met have reached out to offer support.
“We’ve been so grateful for just the community. We didn’t know what to do. We were lost. I feel like we still are. Friends, friends of friends, people we didn’t know, approached us very early on and wanted to help,” Cynthia Russ said.
A GoFundMe was created by a family friend to help Cathleen Russ with expenses. The fundraiser initially sought $20,000, but by early Thursday, it had raised nearly $30,000.
Cynthia Russ said the family has been grateful for the people who have stepped forward, including those who did not personally know Garcia.
“We are all going through a horrendous trauma together,” she said. “Our family is not the same anymore, and it just can’t be. It’s not whole anymore.”

title: Family of missing Hampden man speaks out after AG’s office leak exposed case details
text:
HAMPDEN, Maine (WABI) - The daughter of a missing Hampden man is speaking publicly about her father’s disappearance after confidential case information was included in a document the Maine Attorney General’s Office mistakenly sent to media outlets earlier this month.
Dawn B. Dunphy’s father, Douglas Dunphy Sr., went missing from his home on Kennebec Road in Hampden on Jan. 16. His car was found in Bangor about two weeks later.
The 45-page document mistakenly sent by the Attorney General’s Office contained confidential information on dozens of cases, including Dunphy’s disappearance.
Family remembers Dunphy as Marine veteran, outdoorsman
Dawn Dunphy described her father as a loving father, an outdoorsman and a master electrician who served in the Marines as a plane mechanic during the Vietnam War.
“He was brilliant. He was so smart. He could fix anything,” Dawn Dunphy said. “He could tell every plane and what was wrong with it by the sound of the engine... Took us camping. Taught us survival skills in the woods. Fishing, the whole nine yards, hiking.”
Dawn Dunphy, who now lives out west, said she and her father caught up every Sunday. It has been more than nine months since she last heard his voice.
“My older brother called... And he just said, dad’s missing,” Dawn Dunphy said.
Case remains with state police
The case is now in the hands of Maine State Police. It’s been months since investigators provided any public updates.
“If Dad can be found, and we can put him next to Mom where he belongs, then I can grieve. But I can’t until then. I need to find him,” Dawn said.
Earlier this month, Dawn received a call from a reporter informing her that information on her father’s case had been included in the leak from the Attorney General’s Office.
Dawn said the lack of communication sent her into a panic.
“I need to know what’s happening in order to be informed. It wasn’t real fun to hear about that leak, I’ll tell you. And it wasn’t real fun to be like, okay, could this harm anything?” Dawn said.
Dawn said she later spoke to someone from the Attorney General’s Office, who told her they prioritized notifying families when sensitive information was included and told her that her father’s case was not compromised.
“Every single week, something else happens,” Dawn said. “This is what having a missing relative is like.”
Leak confirmed investigators’ suspicions
Dawn said she has long presumed her father is dead, but the leak marked the first time it was confirmed that investigators believe so as well.
Asked whether finding her father’s body would help her accept what happened, Dawn said it would.
“Definitely. If we could bring him home and put him next to mom. That, that’s where he belongs,” she said.
Dunphy’s family is asking anyone hunting or hiking this fall to keep an eye out and call Maine State Police with any tip, no matter how small, as they hope to bring him home.

title: Portland won’t release police reports about alleged assault by a city official
text:
The city of Portland is refusing to release police reports about a now-former city official who was accused of assault.
First Amendment advocates say the denial of the Portland Press Herald’s public records request violates the state’s Freedom of Access Act and raises questions about whether the city is giving special protections to its employees.
“The city seems to be arguing that just because there’s an employee involved, the records should remain secret,” said Justin Silverman, executive director of the New England First Amendment Coalition, “which is absurd.”
City officials have denied a request and multiple appeals for police documents about an alleged February assault by Gregory Watson, who at the time was the city’s director of housing and economic development.
Watson resigned in August following the allegation. Portland police confirmed in March that Watson was issued a summons for assault, but authorities and city officials have repeatedly declined to share more information about the incident.
In July, the Cumberland County District Attorney’s Office announced it would not be pursuing charges against Watson because the allegations were not provable. He was paid $63,068 while on leave, according to the city.
Watson did not respond to a request for comment at a phone number listed for him.
REASON FOR THE DENIAL
In its denial to the Press Herald’s records request, the city cited Maine law regarding personnel records — specifically, a section that states municipal records containing “complaints, charges or accusations of misconduct” that may result in discipline are confidential.
This isn’t the first time the city has used this argument.
City officials cited the same statute in a denial letter earlier this year after the Press Herald filed a similar records request for police reports about an assault by a former code enforcement officer, Matthew Sarapas.
Police records in Sarapas’ case — which the Press Herald obtained from the Cumberland County District Attorney’s Office, not from the city — showed that Sarapas assaulted a woman while on the job. He was convicted in August.
Because Watson was not charged by the district attorney’s office, county officials won’t provide police records in his case.
City officials contend that their denial was based on the specific circumstances of Watson’s case and would not necessarily apply to all public employees. But they wouldn’t explain why the police reports would be considered confidential personnel records.
Mayor Mark Dion declined to comment on the denial.
City Councilor Kate Sykes said in an interview that the city’s denial seems appropriate because the content of the police reports “is a personnel issue.” She said the city should be protective of personnel documents, and that even city councilors don’t have access to that information.
Sykes also referenced the records denial in Sarapas’ case and said “it seems like the city is following a consistent policy.”
LEGAL IMPLICATIONS
Some advocates, including Sigmund Schutz, an attorney for the Press Herald who specializes in the state’s public records laws, say the city’s interpretation of the law is incorrect and gives municipal employees special protection.
Silverman, the First Amendment attorney, said under Maine’s public records law, public employees should not receive more privacy than any other person who may have been accused of a crime.
“All of this goes to trust and making sure that we have the amount of transparency needed for us to trust that government is working as it should and no special treatment is given to anyone, public employee or not,” he said.
Silverman also said the city’s argument contradicts rulings by other courts in other New England states. He referenced a 2003 case in Massachusetts between the Worcester Telegram & Gazette and a police department in which an appeals court determined that police reports and arrest logs of a police officer did not count as private personnel records, despite the fact they were included in the officer’s internal affairs file.
He also referred to an appeal by the Press Herald against a public records denial by the city of Portland in 2013. The city refused to release a fire department report about a fireboat crash because it was attached to a disciplinary file. A judge ultimately determined that the factual, investigative details from the report should be released and potential disciplinary action could be withheld.
“In the court’s view, the City is interpreting (the personnel records law) too expansively,” Superior Court Justice Thomas Warren wrote in his decision.
Silverman said he understands those rulings to mean that public officials can’t exempt certain records from requests “only because they happen to be involved in a disciplinary proceeding or might be at some point in the future.”
Staff Writer Andrew Rice contributed to this story.

title: These US jobs have the youngest and oldest median ages
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
See the US jobs with the youngest and oldest workforce
The median age of the U.S. workforce in 2025 was 42.1 years, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.
The workforce includes about 163 million people, with median ages varying by occupation. Some service jobs, like hosts, fast-food workers, waiters and more, skew younger. Other occupations, like judges, drivers and clerks, skew older.
Every year, BLS releases age demographics for nearly 600 occupations, including median age and number of people in each field. The Get the Facts Data Team analyzed the data to see how median ages vary across professions.
Which professions had the youngest and oldest median ages?
Other protective service workers, those in specialized or miscellaneous jobs that don’t fall under public safety, had the youngest median age last year, at 21.2 years.
Median age is the midpoint of the age distribution in an occupation. The median is less affected by outliers and can better represent the typical age of workers in an occupation. The BLS reports median ages for professions with more than 50,000 workers. About 380 occupations did not meet the criteria.
Hosts and hostesses had the second-youngest median age at 21.7 years, followed by fast-food and counter workers, at 22.3 years.
Farmers, ranchers and other agricultural managers had the highest median age at 56.1 years. About 810,000 farmers, ranchers and other agricultural workers make up the industry. School bus drivers had the second-highest median age at 55.9 years.
Are certain occupations getting younger or older?
Farmers, ranchers and other agricultural managers have been getting older over the past decade. Their median age rose from 54.8 years in 2015 to 56.1 in 2025, an increase of 1.3 years.
They didn't have the largest age increase in the last decade. Hotel, motel and resort desk clerks had the highest rise, going from 30.3 years in 2015 to 37.9 years in 2025, nearly an eight-year increase. Food processing workers also trended older, going from 38.3 years in 2015 to 44.7 years in 2025.
Aerospace engineers had the largest drop in median age, from 47.3 years in 2015 to 39.5 years in 2025. Animal trainers and motor vehicle operators also trended down, dropping their median ages by 7.7 years and 7.6 years, respectively.
