title: Rockland school district hopes to erase budget deficit in 3 years
text:
ROCKLAND, Maine — Regional School Unit 13 expects to erase its $2.6 million deficit within three years.
The business manager made the pronouncement during a Tuesday meeting of the board’s Budget and Finance Committee.
The 2024-2025 audit reported a deficit of about $2.6 million in the overall budget of more than $41 million at the end of the 2024-2025 fiscal year. The deficit was due largely to the district not receiving the MaineCare reimbursement it had expected to cover some of the special education costs for speech, occupational and physical therapy.
Business Manager Katherine Hunt said for the first few pay periods this year, she expects the district to spend $1.1 million less than budgeted, which would help reduce the deficit.
Former Business Manager Peter Orne attended the meeting via Teams and said the first month is generally the least reliable period to use in a forecast of year-end savings. He said he estimates a range of $400,000 to $1.2 million and would consider $625,000 to be the best projection for savings at this point.
Assistant Superintendent Steffany Tribou pointed out, however, that if the district were to fill about 16 special education educational technician positions that remain unfilled, the savings would be less.
The business manager went through the budget, article by article, to update board members on spending and revenues for the current 2026-27 budget.
She also reminded the board it would need to transfer money from the district’s $100,000 contingency account to cover the costs of the superintendent search.
The board voted 7-1 on Oct. 7 to hire Alma Advisory Group of Chicago, which could cost up to $63,000. That does not include paying for travel or lodging costs for candidates to come to interviews.
Regional School Unit 13 board members voiced concerns at that Oct. 7 meeting about audit findings for 2024-25 that found numerous deficiencies in financial operations in the district. The business manager said at that meeting, the finance department has responded to those findings and is working to ensure they do not occur again.
In March 2026, the Internal Revenue Service filed a $321,867 tax lien against RSU 13 for errors in withholding of federal income taxes, Medicare taxes and Social Security taxes. Nearly $300,000 of the lien is for the tax period that ended in December 2019. Another $10,188 was for the tax period that ended in June 2023. And another is about $11,000 for the tax period that ended in 2024.
This story appears through a media partnership with Midcoast Villager.

title: Boys Soccer Playoffs: County Matchups and a Big Bracket Twist
text:
Aroostook County Boys Soccer Teams Head Into 2026 Playoffs With Plenty of Local Storylines [VIDEO]
The boys' high school soccer playoffs are almost here, and there's plenty to talk about as our local teams get ready for their tournament runs.
Madawaska has earned the top seed in Class D North, Presque Isle has secured a preliminary-round bye in Class B, and Fort Kent is preparing to host a Class C quarterfinal.
Meanwhile, the eight-player tournament has a particularly interesting possibility, with Wisdom and Katahdin potentially meeting in the quarterfinals if the Cougars can get through their preliminary game.
Add in Caribou, Central Aroostook, Fort Fairfield, Hodgdon, Easton, Washburn, Van Buren and Houlton, and there's no shortage of County soccer to follow.
The eight-player preliminary round begins Friday, October 23, with the Class B preliminary games following Saturday, October 24.
Regional quarterfinals are scheduled for October 27 and 28.
Here's a look at the boys' tournament picture.
The 2026 MPA Soccer Championships on 101.9 The Rock are proudly presented by Pineland Farms in Mars Hill.
Class B North: Presque Isle Earns Home Quarterfinal, Caribou Opens in Preliminaries
The Presque Isle Wildcats finished 8-5-1 and earned the fourth seed in Class B North.
That gives Presque Isle a bye through the preliminary round and a home quarterfinal against the winner of fifth-seeded Erskine Academy and twelfth-seeded Skowhegan.
The Wildcats had some memorable moments during the regular season, including an impressive comeback victory over Foxcroft Academy.
Trailing by two goals, Presque Isle battled back to pick up a 3-2 victory in one of the more exciting finishes of the fall.
The Wildcats also swept their regular-season meetings against Caribou and Fort Kent.
Presque Isle's five losses came against John Bapst, Orono and Foxcroft Academy, all teams that have shown they can compete at a high level.
With the fourth seed, the Wildcats have an opportunity to begin their tournament at home and build on what they've accomplished this season.
Caribou Faces Medomak Valley in Preliminary Round
The Caribou Vikings finished 4-8-2, earning the eighth seed and a preliminary matchup with ninth-seeded Medomak Valley, which finished 6-8.
The teams did not meet during the regular season.
Caribou's victories included two wins over Fort Kent and two against Hermon. The Vikings also earned ties against Foxcroft Academy and Brewer.
If Caribou can advance through the preliminary round, the Vikings would face top-seeded John Bapst, which finished 13-0-1.
John Bapst defeated Caribou twice during the regular season, so the Vikings know the level of competition waiting in the quarterfinals.
First, though, they'll need to get past Medomak Valley.
Class C North: Fort Kent Earns Fourth Seed
Fort Kent finished 7-6-1, earning the third seed in Class C North and a home quarterfinal against sixth-seed Washington Academy.
The Raiders finished with a 6-6-2 record.
The Warriors have faced some challenging competition throughout the fall, including games against Presque Isle, Caribou, Orono and Madawaska.
Fort Kent recorded two victories over Madawaska, which finished as the top seed in Class D North, and also earned a tie against top-seeded Class C Orono.
The Warriors split their two meetings with George Stevens Academy/Deer Isle-Stonington and swept Washington Academy.
The Warriors have shown they can be competitive against strong opponents, and they'll be looking to carry that experience into the postseason.
Class D North: Madawaska Leads a Field Filled With County Teams
If you're looking for a bracket with plenty of local interest, Class D North has it.
Seven of the eight teams in the current tournament field are from Aroostook County, with several familiar opponents meeting again in the postseason.
And at the top of the standings are the Madawaska Owls.
No. 1 Madawaska vs. No. 8 MSSM
Madawaska finished 12-2, earning the top seed in Class D North.
The Owls' only two losses came against Class C Fort Kent, and they swept the rest of their regular-season opponents.
Madawaska finished its regular season with a 6-1 victory over Washburn on Senior Night.
Josh Querze scored twice, while Aiden Gagnon, Oliver Pelkey, Bradley Kennedy and Ashton Guerrette each added a goal.
The Owls will begin the tournament against eighth-seeded Maine School of Science and Mathematics from Limestone, which was 1-7-2 in the supplied standings.
Madawaska defeated MSSM during the regular season.
With the top seed and an impressive regular-season record, the Owls have given themselves a great opportunity to make a run through the Northern Maine tournament.
No. 2 Central Aroostook vs. No. 7 Penobscot Valley
Central Aroostook has also enjoyed an outstanding fall, finishing 11-3 and earning the second seed.
The Panthers are lined up against seventh-seeded Penobscot Valley, which enters with a 5-8 record in the supplied standings.
Central Aroostook's only three losses came against Madawaska twice and Fort Fairfield once.
The Panthers also defeated Fort Fairfield in their other meeting, giving them a split against the Tigers.
Central Aroostook picked up victories over Easton and Washburn during the regular season and has been one of the more consistent teams in the classification.
The Panthers did not face Penobscot Valley this fall, so they'll be preparing for a new opponent when the quarterfinals begin.
No. 3 Fort Fairfield vs. No. 6 Washburn
Fort Fairfield finished 6-6-2, earning the third seed in Class D North.
The Tigers are matched up against sixth-seeded Washburn, which was 3-8-2 in the supplied standings.
These teams split their regular-season meetings, with each picking up a victory.
Fort Fairfield also recorded an important win over second-seeded Central Aroostook, along with a victory over Hodgdon.
Washburn, meanwhile, picked up victories over both Hodgdon and Fort Fairfield, showing that the Beavers can compete with teams seeded above them.
With the season series tied at one game apiece, a third meeting in the quarterfinals should be worth watching.
No. 4 Hodgdon vs. No. 5 Easton
Hodgdon has also put together a strong season, sitting at 9-3-1 in the supplied standings and earning the fourth seed.
The Shires are lined up against fifth-seeded Easton, which finished 8-6.
Hodgdon defeated Easton in both regular-season meetings, and the Shires also recorded victories over Penobscot Valley.
Easton had some impressive moments as well, including two victories over Fort Fairfield.
While Hodgdon had the advantage in the first two meetings against Easton, the Bears will have another chance to change that story when the playoffs begin.
It should be an interesting matchup between two County schools that know each other well.
Eight-Player North: Wisdom Moves to Third, Potential Katahdin Rematch Ahead
The eight-player boys' tournament has one of the more intriguing possibilities for County soccer fans.
Wisdom is entering the postseason as the number three seed, while Katahdin is sixth after finishing with twelve victories.
If both teams advance to the quarterfinals, they'll meet for a third time this season.
But there's plenty of soccer to be played before that can happen.
No. 3 Wisdom Awaits Katahdin or Lee Academy
The Wisdom Pioneers finished 11-3 and earned the third seed in eight-player North.
Wisdom receives a preliminary-round bye and will host the winner of sixth-seeded Katahdin and eleventh-seeded Lee Academy.
The Pioneers have had plenty of success against other tournament teams this season, including two wins over Van Buren and two over Penquis Valley.
Wisdom also split its regular-season meetings with Katahdin.
That creates an interesting possibility for the quarterfinals.
If Katahdin advances past Lee Academy, the Pioneers and Cougars will meet for a third time, with a regional semifinal berth at stake.
No. 6 Katahdin vs. No. 11 Lee Academy
Katahdin finished 12-2, one of the best records among the local boys' soccer teams.
Despite that record, the Cougars enter the eight-player tournament as the sixth seed, based on the Heal point standings.
They'll open against eleventh-seeded Lee Academy, which finished 5-7-2.
Katahdin's only two losses came against Wisdom and Van Buren.
The Cougars also earned victories over both teams in their other meetings, giving them a split against each.
Katahdin did not face Lee Academy during the regular season.
Should the Cougars advance, they'll travel to face third-seeded Wisdom in what could be one of the more interesting County matchups of the tournament.
No. 7 Van Buren vs. No. 10 Schenck-Stearns
The Van Buren Crusaders finished 7-6-1, earning the seventh seed.
Their preliminary-round opponent is tenth-seeded Schenck-Stearns, which finished 7-7.
Van Buren defeated Schenck twice during the regular season and will be looking for a third win against the Wolverines.
The Crusaders also recorded a victory over Katahdin and played Mattanawcook Academy to a tie.
The winner will move on to face the second seed in the quarterfinals.
No. 9 Houlton/GHCA vs. No. 8 Penquis Valley
The Houlton/Greater Houlton Christian Academy Shiretowners finished 4-8-2, earning the ninth seed.
Houlton will travel to eighth-seeded Penquis Valley, which finished 7-7.
These teams did not meet during the regular season.
The Shiretowners picked up two victories over Schenck-Stearns during the fall, along with wins against Ashland and Van Buren.
The winner of the preliminary game will advance to face top-seeded Mattanawcook Academy.
Houlton has already faced Mattanawcook twice this season, with the Lynx winning both meetings.
Tournament Championships Coming to Presque Isle
The postseason begins with eight-player preliminary games Friday, October 23, followed by the Class B preliminaries Saturday, October 24.
Quarterfinals are scheduled for October 27 and 28, with regional semifinals October 30 and 31.
The regional championships follow November 3 and 4, and the state championships are scheduled for Saturday, November 7.
Two major championship games will take place right here in Aroostook County.
Presque Isle Middle School will host the Class D North regional championship on November 4 and the eight-player state championship on November 7.
With so many County teams involved, there's plenty of opportunity for some local schools to advance into the later rounds.
I'll have the finalized brackets, results, updates and more photos as the tournament gets underway.
Good luck to all our local boys' teams as they begin their playoff runs!

title: Bangor Beautiful plants native trees, removes invasive species at farmers market
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - The Bangor Farmer’s Market is a favorite spot for many during the fall. One organization is helping to plant trees to make the spot a little more beautiful.
Sixteen tree saplings were planted Thursday morning by the Bangor Beautiful nonprofit. Native plants like pitched pine and serviceberry trees were provided by Maine Audubon.
The organization also helped to remove invasive plant species in the area, including burning bush and buck thorn. The new, native plant species will not only help create ecosystems, but help to reduce runoff, making sidewalks more pedestrian friendly.
“We can’t let our native species decline because the invasive species are coming in. We want to create habitat. This ecosystem needs native plants so that we can feed the caterpillars that feed the birds that make us all happy in the end,” said Bangor Beautiful President Annette Dodd.
The organization had also repainted a shipping container in the area earlier this year. Bangor Beautiful will be planting more trees in the area this coming spring.
You can learn more by reaching out to Bangor Beautiful on their website and Facebook page.

title: Republican Gov. Mike DeWine denounces Ramaswamy ad featuring Democrat Amy Acton's estranged mother
text:
Trump backs Vivek Ramaswamy on controversial ad featuring Democrat Amy Acton's estranged mother
President Donald Trump said Thursday that Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican nominee for Ohio governor, should keep running a controversial ad featuring the estranged mother of Democratic opponent Amy Acton, posting on social media that it was “hitting pay dirt.”
Trump also denounced Ohio Republican Gov. Mike DeWine, who criticized the ad as “deeply, deeply troubling” earlier in the day. Acton previously served in DeWine's administration as a health official. Her mother lost custody of Acton and her brother after her husband — the children's stepfather — was indicted for raping Acton.
“He strongly suggested that Vivek should, ‘take down the Ad,’” Trump wrote. “He probably wants a Dumocrat to win, and certainly doesn’t want someone who will do a much better job than he is capable of doing. I suggested, on the other hand, that Vivek should keep it up, and let everyone listen to the mother of a defective, dishonest, and incapable Candidate, explain how the daughter is a DISASTER who, uncontrollably, lies, cheats, and steals!”
At a gathering with reporters at the Ohio Statehouse, DeWine recalled the painful experiences of rape victims he dealt with as a county prosecutor and state attorney general.
“It's wrong to run this ad,” he said. “And, even at this late time — my wife, Fran, saw the ad just run this morning on TV — I would just urge the Ramaswamy campaign to take this down.”
The term-limited DeWine’s remarks place him at odds with Ramaswamy, whom he has endorsed. The biotech entrepreneur and former presidential candidate plans to spend $4 million to broadcast it online and on television.
DeWine stops short of pulling his endorsement
But the governor stopped short of pulling his backing of the Republican for now. DeWine recalled a previous line of attack by the Acton campaign had mentioned Ramaswamy's mother and said that also was wrong — “family members have always historically been off limits” — though he noted it was never used in a multimillion-dollar ad campaign.
That critique from the summer cited an investigative report into Geetha Ramaswamy's role at a pharmaceutical company run by her son, who Acton and Democrats described as “hiring his own mother to manipulate clinical trial data.”
The Ramaswamy campaign called those claims “slanderous” and said he's being held to a different standard than Acton and other Democrats who have attacked Republicans' families.
“Governor DeWine is correct that the first and only candidate to attack the mother of her opponent in this race was Amy Acton,” spokesperson Connie Luck said in a statement, adding, "We refuse to accept the media's double standards.”
Ohio Republicans divided over the ad
By chiming in, DeWine has entered the fray of a growing rift among Ohio Republicans over the advertisement — as both the governor's race and a race for U.S. Senate appear far tighter than expected in a state Donald Trump won handily three times. The video features Acton’s birth mother, Donna Arthur, calling her “a liar” and insinuating she has mental health issues.
Acton, Ohio’s COVID-19-era health director, has made no secret of facing homelessness and abuse as a child. Arthur lost custody of her children after their stepfather, Arthur's husband, was indicted on a charge of rape involving Acton. Acton's campaign on Tuesday posted a video of her brother, who supported her backstory about living in a tent and being abused.
Republican Vice President JD Vance, an Ohio native son, expressed disgust during an Ohio campaign swing Wednesday with Republicans “whining” about the ad as low and in poor taste. But Republican U.S. Sen. Jon Husted, DeWine's former lieutenant governor — running in a tight retention race against Democrat Sherrod Brown — has said he would not have run the ad, as has Republican Secretary of State Frank LaRose, who is running for state auditor.
Another influential Ohio Republican, former U.S. Rep. Jim Renacci, posted a lengthy essay on X overnight, suggesting that “the floor may have just fallen out from under the Republican campaign for Ohio Governor” and urging every Republican to distance themselves from it.
Amid the turmoil, Ohio Republican Party Chairman Alex Triantafilou posted what sounded like a warning, or a threat.
“The final days of a tough campaign are always the best time to find out who is really with you and who just posts and pretends,” he wrote. “Yes—we are keeping score.” The quote was followed by a winking-eye emoji.
Ad has faced bipartisan rebukes, support in conservative media
The ad is also dividing Republicans nationally.
Nikki Haley, who sparred with Ramaswamy during the 2024 Republican presidential primary over the personal nature of his attacks, called him “a bad guy” in a social media post Tuesday. “It’s a shame he continues to get away with it,” she wrote.
At the same time, Media Matters for America, a left-leaning media watchdog group, has reported that many within the national conservative media are promoting and praising the ad. Ramaswamy's campaign manager, Jonathan Ewing, characterized it as “a campaign-ending moment for Amy Acton.”
Wayne Allyn Root, of Gateway Pundit, called it “absolutely hilarious” and Daily Wire host Michael Knowles described it as “brilliant.”
Police and court records show Cledith Arthur was arrested and charged with the rape of Acton in July 1978, when she was 12, after her biological father lodged a formal complaint against him. The abuse allegedly happened from December 1976 to April 1978. Cledith Arthur failed to show for a court appearance and became a fugitive.
Donna Arthur remained married to him until his death in 2004.

title: Ukulele group brings island vibes to popular South Carolina vacation area
text:
MYRTLE BEACH, S.C. (Aging Untold)— A ukulele group in South Carolina’s Grand Strand is strumming its way into the hearts of listeners with tropical vibes on the East Coast.
Donning Hawaiian shirts, panama hats and flowers in their hair, the musicians who make up Ukes by the Sea transport audiences to paradise with their breezy sound.
“We say that it’s difficult to play a ukulele and frown at the same time,” Tom Woodle, director of Ukes by the Sea, said. “And it’s got such a happy sound.”
Back to the beginning
Woodle began playing the small-stringed instrument at 4 years old, and his talent quickly blossomed. He started playing on live radio when he was 6, joined bands at 11 and began making money from music at 16.
He even made it onto the top 100 chart with his group, The Reedy Creek Band, playing country and bluegrass in Nashville.
The musician traded spotlights for stained glass and returned to the Grand Strand, where he taught at Coastal Carolina and served as senior rector at The Well by the Sea.
He created the uplifting, toe-tapping ukulele band almost three years ago for all to enjoy.
Diverse repertoire and growing membership
“A lot of rock and roll from the ‘60s and ‘70s, and we do some folk songs, and we do some more contemporary things like Africa,” Woodle said. “It could be anything that hits our fancy.”
The band has 25 members, including seasoned musicians and others strumming for the first time.
Woodle scouted out talent like Kristen Toben, who plays the ukulele and now the steel drum.
“I purchased it, and at least with my musical background, it somehow came easy to me, and Tom has always wanted a steel drum in his band,” Toben said. “It really brought my spirits up, and I remembered how much I love music, and it was just a way for me to just continue on my love of music.”
Woodle taught his wife how to play bass so she could be part of the group.
“And to think that most of these people have never touched an instrument two years ago, I think they should be very proud of themselves,” Toben said.
Community performances
When members of Ukes by the Sea are not practicing, they perform with a purpose throughout the community.
“To spread the love of Jesus with happy music,” Woodle said. “And they love it. They have a good time, and people seem to love watching us, so that’s just a good thing.”

title: Stephen King Wrote a Vampire Classic in a Small Maine Garage
text:
Stephen King Wrote a Vampire Classic in a Small Maine Garage
One of the King of Horror’s most recognizable works was written in a small room in a garage here in the Pine Tree State.
👇 KEEP READING: 13 Best Stephen King Movies According to Rotten Tomatoes 👇
According to his official website’s biography, Stephen King gained the financial means to leave teaching and write full time after learning of a major paperback sale for “Carrie” in May 1973.
At the end of that summer, his family moved to southern Maine because of his mother’s declining health and rented a summer home on Sebago Lake in North Windham for the winter.
There, King wrote 'Salem’s Lot in a small room in the garage, initially calling the novel “Second Coming” and later "Jerusalem’s Lot” before settling on its final title.
His mother died of cancer at age 59 during this period.
King’s 'Salem’s Lot follows writer Ben Mears as he returns to the small Maine town of Jerusalem’s Lot, where he spent part of his childhood, hoping to write a novel.
When residents begin disappearing or becoming vampires, Mears joins a small group of townspeople trying to stop the spreading threat.
And there you have it! One of King’s most recognizable horror novels took shape during a pivotal period of his life in North Windham.

title: Cooper Flagg scores 32 points, Mavs lose opener to Rockets
text:
HOUSTON — Kevin Durant and Jabari Smith Jr. scored 30 points apiece and the Houston Rockets used a big second quarter to build a huge lead and coast to a 128-110 win over the Dallas Mavericks on Wednesday night in the season opener for both teams.
The Rockets led by six after the first quarter before outscoring Dallas 38-12 in the second to take a 32-point lead into halftime.
Durant and Smith each scored 16 points each in the first half. The Rockets were up by 15 midway through the second before using a 19-2 run to make it 70-38 at halftime.
Kyrie Irving had 15 points for Dallas in his first regular-season game since tearing his left ACL in March 2025. But it was a tough debut for Dallas coach Dusty May, who led Michigan to the NCAA championship before being hired to replace the fired Jason Kidd.
Cooper Flagg of Newport, the 2025 No. 1 pick and last season’s NBA Rookie of the Year, led the Mavericks with 32 points. P.J. Washington had 10 points and four rebounds.
The Mavericks used a 9-0 run, with six points from Marcus Sasser, to cut the lead to 103-86 with about nine minutes remaining. But Houston used an 8-2 spurt with 3s from Durant and Fred VanVleet to push it to 111-88 about a minute later.
Alperen Sengun added 23 points with 10 rebounds for the Rockets. VanVleet chipped in six points with 11 assists in his return after missing last season recovering from a torn ACL.
Houston’s Tari Eason was ejected with about three minutes left in the first quarter after receiving a flagrant foul 2 for shoving Washington to the court.
Up next
Mavericks: Visit Indiana on Friday night.
Rockets: Play San Antonio in Austin, Texas on Friday.

title: Bruins stay hot, trounce Predators
text:
BOSTON — Michael DiPietro made 28 saves for his first career shutout, David Pastrnak had two goals and two assists, and the Boston Bruins cruised to a 6-0 victory over the Nashville Predators on Thursday night.
Charlie McAvoy had a career-high four assists for Boston, and Casey Mittelstadt, Elias Lindholm, JJ Peterka and Mark Kastelic also scored.
Pastrnak leads the Bruins in goals (six) and assists (10). Boston improved to 6-0-1 in its last seven games, with the only loss coming Tuesday in overtime at Dallas to conclude a four-game trip.
Justus Annunen stopped 25 shots in his first start for Nashville since last season. The Predators have lost four of five.
The Bruins went ahead 3:49 into the game when Pastrnak sent a cross-ice pass to Mittelstadt, who fired it past Annunen’s right shoulder.
Lindholm made it 2-0 on the power play later in the first. Pastrnak scored midway through the second when he deflected McAvoy’s shot past Annunen, and the Bruins captain assisted on Peterka’s goal late in the period.
Pastrnak capped the scoring with 5 minutes remaining and became the eighth player in Bruins history with 20 career four-point games.
The Bruins scored six goals for the third time, tied with the Golden Knights, Kraken, Avalanche and Hurricanes for the most in 2026-27.
McAvoy became the fourth defenseman in Bruins history with 10 career games of three assists or more, joining Ray Bourque, Bobby Orr and Brad Park.

title: Fraternity suspended at University of Arizona after female student reported assault by 2 men
text:
Fraternity suspended at University of Arizona after female student reported assault by 2 men
The University of Arizona has suspended a fraternity's activities after a female student alleged two men sexually assaulted her at the fraternity's house in August.
Related video above: 'You deserve to be safe': bipartisan campus safety bill promises help for survivors
The Sigma Phi Epsilon chapter at the southern Arizona school was already on probation, but the university said it has now imposed an activities suspension, stating the fraternity poses a risk to the university community. An investigation into the allegations continues.
“It has been determined that your organization presents a substantial risk to members of the university community,” said Associate Dean of Students Whitney Mohr in a letter sent to the fraternity on Wednesday.
The local chapter did not respond to calls or emails, but the national fraternity organization said it had ordered members of the Arizona chapter to comply with any investigation.
"Sigma Phi Epsilon does not tolerate sexual assault or sexual misconduct. The Fraternity has suspended those involved while the investigation proceeds," Brian Warren, chief executive officer of Sigma Phi Epsilon, said in a statement Tuesday. It didn't elaborate on the identities of those involved or their connection to the fraternity.
The female student told investigators that she consensually kissed a man and was drinking on the night of Aug. 26, but then woke up to two men sexually assaulting her in the fraternity house, according to search warrant records dated Sept. 9 and published Monday night by KOLD-TV in Tucson.
She told police she remembers feeling one man’s breath on her face and had trouble swallowing the next morning due to possible strangulation, according to the records. The documents also included physical descriptions of the accused. The next day, she reported the incident to police and underwent a forensic exam at a hospital.
Following media coverage of the allegations this week, the university placed Sigma Phi Epsilon on activities suspension, which prohibits the chapter from hosting, attending, participating in, and sponsoring any organizational activities until the case is settled, according to the associate dean's letter.
The letter also accuses Sigma Phi Epsilon members of providing alcohol to minors on Aug. 26, the night of the alleged assault, and on Sept. 29. The fraternity was previously placed on probation, a conditional warning that included fines, following allegations of hazing in July.
The University of Arizona Police Department, which filed the search warrant, said on Tuesday that the investigation was ongoing.
The Tucson-based university has attempted to crack down on Greek-life activities that violate the code of conduct. Earlier this month, the adminstration suspended activities for 21 fraternities amid reports of assault, hazing and drug- and alcohol-related behavior. Only five fraternities remain suspended.
Sigma Phi Epsilon members are prohibited from contacting the alleged victim or her family, according to the associate dean's letter, and any accusations of retribution or intimidation could result in an additional investigation and harsher consequences.
The Pima County Attorney’s Office on Tuesday said the case hasn’t been referred to prosecutors yet.
__
Additional reporting by AP reporter Jacques Billeaud in Phoenix.

title: As the gambling industry changes, Oxford Casino is up for sale. What does that mean for the community?
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
OXFORD — It’s been 13 years since Churchill Downs Inc. bought Oxford Casino, one of only two casinos in the state.
Since then, a lot has changed in the gambling industry, as the rise of online sports betting and prediction markets have eaten away at traditional casino gambling.
Still, local leaders and business owners say, the casino has been a benefit to the area. As Churchill Downs considers selling the property, leaders hope it remains a community asset.
“I do feel like we are very fortunate to have it here,” Oxford Selectman Ernie Fitts said. “There’s pros and cons with everything, but I certainly feel the pros have outweighed (the cons), having the casino here in the town of Oxford.”
CHANGES AT CHURCHILL DOWNS
The American Gaming Association reported that casino revenue was up 2.3% in 2025 over the previous year, while sports betting revenue was up 22.6% and internet gaming was up 27.6% in the same period.
The changes in the gambling industry have a lot to do with why Churchill Downs is considering selling the Oxford Casino, as well as eight other gaming properties in seven other states.
The company has said it wants to focus on live horse racing, its flagship Kentucky Derby, and online betting platform TwinSpires. In an interview last month with Horse Racing Nation’s Rod Flatter Racing Pod, Churchill Downs’ CEO Bill Carstanjen repeated the assertion that the move to sell the nine casinos is all about strategy and not weak performance.
Yet, he also said gaming has become less popular with public company investors, citing competition for funding from sports betting and prediction markets.
Three months after announcing that Churchill Downs was considering the sale of all or some of the nine casinos, no decisions have been made public. Carstanjen said his company is soliciting and weighing bids and that the process is ongoing.
Under state law, a casino license is not transferable or assignable. If the Oxford Casino is sold, a potential buyer would have to apply for licensure as a casino operator and receive the license before the acquisition occurs, so as not to interrupt business operations.
JOBS AND REVENUE
In 2010, the year of the successful referendum to open the casino, western Maine and Oxford County were struggling with a recession. Unemployment in Oxford County peaked at 11% and was among the highest in Maine. Promises of jobs were a factor in the outcome of the statewide referendum, which passed by 4,723 votes — less than 1%.
In the run-up to the vote, backers of the proposed casino in Oxford County said it would generate more than 1,700 year-round jobs and at least $60 million in revenue for education and statewide programs, the Penobscot and Passamaquoddy tribes, and foster economic development.
The reality has not quite kept up with the hype. The casino employs between 400 and 450 people year-round, with an average annual tax revenue of $33 million distributed by statute, with 46% of net revenue from slot machines and 16% from table games providing funding for a number of programs and services. Most of the revenue goes to education to fund essential programs for K-12. Both the town of Oxford and Oxford County get a share of the revenue.
The impact has been felt. Overall, the casino has contributed more than $338 million to the state, county, and town since it opened in 2012.
In 2025, Oxford received more than $2 million from Oxford Casino, which Fitts said is a huge relief for the town of 4,300. The casino revenue has allowed Oxford to keep its property tax rate at $14 per $1,000 of assessed value, when surrounding towns are at $16, $17 and as high as $24.5 in Auburn.
“As a Select Board member, you don’t have to go and worry as much about taxes,” he said. “Property taxes are a big issue in this state.”
Predictions for a rise in crime and rampant gambling problems never materialized. Lori Manson, the gambling services coordinator of ADEPT Maine, said while Maine is not immune to gambling addiction, most people can go to the casino and gamble for entertainment without issue.
Casinos, she said, are the least of her worries. They are very tightly regulated by the Gambling Control Unit, and you have to physically go to a casino to bet. Sports betting, offshore gambling sites, and prediction markets can all be done on your phone.
“Of all the gambling forms, it’s probably the one I’m least concerned about as far as the harm that it does to the citizens of Maine,” Manson said.
IN THE COMMUNITY
The Oxford Casino has been a good community partner, residents say.
“They’re very community friendly,” Fitts commented. “They help out with a lot of things, they donate a lot of money to a lot of different nonprofits and help in the community.”
Cindi Robbins agrees. The owner of Poland Spring Resort has supported the casino from the outset, and has benefitted from its presence. Before the casino hotel and the Hampton Inn were built, the need for hotel rooms as the casino opened allowed her to open her motor lodge year-round.
“I don’t think there’s much publicity about the charity aspect of the casino,” Robbins said, reciting a list of golf events and charitable events that are regularly sponsored by the casino.
Amanda and Aaron Ouellette, who own Daddy O’s Diner in Oxford and Mechanic Falls, attribute part of their success to the casino, which they say brings more people to the region. It’s allowed them to grow their business.
“Sales have gone up, and also we’ve got a second location,” Aaron said. “We went from having 12 employees to like 40, 45 between the two.”
If you or someone you know is struggling with a gambling problem, 211 is Maine’s Problem Gambling Helpline. Call 211 or text your zip code to 898-211 for access to information about services and resources 24/7.

title: Sunday may be Mike Rowe’s final race. Is he the best auto racer in Maine history?
text:
It’s a question Mike Rowe has been pondering for nearly a decade. And now, on the heels of his eighth Super Late Model championship at Oxford Plains Speedway, the 76-year-old driver from Turner might be ready to answer it.
When will the Maine racing legend retire?
The PASS 400 at Oxford Plains Speedway on Sunday could be the final race of his career. After winning the track title last month, Rowe seemed to be leaning closer to retirement than in years past.
“My crew keeps saying, ‘One more year,’ but I’m definitely slowing down,” Rowe said. “I love racing the (Pro All Star Series) races, but the longer races, I don’t think I should do. I don’t really know right now. I should retire, this would be a good time to do it. When you get long in age (it’s something to think about).”
Rowe confirmed Tuesday he is still on the fence about retirement. His focus is on the PASS 400, then he’ll take time to make a decision about his career, he said.
“My son and grandson are racing now, my great-grandson is racing now,” Rowe said. “It’s time for me to sit back and watch them. I don’t really have anything to accomplish, I guess, anymore. I’ve done everything I can do. Especially this year. We didn’t have expectations about running all the (PASS) races this year, but we went out on a good note and kept going.”
Rowe’s career is filled with accolades. He won the Oxford 250 time times (1984, 1997 and 2005), has eight Oxford Plains titles (1976, 1978-81, 1989, 1990, 2026), three Beech Ridge Motor Speedway Pro Series championships (2009, 2010, 2013), a Pro Stock title at Wiscasset Speedway (1991) as well as championships for PASS (South champion in 2006, North champion in 2016), the American-Canadian Tour (1994) and the Northeast Pro Stock Association (1999).
Where does Rowe’s career stack against Maine’s best drivers? He stands alone, according to his peers.
“He’s had a hell of a run and he’s been very good,” said Unity’s Ralph Nason. “Ever since I first raced him … He’s right at the top (of the list).”
Nason, 86, would know. Like Rowe, Nason is a three-time Oxford 250 champion, and the only driver to win Maine’s biggest race in three consecutive years (1998-2000). He and Rowe shared an intense rivalry for years.
“You don’t train to get in the car to be second,” Nason said. “He had the same talent and the same amount of drive (as me), that’s why we were as competitive as we were.”
There are Maine stock car drivers with careers that compete with Rowe.
Ralph Cusack has the most series titles at one Maine track. He won 12 championships at Beech Ridge — the Scarborough track that closed in 2021 after 72 years — including seven Class A championships (1953, 1958-59, 1962-65).
Dick Wolstenhulme was another Beech Ridge legend, winning 10 track championships, including three consecutive crowns from 1960-63.
Both Cusack and Wolstenhulme had excellent success at one track, but not across multiple tracks or multiple series like Rowe.
Rowe is the all-time wins leader at Oxford Plains Speedway, with 157 victories, ahead of Jon Lizotte (113) and David Smith (112).
“It’s pretty cool to have that amount of longevity and success,” said Farmingdale driver Johnny Clark, 46, a seven-time PASS North champion and the 2020 Oxford 250 champion, who has been racing against Rowe for nearly 30 years. “What a way to go out (if this is the end). He’s one of the best, that’s for sure. … I don’t think there is anybody that could get as much out of a car.”
Chelsea native Dave Darveau was a dominant racer at Unity Raceway and Wiscasset Speedway, winning 692 races in a 44-year career (1952-1996). He won the Sportsman series championship at Wiscasset three times (1976, 1978, 1984).
Rodney Maynard was an Aroostook County racing legend, collecting over 100 career wins and five track championships at Spud Speedway in Caribou. Maynard’s most famous victory came in an exhibition race in 1983, when he defeated NASCAR champion Bobby Allison.
The most notable name from Maine at the national level remains Newburgh’s Ricky Craven, now owner of the former Speedway 95 in Hermon. Craven, 60, ran 278 races in the NASCAR Cup Series from 1991-2004, with two victories, and a third-place finish at the 1997 Daytona 500, behind Jeff Gordon and Terry Labonte.
Locally, Craven won track championships at Unity and Wiscasset, and captured the Busch North Series title in 1991, a year that included an Oxford 250 win.
A strong run in the Maine racing scene, but not as strong or as long as Rowe.
If Sunday is Rowe’s final race, there’s no argument that a major piece of Maine racing history goes with him.
“He’s got to go down as one of the best, he’s raced the longest,” Clark said. “I’ve raced with so many great racers in Maine over the years, but you don’t know what they could have or would have done, because you only raced them for 15 years and they just didn’t put in the time that Mike did.”

title: Biddeford residents say car sped through backyard and crashed into a garage
text:
Biddeford residents say speeding car drove through backyard and crashed into a garage
People who live on Laurier Street in Biddeford said a car that sped through their neighborhood Wednesday night drove through a backyard and crashed into a garage.
Residents told Maine's Total Coverage that the car came speeding down the dead-end street, turned into a driveway, drove into a backyard, hit a garage and then wound up back on Laurier Street, where it stalled out.
Some residents said they also had their power lines knocked down.
Jason Colpitts said that he and his wife were sitting on their back patio when the car came through their fence and almost hit their dog.
"It had to have been going 100 miles per hour, it sounded like. It's a very quiet neighborhood, so that was out of the ordinary," Colpitts said. "They ran over the fence through our backyard and now we have got to replace it, so that's cool."
Colpitts said he tried to talk to the people who were in the car, but they ran away from the scene.
Biddeford Deputy Police Chief Steven Gorton confirmed to Maine's Total Coverage that officers responded to 16 Laurier St. Wednesday night, and that the incident remains under investigation. Because the investigation is ongoing, Gorton said he could not share additional information at this time.

title: Kohen Wiley’s family pushes for federal investigation after baby’s shooting deemed justified
text:
SENATOBIA, Miss. (WMC/Gray News) - The family of 1-year-old Kohen Wiley is pushing to have the Department of Justice open an investigation into his death.
Kohen was shot and killed by a Senatobia police officer back on June 14 at the Senatobia Walmart parking lot.
Earlier this week, Mississippi Attorney General Lynn Fitch’s office announced the officer was justified in his actions.
The Wiley family is represented by civil rights attorneys Ben Crump and Van Turner. The two held a press conference alongside the Wiley family and community activists Thursday morning.
“I’m having a difficult time understanding the word justified. I just don’t understand,” said LaSandra Williams, Kohen’s paternal grandmother.
Williams and Kohen’s maternal grandmother, Veronica Roberson, say they remain heartbroken.
According to Crump’s team, the Wiley family was able to review all of the surveillance and body camera footage from the shooting provided by the Mississippi Bureau of Investigation Thursday morning.
“Disgusted me. First, I want to say, the word justified has haunted me since Monday,” said Roberson.
Roberson and Williams said they will not stop pushing for justice.
“We’re going to petition the Department of Justice to open an investigation to make sure that we get justice for this baby. It just won’t end here,” said Turner.
Turner and Crump said the videos from MBI match the results of their independent autopsy.
Kohen was shot through the side, right to left. According to Crump, MBI said a total of three bullets were fired.
“The third bullet from the side, the bullet that killed one-year-old baby Kohen Wiley, was not justified,” said Crump.
After being cleared by the Mississippi Attorney General, Senatobia Police Officer Hunter Foster reportedly resigned, according to Turner.
Kohen’s family, Crump’s team, and the community said they want Foster decertified.
“It’s not a white or Black issue. It’s a right or wrong issue,” said Brackin Camp. “This was way too much force; it’s unbelievable what happened in the Walmart parking lot that day.”
A special meeting was called by the Senatobia Board of Aldermen and the Mayor on Wednesday. WMC news crews were there; however, a motion was passed to turn the meeting into a closed executive session regarding police personnel.

title: ‘There are no words’: Boyfriend accused of killing girlfriend, her 15-year-old son, and her mother
text:
HAPPY VALLEY, Ore. (KPTV/Gray News) — Three people found shot to death inside an Oregon home on Tuesday have been identified, along with the person who police say is responsible.
According to Happy Valley police, 78-year-old Patricia Lynn Campbell, 47-year-old Katie Lynn Kinder and 15-year-old Evan Scott Kinder were found dead inside their home after officers were called to the residence for a welfare check.
Officers said the welfare check was requested after Kinder did not show up to work.
Neighbors told officers they had not seen anyone at the house for a few days.
The Clackamas County Medical Examiner’s Office said Wednesday autopsies showed all three died from gunshot wounds.
Detectives named 45-year-old Edward Villa as the person believed to be responsible for the family members’ murders.
Police said Villa was Kinder’s boyfriend and lived at the home with her, her son and her mother.
Villa was found dead Wednesday in a motel room at the South Jetty Inn in Hammond of an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound, according to Warrenton police.
Members of the U.S. Marshals Service found him after officers watched his car at the motel.
Officials said Villa had worked for the North Clackamas School District since 2007, most recently as a student and community engagement specialist. The district said he did not show up for work Wednesday.
In a statement, family members said they lost a mother, a sister and a nephew. They described Campbell as someone who helped hold the family together and who was loved as a mother and grandmother.
Loved ones described Kinder as a loving aunt who brought joy and laughter to the family. They said Evan was young and had his whole life ahead of him.
“There are no words strong enough to describe the pain, grief, and devastation we are feeling,” the family shared in part.
The family asked for privacy as they grieved and thanked the community for support.
Villa’s ex-wife, Tiffany Villa, said they share a son and her main concern is his well-being.

title: Reny wants to address affordability in bid for Senate District 13
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Sen. Cameron Reny, D-Bristol, wants to continue the work she has started in her two terms representing Senate District 13.
Reny is up against Edwin W. Mitchell, I-Boothbay, to represent Senate District 13, which consists of all of Lincoln County excluding Dresden and including Washington and Windsor. Reny is the current holder of the seat and if reelected, she will enter her third term.
“Public service, it’s important to me,” Reny said. “My communities are important to me and I want our kids to stand a shot at a life here.”
Born and raised in Bristol, Reny continues to live in her hometown. She went to Guilford College in Greensboro, N.C., where she got a community and justice studies degree. She obtained her master’s degree in school counseling from the University of Southern Maine in Portland.
Most of Reny’s professional career before becoming a state senator was spent as a school counselor, a position she said she is “really passionate about.”
“I think when everyone pitches in, we are all better off and I am of a mindset that I want to leave the world better than I found it and school counseling was what I ended up gravitating towards because it’s helping kids and families,” Reny said.
Her career started out at Biddeford Middle School and when she decided she wanted to move closer to home, she worked at South Bristol School for a few years. She would go on to become the counselor at Woolwich Central School. The roles gave her experience dealing with people from different backgrounds and viewpoints, which she said has helped her with her problem solving skills and bringing together different stakeholders.
When she became a senator, Reny said she had a “hunch” that her school counselor skills would be useful in the new line of work.
“What matters when it comes to getting bills passed into law is your ability to relationship build, your ability to bring in all the appropriate stakeholders, your ability to work with people who don’t necessarily see eye to eye with you, which are all skills I’ve been using for years and years, and that have made me a very effective legislator and have made me very effective working across the aisle,” Reny said.
During her time in the school system, Reny said she has served on school-wide and district-wide committees, and served as the president of the Maine School Counseling Association for a few years.
If reelected, Reny said she wants to continue her public service. Her desire to run again also is fueled by her being raised in a “very strong community” that has a heart for helping each other out. This means to not just donate money, but to devote time and effort, she said.
“I feel like we’ve done a good job trying to insulate the state of Maine from sort of the federal uncertainty that has been prevalent over the last few years, and I want to see that work continue,” Reny said.
In this election, Reny said she believes her experience sets her apart. With this, she said she has been a capable legislator and has been effective in getting different policy “across the finish line.” This includes a bill that was passed last session that made it where medical debt will not affect someone’s credit score. Reny said a bill like this makes it where people are now able to access mortgages, business loans, and other financials that previously weren’t able to because they were sick or hurt.
Not only does Reny want to do better for the state now, she said she wants to set up a “bright future” where people can afford to live and raise their families.
“I want my kids and grandkids and everybody’s kids and grandkids to be able to live here and thrive here long after we’re gone,” she said.
Another achievement Reny is proud of from her time in office comes from her first term. She reflected on how when she was a school counselor, she faced the challenge of a student or their family having a mental health crisis and finding that when they needed to go to the emergency room, their insurance would not pay for the counseling they needed. Reny said this was usually because the referral came from an emergency room doctor instead of their primary care physician.
This encouraged her to push forward a bill that allowed emergency room referrals to be used to access counseling services.
“For people who are struggling with those sort of issues, and honestly, just getting an appointment, taking the time off work, getting yourself there, it’s something that’s seemingly simple that is a hurdle for a lot of people, understandably so,” Reny said.
Another effort Reny is proud of is her climate resiliency work. She said her district faces bigger and stronger storms and need to be ready for them.
“I know culverts aren’t sexy, but they’re very important,” she said.
Other work includes healthcare, where she pushed for a bill to strengthen the prescription drug affordability board which she said gave it direction and resources to use for policy. She said her “extremely bipartisan” Federally Qualified Health Center pharmacy bill presents grants to serve rural and underserved populations to expand pharmaceutical services and decrease the cost of prescriptions.
Reny currently serves on the Appropriations and Financial Affairs Committee and the Marine Resources Committee.
She said her time as a senator has allowed her to learn a lot about a wide range of topics. She used the example of how when she first started, she was placed on the Marine Resources Committee and Health Coverage Insurance and Financial Committee. The experience allowed her to fully understand different aspects of government and the people it serves, she said.
“Standing up for, you know, our farmers, our fisherman, our loggers, and really trying to insulate the state once again,” Reny said. “I hate to come back to it, but it’s sort of the weird world we’re in right now. It feels like there’s a lot of chaos coming from the federal level and trying to not let that chaos steer us off course, or harm our friends and neighbors.”
While on the campaign trail, Reny said the biggest concerns she has heard from people in the district is the cost of living.
Affordability issues are directly tied into cost increases controlled at the federal level, such as fuel, energy, and inflation, she said. At the state level, Reny said the legislature can tackle this issue in different ways.
Reny used the example of high energy costs and said she would like to see the state diversify its energy creation production, making sure it finds anything available to it. She said she would like to see more hydropower and the exploration of any alternative energy source.
She said she also wants public advocates to be able to “check” Central Maine Power when necessary by also having ways to pivot.
Affordability makes the economy do better and small businesses do better when people have buying power, Reny said. By creating more accessible and affordable necessities such as energy, childcare, prescription drug costs, and more, Reny said people can not only afford the bare minimum, but also extra to improve their lives.
“I can’t personally control inflation on my own,” Reny said. “You can do things to make life more affordable where you can.”
Affordable housing fits into this through Reny’s efforts to incentive the creation of new housing, as well as protects more affordable options such as mobile home parks. She mentioned previous bills she has worked on to protect mobile home parks from private equity investors that would buy them and raise the rents.
“When you can make other places in people’s lives more affordable, they can at least take a breath,” she said.
Reny has also been thinking of the impending closure of the labor and delivery unit at MaineHealth Lincoln Hospital in Damariscotta. She said the closure of the addiction resource center in Damariscotta is also unacceptable.
To address these closures and prevent more from happening, Reny said she has a few ideas for the legislature. She wants more transparency in the decision making and financials, especially because of the healthcare system’s “virtual monopoly” in the state.
Reny said because of the district’s high need for substance use resources, it is irresponsible to take them away.
“We’re going to have to look into creative solutions and probably some alternative community service possibilities, but we can’t go without,” Reny said. “I don’t accept us going without.”
When it comes to the state’s working waterfront, Reny said there are ways to find balance between those making a living on the water and making sure others also have access for recreation. While she said she does not know a legislative fix for the balance, she said she is willing to listen and learn to see what people need.
Local infrastructure fits into two separate areas for Reny. She said the first is the community resiliency partnership, which is a state level program that provides grants to municipalities to upgrade infrastructure and prepare for weather events.
The other area is the potential for community and economic development partnerships throughout the state. Reny said there are possibilities that can grow out of it, especially since the state has an entire department for it.
In the past year, the state legislature has evaluated ways to change the funding formula for how education subsidy is sent out to different towns. Reny said a part of the reason people are frustrated with rising education costs is not only within the school system, but because of how everything else has raised in cost.
“Everything is so much more expensive that it was before and just the additional burden feels more daunting that I think it would otherwise,” Reny said.
To solve some of these increasing costs, Reny said she would like to see a higher tax rate on non-resident homes and see the homestead exemption raised. She would also like to see the federal government pay 40% of special education costs, but that is out of her control, she said.
Within the cost for education, Reny said if the state can get a handle on health insurance prices, it might ease the burden on residents. She said that if health insurance can be more “reasonable,” less money is needed for every school employee, town administrator, and staff of businesses across the district.
Reny has endorsements from Maine American Federation of Labor and Congress of Industrial Organizations, the Sierra Club, Maine Service Employees Associations, SEIU Local 1989; Planned Parenthood Maine Action Fund PAC, Maine Conservation Voters Action Fund, Committee to Protect Health Care, EqualityMaine PAC, and the Wabanaki Alliance.
The election is on Tuesday, Nov. 3.

title: Are fake spiderweb decorations dangerous to birds and other animals?
text:
Yes.
Fake spiderweb decorations can entangle birds and other wildlife, sometimes causing serious injuries or death.
The Canadian Wildlife Federation says animals caught in the synthetic fibers may be unable to free themselves, leaving them vulnerable to predators, exhaustion and starvation.
WildCare, a California wildlife hospital, has treated various entangled birds. Injuries can include restricted blood flow and tissue damage, according to the National Audubon Society.
The American Bird Conservancy warns that outdoor webbing can trap unsuspecting birds, particularly during fall migration. Other entanglement hazards include fishing line, sports nets, kite strings, wind chimes and balloon ribbons.
Experts recommend only using artificial webs indoors. Outdoor displays should avoid flight paths, trees and shrubs.
The danger is documented by wildlife rehabilitators, although the overall frequency of entanglements and deaths remains unknown. Anyone finding an entangled animal should contact a licensed rehabilitator rather than try to release it.
This fact brief is responsive to conversations such as this one.
The Maine Trust for Local News partners with Gigafact to produce fact briefs — bite-sized fact checks of trending claims. Read our methodology to learn how we check claims.

title: Obituary: Janet Hanson
text:
BIDDEFORD – Janet Hanson passed away on Oct. 19, 2026, at her home. She was born on June 29, 1944, to Lucien and Marsha (Hutchins) Bedard and was educated in Arundel and Kennebunk schools.
She married Wayne Hanson on Jan. 19, 1974. They celebrated 52 years of marriage.
Janet worked as an antique dealer, which was her passion. She enjoyed shopping, telling jokes and laughing, animals of any kind, plants and flowers, and Christmas. She especially loved her adopted daughter, Victoria, and adopted son, Chris. She loved to be called “Ma.”
She is survived by her husband, Wayne; adopted daughter, Victoria, adopted son, Chris; and many cousins and friends.
At her request, there will be no services.

title: Trump backs Ramaswamy on ad featuring Amy Acton’s estranged mother
text:
COLUMBUS, Ohio (AP) — The backlash over an Ohio campaign advertisement attacking Amy Acton, the Democratic nominee for governor, spread beyond the state’s borders Thursday, causing fresh headaches for Republicans with less than two weeks until the midterm elections.
The latest episode began when Gov. Mike DeWine criticized Vivek Ramaswamy, a fellow Republican that he endorsed as his successor, for running an ad featuring Acton’s estranged mother criticizing her. Acton’s mother lost custody of her children decades ago after her husband was indicted for raping Acton as a child.
But President Donald Trump took the opposite approach hours later, posting on social media that Ramaswamy’s ad was “hitting pay dirt” and questioning DeWine’s loyalty to the party.
Trump’s stance only hardened throughout the day. Speaking to reporters at the White House, Trump said, “Amy Acton’s mother said horrible things about Amy Acton” and “she’s fair game.”
And at a campaign rally in Iowa, Trump regaled the crowd with a story about how Ramaswamy called him to ask for advice.
“You’ve got to ride with it,” Trump recalled telling Ramaswamy, a biotech billionaire and former presidential candidate. Trump expressed jealousy that he didn’t have such a strong ad to run during his own campaigns.
“I told him to leave it up and look upstairs and say: ‘Thank you, God, very much. I appreciate it,’” Trump added. “I only wish I could have had an ad like that against somebody.”
Trump’s aggressive defense of Ramaswamy practically guarantees that more of his party’s candidates will face questions about the issue at a moment when they already risk being dragged down by the president’s low popularity.
Rep. Ashley Hinson, the Republican nominee for U.S. Senate in Iowa, was asked about it before appearing with Trump at the rally.
She told ABC News the ad is “absolutely terrible” and “I think they should take the ad down.”
Ramaswamy’s campaign has said it plans to spend $4 million to show the ad online and on television.
DeWine stops short of pulling his endorsement
The controversy has became the latest test of the bounds of acceptable political discourse.
In western Michigan, former Republican Rep. Fred Upton said the ad had spread throughout his community as people heard about it on the radio and television or were asked about it by others.
“They asked me about it at the bank today,” Upton said, adding that the ad “speaks horribly of the gutter politics that some rely on.”
An influential Ohio Republican, former Rep. Jim Renacci, posted a lengthy essay on social media overnight suggesting that “the floor may have just fallen out from under the Republican campaign for Ohio Governor” and urging everyone in the party to distance themselves from it.
Ohio U.S. Sen. Jon Husted, who is being challenged by former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown, said he would not have run the ad. So did Republican Secretary of State Frank LaRose, who is running for state auditor.
At a gathering with reporters at the Ohio Statehouse on Thursday, DeWine recalled the painful experiences of rape victims he dealt with as a county prosecutor and state attorney general.
“It’s wrong to run this ad,” he said. “And, even at this late time — my wife, Fran, saw the ad just run this morning on TV — I would just urge the Ramaswamy campaign to take this down.”
The governor stopped short of pulling his backing for Ramaswamy. DeWine recalled that a previous line of attack by the Acton campaign had mentioned Ramaswamy’s mother, and the governor said that was also wrong because “family members have always historically been off limits.” However, DeWine noted that the topic was never used in a multimillion-dollar ad campaign.
Acton’s criticism cited an investigative report into Geetha Ramaswamy’s role at a pharmaceutical company run by her son, whom Acton and Democrats described as “hiring his own mother to manipulate clinical trial data.” The Ramaswamy campaign called those claims “slanderous.”
“Governor DeWine is correct that the first and only candidate to attack the mother of her opponent in this race was Amy Acton,” Ramaswamy spokesperson Connie Luck said in a statement, adding, “We refuse to accept the media’s double standards.”
Vance supported Ramaswamy
The Ramaswamy campaign video features Acton’s birth mother, Donna Arthur, calling her “a liar” and insinuating she has mental health issues.
Acton, Ohio’s COVID-19-era health director, has made no secret of facing homelessness and abuse as a child. Arthur lost custody of her children after their stepfather, Arthur’s husband, was indicted on a charge of rape involving Acton.
The abuse allegedly happened from December 1976 to April 1978. Cledith Arthur failed to show for a court appearance and became a fugitive. Donna Arthur remained married to him until his death in 2004.
Acton’s campaign on Tuesday posted a video of her brother, who supported her backstory about living in a tent and being abused.
Republican Vice President JD Vance, an Ohio native son, expressed disgust with Republicans “whining” about the ad while he visited the state on Wednesday.
Amid the turmoil, Ohio Republican Party Chairman Alex Triantafilou posted what sounded like a warning, or a threat.
“The final days of a tough campaign are always the best time to find out who is really with you and who just posts and pretends,” he wrote. “Yes — we are keeping score.” The quote was followed by a winking-eye emoji.
While Republicans are at odds over the ad, Democrats have rallied to support Acton.
“Child abuse and sexual assault should never be weaponized to score partisan points,” Democratic Governors Association spokesperson Izzi Levy said. ”Governor DeWine is right — Vivek Ramaswamy’s ad is beyond troubling, and he should take it down immediately and apologize to survivors everywhere and all those hurt by this reprehensible attack.”
Illinois first lady MK Pritzker said she donated $500,000 to Acton’s campaign because of the ad.
___
Associated Press reporters Joey Cappelletti contributed from Washington and Thomas Beaumont contributed from Sioux City, Iowa.

title: 5 candidates running for 2 Brewer City Council seats
text:
Five candidates are vying for two Brewer City Council seats this election.
Kathleen Kramer and Kevin O’Connell are running for a one-year seat that was opened after former Deputy Mayor Bill Kimball resigned in July. Jarod Farn-Guillette, Marissa Worster and incumbent Dani O’Halloran are running for a single seat with a three-year term.
At a candidate forum Thursday held by the Brewer Education Association, the five candidates shared their thoughts on affordability, public safety and the future of the Brewer Municipal Pool, which was closed multiple times this summer because of a leak. Every candidate said they support a city pool.
The candidates appear in alphabetical order.
Jarod Farn-Guillette
Farn-Guillette, a Maine Department of Transportation planner and youth hockey and lacrosse coach, is running on a platform of “persistent, polite policy.” Persistence and politeness is needed to enact meaningful policy, he said.
When asked about how he would navigate council decisions on increasing taxes or modifying Brewer’s services to keep costs down, Farn-Guillette said he’s willing to make unpopular decisions to keep the city out of debt and affordable for residents.
“Nobody wants to cut anything, but to ensure that our city is fiscally solvent, I’m willing to do that,” he said.
In his other responses, Farn-Guillette said he supports Brewer’s police department and sees homelessness across Greater Bangor as a mental health issue that could be helped, but too much assistance may lead to reliance.
“I’m of the belief that when the law ends, the law breaks, and it is not necessarily our purpose and our place to be overly empathetic. We need to provide care, but we also need to protect the people that matter to us,” he said.
Kathleen Kramer
Kramer, a retired teacher and National Guard veteran, is seeking a seat so she can help the council bring in new business and ideas, she said.
With affordability being a main issue for many residents, Kramer said she would not only look to bring more businesses to Brewer, but she would try to find additional revenue from city services. Kramer didn’t immediately have specific ideas for that revenue.
“I’ll know more when you elect me, and if I get in there, I can say, ‘OK, what’s going on? Let’s look at this. Have you considered this?’” she said.
Along with bringing in more business to expand the city’s tax base, Kramer said she wants to improve the city’s communications. The city’s new website has made it easier for residents to find what they’re looking for, but community feedback and her new perspective could further improve it, she said.
Kevin O’Connell
O’Connell, a former Brewer City Councilor and Maine State Representative, is running for the one-year seat after several years away from the council. When he learned that the one-year term would be up for election, he thought he’d return to public service, he said.
Brewer has been successful in keeping tax jumps to a minimum in the past, but if a decision to either modify services or raise taxes came up, O’Connell said he would work with the city staff to know what staffing and funding levels are needed. City staff in the economic development department are already working to expand the tax base, and he would work with them to help, he said.
“I’ve said this before when I was on City Council; I want everybody that works for the city to be able to talk to me and not worry about repercussions. I want to be an open door,” he said.
When asked about the possibility of homelessness increasing in Brewer, O’Connell said he doesn’t “want what’s happening over in Bangor to ever come to Brewer.” Brewer police are helping people get to services, either in Bangor or at the Bangor Area Recovery Network in Brewer, when they’re needed, which has helped Brewer have a lower homelessness rate than Bangor, he said.
In addition to wanting to work with city staff and support the police department, O’Connell said he wants to be able to take action on citizen concerns when they’re brought to the council.
Dani O’Halloran
O’Halloran, who is also running for re-election as a state representative against Pat Jude, has held a seat on the City Council since 2023.
During the candidate forum, O’Halloran said she’s focused on accountability and affordability in both Augusta and Brewer, and “not afraid to speak out on issues” when she disagrees with other elected officials.
“I just want to say that nobody votes across the aisle more than I do in Augusta. When I look at a bill, I never look at the back to see whether it’s a Republican bill or Democrat bill. I look to see if it’s good for Brewer and the state of Maine, and I vote for it,” she said.
When asked about how she would navigate increasing costs possibly leading to cuts in Brewer’s departments, O’Halloran did not say how she would go about those decisions but pointed to a lack of taxation for Maine’s high earners. Without that tax, the state is not bringing in as much revenue as possible, she said.
Similar to O’Connell’s response, O’Halloran said Brewer police are doing what they can to help direct Brewer’s homeless population to services, but a lack of state funding for mental health programs has left many unhoused individuals without proper treatment.
Marissa Worster
Worster, a small business owner, is running to be an approachable councilor who residents can bring their issues to. In her previous interactions with councilors, they’ve not always been as helpful as she said they could be.
In many of her responses to questions during the forum, Worster said she would seek community input before making a decision as a council member. For a specific situation — the challenge of either repairing or replacing the Brewer Municipal Pool — Worster said she would want the issue to go to voters.
“It’s kind of one of those things where if the council makes a decision and they say ‘We’re going to spend $10 million on a new pool or we’re going to spend $3 million on a splash pad,’ somebody’s going to be unhappy,” Worster said.
Worster, who described herself as “not polished,” said she may not have specifics for how she’ll enact policy as a council member, but she has life experience and a desire to listen to citizens that will lead to every resident having a voice on city matters.

title: Respected attorney was battling cancer when foster son murdered her for her money, officials say
text:
SAN DIEGO (KFMB) - A California attorney and foster mother disappeared while battling cancer in 2024. Now, her foster son is accused of poisoning her with fentanyl and burying her body.
Nadine Jett, a 64-year-old attorney and foster mother, disappeared in January 2024. She was battling cancer at the time and failed to show up for a medical appointment. Last year, her remains were found buried on her 20-acre Valley Center property.
The San Diego District Attorney’s Office announced Wednesday that they’ve made an arrest in the case. Jett’s foster son, 34-year-old Cedric von Ferdinand, is accused of poisoning her with illicit fentanyl in order to get his hands on her money.
“This is a case of deadly greed,” said San Diego County District Attorney Summer Stephan.
When Jett disappeared, von Ferdinand had been living with her, pretending to care for her, Stephan says. He allegedly told friends and family she would die soon and that she wanted to be cremated without a funeral service.
Von Ferdinand allegedly told a caretaker that was due to come to the house that she was no longer needed because Jett had died around Jan. 17, 2024. Stephan alleges it’s around that time that Von Ferdinand killed his foster mother.
Von Ferdinand raised suspicions when he tried to sell all three properties Jett owned, Stephan says. He allegedly forged a real estate document using his thumbprint, pretending it was hers. During a search, investigators also found a fake marriage license for von Ferdinand and his foster mother that he is accused of forging with a co-defendant.
“It was signed and notarized well after her death,” Stephan said.
In July 2025, Jett’s remains were found wrapped in a bedsheet in a 6-foot hole about 30 yards from her home. The medical examiner’s office determined she had massive amounts of illicit fentanyl in her system, and her death was ruled a homicide.
Bianca Lucci and her quadruplet sisters are Jett’s foster daughters, and they deeply miss her.
“Nadine took us in at a young age after about 10 foster homes, and she was the mom we needed. She gave us a fair chance at life,” Lucci said. “It is sad we’ll never get to see her again, but I do believe she’s looking from above, proud of us.”
Von Ferdinand is scheduled to be arraigned Thursday on a murder charge as well as two special circumstance allegations.
