title: Death Notice: Merritt Elton Gooding
Norridgewock voters reject moratorium on noisy commercial developments
text:
NORRIDGEWOCK — Town voters at a special town meeting Wednesday night narrowly rejected a 180-day moratorium on certain commercial developments that produce noise.
The tally, announced by moderator Drew Ketterer after town staff counted raised hands several times, was 61 in favor, 65 opposed.
The vote effectively clears the way for the Norridgewock Planning Board to continue its review of site plan applications for two controversial projects, a burnout pit off Ward Hill Road and a gun shop with shooting ranges of up to 1,000 yards off Skowhegan Road.
Town officials, however, can still propose at a future town meeting the new noise regulations they have already started to consider, Town Manager Richard LaBelle said. They just would not be in place for the review of the pending projects.
Even so, the planning board at its meeting earlier this month requested professional noise studies be done for both. It also scheduled a formal public hearing on the shooting range application, to be held at 6 p.m. Nov. 12 at the Mill Stream Elementary School, 26 Mercer Road.
The more than 120 voters who attended the special town meeting made quick work of the moratorium and other municipal business on the agenda. Voters approved updates to the town’s Subdivision Ordinance, Board of Appeals Ordinance, and Street Naming and House Numbering Ordinance; authorized the $2,500 purchase of a small parcel near downtown Norridgewock; and repealed a requirement that the town put notices in the Morning Sentinel for special town meetings.
The only comments on the moratorium came after Ketterer, formerly Maine’s attorney general, called for a vote and there appeared to be some confusion. LaBelle and Select Board Vice Chair Lindsey Lynch briefly explained what a moratorium is and what “yes” or “no” votes would mean.
Had it been approved, the moratorium would have prohibited certain kinds of new developments or changes in use and the town’s processing of applications for such projects for 180 days. It included a provision that pending applications for developments that fall under its scope would have been put on hold until voters had their say on new proposed rules.
The moratorium would have applied to developments such as shooting ranges; facilities used for testing and demonstration of firearms, ammunition, explosives, or pyrotechnic devices; facilities used for motorsport activities; outdoor entertainment venues using amplification systems on a regular basis; and outdoor industrial operations.
The Select Board drafted the moratorium proposal after hearing concerns from residents over the proposed shooting ranges at 255 Skowhegan Road, LaBelle said previously. The goal was to give town officials time to draft new proposed noise regulations for voters to review by the annual town meeting in March.
The ordinance amendments, meanwhile, passed Wednesday without controversy.
The updated Subdivision Ordinance was presented to voters in March and was rejected. LaBelle said that was likely due to a lack of information among voters. The amendments bring the town’s regulations into compliance with state law, and where the town had a choice, the planning board proposed the least restrictive measures, LaBelle said.
The major change to the Board of Appeals Ordinance, LaBelle said, removes a requirement that an appellant pay for legal notices of hearings to be published in a newspaper. Instead, the ordinance now requires notices to be posted at the town office and online and sent to relevant property owner, abutters and town officials.
The Street Naming and Housing Numbering Ordinance outlines a new process for reviewing requests to change road names. Officials proposed it seeking to better define the process and their authority in response to recent matters that came before the Select Board, according to LaBelle.
As for the property acquisition, voters authorized appropriating up to $3,500 from tax increment financing funds to complete the deal, which has an agreed-upon price of $2,500.
LaBelle said the town has no plans to develop the property, a 0.21-acre parcel at the corner of Mechanic and Main streets, along Mill Stream. Officials wanted it to maintain and enhance the appearance of the downtown area. The seller is Wayne Rogers.
In the final warrant article, voters repealed a requirement they enacted in 1983 that the town place notices of special town meetings in the Morning Sentinel for three days, one week before the meeting.
That can be costly, LaBelle has said: notices for Wednesday’s meeting cost the town $820. People are increasingly turning online to get their information, rather than look at the legal notices section in the newspaper, he said.

title: Maine heating oil hits record $6.04 per gallon
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WAGM) - The Maine Department of Energy Resources today released its latest weekly survey of heating fuel prices, showing the average statewide price of heating oil reached a record $6.04 per gallon on Oct. 19. That is an 83% increase from the same time last year.
New record follows last month’s high
The previous record for heating oil in Maine was set last month at $6.02 per gallon.
“Maine has broken yet another record for heating oil prices, putting even more pressure on families as winter approaches,” said Celina Cunningham, acting commissioner of DOER. “With rising costs and cold weather on the way, I encourage Maine people to stay informed of current prices, review incentive options through Efficiency Maine, and to contact their Community Action Agency if they need immediate relief.”
Based on a standard 275-gallon oil tank, residents are now estimated to pay approximately $750 more to fill their tank to capacity than they would have one year ago, prior to the start of the Iran conflict.
Maine’s reliance on heating oil
Maine consumes more residential heating oil per capita than any other U.S. state and consumes significantly more per capita than other New England states. Approximately 50% of all Maine households rely on fuel oil as their primary heat source, although that figure has declined steadily from 70% in 2010.
Governor calls for more federal assistance
Earlier this month, the governor called on Congress to provide additional home heating assistance as President Trump’s war in Iran continues to drive energy prices to record highs. In a letter to Maine’s congressional delegation, Gov. Mills said current federal funding for the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program is insufficient to meet the increased need caused by sharply higher home heating costs.
Assistance programs available
Financial assistance for home heating is available through the Home Energy Assistance Program, administered by MaineHousing. In addition to HEAP, the Energy Crisis Intervention Program, designed to assist low-income households experiencing an immediate energy-related crisis, will open on Nov. 1.
MaineHousing is urging residents to apply for HEAP as soon as possible and to begin the process before they are out of fuel or experiencing a heating crisis. Priority households include those with a member who is 60 years of age or older, has a disability, or is 6 years of age or younger.
Efficiency incentives and winter guide
At current prices, switching from oil or kerosene to energy efficient heat pumps can save Maine households thousands of dollars annually in heating costs. Maine residents are encouraged to explore home efficiency incentives available through Efficiency Maine.
Earlier this month, DOER released its annual Winter Heating Guide for the 2026-2027 heating season. The guide includes home heating and weatherization tips for Maine residents, steps to access energy assistance programs, links to online resources including the latest energy prices, and summaries of programs available through MaineHousing, Efficiency Maine, Community Action Agencies and other partners.

title: Pres. Trump to hold midterm rally in Fort Myers on Friday
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - President Donald Trump is scheduled to host a midterm campaign rally in Fort Myers, Fla. on Friday afternoon.
GOP organizers said the event aims to mobilize Republican voters for the November elections.
“The midterms are a game of turnout, and nobody turns out voters quite like President Trump,” said Emma Hall, RNC Southeast Regional Communications Director.
The event will be held at Florida Gulf Coast University’s Alico Arena, beginning at 2 p.m. eastern.
Southwest Florida is considered one of the most Republican corners of a state that has been known as a GOP stronghold for years.
Hall said the election is critical for the party.
“Protecting our majorities in the House and the Senate is critical to continuing the Republican agenda of tax cuts, safe communities, secure borders, you know, investment booms in states like Florida,” she said.
Republican gubernatorial nominee and Congressman Byron Donalds is also scheduled to appear at the rally.
Donalds and other GOP candidates in the state have been favored in polling for months. But, a new University of North Florida poll found that the party’s leads in the gubnatorial and U.S. Senate races have been lessening.
José Javier Rodríguez, a Democratic candidate running for Florida attorney general, said he sees the president’s visit as a sign of desparation.
“It’s clear that they feel a little desperation to get turnout,” he said. “And to kind of actually give Republicans a reason to vote Republican instead of crossing the aisle. But it’s unclear why they’ve chosen the president as the messenger when, you know, he’s sort of the billboard for broken promises on the economic front.”

title: Strikes and sisterhood: Inside Bangor’s Coffee Cup bowling league
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Thursday mornings at Family Fun Bowling Alley sound like this — pins crashing, cheers, and laughter from the Coffee Cup League.
The league brings together 24 women every week to bowl, socialize and stay active.
Decades on the lanes
For some, bowling is a lifelong love:
- Ruth has been bowling for about 50 years.
- Gloria started about 60 years ago.
- Roxy joined about 17 years ago.
“I joined for exercise and the camaraderie,” Ruth said.
Roxy joined for family: “She talked me into it, she’s my sister.”
A 90th birthday celebration
Thursday was extra special for mother-daughter duo Sherrie Pedersen and Gloria Tapley, as the team celebrated Gloria turning 90 years young.
“There’s three mother-daughter teams,” Sherri said. “Me and my mom, the 97-year-old and her daughter Toby and another couple over here.”
Each week, teams face a different opponent — though scores aren’t the focus.
“We really like it when we get the pins down, we get a strike or a spare,” Sherri said. “Which I’m not doing so hot today,” Gloria laughed.
More than a game
“It’s good for a laugh.” — Roxy
“We all think it keeps everybody young.” — Sherri
“Well, it keeps us on our feet.” — Gloria

title: Get more money to live, work and learn in Maine with these programs, rebates, scholarships and tax credits
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Living in Maine has an inherent richness, but these programs can create real financial breathing room. Whether you’re building a career, caring for family or planning your next chapter, it’s worth taking a closer look at what’s available simply for calling Maine home.
Here’s how you can make the most out of living in Maine.
For education
Maine wants its residents to be well-educated and workforce-ready. There are multiple programs to support students of all ages at different stages.
The Maine Community College System is a smart choice for lifelong learning, providing guaranteed transfer programs to all of Maine’s seven public universities and six private universities. The seven colleges offer many low- or no-cost options, including free Early College courses for high school students, tuition-free associate degrees and one-year certificates for recent high school graduates.
For those looking to learn a new skill or change careers, Kennebec Valley Community College in Fairfield and Central Maine Community College in Auburn offer workforce training opportunities, including no-cost programs in high-demand fields. A new $5 million federal grant is also expanding access to manufacturing training at several Maine community colleges.
The Competitive Skills Scholarship is for residents seeking a degree or credential for a job in a high-wage, in-demand occupation. Via the Alfond Scholars Initiative, The Roux Institute at Northeastern University offers generous graduate school scholarships for Maine residents to earn in-demand degrees in high-growth fields like Applied AI, Biotechnology, Computer Science and more. The average award is $30,000.
Central Maine residents may also qualify for scholarships based on where they live. The Maine Community Foundation maintains county-specific scholarship listings, including the William Bingham 2nd Scholarship for Adult Learners, which supports qualifying residents of Oxford, Franklin and Somerset counties returning to school for degrees, certificates or professional training.
Maybe you’re all done with school? If you live and work in Maine, you could be eligible for the Student Loan Repayment Program (SLRP), which will reimburse you up to $25,000 through state tax credits. Qualified individuals obtained an associate, bachelor’s or graduate degree after 2007 from an accredited school anywhere on planet Earth, were Maine residents during the tax year, and have a certain amount of earned income during the tax year.
For current and future homeowners
The First Home Loan Program is a state-run program that provides low-interest loans and money for repairs to first-time or longer-term, out-of-market homebuyers. Although household income limits and home prices apply, most Maine households and homes are eligible for the program.
If you already own property, Efficiency Maine offers rebates for energy-forward improvements. Whether it’s new appliances, added insulation or EV chargers, Efficiency Maine has many incentives and energy loans for homeowners and commercial property owners.
Central Maine homeowners may qualify for additional assistance through local community action agencies. The Kennebec Valley Community Action Program offers grants and other financial assistance for essential home repairs, accessibility improvements and urgent safety issues.
For families
First, for simply being born in Maine, babies are given a $500 MyAlfond grant deposited into a 529 investment account (known locally as NextGen529) where it will earn tax-free interest for future higher education purposes, whether that’s four-year college, two-year associate degree programs, trade schools, even qualified online courses, at home or abroad. Contribute to your child’s NextGen 529 account and receive 30% of the contribution amount each year in a NextStep Matching Grant, up to a $300 match.
While the state continually expands pre-K programming, the Child Care Affordability Program makes direct payments to child care providers for qualified families making up to 125% of Maine’s median income. Once kids are in public school, all students across the state receive free breakfast and lunch at school, regardless of income. Parents of all backgrounds report feeling relieved at how much time, energy and money they save.
For veterans
Beyond free access to state parks, museums, and free noncommercial fishing and hunting registrations, veterans receive several other employment perks in Maine.
Boots2Roots helps active-duty military members, veterans and spouses find meaningful work and put down roots in Maine. With free, personalized transition services worth thousands of dollars, like resume-writing, career coaching and employer networking, Boots2Roots aims to help their “Teammates” find employment or school within two months of arriving in Maine.
All veterans who apply for a job in the state government get an automatic interview if they meet the minimum qualifications for the job. This law applies to Gold Star spouses as well.
For entrepreneurs
Thinking about starting a business? You don’t have to figure everything out on your own. Maine Small Business Development Centers provide free, confidential advising to entrepreneurs and established small-business owners. Whether you’re developing a business plan, looking for financing or trying to grow an existing operation, professional guidance is available at no cost.
You’ll also want to get to know Live + Work in Maine, a nonprofit helping Mainers and soon-to-be Mainers discover the exciting career opportunities and fulfilling lifestyles that make our state special. Visit liveandworkinmaine.com to connect with employers, peers and networks across the state.

title: Bruins stay hot, trounce Predators
text:
BOSTON — Michael DiPietro made 28 saves for his first career shutout, David Pastrnak had two goals and two assists, and the Boston Bruins cruised to a 6-0 victory over the Nashville Predators on Thursday night.
Charlie McAvoy had a career-high four assists for Boston, and Casey Mittelstadt, Elias Lindholm, JJ Peterka and Mark Kastelic also scored.
Pastrnak leads the Bruins in goals (six) and assists (10). Boston improved to 6-0-1 in its last seven games, with the only loss coming Tuesday in overtime at Dallas to conclude a four-game trip.
Justus Annunen stopped 25 shots in his first start for Nashville since last season. The Predators have lost four of five.
The Bruins went ahead 3:49 into the game when Pastrnak sent a cross-ice pass to Mittelstadt, who fired it past Annunen’s right shoulder.
Lindholm made it 2-0 on the power play later in the first. Pastrnak scored midway through the second when he deflected McAvoy’s shot past Annunen, and the Bruins captain assisted on Peterka’s goal late in the period.
Pastrnak capped the scoring with 5 minutes remaining and became the eighth player in Bruins history with 20 career four-point games.
The Bruins scored six goals for the third time, tied with the Golden Knights, Kraken, Avalanche and Hurricanes for the most in 2026-27.
McAvoy became the fourth defenseman in Bruins history with 10 career games of three assists or more, joining Ray Bourque, Bobby Orr and Brad Park.

title: Iran: Oil tankers are on fire, damaged in key strait as fears grow over return to war
text:
Iran: Oil tankers are on fire, damaged in key strait as fears grow over return to war
Seven oil tankers caught fire or were damaged in the Strait of Hormuz overnight after being hit by Iran or striking naval mines, Tehran said Thursday, a markedly high number as tensions wind upward over concerns about a return to all-out war.
Related video: Could President Trump's rallies sway voters in less than two weeks?
With days before Israel's close elections in which Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu could lose power, and ahead of next month's U.S. midterm elections in which war-linked high prices have sparked voter anger, there are concerns that U.S.-Israeli attacks on Iran could resume.
Iranian state television reported the claims about the latest attacks on ships, citing the Revolutionary Guard Corps navy, which again threatened to strike U.S. military bases in the region if the U.S. keeps helping to guide commercial ships through the strait.
The report did not mention casualties. A British military monitor, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations, did not report the attacks, but monitors in recent days have noted reluctance by some shippers to report incidents. Iran still asserts control over the waterway, a central point of leverage in any talks with the U.S. over the war.
Iran's top diplomat, Abbas Araghchi, on Wednesday said a wary Tehran remains open to diplomacy but is ready to defend itself.
Iran has warned that it has learned important military lessons from the war that began with U.S. and Israeli attacks on Feb. 28. In recent days, Tehran has indicated it could expand targets to include infrastructure such as undersea cables and data centers.
The United States for its part is sending more military assets to the region, including a third aircraft carrier and thousands of troops, to join the largest force of American warships and aircraft in the Middle East in decades.
Mediators, meanwhile, have been trying to bring Washington and Tehran back to formal talks.
Iran is still promoting its latest proposal that would end the war and fully open the strait within a week if the U.S. meets several conditions. Those conditions, which include ending the U.S. blockade of Iranian ports, echo ones in the deal that fell apart within days of Washington and Tehran signing it in June.
U.S. President Donald Trump rejected that latest seven-day proposal, but both sides have acknowledged that indirect discussions have continued. Since that rejection, attacks on ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz have increased.
A return to all-out war would again endanger civilians throughout the region and complicate global deliveries of oil, natural gas and related products like fertilizer from the region and likely bring another spike in prices.

title: ‘He didn’t deserve this’: Family heartbroken after 4-year-old boy killed in dog attack
text:
LOUISA COUNTY, Va. (WVIR/Gray News) - A 4-year-old Virginia boy with his whole life ahead of him was killed in a dog attack. As the investigation into the incident continues, the boy’s family is speaking out amid their grief.
Days after 4-year-old Garcia Welch was killed in a dog attack, his family is sharing memories of the little boy they lost as they continue to mourn.
“Garcia is just someone that if you met him, you loved him,” said the boy’s aunt, Cynthia Russ. “He lit up the room. His smile was just amazing.”
Garcia loved painting, playing video games with his older brother and music. His mother, Cathleen Russ, recalled the times she and her son would walk to the bus stop to get his brother, 11-year-old Gabriel Welch.
Garcia’s aunt remembered how friendly he was.
“He was a beautiful kid. He was fun and sweet and kind, and he made friends everywhere. And he just — he didn’t deserve this,” Cynthia Russ said.
The attack
Garcia was killed in a dog attack around 4:40 p.m. Sunday along a highway in Louisa County.
Deputies with the Louisa County Sheriff’s Office arrived at the scene to find Garcia seriously injured with an American bully still attacking him. The sheriff’s office said deputies had to put the dog down to stop the attack.
Garcia was taken to a landing zone for air medical transport but was pronounced dead before he could be flown to a hospital.
Cynthia Russ said the family is still trying to understand what happened that afternoon.
“There’s a lot of confusion about how this could happen — why this happened. Still a lot of confusion about that,” she said.
Cathleen Russ said Garcia was at his father’s home for the weekend. Recently separated, she and Barry Welch had a formal custody agreement. On Sunday, she received a call from a non-family member about the incident.
Gabriel was also at his father’s home on Sunday and witnessed the events. Cynthia Russ described a conversation with the 11-year-old later that night where he claimed he “tried to stop it.”
“I talked to my nephew that night, and he was just crying and screaming,” she recalled.
The sheriff’s office says its investigation remains active. Investigators have not publicly confirmed all the circumstances leading up to the attack.
A life cut short
Before his death, Garcia was beginning a new chapter as a preschool student at Thomas Jefferson Elementary School.
Although he had only recently started attending the school, Principal Jesse Cleaver said Garcia had already made an impression on those around him. In a message sent to families Monday, Cleaver acknowledged the little boy’s death and expressed condolences to those grieving his loss.
“This is heartbreaking news for our Patriot family. Though Garcia was just beginning his time at Thomas Jefferson Elementary School, he quickly made a meaningful impression on those around him with his kind, friendly, and respectful personality,” Cleaver wrote.
The school division said counseling and support would be available to students and staff affected by his death.
For Garcia’s family, preschool was one of many experiences they had been looking forward to sharing with him as he grew older.
“He just had so much ahead of him, and we were just excited to see it,” Cynthia Russ said.
Community offers support
Garcia’s family is now working to arrange his funeral. In the days since the little boy’s death, friends, neighbors and people the family had never met have reached out to offer support.
“We’ve been so grateful for just the community. We didn’t know what to do. We were lost. I feel like we still are. Friends, friends of friends, people we didn’t know, approached us very early on and wanted to help,” Cynthia Russ said.
A GoFundMe was created by a family friend to help Cathleen Russ with expenses. The fundraiser initially sought $20,000, but by early Thursday, it had raised nearly $30,000.
Cynthia Russ said the family has been grateful for the people who have stepped forward, including those who did not personally know Garcia.
“We are all going through a horrendous trauma together,” she said. “Our family is not the same anymore, and it just can’t be. It’s not whole anymore.”

BELGRADE — Volunteers worked Wednesday to turn donated logs into a lifeline for Kennebec County residents struggling to heat their homes, cutting, splitting and stacking firewood for distribution through the Kennebec Wood Bank.
Modeled after a community food pantry, the wood bank offers free firewood to households facing heating emergencies — temporary assistance to residents struggling to paying for necessities.
The organization relies on donations of hardwood logs from landowners, tree services and other community members. Volunteers cut, split and stack the wood, allowing it to season before winter.
The organization partners with the Kennebec Valley Community Action Program, or KVCAP, to coordinate requests for assistance. KVCAP screens applicants, schedules pickups and provides instructions for collecting firewood. Households do not need to be enrolled in the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program or meet specific income verification requirements to qualify.
Eligible households can receive up to one-third of a cord of seasoned hardwood per heating season, typically enough to provide several weeks of heat when used as a primary heating source. Firewood will be available for pickup at the organization’s locations in Belgrade and Monmouth, with distribution scheduled to begin this fall.

title: Maine heating oil costs just hit a record high — again
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Heating oil costs in Maine just hit a record high for the second time this fall.
The Maine Department of Energy Resources said Thursday that the average gallon of heating oil cost $6.04, breaking the record set last month by two cents. Costs are up by 83% over last October, when that same gallon cost an average of $3.30.
At this price, Mainers will spend about $750 more filling a standard 275-gallon oil tank than last fall.
“Maine has broken yet another record for heating oil prices, putting even more pressure on families as winter approaches,” Acting department Commissioner Celina Cunningham said in a news release.
President Donald Trump and his administration’s officials have long told the public that the U.S. and Israel’s war in Iran, which has constricted the crucial oil passageway of the Strait of Hormuz and driven oil prices up, would be quickly resolved. But Trump said this month that the U.S. would not resume strikes on Iran until after the midterm elections next month, a move that could drag out the conflict.
Since the war with Iran began in late February, Maine heating oil prices have spiked 57%.
With costs at their new record high, Maine’s federally supported heating assistance fund, the Home Energy Assistance Program, won’t go as far as in past winters — even with an early release of those funds and $4 million in a carryover from last year.
Maine, as the state most reliant on heating oil, is most vulnerable to price spikes and stood to gain most from the early release of those federal heating assistance funds. About 45,000 households received the supplemental assistance last year, MaineHousing said — and the primary population served by heating assistance programs are seniors on fixed incomes.
To help ease price concerns, the U.S. Department of Energy announced Wednesday that it would release 315,000 barrels of heating oil through a rarely used emergency stockpile, the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve.
Those 315,000 barrels, which carry about 42 gallons each, would fill about 48,100 standard-size heating oil tanks.
But with the release split between the New England states and New York, which by itself has 1.7 million households dependent on heating oil, it’s unclear how the extra supply will impact prices in Maine.
The Department of Energy is using an “exchange” to release the new heating oil — a process where oil companies bid on and receive at least 25,000 barrels of the strategic reserves, and then must return the entire portion they took, plus at least 5% extra, at a later date. The oil will hit the market next month.
Companies must return heating oil to the federal government by April 2027 or face an additional premium that increases by 2.5% monthly, according to the Department of Energy’s request for bids.
But if the Iran war continues into the spring, long-term supply issues may remain.
Heating oil has become a campaign issue, less than two weeks out from Election Day. Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, and her Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson, have blamed each other for high costs. Gubernatorial candidates have also called for more heating assistance funding.
Applications for heating assistance are open now. Maine residents hoping to apply for HEAP funding or looking for other assistance can contact their local community action program or call 211. The state also releases an annual Winter Heating Guide with cost-saving resources for households of all incomes.

title: Iconic Maine: Amazing video shows a moose family near Katahdin
text:
Iconic Maine: Amazing video shows a moose family near Katahdin, surrounded by fall foliage
Maine is known for many things, including moose and beautiful scenery. A viewer shared amazing video and pictures that combine those two things.
Brandon Warren tells Maine's Total Coverage he was hiking along Sandy Stream Pond near Katahdin in Baxter State Park on October 7 when he spotted a family of moose, including a bull, cow and calf.
Warren also shared several pictures he took of the moose, especially the large bull.
Last year, another viewer shared video with Maine's Total Coverage of a close encounter she had with a large bull moose at Moosehead Lake. That video went viral.
With an estimated population of 40,000 to 60,000, Maine has the largest population of moose in the lower 48 states in the United States.
How to see a moose
The Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife has some tips to give you the best chance of seeing a moose.
Moose are most prevalent and likely to be seen in northern and western parts of the state in their core and peripheral range, but can be seen statewide.
Moose are most commonly on the move in the early morning and late afternoon. Officials do say a little luck and a lot of patience are key to success.
In summer, moose spend a lot of time in water, including rivers, streams, ponds, lakes and bogs - and moose are actually very good swimmers. Plants that grow in water are also rich in sodium, which moose crave and need as part of their diet.
Moose will typically feed in short bursts and then move back into the woods to get shade and digest their food.
Once vegetation dies back as fall arrives, moose have less reason to visit bodies of water and tend to spend more time in young upland sites where there is plenty of young forest growth. This is going to be an area of the forest with dense regrowth of young trees, shrubs, and grasses, meaning there is food.
The end of summer and start of fall also means mating season for moose, known as the rut.
During this time, moose are more active in seeking a mate, traveling around their ranges more and checking in on other moose. Because they are moving more, you may have a better chance of seeing one.
Fall is also hunting season, so be sure to be careful and wear blaze orange. You may also want to get away from other people and find places off the beaten path.
By winter, moose are feeding more in forest cuts and people on snowmobiles tend to be the ones to see the most moose.
Once snow is on the ground and trails are groomed and ridden on, these will become places that moose like to travel, taking advantage of the ability to avoid deep, challenging snow conditions.
If you see moose on the trail, give them lots of space and time to get off the trail.
Moose tracks are large, ranging from 4-6 inches long and 3.5-5 inches wide. Like deer, the pointed end of the hoof is the direction that the animal is traveling.
Moose scat (poop) depends on the season and foraging. During winter months, scat is usually a pile of pellets about 1-1.75 inches in length. During spring and summer months, scat will likely have more moisture and may result in softer pellets or a single patty.
State wildlife experts put together a blog with more information, recommendations and details about moose and activity in Maine to help you plan your trip.

title: InvestigateTV+: Helping families that travel with breast milk
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Mothers at TSA checkpoints say they’ve been forced to dump their breast milk or have it opened and tested. InvestigateTV+ explains how their stories created national change and what it could mean for your family’s next flight.
Plus, an empty seat on a boat inspires a fisherman to create a way to connect anglers who don’t want to cast alone, and a family turned a lifetime of caring for wounded wildlife into a powerful lesson about living to the fullest.
Ending confusion over traveling with breast milk
Emily Calandrelli, an author and former host of “Emily’s Wonder Lab” on Netflix, went viral in 2022 after writing on social media about an experience at a TSA security checkpoint.
Calandrelli said she was on a work trip at the time, writing it was her “first time away from my 10-week-old son, who I’m currently breastfeeding,” and that she “brought my pump and two ice packs.”
Calandrelli said two male TSA agents told her she could not bring the ice packs in a carry-on because they were not frozen solid. She said when she asked to speak to a supervisor, she was asked, “Well, where is the baby?” The supervisor then said if her child was with her, “it wouldn’t be an issue,” according to Calandrelli.
She said she was ultimately escorted from the security line and forced to check her ice packs.
Battling early-onset dementia with new tools
No fishing alone
“It was on this lake right here, Pomme de Terre Lake, I was fishing by myself,” John said. “That day I was feeling a little lonely. And I happened to look at my empty seat and got to thinking, man, why didn’t I bring somebody with me? And then the wheels started turning.”
That day, John bought the domain name coangler.com for $13. His idea was an app where people could connect and book fishing trips together.
Birds in his backyard
A licensed bird rehabilitator in Vermont has spent more than four decades healing injured birds, driven by a childhood memory that shaped his life’s work.

title: U.S. Marshals Apprehend Suspect In Westbrook After Waldo Street Incident In Rumford
text:
They Found Him: U.S. Marshals Catch Up With Fugitive Sought In Rumford Manhunt In Town Of Westbrook Tuesday
Less than a week after he disappeared from the scene of a drug raid in Rumford prompting a statewide manhunt for him, 21-year-old Blake Lachance of Lewiston has been apprehended by authorities.
Read More: Rumford Police Seek Armed Suspect After Waldo Street Raid
The Backstory
Authorities issued a warning to residents that Lachance should be considered armed and dangerous following raid on home on Waldo Street in Rumford. Reports of drug activity and shots fired prompted a large police presence in the area. Once the place was secured, it was discovered that Lachance had fled the scene before police arrived.
What Took Place This Week
The U.S. Marshals Service says they caught up with Lachance this week, and that he is now in custody.
"On October 20, in Westbrook, members of the emergency services units apprehended Lachance after he attempted to flee the residence on foot. A perimeter team subsequently took him into custody without further incident. Lachance was then turned over to the custody of the U.S. Marshals Service and transported to a local jail, where he remains pending his initial appearance on the state charges."
Lachance faces felony state charges including criminal mischief, aggravated assault and aggravated reckless conduct.
As is often the case with serious situations in the state, the U.S. Marshals Service says the Lachance's arrest came about as a result of multiple agencies working in cooperation with each other, including the Homeland Security Task Force, the Maine Violent Offender Task Force, Cumberland County Sheriff's Office, Maine State Police, and the South Police, Westbrook, Rumford and Lewiston Police Departments.
Teamwork Makes The Dream Work
U.S. Marshal David St. Pierre says this cooperation across the board is key positive outcomes and arrests.
“This arrest demonstrates the importance of investigative collaboration among federal, state, and local law enforcement partners who work seamlessly across jurisdictions to identify, locate, and apprehend violent offenders who pose a direct threat to our communities. Joint fugitive investigations such as this one help ensure that individuals accused of violent crimes are brought before the courts and that potential threats to public safety are addressed."

If you have details about individuals who are being sought for alleged crimes, or about criminal activity in your area, authorities encourage you to reach out to your local police departments. title: Financial scams take many forms
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
As technology makes banking, shopping and transferring money more convenient, it also makes it easier for criminals to take advantage of people. Fake websites, phone numbers and emails can appear legitimate, and artificial intelligence can imitate familiar voices.
The financial consequences are significant.
According to the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center, Maine residents reported approximately $35.8 million in internet crime losses in 2025. Nationally, the Federal Trade Commission reported approximately $16 billion in fraud losses, including $3.5 billion from impersonation scams.
Those figures reflect reported losses. Many incidents never reach authorities.
Recognizing the warning signs and protecting yourself
Scammers often create a sense of urgency, offer something too good to be true or convince someone to share private information. Knowing what to watch for can help you avoid becoming a victim.
1 – Verify who’s contacting you. Bank impersonation scams often begin with a call or text claiming suspicious activity on your account. The caller may appear to be using your bank’s number. Never share passwords or verification codes in response to an unexpected message. Contact your financial institution directly using a trusted number.
2 – Be skeptical of easy money. Investment and cryptocurrency scams promise unusually high returns while encouraging increasingly large deposits. Legitimate investments carry risk, and guaranteed profits are a major red flag. Consult a trusted financial professional before committing your savings.
3 – Don’t let urgency override your judgment. Emergency scams often involve someone claiming to be a relative in trouble who needs money immediately. Some scammers use AI-generated voices to sound like someone you know. Before sending money, independently verify the story, especially if you’re told to keep it secret.
4 – Research before paying. Fake retailers, fraudulent charities and dishonest contractors rely on people paying without verifying who’s receiving the money. Check independent reviews, verify charities and get written agreements from contractors. Be wary of demands for payment by gift card, cryptocurrency or wire transfer.
5 – Protect your personal information. Unexpected emails, texts and websites may ask you to click a link, open an attachment or share sensitive information. These can be attempts to steal your identity or access your accounts. Visit official websites directly, use strong, unique passwords and enable multifactor authentication.
Your financial institution can be an ally
If you suspect you’ve been scammed, contact your bank or credit union immediately. It may be possible to stop a payment, dispute an unauthorized transaction or secure an account before more money is lost.
You might also want to report the incident to the Federal Trade Commission at ReportFraud.ftc.gov or the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center at IC3.gov. Maine residents can also seek help from the Maine Bureau of Consumer Credit Protection.
Although no institution can prevent every scam or guarantee recovery of stolen funds, getting help quickly can limit the damage.
A trusted community bank or credit union offers additional protection through fraud monitoring, account alerts, customer education and assistance with suspicious activity. Being able to visit a branch and speak with someone face to face is valuable, too.
Fraud prevention depends on awareness, relationships and communication. Whether you bank with a local credit union or community bank, knowing whom to call and feeling comfortable asking questions can help protect your financial future.

title: F-16 intercepts aircraft minutes before Pres. Trump landed for South Carolina rally
text:
CLEMSON, S.C. (WHNS/Gray Media) - A U.S. fighter jet intercepted an aircraft that violated restricted airspace over Clemson during President Donald Trump’s scheduled rally on Wednesday.
According to the North American Aerospace Defense Command, an F-16 intercepted a general aviation aircraft at about 5:40 p.m.
The aircraft landed safely at a nearby airfield while being monitored.
According to White House pool reports, Air Force One touched down at Greenville-Spartanburg International Airport just after 5:45 p.m., minutes after the intercept.
President Trump got off the plane at 6:08 p.m. and boarded Marine One to head to Clemson.
Marine One landed near the rally venue at Clemson University’s T. Ed Garrison Arena just before 6:35 p.m., according to the pool report. The president began speaking at 7:10 p.m.
NORAD reminded pilots who are intercepted to immediately tune to frequency 121.5 or 243.0 and reverse course until receiving further instructions.
Pilots who violate temporary flight restriction airspace may be met by federal authorities upon landing and face enforcement action.

title: More than 136K Mainers have already voted in November's election
text:
More than 136,000 Maine voters have already voted in the upcoming midterm elections, according to the latest data from the secretary of state. The vast majority of those votes are coming from registered Democrats.
Registered Democrats historically use Maine’s mail and in-person absentee voting more than Republicans and unenrolled voters, but the rate of use this year could signal a significant edge in enthusiasm.
So far, more than 52% of ballots cast have come from Democrats. That’s more than double the 20% among Republicans, as well as unenrolled voters, also referred to as independents.
The pace among Democrats is well ahead of the 2024 election, a high enthusiasm year for Republicans, and about the same as the 2022 midterms, according to state data. Republican voters are well off the pace they set at this point two years ago when President Donald Trump was on the ballot.
This story appears through a media partnership with Maine Public.

title: New development, business openings and investment reshape Central Maine in 2026
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Major redevelopment projects, new businesses and investments in downtown infrastructure have shaped Central Maine’s economic landscape in 2026. From Augusta and Waterville to Skowhegan and Farmington, communities are attracting development while adapting to changes in retail, health care and locally owned businesses.
Here are some of the year’s notable developments, as reported by the Kennebec Journal, Morning Sentinel and Franklin Journal, available at centralmaine.com.
Major commercial projects move forward
In Augusta, developers are moving ahead with Capitol Heights, an 8-acre redevelopment of the former Kmart property at 58 Western Ave. Plans call for 58 market-rate apartments above retail space, a 135-room hotel and two additional commercial buildings.
The Boulos Company began recruiting commercial tenants in March, targeting restaurants, financial institutions, medical offices and other businesses. The project is among Augusta’s largest commercial redevelopments in recent years.
Waterville is also preparing for a major addition to its commercial landscape. Amazon received Planning Board approval in June for a proposed 159,000-square-foot distribution center near Trafton and Junction roads in Waterville and Sidney. The facility could become the company’s third in Maine.
Downtown investments aim to attract visitors and businesses
In Skowhegan, construction began in June on the long-planned River Park, a project intended to transform the Kennebec River waterfront into a recreation destination.
The first phase includes an accessible boardwalk overlooking the river gorge. Future plans call for whitewater paddling and surfing features, improved river access and trails.
A 2025 study commissioned by Main Street Skowhegan projected that the completed park could generate $16.6 million in annual economic activity and support 137 permanent jobs throughout the region. Funding for some of the later phases, including the whitewater park, remains unresolved.
Waterville continues to invest in its downtown as well by improving pedestrian accessibility and experience. The city received an $850,000 federal grant for improvements near the Ticonic Bridge, pedestrian access around Silver Street and a proposed art walk connecting Castonguay Square to Temple Street.
The city’s investment in arts and culture is also producing measurable results. Downtown visitation increased 11% over three years, according to the Central Maine Growth Council. Colby College has invested approximately $85 million in downtown revitalization, including the Paul J. Schupf Art Center and Greene Block + Studios.
Health care and retail spaces find new uses
The former Staples store at 40 Waterville Commons Drive is being redeveloped for ConvenientMD, which plans to open separate primary and urgent care clinics in approximately 17,000 square feet of the 24,000-square-foot building.
The facilities were initially expected to open toward the end of 2026. Harborlight Properties, which owns the building, plans to renovate and lease the remaining 7,000 square feet.
The new clinics could help address demand for medical services following the closure of Northern Light Inland Hospital and associated practices in the Waterville area.
Downtown Waterville is also preparing to welcome Ollie’s Bargain Outlet, a national discount retailer that plans to open its second Maine location at 18 Concourse West, formerly occupied by Northern Light Primary Care. The store is expected to employ 30 to 50 people, with an opening anticipated in late October or early November.
Small businesses open, close and change hands
While larger projects have attracted attention, smaller businesses are also experiencing significant changes.
In Augusta, Capital Bar and Grille opened in February at 228 Water St., bringing a new restaurant and lounge to the downtown dining scene. Owners Andy Chapman, Sotirios Gudis and Mike Akanji are combining their hospitality experience to offer an upscale but casual atmosphere.
In Farmington, the Better Living Center, a natural foods store operating since 1973, announced its transition to the Farmington Food Co-op on April 1. The new community-owned model is intended to preserve the longtime business and its focus on locally sourced food and products.
Another Farmington landmark closed in August when owner Rachel Jackson retired from the Farmington Diner on Wilton Road. El Tequila Mexican Restaurant announced plans to renovate the space and open another location, with hopes of retaining some of the diner’s employees.
Waterville also lost a neighborhood institution when Juliette’s Bakery and Deli closed April 30 after 17 years at 40 Ticonic St. The building has housed a neighborhood market since the 1940s, and the owners had been seeking a buyer who might continue the business.
New opportunities for food entrepreneurs
Skowhegan is investing in another part of its local economy through The Kitchen at 185, a planned shared commercial kitchen on Water Street.
In July, the town approved a $50,000 grant to Main Street Skowhegan to support the project, which is intended to provide commercial kitchen space for dozens of food entrepreneurs.
By giving small producers access to shared facilities, the project aims to reduce some of the costs associated with starting or expanding a food business.

title: How credit card companies profit from your debt — especially if you have bad credit
text:
How credit card companies profit from your debt — especially if you have bad credit
You can be responsible with your credit cards. You can pay your card bills in full each month and never owe a dollar in interest. And for all that effort, your credit card company will still consider you a “deadbeat” — the industry’s term for its least profitable customers.
Credit card companies make most of their money when you stay in debt. People who pay off their balance each month — “transactors,” in industry shorthand — don’t generate much revenue for card issuers. Instead, they count on “revolvers” (cardholders who carry a balance) to keep feeding their bottom line.
Americans owed a collective $1.26 trillion on their credit cards in the second quarter of 2026, which is near the record high of $1.28 trillion set in the fourth quarter of last year, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. These numbers don’t inspire optimism. Credit card debt, after all, is expensive and can be toxic to your financial health. It’s persistent, too: 47% of cardholders report having a credit card balance as of December 2025, and 22% of debtors don’t think they’ll ever pay it off, according to Bankrate’s 2026 Credit Card Debt Report.
For the people carrying those balances, that’s a problem. For the companies that issued the cards, it’s business as usual.
“Credit card companies make a lot of money on people who carry over credit card debt month to month,” says Lauren Saunders, senior attorney at the National Consumer Law Center. “The people’s payments heavily go to interest rather than reducing their principal.”
And the lower a cardholder’s credit score, the easier for the credit card issuer to make money on the debt they carry. Issuers profit from keeping Americans in debt, and consumers like you pay billions in interest and fees. Protect yourself by knowing the facts and avoiding the trap of revolving debt.
Credit card issuers depend on you staying in debt
Credit card companies make money in three ways:
- Interest, or what you’re charged for carrying a balance
- Other card fees, such as late fees, annual fees, cash advance fees, balance transfer fees and others
- Interchange fees, or fees the merchant pays every time a customer uses a credit card for payment
The biggest share of these profits comes from interest. In 2024, consumers paid $160 billion in interest charges, up from $105 billion in 2022, according to CFPB’s Consumer Credit Card Market report. In fact, interest accounts for about 80% of credit card profitability, according to 2022 Federal Reserve research. With other consumer fees making up most of the remaining 20%, it’s safe to say that cardholders who carry a balance drive most credit card revenue — so issuers rely on them and seek them out.
Interest is also a lucrative revenue stream because the issuers keep the rates steep. Currently, the average credit card interest rate is close to 20%, according to Bankrate’s data. For people with bad credit (or a FICO Score below 580), the rate can be even higher, often exceeding 30%. Issuers price their card products with lending risk in mind, ensuring they remain profitable even if more likely-to-default consumers eventually default.
A card interest rate consists of a Prime Rate (currently 7.00%) and a margin set by the issuer, often about 13%. And yet, “you see cards charging 35.99% in any interest rate environment,” says Adam Rust, a financial director at the Consumer Federation of America.
“It’s interesting to see how the margin between the consumer credit rate and the federal funds rate has gone up over time,” he says. “There’s been a consistent widening of that gap… Large issuers generally charge higher interest rates on a risk-adjusted basis, and yet they still get more market share.”
That means that if you expect to carry a balance, you can’t assume that a major bank will give you a competitive rate. You need to shop around and see what smaller issuers offer. For example, federal credit unions currently cap their interest rates at 18%.
Cardholders with lower scores carry a burden
Issuers rely on customers being in debt, and they do little to steer people with low scores away from it. The industry has a significant incentive to extend credit to borrowers who are already stretched too financially thin, rather than steer them away. And issuers purposefully seek out such customers when marketing certain cards.
“The data brokers are providing thousands of granular points of information on consumers,” Rust says. “An issuer doing its homework doesn’t have any trouble identifying which customers are liquidity-constrained and likely to carry a balance. That’s not hard.”
About half of all general-purpose card accounts carried a balance in 2024, according to the CFPB’s 2025 report. That overall rate hides a huge spread by credit tier: In 2024, 83% of cardholders with subprime scores and 88% with deep subprime scores carried a balance.
“It’s natural that people who are struggling more paycheck to paycheck, who have lower credit scores and have had trouble meeting their expenses, turn more to credit cards and have trouble paying them off every month,” Saunders says.
And the reason they turn to cards is usually not what people assume. Among cardholders carrying a balance, 41% said that an emergency or unexpected expense was the primary cause, while another 33% pointed to day-to-day expenses as the biggest cause of their debt, according to Bankrate’s 2026 Credit Card Debt Report. Only 7% carry a balance because of vacations or entertainment.
Carrying that balance costs low-score borrowers more per dollar, too. Cardholders with subprime and deep subprime scores who revolve a balance pay two to four times more in interest and fees than the superprime borrowers, the CFPB found.
To credit card companies, the riskiest borrowers are also the most profitable ones. In fact, prime borrowers are only about half as profitable, according to research published by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York in 2025. Return on assets for subprime borrowers with FICO Scores in the 600s sits at around 11%, then drops sharply and levels off near 5% for prime borrowers above 750.
What it means for you
For every $1,000 in balances, issuers keep about $110 a year from cardholders with scores in the low-to-mid 600s. To compare, they only make about $50 per $1,000 from cardholders with scores above 750. If you carry a balance at a high APR, you’re a lucrative customer for your card issuer — even if you don’t qualify for its lucrative card products.
“Despite a significantly higher charge-off risk, subprime and deep subprime revolvers are some of the best customers for a card issuer,” Rust says. “The returns on revolvers are so much higher even after factoring in all the expenses for operations and rewards, that it’s hard to ignore.”
Issuer profits aside, offering a revolving line of credit to consumers with bad credit is both necessary and exploitative. On the one hand, it allows people who struggle financially access credit without turning to truly predatory options, such as payday or title loans. On the other hand, with how high fees and interest rates are on cards for bad credit, a credit card can easily make a bad situation worse.
“Anybody who has ‘bad credit’ is probably already deep in debt and really shouldn’t be taking on more,” Saunders says.
But while the cardholder is left to pick the lesser evil, the issuer always wins. A credit card company doesn’t need to choose between serving a subprime borrower and profiting from them. It gets to do both.
How credit cards turn into debt traps
While the healthiest credit card habit is paying off the balance in full every month, credit card issuers don’t make it easy.
Saunders explains that the way credit cards are structured doesn’t encourage swift repayment. Minimum payments are very low — often 1% of the balance amount plus any accrued interest. Paying only the minimum can keep you revolving a balance for years and paying interest on interest, until your total interest exceeds what you borrowed in the first place.
“I don’t think people have any idea of how long it would take to repay their credit card debt just making the minimum payments,” Saunders says. “There is a minimum payment warning that is required on statements from the Credit Card Act of 2009, but… unless you’re really looking at that on your paper statement or on the PDF online, which most people probably never [do], you’re not going to see it.”
Then there are the cards designed to be expensive from the start.
“There are some credit cards aimed at subprime consumers that have very high fees,” Saunders says. “Those fees can be monthly fees. Those are fees that really reduce the amount of credit they’re even getting. We call those fee harvester cards that are really just designed to take fees out of people rather than to give them useful forms of credit.”
These offers usually arrive in the mail. To accept, you’re sent to a website that leads with the promise of a credit card, even with bad credit, but buries the terms under easy-to-miss links. If you check the links, you’ll likely find a range of junk fees, including an application fee, monthly fees and fees for “premium design” (which will still be a regular plastic card). These are signs to look elsewhere for a card.
Saunders also warns against potentially predatory credit card types that can get you in a revolving cycle when you don’t expect it. Be wary of deferred interest cards, which advertise 0% or low APR for several months. You’ll often see these at department stores, big-box stores and sometimes in medical and dental offices. No interest sounds like a good deal, but if you don’t repay the balance in full before the promotional period ends, you’ll owe the interest on the entire original balance, retroactive to the day you bought. Those charges can easily total hundreds of dollars.
“It’s a real trap,” Saunders says.
How much it costs to be a revolver
Let’s say you have a $1,000 balance on a card charging 21%. Your budget is stretched thin, so you only make minimum payments (interest + 1% of the balance). It will take you 119 months — almost 10 years! — to get rid of your debt. You’ll also pay $1,125 in total interest charges, more than your original balance.
It seems like a lot. But for many American revolvers, the numbers are even more significant.
In the Fed’s 2022 research, the average light revolver (or someone who revolved a balance for 11 months out of a year or less) spent $637 on their card per month and had a monthly balance of about $1,700, of which almost $1,000 was revolving balance. Light revolvers held about 22% of total revolving balances and comprised a quarter (25%) of all card accounts. They paid around $15 in interest monthly, which makes up about 20% of all interest.
In contrast, the average heavy revolver (or a person who rolled a balance every month of a year) only spent just $206 a month on their credit card. However, their balance was almost $4,500, and they rolled $4,100 month over month. Overall, heavy revolvers held more than half (53%) of total balances and about two-thirds of total revolving balances. They paid more than $60 per month in interest charges on average — and more than 70% of all interest.
Only 1 in 5 credit card accounts (21%) were transactors. However, they accounted for 39% of all credit card purchase volume, with average monthly spending of $826. They also paid almost no interest.
This underscores the dynamic between revolvers and transactors. The people who consistently carry a balance spend the least on purchases and pay the most in interest. The so-called deadbeats spend the most on purchases on average, yet they avoid interest altogether.
And that’s the tension at the center of the credit card business: What’s best for the issuer’s profits is a financial burden for the cardholder. Fewer than half of cardholders in debt (48%) have a plan to pay it off, according to Bankrate’s 2026 Credit Card Debt report. Worse still, almost 1 in 5 debtors (19%) think they might miss a minimum payment at some point in the next six months.
If credit card debt is straining your finances and dragging down your credit score, you’re not alone. But your credit card habits don’t lessen your value as a customer. Quite the contrary: You’re making your issuer more money than someone with a much higher score and a premium card you can’t qualify for.
How to stop being your issuer’s best customer
Your relationship with your credit card issuer is a two-way street. You follow the terms and conditions, pay your bills and spend within your credit limit. In exchange, your issuer offers access to a line of credit and sometimes certain benefits. What you don’t owe them is a monthly contribution to their margin.
Twenty-two percent of cardholders in debt don’t believe they’ll ever get out of it. It’s not easy, but paying off your credit card debt is possible. Pay more than the minimum whenever you can. Attack your highest-rate card first. And move the balance somewhere cheaper if you can qualify — a balance transfer card with a 0% promotional period will generally want a score of at least 670. Whatever approach you pick, the one that works is the one you stick with.
If you feel completely overwhelmed by debt, get help from a nonprofit credit counseling agency, which can set up a debt management plan to pay down your card balances. Be skeptical of any organization that charges upfront fees or promises to settle your debt for pennies on the dollar.
When you clear your balances, you can become a transactor: someone who uses a card for the perks without paying the issuer a dime in interest. If you’re already there, keep using your cards wisely. Your credit card company might call you a “deadbeat,” but that’s exactly what you want to be.

title: Data drives policy for Nutt in House 48 race
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Support for municipalities and data-based decisions are at the heart of Charlotte Nutt’s campaign for House District 48.
Nutt, D-Edgecomb, faces Erik Hobson, R-Boothbay, in the race for the district, which consists of Boothbay, Boothbay Harbor, Edgecomb, South Bristol, and Southport. Rep. Holly Stover, D-Boothbay, is serving her fourth and final term in the seat.
Nutt grew up in Edgecomb, where she lives today. She graduated from Dartmouth College in Hanover, N.H. in 2019 with degrees in earth sciences and economics. She later earned a master’s degree in public policy from the University of Southern Maine in Portland.
After graduating, Nutt worked for the Midcoast Council of Governments, a nonprofit municipal planning organization, as a data specialist. She is now self-employed, working as a consultant for various data and policy organizations.
Improving data accessibility is a priority for Nutt. She said the state government has made progress on digitizing data, but that data quality is not standardized statewide. She pointed to municipalities’ assessor data as an example.
“I was doing a comprehensive plan for one of our towns, and their assessor data just wasn’t correct,” Nutt said. “So having correct and complete data really supports the towns and planning for their own futures. And we’re a home rule state … so that really is absolutely necessary for towns to have access to that data.”
All “good policy” begins with data, Nutt said. With this, she said she believes accessible data is a way to make a big difference for rural communities.
The biggest issue Nutt is focused on is housing. She said there is a shortage of housing units – both affordable and luxury – and that property tax increases are pricing people out of her district, discouraging young families from moving in, and preventing longtime residents from staying.
If elected, Nutt said she would prioritize building housing units while considering the different situations and “community cultures” of municipalities statewide. She said this exemplifies how good data can foster effective policy.
Her plan is to look at the supply and demand in each of the towns to form an understanding of how many housing units are needed.
Nutt said supporting the preservation of existing housing could also ease some Mainers’ housing woes. She references what she called the “classic story,” in which a resident might have be what is considered a “nice, big house” but is not making enough money to keep up with maintenance.
“Their house is their main asset, and that asset is slowly going away because they are not able to keep that up,” she said.
Nutt supports increasing state subsidy given to towns for education. She said voters need to support schools in a way that “doesn’t push our Mainers out of their homes.”
Schools are community pillars, Nutt said, educating but also providing essential resources to students.
“It’s where our coat drives happen, where our boot drives happen, where people get support,” she said.
Healthcare is another key issue for Nutt. She has family members who work in the healthcare industry, and she said their stories have informed her perspective on what changes need to occur.
“My fiance works in the emergency room … the cases that are hardest for him aren’t like the intense, classic emergency room cases,” Nutt said. “It’s more the ones where it’s been years or decades of the state failing someone, and now they’re unhoused, underfed, going through a mental health crisis, and they’re now in the ER.”
She said Mainers need healthcare that is accessible from their homes and that is affordable.
“People, at this point, are trying to make the decision between going to the hospital and being in debt, or just continuing to suffer with their illness,” Nutt said. “That’s simply not OK.”
Nutt also expressed concerns about transparency in MaineHealth’s decision to close the labor and delivery unit at Lincoln Hospital in Damariscotta. She said despite the low number of births, the labor and delivery unit is an important resource for the community, and that Maine needs improved healthcare systems for residents of all ages.
“We are the oldest state in the nation, population-wise, and yet we still need labor and delivery units,” Nutt said. “We need healthcare for older adults as well and that healthcare needs to be in-hospital and also in-home, because people are aging at home.”
Nutt said addressing climate change is another one of her goals, pointing to recent years’ storms that led to severe flooding across Lincoln County. She worries about the impact of sea level rise, ocean acidification, and warming on Maine’s marine industries.
“(There) aren’t going to be as many lobsters in the Gulf of Maine in the future, and I think that we really need to support all of our industries that are dependent on our environment,” Nutt said.
She said climate change policy can enhance infrastructure as well. Nutt suggested expanding bike lanes and pedestrian options as a way to lower carbon emissions and to provide more commuting options. From her house in Edgecomb, she said she could bike to Damariscotta but chooses not to because the “roads are so dangerous.”
While talking about infrastructure, Nutt said that the Legislature also needs to dedicate funding toward improving roadways. She said she has heard from voters whose vehicles have sustained damage from bad roads.
In approaching these issues, Nutt believes the Maine Legislature must keep municipalities at the forefront. She said her previous work with towns including Belfast and Monhegan Island shaped this belief because she saw the varying needs of each municipality.
“We’re made up of a lot of rural communities that are all very unique,” Nutt said. “We at the state can’t forget that Maine is a home rule state, and that so much happens at the local level, and the more that we can support our municipalities through training, through data access … that can make a huge difference in people’s lives.”
For more information, go to charlottenuttformaine.com or email charlotteformaine@gmail.com.
The general election is on Tuesday, Nov. 3.

title: At Cadillac Mountain, a missing Wabanaki marker and the fight over what national parks should tell
text:
BAR HARBOR, Maine — In the soft light of dawn, an Ohio tourist studied the interpretive sign at the summit of Cadillac Mountain in Acadia National Park, reading about how magma formed the ground under her feet.
There is one sign she and the other 4 million-plus tourists who visit Acadia annually can no longer see at the summit: a marker explaining the mountain’s sacred significance to the Wabanaki people in the region. “Today, visitors from everywhere find meaning on the mountain,” it said.
It was among 30 markers removed from Acadia under a Trump administration campaign to strip national parks of materials deemed disparaging to American history, according to the National Parks Conservation Association.
But when park staff took down the summit sign at the orders of Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, they also unraveled some of the trust that took decades to build between Acadia National Park and the Wabanaki people. The Wabanaki Confederacy, also known as “the people of the dawnland,” has inhabited the northern seaboard for over 10,000 years and was the first known stewards of land that includes much of the national park. It was a gathering place to trade, hunt, fish and pick sweetgrass.
Some of the signs removed from Acadia were developed over years of partnerships with organizations including Friends of Acadia, the Schoodic Institute and the Native Plant Trust — with consultation from citizens of the Wabanaki Nations. They know the mountain in Maine as Wapuwoc — “white mountain of the first light.” From October to March, it’s the first place to see the sunrise in the continental United States.
“Getting to a place where our language is in these parks and it is educational … erasing that or setting that back has big implications for how far we’ve come,” said Maulian Bryant, the Wabanaki Alliance’s executive director.
Bryant says the removed signs reflected “the good stuff.”
“These signs don’t say 96% of Wabanaki people died from smallpox, or there were 26 nations and now there’s four,” she said. “If we really want to get into the real history, that’s a whole other slice of cake.”
Other signs removed from Cadillac’s summit addressed issues of climate change, informing visitors that “Acadia’s future will be warmer and wetter” and that “In the last century, average annual precipitation has increased by six inches.”
During their tenure under the Biden administration, former National Park Service director Chuck Sams and former Interior Secretary Deb Haaland — the first Native Americans to hold these positions — aimed to reflect the experiences of all Americans throughout the national parks. Before leaving his post in February 2025, Sams saw parts of his work unraveled by the current administration.
This “attempt to rewrite history into a single narrative … is also counter to our democracy. And counter to the idea that we are a plural nation,” said Sams.
Lawsuit against national park removals advances
Now, a coalition of conservation, history and science organizations are fighting in court to get the Acadia signs and hundreds of other items put back. Under Burgum’s 2025 campaign, signs, books, films and exhibits covering topics such as slavery, climate change and the massacre of Native Americans were flagged and removed from national parks and monuments nationwide.
“Some of it’s been put back, and then some of it has been removed again,” said the Center for American Progress’ Angelo Villagomez. He was part of the progressive policy group’s team that examined a database leaked earlier this year and found that a third of national parks had flagged exhibits featuring history or science. Of those, Black and Indigenous history were most targeted.
Portions of all flagged material have since been reviewed and cataloged by a committee led by Joy Beasley, a National Park Service associate director. However, in a June affidavit, she writes that the spreadsheet is “unlikely to capture every removal, revision, or replacement.”
The Interior Department did not respond to The Associated Press’ questions about the current status of sign and exhibit removal or the ongoing lawsuit filed by the nonprofit coalition in February against the federal government.
The parks “are America’s storytellers,” said Todd Martin of the National Parks Conservation Association, a plaintiff in the lawsuit. “It’s their duty to preserve and interpret American history, the good, the bad, and the ugly.”
Jenny McBurney, a government publications librarian at the University of Minnesota who co-founded the project Save Our Signs, feels it’s more important than ever for park visitors to document revised signs.
“People are going to go to the parks and think that they will get to learn history there when in fact they will be learning an incomplete history,” said McBurney.
Wabanaki culture — past and present — shared in Acadia
Despite the job cuts, threats of land reduction, talks of privatization and even demolition within some parks, Indigenous groups and park partners have persevered.
In Maine, members of the Wabanaki Confederacy — comprised of the Maliseet, Mi’kmaq, Passamaquoddy, Penobscot and Abenaki principal nations — carry on the cultural traditions and spiritual practices that helped them maintain sovereignty and connection to their ancestral land after settlers arrived. That includes sharing their culture with tourists.
Penobscot Nation citizen Jennifer Neptune had mixed emotions about the attempted erasure of her people from Acadia and their ancestral homeland.
“It’s hard to get good signage in national monuments, in national parks,” said Neptune. “It’s a real gut punch when it (removal) happens, not just for Indigenous people, but for Black people, for the people whose stories don’t get shared.”
Over the past decade, she’s seen real change from the National Park Service, playing an integral part in bringing Wabanaki voices to the table to create Indigenous-designed spaces.
In partnership with Acadia, the privately owned Abbe Museum, which is largely overseen by Wabanaki people, hosts a program that brings Native voices into the park through music, arts and culture.
Nick Bear and members of a Wabanaki drum circle perform on Cadillac Mountain annually as part of this collaboration. “That’s just like bringing those ceremonies right back to the original sites,” he said.
In July, Passamaquoddy basket maker Lydia Soctomah demonstrated traditional Wabanaki basketry using pounded ash bark and sweetgrass outside the Sieur de Monts Nature Center. Both the ash tree and sweetgrass are part of the Wabanaki creation story, she said.
“Making a basket is worth 1,000 memories for me,” said Soctomah, whose grandmother was a well-known basket maker. “I was always told it holds a part of your spirit.”
Sweetgrass access an example of shared stewardship
Access to sweetgrass has long been difficult for Wabanaki people as they were pushed from coastal lands onto reservations. In Acadia, it’s been nearly nonexistent since the park’s creation in 1916. But over the past decade, park staff and Wabanaki members have collaborated to change that.
In 2017, scientist Suzanne Greenlaw, a citizen of the Houlton Band of Maliseet Indians, partnered with the U.S. Forest Service, Acadia’s Schoodic Institute and 14 traditional gatherers to conduct a Wabanaki-led sweetgrass study in hopes of allowing tribal access.
“It was really impactful because we had never had those kinds of co-stewardship relationships,” said Greenlaw, adding that those relationships, built over time, have not changed.
By the end of the Biden administration, there were over 400 co-stewardship or co-management agreements with tribes, 159 within the National Park Service alone, says Sams. Programs in Acadia were among them.
These programs, he says, allow tribes to fulfill their obligation to protect, preserve and enhance natural resources, and the federal government to fulfill its obligation to allow tribal access for hunting, fishing, and gathering foods and medicines.
Sams cautiously hopes there will be a rebuilding period for the park service under the next administration.
“There are always ebbs and flows with every administration,” he said. “Nobody has seen that more than American Indian tribes.”
