title: Rockland Police Department wins award for juvenile crime program
text:
ROCKLAND, Maine (WABI) - The Rockland Police Department has received the 2025 Community Policing Award from the New England Association of Chiefs of Police for it’s youth mentorship program. Rockland PD won first-place out of all New England police departments serving under 15,000 in total population.
The department started the program after a spike in juvenile crime in 2022. That year, calls involving juveniles rose 94% from the previous year, according to Rockland Police Department. After starting the program, juvenile crime in 2024 fell 37% and declined again in 2025.
“The program came out of kind of a necessity. And we all kind of put our heads together and said, hey, we need to do something different to address it,” said Deputy Chief Alex Gaylor, Rockland Police Department.
The Youth Mentorship Program introduces young people to law enforcement.
“Every Thursday we have a drop-in at the rec center, kick ball or do other activities with local youth and try to break down those barriers between the officers and the community and the youth particularly,” Gaylor said.
Gaylor said the program’s success would not have come without help from community members support and donations. He said in the last year, the department has received over $1,000 from community partners, local businesses and community members.
Doran Wright, known to the kids as “Pastor D.” Wright is the lead at the Belonging Center, a place for school-aged students to drop in and build connections. Wright is only one member of Rockland PD’s supporting cast for the youth mentorship program.
“Our philosophy is you shouldn’t have to commit a crime to get the help you need, so that’s sort of the underpinnings. Other than that, it’s building relationships, creating strong community,” said Doran Wright, lead, Rockland Youth Diversion Team.
Wright said he has seen the success of the program first-hand.
“There’s a young person I began working with a few years back in Long Creek. Came in as sort of a brash, feisty 15-year-old. And now, just this week, reached out to me to say he’s just started sort of a career move after a few years down the road. And people would have said his prospects for employment are negligible. And, you know, whether it was in Long Creek or whether in his home community, he got support he needed,” Wright said.
Wright and Gaylor said recognition is not the reason they do the work.
“In the end, the credit goes to the kids. Because if the kids are not buying into what we offer, then it’s all for naught, so while police departments and our organization and others, you know, sort of get the plaque on the wall, the ones who really deserve it at the end of the day are the kids who actually give us their trust and welcome our support,” Wright said.
“At the end of the day, this isn’t what it’s about. So, it’s about the work that they’re doing every day, but it does, it always obviously feels good to be recognized for that work, and yeah, we’re just looking forward to continuing to do what we do, look for ways to improve it and keep marching forward,” Gaylor said.
Gaylor said the department is already working to expanding and improving the program. He said Rockland PD applied for a grand to have a social worker to go out with some of the community partners.
The award will be presented Nov. 16 in Warwick, Rhode Island.

title: Portland City Council candidates jointly condemn PAC spending as election nears
text:
A majority of candidates for Portland’s three City Council races have signed on to a joint statement condemning political action committee spending ahead of the Nov. 3 election.
The statement, which was released Thursday and has been supported by all but one council candidate, decries PAC spending as having an outsize influence on local elections — especially as many candidates are enrolled in the city’s clean elections fund, which caps spending.
“We strongly believe spending of this magnitude by outside groups has no place in Portland’s municipal elections,” the joint statement reads. “While we recognize that people outside Portland have an interest in our city’s future, these elections should be decided by the residents who will live with the decisions of the Portland City Council.”
The eight candidates said the statement reflects a united stand against PAC spending on council races, which has been relatively rare in Portland politics until recent elections.
While it was written as a blanket statement against “all outside spending and influence,” it specifically references a PAC known as the Campaign for Responsible Government, which is led by Portland attorneys David Soley and David Farmer. That PAC, formed in 2024, is carrying more than $50,000 in contributions and last week spent $20,500 to support Ilma Lopez in District 5. While other PACs have spent big in previous elections, it’s the only PAC registered in Portland that has been active in this year’s election.
In previous filings, the Campaign for Responsible Government said it planned to support Lopez, Jake Viola in District 4 and Kate Snyder for councilor at-large, though it has so far only spent on Lopez. All three candidates signed the joint statement and have said they do not want PAC support.
Atiim Boykin, who is running against Snyder and Joey Brunelle for at-large councilor, said he chose not to sign on to the statement because it felt like a political move from the candidates most concerned with PAC spending impacting their campaigns — though he noted that he also doesn’t support PACs.
Candidates cannot legally coordinate with PACs, and expenditures on behalf of candidates often occur without a candidate’s knowledge or approval. Lopez, a clean elections candidate, said this week that she doesn’t support “outside expenditures in local Portland races” and that her campaign has not and will not work with any PAC.
The joint statement from candidates says their position “is not an indictment of any candidate who benefits from independent spending.”
“We do, however, want to make our collective position abundantly clear: outside parties of all types should refrain from spending in our races.”
Farmer, administrator of the Campaign for Responsible Government, defended the group this week, saying its donors are simply concerned over the city’s direction but that it has instead been painted as “dark and nefarious.”
‘A STEP BACKWARDS’
The presence of PACs in Portland is a relatively recent trend that can be traced back to several high-profile referendum campaigns.
Spending exploded in 2022 when the Enough is Enough PAC raised more than $430,000 to defeat a slate of citizen-initiated referendums backed by the Maine Democratic Socialists of America to strengthen rent control, restrict short-term rentals and raise the minimum wage.
In 2024, the National Association of Realtors spent more than $50,000 to support four Portland candidates, two years after it had given $100,000 to Enough is Enough.
It was that same year that the Campaign for Responsible Government formed and put its weight behind Sarah Michniewicz, spending $12,700 to support her and about $8,500 against her opponents and the Maine DSA.
The Maine DSA also spent about $16,000 that year to support its slate of candidates and oppose others, including Viola.
Cassidy Lacroix, who is managing Jakobi Delgado’s campaign in District 5, said their campaign spearheaded the joint statement as a stance against all PAC involvement.
“This is about money involved in politics, not one PAC or another,” Delgado said. “The point of clean elections is to make sure people can trust politicians.”
Portland candidates enrolled in clean elections are allowed maximum campaign funding of $12,498 for district races and $32,498 for at-large races.
Brunelle, the at-large candidate, has been outspoken on social media regarding the Campaign for Responsible Government. He said he pushed for Portland to implement its clean elections program in 2023 after large amounts of money from outside Maine began flowing into referendum campaigns, and in hopes of avoiding the same occurring with City Council races.
Brunelle said the recent trend is “running over the hard work people put into this” over several years to implement clean elections in Portland.
“What is happening right now is a step backwards,” he said.
Viola, who is running against incumbent Councilor Anna Bullett in District 4, shared a video last week where he said PAC funding should have no role in Portland politics.
‘MOVE OUR CITY FORWARD’
When asked how the PAC chose its preferred candidates, Farmer said about 45 donors and interested parties researched candidates before the group took a vote on who to support.
“Some of these folks I fundamentally disagree with on issues at the state and federal level,” he said of the chosen candidates. “But on the local level, we agree that the current majority on the City Council has failed the city.”
“We said, ‘Who do we think are the folks who are the most responsible and most able to take a look at these problems and move our city forward,’” he said.
Farmer said the PAC does not intend, as of this week, to spend in District 4 or the at-large race. but that could change depending on “what other groups and other people do.”
The money spent by the PAC so far was for a video advertisement showing Mayor Mark Dion endorsing Lopez. Farmer said the ad is positive and avoids attacks against the DSA-backed Michael Todd Chretien and other District 5 candidates.
Registered PACs in Portland also include Enough is Enough, the James Phinney Baxter Campaign Fund and the Maine DSA Campaign for a Livable Portland, but none have been particularly active this election season. The most recent Maine DSA campaign report shows a cash balance of $892 and no expenditures in support of candidates, while Enough is Enough and Baxter both show no new contributions or expenditures.
Snyder said she signed on to Thursday’s statement because she has already “been clear I don’t need or want PAC spending to influence my candidacy.” But she said some of the information circulating online has falsely tied her to the Campaign for Responsible Government and inaccurately claimed to have given her an unfair advantage.
Brunelle is the only clean elections candidate in the at-large race, but Snyder said she has based her campaign fundraising on the maximum allowed under the clean elections fund.
In 2024, all 12 of the candidates running for Portland City Council were registered clean elections candidates. The next campaign finance reports are due Friday.
PEOPLE BEHIND THE PAC
The Campaign for Responsible Government was formed after the Portland council voted in 2024 to divest in companies doing business in Israel, which Farmer said “changed nothing for the city’s operation” but “divided our community.” (Officials later said the city did not have investments in the companies included on the council’s list.)
The PAC’s top donors have included Bonnie Siegel, a board member of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee who was a strategist on Ted Cruz’s 2016 presidential campaign, and Judy Glickman Lauder, a photographer, philanthropist and wife of former Estee Lauder CEO Leonard Lauder.
The PAC had roughly $40,000 in funds heading into election season and gathered another $13,000 in contributions between mid-July and the end of September. Among the largest donations in that period were from David Soley, an attorney at Bernstein Shur whose family is among Greater Portland’s most prominent property owners; Lenny Nelson, a founding partner at Bernstein Shur; and Dan Kleban, the co-founder of Maine Beer Co. who ran for the Democratic nomination for U.S. Senate.
Also donating were Todd Goldenfarb, a developer with Mile Marker Investments and Portland Music Holdings, which is currently suing the city over halting the proposed Portland Music Hall venue, and Ned Payne, owner of several Portland properties and vice president of the Rental Housing Alliance of Southern Maine.
Its treasurer is Bryan Dench, an attorney who served as treasurer for Republican Gov. Paul LePage’s reelection committee in 2014 and represented LePage in several legal battles. Dench serves on the board of Maine Right to Life, a pro-life advocacy group, and has previously been criticized locally for anti-LGBTQ views.
About a third of its contributions are from non-Maine addresses.
Farmer said donors come from a mix of political ideologies who agree that Portland needs change.
“It’s no different from what many other groups do,” he said.

title: Wrong turn leads stranger to rescue family of 14 from house fire
text:
LYERLY, Ga. (WRCB) - A wrong turn may have saved 14 lives in northwest Georgia after a man driving home to Alabama spotted a house on fire and rushed inside to warn the family.
James Burke fell asleep in his recliner Saturday night while his wife, 11 children and one grandchild slept in their beds. He woke up to a man standing in his living room.
“The next thing I know, some guy was telling me in my living room, ‘Hey, you’ve got to get out of here. Your house is on fire,’” James Burke said.
The man, identified as Mr. Casey, was driving home to Alabama with his son. A wrong turn sent them down Highway 114 south of Lyerly.
“He was on the wrong road. His GPS put him on the wrong path. He’s never been down that road before. And he said that he knew that something kept bringing him down our road. When he saw the fire from the top of the hill, he knew he had to take action,” James Burke said.
Rescue from the home
James Burke said Casey helped pull all 12 children from the burning home and helped get firefighters to the scene.
“If it had been another five minutes, it would’ve been a different situation. We wouldn’t have made it,” Larita Burke said.
Community response
After the shock wore off Sunday morning, the Burkes said they were met with kindness from strangers, this time in their own community.
“It’s overwhelming how much, immediately, people called to ask, ‘Hey, what do you need? What can we do?’” James and Larita Burke said. “It has been a wonderful feeling. There are so many wonderful people in this community that have reached out. I didn’t realize this county was as wonderful as it was until something like this happened.”
Family looks ahead
The Burkes said the loss of their belongings is fresh in their memories and hard for the younger children to understand.
“They keep asking. My little three-year-old keeps asking, ‘Daddy, when do we go home?’ I said, ‘Soon,’” James Burke said.
“They see the burnt house, but we remind them that it’s still our house. It just needs to be fixed,” Larita Burke said.
The Burkes said they are focusing on the future.
“We are traumatized, of course, but you know what? We’re gonna turn this page, and we’re gonna get on with our lives because we have so much to live for. All of our babies made it out,” James Burke said.
The Burkes said they have fostered more than 500 children over the past 15 years. They said they hope to continue fostering once their home is rebuilt.
The cause of the fire remains under investigation.

title: Trump promises cash payments ahead of midterms
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - President Donald Trump is promising a series of cash payments to voters as Republicans seek to maintain control of the House and Senate in the midterm elections.
At the RNC midterm convention in September, Trump pledged to send $5,000 to every American adult if the GOP retains control of Congress.
“Because of our tremendous strength and success economically, I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000,” Trump said Sept. 9.
Since the Dallas convention, Trump has continued to make additional promises.
He said he would send $8 billion in direct payments to U.S. farmers, who he said have been hit by tariffs and record diesel prices.
Trump also announced a new program that would provide as much as $30,000 to any American who reports a tip about government fraud.
In Greenville, N.C., Trump made a promise to Marine Corps veterans who have claims against the U.S. over contaminated water at Camp Lejeune.
“If we win the House and the Senate, I am directing the Department of Justice to settle all remaining legitimate claims as soon as possible,” Trump said.
Democrats have accused the president of trying to buy votes with the many promises made in the final weeks of the campaign.
It remains to be seen whether Trump can deliver on the promises, or whether the proposals will affect the outcome of the midterm election.

title: Why older adults avoid therapy — and how to help them open up
text:
(Aging Untold) — For some older adults, the word “therapy” carries a stigma rooted in a generation that was taught to stay quiet and keep going.
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck says that silence has a cost and the Aging Untold experts have practical, low-pressure ways to help older loved ones start talking.
A generation taught to hide it
“Our age community was raised in a time when mental health was not something that we talked about,” Cradduck said. “Mental health was something that was hidden underneath the rug.”
Cradduck said that stigma meant asking for help was often seen as shameful.
“It was looked at with such distaste that for an aged person to say, ‘I need help,’ or ‘I would like to talk to someone’ — and that’s why there’s so much depression, I think, in our aged community,” Cradduck said.
She connected that silence directly to unresolved pain.
“When you haven’t been able to deal with all of the trauma that life has given you and you haven’t processed through, then there’s such a heavy weight on you,” Cradduck said. “Psychotherapy is absolutely an essential part of just being a human being, I think.”
“Survival is not healing”
Older generations were conditioned to push through hardship rather than confront it, Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said.
“I learned how to survive. That’s the older generation — they were always taught they were very stoic and they survive, but survival’s not healing,” Rogers said. “So they never really had a chance to really even heal or even to recognize, do they even know they’re depressed?”
Rogers added that depression in older adults doesn’t always look like sadness.
“It presents so different. It’s not sadness. They may be irritable. They may just feel like they’re fluttered, you know, or just loss of desire or motivation,” Rogers said. “I don’t think they recognize that they’re depressed.”
Reframing therapy as “education”
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said the word “therapy” itself can shut the conversation down before it starts — so she uses different language.
“When I’ve worked with clients that hear therapy and you can just see their eyes are like, no, no, no, I just don’t call it therapy,” O’Rourke said. “I say education. Let’s take a class, let’s buy a book just to get them kind of initiated into the idea that maybe talking would be helpful.”
She described one example of meeting a client where they already were.
“I had one Catholic client and I said, ‘Why don’t you go to confession?’ And he did,” O’Rourke said. “And in that tradition, he got it all out with the priest, and he felt better. And then he was open to going to therapy. It was the thing that just triggered him, so be open to using anything just to get that motion going.”
Friends, clubs and community can help too
Cradduck said licensed therapy isn’t the only path to processing grief and life’s heaviness.
“You don’t have to be a licensed therapist to be a good friend and lend an ear. Most of us have some good advice we can give,” Cradduck said. “But this is the bootstrapped generation — you were told you had to pull your bootstraps up, you had to keep going. And they were left suffering.”
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose pointed to group settings as another outlet.
“Even like Bible studies, book clubs — you know, where you can have discussions,” Ambrose said. “I have people around the country, they’re doing downsizing clubs, and people are really processing all this stuff, all the grief, all the heaviness.”
Ambrose said those groups often lead to deeper conversations than expected.
“They’re talking about the challenges they have communicating with their spouse or adult children, or with the medical episodes that they’ve had. So it’s very cathartic,” she said.
A Medicare benefit many don’t know about
O’Rourke also flagged a federal resource available to older adults seeking mental health support.
“The other resource that I would want people to know about is Medicare. Go to cms.gov. Medicare covers mental health help,” O’Rourke said.
Hospice is another resource, O’Rourke said.
“And if you’ve been involved in losing someone and you’ve had hospice services, you can get help with that grief for 12 months after death,” she said.

title: How this app helps anglers find their fishing crew
text:
HERMITAGE, Mo. (InvestigateTV) - For many anglers, sometimes it’s not the fish but the memories that are keepers.
“Some of my best memories,” John Bledsoe said, “and the best memories I have with regards to fishing, are always about the people I’m with at the time.”
Without a doubt, this lake is a dream spot for many. But for John, this spot launched his dream.
“Helping people that maybe don’t have the means to get outdoors,” John said about the app, “or maybe people that need help loading and unloading boats, or their wives would feel more comfortable if they had an extra co-angler in the boat with them.”
A chemist by trade, Missouri State’s e-Factory was right next to where John worked. It was there he got advice and attended a 10-month-long coding program.
That led to funding opportunities from various organizations to get Co-Angler launched as smooth as a bass boat off a boat ramp.
“It’s a great way for people to connect and meet each other,” angler Luke Routh said.
Luke’s fished in tournaments all across the nation, but the Co-Angler app is a way for him to have a little more fun.
“A lot of outdoorsmen are good people,” Luke said. “They just want to go outside and have fun, enjoy the lake; a lot of people don’t have access to it.”
“So, if you’re a person that has a boat,” Luke continued, “you ain’t got to show off all your good fishing spots. We’re coming here today, John and I, just fish randomly throughout the lake, and we’ve had a heck of a time.”
“Social media has created this kind of pseudo-social connection, which isn’t really real,” John said. “And so having the ability to use technology in the outdoors to connect people in the real world to go fish together is something I’m really passionate about.”
On the app, you can create your profile, explore trips, rank your activity level, techniques, and target fish you want to catch.
“First and foremost, it’s about human connection,” John said. “It’s about getting people in the outdoors together, sharing each other’s company, having a great time.”
”There’s definitely some natural healing properties to, you know, being around water and the outdoors, and sunshine, getting some of that vitamin D,“ John continued.
Right now, there are over 2,500 users on the app. John says it’s the only app connecting anglers.
Co-Angler is available in the App Store on your cell phone, or you can find it by clicking here to go to coangler.com.
It’s free to join, but you can add on some premium features as well.

title: Nurses raise concerns over Houlton Regional Hospital leadership
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
HOULTON, Maine (WAGM) - A group of nurses is raising concerns about leadership at Houlton Regional Hospital.
The Maine State Nurses Association has released a letter from nurses at Houlton Regional stating they have no confidence in the hospital’s CEO, Jeff Zewe. The letter follows the recent departures of several nurses from Northern Maine Medical Center’s emergency department, which also cited concerns about leadership. Both hospitals are led by Zewe.
Reasons cited in the nurses’ letter
The letter states the following reasons for the nurses’ lack of confidence in hospital leadership:
- Longtime emergency and inpatient physicians being replaced, and virtual doctors providing some overnight care.
- Physicians and surgeons continuing to leave, even as the hospital promises expanded services.
- Nurse turnover, reliance on traveling nurses, and the departure of several longtime nursing leaders.
- Security staffing being reduced following the departure of the hospital’s security director.
- Staffing levels in the Acute Care Unit not meeting the needs of the sickest patients.
- The emergency department working with only two nurses overnight, which can delay care during critical situations.
- Unresolved contract negotiations over staffing protections.
- Hospital leaders relying on out-of-state consultants instead of local staff input.
- The hospital’s culture becoming more corporate and less community focused.
Hospital board responds
Houlton Regional management was contacted for comment on the nurses’ letter. The Houlton Regional Hospital Board of Trustees responded in a letter stating:
“We remain committed to listening to employee concerns and working collaboratively with clinical teams to ensure both staff satisfaction and high-quality patient outcomes. Our priority remains clear: to increase access, provide high quality, accessible healthcare to the people of this region while building a sustainable future for Houlton Regional Hospital.”

title: Everybody sells insurance. What businesses need is a partner.
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
“Everybody sells insurance.” That is how Paul White describes the workers’ compensation marketplace. “What we were looking for was a partner,” he says. “Someone who answers the phone. Someone who shows up. Someone who is invested in your success.”
For Paul White Company, that partnership has helped turn workplace safety into a shared business priority. Founded by White’s parents in 1970 as a tile contractor, the family company has grown to serve residential and commercial customers across Maine, New Hampshire and other parts of New England.
The work is demanding. Flooring installation can be hard on backs, shoulders and knees, while stone and quartz countertops require careful handling. White says the company has focused on removing hazardous steps, improving material handling, addressing trip risks and strengthening protection around cutting tools and fabrication work.
The most meaningful change, he says, came from involving the people closest to the work. Rather than treating safety as a top-down directive, the company asked for input across roles and gave team members ownership of the solutions.
“What I am most proud of is the buy-in from the ground up,” White says. “It was not just an ownership-driven thing. There were a lot of stakeholders in the process.”
That commitment is supported by Chalmers Insurance Group and MEMIC. Luke Goodine, account executive at Chalmers, describes the relationship as a three-pillar risk management program: a client committed to improvement, a carrier with hands-on safety and claims resources and an agency that keeps communication moving among everyone involved.
“When we need help, MEMIC is willing to do what needs to be done,” Goodine says. “The agency ties those pieces together and creates communication between Paul White Company and MEMIC.”
The partners meet quarterly to review claims, discuss changing risks, prepare for key experience-modification dates and make sure open issues do not linger when a conversation could move them forward. MEMIC specialists have also visited the workplace, helped assess risks, shared training resources and collaborated on practical improvements.
White says the approach felt supportive rather than restrictive. “It was very collaborative,” he says. “There was great dialogue about why things were being done a certain way, and then we came up with a quick path forward.”
That sustained effort has produced measurable results. Paul White Company’s experience modification factor improved from 1.37 to a projected 0.82. The data also showed fewer injuries, fewer incidents and faster returns to work.
But the number is not the whole story. Better safety means people go home safely. When an injury does occur, the partnership helps the company respond quickly, keep the injured person connected and build a plan for recovery and a safe return to work.
Both White and Goodine emphasize that safety has no finish line. Risks change as operations change, and progress can slip if attention fades. The answer is consistency: scheduled conversations, clear responsibility, an openness to feedback and a plan for what happens when something goes wrong.
“It is not something we wished would happen,” White says. “It is something we actively made happen.”
Goodine encourages other businesses to take advantage of the expertise already available through their carrier and agent. Start with a conversation, invite a walkthrough, ask questions and dedicate a group with the authority to act.
“Companies may not realize how much MEMIC wants to show up,” Goodine says. “It is in everyone’s best interest that people stay safe and no one has a claim.”
For Paul White Company, Chalmers, and MEMIC, the lesson is simple: workers’ compensation is more than a policy. It is an ongoing business strategy built on listening, shared accountability and trusted partnership.

title: Mother, 4 young children killed in overnight Texas mobile home fire
text:
VAN ZANDT COUNTY, Texas (KLTV/Gray News) - Four young children and their mother died following an overnight house fire, authorities said.
Van Zandt County Fire Marshal Kevin Palmer said firefighters were dispatched shortly after 12:30 a.m. Wednesday to a fire at a mobile home at 482 County Road 4127 with reports of people trapped inside.
Palmer said when crews arrived, three people had escaped on their own, but four children remained inside. Firefighters breached an exterior wall to get in and quickly located the four children.
Officials said three of the children were pronounced dead on scene and a fourth child was flown to a hospital. The children’s mother was also flown to the hospital. Officials later announced the child and mother died at the hospital.
The children were a 3-year-old girl and three boys, ages 5, 8 and 10. The family has not been publicly identified, however Canton Independent School District confirmed some of the children were students.
“It is with profound sadness that we share the heartbreaking news of the loss of students at Canton Elementary and Canton Intermediate Schools. Our thoughts and prayers are with the family, friends, classmates, teachers, and everyone affected by this tragic loss,” the district said.
Two other people were taken by ambulance to the hospital as a precaution, Palmer said.
The Fire Marshal’s Office is in the early stages of investigating the fire.
When the Canton Fire Department got to the fire, the mobile home was half on fire, according to South Van Zandt Volunteer Fire Department Battalion Chief Jason Foster. He and his crew were called in as backup.
“As I got there, I went up to go in and help them search. They handed me the first one out. We pulled him out, started doing CPR immediately, and then they went in searching for the rest,” Foster said.
Foster said the fire was heaviest to the middle and right of the mobile home. The children were found inside a bedroom.
Foster says he’s been a firefighter for 28 years.
“Unfortunately, not my first time in a situation like this. But they never get any easier,” Foster said.
Foster says the fire was controlled in about 20 minutes.

title: ‘Praying for everyone affected’: 2 dead following massive fire at senior assisted living center
text:
CLINTON, Miss. (WLBT/Gray News) - Two people died after a fire at an assisted living center in Mississippi.
According to Hinds County Coroner Jeramiah Howard, one of the victims was an 82-year-old man, and the other was an 81-year-old woman.
Hinds County fire officials said the fire broke out at Brookdale Senior Living on East Northside Drive around 5 p.m. on Wednesday.
Firefighters from multiple departments, including the Jackson Fire Department and the Hinds County Volunteer Fire Department, along with several retired Clinton Fire Department personnel, helped put out the fire.
“We are heartbroken by the loss of two residents as a result of the fire at our Clinton community. Our deepest sympathies are with their families and loved ones during this incredibly difficult time,” representatives with the Brookdale Clinton facility said.
Mississippi Gov. Tate Reeves added that the Mississippi State Department of Health and the Mississippi Emergency Management Agency were also assisting in the response.
“Please continue praying for everyone affected. Thank you to all of the first responders who have quickly sprung into action to help those in need,” Reeves said.
According to Clinton Fire Chief Levius Buckley, 85 residents had to be evacuated, with four needing to be hospitalized with what appeared to be non-life-threatening injuries.
Buckley said the fire impacted several wings of the building, “about 45%” of the facility, and that the building would not be livable for a while.
The fire chief also called a rumor that the facility’s sprinklers were not working “not factual.”
Fire officials said the cause of the fire remains under investigation.

title: Rockland Police Department wins award for juvenile crime program
text:
ROCKLAND, Maine (WABI) - The Rockland Police Department has received the 2025 Community Policing Award from the New England Association of Chiefs of Police for it’s youth mentorship program. Rockland PD won first-place out of all New England police departments serving under 15,000 in total population.
The department started the program after a spike in juvenile crime in 2022. That year, calls involving juveniles rose 94% from the previous year, according to Rockland Police Department. After starting the program, juvenile crime in 2024 fell 37% and declined again in 2025.
“The program came out of kind of a necessity. And we all kind of put our heads together and said, hey, we need to do something different to address it,” said Deputy Chief Alex Gaylor, Rockland Police Department.
The Youth Mentorship Program introduces young people to law enforcement.
“Every Thursday we have a drop-in at the rec center, kick ball or do other activities with local youth and try to break down those barriers between the officers and the community and the youth particularly,” Gaylor said.
Gaylor said the program’s success would not have come without help from community members support and donations. He said in the last year, the department has received over $1,000 from community partners, local businesses and community members.
Doran Wright, known to the kids as “Pastor D.” Wright is the lead at the Belonging Center, a place for school-aged students to drop in and build connections. Wright is only one member of Rockland PD’s supporting cast for the youth mentorship program.
“Our philosophy is you shouldn’t have to commit a crime to get the help you need, so that’s sort of the underpinnings. Other than that, it’s building relationships, creating strong community,” said Doran Wright, lead, Rockland Youth Diversion Team.
Wright said he has seen the success of the program first-hand.
“There’s a young person I began working with a few years back in Long Creek. Came in as sort of a brash, feisty 15-year-old. And now, just this week, reached out to me to say he’s just started sort of a career move after a few years down the road. And people would have said his prospects for employment are negligible. And, you know, whether it was in Long Creek or whether in his home community, he got support he needed,” Wright said.
Wright and Gaylor said recognition is not the reason they do the work.
“In the end, the credit goes to the kids. Because if the kids are not buying into what we offer, then it’s all for naught, so while police departments and our organization and others, you know, sort of get the plaque on the wall, the ones who really deserve it at the end of the day are the kids who actually give us their trust and welcome our support,” Wright said.
“At the end of the day, this isn’t what it’s about. So, it’s about the work that they’re doing every day, but it does, it always obviously feels good to be recognized for that work, and yeah, we’re just looking forward to continuing to do what we do, look for ways to improve it and keep marching forward,” Gaylor said.
Gaylor said the department is already working to expanding and improving the program. He said Rockland PD applied for a grand to have a social worker to go out with some of the community partners.
The award will be presented Nov. 16 in Warwick, Rhode Island.

title: Rather than trying to recruit new nurses, CMMC should reinstate those who already worked there
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Carl Sheline is the mayor of Lewiston.
Last week, Central Maine Medical Center ran a recruitment advertisement on its social media pages seeking registered nurses. For nurses with two or more years of experience, hospital management was apparently willing to offer a hefty $20,000 sign-on bonus.
“Join a collaborative team where your voice is heard, your expertise is respected, and your commitment to exceptional patient care is appreciated every day,” the Instagram post read.
Who do they think they’re fooling? I suspect very few.
In the weeks leading up to the Sept. 24 election in which CMMC nurses voted overwhelmingly to form a union, management fired or suspended 20 nurses. According to union organizers, at least one nurse was escorted out of the hospital in the middle of their shift.
The hospital says these nurses were disciplined for violating established policies and standards. I don’t buy it, and neither should you.
Prime Healthcare, CMMC’s new owner, has a reputation for aggressive union busting. The California-based, for-profit company owns 20 hospitals across the country, including several in Illinois. When nurses at three of its Illinois facilities began organizing, terminations followed, just like they did at CMMC.
After CMMC nurses voted to unionize, management could have voluntarily reinstated the disciplined nurses as a show of good faith. It would have gone a long way toward repairing the hospital’s tarnished reputation.
Instead, management has repeatedly wasted time and money trying to block the nurses’ organizing efforts at every turn. Even now, CMMC management is fighting to invalidate September’s vote, arguing, ironically, that allegations of union busting should have been investigated to ensure nurses could vote without interference.
The reality is that nine out of 10 nurses voted for the union despite management’s alleged attempts to interfere.
It’s not too late for CMMC to do the right thing. As the weeks drag on, the nurses and their families are increasingly feeling the financial strain. The holiday season is approaching, and these families should not have to worry about how they will pay their bills or put food on the table because their employers essentially chose to punish them for standing up for their rights.
At the very least, reinstating the 20 nurses and providing back pay would cost less than trying to lure new nurses with signing bonuses in the hope that they will overlook CMMC’s ocean of red flags that I see.
It would also cost less than relying on travel nurses to compensate for chronic understaffing. Hospitals often pay a premium for temporary nurses, whose travel, housing, and agency costs add up fast.
Rather than paying a small fortune to recruit nurses from out of state, CMMC could reinstate experienced nurses who already know the hospital, its patients, and the community it serves.
What I consider lip service won’t be enough to improve hospital staffing. If management wants prospective hires to believe their voices will be heard, their expertise respected, and their commitment to patient care appreciated, it needs to start acting like it. So far, its actions have demonstrated the opposite to me.
In its recruitment advertisement, CMMC emphasized the importance of investing in its nurses.
“You’ve invested years in becoming the nurse you are today,” the post read. “Now invest your future in a team that’s invested in you.”
What, then, does CMMC owe the 20 nurses who have collectively invested decades of their careers in the hospital?
Before the acquisition of CMMC by Prime Healthcare was finalized, I had an in-person meeting with Dr. Prem Reddy, the CEO of Prime Healthcare.
When I heard about the merger, I had concerns. But after our sincere conversation, I felt better about the future of the hospital. I no longer do.
I was told that Prime Healthcare was going to make substantial investments in CMMC, and maybe they have. But nurses have told me they don’t even have enough bed linens, the most basic of necessities. It’s unacceptable.
If CMMC management wants to repair its relationship with its staff and the community, I think they need to stop fighting the nurses’ organizing efforts and move forward to bargaining. I believe they must reinstate all 20 nurses and provide them with back pay.
Anything less would make its promises to current and prospective employees ring even hollower.

title: A second female lawmaker in Australia is threatened days after alleged car attack
text:
A second female lawmaker in Australia is threatened days after alleged car attack
A man has been charged with threatening an Australian lawmaker’s staff with nunchucks, police said Thursday, days after another legislator was critically injured when a man repeatedly hit her with a car.
Related video: Australia lawmakers on car attack
Nunchucks are a weapon used in martial arts consisting of two sticks or rods connected by a rope or chain.
The incidents are heightening concerns about female politicians’ safety and raising concerns about security in a country where lawmakers are highly accessible to the public.
Man detained after entering lawmaker's office with nunchucks
Police say that a 56-year-old man entered Western Australian state government minister Hannah Beazley’s electorate office in suburban Perth on Wednesday, brandishing nunchucks and making verbal threats. Beazley wasn't in the office at the time.
The man was detained and charged with being armed in a way that may cause fear and with threatening to perform an unlawful act. He spent the night in police custody and will appear in a Perth court later Thursday, police said.
There was no allegation the man’s behavior was connected to the driver who hit federal lawmaker Helen Haines with his car in the east coast state of Victoria on Monday.
Haines' alleged attacker, Brendan Nugent, appeared in a court on Wednesday charged with intentionally causing serious injury, dangerous driving causing serious injury and causing harm to a federal official. He did not enter pleas and remains in custody.
Police are still searching for a motive.
Haines, a 65-year-old independent lawmaker, remained in critical condition on Thursday in a Melbourne hospital where surgeons have amputated both her legs, a health department statement said.
Australians worry attacks threaten tradition of accessible politicians
Both the Haines and Beazley incidents have raised concerns about the safety of female politicians, who account for a growing proportion of lawmakers in Australian parliaments.
Just under 50% of federal lawmakers and a majority of Prime Minister Anthony Albanese’s Cabinet are women.
Australian lawmakers are some of the most accessible in the world and political violence has traditionally been rare. But there are fears that increasingly toxic public debate driven by social media creates additional risks for elected women.
Albanese said the fact that the threat to Beazley came so soon after the alleged attack on Haines was “just heartbreaking.” Beazley is the daughter of Albanese's former federal colleague, Kim Beazley.
“We can have debate and disagreement, but do it in a way without descending into the sort of violence that we have seen in too many parts of the world,” Albanese told Australian Broadcasting Corp. “It’s certainly not who we are as Australians.”
Albanese attended an online security briefing this week for women lawmakers in his center-left Labor Party. Security agencies addressed misogynistic threats directed at them.
Male and female federal lawmakers agree that women are facing the worst of the online abuse.
“Of course people are concerned. They’re anxious,” Albanese said. “There has been a normalization of behavior that can be very aggressive in a way that wasn’t happening a couple of decades ago.”
Beazley says staff were rattled but safe
Hannah Beazley said she was in the state parliament when the man entered her electorate office demanding to see her.
Beazley said two members of her staff had been “rattled,” but had remained safe behind a security screen.
“We don't know his motives at all,” she told reporters on Wednesday.
Governor-General Sam Mostyn, who is only the second woman to ever serve as the British monarch’s representative in Australia, said that she was abused on social media for speaking at a press conference on Wednesday alongside Haines’ husband Phil Haines.
“Like any woman who has stepped up into any position across any part of our society, there is a unique and pernicious form of attack that comes our way,” Mostyn told ABC.
“Women across the country know that there are certain things that are reserved for women in that attack that go to our gender and they are often vicious and just despicable,” she added.

title: Maine-based producer works on song featuring The Pretty Reckless and Foo Fighters members

text:
Maine-based producer works on song featuring The Pretty Reckless and Foo Fighters members Dave Grohl and Pat Smear
A producer based in Portland, Maine, is sharing his experience of working with members of Foo Fighters on a new version of a song he produced for The Pretty Reckless.
Jonathan Wyman helped produce The Pretty Reckless' most recent album "Dear God," which was released in June. The album features the song "About You," which Wyman felt was "in Dave's wheelhouse," referring to Foo Fighters frontman and former Nirvana drummer Dave Grohl.
Wyman said he received a call from Taylor Momsen, lead vocalist of The Pretty Reckless, who said that she and Grohl were going to do a new version of "About You," and Wyman jumped at the chance to work with one of his favorite artists.
Wyman flew out to Los Angeles, where Momsen, Grohl and another member of the Foo Fighters, guitarist Pat Smear, recorded the song. Grohl played drums and guitar on the record while providing backing vocals, while Smear also played guitar on the track.
"It was nuts because growing up in the '90s, Nirvana was huge for me and Foo Fighters sort of came out when I was in college," Wyman said. "I've been a fan of everything Dave's been in."
The song was mixed in Maine and mastered by Grammy-winning mastering engineer Adam Ayan, who is also based in Portland, Maine.
The bonus version of "About You" was released last Friday, Oct. 16, and a music video for the track was released on Monday, Oct. 19.

title: Newborn safely surrendered to Safe Haven Baby Box that has been used 3 times since it was installed
text:
KNOXVILLE, Tenn. (WVLT/Gray News) – A newborn baby was safely surrendered at a Safe Haven Baby Box at a Knoxville Fire Department Tuesday.
Station 17 received a baby box alert around 7:45 p.m., according to Timothy Woods with the fire department.
The crew at the station went to the box, where they found a healthy baby inside, Woods said. The child was quickly removed from the box for further evaluation before being taken to the hospital.
Woods said this baby box was installed in February 2023, marking the first one in Tennessee. There are now 33 in the state, with the most recent being installed in Sevierville.
This was the third time the baby box has been used since its installation, according to Woods.
How does a Safe Haven Baby Box work?
When a baby is placed inside the climate-controlled box, a silent alarm immediately alerts firefighters, allowing personnel to respond within minutes while preserving the anonymity of the individual surrendering the child.
Surrendered babies are typically adopted by a family within 30 to 45 days.
Officials with the Department of Child Services conduct interviews to find a home for the newborn.
“The Safe Haven Baby Box provides a compassionate option that protects the health and safety of babies while offering hope during a crisis,” Brad Bailey, chairman of The Woodlands Township, said. “We are thankful this baby is safe and commend the Fire Department for its commitment to providing this lifesaving resource to our community.”
The baby box was installed at the fire station in April 2025 and operates under the Texas Safe Haven law.
Resources for the parents
“To the parent, thank you! Thank you for keeping your baby safe and trusting us and the fire dept to take it from here,” Safe Haven Baby Box founder Monica Kelsey said. “We are praying for you!”
Safe Haven Baby Boxes offer free medical and counseling resources for the mother, should she need them.
Counseling services are available based on the birth mother’s schedule and are done online via Zoom at no cost.
If you need help finding a Safe Haven location or would like to speak to a licensed counselor, call the National Safe Haven crisis hotline at 1-866-99BABY1.
Women in crisis can call the national 24-hour hotline and receive counseling and assistance free of charge.

title: Letter: Susan Collins helps deliver Donald Trump’s agenda
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
Susan Collins says she’s willing to stand up to Donald Trump. After nearly 30 years in Washington, Sen. Collins should be judged by what she’s done, not what she says.
Collins always reminds us of the federal dollars she brings home. That’s important. But what good is getting money for Maine hospitals while supporting an administration whose policies threaten their financial survival?
Consider her record.
She voted to confirm Robert F. Kennedy Jr., despite his long history of spreading vaccine misinformation. With measles cases surging, she still defends that decision.
She supported Brett Kavanaugh’s confirmation to the Supreme Court, assuring Mainers he respected established precedent. Kavanaugh subsequently helped overturn Roe v. Wade.
Collins often expresses deep concern about Trump’s actions. But concern without meaningful action changes little.
According to an August Bangor Daily News analysis, Collins cast just four decisive votes against Republican-preferred outcomes during Trump’s second administration, through the period examined.
As chair of the powerful Senate Appropriations Committee, Collins has the power most senators can only dream of. Why isn’t she using more of it to challenge Trump’s agenda?
Collins has helped Maine communities. No question. But bringing home federal dollars doesn’t excuse the consequences of her national decisions.
Susan Collins doesn’t sound like Donald Trump. But too often, her votes help deliver his agenda.
Maine deserves better.
Michael Towey
Belfast

title: Sleepover safety: Rite of passage or too big a risk
text:
(Aging Untold) — Parents face a difficult decision when their children are invited to sleepovers, weighing the childhood tradition against safety concerns.
At the McElrath home, Fridays are reserved for family time. After a hectic week of work and school, the family of four enjoys quality time together.
“We started protecting our Fridays. Nothing ever gets scheduled on Fridays,” Chris McElrath, a father of two, said.
The no-sleepover camp
As the McElrath children get older and receive invitations to sleepovers with friends, the parents have made a decision.
“With the exception of a time or two that I can count on one hand, we’re in the no-sleepover camp,” Emily McElrath, a mother of two, said.
The couple said they are not comfortable with their 9-year-old son, who suffers from epilepsy, and their 11-year-old daughter spending the night outside their home.
“Not everybody has the same rules that we have in our household, and that’s OK. I don’t know what their social media policy is. I don’t know if their children have phones or devices,” Emily McElrath said.
She is concerned about what online content might be seen by curious young eyes.
“And just some of the stuff that I’m already seeing kids talk about in her grade. If my child sees it, I don’t necessarily get a do-over. I don’t get to have her un-see it or un-experience it,” Emily McElrath said.
Expert warnings
Kristi McVee, a child safety expert, said sleepovers “can actually be a massive risk for children.”
McVee, a former child abuse detective who has interviewed young victims in Australia, said sleepovers open the door for sexual abuse, and not just at the hands of strangers.
“Sleepovers at cousins’, at grandparents’, at other people’s homes that could be family because for the most part, child sexual abuse is perpetrated by someone known to the child,” McVee said.
According to the CDC, more than 90 percent of child sexual abuse is perpetrated by someone the family knows and trusts.
Balancing safety and experience
“I feel like it’s a hot topic more than it’s ever been a hot topic,” Jessica Saggio, a parenting columnist, said.
Saggio said she does not want to give up on what she believes is right about the sleepover experience.
“You have to be balanced. You can’t just trust anybody. You have to be careful about where your kids go and who they’re with, but also, I’m not a hardline ‘no’ because I want them to experience that side of childhood,” Saggio said.
Her two older daughters, ages 10 and 8, are just starting to attend birthday slumber parties.
“The family was in our neighborhood. We know them quite well, again the mom had everything planned out. There was no wiggle room for shenanigans, if you will,” Saggio said.
Saggio said it was an overall good experience for her daughters.
But experts warn that sometimes sleepovers are an opportunity for children to engage in high-risk behaviors while the adults are not looking.
“It’s actually quite common for sleepover parties today for kids to jump online and go and engage in sexual communications with people. Bullying very much so, whether they get together as a group at the sleepover and bully someone else,” McVee said.
What to consider
Licensed clinical psychologist Dr. Carolyn Ievers-Landis at University Hospitals in Cleveland said there are many things to consider.
“How closely are kids being monitored? How safe is that household?” Ievers-Landis said.
Ievers-Landis recommends focusing on the child’s need for emotional security and comfort.
“Some kids might wet the bed sometimes and they’re embarrassed to go to sleepovers. Some kids might have fears at night or fears of the dark, so they’re afraid to be away from their parent. Some kids might just like to do things the way things are always done and so they’re afraid,” Ievers-Landis said.
Some children may need more time to mature before agreeing to a sleepover.
The late-over alternative
The McElraths opted for what is called a “late-over,” where a child attends the party but leaves sometime before midnight.
“Even if it’s 10:30/11 o’clock, she can stay over and come to the party and hang out with the girls, but we have somewhere to be early the next morning, so I need to come pick her up,” Emily McElrath said.
“Ease into it. Try one of those late overs. Try letting them go until 10, pick them up, then start over the next time and go a little bit later the next time,” Saggio said.
If it is not the right time or a good fit for a child, experts say parents should not force it.
“They don’t have to do a sleepover. You don’t have to do it if you don’t want to do it,” Saggio said.
“Once our kids are in high school, I would be fine with sleepovers I think,” Emily McElrath said.
For now, the McElraths’ no-sleepover policy will stand.
“First and foremost, our job is not to be your friend, it’s to be your parent and keep you safe. That’s kind of how we landed on that decision,” Emily McElrath said.
Safety suggestions
The Child Rescue Coalition offers suggestions for parents who decide their child is ready for a sleepover:
- Make sure you know and trust the adults and that they will be present to supervise.
- Know who else will be there at the same time as your child. Studies show that 40 percent of children are abused by older children.
- Have a pre-sleepover talk with your kids.
- Check in on your child and allow them to call you. Designate a code word your child can say if they feel unsafe, so you will know to pick them up immediately.

title: Setting the record straight on Troy Jackson
text:
Negative ads on TV and mailings are wasting money and spreading rumors.
Regarding Troy Jackson and allegations of intimidation of women: In an incident between Troy Jackson, at age 19, and Lana, his partner of about 40 years, Lana has strongly said Troy was not violent toward her.
Regarding Jackson’s desire to raise taxes on Social Security, he does, but not for ordinary people. Jackson wants the wealthy to pay their fair share into Social Security. This year, according to U.S. News and World Report, only income up to $184,500 is subject to Social Security payroll taxes. If this cap goes away, like Jackson wants it to, we could save the program for those with less.
About “Oh, shut up.” Jackson said this during the fourth debate in an “Oh, come on,” tone. It did not sound harsh — like Susan Collins’ inappropriate comment about the heckler.
Victoria Adams
Kennebunk

title: Man sentenced to 80 years for murdering sex offender who assaulted his relative
text:
GOSHEN, Ind. (WNDU) - An Indiana man convicted of shooting and killing a sex offender who assaulted one of his relatives has been sentenced to 80 years in prison.
According to the Elkhart County Prosecutor’s Office, Nicholas Stanley received 65 years for murder and 15 years for a firearm enhancement he admitted to during his trial.
Stanley, 36, was found guilty last month of killing Allen Cogswell, 35, at the Daylite Inn on Cassopolis Street on June 24, 2025.
Cogswell was released from prison in May 2025 and was living at the motel. Court records showed Stanley was a close family member of one of Cogswell’s past victims.
The Goshen News reported that Stanley testified during his trial that he planned to confront Cogswell and beat him up. He said seeing Cogswell through the motel window caused his brain to “explode like a tsunami” and led him to decide to kill him.
Stanley was said to have gone to his car, grabbed a shotgun, knocked on Cogswell’s motel room door before shooting him twice that early morning.
“I decided that I had to do what I had to do to protect my [family]; I had to kill him,” Stanley was quoted as saying under oath.

text:
MEMPHIS, Tenn. (WMC/Gray News) — A fugitive has been apprehended one year after he was mistakenly released from custody, authorities in Tennessee said.
The Shelby County Sheriff’s Office said deputies and U.S. Marshals agents arrested Anthony Green around 1:25 p.m. Wednesday.
Green had been erroneously released from custody in September 2025.
Background on the case
The Shelby County Sheriff’s Office said Green, then 24, was found guilty in September 2025 in a 2020 murder case after a three-day trial.
The jail had not yet received or processed information from the clerk’s office before Green was released in September 2025 after posting a $2,500 bond in an unrelated misdemeanor theft case, the Shelby County Sheriff’s Office said.
Arrest details
Officers, deputies and U.S. Marshals agents acted on tips and executed a search warrant in the 3300 block of Knights Trail in Memphis.
Green, now 25, was taken into custody and transported to the Shelby County Jail. He faces charges of first-degree murder, attempted first-degree murder and employing a firearm with the intent to commit a felony.

title: Judge orders Trump must sit for a deposition in his defamation lawsuit against the BBC
text:
MIAMI (AP) — A federal judge on Thursday ordered President Donald Trump to sit for a deposition in his $10 billion defamation lawsuit against the BBC by Dec. 11.
The order from U.S. Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett came as lawyers for the British broadcaster complained that Trump had delayed his appearance in his own lawsuit. Charles Tobin, attorney for the BBC, said that with two months left in the discovery period, “we still haven’t been able to depose the plaintiff.”
Meanwhile, it remained uncertain whether former special counsel Jack Smith would be allowed to sit for a deposition. Federal rules require current and former employees to receive permission from agency heads before testifying in court cases. Smith has requested permission but has not received an answer, and the judge ruled that the department must respond to him by Nov. 2.
In arguments about Trump’s deposition, Tobin noted there had been an agreed-upon date of Oct. 16, but Trump had canceled it for a “matter of national importance.” He said the Republican president was in fact campaigning in Georgia that day. “He was participating in party politics and prioritized that over sitting for the deposition,” Tobin said.
Lett said Trump must sit for a deposition by Dec. 11, or face sanctions up to dismissal of his lawsuit — unless the discovery period is extended by the presiding judge.
Discovery, where lawyers for both sides exchange documents and other evidence, is scheduled to end Dec. 18, and the BBC’s attorneys want to make sure they have Trump’s deposition before that deadline. Lett said only the presiding judge assigned to the case can alter the trial schedule, and the defense said it would be open to scheduling the deposition at a later time if the trial schedule was also changed.
Trump, who has often avoided depositions, filed his lawsuit against the BBC last December. He accused the publicly funded broadcaster of defamation as well as deceptive and unfair trade practices related to a documentary, “Trump: A Second Chance.”
The BBC acknowledged that filmmakers spliced together quotes from different sections of the speech Trump delivered to his supporters on Jan. 6, 2021, before the storming of the U.S. Capitol, to make it seem he was directly urging violence. The broadcaster apologized over the editing, and the head of the BBC and its top news executive both resigned. But the BBC has denied Trump’s claims that it defamed him.
Trump’s attorneys also argued against recording his deposition on video, asking for only a court reporter. The judge ruled that the deposition could be recorded on video but only for attorneys, meaning it wouldn’t be released to the public.
It remained unclear whether Jack Smith would be allowed to sit for deposition
To bolster its defense, the broadcaster subpoenaed former special counsel Jack Smith earlier this month. Trump’s lawyers have argued that there is no good reason for Smith, who is not a party to the case, to appear. The BBC has said Smith has extensive knowledge of what happened that day.
At issue in Thursday’s hearing, though, was whether Smith had received the legally required permission from the Department of Justice. Assistant U.S. Attorney Matthew Feeley told the judge that Smith had sent a letter to the department saying he would not testify without permission, and the agency had not yet responded. Lett ordered the department to respond to Smith by Nov. 2.
It seems unlikely that the department would grant Smith permission, or that he would move forward without it.
Earlier in the hearing, Tobin, the BBC lawyer, argued that Smith has not objected to being deposed for this case, meaning the only objection is coming from Trump. Tobin said the BBC is not trying to relitigate the events of Jan. 6, but Smith is one of the leading experts in what happened that day, and his deposition could lead the BBC to evidence that could help their case.
“We can argue later on whether his testimony is admissible,” Tobin said, “but we are entitled to that deposition.”
Trump’s lawyer, Alejandro Brito, said Smith has no personal knowledge of Trump’s Jan. 6 speech or Trump’s state of mind when he gave it. All of Smith’s knowledge about the case is secondhand, Brito argued, and the special counsel’s report, along with Smith’s testimony before Congress, is all public and available to the BBC’s attorneys.
Judge says the BBC can see membership records for Mar-a-Lago
The judge agreed that the BBC should be allowed to see records for the total number of applications for membership at Trump’s Mar-a-Lago resort in Florida from Jan. 6, 2020, through Jan. 6, 2026, as well as the total cost of membership and initiation fees for new applicants.
Tobin said one aspect of any defamation case is showing actual damages, and the popularity of Mar-a-Lago is a significant indicator of Trump’s reputation. The BBC’s lawyer described the private club as “a place where he exhibits his reputation in front of people who are important to him.”
Brito argued that Trump does not actually run Mar-a-Lago, and that his reputation is not associated with the club.

title: John Anderson, Country Music Hall of Fame singer, dies at 71
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WSMV/Gray News) — Country music singer John Anderson has died, according to a statement shared by his family on his official social media pages.
“It is with the heaviest of hearts that we share the passing of our beloved husband, father, grandfather, and best friend,” the family said in the statement.
Anderson was 71.
Family statement
“To the world, he was a gifted country music singer whose voice and songs touched countless lives. To us, he was so much more. He was the heart of our family, the one who made us laugh, loved us fiercely, and made every ordinary moment feel special,” the statement said.
“We are completely heartbroken,” the family said. “His music will live on, but for us, his greatest legacy will always be the love he gave his family and the memories we will carry with us forever. Please keep our family in your thoughts and prayers as we grieve this unimaginable loss.”
Career highlights
Anderson was known for hits including “Straight Tequila Night” and “Seminole Wind.”
Throughout his career, Anderson opened shows for other artists including Merle Haggard, George Jones and Willie Nelson.
Anderson received the CMA Horizon Award and the CMA Single of the Year award for “Swingin’.” He also received the Academy of Country Music Career Achievement Award.
He was inducted into the Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame in 2014.
According to the Country Music Hall of Fame, which inducted Anderson in 2024, he earned 20 top 10 country hits.
Hall of Fame tribute
“John Anderson was a one-of-a-kind song stylist who proved that fresh innovations were best born from time-honored traditions,” said Kyle Young, CEO of the Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum. “Whether he borrowed inspiration from Lefty Frizzell’s vocal bends or the Florida swamp land, he brought dynamic distinction and creative soul to a world that needed to hear his voice. In 1981, John famously gave life to Billy Joe Shaver’s lyric, ‘I’m just an old chunk of coal, but I’ll be a diamond someday.’ He was already a diamond then, and a diamond he always will be.”
Anderson’s family has not released information about what caused his death.

title: Former historic Ellsworth jail gets a new roof amid yearslong rehab
text:
The stewards of Ellsworth’s former county jail, built in 1886, are replacing its antiquated, leaking slate roof — the latest step in an ambitious project aimed at rehabbing the historic building that has survived years of neglect.
The Ellsworth Historical Society is in the middle of a yearslong rehabilitation project that will preserve the old jail’s historic character while ensuring it’s safe for visitors for years to come.
The latest repairs, funded through $500,000 in congressionally directed spending, will replace the roof and guttering system using materials and designs that match their original construction, according to the Ellsworth Historical Society.
“There was a danger that it would be torn down: the county didn’t want to maintain it — they have a modern jail and sheriff’s office that meet today’s needs — so the county commissioners could have had a parking lot there,” Ellsworth Historical Society president Mark Worth said. “The historical society wanted to save this historic building in downtown Ellsworth: it’s a part of the character and history of Ellsworth. We believed it was worth saving because of its historical significance.”
The project is being funded exclusively by grants and donations, without any reliance on taxpayer dollars, Worth said.
The society has owned the former jail, which also housed the Hancock County sheriff and his family, since 1998 but has managed the property since the 1970s, when jail operations were moved to a new wing of the current courthouse that is now used to house the sheriff’s office. The old jail was placed on the National Register of Historic Places in January 2008, according to Betsy Arntzen, the society’s assistant treasurer and grant writer.
The roof — roughly 30% of which will be preserved during construction — will be replaced with locally sourced slate, Arntzen said. The project’s bid was awarded to Hahnel Brothers Co., a more than century-old, family run Maine roofing and sheet metal contractor, and will be completed within two months, Arntzen said.
The society previously repointed the jail’s brick on all four sides, after decades of the antiquated building crumbling, with $200,000 in funding from a National Park Service grant, according to Arntzen. That work was completed in 2024.
The society has won more than $1 million in grants over the past three years, Arntzen said.
Next, the stewards will rehabilitate the jail’s front porch and all windows, work that will total just over $200,000. That construction will begin this fall and be completed by the summer of 2027, according to Arntzen. Future phases will include rehabbing old lead paint from the interior’s jail cells.
Following the restoration, the stewards hope to transform the once decaying jail into a museum with regular hours. They currently only host public tours by appointment.
“Every county’s jail has not survived exactly intact the way this one has — it’s largely unchanged — so it’s one of the unique examples of a county jail in the state of Maine,” Arntzen said. “Its architecture is a paired structure where the sheriff and his family live under the same roof with the inmates. [That] was a common idea for people who were taking care of the incarcerated law breakers, like a lighthouse keeper.”
The sheriff’s family would be involved in caring for the jail: spouses would cook meals for the inmates, some of whom would in turn babysit for the sheriff’s children, Arntzen said, adding that the wives would be “unpaid staff members.”
Among the jail’s most thrilling historical moments was the daring but temporary 1965 escape of Myles Connor, a notorious thief who fled the building after surprising the jail guard with a fake gun, which he had carved out of a bar of soap and blackened with shoe polish. Connor has also been linked to Boston’s infamous 1990 art heist at the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum.
The society will soon collect oral histories from former inmates, family members and friends who lived, worked and spent time in the old jail, they said, adding that they encourage the public to contact them with such stories.
“It’s living history, not some dumb building. It’s where real people lived with their families,” Arntzen said. “It represents a period of time, and it represents real people’s lives who are among us today. It is an untold story.”
