title: Maine needs to double down on its Canadian ties
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Douglas Rooks has been a Maine editor and columnist for 41 years. His biography of Gov. Ken Curtis, “Transformational,” is now available. He welcomes comment at [email protected].
I had the chance to travel for a week in Canada recently. It seemed a good time to compare the two countries while traveling north — or in this case, east.
The Maritime provinces (New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia) recall similarities for Mainers. Though our viewpoint usually extends west — uniquely among the “lower 48” states, Maine borders only one, New Hampshire — New Brunswick is an equally interesting pairing.
The two are almost equal in size, though New Brunswick has just shy of 900,000 people against Maine’s 1.4 million. Cities are larger, though, with three — Moncton, St. John and Fredericton, the capital — exceeding Portland’s population.
Throughout the Maritimes, there’s a familiar feel, with the Acadian forest dominating the coast an extension of Washington County. Yes, there’s lots of trees, though Prince Edward Island, whose economy relies on farming (and tourism), resembles Aroostook’s potato-growing regions.
There have been changes since previous wanderings of mine. A bridge to PEI replaced the ferry in 1997. The U.S. Customs station opened in 2009 is four miles upriver from Calais, while Canada’s is still downtown.
Some changes are more recent. Canadians are united behind Prime Minister Mark Carney to a degree unthinkable a few years ago. When Carney and his Liberal Party stood for election in April 2025 after Liberal Party Prime Minister Justin Trudeau stepped down, Carney was widely expected to lose to Pierre Poilievre’s Conservative Party. Pundits called it “unwinnable” for the Liberals.
Instead, Liberals won their first majority since 2019 and Carney may be carving a larger place for himself on the international scene than Trudeau — himself son of legendary Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau, whose 18 years in office made him the most famous Canadian PM to date.
The elder Trudeau, a Liberal Party member from Quebec, held Canada together against a determined separatist movement by the Parti Quebecois aimed at separating the French-majority province from Canada. This week, separatists in Alberta, the conservative, oil-rich western province, held a referendum to explore independence — and 76% voted “No.”
What prompted these events? The actions of President Donald Trump. Upon returning to office, Trump made ludicrous statements about Canada as “the 51st state,” arguing that America’s (and Maine’s) largest trading partner was defrauding us. He aimed to make the world’s “longest undefended border” a battleground.
Carney differs from the international leaders who make soothing sounds to avoid Trump’s ire. Carney plays it straight, defending his nation’s interests. Trump, after his first trade war was struck down by the U.S. Supreme Court, launched another against Canada.
The immediate results: Canadians are increasingly united, Americans disunited. Yet Canadians seem to bear us no ill will for this distressing performance. Rather the opposite: Americans are still welcome, with the attitude “this too will pass.” In our own response to Trumpian vows to annex Canada, Greenland, Iceland, Venezuela, et. al., we might think instead: cooperation.
Let’s ponder a confederation of Atlantic provinces and states, with Maine a charter participant. Our economies have similar strengths and weaknesses. Unlike much of the world, we could use some more people — young people especially.
Where Maine was abandoned by American paper companies, job losses were mitigated in Canada thanks to companies like Irving, with its forest products and petroleum divisions. Along with McCain, the frozen food giant, Irving is now the largest business investor in eastern Maine and Aroostook. Once viewed as a threat, Canadian investment helps sustain Maine’s rural economies — but is now threatened by irrational trade wars.
Long ago, a Maine governor appreciated Canadian ties and built on them. When I researched Ken Curtis’ administration, one surprise was how vigorously and persistently he pursued those ties. He sought to create a public power authority that could buy cheap hydropower from the then-new Churchill Falls project in Newfoundland; CMP and Bangor Hydro opposed him.
Curtis befriended Richard Hatfield, New Brunswick’s longest-serving premier, and signed numerous agreements, some still in force. He established an Office of Canadian Relations and later served a regrettably brief stint as ambassador to Canada. Though Curtis hoped future governors would maintain these efforts, they didn’t.
Gov. Janet Mills traveled this week to Ireland, exploring both the Republic and Northern Ireland as a gateway to the European market, now that Great Britain has “Brexited” the EU. Perhaps the next governor could explore gateways to Canada.
If as well received as I expect a confederation would be, Maine might attract American Atlantic partners, say Massachusetts, New Hampshire and Rhode Island. Then Maine could be the center of something, rather than at the far margins.
Confederation is a useful concept. It’s how Canada moved toward nationhood starting with a conference in Charlottetown, PEI, in 1864, the height of our Civil War. And on that path — unlike our own — no revolution was required.

title: Tragedy Narrowly Averted After Two Boats Collide
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
By Paul Sylvain
Three very lucky Machiasport men narrowly avoided being claimed by the frigid ocean waters off Cross Island on Oct. 15, following a collision between a Cooke’s Aquaculture vessel and a commercial fishing boat skippered by Eric Wood.
Machiasport Harbor Master David Cale reported Saturday that Eric Wood and his sternman, Stephan Van Hoose, were working off Cross Island when Wood’s boat got T-boned by one of Cooke’s salmon vessels at around 7 a.m. last Thursday.
“Troy Wood was the captain of the salmon boat and hit Eric wide open at 17 knots [nearly 20 mph],” Cale said. “Troy was the only person aboard Cooke’s boat.” Cale said he was told that Troy Wood “wasn't even at the wheel because he got thrown overboard” by the impact.
“If it wasn't for Eric, Troy would have drowned,” Cale said. “Even though Troy was wearing a life jacket, the weight of his clothes and boots was pulling him under.”
Incredibly, even though Eric Wood’s boat had just gotten hit, Eric saw Troy Wood struggling in the 52-degree water and managed to swing his badly damaged boat around to grab Troy and keep him afloat until several salmon pen workers rushed over in their skiff and pulled him out of the water.
“In the meantime, the salmon boat was still doing circles and almost hit them again,” Cale said. “The workers had to chase down the salmon boat and get aboard it to stop it.”
Van Hoose was taken to the hospital to be checked out for possible rib injuries, Cale said, adding that no ribs were broken, but they were pretty badly bruised.
Van Hoose posted on social media Saturday, “I am still processing everything, slowly. I remember every detail, and I see it every time I close my eyes, but it doesn’t feel real.”
Said Van Hoose, “I was standing in the middle of this deck three seconds before impact. Another boat struck us broadside at high speed, sunk our stern underwater, and drove completely over us. Millimeters and microseconds from ending tragically, but we all made it home.”
He went on to say, “My body will heal, but I don’t know about my mind. Hopefully putting [this] out there will help.”
“In the end Cooke’s will be paying [for the damage to Eric Wood’s boat],” Cale said. “Eric’s boat got hit so hard that the impact at full throttle almost flipped it over. Eric told me his boat listed so hard its keel and propeller came right out of the water and, by some miracle, the boat sat back down.”
“I asked Eric on Saturday if he could use help with anything,” Cale said. “Eric said he was disappointed with the Coast Guard because even though he called and reported the accident, he hasn't heard back from them, and they never came to the scene.”
According to Cale, “The same thing happened when Kenny Link’s boat got hit by a salmon company boat. If a boat sinks and no one gets severely hurt, they’re not coming. And Eric has never even heard from Marine Patrol.”
Cale said Eric Wood remains shaken up by the accident. “He’s been friends with Troy since they were kids,” Cale said, “and he was afraid he was going to lose him.”
Cale said the accident is still being investigated.

title: Fox News poll shows Susan Collins and Troy Jackson tied less than 2 weeks out
text:
U.S. Sen. Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson were tied at 49% among likely voters in a Fox News poll released Thursday, the latest survey to show Maine’s Senate race as a coin flip less than two weeks before Election Day.
It is one of the better results this month for Collins, a Republican who has not led a public poll since late September and trailed in every single one in 2020 before handily beating Democrat Sara Gideon. Jackson has a 56% chance of winning, according to Decision Desk HQ.
The toss-up race is one of a handful that will decide control of the U.S. Senate. Collins is seeking a sixth term against Jackson, a former Maine Senate president from Allagash who has been on a dead campaign sprint since becoming the nominee in July. He replaced Graham Platner, who withdrew over a rape allegation from an ex-girlfriend.
Fox’s August poll surveyed only registered voters and had Jackson up 2 points. He holds the same margin among registered voters now, even as most of the remaining undecided voters have picked a side.
Trump is the biggest drag on Collins. Just 37% of likely voters approve of the president’s job performance, and a majority said they are concerned the senator votes with him too often, including 42% who are extremely concerned about that.
But Collins holds a clear path to victory that runs through crossover voters. She leads independents by 13 points in the Fox poll, and 1 in 5 likely voters who disapprove of President Donald Trump are backing her. An AARP poll last month found Collins with more swing support than any other Republican in seven battleground states.
She is running well ahead of her party. More likely voters want Democrats to control the Senate than Republicans, and Democrat Hannah Pingree leads Republican Bobby Charles by 10 points in a governor’s race that has drawn relatively little attention and also includes independent state Sen. Rick Bennett.
Most October polls in the Senate race have looked similar. Jackson led by 2 points in surveys from InsiderAdvantage, Suffolk University and Rasmussen Reports, and by 4 in Marist and Washington Post surveys. Collins’ last lead came in a co/efficient poll from the end of September.
The Fox poll, which surveyed 1,514 likely voters from Oct. 16-20, has a margin of error of plus or minus 2.5 percentage points.

title: As the gambling industry changes, Oxford Casino is up for sale. What does that mean for the community?
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
OXFORD — It’s been 13 years since Churchill Downs Inc. bought Oxford Casino, one of only two casinos in the state.
Since then, a lot has changed in the gambling industry, as the rise of online sports betting and prediction markets have eaten away at traditional casino gambling.
Still, local leaders and business owners say, the casino has been a benefit to the area. As Churchill Downs considers selling the property, leaders hope it remains a community asset.
“I do feel like we are very fortunate to have it here,” Oxford Selectman Ernie Fitts said. “There’s pros and cons with everything, but I certainly feel the pros have outweighed (the cons), having the casino here in the town of Oxford.”
CHANGES AT CHURCHILL DOWNS
The American Gaming Association reported that casino revenue was up 2.3% in 2025 over the previous year, while sports betting revenue was up 22.6% and internet gaming was up 27.6% in the same period.
The changes in the gambling industry have a lot to do with why Churchill Downs is considering selling the Oxford Casino, as well as eight other gaming properties in seven other states.
The company has said it wants to focus on live horse racing, its flagship Kentucky Derby, and online betting platform TwinSpires. In an interview last month with Horse Racing Nation’s Rod Flatter Racing Pod, Churchill Downs’ CEO Bill Carstanjen repeated the assertion that the move to sell the nine casinos is all about strategy and not weak performance.
Yet, he also said gaming has become less popular with public company investors, citing competition for funding from sports betting and prediction markets.
Three months after announcing that Churchill Downs was considering the sale of all or some of the nine casinos, no decisions have been made public. Carstanjen said his company is soliciting and weighing bids and that the process is ongoing.
Under state law, a casino license is not transferable or assignable. If the Oxford Casino is sold, a potential buyer would have to apply for licensure as a casino operator and receive the license before the acquisition occurs, so as not to interrupt business operations.
JOBS AND REVENUE
In 2010, the year of the successful referendum to open the casino, western Maine and Oxford County were struggling with a recession. Unemployment in Oxford County peaked at 11% and was among the highest in Maine. Promises of jobs were a factor in the outcome of the statewide referendum, which passed by 4,723 votes — less than 1%.
In the run-up to the vote, backers of the proposed casino in Oxford County said it would generate more than 1,700 year-round jobs and at least $60 million in revenue for education and statewide programs, the Penobscot and Passamaquoddy tribes, and foster economic development.
The reality has not quite kept up with the hype. The casino employs between 400 and 450 people year-round, with an average annual tax revenue of $33 million distributed by statute, with 46% of net revenue from slot machines and 16% from table games providing funding for a number of programs and services. Most of the revenue goes to education to fund essential programs for K-12. Both the town of Oxford and Oxford County get a share of the revenue.
The impact has been felt. Overall, the casino has contributed more than $338 million to the state, county, and town since it opened in 2012.
In 2025, Oxford received more than $2 million from Oxford Casino, which Fitts said is a huge relief for the town of 4,300. The casino revenue has allowed Oxford to keep its property tax rate at $14 per $1,000 of assessed value, when surrounding towns are at $16, $17 and as high as $24.5 in Auburn.
“As a Select Board member, you don’t have to go and worry as much about taxes,” he said. “Property taxes are a big issue in this state.”
Predictions for a rise in crime and rampant gambling problems never materialized. Lori Manson, the gambling services coordinator of ADEPT Maine, said while Maine is not immune to gambling addiction, most people can go to the casino and gamble for entertainment without issue.
Casinos, she said, are the least of her worries. They are very tightly regulated by the Gambling Control Unit, and you have to physically go to a casino to bet. Sports betting, offshore gambling sites, and prediction markets can all be done on your phone.
“Of all the gambling forms, it’s probably the one I’m least concerned about as far as the harm that it does to the citizens of Maine,” Manson said.
IN THE COMMUNITY
The Oxford Casino has been a good community partner, residents say.
“They’re very community friendly,” Fitts commented. “They help out with a lot of things, they donate a lot of money to a lot of different nonprofits and help in the community.”
Cindi Robbins agrees. The owner of Poland Spring Resort has supported the casino from the outset, and has benefitted from its presence. Before the casino hotel and the Hampton Inn were built, the need for hotel rooms as the casino opened allowed her to open her motor lodge year-round.
“I don’t think there’s much publicity about the charity aspect of the casino,” Robbins said, reciting a list of golf events and charitable events that are regularly sponsored by the casino.
Amanda and Aaron Ouellette, who own Daddy O’s Diner in Oxford and Mechanic Falls, attribute part of their success to the casino, which they say brings more people to the region. It’s allowed them to grow their business.
“Sales have gone up, and also we’ve got a second location,” Aaron said. “We went from having 12 employees to like 40, 45 between the two.”
If you or someone you know is struggling with a gambling problem, 211 is Maine’s Problem Gambling Helpline. Call 211 or text your zip code to 898-211 for access to information about services and resources 24/7.

title: Family of missing Hampden man speaks out after AG’s office leak exposed case details
text:
HAMPDEN, Maine (WABI) - The daughter of a missing Hampden man is speaking publicly about her father’s disappearance after confidential case information was included in a document the Maine Attorney General’s Office mistakenly sent to media outlets earlier this month.
Dawn B. Dunphy’s father, Douglas Dunphy Sr., went missing from his home on Kennebec Road in Hampden on Jan. 16. His car was found in Bangor about two weeks later.
The 45-page document mistakenly sent by the Attorney General’s Office contained confidential information on dozens of cases, including Dunphy’s disappearance.
Family remembers Dunphy as Marine veteran, outdoorsman
Dawn Dunphy described her father as a loving father, an outdoorsman and a master electrician who served in the Marines as a plane mechanic during the Vietnam War.
“He was brilliant. He was so smart. He could fix anything,” Dawn Dunphy said. “He could tell every plane and what was wrong with it by the sound of the engine... Took us camping. Taught us survival skills in the woods. Fishing, the whole nine yards, hiking.”
Dawn Dunphy, who now lives out west, said she and her father caught up every Sunday. It has been more than nine months since she last heard his voice.
“My older brother called... And he just said, dad’s missing,” Dawn Dunphy said.
Case remains with state police
The case is now in the hands of Maine State Police. It’s been months since investigators provided any public updates.
“If Dad can be found, and we can put him next to Mom where he belongs, then I can grieve. But I can’t until then. I need to find him,” Dawn said.
Earlier this month, Dawn received a call from a reporter informing her that information on her father’s case had been included in the leak from the Attorney General’s Office.
Dawn said the lack of communication sent her into a panic.
“I need to know what’s happening in order to be informed. It wasn’t real fun to hear about that leak, I’ll tell you. And it wasn’t real fun to be like, okay, could this harm anything?” Dawn said.
Dawn said she later spoke to someone from the Attorney General’s Office, who told her they prioritized notifying families when sensitive information was included and told her that her father’s case was not compromised.
“Every single week, something else happens,” Dawn said. “This is what having a missing relative is like.”
Leak confirmed investigators’ suspicions
Dawn said she has long presumed her father is dead, but the leak marked the first time it was confirmed that investigators believe so as well.
Asked whether finding her father’s body would help her accept what happened, Dawn said it would.
“Definitely. If we could bring him home and put him next to mom. That, that’s where he belongs,” she said.
Dunphy’s family is asking anyone hunting or hiking this fall to keep an eye out and call Maine State Police with any tip, no matter how small, as they hope to bring him home.

title: Patriots’ comeback falls short against Bears
text:
CHICAGO — Caleb Williams threw for 308 yards and two touchdowns, and the Chicago Bears cooled off Drake Maye and the New England Patriots with a 30-24 win on Thursday night.
Williams was 22 of 33 passing in his second game back after being sidelined by a right hamstring injury. He became the first Bears quarterback to throw for more than 300 yards in consecutive games since Mitch Trubisky had a three-game run in 2018.
Williams outdueled Maye in their second meeting since the longtime friends were part of the 2024 NFL draft. Williams went No. 1 to Chicago, and Maye was selected by New England at No. 3.
Luther Burden had four catches for 130 yards for Chicago (5-2), and Colston Loveland had a 12-yard touchdown reception. Cairo Santos kicked a 58-yard field goal with 1:34 left, a career long and matching the franchise record, after he missed a 53-yard attempt earlier in the final quarter.
Maye was 24 of 31 for 321 yards and two touchdowns. He also threw a costly interception in the end zone in the first half.
New England (4-3) had won three consecutive games behind Maye, who threw 10 TD passes and one interception during the streak.
Rhamondre Stevenson had five catches for 93 yards and a touchdown for the Patriots. Eli Raridon had a 30-yard TD catch in the third quarter.
After Santos’ long field goal, Maye drove New England into range for Andy Borregales’ 47-yarder with 37 seconds to go. But Chicago recovered the onside kick.
It was Chicago’s first home game since Mike Ditka died on Oct. 9. The Bears saluted the Hall of Fame tight end and longtime coach with a pregame moment of silence, and they also handed out fake mustaches to the crowd of 60,520 at Soldier Field.
Ditka’s No. 89 jersey dotted the stands, and fans also donned Bears sweaters in a callback to what Ditka wore on the sideline as a coach.
Chicago opened a 20-7 lead on Burden’s 24-yard touchdown with 14 seconds left in the first half. Burden got the ball on a screen on third-and-17, and Loveland, Kalif Raymond and Darnell Wright helped clear the way for his second TD reception of the season.
Set to receive the second-half kickoff, the Bears were in position to pull away. But the Patriots responded with Stevenson’s 48-yard touchdown reception on the final play of the half.
Stevenson slipped out of the backfield and Maye lobbed the ball over the head of Bears safety Cam Lewis. Stevenson ran away from Lewis and got a downfield block from DeMario Douglas before cutting past Bears cornerback Jaylon Johnson on his way to the end zone.
Injuries
Patriots: Cornerback Christian Gonzalez played after being listed as questionable because of an illness. … Safety Kevin Byard departed after he was checked out by trainers with 9:44 left in first half. He later returned. … Defensive tackle Christian Barmore departed late in the game.
Bears: Cornerback Malik Muhammad left in the third quarter because of a toe injury. … Tight end Cole Kmet hurt his right knee on a reception with 5:34 left.
Up next
Patriots: At Miami on Nov. 1
Bears: At Seattle for a Monday night game on Nov. 2

title: Execution staff warned IV site might have ‘blown’ during Christa Pike’s execution attempt
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (AP) — Tennessee execution team members failed multiple times to establish working IV lines in Christa Pike’s arms before her attempted execution and warned that some of her veins may have ruptured, or “blown,” before she was injected with the lethal drug, her attorney wrote in a court document filed Thursday.
The IV team went through about 10 needles and tried several IV sites on both arms, attorney Randy Spivey wrote in the document, which provides the most detailed account of the execution attempt so far. They even struggled to push saline through the last IV site they established, Spivey wrote.
Pike, 50, was hospitalized after surviving two doses of pentobarbital as the state tried to execute her on Sept. 30 for the 1995 stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer. She was 18 when she tortured and killed Slemmer with her boyfriend, becoming one of the youngest women to be sentenced to death.
State protocol calls for a second dose of pentobarbital if the first doesn’t result in death, but it doesn’t spell out what to do if a person survives the second injection.
After being taken to a hospital, Pike was on a ventilator for several days. At one point, her attorneys did not expect her to survive. She ultimately regained consciousness and returned to prison after being discharged.
The failed execution has brought renewed scrutiny to how Tennessee carries out death sentences. The court document was part of a separate legal proceeding in which people on the state’s death row are challenging Tennessee’s lethal injection procedures.
“Our predictions about the likelihood of botched executions have come true — and will continue to come true — without substantial change,” Kit Thomas, an attorney representing people on death row in the case, said.
Nearly an hour of IV attempts
The execution team began trying to place the two IVs required by Tennessee’s execution protocols at 6:34 p.m., Spivey wrote, and when they struggled Pike helped, advising them to look in her upper arm for a viable vein.
They managed to set an IV in Pike’s right arm within about 6 minutes, but it took them nearly an hour to complete the same process in her left arm.
Pike was “wincing and grimacing” as the IV team members moved the needles around inside her left arm, Spivey wrote, and the team members repeatedly expressed doubts after inserting the needles.
One team member said a vein “might be blowing” at 6:57 p.m. while examining an IV in Pike’s left arm, but two others said they couldn’t tell, Spivey wrote. “One of them said something like, ‘it’s either blood or blown, I need to know,’” Spivey wrote.
The team tried again with a different spot in her left arm, and the needle appeared to be severely bent when they pulled it out, the attorney said. “I think it’s blown,” the attorney recalled one of the IV team members saying at 7:07 p.m. After more attempts, the team decided at 7:13 p.m. that they had successfully placed an IV in Pike’s left arm, and they taped her hands down and hooked her up to a heart monitor.
Pike complained of burning arm pain
A series of phone calls were made to the execution chamber starting about five minutes later. Spivey said it appeared the execution team members responsible for pushing the pentobarbital into the lines — a process that happens in an adjoining room — were asking the IV team for repeated checks of Pike’s left arm.
It’s not clear exactly when the pentobarbital was pushed into the IV lines, but at 7:34 p.m., Pike said her arm was hurting.
“I feel like my arm is about to bust. It burns,” she said, according to her attorney. She continued to talk to her spiritual adviser for the next 10 minutes before she began making an “agitated snoring sound,” Spivey wrote.
Over the next 30 minutes Pike strained, flinched, moved her head and seemed to struggle to breathe, Spivey said, and when he asked to use a phone he was led on a circuitous, seven-minute route through the facility instead of being allowed to use the phone in the execution witness room.
Spivey called fellow attorneys at 8:22 p.m. and asked them to stop the execution because a third dose of pentobarbital isn’t authorized under the state’s protocol. He then went back to the witness room and told the deputy attorney general that Pike needed immediate medical care.
Spivey was told an ambulance was on the way at 8:50 p.m., and 20 minutes later he was told that medical staff were providing life-saving measures, he wrote. An ambulance was seen arriving at the hospital at 9:14 p.m.

title: USDA offers drought assistance to Maine farmers in four counties
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
USDA offers drought assistance to Maine farmers in four counties
The USDA is now offering emergency assistance to eligible Maine farmers to address water needs of livestock, orchards and vineyards impacted by recent drought conditions.
USDA offers drought assistance to Maine farmers in four counties
The USDA is now offering emergency assistance to eligible Maine farmers to address water needs of livestock, orchards and vineyards impacted by recent drought conditions.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture is accepting applications for emergency conservation assistance to help Maine farmers amid the state's ongoing drought.
Farmers in Cumberland, York, Androscoggin and Sagadahoc are eligible.
The program aims to address the farmers' water needs and can cover up to 75% of approved restoration costs, with a maximum payment of $500,000.
Applications are due by county: Nov. 4 for Cumberland County, Nov. 9 for Androscoggin County, and Nov. 13 for York and Sagadahoc counties.
"The Farm Service Agency can help producers and landowners recover from natural disasters that impacted their operation," said CED Laurie Thiboutot, FSA County Executive Director for Cumberland, York, Androscoggin and Sagadahoc Counties. "If you have a need for emergency water for your livestock, orchard or vineyard, please call our offices before beginning any restoration activities in order to determine program eligibility and to request restoration practice approval before taking any action."
The assistance is available to producers who lease federally owned or managed land, including tribal trust land, or state land. Damage or conservation concerns that existed before the qualifying disaster are not eligible.

title: South Portland rallies around 10-year-old girl after a near-fatal illness
text:
Ten-year-old Kathryn Dobson played a flag football game on Saturday Oct. 10. She went to a trick-or-treating event that Sunday. The next night, she went into cardiac arrest.
Her illness had begun as a fever and stomachache, resembling a typical virus. But after she started throwing up blood, her family rushed her to the hospital.
It took medical staff 30 minutes to perform chest compressions to bring her heartbeat back. She remained hooked up to a ventilator for days.
Katie J, as her family calls her, had developed sepsis, and her body began shutting down. She tested positive for the flu, likely the cause of her escalating symptoms, according to Jana Grant, a close family friend.
Katie J remains in the hospital and her parents haven’t left her side.
Testing has shown no lasting damage to her heart and brain. On Wednesday, she was taken off the ventilator, according to her father, J.D. Dobson.
The South Portland community has shown up for the Dobsons, who have long-standing ties in the city. Christine, Katie J’s mother, has taught in the district for more than 25 years (now at Waldo T. Skillin Elementary School), and J.D., her father, coached Little League and youth football.
“It shows what South Portland is all about,” J.D. Dobson said. “When you’re in a crisis like this, having the power of everybody behind you, it just gives you that strength to move forward.”
Grant started a gofundme after receiving dozens of messages from friends and neighbors wanting to help. Within 24 hours, it raised more than $30,000.
Now, it’s raised nearly $50,000. The donations will help the family cover medical bills, meals and other expenses, easing the financial strain caused by Katie J’s unexpected hospitalization.
Well-wishers are also reminding Katie J that she’s not alone.
South Portland Fire Cheerleading, the organization Katie J has cheered with for four years, collected videos of Maine cheerleaders and friends sharing their support for her. The leadership team put together a video compilation of dozens of people cheering her on.
The Facebook post calling for submissions for the video went up Monday at midnight. By the next morning, nearly a dozen high school, college and local competitive cheer programs sent submissions.
“She’s one of those kids that gets along with everybody on the team,” said Nicole Fitzgerald, one of her cheer coaches. “She’s confident, spunky, sassy and also really, really sweet.”
Grant said the little girl is a fearless little fighter always eager to get in the middle of a game of tag or football, and a sister-figure to Grant’s two boys. The families spend summer days together at a lake, where Katie J swims like a fish, Grant said. And she’s not afraid to jump.
At South Portland High School’s homecoming game on Friday, youth cheerleaders from Katie J’s team will join the high school cheerleaders on the sideline, all donning #Cheers4KatieJ bows. Katie J’s flag football team will wear special ribbons, and the football players will wear stickers on their helmets in her honor.
“Everyone’s going to be really rooting for her,” Fitzgerald said.
